That body of yours, O Agni, which is purifying and has entered into the earth—that which is in the fire, that which is in the Rathantara, that which is in the Gāyatrī metre, that which is in the Trivṛt Stoma, and that which is in food—all that of yours he now secures; for that, Svāhā! That body of yours, O Agni, which is purifying and has entered into the intermediate space—that which is in the wind, that which is in the Vāmadevya, that which is in the Triṣṭubh metre...

That [form] of yours which is in the fifteenfold hymn, that which is in the sacrificial animals—this he now secures for you; to it, Svāhā! That form of yours, O Agni, which is your pure body, which entered into heaven, which is in the sun, which is in the *bṛhatī* meter, which is in the *jagatī* meter, which is in the seventeenfold hymn, which is in the waters—this he now secures for you; to it, Svāhā!

Vāta is the breath; that is this Self. You are the soil, beloved by cattle; grant well-being and health to my children and descendants. Grant me progeny. Gharma is the head; that is this Agni. You are the soil, beloved by cattle; cook for us our food, which is well-prepared; grant me cattle. Ārka is the eye; that is yonder Sun. You are the soil, beloved by cattle. O Śukra, that which is your bright abode, your bright body, your bright, imperishable light, and your unassailable name—by that which is unassailable, [protect me].

I have established you; grant me splendor. Those fires which have come together from heaven, from the intermediate space, and from the earth, clothed in food and vigor—having given riches to this Agni, may they, satisfied and pleased, return again to their own abode.
May heaven and earth be favorable; may even the plants be favorable.
May the fires, being of one accord, distinguish me individually for the sake of my seniority.

Those fires which are of one mind and one consciousness, having entered into the plants and the waters—let them all come together toward the sovereign; bestow strength upon us, upon our bipeds and our quadrupeds.
May this Agni be the most excellent; may he be the most glorious; may he be the best of thousandfold givers. He has settled in his well-fashioned womb; therefore, we choose our boons from him.
Varuṇa, the wise one, has sat down among his dwellings, steadfast for the sake of sovereign rule.
Now indeed Brahmaṇaspati utters the hymn worthy of praise, in which Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and the gods have made their dwellings. 14.

Aditi, desiring offspring, cooked rice-porridge; she ate its remains and conceived, and from that the Ādityas were born. This rice-porridge which is being cooked is indeed made as a support and as a foothold. The fuel-sticks are a span long, for the self is thus measured by Prajāpati. That body of Agni which is worthy of sacrifice is in the *aśvattha* tree; with that he united. Ghee is his body characterized by clarity; when he anoints the fuel-sticks with ghee, it is by means of those two bodies that he [unites] him.

He unites him with the pathless [state] and bestows vigor through his exertion; for whatever vigor is performed, it is bestowed through exertion upon the pathless [state]. The year is indeed procreation, and Agni is the progenitor. Thus, that which is procreation, when he places fuel-sticks on the fire before the end of the year, the progenitor causes him to be born from that very procreation. A man is indeed one whose season is not yet assigned, for he does not know which season he will be born into. When he places the fuel-sticks, it is whichever is his own season and whichever is his constellation.

He obtains that which this rice-porridge being cooked represents; for when fuel-sticks are laid on, the womb is thereby prepared, and seed is thereby placed therein. In a year, indeed, seed that has been deposited comes to birth; therefore, when one establishes the sacred fire after a year has passed, he establishes it once it has already been born. It should be established twelve nights before [the completion of the year], for those are the counterpart of the year; or else on three nights, or on two; or else it may be established on the day before. Those very [days] are for one establishing the fire. The Ādityas, indeed, departed from here as the highest ones to that world.

The guardians of the path drive away him who desires to sacrifice; the Ādityas are the sharers of the remnants, so when he anoints the fuel-sticks with the remnant, he announces it to them. Having thus announced it to them, he ascends to the heavenly world. || 15 ||
You, O kings of the sacrifice, invoke for protection Agni— the Rudra, the Hotṛ-priest who truly sacrifices for both heaven and earth,
the one of golden form— before the thoughtless thunderbolt strikes.
O Agni, growing strong among those who are to be drawn forth, for the wind-god, for the powerful one, for the seeker of splendor.
O Agni, what will you say to the surrounding Nāsatyas, to Kṣa, and to Rudra, the slayer of men?
Agni, the Hotṛ, has made our lives auspicious; you purify our lifespans.
O Agni, purify yourself with skillful hands; bestow upon us splendor, heroic vigor, wealth, and nourishment for me.
May Aditi make him sinless who has offered praise to the horse Dadhikrāvan when the fire is kindled at the dawning of the Uṣas; may she, in harmony with Mitra and Varuṇa, grant him this.
Great is the deed of the swift steed Dadhikrāvan, who fulfills the will, the much-desired bull,
whom you two, O Mitra and Varuṇa, gave to the Pūrus— the radiant one, like Agni, the overcomer.
May we abide in the good-will of Vaiśvānara, the upholder of cosmic order.
To Agni, the ordainer, whose food is the bull and whose food is the cow, whose back is laden with Soma—to him we shall pay worship with hymns of praise.
When he has grown strong with food by means of strength, the mighty Agni makes himself a swift messenger.
Consuming it, he clings to the tail of the wind; like a swift steed, he is urged on and the racer is driven forth.
Agni is the lord of wealth; Agni is the lord of great fortune. May he grant these things to us.
O Agni, King, we approach you at the exhilarating sacrifice as the lord of riches among all treasures;
through you, seeking booty, may we win the prize and overcome the hostile attacks of mortals.
O youngest one, protect the men who offer oblations; hear our songs; and guard our offspring with your own self.
To you, O youngest Agni, the peoples bring tribute from near and from afar; take notice of the prayer of him who praises you most beautifully. Great, vast, and auspicious is your protection, O Agni.
Black dust rises from the feet of Jātavedas upon his departure, when Agni spreads across the earth.
In you, O Hotṛ of ancient lineage, the worshipful ones have placed their treasures during the evening and the morning.
In whom, the purifier, all beings and all blessings have gathered like in a desert;
O friends, boldly offer a hymn and a sacrifice to Agni; sing and chant to the Ordainer.
Bring forth the oblation and the well-purified prayer for Agni, for his bright radiance.
He who, through his wisdom, moves among all divine and human births.
With light, with splendor, you have shone forth.
O Agni, shining brightly among the wide dwellings, do thou ward off the sorceresses with thy face.
May we, though ignorant, serve him who is of beautiful aspect, fair to behold, swift-moving, and more wise than the wise.
May he, the Yakṣa who knows all ways and means, proclaim the oblation among the immortals, O Agni. 16.

Yoke, O Agni, like a charioteer, the horses that best invite the gods; sit down as the ancient Hotṛ-priest. And, O god, speak for us to the gods, you who are most wise; grant us full confidence in all desirable things.
For you, O most youthful one, when invoked by the sons of strength, have become the observer of Truth and worthy of sacrifice.
This Agni [is the master] of the thousandfold.
Bend toward this sacrifice, O Aṅgiras, with our joint invocations, as the Ṛbhus bend the felly of a wheel. Draw near!
To whom indeed, O Virūpa, shall you now direct your excellent praise with constant speech—[to] the bull who shines toward heaven?
With the army of this Agni, who looks back from afar, shall we lay low the Paṇi among the cattle?

O Gods, let not the clans of the gods abandon us, as milch-cows leave a lean bull; O inviolable ones, do not desert us. Let not the malice of any malicious hater strike us down, as a wave strikes a ship.
Homage to you, O Agni; the people sing for the sake of your power, O God; with your weapons, crush the enemy.
O Agni, for the sake of our protection, do you bestow wealth upon us; as the maker of wide space, make our domain broad.
Do not let us fall away in this great contest, like those who fail in their grasp; win the wealth together with the prize of victory.
Come hither from the assembly of others; indeed, I shall speak this to you. || 17 ||
Thus ends the seventh section, named Ālobhī, in the Iṭhimikā of the Caraka recension of the Śrī Yajurveda-Kāṭhaka. 7.

Now begins the eighth section: The Section on the Directions. The directions were indeed not yet established, nor did they come into being. Then they caused this eastern direction to shine for Agni—that which is the Kṛttikās. When one establishes the sacred fire under the Kṛttikās, he establishes it in the eastern direction itself. Indeed, he alone goes forward facing east who has established the fire; others go backward. The Kṛttikās are the lunar mansion belonging to Agni. When one establishes the fire under the Kṛttikās, he establishes it in its own lunar mansion. The Kṛttikās are the head of Prajāpati. When one establishes the fire under the Kṛttikās, [he establishes it] in the head.

He becomes preeminent; for there are indeed seven Kṛttikās, and there are seven vital breaths in the head. The vital breaths are the senses; verily, he obtains the vital breaths and the senses. One constellation is exceedingly full; verily, he attains prosperity for his offspring and cattle.

It should be established under Rohiṇī, for under Rohiṇī the gods established it; by that they ascended to prosperity, and that is why Rohiṇī is called Rohiṇī. Under Rohiṇī Prajāpati established it, and by that he ascended to prosperity; that is why Rohiṇī is called Rohiṇī. This world is indeed the heavenly world for a man, in that he becomes more prosperous in this world; therefore, for the sake of prosperity, it should be established under Rohiṇī. There were certain Asuras named Kālakāñjas who were piling up bricks. Indra also piled up one of their bricks, and there was a pair among them.

Then they ascended to heaven; he tore that apart, and those [parts] were scattered. These two are the two divine dogs. That which was torn apart is this very *ūrṇavābhi* (the woolly spider), which is bound together by its own entrails. Indeed, he bestows upon them their vigor and strength. He bestows vigor and strength upon his rival when he establishes the sacred fire under the Citrā constellation. This is the constellation belonging to Indra, the victorious. One who desires, "May I be fortunate," should establish the fire under the Pūrvaphalgunī constellations; for this is the constellation of Bhaga, and thus he becomes fortunate.

One who desires, "May my offspring be inclined toward giving," should establish the fires under the Uttarā-phalgunīs. This lunar mansion belongs to Aryaman; he who gives is indeed Aryaman. These offspring live upon his gifts, and thus they become inclined toward giving for him. He should establish them for a Rājanya, for he lives upon gifts. They should be established by a Brāhmaṇa in spring, for spring is the season of the Brāhmaṇa; he establishes them in their own season. He bestows brilliance and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). They should be established by a Rājanya in summer, for summer is the season of the Rājanya; [he establishes them] in his own [season].

Thus they established him in the seasons; he bestows vigor and strength. In autumn, the Vaiśya should establish the fire, for autumn is the season of the Vaiśya; thus they establish him in his own season, and he bestows nourishment and cattle.

"One should establish the sacred fires with the thought, 'I shall sacrifice with Soma'; for whomever one establishes them at any time, he establishes them intending to sacrifice with Soma, and it is indeed this that he increases when he sacrifices with Soma. They should be established on the full moon of Phalguna; for this is the mouth of the seasons, and thus he establishes them at the very beginning of the season. They should be established in the cool season (śiśira); for the cool season is the birthplace of Agni, and thus he establishes him as one already born. One establishes the fires thinking, 'May I prosper in all directions'; and since Agni is in all directions during the cool season, he indeed prospers in all directions."

He who establishes the sacred fires in the cool season should establish them either on the full moon day or on the new moon day; for this is indeed an auspicious day, and it is on an auspicious day that he establishes them. Therefore, one should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, or with the *Āgrayaṇa*, or with an animal sacrifice, or with Soma, either on the full moon day or on the new moon day. This is indeed the sacrifice; thus he takes hold of the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice itself. ||1||

Or rather, when these two separated, that which was the non-sacrificial part of that [heaven] was cast upon this [earth], and that became salt-impregnated soil (*ūṣa*). In that there are salt-impregnated soils, he establishes him in the sacrificial essence of these two. Salt-impregnated soil belongs to Prajāpati; it becomes more abundant day after day for the sake of procreation. Salt-impregnated soil is indeed the dear abode of cattle; in that there are salt-impregnated soils, he attains the dear abode of cattle. This earth indeed trembled, fearing, "Agni will burn me up"; she was afraid, thinking, "Agni will carry away my luster. She was as if moist.

This [earth] was sinking; the gods made it firm with pebbles. They placed brilliance in Agni because there are pebbles; he makes this very [earth] firm and places brilliance in Agni. This [earth] was indeed seized by Vṛtra; the ants know that place of hers where her living, sacrificial part is. Because there are ant-hills, he places him in the very living, sacrificial part of this [earth]. Water indeed was this world, only a vast expanse. Prajāpati, having become a boar, dived down and dug up earth as far as his mouth reached. That much he lifted up.

This earth was formerly that which was struck by the boar; he thus places him (Agni) directly upon her. Indeed, the boar sees food on this earth, and for its sake she parts asunder; therefore, when there is a place struck by a boar, one obtains that very food. That which it took up is Aditi; that which spread out is Pṛthivī; that which came into being is Bhūmi. When there is a place struck by a boar, it indeed spreads out for him with offspring and cattle. Truly, the foods of animals are diverse: the food of the cow is one thing, that of the horse is another, and that of the sheep is yet another.

The water of the female goat is one thing, and that of the male is another; when he pours out the water, he obtains as much food as there is. These five materials are the five powers in man: by one he produces power, by another he produces it, and by another he does so; thus he attains and secures whatever power there is. These five materials constitute the fivefold sacrifice; verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.

Verily, truth does not nourish strength, nor does food; the Udumbara is strength. When there are [fuel-sticks] of Udumbara wood, he bestows strength upon the food. They are of Śamī wood for the sake of pairing. When Agni was created, Prajāpati kindled him first with a Śamī branch. Since they are of Śamī wood, he kindles him with his own kindling-stick. Having become a horse, Agni departed from the gods; where he stood, there the Aśvattha tree grew up. That is the reason for the Aśvattha’s name as "Aśvattha. When there are [fuel-sticks] of Aśvattha wood...

Whatever part of him was deposited there, that they collect for them. Indeed, Agni departed from the gods by means of men; the gods thought of him, "He will surely become this [world]. The Maruts cut out his heart with thunder; that became the celestial lightning-strike. Whatever part of him was deposited there when a tree is struck by lightning, that they collect for them. There are five vessels made of Palāśa wood, for the sake of the fivefold nature of the sacrifice.

The Brāhmaṇa should establish [the fire] at eight steps; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables and the Brāhmaṇa has the Gāyatrī as his metre. He establishes it for himself, according to his own metre, so that he may be free from enmity. Just as a father invigorates his son, even so does his own metre invigorate him. The Rājanya should establish [the fire] at eleven steps; the Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables and the Rājanya has the Triṣṭubh as his metre. He establishes it for himself, according to his own metre, so that he may be free from enmity. Just as a father invigorates his son, even so does his own metre [invigorate him].

He quickens [the fire] within twelve steps; it is to be established by a Vaiśya. The Jagatī has twelve syllables, and the Vaiśya has the Jagatī as his meter; he thus establishes him from his own meter, from that which is his own. Just as a father quickens his son, so does his own meter quicken him. "I establish the fire so as to hold it unlimited," he says; the fire is to be established in an unlimited space for the attainment of the unlimited. He should establish it at whatever distance he deems right with his eye; the eye is indeed truth; he thus establishes him in truth. In the forenoon...

It should be established during the *puṇyāha* (the auspicious day); verily, he establishes it on an auspicious day. It should be established when the dawn has broken but before the sun has risen; for in this very world Prajāpati created offspring, and they were born. Thus it should be established for the sake of procreation. Night belongs to Agni and the day to Indra. If he were to establish the fire after the sun has risen, he would depart from the color of Agni; if before sunrise, he would depart from the color of Indra. One should establish it after sunrise in the latter part of the night, and before sunrise in the former part; thus he attains both the colors of Indra and Agni. Night is indeed of the nature of Asuras by its color.

He who establishes the fires when the sun has risen establishes the Śukriya-rite; for by what is not yet risen one establishes at night, and by what has risen one establishes by day; he who establishes the fires when the sun has risen establishes by day.

Indeed, men do not know it well, for they deliberate as if about a constellation; for truly, an auspicious day is established by the risen [sun]. He who establishes the fires when the sun has risen establishes it on an auspicious day. "Seven, O Agni, are your fuel-sticks, seven your tongues, seven the seers, seven your beloved abodes; knowing them, fill the seven wombs with ghee. As many as are the bodies of Agni, he who, while establishing them, causes them to be dissatisfied, will himself become dissatisfied. Indeed, there are so many bodies of Agni—sixfold, seven each. These [are they].
Thus he gratifies him; he does not become thirsty. With a full ladle and with his mind, he offers to Prajāpati. Prajāpati is full; verily he attains Prajāpati. || 3 ||

"With the vow of the Aṅgirases, the gods, I establish thee"—with these words it should be established by a Brāhmaṇa. For those among the gods who are Aṅgirases belong to the Brāhmaṇa as his kinsmen: Agni, Vāyu, Speech, and Bṛhaspati. From that is his kinship, from that his path of approach; since his sacrifice is where his kinship lies and where his path of approach lies, therefore it accepts him. "With the vow of Indra accompanied by the Maruts, I establish thee"—with these words it should be established by a Rājanya. For those among the gods who are kings belong to the Rājanya as his kinsmen: Indra, Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, and Tvaṣṭṛ. From that...

His sacrifice is his kinship, and from that it comes; since his sacrifice is his kinship and from that it comes, it accepts him from there. "I establish you with the vow of Manu, the village-chief," [with these words] he should be established by a Vaiśya. The Maruts are indeed the *viś* (clan) among the gods; they belong to the Vaiśya as those who have atoned for sin. Since his sacrifice is his kinship and from that it comes, and since his sacrifice is his kinship and from that it comes, it accepts him from there. Manā was indeed *iḍā*; she went to the Asuras as they were establishing their fires. They first [established] the *āhavanīya*.

Then, having established the *gārhapatya* fire and then the *audanapacana* fire, he said to them: "Having attained prosperity, they have descended back [to earth]; they will be meritorious, but they will also be ruined. He went to the gods as they were establishing their fires; they established the *audanapacana* fire first, then the *gārhapatya*, and then the *āhavanīya*. He said to them: "Having attained prosperity, they have cut off this world; they will be meritorious, but no offspring will belong to them. She (the Earth) then established the fire for Manu; she said, "So be it."

"Thinking, 'I shall establish the fires so that humans will procreate after the manner of the gods,' she first established the Gārhapatya fire, then the Audanapacana fire, and then the Āhavanīya fire, for the sake of securing these two worlds."

Then humans were born after the gods for the sake of procreation; thus, the fire should be established. Moreover, it is for the separation of these two worlds. What Prajāpati spoke first, he spoke as truth alone. He indeed spoke this three times: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svar*. This is the truth of speech; with that which is the truth of speech, he establishes the fire. Truth is indeed conducive to prosperity (*bhūṣṇu*). He who, knowing this, establishes the fire with this [formula] certainly prospers. This world is the latter, *bhūḥ*; yonder world is the former, *bhuvaḥ*; "bhūrbhuvaḥ" is the latter.

In order that the truth which is to be established may not fail to follow, [one recites] "bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ" first; by that, everything is obtained. Speech indeed uttered the deity; for speech is indeed the deity once it has been uttered. Now, that which one swears by with speech, or that which one becomes harsh through it—that is not truth. That deity Speech indeed uttered is none other than these very *vyāhṛtis*. This, indeed, is the divine essence of speech; by that very divine essence of speech, he establishes it. This world (*bhūḥ*) is the latter, and yonder world (*bhuvaḥ*) is the former; thus, "bhūḥ bhuvaḥ" is the latter.

He places both of these together; for this is the womb of that, since it is produced from this. This fire which is within the fire-altar is indeed this one, while that which was previously [placed] is yonder sun. This is he who is produced from yonder; that which is the second light is indeed that very thing. "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ"—this is the first to be placed; he thus places both of these together, for this is the womb of that, since it is offered upon this. That which is offered from yonder is indeed that which is the third light.

By that [fire], he indeed attains this sun; it is laid down facing westward, and therefore this [sun] faces all creatures westward. By means of fire, the gods eat food; food is eaten facing westward. That it is laid down facing westward is for the sake of eating food. Prajāpati created the gods facing eastward and the Asuras facing westward; he drove away the Asuras by means of the Brahman. Fire is the Brahman. That it is laid down facing westward is for the purpose of driving away the rival. They encompass this half [of the world] with fire, and they attend upon this half; thus it belongs to the side of the gods.

The gods move around; approaching this direction, he offers while attending upon her who dwells in the half of the gods. For the gods are indeed in this direction; it is toward that very direction of the gods that he turns and offers. || 4 ||

Agni, indeed, did not wish to go forth toward the east. They carried him out by means of a horse; because they carried him out there where he was previously carried out, he is called *pūrvavāh* (the one who carries first), and that is his nature as *pūrvavāṭ*. Agni is Prajāpati, and the horse is his eye. When they lead the horse in front, he goes forth following his own eye as it sees. The gods, preceded by the *stomas*, drove the Asuras away from these worlds. The horse is produced from the *stoma*; when they lead the horse in front, he drives away the rival from these worlds, being himself preceded by the *stomas*. [When] Agni was born...

The Rakṣases, seeking to injure them, seized hold of them; he drove them away with the horse. When they lead the horse in front, it is for the driving away of the Rakṣases. Verily, having become a horse, the Sacrifice passed beyond men; when they turn the horse back toward him, they think of him as passing beyond; thus they turn the Sacrifice back toward the sacrificer. Agni entered the horse, having become a black antelope; he came to that place where this [spot] is like the hoof-print of a wild animal; therefore it is to be stepped upon. When he makes the horse step upon it, [he does so for that reason].

He secures that very thing; for this is indeed a dwelling-place, and moreover, it is as if hidden, therefore one should not step upon it. Indra, indeed, gave the Yatis to the hyenas; while they were being devoured, the seer Syūmaraśmi entered a horse. Therefore, a horse sniffs its own dung. [The question was asked: "Did anyone exclude both the seer and Agni? [The response was: "We were unable to divide Agni; they divided him by means of the horse. When they lead the horse in front, it is for the sake of dividing Agni.

Those two who are indeed the seer and Agni—those two deities then divide him [the sacrificer]. A horse should be given; for the horse belongs to Prajāpati. In that he gives a horse, all the deities become worshipped and gratified by him. This horse is indeed the supreme sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*). In that he gives a horse, it is for the sake of fulfillment. A draught-animal should be given; for cattle are indeed draught-animals. The sacrifice is the draught-animal of Agni; it serves him. When Agni has been established, gold should be given for the sake of brilliance. He produces a hero, a hundred-fold measure.

He who establishes the sacred fires is a hero who bestows a hundredfold; at the two former oblations, thirty measures of gold are to be given, and at the last, forty measures. By advancing, he indeed prospers through the advancement of the sacrifice. The oblation is the self, and gold is the purifier; thus he purifies him at all the oblations. Agni desired Varuṇānī; his vital energy departed from him and became gold. When one offers gold, he endows him with his own vital energy. One who has offered gold should not establish the fires again.

What was swallowed of it comes out; he becomes pure. Indeed, Varuṇānī desired Agni; she united with him. Of those waters, Varuṇānī, that which was Agni’s seed became gold; that which was of the waters became silver. Therefore, the golden vessel is made of both gold and silver. That which was the impurity of the embryo became base metal (durvarṇa). Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not possess base metal, for it is impurity. He thus offers gold; he endows him with his own very seed.

Indeed, these bodies of Agni are together: this [earth] is the *audanapacana* (the hearth for cooking rice), the intermediate space is the *gārhapatya*, and the sky is the *āhavanīya*. He who establishes the fires without having resolved these [bodies] does not separate himself from evil; Rudra becomes his slayer of cattle. When he pays reverence with these [verses], he thereby resolves them, establishes them each in its own womb, and then establishes the fires; thus he separates himself from evil, and Rudra does not become his slayer of cattle. With the words, "The sky art thou by greatness," he becomes great after having established the fire; with the words, "The earth by the earthiness," day after day.

"He becomes greater; O Goddess Aditi, in your lap, place him—the eater of food—for the sake of food and for offspring. Verily, he places that eater of food for the sake of food and for offspring. He establishes Agni for the sake of food. He who, knowing thus, establishes Agni, eats food.

Now, these are the verses of the Queen of Serpents (*sarp-rājñī*). This earth is indeed the Queen of Serpents; the *sārparājña* verses are food. One who, knowing this, establishes the sacred fire (*agni*) does so for the sake of obtaining food, and he eats food. Spring indeed holds these creatures back for summer; summer [holds them] for the rains; the rains for autumn; autumn for winter; winter for the cool season (*śiśira*); and the cool season holds them back for Agni. Agni [holds them] for the sacrificer for the sake of obtaining food. One who, knowing this, establishes the sacred fire eats food. 6.

The oblation has been poured out and placed near, but it remains unbesprinkled. Then, having sprinkled honey upon the gaming-ground and having cast down the dice, he offers with the verse: "Varuṇa, firm in his vow, has sat down in his dwellings for sovereignty, he of the good wisdom. For three times indeed did the Virāj stride forth—to the Gārhapatya fire, to the Āhavanīya fire, and to the middle gaming-ground. Verily, he causes him to stride after the striding of the Virāj; he stands firm and attains a foundation. He offers with the *dharmadhṛti* (supporter of dharma) verse; verily, he makes him a supporter of dharma. [He offers] to Savitṛ...

They kill the cow that provides sustenance; they gamble with her; they offer her to those sitting in the assembly hall. By this means, she becomes beloved and gratified to him. With the verse "Now indeed, O Brahmanaspati," he offers an oblation in the place of address using a mantra dedicated to the Viśvedevas; thus he secures the mantra for him. Having come together toward him, they deliberate in accordance with that mantra.

Verily, the gods and humans were together at the cooking of the *odana*. Those humans overstepped the gods; the gods, having driven food away from them, stepped up toward the *gārhapatya* fire. They followed after them there, yet those humans still overstepped the gods; the gods, having driven cattle away from them, stepped up toward the *āhavanīya* fire. They followed after them there, yet those humans still overstepped the gods; the gods, having driven the sacrifice away from them—

They stepped forth toward the assembly hall; they followed after them, for those humans indeed surpassed the gods. The gods, having driven away Virāj from them, stepped forth toward the invitation (*āmantraṇa*); from that point on, they did not fall back. These are indeed the stepping-stones of the gods; he who knows this steps upward to ever more excellent worlds. This invitation is truly the unconquered truth of the gods; therefore, one should go well to the morning invitation; he goes to truth itself.

Therefore, one should not go to a summons if it has not been offered as an oblation; therefore, one should not speak untruth when being summoned. He who knows this becomes "Vahni" (the carrier); indeed, the fire for cooking the rice-porridge was originally Vahni, and he for whom this is known is born as Vahni. The Gārhapatya fire is the house; he who knows this becomes possessed of a house. The Āhavanīya fire is the sacrificial hearths; the sacrifice inclines toward him who knows this. The Madhyādhidevana is wide-extending; he who knows this is extended with offspring and cattle. The summons is unattainable; it does not reach him who desires it, provided he knows this.

An uncastrated bull should be given for the sake of obtaining a womb; a garment should be given, for a garment belongs to all the gods, and it is for the propitiation of the deities. An increasing sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given; indeed, by the increase of the sacrificial fee, the sacrificer increases accordingly. A milch cow should be given as a gift, for she brings milk near; indeed, for one who establishes the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), it does not become less. A milch cow should be given to the *hotṛ* priest for the attainment of blessings. An ox should be given to the *adhvaryu* priest; he secures the vehicle of the sacrifice itself. A chariot should be given, for this is indeed the chariot of the gods.

When the sacrifice is performed, he mounts the chariot of the gods as if with a human chariot. A pair of cattle should be given for the attainment of a pair. Six should be given; there are six seasons; verily he finds firm support in the seasons. Twelve should be given; twelve months are a year; it is for the attainment of the year. If he should exceed twelve, he should give twenty-four; the Gāyatrī has twenty-four syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the mouth of the sacrifice; thus he does not overstep the Gāyatrī, the mouth of the sacrifice. There are three oblations.

There are these three worlds; he thus attains these very worlds. Virāj strode forth thrice; he causes him to stride following the stride of Virāj. In that [he kindles] the *pavamāna*, he purifies him thereby; in that [he kindles] the *pāvaka*, food indeed is *pāvaka*—thereby he bestows food upon him; in that [he kindles] the *śuci*, he makes him pure, fit for sacrifice, and worthy of the offering. "May I be possessed of cattle, may I be possessed of offspring, may I be possessed of splendor"—with this thought one establishes the fire. The *pavamāna* is indeed breath; from breath, cattle arise.

When [he offers] to Agni Pavamāna, he thereby causes cattle to be born for him; for the purifying ones are indeed the waters, and from the waters offspring is born. When [he offers] to Agni Pāvaka, he thereby causes offspring to be born for him; for yonder sun is the pure one, the bestower of splendor. When [he offers] to Agni Śuci, yonder sun himself bestows splendor upon him. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict; when Agni was about to depart for victory, he distributed his body in three parts: a third among the cattle and a third in the waters.

The third [offering] is in yonder sun; when these oblations are offered, he thereby gathers together his own bodies. Thus, with his body and with splendor, he is established. These worlds are indeed these oblations. There are separate sacrificial grasses (*barhis*); he thus fills these very worlds. If there were separate sacrificial grasses, he would not leave a gap in the world for procreation; for offspring are born deficient. The two subsequent [oblations] should have the same sacrificial grass; he thus leaves a gap in the world for procreation, and from it offspring are born. We know this.

"We know this world, but we do not see that [other] one, or perhaps we do. Therefore, the two subsequent offerings should be made on the same sacrificial grass (*barhis*). These oblations are indeed cattle: the clarified butter, the cake, and Agni as Rudra. If he were to offer them after the fire has been extinguished (*amnaḥ*), he would deliver the cattle over to Rudra and would become without cattle. They should be offered after a year; by means of the year he pacifies him. This part of the sacrifice is performed loosely when he offers them after a year, for it is without its proper womb (*sayoni*). They should be offered precisely after the fire has been extinguished, so that there may be no looseness and there may be a proper womb.

Agni, indeed, did not desire this world because of what they cook here—namely, flesh—and because they burn a man, and because they cook what is stolen; he did not desire this world for that reason. When he returned to this world, those sacrificial bodies of his that were there, with them he ascended. These are they: the *pavamāna*, the *pāvaka*, and the *śuci*. That body of his which was the *pavamāna* entered the cattle; that which was the *pāvaka* entered the waters; that which was the *śuci* entered yonder sun. The *pavamāna* is indeed breath; by means of breath...

When [he offers] to Agni Pavamāna, he bestows cattle upon him by that means. That body of his which entered the cattle—that is what shines forth like a flame when ghee is offered; that body of his which entered the waters—that is what appears as it were within the waters. When, having washed his hands and bathed, he eats with faith, that very Agni who is in the waters purifies him and makes him palatable. When [he offers] to Agni Pāvaka, he purifies him together with his cattle. This indeed is that [body] of his...

That body of his which entered the waters—that is this flame which, when ghee is offered, blazes up like blood; that body of his which entered yonder sun—that is this light which shines above, like something shimmering, like a luminous glow. It is for the sake of purity, for renown, for fame, and for splendor. That body of his which entered yonder sun—that is this flame which, when ghee is offered, blazes up like gold. When these oblations are set forth, it is those very [bodies] of his that are being offered here.

He brings together the body-parts; thus he is brought to the fire with his body and with splendor. These worlds are indeed these oblations; there are separate sacrificial grasses (*barhis*), for these worlds are established separately.

The *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *gāyatrī* meter; for Agni is of the *gāyatrī* nature and the *gāyatrī* is his metre. This *agnyādheya* (the laying of the fires) is performed for Agni; thus, by means of these offerings to Agni, Agni goes forth establishing himself in Agni. For the two latter oblations, one should use as the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) [the verse] "By Agni Agni is kindled. Urvaśī was indeed the wife of Purūravas. She was pregnant when she departed back to the gods. There, among the gods, Āyu was born. He went after her and asked for her back, but they did not give her to him.

They restored life to him and granted him life, saying, "This is life. They then poured the *ukhya* fire into the fire-pan (*ukhā*) and said, "Place this; by means of it you shall procreate. He suspended the fire on a branch of a tree and entered the village with the [restored] life-force. He returned, thinking, "I have come back," and saw the fire blazing at the top of the tree. He realized, "This indeed is that fire. Taking its two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*), he churned out the fire and established it; by means of it, he procreated. When the two kindling-sticks of the *āroha* are used for procreation, one should offer a pap of ghee to Aditi on the new moon day.

"One desiring cattle should offer this [oblation]. Aditi is this [earth]; upon her cattle are produced. The establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) is the mouth of the sacrifice; by seizing the very mouth of the sacrifice, he obtains cattle. It consists of four portions to eat, for these cattle are paired up to four, in couples, and they are the performers of vigor. On the full moon day, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma. For the Brāhmaṇa has Agni as his deity, and Soma is the king. The establishment of the fires is the mouth of the sacrifice; by stepping upon the very mouth of the sacrifice, he attains self-sovereignty."

The sacrifice did not incline toward the gods; they were distressed, saying, "The sacrifice does not incline toward us. The sacrifice first inclined toward Agni and Soma among them. They perceived, "Agni and Soma indeed first inclined the sacrifice toward us; we desire the inclination of the sacrifice from them. They said, "The sacrifice has first inclined toward you two; may the sacrifice incline toward us through you two. They replied, "Let us choose a boon: let us alone be offered the *ājyabhāga* portions first. Therefore, they offer the *ājyabhāga* portions to Agni and Soma first.

For what is enclosed by water for these two is that he subsequently offers the oblation to Agni and Soma; it is for the non-interruption of the sacrifice, for from there the sacrifice first bowed toward the gods. If he were to subsequently offer anything else, he would separate the sacrifice from its deity. Agni and Soma are indeed a pair; Soma is the placer of seed, and Agni is the progenitor. Agni, indeed, is all this: the waters, the plants, and the trees—all that is Soma. These two are closest to us among the gods, for we see them as it were directly. Just as humans here serve [their guests], so do the gods serve him.

They attended upon him, desiring to know: "By means of this [fire] being taken out, may we conquer. They took it out, and by means of it they conquered. It is for the sake of victory that this [fire] is taken out. Indeed, Agni was afraid of being left without a place of installation; he should not be installed too far away, lest he be left without a place of installation.

When Agni was created, the Agnihotra was created after him; therefore, they follow the fire that has been established with the Agnihotra. The evening oblation belongs to Agni, and the morning oblation belongs to Sūrya. If one were to offer the morning oblation with an offering belonging to Agni, he would exclude the power of procreation from the front and act contrary to the natural order. With a full ladle, he offers mentally to Prajāpati; Prajāpati is full; thus he attains Prajāpati. Prajāpati is indeed full through prosperities and deficient through failures; a person is full through his desires and deficient through prosperities.

By the Full itself, full prosperities have been secured or brought for us; we belong to some other gods, while others have not brought [prosperity] for us. We live by the contact of some, while others [live] by our presence. Of earth, wind, and water—we have been brought by them, we live by their contact. Of fire, sun, and heaven—we have not been brought by them, we live by their presence. Having sacrificed to those very ones, they have brought him [prosperity]; he becomes part of a more excellent host. Men do not master his misfortune, who knows thus.

If one were to touch [the fire] with oneself, one would be liable to die; but since he touches it with clarified butter and herbs, he becomes free from death. He who has established the sacred fires is indeed brought near to the gods; they consume his food. With a full ladle he offers oblations; by means of the full ladle he has made himself sufficient for Agni, and thus he becomes sufficient for himself. The plants and the trees conspired together by day and excluded everything else from here. Prajāpati reflected, "These two have indeed taken possession of this world. Having created Agni, he established him [the fire].

Therefore, he meditated upon them; for this [fire] is established as one that overcomes rivals, yet it is indeed one that has not yet been fed with offerings. Being thus unfit for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), he who has not yet established his fires eats only what is already offered and made palatable by this [meditation]. || 11 ||

"Should the fire be established or should it not be established? they deliberate. "By one who intends to establish the fire tomorrow," [they ask]. "It should indeed be established; for he who is without fire is without sacrifice. A goat should remain tied there that night; for the goat is the very brilliance of Agni—thus he establishes that fire for him. It should be spotted, for it belongs to all the gods. He who intends to establish the fire the next day should observe the vow that night: he should not eat meat, nor approach a woman. For every man possesses fire; otherwise, the fire would depart from him, for this [goat] is his."

For from this very source he is emitted who draws it out; that which is on the right is churned for the sake of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Moreover, by means of these two fires, he makes him of common origin. His attendants should churn it every day; he may fetch it from anywhere, for that is his unappropriated body, and thus he appropriates it. He should fetch it from where it is glowing, for then these deities become manifest, and he appropriates them. He should fetch it from a frying pan for one who desires food; this is indeed his food-eating body.

He thus secures that very body. If a Brāhmaṇa or a Vaiśya should be prosperous like a wealthy man (asura), one should fetch [fuel] from his house; whatever prosperity that is, and whatever food that is, he thereby secures. However, from that time on, he should not eat in that man's house. He lifts it up three times; these worlds are three, and thus he attains these worlds. In that he lifts it up, he thereby attains this world; in that he moves eastward, he thereby attains the intermediate space; in that he places it [on the fire], he thereby attains yonder world. Having placed it, he should not lift it up again; if he does, he departs and becomes worse off.

From his vital breaths, Prajāpati indeed created offspring; they were born by that measure. One should lift [the fire] by that same measure for the sake of procreation. One should not lift it too high, lest Agni carry away his vital breaths and he die. Nor should one place it too low, for then it departs and he becomes worse off. || 12 ||

In former times, the gods were eaters of the unoffered; now this [oblation] turns toward those who eat the offered. Strength departs from him; he wins strength for himself. He makes them sharers in the sacrifice. They sacrifice in that world, they offer oblations in this world, and they cook in that world, so as not to create an interval between them; thus he establishes him in the state of Vaiśvānara. Those who sacrificed with the sacrifice attained the status of Ārṇava; humans do not truly know the sacrifice as it was, and therefore not everyone prospers. In former times, they used to give with [gifts] accompanied by sacrificial fees.

Those who sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices—this rice that is cooked, he gives as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of the success of the sacrifice. Indeed, he performs an *iṣṭi* sacrifice by means of this rice that is cooked; he who cooks this [rice] is indeed one who has performed both *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial and charitable works).

Prajāpati indeed assigned portions to the gods; he thought, "The sacrifice itself has entered within me as my own self. He saw this rice-offering (*odana*) and assigned it to himself as his portion. This is the portion of Prajāpati; one should cook it large and unlimited, for Prajāpati is unlimited—one thus attains Prajāpati himself. The gods and the Asuras were in conflict. Those gods sacrificed to Prajāpati alone, while the Asuras offered to one another. Those gods cooked this rice-offering and presented it to Prajāpati.

Prajāpati, seeing that portion which he had set aside, returned to the gods; then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who, knowing this, brings the *anvāhārya* (the guest-offering) prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. Some gods are to be praised (*īḍyā*), others are to be served (*saparyeṇyā*). The Brāhmaṇas are the gods to be praised, and the *anvāhārya* is the service for those to be served. By means of the sacrifice he gratifies those to be praised, and by the *anvāhārya* he serves those to be served; thus both are pleased with him at the sacrifice. "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati, full of vigor."

"Rich in milk, uninjured; for the sake of non-injury, you are uninjured by name; do not be injured for me! Protect my out-breath and in-breath; protect my common breath and diffused breath; protect my upward breath and form! You are vigor; bestow vigor upon me; come unto me!"—thus he prospers visibly before Prajāpati. || 13 ||

The re-establishment of the sacred fires is performed together with the light of the gods. O Agni, bring hither a thousandfold; form by form, bestow upon us life after life. That which you, when struck by wrath, have caused to fall upon the earth—that the Ādityas, all the gods, and the Vasus have brought back again. That which was cast away by you in anger, or that which was overturned through misfortune—that of yours, O Agni, we restore perfectly; we kindle you anew. Let the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus enkindle you again; let the priests enkindle you, O Agni, the upholder of wealth.
Bestow right here upon us fierce skill, along with horses, cattle, barley, and heroic strength.
May Mitra and Varuna restore you; may Indra restore you; may Bhaga restore you.
Again all the gods and the brahmins have kindled you. Return again with vigor, O Agni, with nourishment and long life; protect us again from sin.

Return with wealth, O Agni; overflow with a stream that provides sustenance for all, from every side. May your signal, O fair-signal, O good-signal, may the Ādityas, being pleased, enjoy this oblation of ours—*svāhā*! Salila, Saliga, Sagara—may the Ādityas, being pleased, enjoy this oblation of ours—*svāhā*! O Light of Heaven, O Radiant One, O Āditya, O Gods, among the gods, bring forth for us this true invocation of the gods—*svāhā* to the Ādityas! 14.

The *punarādheya* (re-establishment of the fires) is indeed a portion of Agni; by desiring to obtain that portion, one diminishes him. If, after having established the fires, one should think, "I am being deprived of this [portion]," he should perform the *punarādheya*. By obtaining that very portion which he previously diminished while seeking it, he indeed increases it. Everything whatsoever is made for Agni; he has given every portion to Agni, and thus he attains all prosperity. "There are no materials to be collected," they say; "there is no need for ritual formulas (*yajus*)," they say. For these [fires] have already had their materials collected and their formulas performed. Therefore, one should not gaze at the sun.

The requisites are indeed the materials; the ritual formula is the task. A garment that has been re-sewn is to be given, an ox that has been let loose again, and a chariot that has been repaired again—these are indeed the forms of the re-establishment of the fire. By means of these very forms, he makes it successful. When Agni goes out, he goes out after the waters and the plants; these Darbha grasses are those very waters and plants. In that there are Darbha grasses with their roots intact, he wins him back from the waters and from the plants.

The gods and the Asuras were arrayed for battle. As the gods were about to achieve victory, they deposited their beloved bodies in Agni, thinking, "If we shall conquer, we will come back to these; if they should conquer us, we will resort to these. Having conquered, they sought them out, saying, "Let them be common to us all. Agni said, "He who shall establish me with my own deity shall become united with these bodies. The gods established him; they became united with these very bodies. He who knows thus becomes united with these very bodies.

The wise Tvaṣṭṛ established this [fire-altar] desiring cattle; these cattle here belong to Tvaṣṭṛ, and by that he prospered. Manu established it desiring nourishment; he nourished these forms of nourishment here, and by that he prospered. Prajāpati established it desiring offspring; these offspring here belong to Prajāpati, and they were born from it, and by that he prospered. Verily, he who established it became united with that wealth (vasu); therefore it is called Punarvasu, and for that reason it should be established under the Punarvasus. He who established it indeed prospered;
therefore they are the Anurādhas, and for that reason it should be established under the Anurādhas. || 15 ||
Like a cauldron, it is heated by the neighboring flames; with well-fashioned hymns, let a great offering be presented to the lover of songs.
Within the raw [cows], you brought forth the cooked; O Sūrya, you caused him to ascend to heaven.
In whom the seven Vasus ascend, ascending from of old.
The seer Dīrghaśravas was indeed the guest of Indra’s cauldron.
O Śatakratu, those senses of yours which are among the five peoples—O Indra, I choose them for you.

It was granted to you for your great sovereign power; it was granted to you entirely for the slaying of Vṛtra. It was granted to you, O Indra, by the gods for dominion, for might, and for the overcoming of men.
To Indra indeed the singers have sung the lofty hymn; to Indra the chanters with their songs; to Indra the voices have cried out.

Thus do the Vasiṣṭhas honor with hymns Indra, the bull whose arm wields the thunderbolt; may he, being praised, grant us wealth consisting of heroes and cattle. And you, protect us always with your blessings.
When your wrath, O Indra, and your wheels have rolled together, then it is in you and in the sun.

O Indra, your greatness is supreme, O fierce one; when the armies, seeking your favor, have come together, let the missile fall from the arm of the hero, and let not your mind wander away in every direction.
O Indra, once born, you made your mind firm; you went forth alone to fight even against many.
Even the stone you shattered with your might, as you discovered the stall of the ruddy cows.
He who, as soon as born, was the first mindful god, who by his power surpassed the gods;
at whose breath the two worlds trembled through the greatness of his manly might—he, O people, is Indra.
May Indra, the good protector, with his own aids, be gracious to us—he who possesses all wealth.
May hatred be dispelled; may he grant us fearlessness; may we become masters of heroic vigor.
May we abide in the favor of that one worthy of sacrifice, and also in his auspicious goodwill.
May that Indra, the protector of his own, be with us; may he drive our enemies far away.
O deliverer from distress, let us offer our inspired hymns, seeking your favor as we choose the most abundant gift.
O Indra, accept this offering; may the desires of the sacrificer come true.

Since the inspired thought has entered me and brought me forth, I shall praise Indra before the decisive day, so that he may carry us across from distress, as both sides invoke him when he comes like a ship.
The Anus fashioned a chariot for your horse; Tvaṣṭṛ, O much-invoked one, forged the radiant thunderbolt.
The Brahmans, magnifying Indra with hymns, strengthened him for the slaying of the serpent.
When the strong ones sang their hymn to you, the strong one, O Indra—the pressing-stones and Aditi in accord;
when the wheel-rims, horseless and chariotless, sped forth impelled by Indra, they overran the Dasyus.
Then, O God, all the gods rejoiced after you, the most wise among the wise, as you slew the dragon.
Wherein, being praised, you grant wide space for the oppressed, for heaven, for the people, and for our own bodies.
Heaven and Earth yielded that power of yours; the immortal gods submitted to you, O Indra.
O doer of all, perform that which is yours to do; bring forth a new hymn of praise through sacrifices.
Boldly, O bold-minded one, bring forth [the bolt]; let great glory abide within you.
May the waters flow forth with speed like mothers; slaying Vṛtra, may we win the light of heaven.
For him, indeed, let the lord, however great he may be, swiftly brandish the thunderbolt against Vṛtra;
may he rend him as one cleaves the joints of an ox, striking across him so that the waters of the floods may flow forth.
And let the people say: "Agni has been born as a slayer of Vṛtra, a winner of wealth in every battle."
O Agni, may splendor be mine.
O Indra, you were born for the sake of sovereign power and strength, O bull among the peoples.
You drove away the man who acts as an enemy; you made wide space for the gods.
Like a formidable beast that wanders and dwells in the mountains, you have come hither from the farthest distance.
O Indra, whetting your sharp bolt and making your blade keen, strike down the enemies and drive away those who oppose us. 16.
May the Revatī cows, who provide abundant strength, be our companions at the feast with Indra; may we, possessing food, rejoice through them.
These wise ones encompass him with homage by the thousands.
Many vows attend him for the sake of ancient perception; may the excellent ones follow his self-rule.
Indrāṇī won the well-won prize with her husband; she disclosed the secret of the husband’s power by means of the *udaṃśu* plant.
Her hips extend thirty yojanas, and her womb bears the ancient Indra.
May Senā by name, the Earth, Dhanañjaya, Viśvavyacas, Aditi, Sūryatvac, Indrāṇī, Prasahā, and Saṃjayantī— the mistress of nourishment— bestow nourishment upon me.
Among these women, I have heard of Indrāṇī as the one with the excellent husband.
For her husband shall not die from old age nor by any other cause; Indra is superior to all.
O Indrāṇī, I have no pleasure apart from my friend Vṛṣākapi, whose dear oblation here goes among the gods; Indra is superior to all.
In the eastern direction you are King Indra; in the northern direction, O slayer of Vṛtra, you are the slayer of Vṛtra.
Where the flowing rivers go, that is conquered by you; O Bull, be worthy of our oblation from the south.
His greatness has indeed surpassed that of heaven, earth, and the intermediate space.
Indra, the self-ruling lord praised by all, the master of his own home, has grown mighty for the battle, irresistible and impetuous.
You, O Indra, are the over-king; you become the sovereign lord of the people. You are the divine subjects and also the ruler; may your sovereign power be vigorous, undecaying, and eternal.
He who is Hiraṇyagarbha, the first-born of breath.
Soma and Pūṣan, progenitors of riches, progenitors of heaven, progenitors of earth—
born as the guardians of the entire world, the gods have made them the navel of immortality.
May these two gods, at their birth, be pleased; may they conceal the unwanted darkness.
Within these two, while they were still raw, Indra brought forth the cooked [milk] among the cows for Soma and Pūṣan.
I invoke by name the beloved ones of you swift Maruts, so that they may come, being satisfied and longing.

For glory, they have mingled themselves with splendors; they are well-disposed with their rays and with those who sing hymns. Armed with axes, impetuous, and fearless, they have found the beloved dwelling-place of the Maruts.
We invoke Indra for you from all sides, away from other people; may he be ours alone.
Come to us with all your aids, being of one mind and graciously accepting our prayer, O Lord of the Bay Horses!
O Indra, with your beautiful jaws, turning repeatedly with the elders, bestow upon us manly vigor.
O Maruts, when we call upon you from heaven with auspicious intent, come hither to us!
O Maruts, being praised, lead us toward greater prosperity away from all oppressors.
O worshipful ones, enjoy our offering; may we be masters of riches.

He, the possessor of martial strength, the maker of the chariot-seat, the equalizer, the great smasher, roaring like a bull, the drinker of the dregs, the stirrer up of vast dust— the sole subduer of human tribes— became the conqueror of all peoples.
When the people, those heroes, rush together with their fury toward the swift rivers, the plants, and the settlements.
And so, O Maruts, sons of Rudra, be our protectors in the battles for our glory. O Indra, bring to us for our aid the most excellent wealth—conquering, ever-victorious, and supreme.

For our well-being, may you, the leader with your swift steeds, come hither; as you sit upon the many ancient nourishments, may we be winners of vast wealth. O Indra, may there be for us fortune accompanied by progeny. Grant to the donor who exerts himself those triple-layered protections which are yours.
May those [gifts] of yours, O Maruts, come to us; bestow upon us wealth, O bulls, together with heroic sons. 17.
Thus ends the eighth section, named "The Station of the Directions," in the *Iṣṭimikā* of the Caraka recension of the *Kāṭhaka* of the glorious *Yajurveda*. 8.

Now the ninth section: On the extinction [of the fire]. When the fire goes out, it goes out following the year. Seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses should be recited; for the year is seventeenfold—there are five seasons and twelve months. This indeed is that year; verily, he secures him from the very year. Regarding this they say: "Only fifteen should be recited, not seventeen; for the fifteen are more closely connected to the year. Fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses are recited in succession; there are fifteen nights in a half-month, and by means of those [nights], they are obtained.

As many as are the syllables of the *sāmidhenī* verses, so many are the days of the year; by those very syllables, those days are attained. Indeed, when Agni goes out, he goes out following the year. The year consists of six seasons; since there are six *vibhakti* formulas, he secures him from the year itself.

Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; there are six seasons, therefore there are six case-endings. Although they consist of two syllables each, they are made to have four syllables, for these domestic animals exist in pairs up to four, and they are the performers of virility. Furthermore, because they distribute Agni in many ways here, and because he has nourished these prosperities, therefore Agni alone attains as many case-endings as these, and no other deity. The fore-offerings (prayāja) are indeed the mouth of the sacrifice; if one were to omit the fore-offerings, one would omit the mouth of the sacrifice. The fore-offerings are indeed food. If...

If he should desire of someone, "May I deprive him of food," he should place the *vibhakti* formulas above the *prayāja*s for that person. The *prayāja*s are indeed vigor, and the *vibhakti*s are vigor; thus, from vigor itself he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call, and he attains swift prosperity. They say, "Is not the offering made to Agni performed separately? Why then do the *prayāja*s have *vibhakti* formulas? These *prayāja*s are indeed sacrificed throughout the year; therefore, it is offered to Agni, and thereby the offering to Agni is not performed separately.

"Return with strength, O Agni; return with food and long life; protect us again from sin"—with these words he should offer before the fore-offerings (*prayāja*). "Return with wealth, O Agni; overflow with a stream that nourishes all, on every side"—with these words he should offer after the after-offerings (*anuyāja*). For he who departs with strength and cattle departs together with them; thus he regains both strength and cattle. Moreover, in this way he secures the blessing of the sacrifice from both sides.

They say, "It is not made separate from Agni; why then do they sacrifice the two *ājyabhāga* offerings? These two *ājyabhāga* offerings are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice. If one were to exclude the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one would exclude the eyes of the sacrifice. One should perform this verse, "O Agni, purify our lives," in the place of the *ājyabhāga* belonging to Soma. Since it belongs to Agni, it is addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*); since it is a *pāvamāna* (purifying) verse, it is addressed to Soma (*saumī*). Thus, it is not made separate from Agni, nor does one exclude Soma. One should perform this verse, "Agni is the head of heaven, the summit," in the place of the *ājyabhāga* belonging to Soma.

Whether for one desiring offspring or desiring cattle, that which is a pair is thereby productive; that which contains seed belongs to Soma; thus it is not made non-Agneya, nor does it pass beyond Soma.

He who neglects the sacred fire is indeed a slayer of the heroes among the gods. A hero is one who bestows a hundredfold. Since these are *akṣarapaṅktis* consisting of a hundred syllables, he thereby recovers for the gods that very hero. For the fire is to be established upon one [earth] for its first installation (*ādheya*), and upon another for its re-establishment (*punarādheya*). He does not truly win over that [earth] for which there is a re-establishment by means of the first installation; rather, it is by the re-establishment that he wins her over. Old age is indeed the lifespan ordained by the gods, for he lives for as many years as that. Therefore they say, "A hero is one who bestows a hundredfold," because these are *akṣarapaṅktis* consisting of a hundred syllables.

He obtains as much vigor as there is; he pervades it with his life-force. Indeed, he who lets the fire go out is deprived of life-force and vigor. Man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a vigor of a hundred [powers]. Gold is life-force and vigor. In that he gives gold weighing a hundred mānas, he recovers both life-force and vigor. || 2 ||

He who neglects the sacred fire is deprived of the sacrifice; for the sacrifice is fivefold, and since the cake is on five potsherds, he thereby secures the sacrifice itself. Regarding this they say: "It should be made on eight potsherds, not on five. The Gāyatrī has eight syllables, Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī, and the Gāyatrī is his metre; thus, that which is the re-establishment of the fire is made pertaining to Agni, and for that reason it should be on eight potsherds. But that is not to be regarded [as final]; it should indeed be made on five potsherds. For when Agni is neglected, he is neglected for a year, and the year consists of five seasons.

The fifty-fifth and the sixty-fourth season came into being. This is common to both the fifty-fifth and the sixty-fourth: that which is the five-potsherd [offering] wins him from the year itself. For the seasons are five, and the seasons are procreation; since it is a five-potsherd offering, it is for the sake of procreation. The seasons are indeed procreation, and Agni is the progenitor; since it is a five-potsherd offering, the progenitor causes him to be born from procreation itself. Verily, all these Ādityas went to yonder world together; having gone to yonder world, they...

They were thirsty; they knew [it was] from the gift of yonder world that he had come here. They established this fire again; by it they prospered. The Ādityas indeed are prosperous in this world, the Ādityas in yonder world; cattle are in this world, the seasons in yonder world. He who, knowing thus, establishes this fire, prospers in both worlds. O Ketu, Suketu, Saketa—may these Ādityas, being pleased, partake of this oblation, Svāhā! O Salila, Saliga, Sagara—may these Ādityas, being pleased, partake of this oblation, Svāhā! From heaven...

"O Jyotis, Vivasvat, Āditya! O Goddesses among the gods, quicken this true invocation of the gods for us; svāhā to the Ādityas!"—with these [formulas] they indeed established that fire, and by it they prospered. When one establishes [the fire] with these, then it is truly established; for the Āditya is indeed the fire to be re-established. || 3 ||

An eight-potherd cake for Agni; a pap for Soma; a twelve-potherd cake for Savitṛ; a pap for Sarasvatī; a pap for Pūṣan; a seven-potherd cake for the Maruts; clotted curds for the Viśve Devas; a one-potherd cake for Heaven and Earth; an eight-potherd cake for Agni; a pap for Soma; an eight-potherd cake for Savitṛ; a pap for Sarasvatī; a pap for Pūṣan; a twelve-potherd cake for Indra and Agni; clotted curds for the Maruts; clotted curds for Varuṇa; a one-potherd cake for Ka. "Homage to you, O Ātāna! O invincible one, go forward along the stream of clarified butter, together with offspring, together with abundance of wealth."
We invoke the Maruts, the devourers, who carry the sacrifice, who are well-pleased with the groats.
O Indra, O God, be with us here in the battles; let there be for you, O Impetuous One, our reverent submission.
The song of the one who possesses the oblation honors the Maruts, the bounteous gods of the earth, with their offerings.

Whatever sin we have committed in the village, whatever in the forest, whatever in the assembly, or whatever in the senses; whatever we have done against the waters, whatever we have done against the law of even a single person—all that we now expiate. Svāhā!
The performers of ritual action have performed their work together with speech that brings well-being; having performed the rite for the gods, go home, O bounteous givers.

In the morning, an eight-potherd cake is offered to Agni Anīkavat; at midday, a pap is offered to the Maruts Sāṃtapanas; and in the evening, rice cooked in the milk of all the cows is offered to the Maruts Gṛhamedhas; the scrapings are set aside for the sake of continuity.
O ladle, fly away full; fly back again well-filled. Like merchants trading wares, let us sell forth food and vigor, O Śatakratu.
Give to me; I give to you. Bestow upon me; I bestow upon you. Take from me what is to be taken; I take from you what is to be taken.
O Śatakratu, bring together for us food and vigor, as if collecting a debt.

To the Maruts, the sportive ones, [there is] a cake on seven potsherds in the morning; together with the rays of the sun, [there is] a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, a pap for Pūṣan, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni, a pap for Indra, and a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman. O Agni, perform the office of the Hotṛ, perform the office of the messenger; standing upright at the sacrifice, may Heaven and Earth protect thee, and may thou protect Heaven and Earth. As the maker of good offerings, be for Indra and for the gods. Enjoying this oblation of ghee, partake of it—Svāhā! || 5 ||

Clarified butter for Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs; a cake on six potsherds for the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass (barhiṣad); parched grains for the Pitṛs consumed by Agni (agniṣvātta); and a stirred drink (mantha) for Agni Kavyavāhana. "This, O father, is for you and those who follow you; this, O grandfather, is for you and those who follow you; this, O great-grandfather, is for you and those who follow you. Come, O Pitṛs, and rejoice here!"
O Maghavan, may we gladden you, who are so beautiful to behold;
now, O you whose chariot-seat is full, being praised, you go according to our desires—yoke now, O Indra, your two bay steeds!
The Soma-loving Pitṛs have departed by their ancient, deep paths.
Having bestowed upon us here what is auspicious wealth, grant us riches consisting of all-heroic sons.
The ancestors have rejoiced.
By this manifestation, generating mighty deeds— for he is indeed the glowing one, the wide path for the sake of space—
he rose up toward the red glow, the summit of the honeyed mead, when his own body impelled his body.
They have eaten and they have rejoiced; indeed, the dear ones have shaken themselves free.
The self-luminous sages have offered praise with a most recent hymn; now, O Indra, yoke your two bay steeds.

Homage to you, O fathers, for your fury; homage to you, O fathers, for your vigor; homage to you, O fathers, for your life; homage to you, O fathers, for your sap; homage to you, O fathers, for your cruelty; homage to you, O fathers, for your strength; homage, homage to you, O fathers! *Svadhā* to you, O fathers! Where, O fathers, is *svadhā*, where you are—may it be with you. Rejoice in it according to your respective portions. Whatever vitality, O fathers, is here, and whatever we are—may we long enjoy that while living among it.
We invoke the mind with the Nārāśamsa hymn and with the prayers of the Fathers.
May our mind return to us again for the sake of wisdom, for strength, and for life, so that we may long behold the sun.
May our fathers and the divine folk grant us back our mind; may we be united with the company of the living.
O Agni, we kindle you, the radiant, the unaging god, so that your most praiseworthy fuel may blaze in the sky;
bring nourishment to those who offer praise.
Whatever harm I have done to the mid-region, to the earth, or to the sky, or whatever I have harmed my father or my mother.
May Agni Gārhapatya release us from that sin, whatever evil deeds we have committed. 6.
I make Rudrākhu your sacrificial animal; with him, I redeem you from the animals. This, O Rudra, is your portion, together with your sister Ambikā; accept it, svāhā!
O Mother, we have propitiated Rudra, the god Tryambaka,
so that he may make us more prosperous, so that he may make us better, and so that he may inspire our resolve.
A medicine for the cow, for the horse, for the man, and a path easy to traverse for the ram and the ewe.
And furthermore, may there be for us a remedy, a truly excellent remedy, so that it may come to pass.
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant one, the nourisher of wealth.
May I be released from death, as a cucumber from its stalk, but not from immortality.

O you who abide in the *bhaga*, may I obtain your *bhaga*. This, O Rudra, is your portion; with this favor, pass beyond the Mūjavat mountains, clad in a skin-garment, with the *pināka* bow in hand and your bow strung. You are fuel; may we prosper through you. You are kindling; may we thrive through you. You are splendor; bestow splendor upon me. 7.

Mind is the sacrificial ladle, mind is the clarified butter; speech is the altar, thought is the sacred grass; intention is the fire, understanding is the fire-kindler; the Lord of Speech is the Hotṛ priest, the mind is the Upavaktṛ, breath is the oblation, and the Sāman is the Adhvaryu. Go to Indra, Svāhā! Earth is the Hotṛ, heaven is the Adhvaryu, Tvaṣṭṛ is the Agnidh, Mitra is the Upavaktṛ. O Lord of Speech, with the most powerful vigor of speech you sacrifice for the sake of the lord of the sacrifice; may the Lord of Speech, performing the rite well, drink the Soma. May he bring forth Indra for the sake of power, Svāhā! Soma [is] of Soma.

The leaders are the *śukra*s; the leaders of the *śukra* are the *śrāta* Soma-offerings for you, O Indra, O Vātāpin, who hears our invocation—*svāhā*! Agni is the *hotṛ*, the Aśvins are the *adhvaryus*, Rudra is the *agnīdh*, Bṛhaspati is the *upavaktṛ*. O Lord of Speech, whose name is known in the heart, the Lord of Speech has drunk the Soma; may he bestow manly vigor upon us—*svāhā*! The leaders are the Soma; the leaders of the Soma are the *śukra*s; the *śrāta* Soma-offerings are for you, O Indra, O Vātāpin, who hears our invocation—*svāhā*!

On the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you. May Varuṇa lead you, O divine Dakṣiṇā; for Yama, I accept this horse; through it may I attain immortality. May there be vigor for the giver, and bliss for me, the receiver. On the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you. May Varuṇa lead you, O divine Dakṣiṇā; for Agni, I accept this gold; through it may I attain immortality. May there be vigor for the giver, and bliss for me.

O recipient, at the impulse of the divine Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you. O goddess Dakṣiṇā, may Varuṇa lead you to Rudra as a cow; through this, may I attain immortality. May there be strength for the giver and joy for me, the recipient.

On the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive thee. The Gnas cut thee; the Apas stretched thee out; the Varutris wove thee. May Varuṇa lead thee, O divine Dakṣiṇā! For Bṛhaspati I accept this garment; may I attain immortality. May there be strength for the giver, and joy for me, the receiver. On the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive thee. May Varuṇa lead thee, O divine Dakṣiṇā!

From the lying-down Aṅgiras, who was breathless, may I attain immortality through him; may there be long life for the giver and joy for me, the receiver. At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you. May Varuṇa lead you, O divine Dakṣiṇā. For Prajāpati, a man; through him may I attain immortality; may there be long life for the giver and joy for me, the receiver. Who has given this to whom? Desire has given it to desire. Desire is the giver; desire is the receiver.

He entered the ocean of desire; with desire I accept you. O Desire, this is your great oblation: the Hotṛ is Satyahavis, the Adhvaryu is Acittapājas, the Agnidh is Acittamanas, the Upavaktṛ is Anādhṛṣya and Apratidhṛṣya, the Abhigara is Ayāsya, and the Udgātṛ is Vācaspati. O Lord of Speech, Vidha is your name; we pay homage to your name. You, Vidha, [pay homage] to our name. May the thread of the gods not be severed, nor that of men. 9.

Agni [is associated] with the *yajus* formulas; Savitṛ with the *stomas*; Indra with the *ukthas* and *madas*; Bṛhaspati with the *chandas* meters; Viṣṇu with the consecration (*dīkṣā*) and austerity (*tapas*); Aditi with the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds; the Ādityas with the clarified butter (*ājya*); Mitra and Varuṇa with the *dhiṣṇya* fires; the Maruts with the waters and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); Tvaṣṭṛ with the fuel-stick (*samidh*); the Aśvins with the milk-mixture (*āśira*); Pūṣan with the utterances of *svagā*; Earth with the fire; Speech with the wind; the army with Indra; the lowing cow (*dhenā*) with Bṛhaspati; the Path with Pūṣan; the Gāyatrī with the Vasus; the Triṣṭubh with the Rudras; the Jagatī with the Ādityas; the Anuṣṭubh with Mitra; the Virāj with Varuṇa; the Paṅkti with Viṣṇu; and the Consecration (*dīkṣā*) with Soma. 10.

Prajāpati desired, "May I exist; may I procreate. He divided himself tenfold. His thought (*citti*) became the offering-spoon (*sruc*); his thinking (*citta*) became the clarified butter (*ājya*); speech (*vāc*) was the altar (*vedi*); what was meditated upon (*ādhīta*) was the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); insight (*keta*) was the fire (*agni*); what was discerned (*vijñāta*) was the fire-kindler (*agnidh*); the Lord of Speech (*Vācaspati*) was the Hotṛ priest; the mind (*manas*) was the Upavaktṛ; the breath (*prāṇa*) was the oblation (*havis*); and the Sāman-chant was the Adhvaryu. Having thus divided himself tenfold and formed a pair, he sought a dwelling-place. He found the threefold (*trivṛt*) as his dwelling-place—the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). From that, he emitted creatures. From that, another rose upward like a blade of grass.

The fifteenfold [breath] that pierced downward was the latter fortnight; with it he created the Asuras. That which pierced upward was the former fortnight; by it he created the gods. As it swelled upward, the gods swelled upward after it. That which pierced downward was the latter fortnight; by it he created the Asuras. As it collapsed, the Asuras collapsed downward after it. Following the right hand he created the gods; they became possessed of vigor. Following the left hand he created the Asuras; they became weak. Therefore, the right side [is superior].

By means of the truth of his own superior vigor, he created the gods; they became truth. By means of untruth, he created the Asuras; they became untruth. By means of the day, he created the gods; they flourished with a white color. By means of the night, he created the Asuras; they became black. He indeed desired that very thing: "In what shall I offer? He beheld Indra as vigor within himself. Everything else had been born. He poured it out, saying, "Go to Indra, Svāhā!
