Breath is indeed vigor, and Indra is vigor; thus he placed vigor into vigor. They [the gods] were established.

With the Caturhotṛ formula, those whose domestic lord was Soma sat down, saying, "Let us generate Indra. Pṛthivī was their Hotṛ, Dyau was their Adhvaryu, Tvaṣṭṛ was their Agnīdh, and Mitra was their Upavaktṛ. They drew these two cups; they sought a place of abode and found the twenty-one-fold as their place of abode; they generated Indra. With the Pañcahotṛ formula, those whose domestic lord was Varuṇa sat down, saying, "Let us go to heaven. Agni was their Hotṛ, the Aśvins were their two Adhvaryus—it was because of the Aśvins that they were called Pañcahotṛs—Rudra was their Agnīdh, and Bṛhaspati was their Upavaktṛ. They...

These two seized them; they sought a resting place; they found the twenty-sevenfold [stoma] as their resting place. They ascended to heaven, having made that a bridge. There the domestic animals were released. They led them away to the deities: a horse to Yama, gold to Agni, a cow to Rudra, a garment to Bṛhaspati, a breathing [animal] to Uttāna Āṅgirasa, and a man to Prajāpati.

When he accepted Yama’s horse, half of his vital power (*indriya*) departed; he accepted it with this [formula], and thus he regained half of his vital power. He who, knowing this, accepts a horse, regains half of his vital power; but he who accepts one without knowing this, half of his vital power departs from him. When he accepted Agni’s gold, a third of his vital power departed; he accepted it with this [formula], and thus he regained a third of his vital power. He who, knowing this, [accepts] gold...

He who accepts [the cow] while knowing this bestows a third part of his sensory power; he who accepts it without knowing this, a third part of his sensory power departs from him. When Rudra accepted the cow, a fourth part of his sensory power departed from him; he accepted it with this [formula], and thus he bestowed a fourth part of his sensory power. He who accepts the cow while knowing this bestows a fourth part of his sensory power; he who accepts it without knowing this, a fourth part of his sensory power departs from him.

As Bṛhaspati was receiving the garment, the fifth power of his senses departed; he received it back with this [formula], and thus he restored the fifth power of his senses. He who, knowing this, receives a garment, restores the fifth power of his senses; but he who receives it without knowing this, the fifth power of his senses departs from him. As Uttāna Āṅgirasa was breathing out while receiving it, the sixth power of his senses departed; he received it back with this [formula], and he...

He who, knowing this, accepts [the gift] while not breathing, bestows a sixth part of his sensory power; he who, not knowing this, accepts it, loses a sixth part of his sensory power. When they accepted the man from that Prajāpati, a seventh part of his sensory power departed. He accepted him with this [formula]; he bestowed a seventh part of his sensory power. He who, knowing this, accepts the man, bestows a seventh part of his sensory power; he who does not know this [loses it].

He accepts [the gift]; he approaches the seventh sense-organ. "Who has given this to whom? Desire to desire," for desire is the giver, desire is the receiver; "he has entered the ocean of desire," for desire is indeed like an ocean, immeasurable. "With desire I accept you; O desire, this is yours"—thus with desire alone he accepts it and establishes it in desire. Indeed, those who know thus do not seek a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in that world beyond when they accept a fee from such a god.

He who knows that one who first led away the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) obtains as much as the leader of the sacrificial fees. He who knows those for whom he led them away becomes worthy of sacrificial fees. He who knows that acceptance by which they accepted them becomes more prosperous; for having accepted them, they became more prosperous. Those gods, having gone to heaven, felt thirst; they knew: "Has he come here from the other world because of his giving?"

They said to the Ṛṣis, "Therefore, give us these seven *hotṛ*s. "By what abode? they asked. "You shall find it right here," [the Ṛṣis replied]. They sat down with the seven *hotṛ*s, having Aryaman as their householder, thinking, "Let us perform the *saṃtana* sacrifice. Among them, Mahāhavis was the *hotṛ*, Satyahavis the *adhvaryu*, Acittapāja the *āgnīdh*, Acittamanas the *upavaktṛ*, Anādhṛṣya and Apratidhṛṣya the two *abhigara*s, and Ayāsya the *udgātṛ*. They drew this cup; they sought an abode, and they found the thirty-three-fold abode. By means of that, this—

This world is indeed continuous through the Saman-tanvan and the Trayastriṃśa, as well as through the Saptahotṛ; whatever is given by gods and men to one another is given to him continuously and without interruption, for one who knows thus.

Prajāpati is the Daśahotṛ; the New and Full Moon sacrifices are the Caturhotṛ; the Cāturmāsya sacrifices are the Pañcahotṛ; the Soma sacrifice is the Saptahotṛ. The Agnihotra is the Daśahotṛ; the New and Full Moon sacrifices are the Caturhotṛ; the animal sacrifice is the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ; the Soma sacrifice is the Saptahotṛ. Breath is the Daśahotṛ; sight is the Caturhotṛ; hearing is the Pañcahotṛ; speech and the self are the Saptahotṛ. The Agnihotra is offered for the sake of life; he who knows this attains a full lifespan. The Full Moon sacrifice is offered for the sake of sight; it is not for the seizing of sight.

He who knows thus: for the sake of the ear, the New Moon sacrifice is offered, not for the sake of seizing the ear; he who knows thus. For the sake of speech and for the sake of the self, the Soma sacrifice is offered, not for the sake of seizing speech nor for the sake of seizing the self; he who knows thus. Prajāpati, the ten-fold Hotṛ, being one, becomes the recipient of the greatest share of the *vyāhṛtis*; being one, he becomes many—he who knows thus. For the sake of splendor, the Full Moon sacrifice is offered; the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni, and Agni is of the *gāyatrī* nature; his metre is the *gāyatrī*. Thus, he has placed both deities in their own proper stations; no other [sacrificer] does so.

He who knows this becomes the lord of security and well-being. For the sake of long life, the sacrifice to Agni is performed on the new moon day; he who knows this attains a full lifespan. For the sake of heaven, the Soma sacrifice is performed; by means of it, he goes to heaven.

He who desires to prevail through offspring and cattle should, having put on the *varāsī* garment, drink hot milk while lying on the ground for twelve nights. On the morning of the twelfth day, having rushed forward toward the east, he should recite the *Daśahotṛ* formula. For this [formula] is indeed without a mate, and thus one does not prevail. Prajāpati is the *Daśahotṛ*; having divided himself tenfold and created a mate, he is propagated with offspring and cattle. One desiring a son should cause him to sacrifice with the *Caturhotṛ* formula. By means of the *Caturhotṛ*, the gods generated Indra; the son is the essence (*indriya*).

He produces for him only a son, and no other is born after him; for he is born with his whole faculty and his whole vigor. The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is a boon, for a son is indeed a boon. One should cause a king to sacrifice with the Caturhotṛ formulas when battle is joined. By means of the Caturhotṛs, the gods produced Indra; he becomes the Indra of one side, and they conquer the battle. He produces Indra for him, and he conquers the battle. Whatever he wins therein, that is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity. One who desires cattle should cause him to sacrifice with the Pañcahotṛ formulas.

By means of the Pañcahotṛ, the gods indeed created cattle; he thus produces all cattle for him. For this [sacrifice], there are these four sacrificial gifts: a horse, gold, a cow, and a garment. One who might become worse off after the completion of a sacrifice should have the Saptahotṛ perform it. He who becomes worse off after the completion of a sacrifice cuts himself asunder; he passes away from his own state. By means of the Saptahotṛ, the gods went to the heavenly world; by means of the Saptahotṛ, they established this [world]. He extends it evenly; he does not become worse off than before.

To whatever extent he knows whom he sacrifices to and which Caturhotṛs are to be gratified at each pressing, he himself is gratified with offspring and cattle, and the Soma-draught inclines toward him. Having explained the Daśahotṛ, he should chant the Bahiṣpavamāna; the Daśahotṛ is Prajāpati, and thus he procreates. Having explained the Caturhotṛ, he should chant with the Ājyas; by means of the Caturhotṛ, the gods indeed generated Indra, and thus he generates Indra for this sacrificer; he makes that pressing possessed of Indra. Having explained the Pañcahotṛ, [he should chant] with the Mādhyandina [Pavamāna].

He should chant the *udgītha* with the *pavamāna* [stotra] using the *pañcahotṛ* formula. By means of the *pañcahotṛ*, the gods drove away the Asuras; by means of the *pañcahotṛ*, they released the cattle. Having driven away his rival, he releases cattle for himself. Having explained the *saptahotṛ* formula, he should chant the *udgītha* with the *pavamāna* [stotra] of the *arbha* [cup]. By means of the *saptahotṛ*, the gods went to the heavenly world; by means of the *saptahotṛ*, they established this [world]. He establishes it in harmony.

While the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, he should pronounce the *daśahotṛ* formula; Prajāpati is the *daśahotṛ*, and thus he brings forth progeny. Before the *prayāja* offerings, he should pronounce the *caturhotṛ* formula; by means of the *caturhotṛ*, the gods indeed brought Indra into being, and so he brings Indra into being for this sacrificer and makes the sacrifice possessed of Indra. While the portions of the oblation are being cut off, he should pronounce the *pañcahotṛ* formula; by means of the *pañcahotṛ*, the gods indeed drove away the Asuras, and by means of the *pañcahotṛ* they released the cattle; having driven away his rival, he releases cattle.

One should recite the Saptahotṛ formula after the after-offerings (anuyājas). By means of the Saptahotṛ, indeed, the gods went to the heavenly world; by means of the Saptahotṛ, they established this [world]. He thus establishes it completely. With the Caturhotṛ formula, he should touch the oblations placed at the full moon sacrifice. By means of the Caturhotṛ, indeed, the gods generated Indra; the full moon is procreation. He thus generates [offspring]. With the Pañcahotṛ formula, he should touch the oblations placed at the new moon sacrifice. By means of the Pañcahotṛ, indeed, the gods went to the heavenly world; the new moon is conducive to the heavenly world. This is the securing of the heavenly world. || 14 ||

The *caturhotṛ* formulas are indeed food; he who knows thus becomes possessed of food. As for what they say: "If there is only one *caturhotṛ*, why are all of them called *caturhotṛ*s?"—it is because these four are sacrifices, and each of them has four *hotṛ*s; that is their state of being *caturhotṛ*s. For one year, one of the four should not eat; that is their vow. This *caturhotṛ* ritual is indeed the sacrifice of one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*); they know it as such for the sake of obtaining food, for the sake of splendor and vigor. On the tenth day, the Udgātṛ should chant with the verses of the Serpent Queen (*sarparājñī*). This [earth] indeed...

The food of the Queen of Serpents and the Caturhotṛ formulas—having obtained food through these, he secures food for himself. Indeed, these Caturhotṛ formulas are unapplied and unsecured; when the Hotṛ recites the Caturhotṛs, he thereby applies them and secures them. This is the indistinct hymn of the gods, namely the verses of the Queen of Serpents; its indistinct chant is the Caturhotṛs. He chants the Prastāva mentally, he sings the Udgītha mentally, and he chants the Pratihāra mentally; thus the Udgātṛs pour forth seed when they recite the Caturhotṛs.

The Hotṛ speaks; verily, the Hotṛ generates the seed that has been poured out. One should explain the Agnyādheya [at this time], for the Agnyādheya is the extraction of the Brahman; the Caturhotṛ formulas are the extraction of the Brahman; and when that sun rises, it creates the entire Brahman. Now, these are the *saṃbhāra* materials. Indeed, once upon a time, the sacrifices of the gods and the Asuras were both extended. Whatever the gods did, the Asuras did the same. Those gods, taking the sacrifice...

As he stepped upon it, he gathered [the materials] together; by that, he overcame the Asuras. Because he gathered them together (*sam-abharat*), that is the reason for the name of the *saṃbhāras*. One who intends to proceed with these [offerings] four by four should offer oblations. Thus, he first grasps the sacrifice and first grasps the deities; he becomes possessed of the sacrifice, while the other remains without the sacrifice. During the initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should cause [the sacrificer] to recite [these verses]. For the sacrifice is as much as this [extent]; having grasped the sacrifice in its entirety, he undergoes initiation. Or, during the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), one should cause him to recite; for the sacrifice is as much as this, namely, as much as the twelve-day rite.

As great as the sacrifice is, so great [is it] when one, having taken up the twelve-cubit [staff], undergoes initiation. Now, these wives [are significant]: from the south, the Asuras indeed conquered the sacrifice of the gods; the *āgnīdhra* shed of those [Asuras] remained unconquered. The gods entered into that with the wives; the Asuras, being ashamed, having exposed the wives, turned back. The gods, rising up after them, then conquered them by means of the midday *pavamāna*. For whomsoever the *āgnīdhra*, knowing the wives, becomes, he overcomes the houses and the cattle of his rival.

No rival shall ascend upon his house or his cattle—he for whom the knowing Agnidh performs the offering to the Patnīvats; he, being wise, satisfies the wife; the satisfied wife conceives seed; from seed offspring are born; he becomes prolific through offspring and cattle. || 15 ||

Having created living beings, he desired, "May I create the sacrifice. He perceived this Saptahotṛ [formula]; having recited it mentally, he offered it. By means of that, he created the sacrifice. Once created, the sacrifice went away from him. He recited it after it with the Grahya [formula] and drew it in; that is the reason for the name of the Graha. One who is about to undergo initiation should offer the Saptahotṛ first; having thus created and seized the sacrifice, he extends it. It becomes a Graha for the support of the created sacrifice. Having created the sacrifice, he desired, "May I create the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

Thinking, "Let me create," he beheld this Caturhotṛ; having recited it mentally, he offered it as an oblation. By means of it, he created the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Once created, the New and Full Moon sacrifices moved away from him. Having recited [the Caturhotṛ] after them, he seized them with a *graha* (libation). That is the reason for the name of the *graha*. One who is about to perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices should offer the Caturhotṛ first. Having created and seized the New and Full Moon sacrifices, he proceeds. It becomes a *graha* for the support of the New and Full Moon sacrifices once they have been created. Having created the New and Full Moon sacrifices...

He desired, "May I create the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. He saw this Pañcahotṛ formula; having recited it mentally, he offered it as an oblation. By means of it, he created the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. Once they had been created for him, they moved away from him. Having recited the formula mentally, he seized them with the Graha cup. That is the reason for the name of the Graha. When about to perform the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, one should offer the Pañcahotṛ oblation beforehand. Having thus created and obtained the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, he proceeds with them. It becomes a Graha for the support of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices that have been created. [This applies] when practicing exorcism.

One should offer with the *daśahotr* formula; for there are nine vital breaths in a person and the navel is the tenth—he thus causes his very breaths to be exhausted. He should offer either on a self-made salt-flat or in a cleft; for this is the part of her seized by *Nirṛti*; verily, he causes *Nirṛti* herself to seize him. He utters the *vaṣaṭ* call; for this is the cruel part of speech—verily, he cuts him off with the cruel part of speech. The *Āṅgirasas* and the *Ādityas* contended for the world of heaven; those *Ādityas*, having perceived this *pañcahotṛ* formula, offered it after reciting it mentally, and then [the Āṅgirasas were defeated].

The Ādityas went to the heavenly world, while the Aṅgirases fell away from it. Those Aṅgirases said to the Ādityas, "Where are you? How shall we carry your oblation? They replied, "In the meters. [They asked further: "The Vasus in the Gāyatrī, the Rudras in the Triṣṭubh, and the Ādityas in the Jagatī. In this very way, the oblation is carried to the existing gods for one who knows thus the instruction regarding the gods; he becomes possessed of the instruction. He who desires the heavenly world should, having mentally recited these five Hotṛ-formulas, offer them; for there are five seasons.

The seasons are the year, and the year is the heavenly world; having established himself in the seasons, that is, in the year, he goes to the heavenly world. If a non-Brahmin, having studied the Veda, does not shine, he should go to the forest, tie up a clump of darbha grass, seat a Brahmin to his south, and explain these Caturhotṛ formulas to him. For that which is the Caturhotṛs is the undefined Brahman of the gods; thus, as it is being defined, it causes him to attain clarity. [He explains them] after tying up a clump of darbha grass.

"Agni indeed is the bunch of darbha grass; he recites while accompanied by Agni. A Brāhmaṇa sits to the south; the Brāhmaṇa is indeed the overseer of creatures; he recites while accompanied by an overseer. Both he who recites and he who sits to the south are liable to lose their glory. To him who sits to the south, one should give a boon; whatever glory reaches that [sacrifice], one secures it by means of that boon. (16)

One who has rivals should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni. Indra and Agni are indeed vigor and strength; by means of that very vigor and strength, he overcomes them. One who desires kinsmen should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni. Indra and Agni are indeed vigor and strength; by means of that very vigor and strength, he draws them down beneath him. Indeed, they do not follow after him as he departs unless they desire it. Indra and Agni are vigor and strength; when he offers to Indra and Agni, he departs having gathered their very vigor and strength. As he departs, they do not follow after him unless they desire it.

They follow after him; he who desires offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni. Verily, when Prajāpati was desiring to emit offspring, Indra and Agni hid away his offspring. He perceived: "Indra and Agni have indeed hidden my offspring. He beheld this offering to Indra and Agni on eleven potsherds; then indeed they restored the offspring to him. Indra and Agni hide away the offspring of that man who, though capable of having offspring, does not obtain offspring; it is to them that he has recourse with their own share. They [restore it].

Being pleased with him, they gave back his offspring; thus the *yājyā* and *anu-vākyā* verses become "restoring the giver" for the sake of prosperity. One who is setting out for battle should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni; Indra and Agni are indeed strength and vigor; by means of that very strength and vigor, he sets out for battle. Having arrived at the battle, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni; Indra and Agni are indeed strength and vigor; by means of that very strength and vigor, he conquers it. Having won the battle, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni; for he [is] indeed by means of strength...

He who conquers in battle is deprived of his vigor; for with all his faculties and all his vigor he conquers. Ojas and vīrya belong to Indra and Agni. When there is an offering to Indra and Agni, Indra and Agni themselves endow him with ojas and vīrya. He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni and a pap to Pūṣan when setting out for gain. Ojas and vīrya indeed belong to Indra and Agni; by means of ojas and vīrya he goes forth. Pūṣan is the bestower of vīrya; because there is an offering to Pūṣan, Pūṣan himself [bestows it] upon him.

He bestows vigor. He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni, a pap to Pūṣan, and a pap to the Lord of the Field for one who desires, "May I prosper in this community. Indra and Agni are indeed vigor and strength; by means of the offering to Indra and Agni, Indra and Agni themselves find a place for him through vigor and strength. Pūṣan is the giver of vigor; by means of the offering to Pūṣan, Pūṣan himself bestows vigor upon him. This earth is the Lord of the Field; by means of the offering to the Lord of the Field, he finds firm support in this very earth.
With what splendor have the Maruts, dwelling together in the same nest, mingled with one another?
With what thought do these bulls come from whence? They sing their strength, seeking wealth.
Whose sacred hymns have the youthful Maruts delighted? Who has turned them toward his sacrifice? Like hawks gliding through the mid-air, by what great thought may we cause them to pause?
From where do you come, O Indra, though being so great, that you go alone, O Lord of the Good? What is this for you?
As you hasten hither, you ask us about our auspicious deeds; O Lord of the Bay Steeds, tell us what you have against us.
The Vedic hymns are my thoughts; the pressed juices are for peace. My vigor stirs; the pressing-stone is set forth for me.
They look toward you and desire the hymn of praise; these two bay steeds carry you toward us.
From there, yoking ourselves with these, we adorn our bodies within our own sovereign power.
With these splendors we now employ thee, O Indra; for thou hast indeed come to us according to our own nature.
O Maruts, where was your self-dependent power when you left me alone in the slaughter?
For I, fierce, mighty, and powerful, have bent down every enemy with my deadly weapons.
O Bull, you have performed many deeds for us with our allied and equal heroic powers.
For indeed, O most powerful Indra, we Maruts shall accomplish many things through our will, whatever we may desire.
O Maruts, with my own power and through my own fury, having become mighty, I slew Vṛtra. With the thunderbolt in my arm, I made these all-glittering waters flow easily for Manu.
O Maghavan, you are unsurpassed; indeed, there is no deity known who is equal to you.
Neither while being born nor once born does he perish; do what you shall do, O you who have grown great!

My power alone is vast; whatever I, being bold, shall accomplish through my wisdom, I indeed am the fierce one known among you, O Maruts. Indra is the lord of these things, he who causes them to fall.
O Maruts, this hymn of praise has honored me here, since you heroes have fashioned for me a prayer worthy of being heard.
For Indra, the bull, the great warrior—for my sake, as friends for a friend—you have done so for your own bodies with your own bodies.
Thus indeed these [Maruts], shining toward me and bestowing blameless glory, have acted.
O Maruts, of moon-like color, having been beheld by me, you have pleased me and indeed continue to delight me now.
Who here has magnified you, O Maruts? Come forth toward your friends, O friends!
May they cause my wondrous hymns to be heard; be mindful of these my sacred rites.
Since the poet has offered praise for my sake, the inspired wisdom of Mānya has turned toward us.
O Maruts, turn toward the inspired singer; let the singer recite these prayers for you.
This hymn is for you, O Maruts; this is the song of Māndārya, the son of Māna, the poet.
May she grant vital strength to our bodies; may we find nourishment and a secure dwelling that bestows swift life-sustenance. 18.
O Maruts, when you [come] from heaven, may you [bring] Indra to us.
O Bull, let your impetuous strength come from behind, from above, from below, and from the front.
Let them come together from all sides toward us; O Indra, bestow upon us resplendent, heavenly glory.
With you as his ally, O Soma, through that friendship of yours, Indra set the waters flowing for mankind;
he slew the serpent, released the seven rivers, and opened the channels that had been closed up.
May I be united with my friend Ṛdūdara, who, when drunk, shall not harm me, O Lord of the Tawny Steeds. This Soma which has been placed within us—for that sake, I extend Indra’s life-span.
O Agni, the star; O Agni, the great one; up that bright [light] of the gods.
Seven pure ones, yoked by themselves—the daughters of the Sun—go with their own yoking.
O divine Sūrya, seven bay horses carry you in your chariot, you whose hair is flame, O far-seeing one.
This Soma, being purified, flows as Pūṣan, as wealth, and as Bhaga; as the lord of the entire world, he has looked out upon both heaven and earth.
The Priyamedha seers, like birds of prey, approached Indra with their supplications.
Drive away the darkness, fill our vision, and release us like those bound in a snare.
Just as indeed that [was done], O Vasus.
Bestow sight upon me for the sake of seeing; bestow sight upon my bodies so that they may look abroad. May we behold this world both together and separately.
O Sūrya, may we behold you, who are so beautiful to look upon; may we, with the eyes of men, see clearly.
O Agni, three are your strengths, three your abodes, and three are your ancient tongues, O you who are born of Truth.
Three are your bodies, beloved by the gods; with them, protect our songs without failing.
We know your three forms, O Agni, in three ways; we know your dwelling distributed in many places.
We know your supreme name which is hidden in the cave; we know that spring from which you have come forth.
O Indra, [grant us] a triple-layered, threefold-protecting refuge that brings well-being.
Bestow vomiting upon the generous patrons and upon me, and keep your missile away from these others.
Pierced through by his unsteady weapon, even the mountains were split at their ridges thrice seven times;
neither god nor mortal can surpass that which the mighty Bull has accomplished.
Bṛhaspati, who dwells in the three abodes, suddenly propped apart the ends of the earth with his roar;
him, the sweet-tongued one, the ancient seers, the inspired sages, beholding him, have established in front.
Having split the fortress, you lay low; from the west, he cut through the three together from the ocean.
Bṛhaspati found the dawn, the sun, the cow, and the hymn, like the thundering sky. || 19 ||
Thus ends the ninth section, named "Utsīdana," in the *Iṣṭimikā* of the *Caraka* recension of the *Kāṭhaka* of the glorious *Yajurveda*. 9.
Now begins the tenth section:
[The offering] to Agni and Viṣṇu.

One who is practicing sorcery, or one who is being practiced against, should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati. Agni indeed is all the deities; Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; Sarasvatī is speech; Bṛhaspati is the sacred formulation (*brahman*). By means of Agni, he counteracts his [opponent's] deities with [his own] deities; by means of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, he counteracts the sacrifice; by means of Sarasvatī, speech, he counteracts speech; by means of Bṛhaspati, the sacred formulation, he counteracts the sacred formulation. Having thus made them equal, whatever he does thereafter, by that he overpowers him. This very same [rite].

One who performs sorcery should offer [this oblation]. Agni is indeed all the deities; Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; Sarasvatī is speech; Bṛhaspati is the sacred formulation (*brahman*). By means of Agni, he joins him with the deities; by means of Viṣṇu, with the sacrifice; by means of Sarasvatī, with speech; by means of Bṛhaspati, with the sacred formulation; thus he overcomes him. One who is about to immolate an animal should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu. He who immolates an animal without having secured both the deities and the sacrifice acts with a defective animal. Agni, indeed, is all the deities.

Viṣṇu is the sacrifice and the deities; having encompassed the sacrifice, he slaughters the victim. One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu in battle. Agni indeed is all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus, by means of the deities and the sacrifice, he conquers him. If he should think, "They are advancing against me," he should make two verses the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) and one the offering verse (*yājyā*); he makes it equal with two and employs it with one. One who is being practiced against with malevolent magic should offer a *caru* oblation of ghee to Agni and Viṣṇu; Agni indeed is all...

Viṣṇu is the deity of the sacrifice, and he enters into both the deities and the sacrifice from the middle. This pair consists of ghee and rice grains; the ghee is the milk of the cow, and the rice grains are those of the ox. By means of this pair, he surrounds himself on all sides for the sake of stability. One who desires sight should offer a pap of cooked rice in ghee to Agni and Viṣṇu. For by the eye of Agni, human beings see, and by the eye of Viṣṇu, the deities see; these two are the bestowers of sight. He approaches them with their own portion, and they grant him sight.

This pair is indeed what is offered: ghee and rice-grains. The ghee is the milk of the cow, and the rice-grains are those of the ox; thus it is a pair. By means of this pair, he produces a pair for him. It is in ghee; ghee is indeed brilliance, and the eye is brilliance; by means of brilliance, he bestows brilliance upon him. He should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni-Viṣṇu in the morning, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati; at midday, an eleven-potherd cake to Agni-Viṣṇu and these two same pap-offerings; [and again] an [eleven-potherd cake] to Agni-Viṣṇu.

There is a cake on twelve potsherds in the afternoon, and these two oblations of cooked rice for one whose rival is sacrificing with Soma. Agni is indeed all the deities; Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; Sarasvatī is speech; Bṛhaspati is the sacred formulation (*brahman*). By means of Agni, he obtains the deities of his rival through his own deities; by means of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice through his own sacrifice; by means of Sarasvatī, speech through his own speech; by means of Bṛhaspati, the sacred formulation through his own sacred formulation. Through the sacrificial cakes, he obtains the pressings; through the potsherds, the meters. This is the sacrifice known as the "Ordinance of the Sacrifice" (*adhvarakalpā*); by it, he obtains the very sacrifice itself. Whatever he gives therein—

As its sacrificial fee, he subsequently offers a cake on one potsherd to Mitra and Varuṇa. By that, he obtains that very cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa which is to be offered as the *anūbandhyā*. It is made on one potsherd; for a person cannot be obtained by means of many potsherds, but rather he obtains him all at once.

The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session (sattra) desiring glory—Agni, Soma, and Indra. They said, "Whatever glory shall come to us, let that be common to us. Glory came to Soma; therefore he is glorious. He went to the mountain; therefore he is on the mountain. Agni followed after him, and Agni and Soma became united. Then Indra felt unsupported, as if loose. He went after them and took refuge in Agni and Soma. They caused him to sacrifice with this offering, with a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Soma; [for] brilliance indeed...

Agni is power (*indriya*) and Soma is brilliance; Agni bestowed brilliance upon him with the offering to Agni, and Soma bestowed power with the offering to Soma. From that, indeed, he became [prosperous]. One desiring prosperity should sacrifice with an eleven-potherd cake for Agni-Soma. Agni is brilliance and Soma is power; Agni bestowed brilliance upon him with the offering to Agni, and Soma bestowed power with the offering to Soma. He certainly becomes [prosperous]. A Brāhmaṇa should offer an eleven-potherd cake to Agni-Soma for the sake of all desires. Agni and Soma are indeed the own deities of the Brāhmaṇa; it is them [he thus pleases].

He approaches them with their respective portions; they grant him all his desires. A Brāhmaṇa desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a cake on eight potsherds of *śyāmāka* grain to Agni and Soma in the spring. Agni and Soma are indeed the bestowers of spiritual luster; he approaches them with their portion, and they grant him spiritual luster. He should sacrifice in the spring, for the spring is the season of the Brāhmaṇa; in his own season he secures spiritual luster. Such indeed is spiritual luster.

Like tawny, like small, like green—verily he unites the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). In that it is on eight potsherds, it belongs to Agni; in that it is black, it belongs to Soma. Thus it does not depart from either; there are two invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) for Agni-Soma, and the two *saṃyājyā* verses are addressed to Soma and Agni. Agni is brilliance and Soma is sensory power (*indriya*); verily, by means of both brilliance and sensory power, having encompassed the splendor of sacred knowledge on both sides, he places it within himself.

One who would eat what is not food, or one who desires to eat it, should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; by means of the year itself, he eats what is purified and made palatable. If he offers after having already eaten, the year itself makes what was eaten palatable for him. One who has acted treacherously against an equal, or one who desires to act treacherously against an equal, should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; this [year] is equal toward him who is equal.

Having obtained the year itself, he commits an offense against the desire that has come to him. He who has been accepted as a gift, desiring gain, should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; they accept that person for the sake of the year whom they accept as a gift. Having obtained the year itself, he wins the gain that was to be won. He who is depositing a gift should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; he thus employs the year.

He who begs releases him for a year; for the year indeed wins this for him that he begs, and thus he makes him a sharer. Whichever [deity] he cleanses last, he should give its rope to his unfriendly rival; for he who begs wanders with a snare, and so he fastens a snare upon his unfriendly rival. He who desires, "May I take away the wealth or the grain of this king or village headman," should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara—for the year indeed...

Agni Vaiśvānara is the year, the giver of food; he approaches him with his own portion, and he bestows food upon him, for offspring are born following the year. One desiring rain should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; that which belongs to Vaiśvānara is the fierce body of the year. With that [body], it stands here scorching and burning, seeking its own portion. He gratifies that very [body] of his, and she [grants] him...

When it rains while he is pleased, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara in battle. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year. Of two who have joined in combat, whichever one lacks a support is defeated; having made the year his support, he conquers the battle.

One who desires a village, prosperity, and spiritual luster should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. He should place green gold in the middle [of the cake] and silver on top. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; the year is vigor, and the self is the green gold. Verily, he places him in the midst of vigor; he attains prosperity and indeed becomes prosperous. As for the silver, he removes it together with the ashes; for he who, though capable of spiritual luster, does not attain it, is seized by impurity.

He becomes possessed of spiritual luster; he indeed drives away evil from him and endows him with spiritual luster. Just as spokes are fastened to the nave, even so the months and the seasons are fastened to the year. In that he places gold in the middle, he makes him the very nave.

Just as the spokes are dependent upon the nave, even so do his kinsmen depend upon him. One who is afflicted by illness, or one seized by Varuṇa, should offer a sacrificial pap of barley to Varuṇa and a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. He who is afflicted by illness is indeed seized by Varuṇa; because the offering is to Varuṇa, he releases him from Varuṇa. It is made of barley, for barley is the portion belonging to Varuṇa; with his own portion, he thus satisfies Varuṇa. It is a span in measure, for man is only as large as this [span] of his.

The vital breaths are as extensive as his very self; he thereby releases him from Varuṇa. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year, and the year is life; verily, he establishes him in the year, in life, and he attains a full span of life. He who, not giving to another, moves about seizing [from others], is seized by Varuṇa. One who desires to practice sorcery against a Kṣatriya, or one who desires prosperity, or one who is seized by Varuṇa, should offer a pap of barley to Varuṇa and a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. Since he is seized by Varuṇa, by means of the offering to Varuṇa, he releases him from Varuṇa; it is made of barley.

He becomes a span in measure; Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year, and the year is vigor; verily he establishes him in the vigor of the year, and he prospers for the sake of prosperity. One who is about to remove the sacred fire should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; this [fire], being removed, does not perish as long as it remains within the year. Having made him a sharer, he removes the fire in accordance with the year. [One should offer] a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara...

One whose full moon or new moon sacrifice is omitted should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the Maker of the Path). He who omits the full moon or new moon sacrifice goes astray from the path; Agni is the maker of the path among the gods. One thus takes hold of him, and he leads him back onto the path. Indeed, one cuts the sacrifice asunder when one performs this intermediate offering while the sacrifice is already extended. Whatever cake on eight potsherds belongs to Agni at the full moon and whatever belongs to him at the new moon—that one should offer to Agni Pathikṛt.

By that very path he returns; he does not interrupt the sacrifice. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vājasṛt in battle. Agni is indeed the winner of the prize among the gods; he who wins a battle runs toward that prize. He pursues him with his own share; he runs toward the prize and wins the battle. Moreover, he becomes as unassailable as Agni himself. He who, having established the sacred fires, should act contrary to his vows, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati. For he who has been initiated belongs to the gods.

The one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) may not eat the food of such a person; for the Lord of Vows (*Vratapati*) takes away the vow of him who, having established the fires, behaves contrary to his vow. Agni is the Lord of Vows among the gods; he approaches him with his own portion and thus recovers his vow from the Lord of Vows. One suffering from illness should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni, the slayer of demons (*rakṣohan*). When Indra was born, the demons (*rakṣāṃsi*) followed him; as he was being seized and touched by the demons, he entered into Agni. Therefore, Agni drove away the demons. The demons follow him who [is ill].

Agni is the sick one among the gods, the slayer of Rakṣases; he approaches him with his own portion, and he drives the Rakṣases away from him. He should sacrifice on a dark night at midnight; for it is on a dark night at midnight that the Rakṣases stir abroad. By this, he casts them out while they are still full. He should sacrifice in an enclosed space to keep the Rakṣases at bay.

These fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, which destroy the Rākṣasas, belong to Vāmadeva. Vāmadeva and Kusidāyī once raced for a prize. As he was racing ahead, Kusidāyī crushed the pole of his chariot; she then turned back toward him, thinking, "I will break their axle. Vāmadeva was carrying the fire in a pan (*ukhya-agni*); he looked at it and saw this hymn: "Make your strength wide like a net... The fire, rushing after her, completely consumed her as she was being burned.
He submerged the lake Kausida; this which is recited here is for the destruction of the Rākṣasas.

The Naimiṣeyas were indeed performing a long sacrificial session (*sattra*). Having risen from it, they drove away twenty-seven heifers among the Kurus and Pañcālas. Vaka Dālbhya said to them, "You yourselves divide these; I shall go to this Dhṛtarāṣṭra Vaicitravīrya, and he will provide me with a household. He went to him, but the king paid no heed to him. Vaka urged him on, saying, "O base Brahmin! Paśupati kills the cows; go, cook them for another! [The king replied: "Of those cows, O King, the meat belongs to Devasū."

He said, "I have killed him," and he cut up his thighs and cooked them. While he was cooking, [the king] cast [the meat] away. He offered an eight-potherd cake of black rice to Agni Rudravat. Whatever belonged to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all of that became scattered and vanished. The fortune-tellers found it and said, "A Brahmin is surely practicing sorcery against you; curse him! He sought him out and gave him much wealth. He offered an eight-potherd cake of white rice to Agni Surabhimat.

Then, indeed, he should cast that [offering] away and offer a cake on eight potsherds of black rice to Agni Rudravat while practicing sorcery; for Agni is Rudra, and thus he delivers him over to Rudra himself. It is of black rice: black, indeed, is darkness, and darkness is death; thus he seizes him with death itself. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat when this god intends harm toward his offspring, or whenever he should desire, "May he perish. For this is the healing body of Agni.

Surabhimatī (the fragrant one) pursues that very [power] as her portion; with it he heals him. One for whom a dead man is heard of should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat. He who is heard of as dead is indeed heard of as putrid. That which is the fragrant body of Agni, that very thing he pursues as his portion; with it he makes him fragrant. One for whom a man has been killed without being slain should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat. He is indeed seized by impurity.

They curse him who has struck down twins; he approaches with his own portion that very body of Agni which is fragrant, and by that he purifies him. He who desires, "May I be an eater of food," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the eater of food; Agni indeed is the eater of food among the gods; he approaches him with his own portion, and he makes him an eater of food. He who desires, "May I be possessed of food," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the possessor of food; Agni indeed is the possessor of food among the gods; he approaches him with his own portion, and he...

He makes this man possessed of food. One who desires, "May I be a lord of food," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the Lord of Food. Agni indeed is the lord of food among the gods; he approaches him with his own share, and he makes him a lord of food. He should perform the offering throughout a year; for the year is the giver of food. He approaches it with its own share, and it makes him an eater of food, possessed of food, and a lord of food. One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, accompanied by the Vasus, for the sake of all desires.
Whatever a Brāhmaṇa obtains, that is indeed the wealth of the gods; Agni is the most wealthy among them. He approaches him with his own portion, and he grants all his desires to him. || 6 ||

One who practices sorcery, or one against whom sorcery is practiced, should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni Yaviṣṭha. The gods and the Asuras were at war with one another; those Asuras released the *visṛṣṭis* (missiles) against the gods. The gods perceived it: "The Asuras have indeed released the *visṛṣṭis* against us. They offered an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni Yaviṣṭha; by that means, they warded off those *visṛṣṭis* from themselves. They release a *visṛṣṭi* against him whom they practice sorcery upon. In that he offers to Agni Yaviṣṭha, by that very act he [wardes it off].

One whose soma has been spilled should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni Yaviṣṭha from his own portion; for those whose two somas collide, they collide with the deities, since Agni is all the deities; thus, by means of Agni Yaviṣṭha, he appropriates their deities.

The gods and the Asuras were arrayed for battle. Whatever [portion] of the gods they did not slay, that alone remained theirs; but those of the Asuras, having been born again, fought once more. The gods knew: "Whosoever among us dies here, Agni indeed slays them. They said, "Do not destroy us! How will you destroy us? He replied, "Let there be a share for me. [They said,] "We will not endure one who has no share for us. They offered a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣamavat (the Enduring). Then indeed he endured for them. To Agni...

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Kṣamavat when this god intends harm toward offspring, or when he should desire, "May they perish. For whoever here dies, it is Agni who kills them; Agni is the most patient among the gods. He approaches him with his own portion, and being pleased, he indeed shows patience toward him. The gods, the fathers, and humans were on one side; the Asuras, Rakṣases, and Piśācas were on the other. They contended with one another. Whatever small amount of blood the Asuras caused to flow from the gods, that [they turned] into nights.

The *rakṣases*, while performing the *sumbha* rite, slew them; they were dead when [the sun] shone upon them. The gods knew: "Whoever among us dies, it is surely the *rakṣases* who perform the *sumbha* rite against them. They invited them [the *rakṣases*] and they said: "Let us choose a boon: whatever we win from these Asuras, let that be ours as well. Thereupon the gods conquered the Asuras; having conquered the Asuras, they drove away the *rakṣases*. [The *rakṣases* thought], "They have committed an untruth (*anṛta*)," and so they settled all around the gods. Those gods sought protection in Agni alone; they [offered] to Agni...

They offered a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pravata, a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vibādhavat, and a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pratīkavat. By [the offering] to Agni Pravata, they drove away those *rakṣases* that were in front; by [the offering] to Agni Vibādhavat, they repelled those that were all around; by [the offering] to Agni Pratīkavat, they pushed back those *rakṣases* that were behind. One who has rivals should sacrifice with this [offering]; he who has many rivals [should offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pravata.

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vibādhavat and a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pratīkavat. By [offering] to Agni Pravat, he drives away that rival who has previously surpassed him; by [offering] to Agni Vibādhavat, he oppresses him who is his equal; by [offering] to Agni Pratīkavat, he repels that rival who stands behind him. Thus, he drives away a superior rival, surpasses one who is his equal, and a worse person does not overtake him—he who, knowing this, sacrifices with this [offering].

The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Gāyatrī stood between them, encompassing vigor, strength, and food. The year itself stood between them. There are twenty-four syllables in the Gāyatrī, and there are twenty-four half-months in the year. They [the gods and Asuras] thought, "Whichever side this one will join, they shall become masters of this world. They called out to her; the Asuras called her "Dābhī," and the gods called her "Viśvakarman. She did not join either side. Then those gods...

He saw this *yajus*: "Thou art vigor; thou art might; thou art strength; thou art splendor; thou art the name of the abode of the gods; thou art the All; thou art all life; thou art everything; thou art all life; thou art the overcomer. With this, she turned toward the gods. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. One who has rivals, or one who is contending, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni. Having approached it, he should touch it with these *yajus* formulas. Indeed, the year is vigor and virility; thus he appropriates the vigor and virility of his rival. Deprived of virility, that rival perishes.
This very sacrifice is named Gāyatrī; moreover, they say it is "the seizure of the kṣatra. ||7||

One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra Gharma-vat. Yonder sun is indeed the Gharma; he is Indra, and he is the bestower of spiritual luster. He approaches him with his own portion, and he grants him spiritual luster. One who desires cattle should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra Indriyavat. Cattle are indeed power (*indriya*); Indra is the bestower of cattle. He approaches him with his own portion, and he grants him cattle. [To Indra Arkavat...]

One desiring food should offer a cake on eleven potsherds; for the *arka* is indeed food, and Indra is the giver of food. He approaches him with his own portion, and he grants him food. One who has been driven from his realm and desires to regain it should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra *Arkavat*; for they drive one to the very end whom they exclude. That which possesses the *arka* is the final body of Indra; thus, he establishes an end for him at the very end. A barren cow is the sacrificial fee, [with the thought] "May she lead me to my desire. One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra *Gharma-vat*.

One who desires prosperity should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Powerful and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Radiant, using the same sacrificial grass for both. In that he offers to Indra the Gharma-sustained, it is because the Gharma is yonder sun and this Indra is the head of creatures; thus he makes himself the head. In that he offers to Indra the Powerful, he bestows power upon himself. In that he offers to Indra the Radiant, it is because the earth is the radiance (arka); thus he finds firm support on this very earth. There should be a pap in the middle to avoid monotony, [and another] to Indra the Wrathful.

One should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds in battle. For it is through fury that one exerts heroism, and through power that one conquers; thus he bestows both fury and power upon these [deities] for the sake of victory. One should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra the Fierce and the Mindful in battle. For it is through fury that one exerts heroism, and through power that one conquers; having made Fury and Power his allies, he bestows their mind for the sake of victory. One who desires to be mindful should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra the Mindful and the Radiant.

"May I be radiant"—for splendor and radiance are indeed the mind; thus he bestows upon him splendor and radiance through the mind. He should not proclaim it before a year has passed; for by means of a year, that which is unattained is attained, and having attained the year, he secures it for himself. (8)

One who has been expelled or is about to be expelled should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Good Protector (*sutrāman*). Indra is indeed the protector and Indra is the expeller; he approaches him with his own share, and he protects him. One who is afflicted by disease should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Deliverer from Evil (*am̐homuc*). He who is afflicted by disease is indeed seized by evil (*am̐has*); that body of Indra which delivers from evil is his healing power. He approaches him with his own share, and he releases him from evil. [To Indra the Deliverer from Evil...]

One who, by himself or through his household, has fallen into distress or is seized by sin, should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds. He who falls into distress or is seized by sin is indeed seized by evil; Indra is the deliverer from evil, so he approaches him with his own share, and he releases him from evil. One who desires, "May the great sacrifice come to me," should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra Arkavat Aśvamedhavat. For this earth is the *arka*, and the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is Indra’s sacrifice; the sacrifice reaches its end for that seeker of sacrifice whom it does not approach.

The sacrifice does not approach those two final bodies of Indra which possess the *arkas*; it is by means of these very two final bodies of Indra that he seizes the sacrifice, and the sacrifice approaches him. He who desires kinsmen should offer an eleven-potherd oblation to Indra-Anvṛju; for sovereignty is indeed power (*indriya*), and by means of power itself, he makes his kinsmen submissive. One who has rivals should offer an eleven-potherd oblation to Indra-Prababhru; for the *prababhru* is a thunderbolt, and with the *prababhru*, Indra [struck] the thunderbolt at the Asuras.

He strikes his rival with the thunderbolt itself; he strikes him down. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Vimṛdha in a battle for the sake of success. The offering to Agni is for prosperity. When Indra had slain Vṛtra, the enemies (mṛdhas) assailed him; he saw this [offering] to Vimṛdha and with it he drove away those enemies. He who desires to win a battle seeks to slay Vṛtra. That body of Indra which was "Vimṛdha," to that very one he has recourse as his portion; through it he drives away the enemies.

He slays Vṛtra and conquers the battle; he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Vimṛdha (the Dispeller of Foes) when danger comes from all sides. The offering to Agni is for prosperity. When Indra had slain Vṛtra, the foes trembled against him on every side; he beheld this [offering] to Vimṛdha and with it he drove away those foes. The foes tremble against him on every side when danger comes from all sides. He approaches that very body of Indra which is "Vimṛdha" with its own portion; by it he drives away the foes from himself. 9.

Prajāpati indeed fastened the thunderbolt upon Indra with the Mahānāmnī verses; by means of it, he conquered. Thereupon, he became [great]. He was afraid, thinking, "The unappeased thunderbolt will burn my neck. Thereupon, he fashioned the Revatī verses for the sake of appeasement. One should offer a pap (caru) to Indra for a Rājanya who desires prosperity. For the Rājanya has Indra as his deity; verily, he generates him from his own womb for the sake of prosperity. He surely prospers. The Revatī verse is the invitatory formula (anuvākyā), and the Śakvarī is the offering formula (yājyā). The Revatī is indeed the thunderbolt, and the Śakvarī is the thunderbolt; [thus] it is the thunderbolt itself.

He unites [the two]; by that he conquers; it indeed becomes a sacrificial pap (caru) for the sake of peace, so that there may be no burning. When an army has risen up, one should offer a pap to Indrāṇī in the king’s house; for the army is Indrāṇī, and thus with the sacred power (brahman) he brings it under control for the sake of victory. Balbaja grass should be used both for the fuel and for the sacrificial strew. These are indeed powerful when grown; thus he leads her forward according to the proper method. Whatever she may find, that shall be the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of prosperity. When an army has risen up against the king, one should offer a pap to Indra and to Indrāṇī.

This is indeed Indra’s discarded wife; he leads her away among the cattle. Balbaja grass is placed both in the fuel and on the sacrificial strew; for these are indeed powerful when born. He leads her away in accordance with the proper order. Whatever she may find, that is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the sake of prosperity. Prajāpati indeed assigned the portions to the gods. His vital power (*indriya*) was left over. Indra said, "Let it be mine! He placed it in him. Yet it remained excessive even in him. It then ascended upwards through these worlds.

He did not obtain it with one, nor with two; having obtained it with the third, he secured it. One desiring prosperity should offer three sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*); these worlds are three, and by obtaining these very worlds, he secures vigor and strength. Each subsequent one becomes larger, for each subsequent of these worlds is larger. First [he offers] to Indra the King, then to Indra the Self-Ruler (*svarāj*), then to Indra the Overlord (*adhirāja*). Indeed, Indra became all these; he who, knowing this, conquers with this [offering], becomes all these.

There are three invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) and they are also the offering verses (*yājyā*). Having recited the first, he offers with the middle; having recited the middle, he offers with the last; having recited the last, he offers again with the first. This is for the continuity of these worlds and for the sake of clear understanding. He makes all [the verses] invitatory and all offering verses. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Those Asuras were more numerous, yet their minds were unconquered; the gods were fewer, yet their minds were more completely conquered. Those gods said, "Consider who among us..."

"Let us exert ourselves following him who is the most vigorous," they said to Indra. "You indeed are the most vigorous among us; let us exert ourselves following you. He replied, "I have these three bodies that are full of vigor; satisfy them for me, and then we shall overcome these [enemies]. "Then tell us what they are," they said. He replied, "This one is 'the Dispeller of Foes' (vimṛdhā), this one is 'the Deliverer from Distress' (am̐homuk), and this one is 'the Endowed with Power' (indriyāvatī). They offered a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Vimṛdha, and [another] to Indra Am̐homuc.

An eleven-potherd cake for Indra the Powerful; an eleven-potherd cake for Indra the Dispeller of Foes. Those who contended with the Asuras, their superiors, were indeed beset by foes; by this [offering] they struck down the foes. Because it was for Indra the Dispeller of Foes (*vimṛdha*), they thereby struck away the foes. Because it was for Indra the Deliverer from Distress (*am̐homuc*), they were indeed seized by distress; by this they were delivered from distress. Because it was for Indra the Powerful, they thereby placed power within themselves. One who has rivals should sacrifice with this [offering], especially one who has many rivals: [he should offer] an eleven-potherd cake to Indra the Dispeller of Foes.

He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Am̐homuc, and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Indriyavat. When he offers to Indra Vimṛdha, he indeed drives away his adversaries (*mṛdhaḥ*), for he who contends with a more excellent rival is beset by adversaries. When he offers to Indra Am̐homuc, he is released from sin (*aṃhas*), for he who has a rival is seized by sin; through this offering, he is released from that sin. When he offers to Indra Indriyavat, he bestows sensory power (*indriya*) upon himself. There are thirty-three deities; he [thereby] wins them all.

He undertook his endeavors with heroic powers; he then conquered the supreme victory over the Asuras. Because there are thirty-three potsherds, he endows himself with all the deities through heroic powers; he indeed prospers. This is the sacrifice named "Victory" (Vijiti); he who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, attains the supreme victory over his rival.

Prajāpati created cattle; they departed from him. Bṛhaspati and [Prajāpati] followed after them with their footstep. Wherever they had settled, there they found the garmut plant growing. They cut it off and brought it away. Bṛhaspati said, "With this plant you shall win; these cattle will surely turn back to you. He offered a pap of rice for Prajāpati, using garmut plants in water. Then indeed the cattle turned back to him. One should offer a pap of rice for Prajāpati, using garmut plants in water.

One who desires cattle, or one who is without cattle, has indeed lost his cattle from this [world]. Prajāpati is the giver of cattle; he approaches him with his own portion, and he brings the cattle back to him again. There should also be cow-urine for the sake of having a common origin. Having created the cattle, Prajāpati made Pūṣan their guardian. They departed from him; Pūṣan followed after them by their tracks. Wherever they settled, he found the dung of those born there. He cut it off and brought it away. With that, he said to Prajāpati: "With this, me—"

"Stay! These cattle will surely come back to you," he said; then Soma became distressed. "This which grows without being ploughed is mine," he thought, and he offered a *caru* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan, containing *garmut* grain in water. Thereupon, the cattle indeed returned to him. One who desires offspring or cattle should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan, containing *garmut* grain in water. Soma is the depositor of seed, and Pūṣan is the progenitor; Soma bestows the seed for him, and Pūṣan causes procreation. He obtains offspring or cattle.

Or for whichever desire he offers [the oblation], there should also be cow’s urine for the sake of providing a common origin. One who desires kinsmen should offer a pap of *priyaṅgu* grains cooked in the milk of a speckled cow (*pṛśni*). The Maruts were indeed born from the speckled one; the Maruts are the kinsmen of either this speech or of the earth. *Priyaṅgu* grains are the natural milk of the Maruts; with their own milk he approaches them. Just as a calf reaches toward the udder, so do his kinsmen reach toward him.

The invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) contains the word "dear" (*priyavatī*), and the offering verse (*yājyā*) contains the word "prosperity" (*śrīvatī*). In that the invitatory verse contains the word "dear," he makes him dear among his kinsmen; in that the offering verse contains the word "prosperity," he leads him to prosperity. The invitatory verse is in the *dvipadā* metre and the offering verse is in the *catuṣpadā* metre; thus he wins both two-footed and four-footed cattle. He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and a *praiyaṅgava* porridge to the Maruts. They should cook that [porridge] behind [the fire]. For whichever Kṣatriya the common people (*viś*) might act in opposition, Indra is indeed the Kṣatra and the Maruts are the people (*viś*); [this serves] for the sake of the Kṣatra itself.

He joins the people together; while that [verse] is being recited, they pronounce it from behind toward the front. Thus he places the people behind him for this sacrificer, so that there may be no separation. He should offer a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra for one who desires, "May I create discord between the people and the nobility. Indra is indeed the nobility, and the Maruts are the people; thus he creates discord between them by means of their respective shares. Having recited a verse addressed to the Maruts as the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the offering to the Maruts, he should sacrifice with a verse addressed to Indra; having recited a verse addressed to Indra as the invitatory verse for the offering to Indra, he should sacrifice with a verse addressed to the Maruts. Thus, he establishes the nobility alone.

He takes away the people by bypassing them; the Viś is distinct from the Kṣatra. He should cut portions from both sides of the sacrificial cake for whichever side he desires to defeat. Thus he sets the Viś on fire from both sides, and they are quickly defeated. One should offer this very oblation when he desires, "May they be settled. He should sacrifice its fore-portion; verily, by means of their own share, he settles them. He who is a Kṣatriya and fears the loss of his subjects, or a Brāhmaṇa [who fears it], should offer a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts; for the Maruts are indeed the Viś.

Verily, he pacifies them by means of their own portion. This hymn of Agastya, the *Kayāśubhīya*, one should recite over the *sāmidhenī* verses; its *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* should also be used. Indeed, Agastya consecrated a hundred dappled bulls for the Maruts, but Indra seized them for himself. Enraged, the Maruts raised their thunderbolt and rushed at him. He beheld this hymn and with it pacified them. When this is recited, it is for the sake of peace. 11.
For you, O Jātavedas, who are widely renowned and take delight in this [offering], O Agni, I generate a beautiful hymn of praise.
O Agni Jātavedas, for that well-doer for whom you shall create a pleasant abode.
Through the Aśvins, he attains wealth consisting of sons, heroes, and cattle for his well-being.
Savitṛ, who makes all these beings hear with his song, impels them forth.
All forms.
May Vāyu, who moves at the head and delights in sacrifice, come to the sacrifice together with his mind, auspicious with his auspicious teams of horses.
O Vāyu, with those teams by which you go toward the donor for the sacrifice in his dwelling.
Bestow upon us wealth that provides excellent sustenance; bestow upon us a hero and the bounty of cattle and horses.
O Pṛthivī, you indeed bear the burden of the mountains as their support; O mighty one, you who possess the sloping plains, you quicken the earth with your greatness.
She who, by her might, firmly sustains even the trees upon the earth.
When the rains of the lightning from your cloud pour down from heaven.
O Agni, bring to us wealth that is all-conquering, most excellent, and invincible in all battles.
O Agni, in every exhilaration, may he of upright intent indeed bestow upon us herds of cattle.
Gather with both hands many hundreds of treasures; sharpen us for wealth and bring it to us.
O lord of beautiful jaws, O master of spoils, O possessor of power, yours are wondrous deeds.
O Indra, bestower of abundant wealth, grant us a share of beautiful cattle and horses by the thousands.
O Revatī, you have overcome us.
May there be consciousness for our cattle by day, consciousness for our horses by night;
may there be consciousness for us from our own kin, consciousness from strangers, and consciousness for us, O Aśvins—bestow that consciousness upon us here.
O Indra, may we grasp wealth and food; may we grasp riches that are manifold, radiant, and reaching to heaven.
May we grasp divine providence, which possesses heroic vigor, is led by cattle, and abounds in horses.
We invoke Indra and Vāyu here, who are beautiful to behold and easy to call upon, so that every person may be well-disposed toward us at our gathering.
May Agni, the first, protect us with the Vasus; may Soma guard us by his own power with the Rudras.
May Indra with the Maruts act according to the seasons, and may Varuṇa with the Ādityas grant us protection.
May Agni together with the Vasus protect us; may Soma together with his Rudra-like forms [protect us].
Indra, to whom oblations are offered, is united with the Maruts; Varuṇa, the possessor of all knowledge, is united with the Ādityas.
Equal are your intentions, equal are your hearts.
May your minds be in harmony, so that you may prosper together.
I have brought your minds together, your vows together, and your thoughts together.
Those who have stood apart from their vows, them we cause to bend down.
Just as the Ādityas cause the sun to swell, and as the imperishable ones rejoice in the imperishable earth,
even so may Indra, Varuṇa, and Bṛhaspati— the guardians of the world— cause me to swell.
Ever new he becomes as he is born; the banner of the days, he goes to the forefront of the dawns.
Arriving, he ordains the portion for the gods; the moon extends long life. 12.

He who was born knowing its kinship proclaims all the generations of the gods; from the midst of the sacred word (*brahman*), he has raised up the sacred word itself, and by his own inherent power, he has established himself from the low to the high.
Great, once born, he propped up the earth; he twice supported the sky and the earthly realm.
From the foundation, by his very birth, he reached the highest point; Bṛhaspati is its sovereign deity.
We invoke you, the Lord of hosts, the sage among sages, possessed of most exalted renown;
the supreme ruler of sacred prayers, O Brahmaṇaspati, hear us with your aids and sit upon your seat.
With his well-praising, chanting host, Bṛhaspati shattered Vala and the Phaliga with a roar; bellowing, he drove forth the lowing, milk-yielding cows that prepare the oblation.
Agni is the appointed priest at the hymn; the pressing-stones and the sacred grass are at the sacrifice.
With a Ṛc I seek the Maruts, Brahmaṇaspati, and the gods for their desirable aid.
Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati; seeking the gods, we entreat you.
Let the bounteous Maruts come forward; O Indra, be swift in our company.
May the noble, bull-like, and most powerful Māyu come, the controller of riches and the protector of our bodies for the one who serves him.
May the thousand-eyed god, the breaker of enclosures with the thunderbolt in his arm, bestow wealth upon us.
O Aryaman, O King, those many paths of the gods that lead to heaven and traverse the sky—
by those easy paths protect us today, and speak for us, O God.
O Indra and Bṛhaspati, bestow upon us wealth consisting of hundreds, abounding in horses, and reaching into the thousands.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below against the malevolent;
may Indra from the front and from the middle grant wide space to us, his friends, as our friend.
Hiraṇyagarbha, who [arose] from the breathing one; and "Up that bright [face] of the gods."
O Sūrya, you are the deliverer, visible to all, the maker of light; you illuminate the entire radiant realm.
The golden ornament of heaven, far-sighted, rises with his goal afar, spreading light and shining brightly.
Truly, impelled by Sūrya, men go forth to their purposes and perform their works. 13.
Thus ends the tenth section, named Āgnāvaiṣṇava, in the Iṣṭimikā of the Caraka recension of the Śrī Yajurveda Kāṭhaka. 10.

Now begins the eleventh section: On the Maruts. One should offer an oblation to the Maruts; for this, there should be a golden disk (*rukma*) of twenty-one *nirbādhas* as a cover. He should cut off portions [of the offering] while holding them away from himself. If he were to place the *viṭ* (the common people) upon the *nirbādhas* of a Kṣatriya, he would indeed pacify the Maruts by means of their own portion, for the Maruts are the *viṭ*. There are twenty-one *nirbādhas*; the hosts of the Maruts are twenty-one. In that there are twenty-one *nirbādhas*, he appropriates their *nirbādhas* by means of the *nirbādhas* themselves. He who desires kinsmen should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and one on twelve potsherds to the Viśve Devas.

Indra is indeed the *kṣatra* (nobility), and these subjects are Vaiśvadevī; he thus unites the people (*viś*) with the nobility. Having taken a portion for Indra, one should then take both portions for the Viśvedevas, and then again for Indra. Indra is the *kṣatra*, and these subjects are Vaiśvadevī; by means of the *kṣatra*, he thus encloses the people on both sides. The invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) should have the colors of Indra and the Viśvedevas for the sake of prosperity. Gold with a raised boss (*upacāyyapṛḍa*) is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); verily, he bestows his kinsmen upon him. This is called the "Anuvartman" (the following path).

He makes these very offerings follow after him. He should offer a *caru* of *śyāmāka* grain to Soma for one who vomits *soma*. Indeed, Indra drank the *soma* of Tvaṣṭṛ without being invited; he was deprived of the *soma*-drinking by Viśvarūpa. Therefore, *soma* should not be drunk by one who is not invited; he becomes deprived of the *soma*-drinking. That which he vomited forth became the *śyāmāka* grains. This *śyāmāka* is indeed that very *soma*-drinking; he thus directly secures the *soma*-drinking. It should be offered to Soma-Indra, for he is deprived of his power (*indriya*).

He who vomits Soma is deprived of the drinking of Soma; for a Brāhmaṇa is connected with Soma by his very deity. When there is an offering to Soma and Indra, it is through his own power that he provides him with the drinking of Soma. The drinking of Soma is indeed unstable for one who vomits Soma; he should leave some grains remaining and throw them back into the boiling [mixture], thereby securing the drinking of Soma for him. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat (the Luminous), a pap to Sūrya, and another cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat above that.

Human beings desire sight from Agni at night, for they see with his eye; from Sūrya by day, for they see with his eye. These two are the givers of sight; he approaches them with their respective portions, and they bestow sight upon him. Since a single deity is divided into two, therefore the eye, though being one, is twofold. Therefore the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses become identical. He cuts off the portion of the Sūrya offering from the middle; thereby he makes this very thing which is between the two eyes. This is for the sake of distinguishing the two eyes. [He offers] three balls of rice.

He offers [the oblations] with the verses, "Upwards that Jātavedas," "He has yoked the seven bright ones," and "The seven bay steeds have harnessed thee for the chariot. This, indeed, bestows sight upon him; for that which belongs to him is sight. This sacrifice is called the *rājanī*; by means of it, Kratujit Jānaki once caused Rajana Koṇeya—who desired sight—to perform a sacrifice. One who desires sight should sacrifice with this very rite: he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, one on eleven potsherds to Indra, and one on eight potsherds to Bṛhaspati. Indra, indeed...

Not being firmly established, he felt as if he were slipping; he sought refuge with both Agni and Bṛhaspati. They caused him to sacrifice with this very *iṣṭi*. In that there was an offering to Agni, they thereby placed splendor (*tejas*) in him from the front; in that there was an offering to Indra, they thereby placed power (*indriya*) in him in the middle; in that there was an offering to Bṛhaspati, they thereby placed spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in him from above. Verily, from that he prospered. One who desires prosperity should sacrifice with this [offering]. In that there is an offering to Agni—Agni being splendor—he thereby places splendor in him from the front; in that there is an offering to Indra, [he thereby places] power...

Or, Indra, by means of that [offering], places power (*indriya*) in the middle; since Bṛhaspati belongs to the Brahman, he thereby places spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) at the top. The [cake] for Indra belongs to the other two; he joins them together at the navel, and thus he places power in the middle of him. That which is for Indra is in the middle, and the other two are on both sides. Agni is brilliance, Indra is power, and Bṛhaspati is the Brahman. By means of both brilliance and spiritual luster, he encloses power on both sides within his self.
There are three *ṛc*s for the *ājyānuvākyās* for the sake of prosperity; this is the oblation named "Three-Layered" (*tridhātu*), for by means of it he established those three heroic powers. || 1 ||

One whose gold has been stolen or carried off, or who desires, "May I find gold," should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, an oblation on eight potsherds to Savitṛ, a barley gruel to Vāyu, and an oblation on one potsherd to Bhūmi. For Agni indeed found gold in food; regarding that, Savitṛ addressed him: "In food, there is that which has not yet been reached by Vāyu. On this earth they find it, and on this earth they purify it. The offering to Agni is for the sake of finding, for he is Jātavedas (the Knower of Beings). The offering to Savitṛ is for the sake of impulsion, for the sake of leading forward.

In this [region] belonging to Vāyu they find gold; in this [region] they purify themselves. These deities indeed have mastery over gold; he approaches them with their respective portions, and they grant him gold. When he finds gold, he should then offer this very [oblation]. Those deities who grant him gold—he makes them sharers in it for his own safety. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra. There should be curds, honey, ghee, parched grains, and rice grains; these should be mixed together. With that, one who desires cattle [should sacrifice].

If it belongs to Agni, he sacrifices to one deity alone; if it belongs to Indra, Indra is the giver of cattle, and he approaches him with his own portion, and he bestows cattle upon him. If it were mixed, [it would be so because] cattle are indeed mixed; thus he wins cattle. It should be made for Indra, for Indra is the giver of cattle. If he were to perform two offerings to Indra together, there would be redundancy (*jāmi*). It should be made for Prajāpati; Prajāpati is the source of cattle; from his own source he causes them to be born. Prajāpati is the giver; he [approaches] him alone.

He approaches with his allotted portion; he grants him cattle. "Revatī" and "Saṃsṛṣṭasya" are the invitatory and offering verses for one [rite], and "Śakkarī" for the other. Revatī is indeed cattle, and Śakvarī is cattle; verily, he wins cattle. These five are combined, and the other two make seven; the Śakvarī consists of seven feet, and cattle belong to the Śakvarī; verily, he wins cattle.

The *pañkti* is also [the sacrifice], and man is fivefold; thus becoming everything, he approaches the cattle. There is clarified butter (*ghṛta*); clarified butter belongs to Agni, and Agni is the impregnator; verily, by means of it, he causes him to impregnate. There is honey; honey belongs to Soma, and Soma is the depositor of seed; verily, by means of it, he bestows seed.
