There are parched grains and rice grains; the form of the day is the parched grains, and that of the night is the rice grains; cattle are born after the pattern of day and night, for they are born either by night or by day—[in] day and night.

Thus he causes them to be born after him. There is curd; for cattle have the nature of curd, and so he wins cattle that are of like form. Honey must not be offered as an oblation; honey is life, and he would be placing life into the fire—he might well perish. Having sacrificed with this [offering], one should sacrifice with the *āyuṣyā* (life-prolonging) rite; having thus won cattle, he attains life. If he does not sacrifice with this [offering], he should give a boon; by means of a boon, he indeed secures a boon.

He should give two, for there are two, namely prāṇa and apāna; he should give three, for there are three vital breaths: prāṇa, vyāna, and apāna; thus he places those very breaths in the sacrificer. He should give only one, but it should be threefold (trivṛt), for the vital breath is threefold. Indeed, he offers various different oblations, and he is liable to assume a different form; therefore, he should give a speckled cow to redeem his forms. He should give all kinds of birds; thus he secures all cattle. If he should not desire [to give], he should give a pregnant four-year-old cow, for she is indeed...

Just as all ages support a calf, by that [offering] he becomes a calf; just as a heifer supports a calf, by that he becomes a heifer; and just as one who has reached the highest age becomes old, by that he becomes aged. Verily, by this very [offering], he wins all cattle. The waters indeed wiped this world clean, and Manu alone remained there. He saw this sacrifice, he took it, he sacrificed with it, he expanded by it, and through it he attained this abundance. He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with this [offering], expands and attains that abundance which Manu attained. 2.

The gods, indeed, could not reach an agreement; they went their separate ways in four groups: Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, Indra with the Maruts, and Varuṇa with the Ādityas. Bṛhaspati said to them, "I shall officiate at your sacrifice; you will surely reach an agreement. He said to Indra, "Let me officiate at your house," [for] "they will agree for the sake of your preeminence. He then offered a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by the Vasus, a pap to Soma accompanied by the Rudras, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and a pap to Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas.

He caused them to perform the sacrifice in the house of Indra; then indeed they came to an agreement, and they came to an agreement for the sake of Indra’s preeminence. He made two *triṣṭubh* verses as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*. The *triṣṭubh* is indeed Indra’s own metre; it is force and vigor. By means of its own metre, he bestowed force and vigor upon him. Therefore, Indra is the most vigorous among the gods. One should cause those who do not agree with one another to sacrifice with this [rite]. For whomsoever one should desire, "May this man become preeminent," in his house they shall surely come to an agreement; these very [verses] lead him [to that].

The deities, agreeing upon their respective shares, cause them to be recognized; one should employ two *triṣṭubh* verses as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*. The *triṣṭubh* is indeed vigor and strength; verily, he bestows vigor and strength upon them. The two *saṃyājyā* verses contain the word "together" (*sam*) for the sake of prosperity. This sacrifice is called the "Concordant" (*saṃjñānī*); they indeed come to an agreement. Prajāpati gave his daughters, the constellations, to King Soma; he dwelt only with Rohiṇī. Because they were not being approached [by him], they returned [to their father]. Therefore, a woman who is not being approached returns [to her family]. He then went after them.

He asked for them back, but he would not give them to him. He said, "Dwell equally among all of them, and then I will give them back to you. He dwelt only among Rohiṇī. While he was there, consumption seized him. Soma the King is indeed Candramas; because consumption seized the King, that is the origin of the Rājayakṣman (the King's Malady). He withered away like a blade of grass. He sought refuge with Prajāpati. He said, "Dwell equally among all of them, and then I will release you from this. Therefore, the moon dwells equally among all the lunar mansions.

He lived in a state of equality; he caused him to sacrifice with a *caru* oblation to the Viśvedevas on the night of the new moon, and thereby released him from consumption (*yakṣma*). He swelled along with that very [moon] as it was swelling. One who fears consumption should sacrifice with a *caru* oblation to the Viśvedevas on the night of the new moon; he releases him from consumption, and he swells along with that very [moon] as it is swelling.

One who is of low birth should offer an oblation of *ānuṣūka* rice to Bṛhaspati. Bṛhaspati was indeed the lowest-born among the gods, yet he attained the foremost place. Bṛhaspati is the deity for one who is of low birth; he thus takes hold of him and leads him to the foremost place. Bṛhaspati is the Brahman, and the Brahman is the father of the Brāhmaṇa. The father has authority over his son, whether from the front or from behind, but not from above. It is the Brahman as father who leads him to the foremost place. These *ānuṣūka* rice grains belong to one of low birth; he thus makes them the foremost.

In that he leads him around and offers the oblation, he takes hold of those very [deities]; they lead him around to the front. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is spread out again, and the fuel-stick (*idhma*) has grown up again, for the sake of prosperity. He who desires kinsmen should offer a pap (*caru*) to Bṛhaspati; for him, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses should contain the word "host" (*gaṇa*). The Brāhmaṇa has Bṛhaspati as his deity; thus he endows his own deity with abundance. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses contain the word "host"; verily, by means of his kinsmen, he makes him possessed of a host.

One who desires, "May my spiritual power (*brahman*) be strength," should offer a *caru* oblation to Brahmaṇaspati; for him, there should be two verses, one for the offering and one for the invitatory prayer, addressed to the Maruts. For Brahmaṇaspati is indeed the spiritual power, and the Maruts are the people (*viś*); he thus causes the people to submit to his spiritual power, and his spiritual power immediately becomes strength. One who desires, "May my subjects be desirous of giving," should offer a *caru* to Aryaman; for he who gives is indeed Aryaman, and these subjects live upon his gift; thus they become desirous of giving to him. [He should offer] a *caru* to Indra-Bṛhaspati...

One should perform this sacrifice for a Rājanya who desires prosperity. The gods were indeed afraid of the Rājanya as he was being born; they followed him and bound him with a cord. Truly, that Rājanya is born bound; for if he were born unbound, nothing at all would exist—he would devour all these creatures. The Rājanya has Indra as his deity, and Bṛhaspati is the Brahman. By means of the Brahman, he thus releases him from the binding. Thus unbound, he exerts himself for heroic power. Gold is the sacrificial fee; it is the very cord that was there before.

One who desires long life should offer a *caru* oblation of rice to Prajāpati, consisting of one hundred *kṛṣṇalas* in clarified butter, for the sake of escaping death. The gods were indeed afraid of death; they sought refuge with Prajāpati, and he caused them to sacrifice with this very offering. Gold is indeed immortality; verily, by means of immortality, he bestowed immortality upon them. Thereupon they became immortal. He who fears death should sacrifice with this [offering]. Gold is indeed immortality; verily, by means of immortality, he bestows immortality upon him. It consists of one hundred *kṛṣṇalas*; man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a strength of a hundred; thus, verily, he obtains life.

He indeed secures vigor; an offering to the Viśvedevas should be made, for he thereby caused all those gods to sacrifice. An offering to Prajāpati should be made; Prajāpati is the source, and thus he finds firm standing in the very source.

Four *kṛṣṇala* seeds each constitute the portion for the offering, for the sake of prosperity. They present it to the Brahman priest; for the Brahman priest is indeed the *brahman*. By means of the *brahman*, he thus bestows life-span upon him in a single whole. One who desires, "May I become more prosperous," should sacrifice with this [offering]. This world is indeed the heavenly world of man, insofar as he becomes more prosperous in this very world. He prospers and becomes more prosperous, whoever, knowing this, sacrifices with this. He whose fortune has departed should offer a pap of cooked rice to Sūrya; its [priestly fee] is a bay horse.

There should be a golden covering above and a silver one below; for that sun is the end, and when men have reached the end of prosperity, they turn back. From the very end he seizes the end; he does not become worse than he was when he sacrificed. That sun indeed was this [world]; it moved about burning this [world]. The gods, having enclosed it with these two [plates], caused it to go to yonder world. It did not shine. They offered five gold *kṛṣṇala* weights in the *prayāja* offerings; gold is indeed brilliance; by means of brilliance they placed brilliance into him. Then indeed—

He took hold of the splendor; he became splendid following these five directions. This [earth] is indeed silver-colored, and that [sky] is golden-colored; having grasped him from both sides with these two, he causes him to go to yonder world. "He does not shine," they say, for he did not shine. During the *prayāja* offerings, one should sacrifice five gold *kṛṣṇala* seeds. Gold is indeed splendor; verily, by means of splendor he unites him with splendor. He becomes splendid following these five directions.

One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation of white rice to Soma and Rudra. The clarified butter for this should be churned from the milk of a cow that has both a white calf and a non-white calf. Svarbhānu, the Asura, pierced the sun with darkness; he did not shine. The gods sought an expiation for him and caused him to sacrifice with this very *iṣṭi*. By means of it, they drove away the darkness from him. He who is capable of attaining spiritual luster but does not possess it is enveloped by darkness. This [sacrifice] drives away that very darkness from him.

He unites him with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). There is clarified butter from a white cow with a white calf; the rice grains are white. For spiritual luster is indeed like this; thus he restores his spiritual luster.

They sprinkle with clarified butter; they cleanse with clarified butter for the sake of peace, for water is indeed peace. On that night, they should not bring water into his house. He should sacrifice in an enclosed space to secure spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). The sacrificial pap (*caru*) is one span high both vertically and horizontally; for man is of this measure, as far as his vital breaths extend. Thus, he strikes away the darkness from his entire self. They proceed together with the rays [of light]; it is the rising sun itself that strikes away the darkness from him. He should sacrifice on the full moon of the month of Tiṣya.

Tiṣya is indeed Rudra, and the moon is Soma; therefore, the plants belong to Soma and are sacred to Rudra. They wither from the east and dry up from the west; they wither from the east and dry up from the west. He prospers by means of these [verses] directly before his eyes. However, he who sacrifices with this [offering] is liable to become afflicted with skin disease, for it strikes away excessively from him. He should recite the verses of Manu among the *sāmidhenī* verses; whatever Manu spoke was indeed medicine, and thus he provides medicine for him. "The rivers flow, bringing refreshment"—this is the *nārāśamsī*.

He bestows it for the sake of peace. It consists of six verses; there are indeed six seasons, and thus he finds firm support in the seasons. However, there is a danger that he may become afflicted with skin disease, for he approaches while ascending through the vital energies (*tejas*). One desiring cattle should subsequently offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan. Soma is indeed the own deity of the Brāhmaṇa, and Pūṣan is cattle; thus he is increased by his own deity through cattle and gains a skin for himself. He should also offer a *caru* to Soma and Rudra made of black rice while practicing sorcery; Soma, indeed, is the lord of these [plants].

Rudra is the lord of creatures; Agni is the lord of that which is to be slain and that which is not to be slain. Having entreated him as the very lord, he consigns [the victim] to Rudra. It is made of black rice; it becomes like darkness, for darkness is death; verily by means of death he causes him to be seized. The sacrificial grass is made of *śara* reeds for the sake of piercing; the fuel is of *vaibhītaka* wood for the sake of splitting. He should offer a pap to Soma and Rudra for the sake of rivalry or for the sake of having a second. Half of it should be all [black], and half of white rice.

Half of the rice should be black, and half should consist of *śara* grass; half of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) should be *darbha*, and half should be of another kind; half of the fuel (*idhma*) should be from the *vaibhītaka* tree, and half from another tree. Soma is indeed the own deity of the Brāhmaṇa; in his own deity he thus produces a second for him when half and half are used, which serves to create that second state. He who suffers from chronic illness should offer a pap (*caru*) to Soma and Rudra. One who is living is connected with Soma, while one who has died is connected with Agni; he who is chronically ill is neither truly alive nor dead.

He redeems him by means of the portion belonging to those two alone. It is in milk; for milk is indeed milk, and man is milk. He for whom there is sickness—that is, he who is ill—suffers from milk. By means of milk, he thus satisfies his milk. Indeed, he who serves as the *hotṛ* priest extracts this [offering] from Soma and Rudra; he is liable to perish. One should give an ox to him; one should kill it and eat of it—that is the expiation in that case. Or, one desiring offspring or desiring cattle should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra. Soma...

Verily, Rudra is Agni, the depositor of seed; he is the progenitor. Soma indeed bestows the seed upon him, and Agni procreates. He obtains either offspring or cattle, whichever desire for which he performs the offering. 5.

One who has been expelled or is about to be expelled should offer a *caru* oblation to the Ādityas who uphold [the world]. The Ādityas are indeed the protectors; the Ādityas are the expellers. He approaches them with their own share, and they establish him firmly. One who desires prosperity should offer a *caru* oblation to the Ādityas who become [all things]. Aditi, desiring offspring, cooked rice-porridge; she ate its remains and conceived a fetus. From that the Ādityas were born. She thought: "If I had eaten first, even more excellent ones than these would have been born from me."

She cooked [the oblation] again; he ate of it both from the front and from behind. She conceived a fetus. While still within the womb, he spoke. The Ādityas thought, "When this one is born, he alone will become all this. They cast him out. Cast out, he lay there. She cooked a third [offering], saying, "Let it be for the Ādityas indeed! [They said,] "He who has arisen from that womb—from which you were created—let him be restored. They restored him. What of him was dead, they cut away; that became an elephant (*hastin*). What was living...

That Vivasvant Āditya was not as he ought to have been; he offered this *caru* oblation to the Bhuvad-Ādityas. One’s own kin are indeed most sympathetic toward one who seeks their protection; it was to his own kin that he resorted, and through them he indeed became successful. The Ādityas are these very subjects; they are one’s own kin and most sympathetic toward one who seeks their protection. He resorts to them alone with their share. When offering the oblation, he should say: "I shall make a portion for you, O Ādityas," and [he should name] this man, the son of such-and-such, of such-and-such a woman.

"Make him understand [the way] to that clan," he says, thereby granting them their due portion. He offers a *caru* oblation to the Ādityas; for the Ādityas are the divine clan (*devaviś*), and the divine clan has mastery over the human clan (*manuṣyaviś*). By means of the divine clan, he causes him to understand the human clan. There are seven shoots of the *aśvattha* tree; he sprinkles them with water even as fuel. They lie upon the altar until the conclusion of the rite. When the rite is completed, he strikes them down in the middle furrow, saying: "Here I bind the Ādityas so that [this man], the son of such-and-such, may understand [his place]."

If he should not find them by the seventh day, having made those [sticks] into fuel-wood (idhma), he should sacrifice with the next [verse], likewise with the second, and likewise with the third; for thrice seven are the Ādityas—seven and seven; as many as the Ādityas are, so many he binds. Having bound him, they, while being released, cause him to find them.

Vigor departed from the people; it entered the *aśvattha* tree. Therefore, this [tree] stands unsteady, its leaves trembling at all times. In that they are made of *aśvattha*, he binds vigor into the people. He should place the footprint of one who is restrained with the words, "O you whose blessing is true, here is the mind"; thus he makes them mindless. With the words, "Come hither, O Maruts, self-strong ones, along with this lord of the people, toward this king," he should walk around [the fire], fanning the people; thus he makes them mindless. He who...

If he should later become a speaker of vulgar speech, they should bring rice from his house; they should separate the white and the black grains. Of those that are white, he should offer a *caru* to the Ādityas, and those that are black he should set aside for Varuṇa. The Ādityas are the divine clan (*devaviś*); the divine clan rules over the human clan (*manuṣyaviś*). By means of the divine clan, he causes him to enter the human clan. "He has entered this clan," they say. But where is the ruling power (*kṣatra*)? When one enters the ruling power, then indeed he enters it. If he should enter it, then of those that are black, he should offer a *caru* to Varuṇa.

He should offer a *caru* oblation; Varuṇa is indeed the *kṣatra*. Varuṇa himself causes him to attain the *kṣatra*, and he attains both kinds of subjects: the divine subjects and the human subjects. In that he offers the white rice to the Ādityas, therefore the Vaiśya is born as if white; in that [he offers] the black rice to Varuṇa, therefore the Rājanya is as if smoky-grey.

Thou art the life of Agni; of thee, who art the life of Agni, men are the bestowers of life; with that [life], bestow life upon this person, N.N.! Indra’s is thy breath; may he give thee breath—svāhā! To him whose breath thou art, svāhā! The Fathers’ is thy breath; may they give thee breath—to those whose breath thou art, svāhā! The Maruts’ is thy breath; may they give thee breath—to those whose breath thou art, svāhā! The Viśvedevas’ is thy breath; may they give thee breath—to those whose breath thou art, svāhā! Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin’s...

May the breath of those two give you breath; to them both, svāhā! Because you did not crawl, you became ghee (sarpi); because you were new-born, you became fresh butter (navanīta); because you moved forward, you became clarified butter (ghṛta).
The stream of clarified butter, the path of immortality, bestowed by Indra and presented by the Maruts.
Viṣṇu perceived the principles; through the principles, Iḍā impelled the cows.

With the *pāvamāna* hymn, with the *gāyatrī* metre, with the path of the *upāṃśu* cup, and with the power of the *upāṃśu*, I lift you up, O [Name]! With the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans], with the *triṣṭubh* metre, with the path of the *śukra* cup, and with the power of the *śukra*, I release you, O [Name]! With the measure of Agni, with the *jagatī* metre, with the path of the *āgrayaṇa* cup, may the god Savitṛ lead you forth for life, for the sake of living, O [Name]! The gods are long-lived; they are long-lived through immortality. Through their longevity, may you be long-lived, O [Name]! Brahman is long-lived; it is long-lived through the Brahmins. Through its longevity, may you be long-lived, O [Name]!

Agni is long-lived; he is long-lived through the trees. Through his life-span, may this sacrifice here be long-lived for [N.N. there. The sacrifice is long-lived; it is long-lived through the sacrificial gifts. Through its life-span, may this [sacrifice] here be long-lived for [N.N. there. Soma is long-lived; he is long-lived through the plants. Through his life-span, may this [Soma] here be long-lived for [N.N. there. The plants are long-lived; they are long-lived through the waters. Through their life-span, may this [plant] here be long-lived for [N.N. there. O Agni, make him long-lived for vigor and splendor; O Varuṇa, sharpen his keen strength.
Like a mother, O Aditi, grant him protection, so that all the gods may grant him a full lifespan.

The breath of the Aśvins—may they grant you breath; live by that! The breath of Mitra and Varuṇa—may they grant you breath; live by that! The breath of Bṛhaspati—he shall grant you breath; live by that! ||7||

One who is about to sacrifice with this [offering] on the previous day should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and [a pap] to Bṛhaspati. Agni indeed is all the deities; Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; Sarasvatī is speech; Bṛhaspati is the sacred formulation (brahman). It is these very deities that he secures on the previous day. The deities are indeed the vital breaths; having thus secured the vital breaths, he observes the fast. On the following day, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Soma, a pap to Aditi, a pap of barley to Varuṇa, and [a pap] to Agni Vaiśvānara.

The offering on twelve potsherds is for one afflicted by disease; indeed, when a man has died, his flesh goes to Agni, his sap to Soma, and his body to the earth—for this earth is Aditi, since he lies upon her. These deities indeed have power over a man; it is from them that he impels him back to life.

The living one belongs to Soma, while the deceased belongs to Agni; he who is afflicted with disease is neither this living one nor the dead. By means of their respective portions, he ransoms him. He who is afflicted with disease is seized by Varuṇa; because the oblation belongs to Varuṇa, he releases him from Varuṇa. It is made of barley and is a span in length. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year, and the year is life; thus he establishes him in the year, his life, and he attains a full lifespan. These offerings are five in number; man is fivefold.

He obtains the man himself. With the words, "Thou art the life-span of Agni," he places gold in the clarified butter; for gold is born from Agni, and men are the bestowers of life upon Agni; by means of these very [beings], he bestows life upon him. With the words, "The breath of Indra"—for the vital breaths have those deities as their presiding powers—he places those very breaths within him. The quarters have those deities as their presiding powers; thus he impels him from the quarters according to their respective deities. He offers these five oblations; the person consists of five parts; verily, he preserves the person.

"All the officiating priests carry [the vessel] around; indeed, all the officiating priests heal him. They carry it around following the hand of the Brahman priest; for the Brahman priest is the Brahman (the sacred word). By means of the Brahman itself, they bestow life upon him in a single way. When he says, 'As the serpent,' this proclaims the origin, the kinship, and the power of the clarified butter. With the words, 'With the purifying hymn,' he heals him with as much as there is—namely, the cups, the hymns, and the meters—with whatever exists. 'I lift up, I release, I draw out'—just as..."

He rescues him who is to be slain, releases him, and elevates him; in this very way he now rescues him, releases him, and elevates him. "The gods are long-lived," he says as he hands it over; these indeed are the long-lived gods, and through them he bestows life upon him. He drinks from it; he drinks life itself. If one were to pour it out as if it were something discarded, [one would lose it]; for gold is brilliance and ghee is life—verily, from brilliance he places life within himself. "O Agni, make this man fit for life and luster," saying this, he fastens on the gold; Agni, indeed, is all.

The deities are life and gold; with all these deities he binds it for him. "O Varuṇa, sharpen his keen vigor"—thus he indeed sharpens him. "As a mother, O Aditi, grant him protection"—this earth is Aditi; upon her he establishes him. "O All-Gods, so that he may reach old age"—he thus makes him subject to death at old age. "The breath of the Aśvins, of Mitra and Varuṇa, of Bṛhaspati"—the vital breaths have these as their deities; he places them in him, spreads them out within him, and makes them not depart from him. ||8||

O east wind, quicken us, bringing wealth—*svāhā*! O fierce one, possessing the wind, raining down, bring wealth—*svāhā*! O terrible one, thundering while raining, bring wealth—*svāhā*! O you who flash with lightning while raining, truly bring wealth—*svāhā*! Having rained for three nights, O purified one, bring wealth—*svāhā*! "He has rained much today," so it is heard; O famous one, bring wealth—*svāhā*! Raining while glowing, O sovereign ruler, bring wealth—*svāhā*! O being, raining while crashing with lightning and thunder, bring wealth—*svāhā*! The gentle, the submissive, the pure, the swift, the moistening, the well-foaming ones.

The luminous ones, the dark ones, the supporters of Mitra, the supporters of Kṣatra, the lords of the realm—protect me here! You are the bond of the bull; for rain, I bind you up. O gods who possess wealth, O Agni, Soma, and Sūrya, give us water! Break open the ocean! From heaven, from Parjanya, from the intermediate space, from the earth—from those places, protect me with rain! O gods who grant refuge, O Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman, give us water! Break open the ocean! From heaven, from Parjanya, from the intermediate space, from the earth—from those places, protect me with rain! O gods who drink together, [give] of the waters...
O you who possess swift horses and impetuous strength, break open the water-holding ocean from heaven, from the atmosphere, and from the earth; through that, protect me with rain.
By day they create darkness with Parjanya, the bearer of waters, when they drench the earth.
O Maruts, raise up the rain from the ocean; you, O possessors of abundance, cause the rain to fall.
Your milch-cows, O wonder-workers, never fail; your chariots have rolled forth following your glorious march.
The bounteous ones have brought down from the treasury of heaven for the donor this [gift] for the man;
may Parjanya release it upon the two worlds, and let the rains flow across the desert wastes.

Send down rain from heaven; fill the ocean with waters. Those gods whose portion is in heaven, those whose portion is in the intermediate space, and those whose portion is on earth—may they protect this sacrifice; may they enter this field; may they settle deeply into this field. You are born of the water, the first-born; you are strength belonging to the ocean. Break open the stream of heaven! You are of the Maruts; you are the vigor of the Maruts. Break open the stream of the waters!
Cause the earth to swell; cleave open this divine sky.
O Lord, grant us divine water; unbind the leather bag.
The bay, well-winged steeds fly up to heaven, clothed in the waters, along the black path;
they have returned to their dwellings at the appointed time, and they have moistened heaven and earth with clarified butter. 9.

There is a black antelope skin, honey, and the halter of a dark-colored horse; having placed these at the edge of the eastern fire, having caused the sacrificer to put on a black garment and to touch [the materials], he offers these oblations. These are indeed the names of the winds; for this one (Vāyu) is the lord of rain: when he causes to swell, when he causes to stir, and when he causes to bestow, then it rains. He approaches him with his own portion, and being pleased, he pours down rain for him. He offers eight of these; there are four quarters and four intermediate directions.

He instructs [the Adhvaryu] according to the directions; from the very quarters he causes the rain to fall. He mixes [the grains] on a black antelope skin; thus he makes it an oblation. He mixes it with honey; for honey is the essence of the waters and the plants. When it rains, it rains from the waters and the plants; thus, when it rains, he pours down the rain from the waters and the plants.

"Māndā," "vaśā"—these indeed are names of the waters, just as they say, "Come here! Come here!"; in this very way, by calling them by their names, he causes them to fall from heaven. They say, "It is not possible to cause rain to fall from heaven by any other [means] than by the Soma-oblation. When the Yatis were devoured by hyenas, their heads flew away and became date-palms (*kharjūra*). That which was the drinking of Soma fell upwards and became the *karīra* fruits. Since there are *karīra* fruits, he pours down rain from heaven by means of the Soma-oblation itself. Therefore...

One should not give *karīra* fruits to a woman nor to a *śūdra*, for this [fruit] is like the drinking of *soma*. "Thou art the fastening of the stallion; I bind thee for rain," he says, for the horse is a stallion and Parjanya is a stallion, for the sake of prosperity. The halter of the dark-grey horse is used, for when he is about to rain, he becomes like a dark-grey horse.

"The gods who are givers of wealth, the gods who are givers of protection, the gods who are sharers of the draught"—these indeed are the deities who rule over rain. Through them alone he desires rain for him day by day. He ties it up in a black antelope skin; the black antelope skin is indeed the form of the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*. By means of the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*, he desires rain for him. If it should rain, then he should perform the sacrifice; if it should not rain, they should remain as they were. Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed day and night, and Parjanya rains according to day and night; for he rains either by night or by day. These two...

These two indeed rule over the rain; he approaches them with their respective portions. Being pleased, they pour down rain for him. He should offer on the following day a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dhāmacchat, a pap to the Maruts, and a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya. Agni, indeed, sends the rain upward from here; having become, as it were, Dhāmacchat, he rains. The Maruts lead forth the rain once it has been released.

When the sun turns back hitherward with his rays, then it rains; for these deities indeed have mastery over rain. He approaches them with their respective portions, and they, being pleased, pour down rain for him. Even if he does not intend to rain, it rains nonetheless. There are these six oblations; for there are six seasons, and thus he causes rain to flow forth from the seasons. That which is the seventh [oblation], by that he causes rain to flow forth from the year itself. Now, there are these four offerings to the Maruts and three to the Pitṛs; of these, he proceeds with three, and sets aside one.

The *ṛc*s become the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*), and the *yajus* formulas become the offering verses (*yājyā*). The Maruts indeed rule over the rain; it is to them that he provides a greater share. The fourth [verse] he offers into the waters when the rite is completed, with the words: "Release the rain from heaven; fill the ocean with waters. By these means he reaches those [celestial waters], and thus he unites both these [terrestrial] waters and those [celestial ones]. With the verse, "O gods who have your shares in heaven," he shakes the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*); he thereby gratifies both the quarters and the deities, and moreover, these very worlds of his become desired and pleased. This is that [rite].
The sacrifice named Kārīrī is such that for a year one who would perform it with this [offering] shall not eat karīra fruits; furthermore, this is its vow for whoever recites it. 10.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, with that body of yours which is powerful, vigorous, protective, and invincible, we shall worship you; with it, release this man—[name], the son of [father's name], from distress. O King Varuṇa, that bond of yours which is among the gods, that I now release for you; to it, Svāhā! O King Varuṇa, that bond of yours which is in food, in bipeds, in quadrupeds, in trees, in plants, in the waters, and on the earth—that I now release for you; to it, Svāhā! O Mitra and Varuṇa, with that body of yours which is powerful and vigorous...
That body of yours which is demonic and to be avoided—by that we ward you off; by it, release this man, the son of such-and-such a father and such-and-such a mother, from distress. 11.
The chariot of the one who favors the gods is swift, like a hero in any battles whatsoever.
The sacrificer who strives to win the minds of the gods shall surpass those who do not sacrifice.
No one can overtake him by ritual action, nor can he be separated from his purpose;
the sacrificer who strives to win the minds of the gods shall surpass those who do not sacrifice.
O sacrificer, you do not come to harm; O presser of soma, you do not suffer, for you are devoted to the gods.
He who, as a sacrificer, desires to worship according to the will of the gods, shall prevail over those who do not sacrifice.
Herein is no heroic strength, nor even that which consists of horses and steeds.
The sacrificer who desires to worship with his mind the gods shall surpass those who do not sacrifice.
With my song, I praise Agni, the ancient god of your treasures.
Worshipping him who is dear to many, like a friend who brings success in the acquisition of fields.
The rivers flow forth as sources of bliss; like milch-cows, they serve both him who has sacrificed and him who is about to sacrifice.
Seeking glory, the streams of clarified butter approach from every side both the one who bestows gifts and the one who fulfills them.
O Soma and Rudra, tear asunder in all directions the disease that has entered our home;
drive Nirṛti far away to a distance, and may auspicious glories attend us.
O Soma and Rudra, bestow all these remedies upon our bodies;
be gracious to us and release from us whatever sin has been committed that is bound within our persons.

O Soma and Rudra, uphold your divine power; let our offerings reach you swiftly. Bestowing the seven treasures in every house, be auspicious to us—bring well-being to our bipeds and well-being to our quadrupeds.
O Soma and Pūṣan, these two gods— O Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman— we choose for ourselves the great protection of you, the great ones, and your mighty favors.
Sacrifice is the [first] of the gods.
The Ādityas, supporting all that moves and stands, are gods and guardians of the entire world;
far-sighted, they protect their divine power, being true to cosmic order and exacting debts.
Supporting the three earths, the three heavens, and the three celestial realms, he maintains the three sacred laws within their assemblies.
O Ādityas, by Truth your greatness is mighty; that is beautiful, O Aryaman, Varuṇa, and Mitra.
These hymns, dripping with clarity, I ever offer with the ladle to the Ādityas, the kings;
may Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, and Varuṇa—the many-born Dakṣa and Aṃśa—hear me.
O Ādityas, may we be free from bondage among the gods and among mortals, O Vasus.
Winning, O Mitra and Varuṇa, may we win; being, O Heaven and Earth, may we be.
Varuṇa, the Asura, has propped up this heaven for me. ||12||
O Agni and Viṣṇu, O Agni and Viṣṇu, you two purifiers, [come] to us; O Bṛhaspati, from heaven, enjoy our [offering].
Bṛhaspati, being first born from the great light in the highest heaven,
seven-mouthed and born with power through his roar, blew away the darknesses with his seven rays.
O Agni, you purify our lives.
O God Agni, granting long life, choosing old age, clothed in ghee, with ghee upon your back—
drinking the ghee and the lovely nectar of the cow— lead this man to old age as a father leads his son.
The nourisher of the earth.
Those abodes of yours which they worship with oblation—may all those encompass this sacrifice.
Increasing the household, furthering us, rich in heroes, not slaying our men, O Soma, enter the dwellings.
Sutrāman, the great one; O Varuṇa, grant this to me; Vaiśvānara, sought after in heaven, [be] for our protection.
Delighting the Maruts with the guileful hawk—swift as thought, vigorous, and well-fashioned—with that [hawk] by which the fierce, released host advances, O Aśvins, clothe it with well-being.
Roar forth, thunder, deposit the embryo; fly around with your water-bearing chariot.
Draw well the leather bag, let it hang down loosened; may the heights become level and the depths be raised up.

Your well-winged birds have been transformed according to their nature; when this occurred, the black bull bellowed aloud. He has come with auspicious, smiling [waters]; the mists fall and the clouds thunder.
The black path, the bay steeds, the fair-winged birds, clothed in the waters, fly up to heaven;
they have returned from the seat of Order, and since then the earth is moistened with clarified butter.
Like a lowing cow, the lightning bellows; like a mother following her calf, she follows close when their rain has been released.
O Maruts, bestow rain upon us from heaven; cause the streams of the stallion to swell.
Come hither with this thundering, pouring down the waters, O Asura, our father.
He who has measured out the ends of heaven and earth with his ray—he has filled both world-halves with his greatness.
Moving with your most swift steeds, you go weaving the thread, O God, spreading out the black garment. The rays of the Sun, quivering, have driven away the darkness within the waters like a hide.
Thus ends the eleventh section, named Māruta, in the *Iṣṭimikā*, within the Caraka recension of the venerable *Kāṭhaka* Yajurveda. 11.

Now begins the twelfth section: the section on the *payasyā*. One who is afflicted by disease should sacrifice with the *payasyā*. For a Brāhmaṇa, it should be dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa; for a Rājanya, to Indra and Varuṇa; for a Vaiśya, to Agni and Varuṇa. The *āgrayaṇa* itself is dedicated to Agni. The Brāhmaṇa is by nature related to Mitra, while he who is afflicted by disease is seized by Varuṇa. He thus approaches his own deity with its proper portion, and by means of that which belongs to Varuṇa, he releases him from Varuṇa. The Rājanya is by nature related to Indra, while he who is afflicted by disease is seized by Varuṇa. He thus approaches his own deity with its proper portion, and by means of that which belongs to Varuṇa, [he releases him] from Varuṇa.

Agni releases all the deities therein; even for a Vaiśya, he who is afflicted by disease is seized by Varuṇa. He approaches his own deity with its allotted portion; by means of that which belongs to Varuṇa, he releases him from Varuṇa. There is a dish of curdled milk (*payasyā*); curdled milk is indeed milk, and man is milk. That part of him for whom there is disease—that is milk. By means of milk, he satisfies the milk of this man.

There is a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); having thus provided him with bone, he establishes him [in life]. Man is indeed an animal, and the sacrificial cake is an animal; by means of an animal, he rescues the animal. He cuts off [the portions] after separating them, just as one extracts a splinter by breaking it apart; even so does he extract the consumption from his very midst. Having gathered them together, he cuts off for Agni; just as, having extracted a splinter and brought it together, one binds it up, so is that. Now these [other cakes] are on single potsherds; for man is not...

One should obtain him by means of skulls; one obtains him all at once. There are eight; for there are eight hooves of a man, and thus one obtains him hoof by hoof. He offers them in successive order; for wherever there is a noose of Varuṇa, from right there he releases him from Varuṇa.

That offering which one makes in what is not fire is indeed unsuccessful; all offerings should be made in the fire, for Agni is all the deities. By that very means he wins those desires and does not offer an unsuccessful oblation. One who desires kinsmen should sacrifice with curd-mixture (*payasyā*), for it leads to prosperity. The *āgneya* cup belongs to Agni, and the *maitra* cup belongs to Mitra by deity. He who, though capable of being among his kinsmen, is not born as one of them, is seized by Varuṇa. He approaches his own deity with his own portion, and by means of the *vāruṇa* cup, he releases him from Varuṇa. It is a curd-mixture, for the curd-mixture is indeed milk.

Born from milk, he wins milk by means of milk itself. He spreads them out; he satisfies the quarters. He brings them together; he brings his kinsmen together for him. The Brāhmaṇa regarding the cakes on a single potsherd is the same. One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *payasyā* (curd-mixture); it is for prosperity. That which belongs to Agni and that which belongs to Mitra are the two portions of the Brāhmaṇa by deity. He who, though fit for cattle, becomes destitute of cattle, is seized by Varuṇa. He has recourse to his own deity with her portion; by means of the offering to Varuṇa, he releases him from Varuṇa. It is a *payasyā*; indeed, the *payasyā* is milk, and milk is [the essence].

Through milk alone he wins milk for himself; he spreads out [the offering], he satisfies the quarters, and he gathers it together; verily, he gathers cattle for him. The Brāhmaṇa concerning the cakes on one potsherd is the same. One who desires prosperity should sacrifice with the *payasyā* (curd-mixture); it is for the sake of success. That which belongs to Agni is the Maitra-Brāhmaṇa by deity; he who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it, is seized by Varuṇa. He has recourse to his own deity with her portion; through the *vāruṇa* [offering], he releases him from Varuṇa. It is a *payasyā*; indeed, the *payasyā* is milk, and man is milk.

By means of milk itself, he secures milk; he distributes [the oblations] toward the quarters and satisfies them; he gathers them together and thus gathers prosperity for him. The Brāhmaṇa regarding the cakes on one potsherd is the same.

You are firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen; may my kinsmen be firm in me. You are fierce, a guardian, a finder of wealth, a conqueror; may I be a conqueror over my kinsmen, a guardian, a finder of wealth. You are encompassing; may I be encompassing of my kinsmen, a guardian, a finder of wealth. You are a patron; may I be a patron among my kinsmen, a guardian, a finder of wealth. O gods, those who are my kinsmen, who are of one mind, whom I desire in my heart—may they desire me in their hearts; make them well-disposed toward me.

Svāhā! O gods who possess a common mind, those women who are of one mind with me—may they love me with their hearts; make them well-disposed toward me with their hearts, svāhā! O gods who possess a common mind, those sons and those cattle who are of one mind with me—may they love me with their hearts; make them well-disposed toward me with their hearts, svāhā!

The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict; the Asuras were more mindful, while the gods were as if less mindful. Those gods saw this *saṃgrahaṇa* (the rite of seizing); with it they seized the minds of the Asuras, and consequently, being of one mind [with them], the Asuras were defeated. Verily, he seizes the mind of his rival; thus, being mindless toward him, the rival is defeated. One who desires cattle should sacrifice with this; for with this the gods seized the cattle of the Asuras, and consequently those cattle were defeated. Verily, [he seizes] the cattle themselves.

He seizes the mind of his rival; thus he becomes deprived of cattle and perishes. One who desires kinsmen should sacrifice with this [offering]. This is indeed a seizing of the mind; for kinsmen are like those possessed of mind. He seizes the minds of as many kinsmen as there are; their minds being seized, they do not depart from him.

The Vaiśvadeva offering must be performed, for the kinsmen are indeed Vaiśvadeva. It is prepared from the milk of a speckled cow with a speckled calf; for the speckled cow belongs to the Viśvedevas. They collect the clarified butter from all the kinsmen to ensure its Vaiśvadeva character, for the kinsmen are indeed Vaiśvadeva. With the words, "Thou art firm," he lays down the enclosing sticks; thus he establishes the kinsmen as a foundation for him. Having caused them to touch [the oblation] with the words, "O gods, of the mind," he offers the sacrifice. This is indeed a seizing of the mind; thus are the kinsmen—as women, as men, as boys—as many as there are.

Thus, being of the same origin, they seize their minds; with their minds seized, they do not depart from him. He indeed cuts the sacrifice asunder when he offers these intermediate oblations while the sacrifice is still extended; they should be offered when it is completed. If he were to offer them when it is completed, he would place his kinsmen outside of himself. He should offer them between the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. The *prayājas* are indeed the out-breaths (*prāṇa*), the *anuyājas* are the in-breaths (*apāna*), and the oblation is the self (*ātman*). Thus, in the very middle of the self, he establishes his kinsmen. He should offer with a wooden ladle if he should desire: "May [the result] come to me quickly."

"May my kinsmen come quickly and may they depart again quickly"—for even so are the lords of the forest: unstable, as it were, moving and unmoving. If he should desire, "May my kinsmen come for a long time and may they depart for a long time," he should offer with a vessel made of clay; for even so is this earth: stable, as it were, firmly established, moving and unmoving. ||2||

Indra indeed raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra. He said, "This strength is in me; I will give it to you, but do not strike me. He gave it to him. Indra knew, "Truly, there is strength in him. He raised a second [thunderbolt] at him, and a third. He said, "This strength is in me; I will give it to you, but do not strike me. He gave it to him. Truly, he gave him the sacrifice; he gave the sacrifice to Indra; he gave it to Indra.

Therefore, there is an oblation to Indra and Viṣṇu. He indeed bestowed vigor upon him; having become devoid of vigor, he lay prostrate. Viṣṇu supported him with his own powers. He said, "Place me once, O Viṣṇu! Place me twice, O Viṣṇu! Place me thrice, O Viṣṇu! That is the reason for the *traidhātavī* sacrifice's name as *traidhātavī*. Having slain Vṛtra, Indra indeed cast him onto the corpse of Mānava. Vṛtra is Soma, and the corpse of Mānava is the belly; therefore, Soma is drunk in the belly.

Therefore they say, "Vṛtra has been slain, but he has not been struck down. Indeed, the sacrifice fled from the Asuras; having placed the vessels in its lap and assumed this form—namely, that which they sew together when making the *tārpya* garments—it returned to Indra. With it, Indra sacrificed. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with this [rite], prospers in himself and his rival is defeated. The sacrifice returned to Indra; therefore there is an oblation for Indra and Viṣṇu. Verily, the Ṛc verses come to his aid.

Then he offered the Sāmans before him, and then the Yajus; for this is indeed the womb of the Brahman, from which all this was created—the Ṛcs, the Sāmans, the Stomas, and the Yajus. Thus, he takes hold of the very womb of the Brahman.

He transcends all this; with this [sacrifice], indeed, the Sṛñjayas sacrificed, and they transcended all this. Therefore, it shook them off as it was being performed repeatedly; for that reason, it should not be performed repeatedly. Verily, he who sacrifices with this cuts himself asunder; yet one may cause even his son to sacrifice for the sake of continuity. By its power, Vṛtra grew day by day a span high and a span across; and furthermore, whatever space there was, he grew back into it again. He who knows thus prospers with offspring and cattle.

The wise man sacrifices with this; he should sacrifice for all desires, for this entire sacrifice—the Soma-rite—is indeed employed for all desires. One practicing exorcism should sacrifice; he should not give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Having made him a "malignant spirit" (meni), he employs him against [the enemy], for one who is without a dakṣiṇā is indeed a malignant spirit.

One desiring prosperity should offer three sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). These worlds are three; having attained these very worlds, he secures vigor and strength. Each subsequent one becomes larger, for each subsequent of these worlds is indeed larger. They are arranged from bottom to top, for even so are these worlds. There are twelve potsherds; for those [three cakes] consist of four potsherds each, which is for the sake of success. He makes an offering from all of them to avoid a useless sacrifice; for if he does not make an offering from one, he performs a useless sacrifice, and what is useless does not proceed for him.

The first [cake] consists of rice, then one of barley, then one of rice; for rice is indeed red, and this world is as it were red, and yonder world is as it were red; barley is white, and the intermediate space is as it were white; by means of the intermediate space these worlds are connected; thus it is for the continuity of these worlds. He should make the last one of wild rice (nīvāra) to avoid monotony.

There are three milch-cows as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), three garments of *tārpya* silk, and three pieces of gold. These garments of *tārpya* silk are indeed the form of the *Yajus* formulas; the gold pieces are the form of the *Sāmans*; and the milch-cows are the form of the *Chandas* meters. These are truly the forms of the sacrifice; by means of these very forms, he secures the sacrifice. The garment belongs to all the deities; in that he gives garments, he secures all the deities. Gold is brilliance and Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*); in that he gives pieces of gold, he secures brilliance and Vedic luster.

The cow is thrice-perfected: herself, the calf, and the milk; when he gives a cow, he makes him thrice-perfected. He should recite all the meters, for this sacrifice is everything, since all the meters are recited at the Soma-sacrifice. When the sacrifice was created, its caul enveloped it, and that became the *tārpya* garment. Since the *traidhātavyā* is the sacrifice, when the sacrificer puts on the *tārpya* garment, he clothes himself in his own womb. [He recites] the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* verses.

He should also recite the *sāmidhenī* verses in the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters; for the *kakubh* is the vigor of the *uṣṇih*, and thus he secures both of them with vigor. He should not conclude with a *jagatī* verse, for this is the end of the meters; by using it, he would go to the end and cut off the sacrifice. With the *triṣṭubh* verse, "O Agni, three are thy powers, three thy stations," he concludes; for the *triṣṭubh* is vigor and strength. Thus he does not go to the end, but establishes him in vigor and strength. 4.

The gods were about to enter into the service of the Asuras, but Indra did not enter it. Their powers departed from them: the *Rathantara* from Agni, the *Bṛhat* from Indra, the *Vairūpa* from the Viśvedevas, the *Vairāja* from Savitṛ, the *Śakvarī* from the Maruts, and the *Revatī* from Tvaṣṭṛ. Indra encompassed these; he followed after them in common. He saw this offering to Indra on twelve potsherds; with it, indeed, he regained those powers and strengths. Thereupon he became preeminent, and by means of this, the gods followed after him and attained him.

One who desires prosperity should sacrifice with an offering on twelve potsherds to Indra; thus he secures these very powers and virilities and indeed becomes prosperous. His own kinsmen follow after him and prosper. It is offered on twelve potsherds for the sake of its being dedicated to the Viśvedevas. He places it upon the potsherds while they are turned face upwards; he makes it a *caru* (gruel) for the sake of appeasement and to prevent burning. All these *pṛṣṭha* stotras are indeed powers and virilities; they are liable to sweep away this sacrificer if they remain without a foundation. He should interweave the *yājyā* and *anu-vākyā* verses, saying: "Recite for Indra associated with the *Rathantara*!"

Having recited a verse of the Rathantara, one should offer with a verse of the Bṛhat, saying, "Recite for Indra associated with the Bṛhat. Having recited a verse of the Bṛhat, one should offer with a verse of the Rathantara, saying, "Recite for Indra associated with the Vairūpa. Having recited a verse of the Vairūpa, one should offer with a verse of the Vairāja, saying, "Recite for Indra associated with the Vairāja. Having recited a verse of the Vairāja, one should offer with a verse of the Vairūpa, saying, "Recite for Indra associated with the Śākvara. Having recited a Śakvarī verse, one should offer with the Revatī verse, saying, "Recite for Indra associated with the Raivata. Having recited the Revatī verse, [one should offer] with the Śakvarī.

One should sacrifice with these very senses and powers, thereby firmly attaching oneself to them so as not to lose them. One should not utter the *vaṣaṭ* call with a *bṛhatī* verse; for by means of the *bṛhatī*, this world attains freedom from weariness, and offspring are produced. [If one were to use it thus,] one would obstruct procreation. The *bṛhatī* is indeed cattle, and Agni is Rudra; [if one used a *bṛhatī*], one would consign the cattle to Rudra, and one would become destitute of cattle. One should add four syllables from the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) to the offering verse (*yājyā*). In that way, they both become a *paṅkti* and an *anuṣṭubh*. For one who desires offspring, the invitatory verse should be an *anuṣṭubh* and the offering verse a *paṅkti*.

Or for one desiring cattle: Prajāpati was this [universe]; Speech was his second. He united with her; she conceived; she departed from him; she created these creatures; she entered Prajāpati again. In that the *anuṣṭubh* is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) and the *paṅkti* is the offering verse (*yājyā*), and since the *anuṣṭubh* is speech and the *paṅkti* is the year, and Prajāpati is the year—he thus unites the bull with speech during the year. He thereby creates a pair for him. [He does this] all around, enclosing it.

He should cut portions from the *puroḍāśa* cake; by means of these very powers and strengths, he surrounds himself on all sides. One should perform this sacrifice with the intent to strike down [an enemy]. For the gods do not eat the food of one whom they accuse of having killed [an innocent person]; when he is thus shunned by the gods, men do not eat his food. Therefore, even if people should falsely accuse someone, one should not eat that person's food. The *pṛṣṭha* chants belong to all the gods; since he sacrifices with the *sarvapṛṣṭhya*, [he pleases] the deities.

Thus he makes his food savory; when it has been purified and made palatable, men eat that food. This is the sacrifice named "All-Backed" (sarvapṛṣṭhā); he who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice becomes the back—that is, the preeminent one—among his equals.

Like a horse that has been accepted, he who accepts this [horse] spits out his own power and vigor; therefore, it should not be accepted. Varuna indeed accepted it first; he fell into his own deity, and Varuna seized him. He sacrificed with this oblation to Varuna to be released from Varuna’s power. He who accepts a horse should sacrifice with this oblation to Varuna to be released from Varuna’s power. It consists of a cake on four potsherds, for the horse is four-footed; thus he directly [releases] him.

He releases him from Varuna’s nooses. Regarding this they say: "Surely he is not released from others by that which releases him from only one. As many horses as he may receive, so many four-potherd cakes he should offer; for wherever there is Varuna’s noose, it is precisely from there that he releases him from Varuna. One cake remains over; he is thereby released from him upon whom they do not place [the debt]. Moreover, he performs an expiation for Varuna regarding what is yet to come; indeed, Varuna seizes him more firmly who [does not perform this].

Having sacrificed with this [offering], he accepts the horse that is not excellent; if he should be about to accept a horse that is not excellent, he should perform an offering to Sūrya and Varuṇa. Verily, he accepts this world from the god Sūrya, and by means of the [offering] to Varuṇa, he releases him from Varuṇa. There is also a pap for Apāṃ Napāt; for the horse is indeed without a womb, being born from the waters. Having thus provided it with a womb, he establishes it. There are twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses; the year is indeed twenty-onefold: five seasons, twelve months, these three worlds, and yonder sun.

The Āditya is the twenty-onefold; he is Prajāpati, and the horse belongs to Prajāpati. Verily, he obtains the horse itself. "O King Varuṇa, that noose of thine which has the Gāyatrī metre—this I release for thee; to it, Svāhā! O King Varuṇa, that noose of thine which has the Triṣṭubh metre, the Jagatī metre, and the Anuṣṭubh metre—this I release for thee; to it, Svāhā! So many indeed are the metres, and the metres are the nooses of Varuṇa. With them, he seizes him whom Varuṇa seizes. Wherever there is a noose of Varuṇa, right there [he releases it].

Then he releases him from Varuṇa by means of the Varuṇapāśa. Two oblations for Apāṃnapāt are offered; by those two bonds of his which are in the waters, he releases him from them. He offers these six oblations; there are six seasons; verily, he finds firm support in the seasons.

When the plants had ripened, the gods indeed set a race for them. Indra knew, "Agni will surely win. He said, "Whichever of us two wins, let that be for both of us. Agni won first; Indra won after him. Therefore, the offering should be dedicated to Agni-Indra or Indra-Agni, for Agni won first and Indra won after him. For the sake of victory, the Āgrayaṇa cake consists of twelve potsherds, for it arises from the year. There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

For this [earth] comes into being from the year. At that time, there was but one handful of rice, one of barley, one of beans, and one of sesame. Those Viśvedevas said, "Let there be a share for us; we shall spread this out. They made this a share for them, and from that this world spread out. It belongs to the Viśvedevas for the sake of expansion; by means of this [offering], he causes it to expand. It is prepared in milk for the sake of its belonging to the Viśvedevas, for milk indeed belongs to the Viśvedevas. Then this [earth] spoke: "Upon me, indeed, does yonder [sky] cook this through rain."

"By means of us two you shall conquer immortality"—thus they made this portion for the two [heaven and earth], a cake on one potsherd, for the sake of stability. The *dyāvāpṛthivya* offering: some plants are domestic, others are wild; by this [offering], both kinds become sacrificed for him. Soma is the overlord of plants; this is his special share (*uddhāra*), namely that which ripens without being ploughed. This is indeed his share as a special portion, since it is what grows in the wilderness. By this [offering] its excellence is established; that which is ploughed belongs to the other [deities]. A first-born calf is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); it is seed indeed.

For he who has not yet fathered offspring is now consecrated for procreation. Indeed, this Āgrayaṇa cup at the Rājasūya is consecrated for all; thus he secures food for himself, and it becomes for him well-prepared and palatable. He who has established the sacred fires has indeed been brought into the presence of the gods; they eat his food. If one were to eat of the new grain without having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, he would be eating the portion of the gods that has already been assigned to them, and he would meet with calamity. Therefore, one must not eat of the new grain without having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice. By means of this, the gods attained the first place.
Thus, by way of its sequence, the Āgrayaṇa possesses the quality of being the first-offering; he who, knowing this, sacrifices with the Āgrayaṇa, goes at the very head of his equals.

The meters of one who sacrifices with Soma become exhausted for a year. The Devikās are the meters; he thus makes the meters fresh again and restores their power. A six-year-old cow that has not been covered by a bull is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); for she is the quarter (*āśā*), and he is consecrated as a king over the quarters; verily, he bestows the quarters upon him. One who desires cattle should sacrifice with the Devikās. The Devikās are the meters; the meters are a pair. Gāyatrī is Anumati, Triṣṭubh is Rākā, Jagatī is Sinīvālī, Anuṣṭubh is Kuhū, and Dhātṛ is the *vaṣaṭ*-call. When there are two...

The two lower ones and the two higher ones constitute a pair; the Dhātṛ and the Vaṣaṭkāra constitute a pair. From that very pairing he produces cattle for him. That which is the earlier full moon is Anumati, and that which is the later is Rākā; that which is the earlier new moon is Sinīvālī, and that which is the later is Kuhū. The Dhātṛ is the Moon itself: when it is full in one [night] and deficient in the other, that constitutes a pair; when one sees it in one [night] and not in the other, that constitutes a pair; and when the Moon is born from the new moon (amāvāsyā), that constitutes a pair.

Therefore, from that very pair, he causes cattle to be born. One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the Devikā offerings; he should place Dhātṛ last. The Devikās are indeed females, and Dhātṛ is the male. Offspring deposit their seed in the direction of the females; thus, the seed is deposited in those very females. Regarding this they say: "He does not truly deposit it by means of that [offering] which is performed first. He should interpose Dhātṛ; he thereby makes all of them fragrant with the scent of the bull.

He obtains a son afterwards, for he becomes like one who moves behind; indeed, women lead him around from behind. If [the son] should be born, having placed Dhātṛ in front, he should then offer this very oblation; thus he leads him around in the foremost position. One who is afflicted by disease should sacrifice with the Devikā offerings; he should place Dhātṛ in the middle. Dhātṛ is indeed the year, for it is the year that has been seized by this man and then afflicts him. Having thus arranged the year in the middle for him, he then restores him from this union.

These unappeased meters produce lords for him; he should immolate a goat for appeasement so that there may be no wandering forth. Some animals have heroes as their support, others do not. Those cakes which are in front have heroes as their support; those cakes which are behind do not have heroes as their support. Those with heroes as their support remain standing while eating; those without heroes as their support perish. Those cakes which are in front have heroes as their support; they are released into Prajāpati as their foundation. In those [cows]...

The Soma juices are in the vessels; in them he should perform the Devikā offerings, for Soma is the placer of seed. He should sacrifice with the Devikās; for he who gives away everything is deprived of cattle. The Devikās are the meters, and the meters are cattle. At the point where he distributes these [cattle], he sees them last; at that very point where he sees them last, from there he causes them to be born again. Whoever sacrifices with Soma, let him sacrifice with the Devikās;
the Devikās are the meters, and thus he makes the meters fresh again, having restored their vigor. 8.

I mix you, who are sweet, with what is sweet; O sharp one, with what is sharp; O goddess, with what is divine; the bright with the bright; the immortal with the immortal. Be mixed together with Soma! Be full of milk for the Aśvins; be prepared for Sarasvatī; be prepared for Indra the Good Protector.
May the daughter of the Sun purify your pressed Soma with her eternal, continuous fleece. Purified by the filter, Soma has become Vāyu’s envoy, facing westward—the worthy friend of Indra.
Come hither, O you who possess barley; just as those who have barley reap it, separating it in due order.
Prepare food for those who have not come to the trimming of the sacred grass with their homage.

"You are taken with a support; I take you, the flawless one, with the flawless [ladle], acceptable to the Aśvins. This is your womb; for the Aśvins, you are taken with a support. You are taken with a support; I take you, the flawless one, with the flawless [ladle], acceptable to Sarasvatī. This is your womb; for Sarasvatī, you are taken with a support. You are taken with a support; I take you, the flawless one, with the flawless [ladle], acceptable to Indra the Good Protector. This is your womb; for Indra the Good Protector, you are taken."

With the words, "Thee, sweet, with the sweet," he unites it with the Brahman itself. It remains united for three nights, for Soma, once purchased, remains for three nights. With the words, "Be cooked for the Aśvins; be cooked for Sarasvatī; be cooked for Indra Sutraman," for it is indeed for these deities that it is cooked. With the verse, "Vāyu, purified by the filter," he should purify one who has failed or been over-purified; this single *puroruc* bestows power upon him all at once. It is undefined, belonging to Prajāpati; Prajāpati is undefined, and thus he attains Prajāpati himself. 9.

Viśvarūpa, the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ and nephew of the Asuras, used one head to drink Soma, one to consume solid food, and one to drink Surā. Indra thought, "He will surely take over this [world]," and so he struck him down. He fell upon a yoke-pin; he said to a carpenter who was standing there, "Run and cut off these heads of his. The carpenter ran up and cut off the heads with an axe. Therefore, the head of a carpenter is held sacred, and therefore his food is to be eaten.

That which was his head for drinking soma became the kapiñjala; that which was for eating food became the tittiri; and that which was for drinking surā became the kalaviṅka; therefore, it speaks as if with its beak closed.

Tvaṣṭṛ, whose son had been slain, prepared the Soma for Indra; he pressed it in a vessel with a thousand holes—or, as some say, one with a hundred holes—and Indra, having forcibly snatched it from him, drank it through a reed. He was deprived of his Soma-drinking power on all sides; therefore, Soma should not be drunk by one who has not been invited, for he becomes deprived of the Soma-drinking power. That which was released from his nose became two lions; that from his eyes, two tigers; that from his ears, two wolves; and that which was below became the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.

What he spat out first became the *kuvala* fruit; what he spat out second became the *badara*; what he spat out third became the *karkandhu*. The Aśvins healed him and caused him to sacrifice with this Sautrāmaṇī. Whatever vital powers (*vīrya*) he had lost, they recovered those for him and placed them within him. One should perform this sacrifice for one whose *soma* has flowed over. Indeed, he whose *soma* flows over is deprived of vital power. Whatever vital power there is, that they place within him. This same [rite] also occurs in the Rājasūya; for he is indeed deprived of vital power.

He who is consecrated by the Rājasūya perishes, for he slays Vṛtra; as much power as there is, that they place in him. With this very [offering], a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya who desires to prosper should sacrifice; as much power as there is, that they place in him. Regarding this, they say: "This is a sacrifice for one who is afflicted; one who is not afflicted should not sacrifice with it. To this they reply: "One must certainly sacrifice, for every man is afflicted and everyone desires to prosper; therefore, one must sacrifice. As for the offering to the Aśvins, it is because the two Aśvins were physicians; as for the offering to Sarasvatī..."

Sarasvatī is indeed speech, for by means of speech the two physicians [the Aśvins] healed him. When it belongs to Indra, it is because they both placed that heroic power in Indra. He mixes the portion for the Aśvins with *kuvala*-flour, that for Indra with *badara*-flour, and that for Sarasvatī with *karkandhu*-flour. Sarasvatī is indeed speech; verily, he places sweetness in his speech. Moreover, whatever foul thing that speech says against him, she makes it say auspiciously again. The Adhvaryu should meditate in his mind on lions, the Pratiprasthātṛ on tigers, and the sacrificer on wolves—the surā being their food.
By those very same powers through which one is deprived, they, having attained them, bestow them upon this person. ||10||

He should set it down on the head of a Brāhmaṇa; thereby it becomes pure, for Sura is indeed pure food, and by that it becomes pure. There is one *puroruc* verse, one *yājyā* verse, and [it is offered] once; thus he bestows vigor upon him in a single stroke. He offers it as a complete oblation (*sarvahuta*); thus he bestows all vigor upon him. He should cause a Brāhmaṇa to drink it; thereby it is made into an oblation. He himself should not drink it; he places the vigor within himself. That [practice] is not to be disregarded. Sura is indeed evil; he who passes over it in the middle is seized in the middle by evil. [By this act], he frees him from evil in the very middle.

If he were to offer it in the northern fire, he would not turn away from evil; medicine would be prepared. Since he offers it in the southern fire, he turns away from evil and medicine is prepared. As for why he lets it flow out: indeed, this [fire] flows out.

Whatever of this [soma] has been injured or has perished, that the fathers have consumed; they consecrate it with verses addressed to the fathers, and thus they cause it to flow forth from the fathers themselves. Because there are three [verses] each, and because the fathers are in the third world, [it is so]. Because there are four [sets of verses], they cause it to flow forth from these very four directions. It consists of a hundred syllables; man indeed has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundredfold vigor; verily, he wins life and vigor. He buys the sprouts with lead from a eunuch; for the eunuch is untruth, lead is untruth, and the sprouts are untruth.

By means of liquor and falsehood, he indeed purchases a greater falsehood than falsehood itself; the mare is the sacrificial fee, for she is swift-moving, and liquor is like something swift-moving—this is for the sake of prosperity. ||11||

One should sacrifice a goat to the Aśvins, a ewe to Sarasvatī, and a bull or a ram to Indra. They proceed with the omenta in this very manner; since the omentum of Indra is the last among the omenta, Indra thereby prevails over him. When they proceed again with the first [offering] dedicated to Indra while performing the ritual, they thus seize Indra once more for the sake of his presence. As for the one for the Aśvins, it is because the Aśvins were the physicians. As for the one for Sarasvatī, Sarasvatī is indeed Speech; he thus finds firm support in Speech. The omentum of Indra is the last among the omenta.

The first cake belongs to Indra; Indra is indeed vigor, so they endow him with vigor. The one for Savitṛ is for instigation; the one for Varuṇa is for release from Varuṇa’s noose, for he is seized by Varuṇa in the middle. Since she was created from behind with her head turned backward, the cakes being placed on top serve for concealment and to prevent leakage. The portions are collected together, and they invoke the *iḍā* together, both for the sake of cohesion and to avoid the exhaustion of the *iḍā*.

Whatever in the Sautrāmaṇī was unsuccessful, that became successful for this [sacrifice]. In that the animals have different deities and the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) have different deities, this indeed was its unsuccessful part which then became successful. Through these [different elements], he secures various powers. Half of Prajāpati was fortitude (*dhairya*), half was frivolity (*mālvya*). That which was fortitude, he carried around in front; that was Soma, and from that he created the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, every Brāhmaṇa is a *brahmán* and is steadfast (*dhīra*). That which was frivolity—

After that, he winnowed it; that was indeed *surā*, and from it he created the *rājanya*. Therefore, both the elder and the younger, the daughter-in-law and the father-in-law, sit together and chatter after drinking *surā*. *Mālvya* is indeed evil; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa does not drink *surā*, lest he be united with evil. This very [fact] one should explain as a sacred teaching (*brāhmaṇa*) for the Kṣatriya: "Drinking *surā* does not harm him who drinks it knowing this. For this is the body of Prajāpati, his vigor; Prajāpati is vigor; verily, he bestows vigor upon him.

Svarbhānu the Asura pierced the sun with darkness; he did not shine. Therefore, the gods dispelled that darkness. That which they first dispelled became the black cow (kṛṣṇā); that which they secondly dispelled became the pale-red cow (phalgū); that which they thirdly dispelled became the white-spotted cow (balakṣī). That which was upon it [the sun] they dispelled became the barren cow (avaśā). Now, this earth at that time was hairless and without wool. The gods slaughtered that [barren cow] for Aditi out of desire. With her, they caused hair to grow upon this [earth]; from that, indeed, this [earth] acquired its hair. One should slaughter this very same one for Aditi.

For the sake of desire, whatever desire one desires, that he obtains. From yonder, a ray of the sun descended hitherward toward the *cātvāla* pit; there these two became a pair: the ram became the male and the ewe the female. At that time, these plants were indeed fruitless. The gods offered them to the Ādityas for the sake of their desires; by means of that [offering], they caused them to grasp fruit. Therefore, these [plants] grasped fruit. One should offer these two in this manner: one to the Ādityas for the sake of a specific desire, and the other to the Ādityas for the sake of desires in general; thus, by both [offerings], he accomplishes his purpose.

With two [female] goats he sacrifices for desire; he should sacrifice a ewe to Sarasvatī for one from whom speech departs. Sarasvatī is indeed speech; Sarasvatī departs from him from whom speech departs. In that there is a ewe to Sarasvatī, he obtains and secures speech itself before his very eyes. It should be one whose teeth have not yet fallen out, for the sake of completeness; it should be unspilled, for the sake of prosperity. If one should be born as the last among three [brothers], he should sacrifice a goat to Ūrj (Nourishment), desiring nourishment. These two [breasts] are born separately, but this one is born unto nourishment itself.

By this, having obtained vigor, he secures it; the sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood. When the gods divided vigor among themselves, from that the Udumbara was born; therefore, by means of the Udumbara post, one secures vigor. One who desires offspring or cattle should sacrifice this victim to Soma and Pūṣan. Soma is the depositor of seed, and Pūṣan is the progenitor; Soma bestows seed upon him, and Pūṣan procreates. He obtains either offspring or cattle, whichever he sacrifices for the sake of. He should sacrifice a white goat to Vāyu.

One who desires to prosper should resort to Vāyu, for Vāyu is indeed the swiftest among the gods; he approaches him with his own portion, and he leads him toward the most rapid attainment of prosperity. He wipes it, he runs forward; thus he indeed leads him toward prosperity.

He indeed becomes both prosperous and meritorious. Furthermore, one who desires kinsmen should offer a white goat with speckled ears to Vāyu Niyutvat. These creatures follow after Vāyu as if led by the nose, moving here and there; Vāyu is the breath, and Vāyu is the leader of the divine clans (*viśas*). He approaches him with his own share, and he leads the clan to him for him. By offering to Vāyu Niyutvat, he provides a means of support. One should offer a white goat to Vāyu for the purpose of clearing away obstacles.
He who desires desires only a small thing compared to desires; Vāyu blows as the smallest among the gods. He approaches him with his own portion, and he (Vāyu) blows according to his desires. 13.
O Mitra and Varuna, stretch forth your arms toward us.
I choose for myself the protection of Indra and Varuṇa, the two sovereign kings; may they both be gracious to us in such a state.
O gods Indra and Varuna, being praised, bestow wealth upon us for the sake of glorious renown.
Thus praising the host of the Mighty One, may we cross over difficulties as if crossing waters by boat.
O Agni, you are ours; O Agni, you are ours; may they be auspicious for us in every contest.
May Indra be our advocate at all times; may we, unassailed, win the prize.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this.
Through this hymn of praise, may we, accompanied by Indra and with all our heroes, prevail in the assembly;
may Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this.
Agni is the head.
O Agni, he prevails through your protections that grant heroic sons and bring forth strength—for you choose his friendship as your own. O Agni, [grant] strength; O Agni, three are yours.

We impel you both with our ritual act and with nourishment, O Indra and Viṣṇu, across the expanse of this work. May you enjoy the sacrifice and bestow wealth upon us, carrying us across by paths that are free from harm.
Both of you have conquered; you are not defeated, nor has either of you been vanquished. O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two strove together, you divided the thousandfold [booty] into three parts.
Milking the well-yielding cow that provides all sustenance, for the sake of the sacrificer who loves the sacrifice and presses the Soma.
O Agni, dripping with clarified butter, shining through the three Ṛta-periods, you of excellent wisdom, go around the path of the sacrifice.
Three are your lifespans, O Jātavedas. ||14||
