I honor with my song your messenger, the all-knowing, the immortal bearer of oblations, the most skilled in sacrifice.
For he indeed knows the great abode of wealth, the ascent to heaven; may he bring the gods here to us.
That god knows how to bend the gods to his will for the sake of the one who upholds the cosmic order in his home; he bestows even the most cherished treasures.
He, the Hotṛ, being wise, goes between as a messenger, knowing the ascent to heaven.
May we be those who have honored Agni with offerings of oblations, they who nourish him and kindle him.
They have become renowned as wealthy, possessing excellent heroes, and most bountiful—those who have offered worship to Agni.
We praise you, O Hero; indeed, we invoke you alone.
O Indra, even if there were a hundred heavens and a hundred earths belonging to you, [they would not equal your power].
Not even a thousand suns, O wielder of the thunderbolt, nor the two worlds, are equal to you at your birth.
O Maghavan, graciously accept this speech of mine, this hymn of praise which Vasiṣṭha recites for you; enjoy these sacred prayers at our common feast.
These wealthy ones, through homage, have [attained] his power; O Varuṇa, I entreat you for this according to the truth.
Varuṇa carved out paths for the sun and opened the channels of the oceanic rivers; like a released flood of mares, he, following the cosmic order, set the great waters flowing toward the days.
Sing forth a lofty and profound prayer, dear to the renowned Varuṇa, the sovereign lord, who,
like a butcher spreading out a hide, has spread the earth wide for the sun.
Seeking booty, I have approached you with eloquent speech; may the Eater accept my songs with pleasure.
Will the Son of the Waters, who impels swift horses, make them well-adorned? For he shall surely take delight [in them].
To him, from our own heart, let us speak this well-fashioned hymn; will he not surely take note of it?
The Son of the Waters, by the greatness of his divine power, has brought forth all beings as a noble lord.
The waters are wealthy.
O Waters, bestow healing medicine as a protection for my body, so that I may long behold the sun. 15.
Thus ends the twelfth section, named the Payassthānaka, in the Iṭhimikā of the Caraka recension of the Śrī Yajurveda Kāṭhaka. 12.
Now begins the thirteenth section.
The Animal Sacrifice:

One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice three white, hornless, pregnant goats—one to Agni in spring, one to Sūrya in summer, and one to Bṛhaspati in autumn. Because the goat for Agni is sacrificed first, he thereby bestows brilliance upon the beginning; because the goat for Sūrya is sacrificed in the middle, he thereby bestows radiance upon the middle; because the goat for Bṛhaspati is sacrificed last, he thereby bestows spiritual luster upon the end. They are sacrificed throughout the year; the year is indeed vigor, and thus he attains vigor through the year. That they are white is the very form of radiance.

The embryo is indeed the sense-organ; verily, he secures the sense-organ for himself. He should sacrifice three pregnant cows with pendulous udders: a white one to Vāyu, a ewe to Sarasvatī, and a dark-grey goat to Aditi. Or rather, he may sacrifice a ewe to Manu. For it is by means of the mind that they drive him away; Vāyu is the mind. By means of the wind-deity (Vāyavyā), he pacifies their minds. For it is by means of speech that they drive him away; Sarasvatī is speech. By means of the Sarasvatī-deity, he pacifies their speech. He who is without a firm foundation...

This is that which Aditi encompasses; when they encompass it, he finds firm support in her, for she is Aditi. This is indeed a mantra among these [verses] which they encompass; the mantra is the womb of speech, and since they are pregnant with it, they have made him a womb of speech; thus he makes him a mantra. Power indeed departs from him whom they encompass; the mantra is the womb, and since they are pregnant with it, he secures power for himself. One who has committed an offense against a neighbor, or one who intends to commit such an offense, should sacrifice a black ram to Agni Vaiśvānara.

Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; he prospers for the sake of the year for whomsoever he prospers. Having attained the year, one commits an offense against his own desire. One should sacrifice a hornless goat of all colors to Prajāpati; Prajāpati is the source, and from the source itself one is born. Prajāpati is the giver; one approaches him with his own portion, and he bestows all desires upon him. Indeed, this [sacrificial animal] has the head of a horse, the ears of a donkey, and the body of a man.

The goat becomes like the beard of a bull, like its two front feet, like its two hind feet, and like the hair of a dog; for these indeed are the domestic animals, and by this [rite] he attains and secures them. There are twelve milch-cows as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), a garment of silk (*tārpya*), gold, and an upper garment. Those *sāmidhenī* verses which belong to Prajāpati are the *sāmidhenīs*; those *āprī* verses which belong to Prajāpati are the *āprīs*. The *āghāra* libation contains the verse beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha," and the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* belong to this hymn. Indeed, by this [rite], Upaketu prospered; he who sacrifices with this prospers.

He indeed distributed the portions of the *prāśitra* in twelve ways; there he gave twelve cows for each. In that he gives twelve, that is its symbolic correspondence (*pratimā*). By means of the linen garment, the gold, and the upper garment, he wins what is truly unlimited.

One who is ill, or has been long ill, should sacrifice a black ram (*petva*) with one white foot to Varuṇa. Prajāpati created offspring; they transgressed against him, and as they were transgressing, he caused them to be seized by Varuṇa. They lay prostrate and breathless, seized by Varuṇa. A black ram approached them and, seizing its foot, stepped upon it; it was torn out, and thus it became one with a white foot. Those creatures then appealed to Prajāpati. He saw: "This one here is not seized by Varuṇa; through him I shall release these from Varuṇa. That—

He offers a victim to Varuṇa; by that he released them from Varuṇa. He who is ill is seized by Varuṇa; because the victim is for Varuṇa, he releases him from Varuṇa. He should sacrifice on an island; the waters are indeed Varuṇa; he thus releases him from Varuṇa face to face. Prajāpati, having created cattle, sent forth Varuṇa as a suitor; he chose this [victim], therefore it has Varuṇa as its deity. He who is ill is seized by evil; evil is, as it were, black; because it is black, he drives away evil. Because one foot is white-spotted, he thereby [releases] the noose of Varuṇa.

"Release [the fire]! One who desires prosperity should sacrifice a goat to Agni and a black ram to Varuṇa. The goat belongs to Agni for the sake of prosperity; he who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it, is seized by Varuṇa. Because the ram belongs to Varuṇa, it releases him from Varuṇa. Half of a man indeed belongs to Agni and half to Varuṇa: the bones belong to Agni and the flesh to Varuṇa. By means of their respective portions, he ransoms him."

Having thus become free from debt, he indeed becomes [debt-free]; one practicing exorcism against an enemy should sacrifice a black bull sacred to Varuṇa. Varuṇa is indeed death; by means of death itself, he causes him to be seized. This black color is indeed the form of evil; evil is, as it were, black. Since it is black, he overcomes him by means of evil itself.
I bind this animal for King Varuṇa; for Indra, the bull is the exclusive portion.
May the gods enter into its limbs; may Yama seize it, and Nirṛti seize his enemies.
Indeed, these deities hold power over a person; having redeemed him from them, Death, as Yama, causes him to be seized by death itself. ||2||

One who has rivals should sacrifice a dwarf bull to Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu indeed conquered these worlds; he drove away the Asuras from these worlds. [The sacrificer] thus conquers these very worlds and drives away his rival from these worlds. He should sacrifice on uneven ground, for these worlds are, as it were, uneven. One should sacrifice a bull with speckled thighs to Indra and the Maruts for a Kṣatriya from whom the common people (Viś) act oppressively. Indra is the Kṣatra and the Maruts are the Viś; he thus subjects the Viś to the Kṣatra. It has speckled thighs.

He places it behind him unevenly for the sake of non-confusion. One desiring cattle should sacrifice a bull with a prominent hump dedicated to Indra. Indra indeed unbarred Vala; a thousand [cattle] followed after him. He (the bull) sprang up before him. He (Indra) stepped forward, seeing these worlds as he was about to leap up to win the prize. Therefore, this one is "stepped upon" (*samīṣita*), with his neck bent back. One should sacrifice this very bull in front of a thousand [cattle]; he obtains a thousand cattle and unbars Vala itself. When he has obtained a thousand cattle, then [he should sacrifice] one to Viṣṇu.

One should sacrifice a dwarf for stability; for it was upon this [dwarf] that the thousand stood, and as it was being stepped upon, it expanded; therefore, this one appears somewhat bent sideways. One should sacrifice these [other animals] on both sides in this manner for the securing of the thousand. The Sacrifice indeed desired Dakṣiṇā (the sacrificial gift); he united with her, and she conceived. Having aborted him, she ran away. Aditi noticed him lying there after he had been aborted; she brought him back and placed him beneath her thighs.

He grew from below the thighs; therefore, he is as if bent sideways, for he grew from below the thighs. Viṣṇu perceived him; he addressed him, and they both asked him a question. They reported him to Viṣṇu; therefore, they say, "The son belongs to the doer alone. With a dwarf (vāmana) [oblation] one should desire to overcome [an enemy]; one should first offer a pap (caru) to Aditi. Verily, it was Aditi who made him grow; she herself redeems him. By means of him, being debt-free, redeemed, pure, and impelled, one truly prospers. It is dedicated to Soma.

One who desires kingship should sacrifice a reddish-brown bull with white spots on its forehead; Soma is indeed the king of the gods, and Soma is the deity of him who desires kingship. He thus approaches his own deity with its share, and she leads him to kingship. Because it has white spots on its forehead, that is the form of virility. One should sacrifice a red bull with white spots on its forehead to Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, for a Kṣatriya who practices sorcery or one who desires preeminence; for the Kṣatriya has Indra as his deity, and the thunderbolt is his [weapon].

He places the thunderbolt itself into this [bull]; by it he conquers and indeed becomes successful. That which is born first is the form of vigor; he should release him. If two are born, he should release both. If a second is born within a year, he should release him at the end of that year. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni for those two who have been born; for cattle belong to Agni, and thus he ransoms them from him. At the end of the year, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara.

The year is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara; verily, he ransoms them from the year. They shall become fit for sacrifice. Year after year, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. The year is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara; verily, he ransoms them from the year.

When these two have been ransomed on all sides, being pure and productive, he indeed prospers through them. On this very day Indra was born; he was the most heroic among the gods. Therefore, whatever animal is born on the Ekāṣṭakā becomes heroic; he who, knowing this, sacrifices with these two, becomes heroic. He should first offer to Indra Abhimātihā (the slayer of the adversary); for the adversary is evil—thus he strikes away evil. Then he should offer to Indra Vṛtratūr (the overcomer of Vṛtra) as the second; for the adversary is evil.

Having indeed struck away evil, he then becomes a slayer of Vṛtra by means of this [sacrifice] and attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). No one among his equals becomes more prosperous than he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with these two. A hundred cows are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for one, and a stallion that leads the way is the fee for the other. If one should immolate those two which have not been released in this manner, even though they are of the same lineage, he prospers by means of them alone; whatever else he gives therein, that constitutes the sacrificial fee.

One should offer a spotted bull with a mark on its forehead to Indra Manyumat in battle. For by means of fury (*manyu*) one performs valor, and by means of power (*indriya*) one conquers; thus he bestows both fury and power upon these [deities] for the sake of victory. Because it is spotted (*lalāma*) on the front, it serves for the fulfillment of fury. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict; they did not achieve victory. They said, "Let our *menī* (female spirits) win by means of the sacred formulation (*brahman*). They released two bulls: the white, ruddy, hornless one belonging to the gods was Śvaitreya, and the grey, iron-horned one belonging to the Asuras was Śyeneya.

The two of them struck him; Śvaitreya pierced him through with a ritual agreement (*samaya*). That speech which was defeated fell downward; he caused it to sacrifice, and it rose upward from there. Therefore, he whose speech is directed downward is unfit for the office of a priest (*anārtvijīna*), for that is a non-divine (*asurya*) class. Therefore, he whose speech is directed upward is fit for the office of a priest, for he is indeed among the gods. One seeking to practice sorcery against an enemy should sacrifice a reddish-brown, hornless goat to Bṛhaspati. Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; verily, by means of the Brahman, he overpowers him. By this [sacrifice], the gods indeed overthrew the Asuras; because it is hornless (*tūpara*), it is for the sake of overthrowing (*stṛti*). Indra...

Indeed, he slew Vṛtra; having been slain, he encircled him with seven coils. From his head, the Vaidehī cows rose up; they stretched out toward the east, and therefore they are called *puraḥ* (cities). He thought of the bull Vaideha as the last one rising up: "I would now seize this one; by means of it, I might be released from here. He seized it, but he was not released by it. He then seized a goat sacred to Agni and a bull sacred to Indra. By means of the goat to Agni, he burned away those coils of evil with fire; then, by means of the bull to Indra, he placed sensory power and vigor within himself.

Then indeed he became [prosperous]; one who desires to prosper, or who thinks himself as if seized by evil, should sacrifice a goat to Agni and a bull to Indra. Evil indeed surrounded him with seven coils; he who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it, is surrounded by the coils of evil. Because the goat belongs to Agni, he burns away the coils of evil by means of Agni; then, by means of the bull belonging to Indra, he places sensory power and vigor within himself, and thus he truly prospers.

The gods and the Asuras were both in this world. Those Asuras oppressed the gods from this world. The gods sought protection from Prajāpati; he created these: a bull and a cow, Yama and Yamī. Therefore, when twins are born as a pair, one is a bull and the other is a cow. He offered a cow to Viṣṇu and Varuṇa and a bull to Indra. By that, having caused the Asuras to be seized by Varuṇa, he drove them away with Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, and then [he gained] power through Indra.

He placed vigor within himself; then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. One who contends with an enemy should sacrifice these very animals: a barren cow to Viṣṇu and Varuṇa, and a bull to Indra. Having caused his enemy to be seized by Varuṇa, he drives him away by means of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice; then, by means of Indra, he places power and vigor within himself. He prospers in his own person, and his enemy is defeated. One desiring offspring should sacrifice a cow that has miscarried to the plants; for she is indeed dear to the plants. To her...

They press around the mare; therefore, she is dear to all animals. Water is the plants; they dig for water. He approaches them with their own portion; they dig out offspring for him. As many as run after that mare, they are the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) for the sake of success. One who desires to prosper should sacrifice a barren cow to Indra. From her, indeed, Indra was born; he looked back again and thought, "Whoever else shall be born from this [mare] will become my rival."

Reflecting upon it, he enveloped the womb; therefore, this [cow] did not bring forth another. The Rājanya is of the nature of Indra by deity; verily, he causes him to be born from his own womb for prosperity, and he indeed prospers. He who is born from her, one desiring power should sacrifice to Indra; for power indeed is born from her. Having obtained that very thing visibly, he secures it. One who desires, "May I be pre-eminent," should sacrifice to Brāhmaṇaspati for pre-eminence; for the tongue of Agni is pre-eminence.
Brahmaṇaspati stands over all this; verily, he endows him with form and makes him pre-eminent.

One whose father and grandfather have been virtuous should offer a goat to Agni and a bull to Soma; yet he may not attain that [reward]. Agni is all the deities; he offers the deities at the very beginning. He whose father and grandfather have been virtuous is indeed deprived of the power of the Soma-drink when he does not attain it. The Soma-offering belongs to the Brāhmaṇa by virtue of his deity; the Soma-drink is his power. Because it is for Soma, he endows him with power and the Soma-drink. [He should offer] a cow to Heaven and Earth.

One who has been obstructed for a long time should sacrifice a *paryāriṇī* cow. He who is obstructed for a long time is excluded from both Heaven and Earth; when he sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, he causes him to share in Heaven and Earth. He who is obstructed for a long time is indeed a *paryārin*; the *paryāriṇī* cow is his deity. By means of the *paryāriṇī*, his animal victim belongs to its own proper deity. On the very same day, he should sacrifice a calf dedicated to Vāyu. Vāyu is the calf of these two [Heaven and Earth]; he makes them swell and he causes them to bestow [rain]. It is to him [Vāyu] that he [the sacrificer] resorts.

He approaches with his allotted share; he causes these [desires] to be granted to him. He should sacrifice this consecrated (anusṛṣṭa) victim to Indra and Agni, whose father and grandfather have not drunk Soma and who now desires to drink it. Indeed, he whose father and grandfather have not drunk Soma is deprived of the power of Indra and the drinking of Soma. The Brāhmaṇa is by nature connected to Agni; his power and the drinking of Soma reside in Indra. By sacrificing to Indra and Agni, he continues the drinking of Soma through his own very deity. The drinking of Soma is indeed interrupted for him whose father [did not drink it].

The Grandfather does not drink Soma because he was excluded; therefore, his sacrificial animal is his own. One should offer a two-year-old bull to Tvaṣṭṛ that is speckled and has a white spot on its forehead to him who desires, "May a son be born to me who is a skilled cook. Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of forms; he approaches him with his own portion, and he fashions forms for him. One who has rivals should offer a black-spotted bull to the Aśvins. The gods, indeed, drove out the Asuras from the day; whatever belonged to them, whatever wealth they had, and whatever property they possessed, by that [they were driven].

The gods met together at night and saw this black-spotted horse dedicated to the Aśvins; they seized it and by means of it pursued them through the night. The Aśvins are indeed Heaven and Earth; having bound their enemies below with Heaven and Earth and above with the Sun, they drove them out during the night. They seized whatever was their own, whatever wealth they possessed, and whatever was to be known. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. The Aśvins are indeed Heaven and Earth; by means of Heaven and Earth, he binds his rival below.

Having bound him with the sun beyond day and night, he drives him away; whatever is his own, whatever is his wealth, and whatever is to be known—that he seizes. He prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated.

That which is the white form of the day, and that which is the black form of the night—by both these colors he drives him away. Indra, indeed, desired the Dānavī woman Vilistengā. He moved among the Asuras; he became like a woman among women, and like a man among men. He felt as if seized by Nirṛti (Destruction). He saw this Aindrānairṛta victim, a *vipuṃsaka* (neuter/impotent), with which form he had been moving. He sacrificed it. Of that [victim], whatever was not fit for cutting off (*anavadānīya*), with that he proceeded first. Having gone to the south, he offered it on a self-made salt-flat (*iriṇa*) with the words, "Enjoying... (juṣāṇā).

"May Nirṛti accept [this], svāhā! Having said this, he returned and completed the other [offering] to Indra. He first made expiation for Nirṛti and then, by means of the offering to Indra, took power and vigor into himself; from that he indeed became pre-eminent. One who desires to prosper, or one who feels as if seized by Nirṛti, should sacrifice a male Aindrānairṛta beast. Whatever part of it is not fit for being cut off (anavadānīya), with that he should proceed first. Having gone to the south, he offers on a self-made salt-flat with the formula, "May Nirṛti accept [this], svāhā! Then the other [part].

He should return and conclude with the offering to Indra; having first appeased Nirṛti, he then bestows power and vigor upon himself through the offering to Indra and thus prospers. One who desires, "May this battle not be won by [my enemy]," should sacrifice a large bull to Indra. Indra is indeed the leader of battle; Indra is the victor. He approaches him with his own portion, and he leads them away. Because it is large (*viśāla*), that is the form appropriate for Indra the Destroyer (*vighana*); one should sacrifice a large bull to Indra the Destroyer in battle.

If one should desire between two peoples, "May I overcome both peoples," he indeed overcomes both peoples; they move about striking each other, and by means of the *viśālā*, he causes them to go to their destruction.

One seized by an unknown malady should sacrifice a draft-ox dedicated to Agni and Varuṇa; for that which is a woman yet is a draft-ox is known as an "unknown malady. Therefore, one seized by an unknown malady should sacrifice it. Agni is all the deities: whatever of his has been seized by the deities, he releases that through Agni; whatever has been seized by Varuṇa, that through Varuṇa; insofar as she is a draft-ox, she belongs to Agni; insofar as she is a female yet is tamed, she belongs to Varuṇa; therefore, she is dedicated to Agni and Varuṇa. One desiring cattle should sacrifice a bull with a cleft hoof dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ, for it is a pair.

He who is this Aditya is the seer and the progenitor of pairs; he approaches him with his own portion, and he causes cattle to be born for him from that pair. He whose consumption (yakṣma) seizes him while he is trembling should offer a dark-grey, white-throated animal to Varuna. Verily, Varuna seizes him whose consumption seizes him while he is trembling; in that it is dedicated to Varuna, he releases him from Varuna. He who is ill is seized by evil; evil is like the dark-grey color; in that it is dark-grey, he strikes away the evil.

With that [rite] by which Śitikaṇṭha released Varuṇa’s noose, one should release him. One who desires to make a bad Brāhmaṇa drink Soma should offer a smoke-colored bull with a mark on its forehead to the Aśvins. For the Aśvins were among the gods those who did not drink Soma; they subsequently obtained the drinking of Soma. The Aśvins are the deity of this [sacrificer] who drinks Soma later; he has recourse to them with their own portion. They lead him forward to the drinking of Soma. He should sacrifice as if faltering, for a bad Brāhmaṇa wishes to become a Brāhmaṇa as if faltering. Or rather, like smoke...

This one who is a bad Brahmin—by means of the smoky color, he drives away his very smokiness; by means of the freckle on the face, he bestows brilliance upon his face. One should sacrifice a female calf that has miscarried to Sarasvatī for one whom his enemies would, as it were, cause to gasp; for they cause him to gasp with their speech. Sarasvatī is Speech; since the victim is for Sarasvatī, he silences their speech with his own speech.

This [cow], though being a cow, does not yield milk; therefore she is called *dhenuṣṭarī*. In that she is a *dhenuṣṭarī*, she indeed makes their speech barren. One should sacrifice a barren cow to Sarasvatī for one whom they should accuse after he has been killed. Speech indeed reaches him who they accuse after he has been killed. Sarasvatī is speech; in that it is to Sarasvatī, she pacifies their speech by means of speech. This [cow], though being a cow, does not yield milk; therefore she is called *dhenuṣṭarī*. In that she is a *dhenuṣṭarī*, she indeed [makes] their speech...

He makes [the victim] barren; he should sacrifice a *punarutsṛṣṭa* (one released again) dedicated to Savitṛ. He who, having previously been virtuous, later becomes more wicked—by whatever deity he was previously virtuous, that very deity indeed releases him, and then he becomes more wicked. Savitṛ is the impeller of prosperity; he approaches him with his own share, and he impels him toward prosperity once again. He who, having previously been a bull, later becomes a steer (*ukṣan*), attains prosperity just as he did before;
in this very way, [the sacrifice] causes him to attain prosperity. 6.

In the spring, he should sacrifice three ruddy bulls with white spots on their foreheads; in the summer, three with white spots on their humps; in the autumn, three with white spots on their rumps. By those with white spots on their foreheads, he places brilliance in his face; by those with white spots on their humps, he places luster in his middle; by those with white spots on their rumps, he places spiritual splendor in his upper part. They are sacrificed over the course of a year; the year is indeed vigor, and thus he attains vigor through the year. There are nine of them; there are nine vital breaths, and thus he places the vital breaths within himself.

One who desires to prosper should sacrifice with these [offerings] dedicated to Indra; for that sun is indeed Indra, and by means of these he became so. By means of these, he placed splendor and vigor within himself. He who, knowing this, sacrifices with these, truly prospers and places splendor and vigor within himself. One should offer an animal of all forms to Prajāpati when the year has elapsed, for the attainment of the year. Prajāpati is the womb; verily, he finds firm support in the womb.

He becomes possessed of all forms for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything. There are ten [cows]; the vital breaths are ten; the vital breaths are vigor; verily, he finds firm support in vigor. He should offer two milch-cows to Heaven and Earth if he desires food. Heaven and Earth indeed rule over the eating of food; from yonder it rains, and upon this earth one finds support. These two are the bestowers of food; he approaches them with their own portion, and they grant him food. They are "the two who nourish" (*saṃmātarau*); for these two are indeed like mothers who nourish.

Of these two, one should on the morrow sacrifice a calf to Vāyu; for Vāyu is the calf of these two, he causes them to swell, and he causes them to bestow [their milk]. One pursues him with his own portion, and he causes these two to bestow [their milk] upon him. One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice a white-backed animal to Bṛhaspati; for Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and Bṛhaspati is the bestower of spiritual luster. One pursues him with his own portion, and he bestows spiritual luster upon him.

He who exists as one who is surpassed becomes like a back; by [offering] a black-spotted [animal], he makes him a back. One who is surpassed in rank should sacrifice a black-spotted animal to the Aśvins. The Aśvins, indeed, were the ones among the gods who were surpassed in rank; they attained the foremost place. The Aśvins are the deity of him who is surpassed in rank; he takes hold of them, and they lead him to the foremost place. He who is surpassed in rank is seized by evil; evil is, as it were, black. In that it is black, he drives away evil. In that it is spotted on the forehead (*lalāma*), he thereby bestows splendor upon his face.

One who is afflicted by disease should sacrifice a black-spotted animal dedicated to the Aśvins. The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; they are the deities of him who is afflicted by disease. He thus approaches them with their own portion, and they heal him. He who is afflicted by disease is seized by evil; evil is, as it were, black. In that the animal is black, he drives away evil. In that it is spotted on the forehead (*lalāma*), he thereby bestows brilliance upon his face.

One desiring offspring or desiring cattle should sacrifice a male-less (neuter) animal dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ. Prajāpati, indeed, when desiring to create offspring, did not find a second mate; having assumed this form, he united with himself by means of his thumb, and from that he created offspring. Tvaṣṭṛ is the progenitor of the pair; it is to him that one has recourse with his own portion. He produces cattle for him from this very pair. By this very form indeed did Prajāpati create offspring—by that same form through which Prajāpati [created them].

He created offspring from that very form; therefore, one is propagated with offspring and cattle. One who fears impotence should sacrifice a bull to Indra. Indeed, Indra struck off this skin and this evil; he approaches that very [deity] with his own portion. He strikes off that skin and that evil from him. A bull is the sacrificial fee; the bull is indeed vigor; verily, he bestows vigor upon him. ||7||

The *chandāṃsi* (Vedic meters) indeed set their minds upon the sacrifice; that *vaṣaṭkāra*, having approached, cut off the head of the *gāyatrī*. From that, the essence which flowed forth became the *vaśā* (the cow). Because it flowed forth (*avaśrat*), that is the etymology of the *vaśā*'s name. What flowed forth first was indeed blood; Bṛhaspati caught that, and she who became the ruddy (*rohiṇī*) cow was she [that essence]. Therefore, she belongs to Bṛhaspati. What flowed forth second, Mitra and Varuṇa caught that; she who became the two-colored (*dvirūpā*) cow was she. Therefore, she [belongs to them].

That which flowed as the third [stream] for Mitra and Varuṇa, the Viśve Devas received; it became that which has many forms, therefore it belongs to the Viśve Devas. That which overflowed, Bṛhaspati seized; it became a bull, and that is the bull-nature (*ukṣatva*) of the bull. That which was released became these other forms. One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice a reddish-brown cow to Bṛhaspati. He who is capable of spiritual luster but does not possess it is indeed deprived of its essence. This [victim] belongs to the meters.

The essence is Brahman; Bṛhaspati is Brahman. By means of Brahman, he bestows brilliance and essence upon this [sacrificer]; he becomes endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasī*). One desiring rain should offer a two-colored cow to Mitra and Varuṇa. Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed day and night; Parjanya rains according to day and night—for it rains either by night or by day. These two are the lords of rain; he approaches them with their respective portions, and they, being pleased, pour down rain for him. One desiring offspring should offer a two-colored cow to Mitra and Varuṇa; Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed day and night.

Offspring are born following the day and night; for offspring are born either by night or by day, he thus causes them to be born following the day and night. He should sacrifice a multi-colored cow to the Viśvedevas for the sake of his desires; the Viśvedevas are indeed desires, so he has recourse to them with their own portion, and they grant him all his desires. He who desires prosperity should sacrifice a bull to Bṛhaspati; he who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it, is deprived of the essence. This bull is the essence of the meters; it is Brahman.

Bṛhaspati bestows prosperity and essence upon him by means of the sacred word (*brahman*); he surely prospers. One who desires splendor should sacrifice a white cow to Sūrya; for yonder sun is indeed the giver of splendor. He approaches him with his own portion, and he grants him splendor. One practicing sorcery should sacrifice a brown cow to Brāhmaṇaspati; for Brāhmaṇaspati is the sacred word. By means of the sacred word, he thus overpowers him. Brown is indeed the form of the sacred word; by its very form, he brings him to ruin. 8.
May Dhātṛ, Rāti, Savitṛ, Prajāpati, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni take pleasure in this.
May Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu, bestowing harmony through progeny, grant wealth to the sacrificer.
Turn it around, bring it back; O Turner, turn it! O Bringer-back, bring it back!
O Indra, Nanda-bala, from the four quarters of the earth—those are the well-spoken verses—from them we turn you back.
I split open your womb, I split open the birth-canal, and I split open the surrounding membrane; I split apart both mother and son, and the embryo and the placenta.

May the *bāl* be outside thee; the wise Indu, the purifying one, has anointed the embryo—multiform and full of wondrous power. May beings with one foot, two feet, three feet, and four feet spread throughout the worlds.
The embryo that is worthy of sacrifice, the womb that is golden for you, and his limbs that are unimpaired—those the gods have fashioned together.
May Heaven and Earth, the broad ground, sprinkle this sacrifice for us; may they fill us with nourishments.
Homage to your greatness and to your eye; O father of the Maruts, we celebrate that [deed] for you.
Offered with oblations, go by the paths traveled by the gods; take your stand among the plants with your bodily parts.
This was the grievance of the gods: "The Lord of Waters [has taken] the plants."
Pūṣan chose the drop of Soma; the great rock became that which was there at that time.

He is the father of the calves, the lord of the cows; he is the father of the great jars. He is the embryo, the afterbirth, the fresh milk, the colostrum, the curdled milk, the whey, and the clarified butter is his source.

The drop has fallen upon the earth and across the sky; following this womb and that which was before, I offer the drop as it moves along toward the common womb, according to the seven priestly offices. 9.

When he perceives that [the vessel] has become eightfold, he should offer it into the Āhavanīya fire with the *sruva* ladon, saying, "May Dhātṛ, Rāti, and Savitṛ enjoy this. Thus he announces it to the deities. With the words, "Turn back! Return! he causes Indra himself to turn back from the quarters for the sake of expiation. With the words, "I split apart thy joint," he indeed brings forth [the embryo]. They strike between the two buttocks for the sake of procreation. With the words, "O thou who art much renowned," he places the vessel down to prevent spilling. With the words, "One-footed, two-footed," he indeed spreads it out.

If he were to cut out the portions, he would exceed them; if he were not to cut out, he would fail to cut from the animal that has been immolated and would meet with calamity. He should cut one portion from the front of the navel and another from behind it. For the breath is in front of the navel and the downward breath is behind it. As great as the animal is, so much of it does he cut out; thus it is not in vain. In that he distributes the essence among the portions, by that very act the cutting of all the limbs is accomplished. Gold with eight knobs is the sacrificial fee; for this self consists of eight parts.

This [sacrificial cake] has nine layers; the rim is the ninth for the attainment of cattle. It is wrapped with a turban in the third inner compartment; he should make the compartments as if hollow, for thus does the animal consist of hair, skin, flesh, bone, and marrow—he thereby obtains the animal itself. He offers it to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. That which is the abundance of cattle, that which is redundant, is Viṣṇu’s Śipiviṣṭa. This [cake] is indeed redundant, and Śipiviṣṭa is redundant; by means of the redundant, he obtains the redundant. Moreover, in the redundant itself, he places the redundant.

He places [the earth]. With the words, "The embryo which is thine, worthy of sacrifice," he makes it indeed worthy of sacrifice. With the words, "The womb which is thine, golden," he makes it indeed golden. With the words, "Whose limbs are unimpaired, him the gods have fashioned together," he fashions it into a complete whole. With the words, "May the great Heaven and Earth for us," he scatters [earth] upon the animal-cooking hearth; for this embryo belongs to these two, and thus he establishes it in these two. With the words, "Homage to thy greatness and to thy eye," he acts with one who has failed in respect to the animal for whom these [mantras] are not recited.
When he performs these [rites], he gathers everything—[the fire] together with its vigor, its womb, and its body—for the sake of prosperity. ||10||
O Vāyu, drinker of the pure, come to us; a thousand are your teams, O possessor of all boons.
I offer to you the intoxicating juice, since you, O God, have established the right to the first draught.

For intention thee, for desire thee, for prosperity thee! *Kikkiṭā*! Thy mind to Prajāpati, svāhā! *Kikkiṭā*! Thy eye to Sūrya, svāhā! *Kikkiṭā*! Thy hearing to Heaven and Earth, svāhā! *Kikkiṭā*! Thy speech to Sarasvatī, svāhā! *Kikkiṭā*! Thy breath to Vāta, svāhā!
You are a cow, a controller; once impelled by mind, you have conceived the embryo. As a cow, a controller, go to the gods; may the desires of the sacrificer come true.

Unborn, you are the abode of wealth; sit upon the earth! Rise up and take your station in the intermediate space; in heaven let your light be vast—*svāhā*! Follow the stretched thread, the radiance of the mid-region; guard with your wisdom the luminous paths fashioned by thought.
Weave the web of the singers without flaw; become Manu and bring forth the divine race.

You are the oblation of austerity, the color of Prajāpati. May I become a partaker of your limbs. Sūrya for those dwelling in heaven by day; Dhātṛ for the sovereignty, Vāyu for the progeny. May Bṛhaspati offer you, the luminous one, to the luminous Prajāpati—svāhā! 11.

These two, heaven and earth, were together; Vāyu blew between them, and they conceived a fetus. From that, the ewe-goat (vaśā) was born. Agni swallowed her, and Prajāpati ransomed her with this sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). In that there is a cake for Agni, it is for the sake of ransom. Because Vāyu blew between them, it belongs to Vāyu. Because heaven and earth conceived a fetus, it belongs to Heaven and Earth. These two were indeed together; just as two bamboos are joined together, so were they joined. That speech which existed became the ewe-goat; therefore—

This [cow] belongs to Sarasvatī; for it was she who bellowed toward these two, the Sun and the Moon, and they deposited the embryo within her; from that the ewe was born. Therefore, it belongs to Sūrya. One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a cow to Vāyu; Vāyu is a swift deity, and he quickly attains prosperity. One should sacrifice a cow to Heaven and Earth if one desires agriculture; for one who desires agriculture must seek a firm foundation. In that there is a cow for Heaven and Earth, he finds a firm foundation in Heaven and Earth themselves, and Parjanya becomes rain-giving for him. This very [cow]—

The Kaṇvas, the descendants of Śrava, know this: one should sacrifice a female Sarasvatī cow for whom speech has departed. Sarasvatī is indeed speech; Sarasvatī departs from him from whom speech departs. By [offering] a female Sarasvatī, he wins back speech itself. The Prāvareyas know this same [cow]: one who desires luster should sacrifice a female Saurya cow. Yonder sun is indeed luster; he is the giver of luster; he bestows luster upon him. The Yaskas, the Gairikṣitas, know this same [cow]: one who desires the office of a domestic priest should sacrifice a female Agnendra cow. For the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni, and [the king] belongs to Indra.

The Rājanya and the Brahmin make the Kṣatra and the Brahma united; the Kāpeyas know this as the Agniṣomīyā. One desiring food should sacrifice it; for Agni is the eater of food among the gods, and Soma is the food. By means of Agni he eats the food, and by means of Soma he secures it. The Āruṇas know this [verse]: "O Vāyu, come hither, O drinker of the pure, near us. He who generated her—therefore one secures her from him. "For intention (ākūti) thee!"—for she is sacrificed for intention. "For desire (kāma) thee!"—for she is sacrificed for desire. "For prosperity (samṛdh) thee!"—for prosperity.

"Kikkaṭā! Your mind, to Prajāpati, svāhā!"—thus he causes her mind to go to Prajāpati. "Kikkaṭā! Your eye, to Sūrya, svāhā!"—thus he causes her eye to go to Sūrya. "Kikkaṭā! Your ear, to Heaven and Earth, svāhā!"—thus he causes her ear to go to Heaven and Earth. "Kikkaṭā! Your speech, to Sarasvatī, svāhā!"—thus he causes her speech to go to Sarasvatī. "Kikkaṭā! Your breath, to Vāta, svāhā!"—thus he causes her breath to go to Vāta.

He causes [them] to go. He offers with the words, "kikkiṭā te. Therefore, domestic animals approach with the sound *kikkiṭā*, while wild animals flee from the sound *kikkiṭā*. He offers these five; cattle are fivefold; as great as the animal is, he causes it to go to the heavenly world. With the words, "Thou art a cow, thou art powerful," he indeed invokes a blessing. With the words, "Once with her mind she conceived the embryo," he causes [the offspring] to be born. With the words, "Thou art unborn, abiding in wealth upon the earth..."

"These two sink; he thus brings these worlds into distress. 'Stand upright, enter the atmosphere; in heaven let thy great light be, svāhā!'—he thus causes them to go to the heavenly world. 'Follow the stretched thread, the radiance of the region,'—he thus invokes a blessing. 'Guard the luminous paths made by the sacred thought (*dhī*)'—this is for the striking away of the Rākṣasas. 'Weave the unloosened work of the singers,'—he thus weaves it without loosening. 'Become Manu, generate the divine folk,'—he thus generates them. 'Thou art the oblation of fervor.'"

"The color of Prajāpati; may I become a sharer in your limbs"—thus he invokes a blessing. That which he scatters in the waters is a failure; that which he offers in the fire is a consecration (*svagākṛti*); that which he immolates for the cloud is a failure. Therefore, at that time, he is indeed childless. This [offering] is successful through the *vīdhra* (the cloud). One who is barren should sacrifice with this. It is appropriated by three types of people: those who dwell in the *saṃvatsara-sadas* sacrifice, householders, and those who perform the *sahasra-yajña*; these alone should sacrifice with it. "Sūrya, the god among those dwelling in heaven; Dhātṛ of the sovereignty; Vāyu..."

"May Bṛhaspati offer you, the luminous one, for Prajāpati, the luminous one; svāhā!"—Bṛhaspati is indeed Brahman; thus with Brahman he offers her, the luminous one, for Prajāpati, the luminous one. ||12||

Agni, indeed, when born, did not shine. He desired, "May I be radiant. He offered a black-necked goat to Agni Tejasvin (the Radiant). Thereupon he became radiant. He desired, "May I prevail everywhere. He offered a black-necked goat to Agni Vibhumat (the Pervasive). Thereupon he prevailed everywhere. He desired, "May I have a share everywhere. He offered a black-necked goat to Agni Bhāgin (the Shareholder). Thereupon he came to have a share everywhere. Whoever [does this]...

If he should desire, "May I be radiant; may I have power everywhere; may I have a share everywhere," let him sacrifice these goats dedicated to Agni with black necks. He becomes radiant, he has power everywhere, and he has a share everywhere.
O divine Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for his prosperity.
May the celestial Gandharva, the purifier of intentions, purify our intention; may the Lord of Speech make our speech sweet today.
Now, at the impulse of strength, we celebrate with our speech the Great Mother named Aditi.
In her, into whom this entire world has entered, may the divine Savitṛ impel dharma for us.
Within the waters is immortality, within the waters is healing; and in the praises of the waters, O you who possess strength, become swift horses.
Either Vāyu has yoked you, or Manu, or the twenty-seven Gandharvas;
they first harnessed the horse, and they placed speed in him.
O Son of the Waters, whose wave is swift-moving, impetuous, and humped, winner of the prize—by that, win us the prize.

In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, whose impulse is true, may I ascend the highest firmament. In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, whose impulse is true, may we, through Bṛhaspati, the prize-winner, win the prize. O prize-winners, win the prize; holding the course steady, measuring out the leagues, reach the goal!

May the Vājins be auspicious to us in our invocations, they who are swift as measured paces, well-praised in the assembly of the gods; crushing the serpent, the wolf, and the demons, may they drive away all maladies far from us.
In every contest for booty, O swift ones, protect us; O wise, immortal, and truth-knowing ones, drink of this honeyed mead and rejoice. Satisfied, go by the paths traveled by the gods.

May all those swift coursers, who hear our invocation, hear our call— the prize-winners of measured speed, eager to win at the gathering of the sacrifice, winners of thousands, who have seized great riches in the battles.
This vigorous steed, bound by the neck, at the flanks, and in the mouth, hastens toward the whip; Dadhikrā, following his own will, has sped along, springing repeatedly over the curves of the paths.
And indeed, as he runs and hastens forward, eager for the prize, the wind blows after him like the wing of a bird;
as Dadhikrāvan speeds along, he overcomes all with his vigor like a swooping falcon.
O Soma, you have generated all these plants; you have generated the waters and the cows.
You have stretched out the wide mid-air; with light, you have dispelled the darkness.
Those abodes of yours which are in heaven, those on earth, those on the mountains, in the plants, and in the waters—
with all of them, O King Soma, being well-disposed and free from anger, accept our offerings.
May the path always be easy to traverse and rich in nourishment; O gods, blend the plants with honey.
O Agni, may fortune never fail me in your friendship; may I attain the dwelling of the one who possesses much food, which is full of strength.
Taste the offerings; shine forth with nourishment toward us; measure out for us glorious renown.
O Agni, conquer all those enemies in battles; as a slayer, shine upon us with a gracious mind.
Hither come those who kindle Agni and spread the sacrificial grass in due succession—those whose youthful Indra is their friend.

Performing good deeds, radiant, seeking the gods, like smelters blowing upon the births of metal, the gods have come; kindling Agni and strengthening Indra, they have approached, encompassing the vast stall of cattle.
This ancient praise of yours, O Indra and Agni, has arisen from my beautiful thought, like rain from a cloud.
O Indra and Agni, slayers of Vṛtra, may you today accept this pure, newly-born hymn of praise;
for I invoke you both, who are easily summoned, as those who most swiftly bestow strength upon the one who desires it.
May all the gods, who increase the cosmic order and hear our invocation according to the seasons, enjoy the appropriate milk.
Whosoever among the great ones, possessing wondrous power, were born upon the earth, from heaven, or in the gathering place of the waters—
may those gods grant us all life for our nourishment, bestowing wide space through nights and dawns.

The earth and the sky are rich in ghee, the glory of all beings; they are wide and broad, yielding honey. The well-adorned Heaven and Earth are held apart by the law of Varuṇa; they are undecaying and full of abundant seed.
To him who possesses a hundred weapons, a hundred powers, and a hundred aids, the overcomer of enemies—
he who has led us through a hundred autumns to the further shore of all distress— Indra.
These four paths of dust travel between heaven and earth;
whichever of them shall bring us invincibility, O all you gods, entrust that one to us.

Spring, summer, the honey-sweet rains, autumn, and winter—may these bestow prosperity upon us. May we, as those worthy of sacrifice, long remain alive and unslain within the benevolent favor of these seasons.
To the Saṃvatsara, the Parivatsara, the Idāvatsara, the Anuvatsara, and the Udvatsara, offer great homage!
May we abide in the favor of these worthy of sacrifice; may we dwell in their shelter, free from fear.
May this [year]—the Saṃvatsarīyā, the Parivatsarīyā, the Idāvatsarīyā, the Anuvatsarīyā, and the Udvatsarīyā—bear us across, not being angry. May I attain this day from this day; Svāhā!
May Prajāpati generate offspring for us; may Dhātṛ, being well-disposed, bestow it upon us.
May the Year, in harmony with the seasons, and the Lord of Prosperity, bestow nourishment upon me.
May Agni eat first, for he knows how the oblation is; may he, who beholds all people, make the plants auspicious for us.
O gods, you have led us from good to better; through you as our protection, may we attain you.
O father, enter us here as honey-sweet; be auspicious to our offspring and to our bodies.
This very barley, mixed with honey, they plowed upon the bank of the Sarasvatī.
Indra, the lord of a hundred powers, was the master of the plow; the bounteous Maruts were the plowmen. ||15||
May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drink; may they flow toward us with peace and well-being.
This very day the young maidens bow down when they, desiring him, approach him who desires them;
with one mind they agree, and the Adhvaryus and the divine Dhiṣaṇās and the Waters have prepared themselves.
The plants are called mothers.
The herbs that were born first, three ages before the gods— of those brown ones, I now take heed of their hundred and seven abodes.
The cows are Bhaga; the cows have appeared to me as Indra. The cows are the first draught of Soma.
O people, these are the cows; with my heart and mind, I truly desire Indra.
The dust-raising chariot does not overtake them, nor do they go toward the place of preparation;
those cows of the mortal sacrificer roam along that wide-striding, fearless path.
Night, approaching, has shone forth in many places with her eyes; she has clothed herself in all splendors.
I have brought [this] near to you like cattle; O Night, daughter of Heaven, accept my hymn as one who has conquered.
Behold that wonderful light of the gods.
Do thou, O Anumati, grant us thy approval; think of us and bestow welfare upon us. Grant nourishment to our offspring and prolong our lives.
O Anumati, well-guided one, whose name is easy to invoke, who art approved and bounteous—
by that [name], O Goddess, pour forth for us a gracious mind, nourishment possessing all boons and excellent heroes.
May Rākā, who is easily invoked, be present through our excellent praise; may she, the fortunate one, hear us and take notice of us by herself.
May she sew with a needle that does not break, and may she grant a praiseworthy hero who bestows a hundredfold gifts.
O Rākā, those benevolent thoughts of yours which are well-formed, by which you bestow riches upon the donor—
with those, come to us today with a gracious mind, O fortunate one, granting thousandfold prosperity.
O Sinīvālī of broad tresses, you who are the sister of the gods, accept the offered oblation; O goddess, grant us progeny.
To her who has beautiful arms, lovely fingers, and beautiful thighs, who brings forth many sons—to that Sinīvālī, the mistress of the people, offer the oblation.
I repeatedly invoke Kuhu, the one of good invocation, who performs good deeds with wisdom at this sacrifice;
O Goddess, we shall worship you with an oblation—you who grant us the renown of our ancestors.
May Kuhū, the wife of the gods and of immortality, hear our invocation of this oblation;
may she, the sister of the gods, exalting him, bestow upon this wise one the increase of wealth.
May Dhātṛ, the lord of the moving world, bestow wealth upon us; may he favor us with abundance.
May Prajāpati delight the subjects here; may Dhātṛ, being well-disposed, establish them.
May the Lord of Nourishment, fashioning the year with its seasons, bestow nourishment upon me. 16.
Thus ends the thirteenth section, named Paśubandha, in the Iṣṭimikā of the Caraka Śākhā of the Śukla Yajurveda. 13.
Now begins the fourteenth section:
The Vājapeya.
Speak the word for Indra; converse the word for Indra; cause Indra to win the prize; O Indra, conquer the prize!
May the impulse of strength come to me; may Heaven and Earth, the two of all forms, come to me;
may my father and mother both come to me; may Soma come to me with immortality.
This has become true for you, O cows, whom you have joined together with Indra.
O trees, cause Indra to quicken; release the prize of strength!

May the two prize-winning steeds, having won the prize, smell the portion of Bṛhaspati; may the prize-winning steeds, having won the prize, wipe themselves upon the portion of Bṛhaspati. O wife, ascend to the heavenly world! Ascend to the heavenly world! Let us both ascend to the heavenly world! Let us both ascend to the heavenly world! Let us both ascend to the heavenly world! Let us both ascend to the heavenly world! Let us both ascend to the heavenly world! May life be perfected through sacrifice; may mind be perfected through sacrifice; may breath be perfected through sacrifice; may sight be perfected through sacrifice; may hearing be perfected through sacrifice; may speech be perfected through sacrifice; may the self be perfected through sacrifice.

May Brahmā prosper through the sacrifice; may the back prosper through the sacrifice; may the sacrifice prosper through the sacrifice. We have gone to the light, O gods; we have become the offspring of Prajāpati; we have become immortal. Svāhā! To strength, svāhā! To impulsion, svāhā! To the after-born, svāhā! To creative power, svāhā! To the Lord of Speech, svāhā! To Vasu, svāhā! To the one whose head is the sky, svāhā! To the head, the descendant of Vyaśva, svāhā! To Vyaśva, the final, svāhā! To the final, the descendant of Bhuvana, svāhā!
To the Lord of the World, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To the Overlord, svāhā! For food thee, for strength thee, for the winning of strength thee! 1.
In the beginning, the impulse of strength brought forth King Soma in the plants and in the waters;
may they be sweet for us, and may we, with the domestic priest at our head, remain vigilant in the kingdom.
This has come into being through the impulse of strength; all these worlds are encompassed on every side.
Knowing well, Soma causes him who desires to give to bestow; he shall bestow wealth together with heroic sons.
The impulse of strength has now taken its place; the sovereign lord has entered all divine beings and all worlds. Knowing all, he moves about as the Virāj, increasing progeny and prosperity for us.
Impel King Soma for our protection, Indra for the sake of giving,
Viṣṇu, Vāc Sarasvatī, and the vigorous Savitṛ.
May Aryaman grant us [blessings], may Pūṣan, may Bṛhaspati; may the goddess Vāc grant them to us.
O Agni, speak here to us; turn toward us and be well-disposed.
Bestow wealth upon us, O Lord of the People; you are the giver of riches to us.
We invoke Indra and Vāyu here, who are beautiful to behold and easy to call upon, so that every person may be well-disposed toward us at our gathering.
We take hold of King Soma, Varuṇa, and Agni; Āditya, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati the Brahman.

At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the speech of Sarasvatī, by the restraint of the Restrainer, I consecrate this [person], the son of such-and-such a father and such-and-such a mother, with the sovereign power of Bṛhaspati; I consecrate him with the sovereign power of Indra. 2.

You are taken with a support; I take you, who sit upon the wood, who sit among men, who sit in life, as one pleasing to Indra. This is your resting place; for Indra, you are taken with a support. You are taken with a support; I take you, who sit in the waters, who sit in the clarified butter, who sit in existence, as one pleasing to Indra. This is your resting place; for Indra, you are taken with a support. You are taken with a support; I take you, who sit upon the earth, who sit in the intermediate space, who sit in the firmament, as one pleasing to Indra. This is your resting place; for Indra, you are taken with a support. You are taken with a support, O cup, belonging to all people; O sage, sit down within.
Of those three supreme divine vessels that are overturned, I have gathered together the food and the strength from their various openings.
This is your womb; for Indra you are taken with a support.
The essence of the waters, risen up, bright and gathered by the sun—the most excellent essence of the essence of the waters, that I take from you.
This is your source; for Indra, you!
By this manifestation, generating mighty deeds— for he is indeed the glowing one, the wide path for the sake of space—
he has risen up toward the ruddy summit of the honeyed mead, when his own body impelled his body.
You are taken with a support; for Prajāpati you are; this is your womb; for Prajāpati you.
Come now, O masters of barley, just as those who possess barley reap it in due order, separating it out;
bring here the food for those who have not come to the trimming of the sacred grass with their homage.
You are taken with a supporting formula; for Prajāpati you! This is your womb; for Prajāpati you!

Agni [obtained] the one-syllable [meter], the Aśvins the two-syllable, Viṣṇu the three-syllable, Soma the four-syllable, Savitṛ the five-syllable, Pūṣan the six-syllable, the Maruts the seven-syllable, Bṛhaspati the eight-syllable, Mitra the nine-syllable, Varuṇa the ten-syllable, Indra the eleven-syllable, the Viśve Devās the twelve-syllable, the Vasus the thirteen-syllable, the Rudras the fourteen-syllable, the Ādityas the fifteen-syllable, Aditi the sixteen-syllable, Prajāpati the seventeen-syllable, and Agni [again] with the one-syllable.

By means of a word of two syllables, the Aśvins won speech; by means of a word of three syllables, Viṣṇu won these three worlds; by means of a word of four syllables, Soma won four-footed cattle; by means of a word of five syllables, Savitṛ won the five directions; by means of a word of six syllables, Pūṣan won the six seasons; by means of a word of seven syllables, the Maruts won the Śakvarī meter; by means of a word of eight syllables, Bṛhaspati won the eight directions—the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate points; and by means of a word of nine syllables, Mitra won the nine [regions].

Varuṇa won the vital breaths with the ten-syllabled [meter]; Indra won the Virāj with the eleven-syllabled [meter]; the Viśvedevas won the Triṣṭubh with the twelve-syllabled [meter]; the Vasus won the Jagatī with the thirteen-syllabled [meter] and won the thirteenth month; the Rudras won fourteen nights with the fourteen-syllabled [meter]; the Ādityas won these intermediate half-months with the fifteen-syllabled [meter]; Aditi won the sixteenth; Prajāpati was the seventeenth; Agni won the month with the one-syllabled [meter]; the Aśvins [won] this earth.

With a two-syllabled [meter] Viṣṇu won the measuring-line, the intermediate space; with a three-syllabled [meter], the image, the heavenly world; with a four-syllabled [meter], Soma won the rivers and the stars; with a five-syllabled [meter], Savitṛ won the *paṅkti* meter. For that which is the five-syllabled *paṅkti* is indeed the *paṅkti*, since it consists of four sets of five syllables each.

Pūṣan won the Gāyatrī by means of six syllables, for it has four quarters of six syllables each; the Maruts won the Uṣṇih by means of seven syllables, for it has four quarters of seven syllables each; Bṛhaspati won the Anuṣṭubh by means of eight syllables, for it has four quarters of eight syllables each; Mitra won the Bṛhatī by means of nine syllables, for it has four quarters of nine syllables each; Varuṇa won the Virāj by means of ten syllables; and Indra [won it] by means of eleven syllables.

By means of the twelve-syllable [foot], the Viśvedevas conquered the Triṣṭubh; by means of the thirteen-syllable [foot], the Vasus conquered the thirteenth month; by means of the fourteen-syllable [foot], the Rudras conquered fourteen nights—those which lie between the half-months; the Ādityas conquered the fifteenth; Aditi conquered the sixteenth; and Prajāpati is the seventeenth. ||4||

The gods indeed saw the sacrifices separately, saying, "This one for me, this one for you. Then they all saw this [sacrifice] together; they exerted themselves toward it and they ran a race for it. Bṛhaspati won it. Bṛhaspati was indeed the domestic priest (*purohita*) of the gods; whatever the domestic priest hears as the sacred word (*brahman*), that belongs to the king. With that, he caused Indra to sacrifice, and he attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). This is that self-sovereign sacrifice; he who performs this sacrifice attains self-sovereignty. Because Bṛhaspati won it, therefore a Brāhmaṇa should perform the sacrifice.

Because he caused Indra to sacrifice with it, therefore the Rājanya [is so called]. Indeed, the gods brought various sacrifices; then Prajāpati brought this one. The gods desired a share in it; he gave the *Chandāṃsi* (metres) as the *Ujjitis* (victories) to them. Then Prajāpati sacrificed with this; he attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). This is the self-sovereign sacrifice; he who sacrifices with this attains self-sovereignty. Food is indeed *vāja*; he who, knowing thus, eats food, causes himself to be victorious (*vājayati*). Soma is the *Vājapeya*; he who, knowing thus, [drinks] Soma...

He drinks and indeed attains *vāja* (strength/victory). For as many gods as drank the *soma*, they attained *vāja*; therefore, everyone desires to drink the *soma*. Speech (*vāc*) is indeed the source of *vāja*. That speech, when perceived, became fourfold: three quarters are in these worlds, and one quarter is in animals. That which is in heaven is in the *bṛhatī* [meter] and in thunder; that which is in the intermediate space is in the wind and in the *vāmadevya* [sāman]; that which is on earth is in the fire and in the *rathantara* [sāman]; and that which is in animals—of that speech, what remained over, she placed in the *brāhmaṇa*.

They deposited it; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa speaks both kinds of speech, the divine and the human. He who knows thus produces power through his speech. That [power] which is in the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans], by that he comes to the sacrifice; that which is in the cattle, by that he calls him to the sacrifice. He who knows thus approaches him even before he is seen. For as much as speech is, so much he knows; for by speech it is given, and by speech it is bestowed. He who wins [something] with a Gāthā or a Nārāśaṃsī verse, there is nothing to be accepted from him, for he wins by untruth, for untruth indeed...

One should not accept a false verse or a Nārāśamsī from one who is intoxicated, for what is spoken by an intoxicated person is false; indeed, when he becomes sober, then he understands that [which was said]. || 5 ||

These seventeen cups are of two kinds; they belong to Prajāpati, for man is seventeenfold and belongs to Prajāpati: four limbs, the head, the neck, the trunk, and speech as the seventh; then ten vital breaths. Indeed, evil has clung to every limb of man; in that he draws the cups in an interlocking manner, he releases him from evil limb by limb. Soma is prosperity, while the *surā* with its *upayāma* vessels is evil. When the time arrives, they move forward with the Soma cups and backward with the *surā* cups with *upayāmas*; thus he purifies him from evil.

Therefore they say, "One who has sacrificed with the Vājapeya is indeed purified," for it purifies him from evil. These five cups are drawn; the sacrifice is fivefold; verily he wins the sacrifice itself. They all belong to Indra; verily he bestows sensory power upon him in a single unitary form.

Soma is indeed the highest food of the gods; surā is the highest food of men. When the Soma cups and the surā cups are drawn together, by means of the higher food he secures the lower food. Soma is the brilliance of the *brahman*; surā is the impurity of food. When the Soma cups and the surā cups are drawn together, by the brilliance of the *brahman* he places brilliance in himself, and by the impurity of food he casts off impurity; [he wins] the world of the gods.

With the *soma* cups he conquers the world of men; with the *surā* cups he gratifies the self; with the *surā* cups [he gratifies] the wife. Therefore they say: "The sacrificer of the *Vājapeya* is reborn in that world," for by means of the sacrifice he has conquered it. With the verse addressed to Savitṛ—"O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice toward fortune"—he offers at every joint of the body. For this is a sacrifice whose parts have been scattered; who indeed knows how much they place upon it? It is for the sake of completeness and for impulsion.

With the verse, "At the impulse of strength, the great mother," he brings down the chariot; thus, impelled by both this [earth] and Savitṛ, he brings it down for the winning of strength. With the words, "In the waters is immortality, in the waters is healing," he washes the horses; for the horse is born from the waters, so he produces them from their own womb, and furthermore, he makes them pure and fit for sacrifice. With the formula, "Vāyu has yoked thee, or Manu has yoked thee," he yokes them; for no human is worthy to yoke these; he yokes them by means of the deities. Of the waters...
With the formula, "O swift-goer, do not fall," he wipes the forehead-ornaments; this merely restates what has already been explained previously.

The whole [sacrifice] consists of seventeen; Prajāpati is seventeenfold; verily he attains Prajāpati. They cause the drums to resound; for speech entered the forest, and it is that very [speech] he wins. "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, of true impulse," [he says]; impelled by Savitṛ, he indeed mounts the thunderbolt. "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, of true impulse," [he says]; impelled by Savitṛ, he indeed mounts the chariot for the winning of booty (*vāja*). The Brahman priest follows after; the Brahman is indeed Prajāpati of the sacrifice.

Prajāpati impelled Indra; Prajāpati himself impels him away from the thunderbolt. He sings the Sāman; the Sāman is indeed truth; by means of truth he causes him to rise up. He recites the verses of the Vājins for the winning of strength. They race with chariots that have been assigned; for by means of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) the gods went to the world of heaven. In that they race with chariots that have been assigned, he goes to the world of heaven by means of the sacrificial fee itself.

The garment is made of *darbha* grass for the sake of purification; he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the *ujjitī* verses, for the *ujjitīs* are speech—it is speech indeed that he conquers. The gods, when the plants were ripe, entered into a race; Bṛhaspati won it, and he chose the wild rice (*nīvāra*). That is why wild rice is called *nīvāra*. Bṛhaspati indeed won this [sacrifice]; he makes him a sharer in that very [conquest]. He deposits [the grain] in the *cātvāla* pit; for here indeed was this sun; the gods, having enclosed it with these two [worlds], caused it to go to yonder world. It is for the attainment of the heavenly world. "Come to me... [he says].

"May the impulse of strength come hither"—with these words he offers oblations when they have returned; thus he places within himself that very strength which they have won. "This has become your true agreement, which you made with Indra"—[he says this]. "O trees, you have caused Indra to win; be unyoked!"—with this *yajus* they are indeed yoked, and with this *yajus* they are unyoked. "The two steeds, winners of strength"—with these words he makes the draft animals smell [the offering]; thus he makes them sharers. "O steeds, winners of strength"—thus he assigns [the portions]; verily, he gratifies them at the pressing.

They carry away half-loads and portions fit for the gods; those who run the race, from them he purchases by that means whatever prize they win. They carry away a honey-mixture for the Brahman; by that he purchases it for the Brahman alone. The prince eats the *kakubha* fruits; the *kakubha* is indeed vigor, and the prince is vigor; thus he bestows vigor upon vigor. "O wife, ascend the chariot!"—thinking "I shall ascend," he converses with the wife by way of the *svara* (tone); this is the wife's taking hold of the sacrifice, and furthermore—

He places the pair itself at the beginning of the sacrifice for the sake of procreation. With the words, "May life be perfected through the sacrifice," the person indeed becomes whole and goes to the heavenly world. The *caṣāla* (top-ring) is made of wheat; wheat belongs to Prajāpati, being half of all plants; thus he goes to the heavenly world together with food. With the calls, "To strength, svāhā! To impulse, svāhā! there are these thirteen oblations. There are thirteen months in a year, and the year is the heavenly world; verily, he wins for him the year in the heavenly world.

He establishes himself upon that world as its support. They present him with bags of saline soil; saline soil belongs to Prajāpati, so it is with food that they present him. Indeed, he who goes to yonder world departs from this world; in that they present him with bags of saline soil, by that he does not depart from these worlds. He descends onto a goat-skin and a gold plate; the goat-skin is cattle, so in that he descends onto the goat-skin, he establishes himself in cattle. Gold is brilliance; in that he descends onto the gold plate, he establishes himself in brilliance.

It becomes firmly established; it is a *śatamāna* [weight], for man has a lifespan of a hundred years and possesses a hundredfold vigor; thus he secures both life and vigor. He offers with each kind of food using the *vājaprasavyā* verses, for the securing of food. There are seven [verses], for there are seven meters; by means of the meters, he secures food. The meters are indeed speech; by means of speech, he secures food. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the speech of Sarasvatī..."

"By means of the chariot-pole, with the chariot-pole, I consecrate this one, the son of such-and-such a lineage, the son of such-and-such a mother, with the sovereign power of Bṛhaspati"—if a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, for this is the Bṛhaspatisava; "with the sovereign power of Indra"—if a Rājanya, for this is the Indrasava. (8)

Now, these *atigrāhya* cups are for the attainment of that supreme food which has not yet been secured. These animals are for the attainment of the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*). By means of the offering to Agni, he obtains the *agniṣṭoma*, for the *agniṣṭoma* is established upon Agni. By means of the offering to Indra and Agni, he obtains the *uktha* chants, for the *ukthas* belong to Indra and Agni. By means of the offering to Indra, he obtains the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, for the *ṣoḍaśin* belongs to Indra. Through the *agniṣṭoma* he preserves his very self; through the *uktha*, his out-breath and in-breath; through the chant of the *ṣoḍaśin*, his vigor; and through the *atirātra*, his speech.

Through the *bṛhat* chant he establishes progeny in this very world; through the *agniṣṭoma* he establishes himself in the intermediate region; through the chant of the *ṣoḍaśin* he establishes himself in the heavenly world; through the *atirātra* on those paths that lead to the gods; and through the *bṛhat* chant on the firmament (*nāka*). Indeed, there are only so many worlds of the gods as there are these; he attains all the worlds of the gods. Now, this ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī is for the attainment of that seventeenth chant which has not yet been secured. And this spotted cow dedicated to the Maruts—for the gods and...

The Asuras were also in this world; these were not the gods, nor were these the Asuras. Those gods saw this speckled barren cow belonging to the Maruts; they seized her and with her they appropriated the second world—the world of the Asuras. That from which they cut portions is the world of the gods; that from which they do not cut portions is the world of the Asuras. By means of this [cow], he appropriates the second world, indeed the world of his rival, for the rival is in the second world. Of these five [animals], the one dedicated to Sarasvatī is the last; of the other seventeen, the one dedicated to Sarasvatī is the last. Speech, indeed, is Sarasvatī.

Sarasvatī continues the sacrifice by means of speech itself. Whatever the learned man fails to do for the sacrifice, or whatever the unlearned man omits, that is a flaw; Sarasvatī makes that right through speech alone. These seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati are sacrificed; Prajāpati is seventeenfold; thus he attains Prajāpati. They are of a single form; thus he bestows vigor upon him in a single way. The one for Sarasvatī is the last; Sarasvatī is indeed speech; verily, he finds firm support in speech. || 9 ||

The *Rathantara* Sāman is used for the sake of blessing and victory. This earth is indeed the *Rathantara*; it is upon this very earth that he is consecrated. The Vājapeya is of diverse origin; being undefined (*anirukta*), it belongs to Prajāpati, and its Sāmans are undefined. Because of this, it is of diverse origin. Since the morning libations (*prātassavana*) are undefined, it is of common origin. The morning libations are undefined, and Prajāpati is undefined; thus he attains Prajāpati himself. At midday they chant with verses containing the word "strength" (*vāja*); strength is indeed food, and this is for the attainment of food. At the Ārbhava Pavamāna, they chant with verses containing the word "wonderful" (*citra*).

It becomes the best of the *ukthas*, reaching as far as the very jaws of heaven; thus he extends [the sacrifice] forward toward the later hymns. The *Bṛhat* Sāman is used; for that which exceeds [the norm] exceeds toward that world (heaven), and the *Bṛhat* is worthy to reach that world. The *Bṛhat* is sensory power and vigor; verily, he establishes himself in sensory power and vigor. They chant on verses addressed to Viṣṇu containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*; for this body of Prajāpati, which contains the word *śipiviṣṭa*, is rich in cattle; therefore, they chant on verses containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*.
They praise with an extra [verse]; this [victim] is indeed extra, Śipiviṣṭa is extra; by means of the extra, he obtains the extra.
Thus ends the fourteenth section, named Vājapeya, in the Iṣṭimikā of the Caraka recension of the Śrī Yajurveda Kāṭhaka. 14.

Now begins the fifteenth section: The Śrī-Rājasūya. There is a cake on eight potsherds for Anumati; a milch-cow is the sacrificial fee. That which remains behind when the [stakes] are driven westward beyond the yoke-pin is for Nirṛti on one potsherd; these two cakes they bake together. They proceed with the rite for Nirṛti first. Having gone southward, having placed a single firebrand on a naturally formed saline spot, he offers oblations with two stalks of *visraṃsikā* grass, saying: "May Nirṛti enjoy it, Svāhā! A garment with a torn edge is the sacrificial fee. Those [stakes] which remain behind when driven northward, having gone toward the water and having dug up a mound of earth from an anthill—

"I offer this; I drive away the *kṣetriya* (hereditary disease) of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, svāhā! I cover up the *kṣetriya* of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so," thus he says as he covers it. There is a rice-porridge (*caru*) in ghee for the Adityas who are present (*bhuvad-vat*), with a choice bull as the sacrificial fee. For Agni-Viṣṇu there is a cake on eleven potsherds, with a dwarf ox as the sacrificial fee. For Agni-Soma there is a cake on eleven potsherds, with gold as the sacrificial fee. For Indra-Agni there is a cake on eleven potsherds, with a bull-ox as the sacrificial fee. For Agni there is a cake on eight potsherds, and for Mahendra there is curd, with a linen garment as the sacrificial fee.

There is a gentle offering of śyāmāka grain; a brownish-pigmented animal for Indra and Agni on twelve potsherds; an offering of śyāmāka grain for the Viśvedevas; and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth. A first-born calf is the sacrificial fee. ||1||

There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, a pap for Pūṣan, milk or barley-gruel for Vāyu Niyutvat, a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra Śunāsīra, and a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya. A pair of camels is the sacrificial fee, or else a plough with twelve oxen. There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake made of barley on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, a pap of Gavidhuka seeds for Rudra, and a cooked oblation (sānnāyya) for Indra; a milch-cow and a draft-ox are the sacrificial fees. From the place where the waters flow down, they bring Apāmārga plants; these they grind into flour.

They perform these [rites] for them; he offers with a ladle made of *parṇa*-wood, having gone to the south, upon a self-made saline depression, at the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, and with the vigor of Indra: "Thou art a slayer of Rākṣasas, svāhā! The Rākṣasa is slain; we have struck down the Rākṣasa. The boon is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."

May those gods who sit in the east, led by Agni, slayers of demons, protect us; may they aid us; to them, Svāhā! May those gods who sit in the south, led by Yama, slayers of demons, protect us; may they aid us; to them, Svāhā! May those gods who sit in the west, led by the Maruts, slayers of demons, protect us; may they aid us; to them, Svāhā! May those gods who sit in the north, led by Mitra and Varuṇa, slayers of demons, protect us; may they aid us; to them, Svāhā! May those gods who sit above, led by Soma...
