The *gāyatrī* is brilliance, the *anuṣṭubh* is the sacrifice, and the *triṣṭubh* is power. Verily, with both brilliance and power, he encloses the sacrifice on both sides within his own self.

He digs with two verses addressed to Savitṛ for the sake of impulsion; he finds smoke with the first and light with the second. With two [verses], the sacrificer is established, for he is two-footed. "Thou art the back of the waters, the womb of Agni"—with these words he takes up the lotus leaf; for this is indeed the back of the waters and the womb of Agni. He gathers [the materials] with the lotus leaf; verily, he gathers it with its own womb for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. He gathers with a black antelope skin; the black antelope skin is the sacrifice; verily, by means of the sacrifice he gathers the sacrifice so that it may not be spilled.

For indeed, no sacrifice is spilled in a sacrifice; this black antelope skin is truly the form of the Brahman. With the Brahman and with the Ṛg and Sāman, he prepares it. He spreads it [the two skins] with the words, "You two are a shelter, you two are a shield. This lotus leaf is indeed this [earth], and the black antelope skin is that [sky]; thus he spreads these two together. "Both of you, unbroken and broad"—for these two are indeed unbroken and broad—"both of you, wide-extending"—therefore these two are wide-extending—"support Agni Purīṣya"—for he is indeed Purīṣya—"dwell together."

"Finding the light, facing each other with their breast, by themselves"—therefore these two, though being separate, face each other, intending to bear Agni within; "the luminous one, unaging"—he thus bestows eternal light upon him. "Thou art the filler of the soil, the sustainer of all"—for he is indeed the filler of the soil and the sustainer of all. "Atharvan was the first to churn thee forth, O Agni"—Atharvan is Prajāpati; Prajāpati churned him forth in the beginning; thus Prajāpati himself generates him. "Thee, Dadhyañc the Ṛṣi..."—Dadhyañc was...

The Atharvaṇa was full of splendor; with that very [splendor] he gathers him together. With the verse, "Thee, O Pāthya, the bull," he repeats what has already been said before. He pours it out with four [verses]. For there are four meters; with the meters he thus pours him out. He should pour it out for a Brāhmaṇa with Gāyatrī verses, for the Brāhmaṇa is of Gāyatra nature; for a Rājanya with Triṣṭubh verses, for the Rājanya is of Traiṣṭubha nature; for a Vaiśya with Jagatī verses, for the Vaiśya is of Jāgata nature. Or, if he should so desire, he may pour it out with both kinds of verses according to their respective meters.

"May he become more prosperous"—the Gāyatrī is indeed splendor (*tejas*) and the Triṣṭubh is power (*indriya*); thus he bestows both splendor and power upon him in a harmonious manner. He mixes [the clay] with eight verses; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of Gāyatra nature; as great as Agni is, so much of him he gathers together. With "Sit down, O Hotṛ," he causes the deities to settle within him; with "Settle down, O Hotṛ," he causes the human beings to settle; with "Do thou sit down," he causes the birds to settle. With "For the noble one was born at the beginning of days," he causes the gods and humans who have settled within him to be procreated. 4.

"Release the divine waters, full of sweetness"—this is for the establishment of plants. "From their place may the plants rise up with goodly fruit"—therefore the plants bear fruit. "May Vāyu Mātariśvan bestow [it] upon thee"—therefore Vāyu carries rain; Vāyu is indeed breath (prāṇa); verily he bestows breath upon him. "To him, O God, let there be *vaṣaṭ* unto thee"—the seasons are six; verily he places rain in the seasons; therefore it rains season by season. That which is the manifest *vaṣaṭ*—

If he were not to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, the sacrifice would become stale; if he were not to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, the Rakṣases would destroy the sacrifice. Therefore, [he says], "O God, let there be *vaṣaṭ* for thee!"—thus, being spoken indirectly, the *vaṣaṭ* call does not become stale, and the Rakṣases do not destroy the sacrifice.

If he were to offer with clarified butter, he would afflict the earth with heat; he pours out water for the sake of pacification, so that there may be no burning. With the words, "Well-born, with light," he does so, for it is at this very moment—when it is being gathered—that it is born; thus, while it is already born, he bestows light upon it. With the words, "He has sat down in the protection, the refuge, the light," he establishes it in the *brahman*, for the protection and refuge are indeed the *brahman*. With the words, "O Agni, Vibhāvasu, clothe yourself in the all-formed garment," the meters are indeed the garment of Agni; thus, by means of the meters, he clothes it. Or rather, it is the *anuṣṭubh* [that is the garment].

The dear body of Agni—verily, with his own dear body he encloses him. He who knows thus becomes a possessor of clothing. This [fire] when bound is indeed the shaft of Varuṇa; with the verses, "Arise, O you of fair sacrifice," and "Upright for our protection," he raises up the shaft of Varuṇa. With two verses he does so, for the sacrificer has two feet; it is for stability. "Once born, you are the embryo of the two worlds"—these two are indeed the two worlds, and this [fire] is their embryo; verily, he establishes him in these two. "O Agni, beautiful one, distributed among the plants."

Therefore, Agni goes forth toward all plants, neighing loudly from his mothers; for the plants are indeed his mothers, and it is from them that he leads him forth. With the words, "Be firm, O strong-limbed one," he bestows stability upon the donkey itself; therefore, among animals, it is the bearer of the greatest burden. With the words, "Be auspicious to the human offspring, O Aṅgiras," he pacifies him, for at this time he indeed causes distress to the offspring. This is for the sake of peace.

"Do not scorch heaven and earth; do not [scorch] the atmosphere; do not [scorch] the trees"—thus he pacifies him for these very worlds. "Let the prize-winner go forth, neighing loudly"—this is for the sake of complete attainment. "May he not fall before his full span of life"—verily, he bestows life upon him; therefore the donkey reaches its full span of life, and therefore people are afraid when a donkey dies. "The male, bearing Agni, the male"—for he is indeed a male, and he bears the male. "The embryo of the waters, belonging to the ocean"—for he is indeed the embryo of the waters, belonging to the ocean. "O Agni, come for the feast."

"Thus, by means of Agni, the gods first moved across this [world] for the sake of pervasion (*vīti*). This [Agni], having now departed from his abode and not yet reached a firm foundation, thinks ill of both the sacrificer and the *adhvaryu*. [The *adhvaryu* says: 'Right (*ṛta*), truth (*satya*)! Right, truth! This earth is indeed Right, and yonder sky is Truth; he thus establishes him upon these two. [He says: 'O plants, receive this Agni, auspicious as he approaches you here! The plants are indeed his portion; with them he makes him well-settled. And furthermore, those [plants]..."

He causes it to move forward; by means of its own essence, he establishes it. With the words, "Flowering, with good fruit," therefore the plants take on fruit. He brings it down with two verses; the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability. With the words, "With wide power," he loosens it; he thus releases Varuṇa’s noose. With the words, "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," he pours out water; the waters are peaceful, and by means of the peaceful waters, he pacifies his impurity. With three verses—Agni is indeed threefold—he pacifies the impurity of Agni as far as Agni extends.

He pacifies it with the hair of a goat; for the goat is the dear body of Agni—verily, he unites him with his own dear body. He mixes it with pebbles for support, and with potsherds from an earthen vessel; verily, he afflicts the wild animals with pain. If he were to mix it with [hair from] domestic animals, he would afflict domestic animals with pain. Therefore, among animals that are being born, these are the smallest; for they have been afflicted with pain. ||5||

"Mitra, having united with the earth"—for this is indeed Varuṇa’s curse; by means of Mitra, he thus approaches Varuṇa’s curse. "Rudra, having united with the earth, [unite] with the Vasus and Rudras"—by these very deities Prajāpati created her; by them alone he unites her. He restrains her with some [verses] and addresses her with others; thus he creates a pair. Moreover, he thereby secures the blessing from the very middle of the sacrifice. "Thou art the head of Makha"—Makha is indeed the sacrifice; [it is] for the sake of the sacrifice itself.

"He makes the head with the words, 'May the Vasus make you with the Gāyatrī metre'—with these very deities Prajāpati made it, and with them he now makes it. He makes it with three elevations; these worlds are three, and thus he obtains these very worlds. He makes it with five elevations; the sacrifice is fivefold, and thus he wins the sacrifice."

"May you sustain offspring for me"—this is indeed a blessing; it is the milking of the meters. He should make it a cubit long, for the sacrifice is commensurate with man; thus he makes it commensurate with the man who is the sacrifice. Or he should make it as long as he can span with his two arms, for so much strength is there in man; thus he makes it commensurate with strength. Or he should make it a span long, for the mouth is this much; Agni is the mouth of the gods; thus he makes it commensurate with the mouth. Or he should make it of unlimited size, for the attainment of the unlimited. He should make it four-teat, for the milking of Aditi.

One should milk the six teats for the seasons; one should milk the eight teats for the sake of milking the *gāyatrī*; one should milk the two teats of Heaven and Earth. One should fashion a nine-edged [spoon] for malevolent magic. The *trivṛt* is a thunderbolt; verily he hurls the thunderbolt at his enemy. "Thou art the girth of Aditi; may Aditi grasp thy hollow," with this *yajus* he fashions the hollow; for men fashion it without a *yajus*, and thus they distinguish it from a human vessel. If this [spoon] were to break before the cooking is finished, the sacrificer would meet with ruin and his sacrifice would perish.

Having made [the fire-pan] with the verse, "Having made this earth-mouthed," he thus entrusts it to the deities. With the formulas, "May the Vasus fumigate thee with the Gāyatrī metre," and so forth, he fumigates it; for by these very deities Prajāpati fumigated it, and so he fumigates it with them. He fumigates it with horse-dung; the horse belongs to Prajāpati, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati; [he does this] for the sake of common origin. He fumigates it with seven [verses]; the fire-pan is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and there are seven vital breaths; he thus places the vital breaths in the head. Therefore, there are seven vital breaths in the head. 6.

“May Aditi, the goddess, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, [establish] thee”—for Aditi is indeed this earth; thus with Aditi he digs into Aditi, so as not to cause injury to her, for one does not harm oneself. “The wives of the gods, thee”—for the wives of the gods first established her here; with them he establishes her. “The Dhiṣaṇās, thee”—the Dhiṣaṇās are indeed knowledge; thus with knowledge he kindles her. “The Varutrīs, thee”—the Varutrīs are indeed the Hotṛ-offices; with the Hotṛ-offices he cooks her. “The Gnās, thee”—the Gnās are indeed the meters.

With the *gnā* verses and the meters he cooks her; with the words "O *janayas*, you of unsevered wings,"—the *janayas* are indeed the wives of the gods, for they cooked her first; it is with them that he now cooks her.

"May it ripen twice," he says; therefore, the grain ripens twice in a year. He cooks with six [verses]; for there are six seasons; by means of the seasons the gods cooked these wives of the gods, and by them he cooks her. "Varuṇa’s fetter is indeed this [fire] when kindled," [he says]; "of Mitra, the supporter of men"—thus by means of Mitra he approaches Varuṇa’s fetter. "May the god Savitṛ lift thee up," he says; he lifts her up with a verse addressed to Savitṛ for the sake of impulsion. "Unwavering, fill the regions and the quarters on earth," he says; therefore Agni shines throughout all the quarters. "Arise! [he says].

"O Great One, stand upright; may you remain firm"—with these words he indeed makes it firm. For if this [pot] were to break, the sacrificer would meet with ruin and his sacrifice would perish. "O Mitra, I entrust this fire-pan to you"—Mitra is indeed the Brahman; thus he entrusts it to the Brahman.

If it should break, one should join it with those potsherds and make another; that itself is the atonement for the sacrifice from that point. With the words, "May the Vasus moisten thee with the Gāyatrī metre," it is indeed by means of the metres that this [vessel] is made, by the metres it is heated, and by the metres it is baked. It is the metres themselves that they moisten with the metres. An unmoistened vessel is indeed demonic; in that he moistens it, he makes it belong to the gods. He moistens it with goat's milk, for that is most related to Agni and is perfect; moreover, it is with the highest milk.

Now, these animals are sacrificed for the fires, which are indeed desires; by means of these, he conquers all desires and secures all desires. If he were not to sacrifice the animals, his cattle would remain unsecured; if he were to let the rite conclude [without them], the heads would become exhausted; if he were not to let it conclude, he would cut off the sacrifice. In that he sacrifices the animals, he thereby secures cattle; in that he releases them after they have been carried around the fire, it is to prevent the exhaustion of the heads; with one [animal] he brings the rite to completion.

For the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice—since Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice—he thus establishes the sacrifice in the sacrifice and does not interrupt the sacrifice. Those bulls which are castrated belong to Indra; if they, being dedicated to Indra, are offered to the fires, he creates discord between the deities. He should therefore use *triṣṭubh* verses addressed to Agni as the invitatory and offering formulas; since *triṣṭubhs* belong to Indra, by that very fact they are made to belong to Indra, and he does not create discord between the deities. Now, this...

The hornless white goat belongs to Vāyu. This hornless goat is offered in place of all animals: by its being hornless, it represents the horse; by its having a beard, it represents man; and by its being eight-hoofed, it represents the eight-hoofed animals. One should use two verses addressed to Vāyu as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for the sake of the sacrificer’s stability and to prevent madness. If they were not addressed to Vāyu, the sacrificer would either go mad or fall down. The [verses] should be addressed to Vāyu and contain the word "bright" (*śukra*), for Vāyu is the brilliance of Agni; therefore, when the wind blows sideways, Agni follows after it.

That very brilliance of his follows him; for Vāyu is the dear abode of cattle, and Vāyu is the breath. When there is an offering to Vāyu, the cattle, recognizing him, wait upon him. They deliberate: "Should it be made for Vāyu? Or for Prajāpati? If he were to make it for Vāyu, he would depart from Prajāpati; if he were to make it for Prajāpati, he would depart from Vāyu. Whatever animal is sacrificed in the fire, for that one he should prepare a cake for Agni Vaiśvānara; by the fact that the animal is for Vāyu, he does not depart from Vāyu; and by the fact that [the cake] is for Prajāpati, [he does not depart from Prajāpati].

The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) does not depart from Prajāpati because of that; in that it is on twelve potsherds—the year has twelve months, and Agni Vaiśvānara is the year—it does not depart from the nature of Vaiśvānara because of that. ||8||

He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu. Agni is indeed all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus he obtains both the deities and the sacrifice. Agni is the mouth of the gods, and Viṣṇu is their ultimate end; he has thus grasped both ends of the sacrifice. Then there is a pap of ghee for the Ādityas. The Ādityas indeed went from here to yonder world; the Ādityas are these creatures, and they are closest to the Ādityas. He approaches his own deity. It is prepared in ghee, for the Ādityas have ghee as their portion. Then [he offers] to Agni Vaiśvānara.

The year is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara; there are twelve months in the year. [This is] for the attainment of the year. When one piles a fire-altar that is not provided with a womb, it enters the womb of the sacrificer and consumes him. The year is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara, and the year is the womb of Agni. In that he offers to Agni Vaiśvānara, he piles the altar as one truly possessed of a womb. This body of Agni which belongs to Vaiśvānara is his dear form. In that he offers to Agni Vaiśvānara, he prepares an oblation for his own dear body.

Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed desire; he takes up the desired body. When one offers to Agni Vaiśvānara, he attains that desire for which the offering is made. As to why it is on twelve potsherds: the year has twelve months. Those offspring that fall away do so from the year; those that find support find support in the year. Having found support in the year itself, he bears Agni. ||9||

He offers six yajus formulas that have been studied; for there are six seasons, it is by means of the seasons that he consecrates him, and by means of the seasons he raises up his vital power. He offers these seven; for there are seven breaths, it is by means of the breaths that he consecrates him. He offers them separately; therefore the breaths have separate powers—eye, ear, and speech. He offers the last with an anuṣṭubh verse; for the anuṣṭubh is speech, and thus he bestows speech as the highest. Therefore speech is the highest of the breaths, and it speaks what is ordained. Indeed, the anuṣṭubh comprises all the meters.

Cattle are the meters; cattle are food. Verily, he wins cattle and the eating of food. In that he heats it over the flame, he thereby wins what has been; in that [he heats it] over the embers, he thereby wins what is yet to be. He should heat it over the embers, for what is yet to be is more than what has been. "Do not be afraid, do not be harmed," [he says]; verily, he makes it firm. "Unharmed, rise up in this sacrifice," [he says] for the sake of attainment. He heats it with two verses; the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability.

The consecrated one is, as it were, the embryo of him who desires to become pre-eminent; from that very source he produces him. Having churned [the fire], he should place [the wood] upon it when its luster has departed, for it has already come into being and thus approaches its own deity. He should fetch [wood] from elsewhere and place it upon it if he should desire, "May I produce a rival for him"; verily, he produces a rival for him. He should place it upon wood that has been roasted for one who desires food; for food is prepared on what is roasted; verily, he secures food from its own source. He should place it upon a tree that blazes at the top.

This [offering] belongs to one desiring heaven; it is the heavenly one among the fires for the attainment of the world of heaven. With the words, "The flowing [substance], mixed with ghee," he places a piece of *kṛmuka* wood that has been smoothed and anointed with ghee. For the *kṛmuka* entered the dear body of Agni; ghee is brilliance. Thus, he anoints his dear body with brilliance. He places *muñja* grass [on top]; the *muñja* grass is indeed strength (*ūrj*); verily, he bestows strength upon him. With the words, "From the highest gathering-place," he places a piece of *udumbara* wood; the *udumbara* is indeed strength; verily, he bestows strength upon him.

With the verse, "From the highest distance," he offers a fuel-stick of *vikaṅkata* wood; for when Agni was created, the *vikaṅkata* luster reached him, and thus he secures that very [luster]. With the verse, "O Agni, whatever [beings]..."—formerly, indeed, Agni would not burn what had not been cut by an axe; the seer Prayoga made it palatable for him with these [verses]. In that he places these kindling-sticks, he makes the fuel-pile palatable for him; his food becomes palatable for him who knows thus. The meters are indeed the womb of Agni; in that he places [the sticks] with the meters, he [places them] in his own womb.
"With the womb he bears [the child] night after night, never failing"—with this he indeed invokes a blessing; "kindling Agni at the navel of the earth"—with this he conquers hostile armies.

With the verse, "With that army which is fearless," the gods, seeing that the *rakṣases* sought to slay Agni as soon as he was born, beheld these *ṛc*s; with them they struck away the *rakṣases* from him. When he places these kindling-sticks (*samidh*) on the fire, it is for the striking away of the *rakṣases*. Now, regarding this *mālimlava*: the gods and the Asuras were contending; those gods beheld this *mālimlava*, and by means of it they overcame the Asuras. When he places the kindling-sticks with this [verse], it is for the overcoming of his rival. Therefore, in whatever year they pile the fire-altar, [they do so].

Those who seize him become thieves; with the words, "With those jaws of yours that are unafraid," he takes a branch of *udumbara* wood. Indeed, when the gods divided the vital strength (*ūrj*), from that the *udumbara* was born; thus, for one who has been born, he bestows vital strength. With the words, "O Agni, with your two jaws, [seize] the robbers," he takes a branch of *aśvattha* wood. This is indeed the conqueror of rivals among the trees; it serves for victory. When he says, "with your two jaws," he should mentally contemplate the one whom he hates; for thought is swifter than speech. Having thus turned him into an oblation, he presents him to Agni. [The verse continues: "Those among the people..."

"Malimlava," [with these words] he takes a splinter of *vaikaṅkata* wood; for when Agni was created, his radiance reached the *vikaṅkata* tree, and thus he secures that very radiance. "May he who acts with hostility toward us... [with these words] he takes one of *śamī* wood for the sake of pacification; "may he who reviles us and seeks to harm us... [with these words]. Therefore, one who has piled the fire-altar should not utter anything vulgar. "Sharpened is my spiritual power (*brahman*)," [he says]; by means of the *brahman* he sharpens the ruling power (*kṣatra*), and by the ruling power he sharpens the *brahman*. Therefore, the ruling power with the *brahman* as its domestic chaplain surpasses other ruling powers; therefore, the *brahman* with the ruling power as its protector surpasses other *brāhmaṇas*. He incites them.

"May my arms be exceedingly lustrous, and likewise my strength"—thus he invokes a blessing. "With the sacred word (*brahman*) I destroy the enemies; I raise up my own people"—this is according to the sacrificial formula (*yajuḥ*).

"The shining gold disk has shone far and wide"—with these words he should fasten on the gold disk. Agni is death, and gold is immortality; verily, by means of immortality he places a barrier between himself and death. It has twenty-one knobs for support; there are twenty-one worlds of the gods; from them he drives away his rival. He should place the knobs on the outside; verily, he drives him away from this very world. He turns it over on both sides while fastening it on; verily, he excludes him from both worlds.

With the verse "Night and Dawn," he encompasses him by means of day and night. With the words "The gods, the givers of wealth, uphold Agni,"—the gods who give wealth are indeed the vital breaths—he upholds him by means of the vital breaths. There is a sling with six supports; the seasons are six, so he encompasses him by means of the seasons. It has twelve supports; the year consists of twelve months, so he encompasses him by means of the year. It is made of *muñja* grass; *muñja* is strength, so he encompasses him by means of strength.

One should not wear it below the navel; Agni might burn up his seed. One should wear it above the navel; for above the navel is Agni together with all the deities. Thus he wears the deities together with the deities themselves. With the verse, "All forms," he fastens it on for the sake of impulsion. He fastens it while sitting; therefore offspring are born sitting. "Thou art a fair-winged bird, a Garuḍa"—these are indeed the materials of Agni; by these he gathers Agni himself. This is the dear abode of Agni; verily, he wins that. "Go to heaven! [he says].

"O Lord of Heaven!"—this was for the sake of the total conquest of the heavenly world. These worlds belonged to the Asuras. The gods said to Viṣṇu, "As far as this youth strides, so much shall we give you. He strode across this [earth] once with the Gāyatrī metre; he strode across the intermediate space once with the Triṣṭubh metre; he strode across the sky once with the Jagatī metre; and he strode across the quarters once with the Anuṣṭubh metre. The gods thus recovered these worlds from the Asuras. Then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who knows thus...

As he strides forward, he takes possession of these very worlds from his rival; he prospers by himself, and his rival is defeated. With the verse, "Agni has cried out," Vatsapri Bhalandana indeed obtained the dear abode of Agni; by this [verse], one obtains the dear abode of Agni. With the verses, "O Agni, come hither! O Agni Angiras, return with strength and wealth," he returns; therefore, domestic animals return from the forest to the village in the evening. He uses four [verses], for cattle have four feet; the sacrificial fee consists of cattle.

It turns around; therefore the right half of the self is more vigorous. With "I have brought thee hither," he brings it, for he indeed brings it. With "May all the people desire thee; establish the kingdom upon us," he should meditate in his mind upon whomever he desires, thinking, "May he become the ruler"; verily he becomes the ruler. With "O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us," Śunaḥśepa Ājīgarti, seized by Varuṇa, saw this [verse]; by it he was indeed released from the bond of Varuṇa. By this very verse one releases the bond of Varuṇa at the outset.

"Greatly has he risen erect at the dawns," he says; darkness is indeed evil, and by this [verse] he drives away evil. "The swan dwelling in purity"—he thus goes to the seven [verses] and gratifies them. With the word "sitting" (sad), he establishes him firmly in his proper place. He places him upon a stool; for he who is carried in the fire-pan is consecrated among the fires, therefore he places him upon a stool. If he were to place him below, the embryos would be prone to miscarriage; he places him above for the support of the embryos so that they do not miscarry. He worships with three [verses]; there are three worlds.
The vital breaths are prāṇa, vyāna, and apāna; he places those very breaths in the sacrificer. These are the three worlds; he prospers in these very worlds. ||11||

Now, this is the Vātsapra hymn. By means of it, Vatsaprī Bhālandana won for himself the beloved abode of Agni; by means of it, one wins the beloved abode of Agni. By means of it, he indeed defeated the censure of the seers; by means of it, one defeats evil censure. By means of it, he indeed conquered the curses; he who, knowing thus, worships with this hymn, conquers the curses. In that he takes the steps, he thereby establishes his journey; in that he worships, he thereby establishes his rest on the preceding day.

On the following day he departs; on [the next] day he returns. Therefore, while the minds of some other creatures are set on wandering, those of others are set on security. Therefore, the wanderer is the master of security; therefore, the wanderer settles in a place of security. It consists of eleven verses; the Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables, and the Triṣṭubh is vigor; verily, he wins vigor.

In ancient times, it belonged to the Ekepas; then the seers saw this as a "dvīṣam" (double-layered) installation for Agni, and therefore they perform the installation of Agni with a dvīṣam. This [installation] is now made in imitation of that dvīṣam. With the words, "Thee, O All-Gods," he raises him up; the All-Gods are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); verily, by means of the vital breaths, he raises him up. "The All-Gods are indeed men"; verily, by means of men, he raises him up. With the words, "O Agni, may they bear thee with their thoughts," he prospers him with that very thought for which he raises him up. "Forward, O Agni..."

With the words, "O luminous one, go forth," he indeed causes these creatures to suffer heat at this time; [therefore] he should follow with the mantra, "Agni has cried out for peace. If he should sneeze, he should recite, "For they carry thee on a wagon; therefore the wagoner and the charioteer are most honored among guests. With the words, "O Lord of food, give us food," he makes the food palatable for him. With the words, "of the healthy, the vigorous," he means "of the disease-free. With the words, "Further the giver; give us strength for our bipeds and quadrupeds," he invokes a blessing. [He offers] with the fuel-stick to Agni.

Having anointed the fuel-stick with ghee, he places it on the fire with the words, "Make it burn brightly. Just as one cooks a meal rich in clarified butter for a Brāhmaṇa guest, even so should he place the stick with a *gāyatrī* verse for a Brāhmaṇa, for the Brāhmaṇa is connected to the *gāyatrī*; with a *triṣṭubh* verse for a Rājanya, for the Rājanya is connected to the *triṣṭubh*; and with a *jagatī* verse for a Vaiśya, for the Vaiśya is connected to the *jagatī*. Thus, according to their respective metres, he scatters the ashes into the water with the words, "O divine waters, receive these ashes," for water is the womb of Agni; he thus causes him to go back to his own womb.

With three [verses], for Agni is indeed threefold; as great as Agni is, him he causes to reach a firm foundation. He who throws the ashes into the waters casts away the fire. [With the verse], "Having been united with thy mothers, do thou, full of light, sit down again," he bestows light upon him. He who throws the ashes into the waters is deprived of vigor and cattle. [With the words], "Again with vigor, together with wealth," he regains vigor and cattle. [With the verse], "Be mindful of this my word, O youngest one," therefore offspring that have slept wake up.

He is the wise Maghavan; therefore, having gone forth and wandered about, the sacrificial animals return and sit down according to their respective places. There are two-footed [animals] for the sacrificer’s firm establishment. ||12||

May the divine *barhis* be well-divine among the gods, rich in heroes through its heroes; may it be spread at dawn and gathered at evening, surpassing others with wealth. May we rejoice as possessors of the *barhis*. May he partake of the gift of wealth in the winning of riches. Sacrifice! The divine Doors, firm, unshakable, and steadfast, have been opened wide for the gathering of the gods at this invocation of the deities. May a young calf, or a newborn boy, or a child measure them out. Let not a wild beast, a dust-raising steed, or a hoof-striking horse come near them. May they partake of the gift of wealth in the winning of riches. Sacrifice! The two divine goddesses, Dawn and Night, have both been invoked here as this sacrifice proceeds.

Surely you two have come as the divine clans; well-pleased and well-disposed, O givers of wealth, partake of the gift of riches. Sacrifice! Sacrifice to the two goddesses, the Delighters, the repositories of wealth, of whom one drives away hostilities and the other brings desirable treasures to the sacrificer. O givers of wealth, partake of the gift of riches. Sacrifice! Sacrifice to the two goddesses, the Offerings of Strength; may one bring nourishment and strength, and the other bring the shared meal and the drinking together. May we, sharing with the new, be mindful of the old, and with the old, of the new. Those two goddesses, the Offerings of Strength, bestowing strength, have established that strength for us. May they partake of the gift of wealth; sacrifice to the divine Hotṛs, Potṛs, and Neṣṭṛs, who have struck away the evil-speaker, who bring wealth—sacrifice to those who partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of gaining wealth. Sacrifice to the three goddesses, the three divine Ṛtvijs: Sarasvatī, Bhāratī, and Dyā Bhāratī. Bhāratī has touched heaven with the Ādityas; Sarasvatī has protected this sacrifice here with the Rudras. May we rejoice in the common feast with Iḍā, the possessor of wealth—for the sake of gaining wealth, for the gift of wealth, may they partake; sacrifice! The divine Narāśaṃsa is three-headed and six-eyed; a hundredfold is he.

The white-backed ones carry her; a thousand draw her forth. O Mitra and Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati is worthy of this office of the Hotṛ, and the Aśvins of the office of the Adhvaryu. For the winning of wealth, let him partake of the gift of wealth; sacrifice! The divine Vanaspati, the rain-protector, clothed in ghee, has touched the sky with his front, filled the mid-air with his middle, and made firm the earth with his base. For the winning of wealth, let him partake of the gift of wealth; sacrifice! The divine Barhis, the establisher of the waters, the unshakable support of those who move forward, the bearer of all desires.

With this glorious sacrificial grass, which is desirable for men, may we surpass all other sacred grasses. O bestower of wealth, may he partake of the gift of riches; sacrifice! May the divine Agni Sviṣṭakṛt—the giver of good wealth, the delightful sage, the true sacrificer, the invoker, more skilled at sacrificing than any other invoker—O Agni, those gods whom you have sacrificed to and whom you have sent forth, and who have rejoiced in your office as invoker, bring them together; send this sacrifice to the gods in heaven, O divine Sviṣṭakṛt. And you, O Agni, have become the invoker for the bestowing of wealth; accept the word of homage and sacrifice today!

This sacrificer has chosen him as his *hotṛ*, cooking the cooked offerings, cooking the sacrificial cakes, and binding a goat for Bṛhaspati. Today the divine Vanaspati has become well-situated, binding a goat for Bṛhaspati. Today the divine Vanaspati has become well-situated, binding a goat for the Aśvins. Binding a ewe for Sarasvatī and a ram for Indra, today the divine Vanaspati has become well-situated. With the ram for Indra, he has sacrificed; he has taken them from the fat; they have increased.

With sacrificial cakes, O Ṛṣi, descendant of Ṛṣis, this sacrificer has chosen you today from among many who have assembled, saying: "This man shall sacrifice for me among the gods for desirable wealth. Those divine gifts which the gods bestowed, proclaim them to him and give them voice; you, O Hotṛ, are impelled for auspicious speech. Sent by man for the Sūktavāka, recite the hymn! 13.
O Agni, [grant] lifespans; O Agni, purify [us]; O Agni, the Purifier, with your radiance.
O Agni, purifier, shining one, bring the gods here to us, to our sacrifice and our oblation.
For him indeed, the gods ever praise with the ladle dripping with ghee—Agni, so that he may carry the oblations.
I place Agni at the forefront as my messenger.
He, the immortal bearer of oblations, the eager messenger who is well-disposed, Agni, brings [the gods] together through our prayer.
Awaken Agni with a hymn of praise, enkindling the immortal one; may he place our oblations among the gods.
O Agni, this [sacrifice] is kindled; O Agni, may we milk from Sarasvatī’s swelling breast—she who is visible to all—the offspring and the nourishment.
O Sarasvatī, those waves of yours which are honeyed and dripping with clarified butter—with those, be our protector.
I invoke for protection Sarasvatī, the divine, the well-winged, the great bird, the lord of waters, the bull of plants, who from every side satisfies us with his manly powers.
I invoke for protection that Sarasvant, whose vow the waters attend, in whose vow all cattle move, and in whose vow the Lord of Prosperity is established. 14. {1580}
Thus ends the nineteenth section, named Sāvitra, in the Madhyamikā branch of the Caraka school within the illustrious Kāṭhaka Yajurveda. 19.

Now follows the twentieth section. "Go away, depart, and creep away from here!"—with these words he settles upon the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*). If one builds the fire-altar (*agni*) on this earth without having asked its overlord for the place of sacrifice, those fires are built for Yama; Yama is the overlord of this earth. By asking Yama, the overlord of this earth, for the place of sacrifice, one builds the fire-altar for oneself. Desiring the immortal [portion] of this earth by means of the tip of an arrow, they did not find it. In that he settles upon the place of sacrifice with this [formula], he builds the fire-altar upon the very immortal portion of this earth. Sanācchava said: "This [is mine]..."

"Having moved a few steps from the locus of the *yajus*, [it is said]: 'In the beloved abode of heaven, Agni is to be piled. The saline soil (*ūṣāḥ*) is indeed the beloved abode of heaven; when he scatters saline soil, he piles Agni in the very beloved abode of heaven. These sand-grains are indeed bricks belonging to Vaiśvānara, measured out by the *ari*. When he scatters sand-grains, he secures those very bricks. Sand-grains are the beloved body of Agni Vaiśvānara; when he scatters sand-grains, he secures that very body. 'This is that Agni'—this is the verse of Viśvāmitra."

This hymn indeed enabled Viśvāmitra to win the beloved abode of Agni; by this [hymn], he wins the beloved abode of Agni. He lays down four bricks facing east; for there are four meters, and by means of the meters the gods went to the heavenly world. Their quarters collapsed; they saw these "quarter-bricks" (diśyā), and by them they made the quarters firm. As for why he lays down two in front facing each other and two behind—it is for the support of the quarters. He lays down eight of these; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the heavenly world.

One quickly knows the world through the knowledge of the heavenly world. He lays down these eight bricks; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī; as great as Agni is, so much of him he builds. Having laid down these eight, he lays down thirteen Lokampṛṇā bricks. These amount to twenty-one. The twenty-onefold is indeed the foundation of the Stomas, and the Gārhapatya fire is the foundation. By means of the Gārhapatya, he finds a foundation following the foundation of the twenty-onefold; he stands firm, having built the fire, for one who knows thus.

One building the altar for the first time should pile it with five layers; the sacrifice is fivefold and cattle are fivefold; verily he wins both the sacrifice and cattle. One building it for the second time should pile it with three layers; these worlds are three; verily he prospers in these very worlds. One building it for the last time should pile it with a single layer; as one who is singular, he goes to the heavenly world. There are five layers and five fillings of earth; that makes ten. The Virāj consists of ten syllables; the Virāj is food. Verily he finds firm support in the Virāj, in the eating of food. Indeed, the brick is bone.

Flesh is the soil; when he covers the brick with soil, therefore the bone is covered with flesh, and one who knows thus does not become diseased of skin. With the words, "Be united, may you two agree," he pours [the soil] together. That which is carried in the fire-pan and that which is piled up—these two constitute the nobility (*kṣatra*) among the fires. By means of the sacred word (*brahman*), the nobility is brought into union. The sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is the sacred word; verily, by means of the sacred word he brings these two together. He pours them together with four [verses]; for there are four meters; verily, by means of the meters he brings these two together. This indeed...

The *chandases* are the dear body of Agni; by means of that very dear body he consecrates them. In that, having piled them together, he spreads them out, therefore the *kṣatra* (the nobility) comes together with the *brahman* (the priesthood) and departs through the *brahman*. With the words, "Like a mother her son, the earth, rich in soil," he consecrates him by means of the seasons and releases him by means of the seasons. With the words, "May Prajāpati Viśvakarman release [you]," he makes Prajāpati himself his releaser.

Then there are these three *nairṛta* offerings of black rice cooked with husks; for black is the color that attends him whom Nirṛti seizes. This indeed is the portion of Nirṛti: by means of the husks as the form and the husks as the portion, he makes expiation to Nirṛti. With the verse, "That which is beyond this region," he takes [the offering] with one addressed to Vaiśvānara; thus he makes it palatable. They carry it toward this direction, for they carry him toward this direction whom Nirṛti seizes. This is indeed the direction of Nirṛti; in his own direction, he thus makes expiation to Nirṛti.

He places them on a self-made barren spot; for that part of her which is seized by Nirṛti is precisely where he appeases Nirṛti, wherever she has seized her. He places them facing away; thus he appeases Nirṛti in a direction turned away from him. He places three; man is indeed divided threefold, and so he appeases Nirṛti from the whole extent of his body. With the words, "The noose which the goddess Nirṛti bound upon thee," he hangs a sling over it; for the noose belongs to Nirṛti, and thus he releases him from the noose of Nirṛti. These [bricks] belong to the world of the Fathers.

Those who perform rites with southern fires go to the realm of Nirṛti; the Āhavanīya fire belongs to the world of the gods. When he stands by the Āhavanīya, he returns to the world of the gods. He stands by it with a Triṣṭubh verse; the Triṣṭubh is indeed vigor; verily, he bestows vigor upon him. With a single [verse] he stands by it; verily, he bestows vigor upon him all at once.

As long as a man is with his arms raised, so long a bamboo pole he measures; for so much indeed is the vigor in a man; verily, by means of vigor he measures him out. He measures three men forward and four across; therefore, one who has piled the fire-altar eats food from seven men: three beyond him, three below him, and himself as the seventh. He places [bricks] on the two wings measuring a cubit (aratni) and on the tail measuring a span (prādeśa). By the man (puruṣa) the sacrifice is measured; it is measured according to the man-sacrifice (yajñapuruṣa); therefore the wings extend further.
He ploughs with six oxen; for there are six seasons, and thus he unites the furrows three by three according to the seasons; for Agni is threefold, and those [furrows] amount to twelve.

There are twelve months in a year; he conforms to the very ordinance of the year. Moreover, having ploughed by means of the seasons, he establishes himself in the year. This earth, indeed, was afraid of being over-burnt by Agni; she made this twofold—both ploughed and unploughed. That there is both ploughed and unploughed is so that it may not be over-burnt for her, and also so that he may exert his strength upon her by means of that which is twofold. So many indeed are the animals—both bipeds and quadrupeds—and these he places in Agni when [he sows] towards the north.

If he were to release [the ox] for Rudra, he would confine the cattle; he would be without cattle. If he were to let it loose toward the south for the ancestors, it would be exhausted. If he were to drive it westward, he would strike down the *rakṣases*. By releasing it toward the south, he releases it toward the east; the sun is indeed the breath of cattle; verily, he releases them toward their own breath. He sows the shoots of plants with the verses of the plants; verily, by its form, he wins food. He sows every kind of food; verily, he wins all food. That for which he does not sow, from that he is deprived. For that for which he might not sow, he should do so mentally.

He should meditate upon it; by that very means he obtains it. He sows with fourteen [verses]. There are indeed seven cultivated plants and seven wild ones; thus he obtains both kinds. The *arka* is food, and Agni is the *arka*; it is the *arka* itself that is being built up here. He sows on ploughed ground, for on ploughed ground plants take firm root most quickly. He sows along the furrows for the sake of procreation. He sows in twelve furrows; the year has twelve months; by means of the year, he cooks food for him.

He throws clods of earth from the quarters; he gathers strength from the quarters, and thus he piles Agni with strength. From whichever direction he hates a people, from that direction he should bring [the earth], saying, "I have taken food and strength from here. Verily, he takes away their food and strength, and they become hungry. He pours out [the earth] for the high altar (*uttaravedi*), for on the high altar Agni is piled; moreover, he does not exclude a member of the sacrifice. The high altar is indeed cattle; verily, he wins cattle. With the six-verse hymn, "O Agni, thine is glory and vigor," he pours it out; for there are six seasons.

The seasons are the year, and Vaiśvānara Agni is the year; by means of his very form, he secures Vaiśvānara. The first [verse] has eight syllables; cattle have eight hooves; verily, he secures cattle. They are deficient and redundant, forming a pair for the sake of procreation. This metre of Prajāpati is indeed named "the ocean"; from the ocean, cattle are born; it is for the procreation of cattle. Indra, indeed, hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra; it became threefold: one-third became the wooden sword (sphyá), one-third the sacrificial post (yūpa), and one-third the chariot (rátha). That which was shattered—

Those pebbles: Agni is indeed cattle, and the pebbles are the thunderbolt; in that he measures [the altar] with pebbles, he encloses cattle for him by means of the thunderbolt. Therefore, cattle are held apart by the thunderbolt; therefore, one who is more stable does not take away from one who is less stable. He should measure with ten at a time for one who desires food; the Virāj has ten syllables, and the Virāj is food; verily, he finds firm support in the Virāj, in the eating of food. He should measure with nine at a time for one practicing sorcery; the thunderbolt is threefold; verily, he hurls the thunderbolt at his rival. With seven at a time—

For one desiring cattle, there are seven vital breaths; from the vital breaths, cattle are produced. For the sake of the procreation of cattle, he should spread out pebbles and sand without measuring them. If he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he pours out his seed without enclosing it, and he becomes without cattle. Having measured them, he should spread out pebbles and sand if he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle"; he pours out his seed for him with it enclosed, and he becomes rich in cattle. The meters are indeed the womb of Agni, and Soma is the placer of the seed; having strewn [the altar] with the meters...

"O gentle one, he arranges [the verses] in the womb itself; he deposits the seed in the womb, he arranges it. Therefore embryos grow in the womb. They have the same beginning but different endings; therefore, from a common womb, offspring of various forms are born. He should arrange [the verses] for a Brāhmaṇa with a Gāyatrī verse, for the Brāhmaṇa is connected to the Gāyatrī; for a Rājanya with a Triṣṭubh verse, for the Rājanya is connected to the Triṣṭubh; for a Vaiśya with a Jagatī verse, for the Vaiśya is connected to the Jagatī—thus according to their respective meters. (4)

The fire is indeed indistinct at this time when it has not yet been separated [from its elements]; therefore, he recites softly. He recites the meters; for by means of the meters Agni reached the high altar (uttaravedi); therefore, he recites the meters. They go along the path of the sun when they make the horse step forward and backward; therefore, that Āditya goes both eastward and westward. The horse belongs to Prajāpati; when he makes the horse step [upon the altar], he piles it with Prajāpati himself. "Thou art the back of the waters."

"The womb of Agni"—with these words he places a lotus leaf; verily he piles it in its own womb for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. "Growing great, O lotus..."—for he who exists indeed grows. "Spread yourself out with the measure and width of heaven"—verily he causes it to expand. "The Brahman, first born in the east..."—with this verse he places a gold disk (*rukmam*); by means of the *brahmamukha* bricks, Prajāpati prospered through his offspring; it serves for prosperity. It has twenty-one knobs (*nirbādha*) for the sake of stability.

There are twenty-one worlds of the gods; from them alone he drives away his rival. He should make the enclosures below for the suppression of the rival. Fire is not to be piled on earth, nor in the atmosphere, nor in heaven. If he were to pile it on earth, he would burn up the plants with its heat; if in the atmosphere, the birds; if in heaven, the immortal sky. Gold is the immortal; in that he places the gold plate, he piles the fire in the immortal itself.

With the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," he places the golden Puruṣa; by this, he indeed establishes the world of the sacrificer. Moreover, he piles the fire so that there is light in its center. With the words, "The drop has fallen," he touches it; he thus establishes it in the Hotṛ-offices and in truth. He worships with the heads of serpents; he entrusts him to the Deaths themselves, and moreover, he wins that brilliance which is in the serpent. If he were to place [the heads] down, he would be liable to die prematurely. If...

He should place it with the other heads turned toward the same direction; otherwise, domestic animals would become prone to stinging insects. If he were to place it facing in various directions, wild animals would suffer the same. He should simply recite the *yajus* formula; by that alone he secures that brilliance and pacifies it. Indeed, in former times, people could look upon the one who had built the fire-altar, for he had secured all these splendors—those in the fire, those in the serpent, and those in the sun. Now, this [hymn] of Vāmadeva is a slayer of Rākṣasas. At every commencement of the sacrifice, the Rākṣasas seek to destroy the sacrifice; [this hymn is used] for the striking away of the Rākṣasas. It consists of five verses.

The fire-altar consists of five layers; as great as the fire-altar is, so great it is, and from that it drives away the Rakṣases. He offers oblations moving around all the quarters; thus he strikes down the Rakṣases from the quarters. He places them with a ladle; verily, he thus places these two [arms]. He places them silently, for these two cannot be obtained by means of a Yajus formula. Man is indeed the self, and the two ladles are the two arms; in that he places them with a ladle, it is for the sake of having a body. To the south, the Rakṣases were snatching away the offerings of the gods; they (the gods) interposed the Kārṣmarya wood against them. That...

He places bricks made of *kārṣmarya* wood on the south for the purpose of excluding the Rakṣases. He fills them with clarified butter; the *kārṣmarya* is indeed a thunderbolt and clarified butter is a thunderbolt; verily, by means of the thunderbolt, he bestows the thunderbolt. He places them with a *gāyatrī* verse; Agni is indeed of the *gāyatrī* nature and has the *gāyatrī* as his metre; verily, he prospers him by means of his own metre. He fills a brick of *udumbara* wood with curds; curds are indeed food and the *udumbara* is strength; verily, he bestows strength upon food. He places it with a *triṣṭubh* verse; [it belongs] to Indra.

The *triṣṭubh* is food and power; verily, he secures for himself power and the eating of food. This earth is indeed made of *kārṣmarya* wood, and that [sky] is made of *udumbara* wood; in that he places the *audumbara* one on top, therefore that [sky] is above this [earth]. It possesses a head; by these two, a head is created for them. The fire-altar is to be built upon the *virāj*; the *virāj* is indeed the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*). In that he places the two ladles, he builds the fire-altar upon the *virāj*.

Whatever first brick the unlearned Adhvaryu lays down, with that he obstructs the breath of the sacrificer, as well as his offspring and his cattle. There is a naturally perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇṇā*); it serves to release the vital breaths and to provide an opening toward the heavenly world. The horse belongs to Prajāpati; when he causes the horse to tread upon [the brick], he builds it up by means of Prajāpati himself. This naturally perforated brick is indeed this earth; thus he lays down this very earth. If he should think, "An enemy has surpassed me," he should push it forward; whoever [surpassed] him...

The enemy who has passed before is driven away by this [line]; if he should think, "My enemy is behind me," he should push it westward; thus he drives away the enemy who is behind him. He drives away a superior enemy and drives back a weaker one.

If he should think, "I am equal [to others]," he should displace it; for those subjects who were shaken off became perished, and so he now shakes him off. Now this is the *dūrveṣṭakā* (durva-grass brick). Agni is indeed cattle, and cattle do not delight in being driven away; he thus provides a dwelling for cattle, for the support of cattle. With the words, "Rising up from joint to joint," it is for the sake of stability. With "By a thousand and by a hundred," it possesses a thousandfold power; it is commensurate with Prajāpati. He who knows thus attains thousandfold prosperity of cattle.

The wise man lays down this brick. Now, this is the Vāmabhṛt; by means of it, the gods indeed seized the desirable cattle of the Asuras. By means of this, he seizes the desirable cattle of his rival. It consists of two Yajus formulas; by the two Yajus formulas, he strikes down the world of his rival, for the rival exists in the second world. It has a golden head; verily, with golden light, he goes to the heavenly world.

The two are struck together side by side; therefore the eyes are side by side. Now these two are the "semen-possessing" (retassicā). That one is indeed the Svarāj, and this one is the Virāj. Upon a woman lying on her back, a man pours his semen; he (the Svarāj) pours his semen upon her (the Virāj), and she brings forth offspring. Agni eats that which is without semen; he who piles the fire-altar thus becomes procreated. He who, knowing this, lays down these two bricks, [attains success]. With the words, "Thou art the Svarāj," he lays one down on the south; therefore a man lies on the right side of a woman. If he should pile the altar for one who is in the first stage of life, he should lay them down both together.

He should place them on the first layer; thus they pour seed for him in unison. He should place one or the other on the layer of whom he may be hostile; by means of that very seed, he deprives him of his virility. If he builds [the altar] for one in the latter part of life, he should place one on the first layer and the other on the last; thus he encloses the poured seed with both. He places the two seasonal bricks for the separation of the seasons. He places them two by two, for there are two seasons each. Now, this [brick] is marked with three lines; for the gods and the Asuras were once exactly equal.

In the sacrifice, whatever the gods did, the Asuras did that too. Those gods saw this triple-lined brick; they laid it down with its marks facing upward. Consequently, the Asuras could not follow after them; then the gods prevailed and the Asuras were defeated. He who, knowing thus, lays this brick down with its marks facing upward does so for the sake of his rival’s inability to follow after him; he himself prospers and his rival is defeated. However, he should lay it down with its marks facing downward if he should hate someone.

Verily, he causes him to fall into the very womb of the Asuras. These worlds are indeed marked with three lines; by this [verse], he obtains these very worlds. He should make this [brick] from the same clay from which they make the fire-pan (ukhā); thereby all his bricks become possessed of light and accompanied by sacrificial formulas (yajus).

The tortoise is indeed the sacrificial essence (*medha*) of animals; by placing the tortoise [on the altar], animals attend upon it, recognizing it as that very essence. He places it while it is alive, for it is then sacrificially pure. It has four feet; thus he establishes himself in the four quarters. With the verse, "May the great heaven and earth... he thereby maintains the forms of heaven and earth. He anoints it with curds and honey; for honey is the essence of the waters and of the plants.

In that he anoints [the tortoise] with honey, he secures the sap of the waters and the plants; for curds are the essence (*medhas*) of cattle and the vigor (*ūrj*) of cattle—in that he anoints it with curds, he bestows both essence and vigor upon the cattle. One fire-altar is built of bricks, while another is built of cattle; in that he places a living tortoise, he thereby makes this altar one built of cattle. This [tortoise] is indeed the highest step to the heavenly world; just as one who knows the way, being cognizant, leads others directly to their destination, even so does he lead this [sacrificer] toward the heavenly world.

Agni is to be piled upon the navel of Viṣṇu. He who piles Agni not upon the navel enters the navel of the sacrificer and consumes him. This mortar (ulūkhala) is indeed the navel of Viṣṇu; when he places it down, he piles Agni upon the very navel of Viṣṇu. It is made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is strength (ūrg); verily, he bestows strength in the middle, both upon the sacrificer and upon his offspring. Therefore, offspring find strength in the middle; they thrive with vigor from the center.

It is a span in measure, for so great indeed is the navel of Viṣṇu; he places it upon the Vaiṣṇavī brick, for this is a rite performed [for Viṣṇu]. Now, this fire-pan (ukhā) is gathered strength and vigor; verily, he wins strength and vigor. He wins the light of these worlds; he places the light in the middle; he piles the fire with light in the middle; therefore, they worship the light in the middle. He fills it with sand; this is the ash of Agni Vaiśvānara, its own proper abode.

In that he [uses] sand, he wins Vaiśvānara in his very form. If he were to place it upon the *ūna* bricks, the sacrificer would be liable to hunger; he places it full, so the sacrificer does not hunger. He eats food that is never exhausted. He fills it with ghee; ghee is indeed the dear abode of Agni. Verily, he prospers him by means of his own dear abode.

Having bartered for twenty-one beans, he brings the human head; beans are indeed impure, and the human head is impure; thus, by means of the impure, he purchases the impure. There are twenty-one [beans], for man is twenty-one-fold; as great as his self is, that much he purchases. He replaces it with an ant-hill from which seven layers have been dug out; for this [head] is deprived of the vital breaths, as there are seven vital breaths in the head; verily, by means of the vital breaths, he makes it complete. He sings the *Yamagāthā* verses; verily, he snatches it away from the world of Yama. Three...

He sings; these three worlds [are sung]. From these very worlds he excludes him. Therefore, one should not give to a singer, for it is by means of the song that he excludes him. Indeed, power (indriya) departs from him: breath from the head, vigor, sight, hearing, and speech. This is a failure of power, this is impure, this is a "dead head," so they say. Gold is pure. When he scatters gold chips over it, he makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. Having covered it with the fire-pan (ukhā), he scatters [the chips] over it.

Having established it in its foundation, he causes it to prosper through the vital breaths (prāṇas). With the words, "Thou art the giver of a thousand; for a thousand thee," he places the head of the Puruṣa. For the Puruṣa indeed bestows a thousand cattle, while other animals are [only] in thousands. In that he places the head of the Puruṣa in the middle, it is for the sake of stability. Now, as for these heads of animals: these bricks are indeed "thousandfold" (sāhasrī). Somadakṣa Kauśreya placed them for Śyāmaparṇa; from that time on, he attained thousandfold prosperity in cattle, and one attains thousandfold prosperity.

He who, knowing this, lays these down, [attains] the prosperity of cattle. He places the head of the horse facing west from the front; he places the head of the bull facing east from the back. Thus, he provides him with cattle facing toward one another. He should place them facing toward one another for one whom he desires, "May he be rich in cattle"; verily, he provides him with cattle facing toward one another. He should place them facing away from one another for one whom he desires, "May he be without cattle"; verily, he makes his cattle face away from him.

The Adhvaryu should not place the animal heads in between; for this Agni is indeed named Yaviṣṭha, and he would seize his vital breaths, and he would die. Having placed one [brick], he should worship with all these [verses]. Alternatively, he should set them down by moving around them on all sides; thus all are placed, and the Adhvaryu does not meet with misfortune nor fall into error. So many indeed are the animals—both bipeds and quadrupeds—and it is these he afflicts with pain. With the words, "I assign that wild one to thee," he [assigns] the wild animals away from the domestic ones.
He does not release the sacrificial victim from its impurity; therefore, among animals being born, these are the smallest, for they have been struck by impurity.

Agni is indeed an animal; this womb of the animal is being prepared. The *apasyā* bricks are seed; in that he lays down the *apasyā* bricks, he places seed in the very womb. When an animal rolls over, then it is born. The *chandasyā* bricks are cattle; in that he lays down the *chandasyā* bricks following the *apasyā* bricks, it is for the procreation of cattle. He lays down five; cattle are fivefold; as great as the animal is, so much does he generate. This earth, indeed, was afraid of Agni’s burning; she created these *apasyā* bricks and laid them down. In that the *apasyā* bricks are laid down, [it is] upon her...

He said, "It is for the sake of not burning [the sacrificer] that one should give food to a Brahmin, he for whom these [bricks] are laid down. He who, knowing thus, lays down these [bricks], eats food through the Brahman. He lays down five in the east facing west; therefore an animal is born in the east facing west. He lays down five in the south facing north; therefore a man lies upon a woman from the south.

Five [bricks] are placed towards the east from the west; therefore, semen is deposited from the west towards the east. Five *chandaḥyā* bricks are placed towards the north; the *chandaḥyā*s are indeed cattle, and cattle have the north as their abode; he thus encloses the cattle that have been born within their own abode for the sake of the non-injury of cattle. He should not place the *apasyā* bricks towards the north; if he were to place them there, Varuna would seize his offspring from the front. Following the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks, he places the *apasyā*s; when the semen has been infused, he thereby bestows breath, mind, sight, hearing, and speech. Therefore...

"Breathing, seeing, hearing, speaking—this beast is born here before," with these bricks containing the word "breath" (*prāṇa*), he places them in front; verily, he places breath in front. Therefore, a beast breathes forward. "This one on the south, Viśvakarman," with these bricks containing the word "mind" (*manas*), he places them on the south; verily, he places mind on the south. Therefore, the right side is more mindful; therefore, they attend to the mind from the south. "This one behind, Viśvavyacas," with these bricks containing the word "eye" (*cakṣus*), he places them behind; verily, he places the eye [behind].

He places them behind; therefore an animal looks forward. "This from below, heaven from above"—those bricks which possess ears he places from above; verily he bestows the ear from above, and therefore an animal hears more clearly from above. "This earth, thought above"—those bricks which possess speech he places in the middle; verily he bestows speech in the middle, and therefore speech speaks from the middle. He places them crosswise; therefore animals move their limbs crosswise when walking. With those which he places in front, Vasiṣṭha prospered by means of them.

With those on the south side Bharadvāja [is associated], with those behind Jamadagni, with those on the north Viśvāmitra, and with those in the middle Viśvakarman. He who thus knows their prosperity prospers; he who thus knows their arrangement is successfully arranged; he who thus knows their kinship becomes possessed of kin; he who thus knows their foundation becomes possessed of a foundation; he who thus knows their abode becomes possessed of an abode; and he who thus knows their support attains it.
He who knows thus becomes possessed of a foundation, possessed of a cause, and possessed of a basis. 9.

Now, these are the Āśvinī bricks. This Agni is indeed a sacrifice that has been interrupted; for who knows how much of him is not yet performed, or how much is not yet piled? With these [bricks], he makes him whole and heals him. He lays down five of them; Agni is fivefold: for as great as Agni is, for him he provides a remedy. By means of these, he arranges the quarters of Agni. "I set thee on the back of Aditi"—with this [verse], he supports these very worlds. He lays down the seasonal (ṛtavyā) bricks for the arrangement of the seasons. He lays down five; for there are five seasons, as many as there are.

Thus he differentiates them; they have the same beginning and the same conclusion, for the seasons have the same beginning and the same conclusion. He separates them with a single *vyāhṛti*; therefore the seasons are separated.

Therefore, he places the seasonal bricks (ṛtavyā) following the Ashvini bricks, which are of various forms within the uniform year; thus, having deposited the seed, he deposits the seasons. Therefore, having deposited the seed, it is born along with the seasons. He places the Vayavya bricks following the seasonal bricks; thus, he places vital breath (prāṇa) within the seasons. Therefore, these [breaths], though circulating together, do not decay. Therefore, Vāyu revolves along with the seasons. He places the Apasyā bricks following the Vayavya bricks; therefore, Vāyu carries rain. By means of these [Apasyās], he wins rain.

If he were to place them down all at once, it would rain for only one season; he places them without going around [the altar], therefore it rains season by season. He places the *vayasyā* bricks after the *apasyā* bricks; the *vayasyā*s are indeed cattle. Because he places the *vayasyā*s after the *apasyā*s, therefore cattle have different minds and different ways of acting, yet they are of one mind toward water. Having placed the *apasyā*s, he should place the *vayasyā*s if he should desire, "May I be rich in cattle"; for water is the means of unifying cattle. It is in the unification of cattle that he piles the fire-altar.

He becomes possessed of cattle. Having laid down the *vayasyā* bricks, he should lay down the *apasyā* bricks if he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle. He piles the fire-altar in the non-perception of cattle; he becomes without cattle.

He places four in front; therefore the animal is to be led forward. Therefore there are four forms of the eye: two white and two black. They have heads; therefore the head of animals is in front. Five each on both sides for the stability of the animal; therefore the animal inclines forward. With "The goat is the age," he places one on the south; with "The ram is the age," one on the north; thus he places the shoulders of the animal. With "The tiger is the age," [he places one] on the right wing; with "The lion is the age," on the left.

He bestows vigor upon the two wings: with "The tiger is the bird," he places the first; with "The lion is the bird," the second. Therefore, the tiger is born in front and the lion behind. With "Man is the bird," he places the middle. Therefore, man is the lord of animals.

"O Indra and Agni, you two make firm the unshaking brick"—for Indra and Agni are indeed vigor and heroism, and this layer is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). The intermediate space is, as it were, loose; [therefore,] he places vigor and heroism in the offspring, for offspring are the intermediate space. There is a naturally perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇṇā*); it serves to release the vital breaths and to reach the world of heaven. The horse belongs to Prajāpati; when he makes the horse smell [the brick], he piles it up with Prajāpati himself. Now, these are the bricks belonging to the quarters. When the gods were going to the world of heaven, their...

The quarters collapsed; they saw these *diśyā* bricks and with them they stabilized the quarters. When these are laid down, it is for the support of the quarters. "Thou art the queen, the eastern quarter"—therefore she is the queen of the quarters. "Thou art the *virāj*, the southern quarter"—therefore she shines as the *virāj* among the quarters. "Thou art the sovereign (*samrāj*), the western quarter"—therefore there is sovereignty here. "Thou art the self-ruler (*svarāj*), the northern quarter"—therefore there is self-rule here. "Thou art the overlord (*adhipatnī*), the great quarter"—therefore she is the overlord of the quarters. All these [bricks] are indeed these [quarters].

He who, knowing thus, places these [bricks] down with the formula, "Protect my life," places ten in front. There are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, and the navel is the tenth; he thus bestows the vital breaths upon him. With the formula, "Bestow light upon me," he places the last one; he thus bestows the highest light as the highest. Therefore, speech is the highest light among the vital breaths. He places ten of these; the *Virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the *Virāj* is the light among the meters. Sight is light; he thus places sight in front of creatures. With the formula, "The *Mā* meter," he places them on the south.

He places them; therefore the months turn toward the right. With "The earth is the metre," he places one behind for support. With "Agni is the deity," he places one to the north; Agni is indeed vigor (*ojas*), so he bestows vigor from the north. Therefore, he who advances from the north is victorious. He places twelve on the south, twelve behind, and twelve to the north; these amount to thirty-six. The *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables; the *bṛhatī* among the metres attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). He who, knowing this, lays down these [bricks], attains self-sovereignty.

These are thirty-six; the Bṛhatī consists of thirty-six syllables. Cattle are connected with the Bṛhatī; the intermediate space is this layer. [Thus] he places cattle in cattle, and the intermediate space in the intermediate space. Some vital breaths have the Ādityas as their abode, others have the Aṅgirases as their abode: those which are in front have the Ādityas as their abode, and those which are behind have the Aṅgirases as their abode. With the words, "Thou art the head, the ruler," he places them in front; thereby he supports those vital breaths which have the Ādityas as their abode. With the words, "The controller, the ruler," he places them behind; thereby he supports those vital breaths which have the Aṅgirases as their abode.

He places seven in front and seven behind; therefore, the lower vital breath shares in half of the vital breaths that are above. Having created living beings, Prajāpati desired, "May I be their head. He saw these Mūrdhanyā bricks and raised himself up by means of them; he became their head. That is why the Mūrdhanyās have their name. He who, knowing this, lays down these bricks becomes the very head among his peers.

"Swift is the Trivṛt"—with these words he places [the brick] in the east; for the Trivṛt is the mouth of the sacrifice, and thus he extends the mouth of the sacrifice in the east. "The Sky is the Saptadaśa"—with these words [he places it] on the south; for the Saptadaśa is food, and food is produced in accordance with the seventeen-year cycle; thus food comes to be on the south. Therefore, a man eats food with his right hand. Because he places bricks characterized by the Saptadaśa on the south, therefore birds wheel around the right wing. [He places] one characterized by the Ekaviṃśa...

[He places it] behind for stability, for birds settle from behind. [He recites] a verse containing the word "fifteen" on the northern side; the fifteenfold [stoma] is indeed vigor; verily he bestows vigor upon the north. Therefore, one who advances from the north conquers. With the words, "Thou art Agni’s portion, the lordship of consecration," he places two [verses] containing the word "triple" (trivṛt) in front; thus he spreads out the mouth of the sacrifice from the front toward the rear. On the right side [he places verses] containing the word "fifteen," and on the left side those containing the word "seventeen," for the sake of steadiness. The seventeenfold [stoma] is food; in that there are [verses] containing the word "seventeen" on both sides...

He places them down; verily he bestows food on both sides. Therefore, having grasped it with both hands, a man eats food. It consists of twenty-one bricks for the sake of stability. "Thou art the portion of Agni, the overlordship of Dīkṣā"—by these [bricks], the gods indeed won this [world]; by these he wins this very thing. These bricks are called *spṛtis* (winners). "With one they praised; offspring were produced"—by these the gods indeed created this [world]; by these he secures all this. This is indeed the *arkya*.
In accordance with the ritual ordinance food is prepared; the sun is Agni, and he eats the food for one who knows this, for whom the food is thus ordained. ||12||

The gods and the Asuras performed the sacrifice equally; whatever the gods did, the Asuras did that too. The gods perceived this fourth layer; they recited the formulas for it in one way and laid it down in another way. The Asuras could not follow that, and consequently the gods prevailed while the Asuras were defeated. He who, knowing thus, lays down this fourth layer, does so to prevent his rival from following after him; he prospers himself, and his rival is defeated. "Swift is the Trivṛt"—with these words he lays [the brick] down in front.

The *trivṛt* is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice; verily, he places the mouth of the sacrifice in front. With "The sky, the seventeenfold," he places it on the south; the seventeenfold is food; verily, he secures food from the south. He places one with the twenty-onefold on the west for support. He places one with the fifteenfold on the north; the fifteenfold is strength; verily, he bestows strength from the north. Therefore, one who advances from the north conquers. With "The onset, the eighteenfold," he places two [stomas] at the front, in the very beginning, at the mouth of the sacrifice.

"He places the *abhīvarta* with 'the twenty-onefold' on the south; the twenty-onefold is indeed food; verily, he secures food for himself from the south. With 'the splendor, the twenty-two-fold' [he places it] behind; because there are two, and the sacrificer is two-footed, it is for stability. Because there are twenty, and the *virāj* consists of two, and the *virāj* is food, he is established in the *virāj*, in the eating of food. With 'the heat, the nineteen-fold' [he places it] on the north; therefore, of the two hands, the left is the more laborious, as it undergoes the contraction of the arm. With 'the womb, the twenty-four-fold' [he places it] in front; the beginning of the sacrifice is indeed..."

The twenty-fourfold [stoma] he places in front as the very mouth of the sacrifice; "the embryos are the twenty-fivefold," he says on the south side; the twenty-fivefold is indeed food, and thus he secures food for himself from the south. Because there are ten [stomas], and the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food—he stands firm in the Virāj, that is, in the eating of food.

That which is fifteenfold—the sacrifice is fifteenfold—he thereby places the thunderbolt above for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. "The twenty-sevenfold is vigor," he says from behind; these worlds are indeed the twenty-sevenfold; verily, he finds support in these very worlds. "The twenty-threefold is the means of gathering," he says from the north; therefore, the left hand is more capable of gathering. "The thirty-onefold is the creative power (kratu)," he says from the front; the thirty-onefold is speech; verily, he places speech at the mouth of the sacrifice. "The thirty-fourfold is the station of the sun," he says from the south; that, indeed, is the sun.

The summit of the sun is spiritual luster; this Āditya [brick] is spiritual luster itself, and thus he secures spiritual luster from the south. "The support, the thirty-three," [he says] from the west; there are thirty-three deities, and thus he finds firm standing among the deities themselves. "The vault, the thirty-six," [he says] from the north; the vault is indeed the heavenly world; thus he establishes the sacrificer in the heavenly world. ||13||
Come here; indeed, I shall speak to you.
Wherever you set your mind, O Dakṣa, as your superior power, there you shall make your seat.
O Vasu, you have not failed to grant these prayers of ours; therefore, you shall accept our worship.
Agni, the descendant of Bharata, the slayer of Vṛtra, the one of many insights, has come as the true lord of Divodāsa.
For he, by his greatness, bestows wealth that overcomes all earthly things—he who is unassailable, unconquered, and victorious.
O Agni, as of old, with your newest and enduring splendor, you have spread far and wide with your lofty light.
O Agni, come hither for the feast, being praised for the giving of the oblation; sit down as the Hotṛ-priest upon the sacred grass.
We choose Agni as the messenger, the invoker, the all-knowing, the one of excellent wisdom for this sacrifice.
May Agni strike down the Vṛtras; by Agni is Agni kindled. Awaken Agni with a hymn of praise. Agni is the head; well-kindled is Agni. I honor Agni as the Hotṛ-priest.
