Through these our hymns, O Agni, come hither toward us; like the light of heaven, be well-disposed toward us with all your faces.
For indeed, O Agni, you have become the charioteer of auspicious will, of effective and righteous power, and of the great cosmic order.
The mortal who, through his prayers and meditations, has taken pleasure in the service and devotion toward Agni—may he, shining brightly, choose for us abundant food as our aid from of old.
Desiring wealth from the god, we meditate today upon the effective hymn of praise for Agni, which reaches unto heaven. 14.
Vaiśvānara for our protection, he who is enthroned in heaven.
Sing forth to Parjanya, the son of Dyaus, the bounteous one; may he seek out pasture for us.
May these words be close to the heart of Parjanya, the self-ruling lord; may he take pleasure in them.
May there be life-giving rains for him, and may the plants, protected by the gods, bear fine fruit.

May the *samidhs*, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may Tanūnapāt, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may the *iḍas*, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may the *barhis*, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may the doors, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may the doors, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may the *iḍas*, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may the *barhis*, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may the doors, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may Dawn and Night, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may the two divine Hotṛs, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter; may the three goddesses, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter.

Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Savitṛ! Svāhā to Sarasvatī! Svāhā to Pūṣan! Svāhā to the Maruts, the self-strong! Svāhā to the All-gods! Svāhā to Heaven and Earth! Svāhā to Agni the Hotṛ! Svāhā! May the gods who drink the clarified butter, being pleased, partake of the clarified butter. O Agni, you are far-extending; O Soma, you are great fortune. Agni is the head, the bull of the sacrifice on earth. O Soma, those which are your abodes—those are all forms. Purifiers, come to us! From heaven let Pūṣan follow our cows. Your other [form] is bright.
I choose here the wide-spreading protection of the Maruts, who possess the splendor of the sun and are masters of their own power.
Bring forth a brilliant hymn for the swift Marut host, who possess their own inherent strength, for the singer;
they who by force overcome all powers—O Agni, the earth trembles before these mighty ones.

O Viśve Devās, whoever you are upon the earth, and O great, ghee-rich Dyaus, satisfy the gods. Let the divine *barhis* (sacrificial grass), the god of the gods, partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of the bestowal of riches. Let the divine Doors partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of the bestowal of riches. Let the two goddesses Dawn and Night partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of the bestowal of riches. Let the two goddesses who delight [the gods] partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of the bestowal of riches. Let the two goddesses, the offerings of strength (*ūrjāhuti*), partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of the bestowal of riches. Let the two divine Hotṛ-priests partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of the bestowal of riches. Let the three goddesses, the three [times], partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of the bestowal of riches.
May the divine Narāśaṃsa partake of the gift of wealth; may the divine Agni Sviṣṭakṛt partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of gaining riches; may they be auspicious to us in every contest. 15.
Thus ends the twentieth section, named *Apeta-vītam*, in the *Madhyamikā* portion of the *Caraka-śākhā* of the illustrious *Kāṭhaka-Yajurveda*. 20.

Now follows the twenty-first section: the Pañcacūḍa. "Thou art the portion of Agni; the lordship of Dīkṣā," with these words he places it in the east. For Agni is the mouth of the sacrifice, and Dīkṣā is the mouth of the sacrifice; Trivṛt is the mouth of the sacrifice; thus he places the very mouth of the sacrifice in the front. "Thou art the portion of the Nṛcakṣases; the lordship of Dhātṛ," with these words [he places it] on the south. Those who are wise are the Nṛcakṣases; Dhātṛ is food, and the Saptadaśa is procreation; thus he bestows food upon the subjects already born. Therefore, once born, one reaches for food. "Thou art the portion of Mitra..."

"Varuṇa’s overlordship," he says for the west; Mitra is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and Varuṇa is the in-breath (*apāna*); thus he bestows both out-breath and in-breath upon the sacrificer. "Thou art Indra’s portion, Viṣṇu’s overlordship," he says for the north; Indra is vigor (*ojas*) and Viṣṇu is vigor; fifteen is vigor; thus he bestows vigor from the north. Therefore, one who advances from the north is victorious.

"Thou art the portion of the Vasus; the overlordship of the Rudras"—thus [he says] in front. The Vasus are indeed the mouth of the sacrifice, and the Rudras are the mouth of the sacrifice; verily, he places the mouth of the sacrifice in front. "Thou art the portion of the Ādityas; the overlordship of the Maruts"—thus on the south. The Ādityas are indeed food, and the Maruts are food; the twenty-five-fold [Stoma] is food; verily, he secures food from the south. "Thou art the portion of Aditi; the overlordship of Pūṣan"—thus behind. Aditi is indeed a firm foundation, and Pūṣan is a firm foundation; [verily, he establishes] a firm foundation.

The Triṇava is for stability. "Thou art the portion of the god Savitṛ; Bṛhaspati’s overlordship"—thus [he says] from the north. Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; the Catuṣṭoma is the Brahman. Verily, he bestows spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) from the north. It contains the word "Savitṛ," therefore the gift bestowed upon the Brāhmaṇas flows toward the north. "Dhartṛ, the Catuṣṭoma"—thus [he says] from the east. The Catuṣṭoma is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice; verily, he places the mouth of the sacrifice in the east.

"Thou art the portion of the Yavas, the overlordship of the Yavas"—thus on the south; for the months are indeed the Yavas, and the months are food; verily he secures food from the south. "Thou art the portion of the Ṛbhus, the overlordship of the Viśve Devas"—thus behind; for there are thirty-three deities; verily he finds support among the deities. "The turning-point, the forty-eight"—thus on the north; therefore the two hands have equal strength. This [altar] is constructed according to the form of the Arka; the Arka is food, and Agni is the Arka; he eats food for whom this [altar] is thus known.

Those which are prescribed as "foremost" he places in front; for him who knows thus, a foremost son is born. Those which are "possessing food" he places on the south; for him who knows thus, he becomes an eater of food. Those which are "possessing support" he places behind; he goes to a firm support for him who knows thus. Those which are "possessing vigor" he places on the north; a powerful son is born to him for him who knows thus. He who knows thus the prosperity of these [bricks] prospers.

"O Agni, drive away our born enemies," with these words he places [the brick] in front; by this means he drives away that rival who has previously surpassed him. "By force, those who are born," with these words he places [it] behind; by this means he repels that rival who is behind him. He drives away a more excellent rival and repels one who is worse. "The forty-fourfold Stoma," [he says] on the south; "The sixteenfold Stoma," [he says] on the north. The sixteenfold is indeed the thunderbolt, and the Triṣṭubh is the thunderbolt.

The *traiṣṭubha* brick consists of forty-four syllables; it is a thunderbolt (*vajra*) that seizes from the left and releases on the right. Having driven away the rival, he hurls the thunderbolt after him. With the words, "The forty-fourfold hymn-form (*stoma*)," he places it on the south. The forty-fourfold is indeed spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); thus he secures spiritual luster for himself on the south. With the words, "The sixteenfold hymn-form," he places one on the north. The sixteenfold is indeed vigor (*ojas*); thus he bestows vigor upon the north. Therefore, one who advances from the north is victorious.

"Thou art the soil of the earth," [he says] as he places the soil in the middle; for the middle of the self is indeed the soil. Thus he piles the fire-altar as the self itself. These bricks are called "the foeless" (*abhrātṛvyā*); no enemy comes to him who, knowing this, lays them down. Now these are the *virāj*s; he thus places the *virāj* as the highest among cattle, and therefore one who possesses cattle speaks the highest speech. He lays them down ten by ten for the sake of stability. When the gods were going to the heavenly world, those meters of theirs which were unexpressed...

They were conducive to heaven; together with them, the gods went to the heavenly world. The seers desired to understand them; he fashioned them out of bricks. These are the meters that do not carry the sacrifice; they are those very meters of the gods which are undefined and conducive to heaven. He who, knowing this, lays these down, goes to the heavenly world together with them.

Now, these are the *stomabhāgas*. Bṛhaspati indeed brought this foundation of the sacrifice when these are laid down; it is for the firm establishment of the sacrifice. Bṛhaspati indeed gathered together that splendor of the sacrifice when these are laid down; he thus piles the fire-altar with its splendor. Prajāpati created offspring; he created them by means of the *stomabhāgas* themselves; when these are laid down, it is for procreation. On the right side, the sacrifice of the gods collapsed; they propped it up again with the *stomabhāgas*; when these [are laid down]...

They are placed on the south, facing north, for the support of the sacrifice. He places them seven by seven for the sake of possessing strength; three in the middle for stability. Now, these are the *nākasads*; for by means of the *nākasads*, the gods went to the heavenly world. When these are placed, it is for the conquest of the heavenly world.

There is nothing that is not heaven for one who has gone to that world; therefore, those who dwell in heaven possess the nature of being "heaven-dwellers" (*nākasat*). These bricks are called *sarvapṛṣṭhā*; whatever is indeed called *pṛṣṭha* bricks, whatever is the splendor of the *pṛṣṭha* hymns—that he obtains, who, knowing thus, lays these down. Now, these are the *pañcacūḍā* bricks. The wives are indeed the station of the sacrificer; in that he lays the *pañcacūḍā* bricks upon the *nākasat*s, he establishes the sacrificer in heaven. These are indeed Apsarases who have assumed this form as wives.

Having come into being in that other world, they lie down behind the sacrificer; he places one [brick] facing eastward from behind, therefore the wife sits behind him facing eastward. These are indeed the protectors of the body for the sacrificer; all his life-span goes away for him who, knowing this, lays these down. These deities are indeed heavenly; through them alone he goes to the heavenly world. These deities are indeed those to be employed for sorcery: regarding one whom he hates, he should say, "I place him in your jaws! He cuts him off from these very deities, and he quickly perishes.

With the words, "I set thee down in the seat of Āyus," he bestows life as the ultimate; therefore, life is the highest of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). It is a self-perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇṇā*), for the release of the vital breaths and for the reaching of the heavenly world. The horse belongs to Prajāpati; when he makes the horse sniff [the altar], he piles it up by means of Prajāpati himself. Now this is the Vikarṇī brick. The Vikarṇī is indeed the stride of the gods; verily, he causes him to stride following the stride of the gods. It contains the word "Vāyu"; Vāyu is breath, and the self-perforated brick is life; thus, he bestows both life and breath upon him.

He bestows vital breath and the two joined ones; he thus kindles him when he piles [the fire], or rather, he inflames him with a verse addressed to Vāyu. Having carried the fire in the pan for a year, one should pile the fire. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; its bricks are the days and nights. Thus, he piles him as one consisting of bricks and attains success. If he were not to pile it in this manner, he would deprive him of his dear body; but since he piles it in this way, he endows him with his dear body. Thus, Vaiśvānara is piled together with his own body. He lays down the seasonal bricks for the sake of the seasons.

He lays them down two by two for support, for there are two seasons each. He lays four on the middle layer; for this middle layer is like the intermediate space (antarikṣa), and the intermediate space is, as it were, loose. There are four quarters; verily he finds firm support in the quarters. The gods fashioned these from the seasons; that is why they are called ṛtavyās. He who, knowing thus, lays these down, finds support in every season as it arrives.

There are various beginnings but they have a common end; therefore, after laying down the *avakā* grass—one of the various forms of the year—he lays down a brick. This *avakā* is indeed the womb of Agni Vaiśvānara; he thus places them in their own womb for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. He who, knowing this, lays these down prospers. Now, these are the Viśvajyotis bricks; these are the breath-supporters of the sacrificer. By the first [brick] he supports the out-breath (*prāṇa*), by the second the diffused breath (*vyāna*), and by the third the in-breath (*apāna*). These indeed...

These are the deities that lead to heaven; by means of them alone one goes to the heavenly world. These deities are indeed luminous: Agni becomes his light in this world, Vāyu in the intermediate space, and Sūrya in heaven; all these worlds become luminous for him. They possess sovereignty; through them he attains sovereignty. With the words, "Fill the world! Fill the gap! he fills whatever of it is deficient or has a gap. Then, with the words, "Sit down, you are firm," he makes it firm. With the words, "Indra, Agni, Bṛhaspati [have established] you," he bestows vigor.

"Indra and Agni are indeed vigor; with vigor and strength he piles him up. "Those [cows] of his yield the sacrificial food (sūdadohas)," therefore they mix the Soma with curds at every joint. "'The dappled ones (pṛśnayaḥ)'"—the dappled one is food; verily he wins food. "'In the three bright realms of heaven,'" there are three pressings; verily he piles him up in the pressings. The Anuṣṭubh is the following verse; the Anuṣṭubh is indeed breath, therefore breath moves through all the limbs. Or, the Anuṣṭubh is speech: whatever part of this [altar] is not performed here, whatever is not piled, that he rectifies by means of speech and heals. 3.

With those three Gāyatrī verses addressed to Agni that contain the word "head" (*mūrdhanvatī*), he places three bricks in the eastern half; then with Triṣṭubhs, then with Jagatīs, then with Anuṣṭubhs, then with Paṅktis, and then whatever other verse addressed to Agni there may be—three with one metre, three with another—he thus lays down the entire Agni. Yajñasena Caitra indeed discovered this layer; verily, he who, knowing this, lays these down prospers. The metres are indeed cattle and desirable wealth.

He appropriates the cattle and the desirable wealth of his rival from the gods. The Āhavanīya fire is indeed the self, while the *dhiṣṇya* hearths are the rival; if he were to lay them down on the Gārhapatya, he would bestow the desirable wealth and cattle upon his rival. He lays them down on the Āhavanīya; thus he places the desirable wealth and cattle within his own self. This is the layer named the *uttaravedi*; therefore, these are laid down in the highest layer. He who, knowing this, lays these down becomes the highest among his peers. Agni is indeed cattle; Prajāpati created cattle with Agni as their mouth.

Because there are five layers, cattle are said to be fivefold (*pāṅkta*). Because there are three [layers], Agni is threefold (*trivṛt*); because there are two, the sacrificer is twofold for the sake of stability. Hair has two syllables, skin has two syllables, flesh has two syllables, bone has two syllables, and marrow has two syllables; that makes ten. The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; therefore, cattle are said to be of the nature of the *virāj*. That which is knee-high is piled with the *gāyatrī*; that which is navel-high is piled with the *triṣṭubh*; that which is man’s height is piled with the *jagatī*; [and] the *śyenacit* (falcon-pile).

One desiring heaven should pile the bird-altar; for the hawk is the swiftest of birds, [and this serves] for the complete attainment of the heavenly world. One desiring stability should pile the bird-altar with four furrows, laid out like an *alaja* bird; [for] there are four quarters, and he becomes established in the very quarters. He who desires, "May I be possessed of a head in yonder world," should pile it with a head like a heron; verily, he becomes possessed of a head in yonder world.

One should pile the *prauga-citi* if he thinks, "An enemy has surpassed me from the front. By means of the *prauga-citi*, the gods repelled the Asuras who had previously surpassed them; thus, by that very means, he repels the enemy who has previously surpassed him. He should pile it with *praugas* on both sides if he thinks, "An enemy is behind me. By that very means, he drives away the enemy who is behind him. He repels a superior enemy and repels an inferior one.

One practicing sorcery should pile it in the form of a chariot-wheel; for indeed, the gods hurled a thunderbolt at the Asuras who were thus disposed, saying, "Against those who are so disposed! He hurls a thunderbolt at his rival and strikes him down. One desiring cattle should pile it by sweeping together; for the loose earth (purīṣa) is indeed cattle—he piles up cattle for him. He pours out the high altar (uttaravedi) on all sides; for the high altar is cattle—he secures cattle for himself.

One who desires kinsmen should pile the *paricāyya* altar; for kinsmen indeed surround one, and by means of kinsmen he piles it around himself. One who desires food should pile the *droṇacit* altar; for food is eaten with a bowl, and by that very mouth he eats food. One who desires, "May I prosper in the world of the fathers," should pile the *śmaśānacit* altar; for by means of the *śmaśānacit*, Yama prospered in yonder world, and so he prospers in the world of the fathers.

One who desires heaven should pile the bird-shaped fire-altar consisting of the Gāyatrī. Indeed, Agni, having become a bird, flew to the heavenly world; as they say, "The Gāyatrī, having become a bird, flew to the heavenly world. This is for the complete attainment of the heavenly world. Other fire-altars are piled facing upwards, others facing downwards. Those that are piled facing upwards are for that world (the sky); those that are facing downwards are for this world (the earth). When he sprinkles with gold chips while standing upright, by that very act he piles it upwards, for the complete attainment of the heavenly world.

Through initiation (*dīkṣā*), the *virāj* is to be attained. One should remain initiated for three nights; the *virāj* has three feet; he attains the *virāj* itself. One should remain initiated for six nights; there are six seasons, and the seasons are the year; the year is the *virāj*; he attains the *virāj* itself. One should remain initiated for ten nights; the *virāj* has ten syllables; he attains the *virāj* itself. One should remain initiated for twelve nights; there are twelve months in the year; the year is the *virāj*; he attains the *virāj* itself. One should remain initiated for thirteen nights; there are thirteen...

The month is a year; the year is the Virāj; verily he attains the Virāj. He should be consecrated for fifteen nights; there are fifteen nights in a half-month; by the half-month the year is attained; the year is the Virāj; verily he attains the Virāj. He should be consecrated for twenty-four nights; there are twenty-four half-months in a year; by the half-month the year is attained; the year is the Virāj; verily he attains the Virāj. He should be consecrated for a month; that which is a month is a year; the year is the Virāj... [the year is the Virāj; verily he attains the Virāj].

The Virāj attains the Virāj itself. He should remain consecrated for four months; for it was during these four months that the Vasus bore him and they conquered the earth and the Gāyatrī metre. The eight Rudras conquered the intermediate region and the Triṣṭubh metre. The twelve Ādityas conquered the sky and the Jagatī metre; from that, indeed, they attained distinction and preeminence among the gods. Therefore, having been supported for twelve months, one should pile the fire-altar; [twelve months].

The month is a year; the year is Agni Vaiśvānara. Its bricks are days and nights. He piles him with bricks that have been obtained; he prospers and attains distinction among his equals. He sings the Gāyatra first. The Gāyatra is the head of the gods, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatra; therefore, he sings the Gāyatra first. [He sings] the Āgnipāvamānī verses. He who blows here is indeed this breath, and Agni is the mouth of the gods. Thus, he places breath in the mouth; therefore, breath is in the mouth.

He sings the Rathantara on the northern side and the Bṛhat on the southern side; thus he lays down its two wings. The Rathantara is this [earth], and the Bṛhat is that [sky]; verily by these two he encloses it. He sings the Yajñāyajñīya on the tail and the Vāmadevya on the hip. The Yajñāyajñīya is the self and the Vāmadevya is the body; verily he piles it up with its own self and its own body. The heart is in the armpit (apikakṣa); therefore the heart is in the armpit. It is without a verse (anṛca); therefore the heart is boneless. He sings around it with the Arkya verses; Agni is indeed the Arka;
verily he sings around him with the Arkya for the sake of peace.

The year, indeed, lies between the darkness and the heavenly world; these golden chips are thousandfold bricks full of light. When he sprinkles them with golden chips, he causes the year to shine forth for him by means of light. "Thou art the measure of a thousand, thou art the image of a thousand," he says, for these worlds are commensurate with a thousand. Verily, they strike at this Agni when that part of him is not performed here or is not piled up. Gold is immortality; when he sprinkles with golden chips, he fills his body with immortality. "These, O Agni, are my bricks..."

With the words, "May they be milch-cows," he indeed makes them into milch-cows; these, as wish-fulfilling cows, attend upon him in that world. Verily, the gods excluded Rudra from the sacrifice; he turned toward the gods with his bowstring drawn. The gods saw this Śatarudriya; by it they appeased him. In that he offers the Śatarudriya, he thereby appeases him.

He offers first at knee-height; thus he expiates Rudra from this [earth] itself. Then at navel-height; thus he expiates Rudra from the intermediate space itself. Then at man-height; thus he expiates Rudra from the heavenly world itself. Thus he expiates Rudra from above here. Then at man-height, then at navel-height, then at knee-height; thus he expiates Rudra from below in the immortal realm itself. That makes six; for there are six seasons; verily from the seasons he completely expiates Rudra, with either *gavīdhuka* groats or *jartila* seeds.

He offers with either *kusaya* grass mixed with clarified butter or with deer's milk. If he were to offer with domestic [milk], he would make Rudra a dweller in the village; by means of wild [milk], he expiates Rudra in the wilderness itself. He offers with an *arka* leaf; for Agni is indeed the *arka*, and thus by means of the *arka* he expiates him from the *arka*. He offers on the last brick of the northern wing; this is indeed the quarter of Rudra, and so having turned Rudra toward his own quarter, he expiates him. Agni is indeed an animal; he is born at this very time when he is piled.

Just as a newborn calf seeks the udder, even so does he now seek his portion; he meditates upon both the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu when he offers the Śatarudriya. Verily, by means of that portion, he pacifies him. When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, they poured the Gharma offering onto a goat-skin; it, being scorched, touched a leaf, and that became the Arka. That is the essence of the Arka's name. When he offers with an Arka-leaf, it is for the sake of providing a common origin. [He should offer] at the place where the cattle of one whom he hates pass.

Whichever animal he assigns first, that one comes to ruin; those which are last, he should cause the sacrificer to recite over them. These deities indeed lead to heaven; through them alone he goes to the heavenly world. These deities are to be employed for sorcery: regarding one whom he hates, he should say, "I place him in your jaws. He cuts him off from these very deities, and he perishes instantly.

With the verse, "O stone, the strength resting in the mountain," he sprinkles [it] with water. Water is indeed the essence of Prajāpati; thus he satisfies him with the very essence of Prajāpati. Satisfied and gratified, he attends upon [the sacrificer] without hunger. With the words, "O stone, that which we hate in you—let your heat reach it! he afflicts with both hunger and heat whomever he hates. He sprinkles three times; these worlds are three; thus he pacifies him for these very worlds. Then he goes around three times again, sprinkling [water] behind him. That [is done].

It amounts to six; there are six seasons; verily, from the seasons he pacifies him. If he should practice sorcery, having gone around three times again without sprinkling, he should pour it out on that which is the southern buttock, saying: "Here I destroy so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, the descendant of such-and-such. Whatever scorching heat he takes from the fire, with that he afflicts him; following him as he is being split apart, ruin overtakes him. By taking his name, he cuts off his very root.

This piling is indeed Varuṇa’s arrow; he draws it along with a frog, and thus it passes away by the life-span of the frog. It does not harm domestic animals, nor does it harm wild ones; therefore, this [fire] approaches him in both spring and the rainy season, for these two are seasons of heat. He draws it along with *avaka* grass and a reed-shoot; for the *avaka* is the strength of the waters, and the reed is their nourishment. The waters are peaceful; by means of these peaceful things, he pacifies his heat. He does so with three [verses], for Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, he pacifies his heat.

Prajāpati created offspring; they became hungry, and he gave them food. They said, "Food has come to us. This is why [the verses] contain the word *pāvaka* (purifying); it serves for the sake of eating food for one who has piled the fire-altar. He rubs with seven [verses]; there are indeed seven meters; verily by means of the meters he pacifies his heat. He rubs with eight [verses]; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables; Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī; as great as Agni is, so much of his heat he pacifies.

Having gathered [the ashes], he deposits them on the rubbish-heap; for this [earth] is indeed pure, and thus he places impurity upon that which is pure. If he should hate someone, he should deposit [the ashes] upon him; verily, he afflicts him with impurity. He pours fivefold-drawn clarified butter and throws five chips of gold into it; gold is brilliance and ghee is life—verily, by means of brilliance he bestows life upon him. Moreover, he touches the fire with a fivefold oblation. With the words, "Homage to thy heat, to thy flame," he steps across; for having paid homage, one approaches a superior. He sprinkles transversely to avoid monotony.

"O thou who sittest among men, Veḍ!"—this is for the sake of stability. Some gods are eaters of oblations, others are non-eaters of oblations; by this [formula], the piler of the fire (agnicit) wins both. When he offers an oblation and when he sprinkles [the remains], he gratifies them and wins them; thus both of these, being gratified, participate in his sacrifice.

He sprinkles with the "teacher’s fist," for he is most closely related to Prajāpati; therefore, for him, it is neither an oblation offered nor an oblation not offered. He makes shoes from a black antelope skin; the black antelope skin is indeed the form of Brahman, and Agni is Death. By means of Brahman, he places a barrier between himself and Death; he places a barrier between himself and Death. He should make one of the two shoes [from the skin] as a barrier against food; thus he places a barrier between himself and Death and secures food for himself. He who piles the fire-altar is deprived of his vital breaths and his cattle. The first [of the priests] steps upon it; he is the giver of breath.

"Bestowing breath," he says; verily, he endows him with vital breaths. "Bestowing luster, bestowing space," he says; luster is indeed offspring, and space is cattle; verily, he endows him with both offspring and cattle. "Bestowing out-breath, bestowing in-breath," he says as he descends; this is by means of their very forms. He uses two verses, for the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability.

Indra indeed slew Vṛtra; having slain him, he bound him with sixteen coils. He [Indra] burned away the coils of evil with fire and was released from evil by means of two verses addressed to Viśvakarman. When one offers with a verse addressed to Agni, one burns away the coils of evil with fire and is released from evil by means of the two verses addressed to Viśvakarman. One should offer with each verse separately if one should desire, "May he be released from evil for a long time"; verily, he is released from evil for a long time. One should recite all [the verses] together once and offer with the final verse if one should desire, "Swiftly..."

"May he be released from evil"—he is indeed quickly released from evil. It consists of sixteen parts; man consists of sixteen parts. As great as his self is, from that he releases him from evil. Moreover, with sixteen offerings he offers to him with the sword [of the ritual] and with various hymns (*sūkta*s), for the sake of providing different powers to the two hymns. He lays on fuel-sticks; he thus provides a share for him. Just as one provides fodder for a person who is coming, even so this hospitality is performed for Agni. He lays on three [fuel-sticks].

The fire-altar is threefold; as great as the fire-altar is, for it he performs the guest-offering (*ātithya*). They are made of *udumbara* wood; the *udumbara* is indeed strength (*ūrj*); verily, he bestows strength upon it. He anoints them with ghee; ghee is indeed the dear abode of Agni; verily, he performs the guest-offering for him with his own dear abode. With the words, "May all the gods lift thee up,"—the "all-gods" (*viśve devāḥ*) are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); verily, he lifts him up by means of the vital breaths. The "all-gods" are indeed men; verily, he lifts him up by means of men. With the words, "O Agni, may they bear [thee] with their thoughts"—for whomsoever he [intends] this...

He exerts himself with his mind; therefore, he brings this [sacrifice] to fulfillment. "The five directions"—thus he leads him forward along the very directions. Two [verses] contain the word "enclosing" (*parigṛhya*); this is for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. "The golden-haired one, the sun-rayed"—this is for the impulsion of Savitṛ. "The gods, performing the sacrifice for the gods, stood firm"—this is indeed the milking of blessings. "He is the measurer"—this is the measuring out of the heavenly world itself. "The bull, the ocean, the ruddy one, the fair-winged"—with these words he places the stone upon the Āgnīdhra altar; for, as it were, there is no support [for the sacrificer].

The intermediate space is, as it were, no proper abode; in that he places [the cup] in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed—which is the intermediate space—he makes it a proper abode. With the words, "The speckled one is placed in the midst of heaven," he obtains food, for the speckled one is food. He sets it down with two verses: the sacrificer has two feet; [this is] for stability.

They proceed with six verses beginning with the Āgnīdhra; for there are six seasons, and thus they proceed by means of the seasons. With four verses they proceed as far as the tail; for there are four meters, and thus they proceed by means of the meters. "To Indra"—verily he wins power. "They have strengthened"—verily he attains increase. "Victuals" (*vājāḥ*)—victuals are indeed food; verily he wins food. They proceed with an *anuṣṭubh* verse addressed to the Viśvedevas; for the *anuṣṭubh* belongs to the Viśvedevas, and speech is the *anuṣṭubh*. Speech indeed contains all forms, and all forms are fashioned upon the piled fire-altar; therefore they proceed with this verse. "The summoner of favor"—this is the sacrifice.

Verily, he wins bliss and the sacrifice itself. With the words, "By the impulse of strength, with the lifting-up, I have lifted myself up," [he acts]. The lifting-up is indeed the Brahman; the pressing-down is the Brahman. That Āditya, rising, is the lifting-up; setting, he is the pressing-down. By means of the Brahman, he thus lifts himself up; by means of the Brahman, he presses down his rival. Then, with the words, "May Indra and Agni scatter my enemies in all directions," [he acts]. Indra and Agni are indeed vigor and heroism; by means of that very vigor and heroism, he drives away his rival. 8.

"Step by step with Agni, ascend to the firmament"—this is the ascent to the heavenly world. "Go forward along the eastern quarter, O wise one"—thus he turns toward the world of the gods. "Shining, illumine all the quarters"—therefore Agni shines in all directions. "From the earth I have ascended to the intermediate space; from the intermediate space I have ascended to heaven"—these are the steps for these very worlds. "Going to heaven, they look not back"—this is for the attainment of the heavenly world. "O Agni, go first as the leader to the gods"—thus [he attains] among the gods.

And with the words, "Bestowing sight upon men, in harmony with the Bhr̥gus," he who is free from envy causes him to go indeed to the heavenly world. He strides across with five [verses]; for Agni is fivefold; having paid homage to Agni as far as he extends, he strides across.

With the two *saṃhitā* verses, "Night and Dawn, O Agni, thousand-eyed," he offers; verily he unites day and night, and therefore day and night are joined together. He offers with [the milk] of a black cow that has a white calf; verily by means of the day he causes the night to be granted to him. Animals are indeed of various forms and various natures; he thus provides them with their own respective forms. He offers with milk; verily the animals, recognizing him thereby, attend upon him. He offers with curds upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* (self-perforated brick); yonder sky is indeed the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, and curds are vigor; verily he places vigor in yonder sky.

Therefore, from that [heaven], they draw upon the downward-flowing nourishment. With the verse, "Thou art the fair-winged Garutman," he settles it with a Gāyatrī; verily, he makes him step upon this [earth]. With the verse, "With thy light fill the mid-air," he settles it with a Triṣṭubh; verily, he makes him step upon the mid-air. With the verse, "The well-faced one, being invoked, in front," he settles it with a Jagatī; verily, he makes him step upon yonder [heaven]. Having thus made him yoked together with these very deities, he establishes him. He does so with three verses; for Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, him he causes to reach his firm foundation.

With the verse beginning "Of that Savitṛ," he places a stick of Udumbara wood; this is for the sake of impulsion. The Udumbara is indeed vigor; verily, he bestows vigor upon him. Truly, the fire-altar milks the one who has piled the fire, or rather, the one who has piled the fire milks the fire. Kaṇva indeed discovered the milking of this [fire] made of iron; just as one milks a cow that has been let loose to calve, even so does the fire-piler milk the fire by means of this [verse]. With the words "O Agni, we worship thee," he offers for the sake of prosperity. He places a stick of Vikaṅkata wood; for when the fire was created, its radiance went to the Vikaṅkata; thus he recovers that very [radiance]. "O Agni, shine forth, well-enkindled," [he says] for the front.

"No," he says, for the sake of peace. This is a fire-pan made of *śamī* wood, shaped like a *virāj* and provided with ears. Somadakṣa Kauśreya once asked those engaged in a sacrificial session, "Do you know this fire-pan with its ears? They replied, "We know it as that which is in the forest. Indeed, the ears of this pan are cattle; verily, he wins cattle.

With this very [verse], the gods indeed hurled the hundred-edged thunderbolt at the Asuras, saying, "Against you!"—thus he hurls the thunderbolt at his rival and lays him low. With the verse, "Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni," he gratifies the sevens by means of this [offering]. He offers with a full ladle; just as one provides the udder for a newborn calf, even so does he provide this portion for him. He offers curds first and ghee afterwards; curds are strength, and ghee is luster; [he thus bestows] strength...
And he places both brilliance and Samīcī in him as the two highest; moreover, he causes these very two to bestow gifts upon him. ||9||

Now, this is the *Apratiratha* hymn; by means of it, the gods indeed conquered the Asuras irresistibly. That is why the *Apratiratha* is called "irresistible": with it, one conquers the rival irresistibly. This is indeed the Gāyatrī with wings of light; by means of it, one goes to the heavenly world. It consists of ten verses; the Virāj has ten syllables, and the Virāj is food. Thus, he finds firm support in the Virāj, which is food-eating. With this hymn, Bharadvāja used to go forth against Pratardana while preparing for battle; from that, he indeed became the sovereign (*rāṣṭra*). For whomsoever one desires sovereignty—

Thinking "it may be so," one should proceed while girding oneself with this; thus he becomes the very kingdom. This is the oblation named *bhuvanacyava*; by means of it, from every station, he repels his rival. He should perform it in battle. The fuel should be *taijana* or *bāndhuka* wood. If the embers roll back toward him, the army of his enemies rolls back. Then there is an offering on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; that which belongs to Vaiśvānara is the dear body of the year. As for [the offering] to Agni...

He thus prepares hospitality for Vaiśvānara’s own dear body. Vaiśvānara is the nobility (*kṣatra*) and the Maruts are the people (*viś*); in that the Maruts are invoked after Vaiśvānara, he thereby subjects the people to the nobility. He sacrifices to Vaiśvānara aloud and offers to the Maruts in a low voice; therefore the nobility speaks over the people. Agni is indeed cattle, for Prajāpati created cattle with Agni as their mouth; the Maruts are cattle. In that the Maruts are invoked after Vaiśvānara, it is for the procreation of cattle. If [he were to sacrifice] facing east...

The host of gods would turn away; if [the oblation were] toward the south, it would belong to the Pitṛs; if toward the west, it would belong to the Rakṣases; if toward the north, it would belong to humans. It should be offered straight and firmly established for the sacrificer’s firm establishment. Now, these cakes for the Maruts are on seven potsherds each, for the Maruts are seven by seven; having run after them group by group, he offers them group by group, and thus he satisfies the Maruts group by group.

He offers in the middle with that group which is to be recited in the forest; for this [group] is the nobility (*kṣatra*) of the Maruts, while the others are the common people (*viś*). Thus he makes the nobility stand in the midst of the common people. If he should desire, "May I strike down the nobility with the common people," he should confuse the group to be recited in the forest with the other groups; thus he strikes down the nobility with the common people. If he should desire, "May I strike down the common people with the nobility," he should make the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses in the *triṣṭubh* meter. The *triṣṭubh* is indeed vigor and strength; having taken vigor and strength from the common people, he [strikes them down].

He covers [the chariot] for the sake of the *kṣatra*. If he should desire of someone, "May I drive him away from his *kṣatra*," then with that troop which is to be addressed in the forest, he should move the chariot-stand placed upon the fire-altar. For this indeed bears the *kṣatra* of the Rājanya; it is the *kṣatra* of the Maruts. By means of the *kṣatra* of the Maruts, he drives him away from his *kṣatra*. With the words, "The divine subjects, the Maruts, follow Indra as their path"—for this is indeed the following-path of the gods—he thereby creates a following-path for the sacrificer by means of the very following-path of the gods. In that he piles [the altar], he kindles him; he makes him blaze with those names of the Maruts.

He offers the *vasordhārā* (stream of wealth), for it is indeed offered as "the stream of wealth. It is a stream of clarified butter that attends upon the sacrificer in yonder world. He offers it continuously for the continuity and non-interruption of food; he should interrupt it for one whom he hates, for he thereby cuts off his food. He offers with clarified butter, for clarified butter is brilliance; the stream of wealth is brilliance; verily he places brilliance in brilliance. This offering is made for the ordering of what is disordered, and for the securing of what is unsecured.

For the sake of conquering what has not been conquered, he says, "Out-breath and in-breath"; verily, he bestows out-breath and in-breath upon the sacrificer. He says, "Food and sight"; for this is the form of food; by means of its very form, he wins food. He offers twelve of these sets of twelve; the year consists of twelve months; by means of the year, he wins the eating of food.

"Agni and water"—this, indeed, is the womb of food; verily, he wins food from its own womb. He offers the *ardhendrāṇi* oblations to win the gods; because he offers the *ardhendrāṇi*, therefore Indra has the largest share among the gods. He places Indra last; verily, he establishes the sacrificer in power (*indriya*). "The *aṃśu* and the *raśmi*"—the *aṃśu* and the *raśmi* are indeed the mouth of the sacrifice; verily, he wins the very mouth of the sacrifice. "The *sruva*-ladles and the *camasa*-cups"—these are the forms of the sacrifice; verily, by means of these forms...

He secures the sacrifice, the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and the cry of "Svaga. This is for the sake of stability. "Agni and Gharma"—this indeed is Agni’s splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasya*); he secures that very thing. "The three-year-old bull and the three-year-old cow"—there are indeed these many stages of growth among cattle; he secures cattle of equal age. "One and three"—one and three are the meters of men; he secures the meter of men. "Four and eight"—four and eight are the meters of the gods.

Verily, he wins the meters of the gods. The even and the odd *stomas* are a pair for the sake of procreation; by means of the two that increase by two, he creates a pair. By means of the four-increasing [series], he causes [beings] to be born. He offers from "one and three" up to thirty-three; there are thirty-three deities, and thus he wins the deities. From "four and eight" up to forty-eight; the *jagatī* consists of forty-eight syllables, and cattle are of the *jagatī* nature; verily, he wins cattle in this very world.

With the human metre he prospers in this world; with the divine metre he conquers both worlds. "Vāja and Prasava"—these are thirteen utterances (*vyāhṛti*s). Thirteen months are a year; thus, from the very end, he ascends to the year. "May life be perfected through the sacrifice"—this is the perfection of the sacrifice itself. "The *ṛc* and the *sāman*"—the stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*) is indeed food; verily, by means of the stream of wealth, he secures food and becomes an eater of food. "The *stoma* and the *yajus*"—the *stoma* and the *yajus* are indeed the domain of the gods (*devakṣatra*); verily, from the very end, he attains the domain of the gods.

The gods indeed entered a race for the sake of the *vājaprasavya*; Agni won it. In that he offers the *vājaprasavya*, it is for the winning of food; he offers of every kind of food and thus secures all food. He is deprived of that food for which he does not offer. For that of which he might not offer, he should sprinkle even upon the fuel-wood; by that very act he secures it. He offers with a ladle (*sruva*) made of *udumbara* wood; the *udumbara* is strength, and thus he secures food through strength. This is indeed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of Agni; therefore, one who has piled the fire-altar (*agnicit*) does not [fear] when it rains.

He runs; indeed, he runs for food, he runs for nourishment. Now these are the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* (sustainers of the kingdom). This [Agni] who is built up is the sovereign power (*kṣatra*) among the fires, and these [bricks] sustain his kingdom; that is why they are called *rāṣṭrabhṛt*. By means of them, he bestows the kingdom upon him. There are six of these; for there are six seasons; verily by means of the seasons he bestows the kingdom upon him, and moreover, he finds firm support in the seasons.

The offerings are in pairs for the sake of procreation; there are twelve months in a year; verily, by means of the year, he bestows the kingdom upon him, and moreover, he finds firm support in the year itself. He offers the thirteenth oblation at the front of the chariot; the chariot is indeed a thunderbolt; verily, by the thunderbolt he conquers the quarters, and those conquered quarters are traversed by means of the chariot. He offers the oblation to Vāta; verily, he wins Vāta himself. Indeed, this [wind] blows toward him in yonder world as one who has piled the fire-altar. He offers three times; these worlds are three; verily, from these very worlds...

He wins the wind from the worlds; these worlds blow the wind for him. He offers with joined palms; the wind indeed has hands as its portions, and one cannot truly reach the wind with sacrificial portions; thus he reaches it all at once. "Thou art the ocean, full of mist"—these are indeed the forms of the wind; by means of these very forms, he wins the wind.

The out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the *gāyatrī*, the *gāyatra* is the *havirdhāna*; the diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the *triṣṭubh*, the *traiṣṭubha* is the *āgnīdhra*; the downward breath (*apāna*) is the *jagatī*, the *jāgata* is the *sadas*. "The speckled one with rays is placed in the midst of heaven"—the speckled one with rays is indeed the vital breath (*asu*); verily, he places the vital breath between the out-breath and the downward breath for the separation of the out-breath and the downward breath. He lays down twenty-one bricks in the place of the Hotṛ; the twenty-onefold is indeed the foundation of the *stomas*, for the sake of stability. Eleven [bricks] in the place of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; the *triṣṭubh* has eleven syllables, and the *triṣṭubh* is vigor.

Verily, he wins vigor. There are eight on each of the others; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables; verily, he finds support in the Gāyatrī. There are six on the Mārjālīya altar; for there are six seasons, and the seasons carried him [Agni] as sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās); the seasons are the ancestors (pitaraḥ); therefore, six are placed here.

This is the pure hymn of my mind for you; O Maruts, [the hymn] which [arises] from heaven; that protection of yours [which is] for us; this [prayer] of mine, O Varuṇa, I implore you; with what [splendor] shall the wonderful one [come] to us?

By what power is he heard as the most powerful, by which he, the lofty one, acts at every moment? He who is most effective in dispersing the distress of the liberal donor, then bestows wealth upon the singer.
Release us from the highest bond; loosen the middle one; untie the lowest so that we may live.
O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us; O Agni, do thou [loosen] it for us; O Agni, do thou [loosen] it for us.
We invoke Agni, who possesses many forms, for our protection with our prayers; may he carry us across our enemies.

With a well-guided army, may he be gracious toward us; as the best of sacrificers, may he worship the gods for our well-being. O Agni, undeceivable guardian and our protector from afar, shine forth with splendor and wealth.
O Maruts, you who consume the enemies, may you graciously accept this oblation of the Sāṃtapanas; [it is] for your assistance.
O Maruts, O Vasus, whatever mortal of evil intent seeks to strike down our thoughts from the side, may he be released into the snare of malice;
slay him with your most scorching heat!
O Maruts, destroyers of enemies, you who dwell in the home, do not abandon us; release us from distress.
Your great powers from the depths stir forth; O you who are worthy of sacrifice, extend your names.
O Maruts, take pleasure in this thousandfold domestic portion, this offering belonging to the household sacrifice.
Sing forth, O Kaṇvas, to the Marut host that plays at will, the irresistible, which shines upon their chariot.

Like swift horses, the Maruts move in their own direction; like youths eager for the sight of the sacrifice, they have adorned themselves. Established in their mansions, they are radiant like children; like playful calves, they are the givers of milk.
Indra and Agni have pierced Vṛtra; come quickly to us, O Indra! You, O Indra, are great, O Indra!
O Viśvakarman, strengthened by the oblation, sacrifice yourself to the earth and to heaven!
Let other people around us be confounded; here let the bountiful patron be our benefactor.
For our protection, let us today invoke Viśvakarman, the Lord of Speech, who is swift as thought, for the sake of booty.
May he, who brings welfare to all and performs righteous deeds, find pleasure in our invocations most closely for our protection. 13.
Desiring you, we invoke you; desiring you, we kindle you.
Desiring them, bring the desiring ancestors here to eat the oblation.
O Soma, you are distinguished by wisdom; you lead us along the straightest path.
By your guidance, O Indu, our wise ancestors obtained their share of treasure among the gods.
For our ancient fathers, O Soma, the wise ones, performed their sacred rites through you, O Pavamāna.
Striking down the unassailable ones, open wide the enclosures; O Maghavan, be ours with heroes and horses.
O Soma, in harmony with the fathers, you have extended yourself across heaven and earth. To you, O Indu, we pay worship with this oblation; may we become masters of riches.
O Pitṛs who sit upon the sacrificial grass, come hither with your aid; we have prepared these oblations for you—enjoy them!
Come to us with most auspicious protection, and then bestow upon us health, well-being, and freedom from harm.

I have found the benevolent fathers, and the descendant, and the wide stride of Viṣṇu. Those who sit upon the sacrificial grass and partake of the pressed juice with the funeral offering (svadhā)—they are most eager to come here to this food.
The Soma-loving ancestors have been invited to their dear offerings placed upon the sacred grass;
may they come hither, may they hear us here, may they speak for us, and may they protect us.

O Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, come here; take your seats in every assembly, O excellent leaders. Eat the oblations presented upon the sacrificial grass, and then bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroic sons.
O Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, increasers of cosmic order, be gracious to us; release us from distress.
We invoke the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs who follow the seasons, who have attained the drinking of Soma through Narāśaṃsa.
May they come hither; may they hear us here; may they speak for us; may they protect us.
By means of his ancient invocation and his wisdom, he brought forth these progeny of men.

With Vivasvat as his eye, the gods, the givers of wealth, established Agni as the sustainer of heaven and earth. That Agni who is the bearer of oblations to the ancestors, who shall worship the Fathers who increase the Truth—may he announce the offerings to both the gods and the Fathers.
From you, O Agni, come poetic insights; from you, inspired thoughts; from you are born the attainable boons.
From you comes wealth adorned with heroes for the mortal who offers oblations with such devotion.
The wind is the foremost leader with which you go forth.
The seers yoke the ploughs; they stretch out the yokes separately—the wise ones, for the sake of Indra’s favor.

May we invoke the bounteous Indra with prosperity in this battle, the most heroic in the winning of booty—the fierce one who hears us, for our protection in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the winner of riches.
Behold that wonderful light of the gods.
We invoke Indra Śunāsīra at this sacrifice; here we call upon the god who bestows abundant wealth.
We take hold of Indra, the lord of wealth, the son of Anu; may he, the sovereign, grant us protection like a father to his sons. ||14||
Thus ends the twenty-first section, named Pañcacūḍa, in the Madhyamikā branch of the Caraka school within the glorious Kāṭhaka Yajurveda. 21.

Now the twenty-second section: On Heaven. Indeed, for the sake of the heavenly world, the chariot of the gods is yoked; for the sake of desire, the chariot of men is yoked. With the words, "I yoke Agni with power and ghee," he yokes the very chariot of the gods. Being thus yoked, it carries him toward the heavenly world. If he were to yoke [Agni] with all [the verses], his fire would be yoked but the oblations would be without a foundation. He yokes with three verses; for Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, so much of him he yokes. When he is yoked, the sacrifice is established. He does not yoke with two more than those two [initial verses], for the sake of the stability of the oblations; [he yokes] with two.

At the *yajñāyajñīya* chant, he touches [the sacrificial post], saying: "The sacrifice is indeed as great as the *agniṣṭoma*; more than that is performed hereafter. As great as the sacrifice is, as great as the *agniṣṭoma* is, so does he finally ascend after it to the heavenly world."

These two fires—the Agniṣṭoma and the Vaiśvānara—indeed burn together; he touches them with two verses containing the word *apasvatī* for the sake of pacification. With two verses, [he does so] because the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability. "May the years, O Agni, and the seasons increase thee"—with the years he thus increases the seasons, and with the seasons the year. "Shine forth together with the heavenly light"—therefore Agni shines throughout all the quarters. "The Aśvins have warded off death from him"—these [verses] he should perform for one who is ill, for it is death itself that he wards off from him.

With the verse, "He drives away [the darkness] from around the rising,"—for darkness is indeed evil—he thereby repels evil. With the words, "Beholding the higher light,"—for yonder sun is indeed the highest light—he attains union with that very sun, yonder Aditya.

Those verses which contain the word *apasvatī* he should employ for the sake of peace. There are twenty-four of them; there are twenty-four half-months in a year. Indeed, the year does not stand still, nor does the prosperity of one for whom these are performed stand still. Now, these are the *āprī* verses. Having created offspring, Prajāpati felt as if he were depleted. He beheld these *āprī* verses; with them he gratified himself. Prajāpati is the sacrifice; in that there are *āprī* verses, he gratifies the sacrifice itself. They are deficient and redundant, forming a pair for the sake of procreation. It is indeed hairy...

This is the metre of Prajāpati; hairy animals are produced [by it], for the procreation of cattle. Indeed, all these are forms; all forms are employed in the piling of the fire-altar. Therefore, these belong to the piled fire-altar.

Just as the *punarādheya* (re-establishment of the fires) is, so is the *punaścit* (re-building of the altar). He who does not prosper through the *agnyādheya* establishes the *punarādheya*; if he should not prosper with the piled fire-altar (*citya*), he should pile the *punaścit*. He indeed prospers. The first layer is the self; the second is offspring; the third is descendants. When piling the third fire-altar, one should place these bricks in the middle layer for the sake of continuity. What is this fire-altar called? It is "Napāt" (the descendant); it eats food. He who, knowing thus, places these [bricks], attains them—these eight.

He lays them down; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and thus he finds firm support in the Gāyatrī itself. Whatever oblation a builder of the fire-altar offers on a place where no brick has been laid, it flows away; as that oblation flows away, the sacrifice flows away after it, and the sacrificer follows after the sacrifice. When these [bricks] are laid down, it is for the stabilization of the oblations.

As they become firmly established, the sacrifice becomes established; following the sacrifice, the sacrificer becomes established. He lays down eight of them; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī: as great as Agni is, him he builds up. Having laid down these eight, he covers them with loose soil (*purīṣa*). The Gāyatrī has eight syllables and the Gāyatrī is the Brahman; verily by means of the Brahman he builds him up. Having laid down eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the Gāyatrī metre, he covers them with loose soil. The Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables and the Triṣṭubh is vigor; verily by means of vigor he builds him up, with the Triṣṭubh metre.

Having laid down twelve *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the *chandas* metre, he covers it over with loose earth (*purīṣa*). The *jagatī* consists of twelve syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the *jagatī*; verily, by means of cattle, he piles this [altar]. With the *jagatī* metre, there are three layers and three coverings of earth; that makes six. There are six seasons; verily, he finds firm support in the seasons. Regarding this they say: "If his former fire-altar has already been piled, he should sacrifice after settling upon it. Just as one adds more fuel to a fire that is already blazing, even so does he place that former [fire] upon this one.

He bestows brilliance upon it. Regarding this they say: "Who is fit to awaken one who is sleeping better than another? If he sacrifices, he causes him to grow by means of the oblation. In that he piles the fire-altar, he indeed constructs a house; or rather, whatever he obtains from elsewhere, that he brings as his house. Whether he should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, or with an animal sacrifice, or with Soma—if his former fire-altar has been piled, he should sacrifice after settling down beside it. Just as one, having obtained something from elsewhere, brings it to his house, so too is that.

Having maintained the fire for one year as the primary period, when the second year has elapsed, he should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, on eleven potsherds to Indra, on twelve potsherds to the Viśvedevas, a pap to Bṛhaspati, and on three potsherds to Viṣṇu. When the third year has elapsed, he should sacrifice with the Abhijit rite. In that there is an offering on eight potsherds—the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and the morning pressing belongs to Agni and is of the Gāyatrī type—he thereby supports the morning pressing and the Gāyatrī metre. In that there is an offering on eleven potsherds—the [Triṣṭubh] has eleven syllables...

The Triṣṭubh belongs to Indra; the midday pressing is connected with the Triṣṭubh. By this, he supports the midday pressing and the Triṣṭubh metre. As for the cake on twelve potsherds—the Jagatī has twelve syllables, the third pressing belongs to the Viśve Devas and is connected with the Jagatī—by this he supports the third pressing and the Jagatī metre. As for the offering to Bṛhaspati: Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; by this he supports the Brahman. As for the offering to Viṣṇu: Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; by this he supports the sacrifice. As for the Abhijit...

He sacrifices for the sake of conquest. In that he carries the fire in the *ukhā* for a year, he wins this world; in that he piles the second layer, he wins the intermediate space; in that he sacrifices, he wins yonder world. Indeed, Para Āṅgiras, Kakṣīvat Auśija, Trasadasyu Paurukutsa, and others, desiring offspring, piled this very altar. Thereupon they each obtained a thousand sons. He who, knowing thus, piles this altar, attains that same abundance which they attained. 3.

Prajāpati indeed built this fire-altar first, with the seasons and the year: with spring the eastern half, with summer the right wing, with the rainy season the left wing, with autumn the tail, and with winter the middle. With the *brahman* he built its eastern half, with the *kṣatra* the right wing, with the *viś* the left, with cattle the tail, and with hope the middle. As much as there is, so much does he secure; they hear him when he has piled the fire-altar; he eats food; it shines forth. What is the first?

"What is the filling soil? the exponents of Brahman say. "This [earth] is indeed the first layer; the plants are the filling soil. The atmosphere is the second layer; the birds are the filling soil. The sky is the third layer; the stars are the filling soil. The sacrifice is the fourth layer; the sacrificial fee is the filling soil. The self is the fifth layer; offspring are the filling soil. If one were to pile only three layers, he would exclude the sacrifice, the sacrificial fee, the self, and offspring. Therefore, it should be piled in five layers. As for the fact that there are three layers: Agni is threefold. As for the fact that there are two [additional layers]: the sacrificer is two-footed. These worlds are three; verily, he prospers in these very worlds. ||4||

In harmony with the years and the days; in harmony with the ruddy dawn and her crimson rays; in harmony with Sūrya and his steed Etaśa; in harmony with the Aśvins and their wondrous deeds; in harmony with Vaiśvānara, with the sacrificial food and the clarified butter—Svāhā!
The brilliant face of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
The Sun has filled heaven, earth, and the intermediate space; he is the soul of all that moves and stands still.
Yoke, O Agni, like a charioteer, the horses that best summon the gods; sit down as the ancient Hotṛ-priest.

O Agni, yoke indeed those horses of yours, O God, which are well-trained and swift, carrying you readily. You are the path of Agni; you are the path of Vāyu; you are the path of the Gods; you are the path of the atmosphere; you are the one who sits in the atmosphere; sit in the atmosphere.

Thou art the barley, thou art the wild barley, thou art the auxiliary; thus [I place thee] for the sake of the year, for the sake of the ocean, for the sake of the unique water, for the sake of the grape, for the sake of the *satīkā* plant, for the sake of the intention, for the sake of the wise one, for the sake of heaven, for the sake of light, for the sake of Vivasvat, for the sake of the Ādityas, for the sake of the *ṛc*, for the sake of radiance, for the sake of luster, for the sake of brilliance, for the sake of light, for the sake of Sūrya. Thou art the winner of the east wind, thou art the winner of the cloud, thou art the winner of the lightning, thou art the winner of the thunder, thou art the winner of the rain. With the eastern quarter, with Agni as the deity, with the *gāyatrī* metre, I place thee upon the head of Agni.

With the Gāyatrī metre, with the head of Agni, I place the head of Agni. With the southern quarter, with Indra as the deity, with the Triṣṭubh metre, I place the side of Agni. With the Triṣṭubh metre, with the side of Agni, I place the side of Agni. With the western quarter, with Savitṛ as the deity, with the Jagatī metre, I place the tail of Agni. With the Jagatī metre, with the tail of Agni, [I place the tail] of Agni.

I place the tail; with the northern quarter, with Mitra and Varuṇa as the deity, with the Anuṣṭubh metre, I place the side of Agni; with the Anuṣṭubh metre, with the side of Agni, I place the side of Agni. With the upward quarter, with Bṛhaspati as the deity, with the Paṅkti metre, I place the back of Agni; with the Paṅkti metre, with the back of Agni, I place the back of Agni.

Saṃyac and Pracetas are the overlords of Agni, Soma, and Sūrya; whomsoever we hate and whoever hates us, him I place within their jaws. Ugrā and Bhīmā are the overlords of the Pitṛs, Yama, and Indra; whomsoever we hate and whoever hates us, him I place within their jaws. Dhruvā and Pṛthivī are the overlords of Savitṛ, the Maruts, and Varuṇa; whomsoever we hate and whoever hates us, him I place within their jaws. Yantrī and Yamanī...

And [the quarters] of Mitra and Varuṇa, of Mitra, and of Dhātṛ—these are your overlords; him whom we hate and he who hates us, him I place within their jaws. The eastern and the western [quarters] of the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas—these are your overlords; him whom we hate and he who hates us, him I place within their jaws. ||5||

"May he be united with years and with days. The year, indeed, is the "year" (abda); the months are the "days" (āyavaḥ); the dawn is the ruddy one; the sun is Etaśa; these two are the Aśvins; Agni Vaiśvānara is the year; *iḍā* is cattle; ghee is cattle. Cattle are born after the pattern of the year; verily, from the year itself he causes cattle to be born for him. He offers on a clump of darbha grass. Whatever immortal essence and whatever vigor there is in this [earth], that hereupon rises up; it is upon that immortal essence and vigor of hers that he offers. One who has piled the fire-altar does not die prematurely.

For him over whose human head they thus offer with the verse, "The brilliant face of the gods has risen," he offers; Mitra is indeed the day and Varuṇa is the night—whatever exists is as much as this—and so he wins that which exists. He offers with a verse addressed to Sūrya; therefore, the human being faces the sun, while other animals face downward. Because he offers twice with the same verse, therefore a single person has two feet.

Whoever indeed does not yoke the fire when the time for yoking has arrived, does not yoke it among those who are yoking; [he should recite: "Yoke, O Agni, those most fit for the invocation of the gods; yoke those that are thine. He thus yokes the fire when the time for yoking has arrived and yokes it among those who are yoking, provided he knows this. He yokes with two verses, for there are two parts to a non-defective chariot. Whoever indeed does not unyoke the fire when the time for unyoking has arrived, does not unyoke it among those who are unyoking; [he should recite: "As a mother her son, so may the earth release the one rich in soil. He thus unyokes the fire when the time for unyoking has arrived and unyokes it among those who are unyoking.

He who knows thus releases [the breaths]; now, these are the *saṃyānī* verses; these indeed are the deities that lead to heaven; through them he goes to the heavenly world. This Gāyatrī has light for its wings; by it alone he goes to the heavenly world.

Just as water flows from one vessel of water into another, even so does the builder of the fire-altar (Agnicit) go to his world by means of these [bricks]; that is why they are called *saṃyānī*s. Now, these are the names of the seasons; verily, he wins the seasons themselves. "Sumeka" [is said]; the year is indeed *sumeka*; verily, he wins the year. Now, these are the Āditya-bricks. The Ādityas take away the splendor of him who has built the fire-altar and yet does not shine. When these are laid down, it is just as when one adds more fuel to a blazing fire; even so, he places that [splendor] upon him.

First he bestows radiance; the Ādityas do not take away his radiance. As it is among the gods, so it becomes among men. Now, these are the ghee-bricks (*ghṛteṣṭakā*): Agni is indeed radiance, and ghee is radiance; verily, he places radiance into radiance. Now, these are the rain-winning bricks (*vṛṣṭisani*): by means of these, he wins rain. By means of these, it rains for the one who has piled the fire-altar (*agnicit*) there in yonder world according to his desire; that is the "rain-winning" nature of the rain-winners. Now, these are the self-bricks (*ātman*). Regarding this, Śaṅkha Kauṣya said to his son concerning the fire-altar:

"Did we build Agni with the *acchāvāk* verses? "Yes, we did. "Then why did you not sing all the *ātman* [verses]? "Surely we did not know them," they said. Now, when these [bricks] are laid down, one builds the fire-altar with its very self (*ātman*). They are pressed down again; he thus joins breath to breath. Now, this is the sixth layer. He who, having built the fire-altar, does not find firm standing, should lay down this sixth layer. There are six seasons in the year; he thus finds firm standing in the seasons, in the year. These indeed...

The deities are sixfold; by means of them one goes to the heavenly world. These indeed are the deities to be employed for sorcery. Whomever one hates, he should say of him, "I place such-and-such a one in the jaws [of these deities]"; verily, he cuts him off from these very deities, and he perishes instantly.

By means of fire, the gods went to the heavenly world. As they were turning away, the Rakṣases pursued them from behind and sought to strike them. Those gods saw these *vitṛṇṇī* bricks; with them they struck down the Rakṣases. In that he lays down two in front and two behind, he places sight on both sides for the striking away of the Rakṣases. They are self-perforated (*svayamātṛṇṇā*) for the release of the vital breaths and for the reaching of the heavenly world. There are four of them; therefore there are four forms of the eye: two white and two black.

The fire-altar is indeed built for the sake of the heavenly world; if he were to perform the set of eleven animals, he would be hemmed in from the front by the thunderbolt and would not attain heaven. If he performs a non-set of eleven, his cattle would remain unsecured. Therefore, he should immolate eleven animals at a single sacrificial post; thus it is conducive to heaven, and thereby he secures cattle.

One should not measure [the sacrificial post] according to the wings; for if one were to measure it according to the wings, he would enter upon a lesser sacrificial rite, and his offspring would become more wretched than himself. Regarding this, Jāta Śākāyanya said to Śaṅkha Kauṣya: "Having heard that you have measured the set of eleven posts according to the wings, you have entered upon a lesser sacrificial rite, and your offspring will become more wretched than yourself. From that time on, they indeed consider him to have been defeated. One should measure [the post] according to the altar; thus one enters upon a more excellent sacrificial rite.

His offspring does not become more wicked than he himself. "For what purpose is the fire-altar built? they ask. "It is built so that the gods may know him," they say. He who, knowing this, builds the fire-altar—the gods know him. "For what purpose is the fire-altar built? they ask. "It is built so that I may have a home," they say. He who, knowing this, builds the fire-altar becomes possessed of a home. "For what purpose is the fire-altar built? they ask. "It is built so that I may eat food," they say. He who, knowing this, builds the fire-altar eats food; this is his vow.

Having piled the fire-altar for the first time, one should not approach a woman; having piled it for the second time, one should not approach the wives of others; having piled it for the third time, one should not approach any woman at all. For when one piles the fire-altar, he deposits this seed; if he were to approach a woman, he would be deprived of his seed. Regarding this they say: "Those very *iṣṭakās* which are the 'seed-holders,' they sustain the seed of the fire-piler; therefore, one may approach her. One who is piling for the first time should pile with a thousand bricks, for this world is measured by a thousand. One who is piling for the second time [should pile] two thousands, [measured] by the intermediate space.

It is commensurate with three thousand; he who piles the third [layer] piles it commensurate with these three worlds. Prajāpati indeed bore the fire in the pan (*ukhya*); by means of it, he created offspring and entered into them. He said, "He alone among my offspring shall prosper who shall pile this for me. Agni is Prajāpati; when one piles the fire, one piles Prajāpati himself and prospers—this is the reason for the name of the piling (*citya*). He gave it to the Vasus; by means of it, the Vasus [attained] three hundred.

The Vasus created thirty-three [beings] and gave them to the Rudras; with that, the Rudras created three hundred and thirty-three. The Rudras gave them to the Ādityas; with that, the Ādityas created three hundred and thirty-three, of whom the fire-pan (ukhā) was the thousandth. He who thus knows the fire-pan as the thousandth attains a thousandfold prosperity of cattle.

In whatever form the fire-altar (Agni) is to be built—verily, for him who builds the fire-altar in its proper form, no misshapen thing is born to him—one should touch the first layer when it has been completed with a *gāyatrī* verse, the second with a *triṣṭubh*, the third with a *jagatī*, the fourth with an *anuṣṭubh*, and the fifth with a *paṅkti*. Thus he builds the fire-altar in its proper form, and no misshapen thing is born to him. The first layer is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the second the through-breath (*vyāna*), and the third the in-breath (*apāna*); verily, by means of the out-breaths and in-breaths, he kindles it. This is indeed a division of the *iḍā*; the *iḍā* is cattle.

Verily, he piles it with animals. Having announced it to Prajāpati, the fire-altar is to be piled. For whoever piles the fire-altar without having announced it to Prajāpati meets with ruin. Two horses should stand on either side: a dark-brown one to the north and a white one to the south; holding them, he should lay down each brick. This is indeed the form of Prajāpati, for the horse belongs to Prajāpati. Having thus announced it to Prajāpati, he piles the fire-altar and does not meet with ruin.

He gives a golden vessel full of honey to the Brahmin; he becomes worthy of sweetness. It is a *śatamāna* weight; man indeed has a life of a hundred years and a hundredfold vigor; verily, he secures for himself life and vigor. With the verse, "The brilliant face of the gods has risen," he gazes at it with a verse containing the word "brilliant"; verily, he becomes brilliant. At midday, he causes the horse to smell [the offering]; yonder sun is Indra, he is Prajāpati, and the horse belongs to Prajāpati; verily, he prospers him visibly. He who knows the attainment of Agni attains that desire for which [he performs this rite].

The fire-altar is piled for the sake of desire. One who is about to depart should worship the piled fire with the formula: "By initiation I have attained you; by austerity I have attained you; by the Soma-pressing I have attained you; by the purificatory bath I have attained you; by the *vaśā* cow I have attained you. This makes five; for there are five seasons, and the year consists of the seasons. The fire-altar is Vaiśvānara, the year; he attains that very desire for which the fire-altar is piled.

"The single brick," say the exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*); "Speech is the single brick," they say; "The Brāhmaṇa is the single brick," they say. Indeed, they have also said this regarding these worlds: "We know the fire-altar to be built as consisting of only three bricks—namely, these very worlds. The fire-altar is to be built with truth. With "Bhūḥ! he should touch the first layer; with "Bhuvaḥ! the second; with "Svaḥ! the third. This is indeed the truth of speech; verily, he builds the fire-altar with truth.

"Is it with truth that one piles the fire, or is it with untruth? so ask those who discourse on Brahman. "He indeed piles it with truth who piles it in this manner. "For which deity is the fire piled? so ask those who discourse on Brahman. "It is for Prajāpati alone. "What is its oblation? "The self itself."

In the beginning, this world was indeed water, a mere ocean. That Prajāpati, having become the wind, moved restlessly upon a lotus leaf; he found no firm support. He beheld this nest of the waters; that Prajāpati built this fire-altar in the midst of the waters, and it became this earth. Upon it he established himself. This earth is indeed Agni; therefore, when they dig into it, they pierce through the brick, through the pebble, and through whatever else lies before it. That [brick] which he placed in front became the head; that was the eastern direction. That which he placed on the south... he...

That which was on the right became the right wing; that was the southern quarter, which he placed behind—that became the tail; that was the western quarter. That which was on the left became the left wing; that was the northern quarter, which he placed in the middle—that became the back; that was the upward quarter. This Agni indeed consists of five bricks. He who knows thus is propagated, attains a firm foundation. The Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni; therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, there is prosperity in all directions, for he follows his own very quarter.

Indeed, this [earth] shines at night for all birds to see; therefore, birds do not sit upon it at night. This is indeed the nest of the waters; therefore, the waters seek to destroy it, for this is the nest of the waters.

If he should think, "My rival has surpassed me," he should place eight *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks before the *bahiṣpavamāna*, eleven before the *mādhyandina-pavamāna*, and twelve before the *ārbhava-pavamāna*. This one who blows is indeed the *pavamāna*; Vāyu is Agni’s brilliance (*tejas*). He thus drives away with brilliance that rival of his who has previously surpassed him. If he should think, "My rival is behind me," he should place them behind these.

One should place [the bricks] of the *pavamāna* verses; he who blows here is indeed the *pavamāna*, and Vāyu is the brilliance (*tejas*) of Agni. Whatever rival (*bhrātṛvya*) is behind him, him he repels with brilliance; he drives away a superior rival and drives back a weaker one.

This very Prajāpati, who is built up by the pressings, bore the fire in the pan (ukhya). His head fell away; with it the gods toiled, and they restored that head of his which is the pan.
