Agni-Prajāpati ascended [to life] after a year. In that he bears the fire in the pan for a year, he restores the very head of Prajāpati. Therefore, the fire in the pan must be borne for a year; if one bears it for less than a year, he is indeed a mere stump.

"By which the gods went upward to the light, by which the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Rudras [went], by which the Aṅgirases attained greatness—by that may the sacrificer go to well-being. Having anointed the fuel-stick with ghee, he places it on the fire. This is indeed its kindling; moreover, this is performed as a rite for the sacrificer's well-being.
Those fires which are full of soil and have entered upon the earth—you are the highest among them; impel us toward life.
Thus he should stand by his own piled fire; he attains a full lifespan with this three-verse hymn beginning "Upa tvāgne dive dive"; for others, that [standing] is merely a benediction.

When the hearth-stones (*dhiṣṇya*) are laid down, then he lays down three with verses addressed to Bṛhaspati on the south; then three with verses addressed to Yama on the east; then three with verses addressed to Rudra on the north from the south [of the animal-cooking fire]; then three with verses addressed to Varuṇa at the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) on the south. For the Rakṣases sought to destroy the sacrifice of the gods from the south; they drove them away by means of the *brahman*. Bṛhaspati is the *brahman*; therefore, those [bricks] addressed to Bṛhaspati are laid down on the south.

Now, those belonging to the *Rakṣases* are for the driving away of the Rakṣases. Then there are those belonging to Yama; by means of these, indeed, these worlds—both those turned hitherward and those turned awayward—became manifest to Asita Devala. For whomsoever these are laid down, these worlds, both turned hitherward and turned awayward, shine forth for him. Now, those belonging to Rudra: this fire-altar is indeed Rudra, and the animal-cooking hearth is his very self. He is liable to rise up after this [altar] and destroy it; in that he lays down the bricks belonging to Rudra, he thereby pacifies Rudra. Now, those belonging to Varuṇa: Varuṇa is indeed the waters. He is liable to seize him after he has followed the sacrificial bath (*avabhṛtha*);
in that he lays down the bricks belonging to Varuṇa, it is for the sake of release from Varuṇa’s noose. ||11||

If, while the fire-pan (*ukhya*) is being carried, this god should take ill-will toward the creatures, one should place three fuel-sticks each time with three verses addressed to Agni that contain the word "physician" (*bhiṣagvatī*). For it is indeed he who takes ill-will toward the creatures when one places the sticks with verses containing the word "physician"; thus one provides a remedy, for that is indeed peace. If, while the fire-pan is being carried, one should desire, "May it rain," one should place three fuel-sticks each time with three verses addressed to Sūrya that contain the word "ray" (*raśmivatī*). For it is indeed he who afflicts the creatures with heat when Parjanya does not rain.

In that he places [the kindling-sticks] with those verses containing the word "ray" (*raśmi*), he pours down rain; it rains quickly. If, while the fire-pan (*ukhya*) is being carried, he should desire, "May it not rain," he should place three kindling-sticks with those three verses addressed to Sūrya that contain the word "splendor" (*bhrājasvatī*); thus he produces splendor, and it does not rain during that year. If the fire-pan should be lost while it is being carried, he should worship with these four verses: "O Agni, come back... O Agni Aṅgiras, with strength and wealth again. He certainly finds it. 12.

They construct a hall with its ridge-pole facing east; the east is the quarter of the gods, so he turns toward the world of the gods. He goes forward; he thus ascends after that very sun. They cause him to sacrifice within an enclosed space; having encompassed the world of the gods, they consecrate him therein. Indeed, he who goes to that world departs from this world; for that world is, as it were, hidden from here. He should make the *atīroka* openings at the corners; thereby he does not depart from this world. He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; Agni, indeed, is all the deities.

Viṣṇu is the sacrifice and the deities; having taken hold of the sacrifice, he undergoes initiation. Or rather, Agni is the sacrifice and Viṣṇu is the purifier; thus, purified by the purifier, he takes hold of the sacrifice. In that it is on eight potsherds, it belongs to Agni; in that it is on three potsherds, it belongs to Viṣṇu; thus he does not depart from either. He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu. Agni is indeed the lowest of the gods, and Viṣṇu is the highest. Just as one grasps the two ends of a shuttle, even so, having grasped both ends, he pours in the deities in the middle.

There should be a *puroḍāśa* cake for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); for the *puroḍāśa* is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *puroḍāśa* is spiritual luster; thus he becomes possessed of spiritual luster. There should be a *caru* oblation in ghee for one desiring offspring or desiring cattle; for ghee and rice grains constitute a pair, and the ghee is the milk of a cow while the rice grains are from a bull—thus he places a productive pair at the mouth of the sacrifice for the sake of procreation. For this form, the *caru*, is indeed moving; for the consecrated one goes toward that world, as he is indeed that [world].

He consecrates himself for the world; that there is a sacrificial pap (*caru*) is for prosperity. He anoints his eyes, he anoints [his body], he eats, and he puts on a garment—these indeed are the bodies of man; having thus become complete in all his limbs, he enters the consecration (*dīkṣā*). Man is indeed full of holes and internally impure; when he eats, it is for the sake of purity and for the sake of being without holes. In that world over there, one should observe a vow exactly as one does here when being consecrated; just as one might think, "In this way it will not distress me," so should one observe the vow. Moreover, from whatever point one might intend to observe a lesser vow while being consecrated, [one should do so].

He should eat in that manner; he shaves his hair and beard, clips his nails, and cleanses his teeth. This [food] is indeed the nectar of man, yet it is impure; having struck away the impurity, he attains purity. When he bathes, he takes hold of that very consecration (*dīkṣā*); for the Aṅgirases, having deposited the consecration in the waters, went to the heavenly world. It should be bathed in water reaching up to the neck, for they went after depositing it at the height of the neck. However much or however little water he uses when bathing, by that very means he takes hold of that consecration. He does not...

If he were to bathe in flowing waters, he would attain the glory of the *kṣatra*; if he were to bathe in waters from a well, he would attain the glory of the *viś*. He should bathe in still waters; for these still waters are the consecrated (*dīkṣita*) ones among the waters, rich in cattle. Those that are still, hairy, and continuous—since cattle are hairy—he causes the sacrificer himself to attain glory. He should bathe at a *tīrtha* (ford); thus he becomes a ford for his peers.
May Mādhava, who is rich in sweetness, protect us;
may Agni, the god whose course is difficult to overcome and who is undeceivable, protect us; may this sacred prayer bring us life; may he protect us.
May the Rathantara protect us with the Sāmans; may the Gāyatrī, the multiform among meters, protect us;
may the Trivṛt Stoma with its various forms, the ocean, and the wind fulfill this vigor for us throughout the days.
Fierce, the conqueror of the quarters, bestower of vitality, pure, bright, born on the day of light— may you,
with Indra as your sovereign lord, protect us from this [hostility] and maintain this great dominion for us on every side.

The Bṛhat Sāman, which sustains dominion and possesses increased virility; the Triṣṭubh, which is adorned with vigor and possesses fierce heroes—O Indra, protect this power with the fifteenfold Stoma and with the wind that accompanies the battle-cry.
May the All-Gods, who dwell together in the eastern quarter, finders of light through the rainy days of the year,
grant this dominion that is invincible, inviolable power, thousandfold and victorious.

By means of the Vairūpa Sāman may I be able to accomplish that; by means of the Jagatī meter I cause him to enter into the subjects. O All-Gods, with the seventeenfold Stoma, place this ruling power, this ocean, and the fierce wind in the center.
The controller of the quarters has established this Kṣatriya power; the regions are its seat, and this vigor is possessed of friends.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who move through the days with the autumn, this inviolable Kṣatriya power is indeed our strength.
My thought is fixed upon the Vairāja Sāman; through the Anuṣṭubh, it has been gathered as invincible power.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you whose gifts are moistening, protect this ruling power with your sovereign dominions, like a friend.
May the Sovereign of the quarters, accompanied by the thousandfold hymn, the thousandfold one, may the winter season fulfill our needs with its appointed place.
May the wind, seeking aid, like the great Śakvarī verse, protect this sacrifice—she who is dripping with ghee.
May she who is rich in sound, easy to milk, full of milk, and dripping with clarity protect this sacrifice;
O Bṛhaspati, you are our protector, helper, and leader—yoke your voice to the path of the Yāmīs.

May the upward direction, the delight of the quarters, the plants, and Savitṛ with the year among our days [protect us]. O wealthy Sāman, O Aticchandas meter, and you, the meter—be you of easy invocation for us, O Unborn Enemy.
O Stoma of thirty-three, O Mistress of the World, O Vivasvat, O Vāta, favor us with your song!
Under the sovereignty of Savitṛ, may there be for us a refreshing quarter, rich in ghee and full of milk.
He who is Hiraṇyagarbha, the one who breathes through all living beings.
May Virāj, the mistress of the quarters, the wife of Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the face of Aghorā, she who is the mental inspirer of the powerful,
the all-pervading, the nourishing, and the well-being— may that Aditi be auspicious to us in her lap.
The support of heaven, the upholder of earth, mistress of this [world], the consort of Viṣṇu born of strength—
may Bṛhaspati, Mātariśvan, and Vāyu, along with the roaring winds, sing our praises.
May Vaiśvānara, sought after in heaven, find us for our protection; O Anumati, that which is your name—[may it be ours]. 14.
I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise one, whom many kindle as the one belonging to the five peoples;
entering into every clan, we implore him: may he deliver us from distress.
I praise Agni, whose alone is all that breathes and blinks, that moves, and all that has been born and is being born; seeking protection, I call upon him repeatedly: may he deliver us from distress.
I meditate upon Indra, the first, the wise slayer of Vṛtra; may his hymns come hither unto me.
He who goes to the call of the liberal, well-doing worshiper—may he deliver us from distress.

He who conquers the battle by his own power in combat, he who brings together the three kinds of nourishment—I praise Indra; seeking protection, I call upon him repeatedly. May he deliver us from distress.
We meditate upon the ordinances of Vāyu and Savitṛ, you two who bear that which possesses a soul and whom you protect;
you two who have become the sovereign lords of the universe—deliver us from sin.
May our most excellent blessings rest upon the law of the two gods;
I praise Vāyu and Savitṛ, and in my need I call upon them repeatedly: may you two deliver us from sin.
I think of you both, O Mitra and Varuṇa; take note of that, O you who possess true power and are firm, whomsoever you two drive away.
You two kings who travel in one chariot, O fierce ones, deliver us from sin.

That chariot of yours which, with straight reins and true laws, approaches the one who acts deceitfully to corrupt him—I praise Mitra and Varuṇa, seeking protection I call upon them; may they two release us from sin.
I invoke for protection the two best of chariot-warriors among chariot-warriors, who go most brilliantly with their swift, well-governed horses;
O gods, you whose power is most unassailable among the gods, deliver us from sin.

When you two came to the wedding procession of Sūryā with your three-wheeled chariot, seeking a place in the assembly—I praise the divine Aśvins, imploring them, I call upon them repeatedly; may they two release us from sin.
I call upon the Maruts; may they speak for us, and may they all protect this entire speech.
I invoke the swift ones, easy to guide, for our protection; may they release us from sin.
I praise the sharp weapon, the praised one, the victorious divine host, triumphant in battles; I laud the gods, the Maruts, and as one in need, I cry out to them: may they release us from sin.
I meditate upon all the gods; may they speak for us, and may all of them protect this speech of ours.
I invoke the swift ones, easy to control, for our protection; may they release us from sin.
Whatever offense we have committed against men or gods, may there be a sacrifice for bipeds and quadrupeds;
I praise all the gods, I call upon them in my distress—may they release us from this sin.
O Anumati, do thou find favor; that name of thine which Vaiśvānara, sought in heaven, possesses for our protection.
Those two who have spread out with immeasurable powers, who have become the foundations of all treasures—may they release us from distress.
O wide Heaven and Earth, create space for us; O two wives of the field, speak in our favor.
I praise Heaven and Earth; seeking protection, I call upon you repeatedly. Deliver us from distress. ||15||
Thus ends the twenty-second section, named "Heaven," in the Madhyamikā recension of the Caraka branch of the glorious Yajurveda-Kāṭhaka. 22.

Now begins the twenty-third section. Regarding the consecrated one: the consecrated one is indeed the sacrificial oblation (*havis*); the oblation does not attain its essence unless it is anointed with ghee. When he anoints him, he truly provides for him with ghee for the sake of his fitness for sacrifice (*medhyatva*). Ghee is for the gods when it is cooked; for humans when it is melted; for the Gandharvas when it is self-melted; and for Āditya when it is fresh butter (*navanīta*). That which is fresh butter belongs neither to the gods nor to humans; likewise, he who is consecrated belongs neither to the gods nor to humans, as he has departed from this world but has not yet reached that one. When he anoints himself with fresh butter, it is for the sake of prosperity. He puts on a garment, [which is] the wool of Agni.

The *nīvira* belongs to the ancestors; the *praghāta* to the plants; the *vātapā* to Vāyu; the *otavas* and *tantavas* to the Viśve Devas; the *atīrokās* to the Nakṣatras; the garment (*vāsas*) belongs to all the deities, and the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*) belongs to all the deities. Verily, he causes him to prosper through all the deities. He anoints himself. When Indra had slain Vṛtra, the Rakṣases attached themselves to him; he separated them by means of the ointment-mountain (*añjana-giri*). The Rakṣases attach themselves to this man who undergoes consecration, for he becomes [one of them]. In that he anoints himself, it is for the purpose of excluding the Rakṣases. Indra, indeed...

When Vṛtra was slain, his eye flew away; it entered the *trikakubh* [plant]. When he anoints [the eyes], it is for the attainment of that very eye. He anoints the right eye twice and the left once; the sacrifice is threefold, and thus he seizes the sacrifice from its very mouth. He anoints the right eye thrice and the left twice; the sacrifice is fivefold, and thus he wins the sacrifice. He anoints the right first, for men anoint the left first; this is for the sake of distinction. He anoints with a *yajus* formula, for men anoint without a formula; this is for the sake of distinction.

He anoints it facing away; he does not turn back, for men anoint themselves facing forward or backward for the sake of distinction. He anoints with a reed-shaft; for men anoint themselves with a porcupine quill for the sake of distinction.

Maitrī is possessed of *tūla*; Vāruṇī is indeed possessed of *tūla*, being scattered. The consecrated one belongs to Mitra. That which is the eye is, as it were, deficient and perforated; when he anoints it, he thereby fills it for the sake of non-perforation. He purifies [the water]. Indra, indeed, slew Vṛtra; he slew him right within the waters. Of those waters, whatever was sacrificial and pure went forth and became plants. Whatever brilliance was theirs became *darbha* grass; therefore, that is a means of purification (*pavitra*). Therefore, they purify the waters with *darbha* grass. When [he uses] *darbha*-stalks...

He purifies him; he purifies him with the brilliance of the waters and of the plants. He purifies him with two [verses]; truth and falsehood are two, and by truth alone he purifies his falsehood. With two [he purifies], for out-breath and in-breath are two. He purifies him with three; for the gods are threefold in truth, and moreover, there are three vital breaths—out-breath, diffused breath, and in-breath—and it is these very breaths that he places in the sacrificer. He purifies him with five; man is fivefold, so he purifies his entire self. He purifies him with seven; for the meters are indeed seven.

He purifies him by means of the meters; he purifies him with nine [verses]. There are nine vital breaths; verily, he purifies him by means of the vital breaths. He purifies him with twenty-one [verses]. Man indeed consists of twenty-one parts: ten fingers of the hand, ten toes of the feet, and the self as the twenty-first. As great as his self is, that he purifies. With the words, "May the Lord of Thought purify thee,"—the Lord of Thought is indeed the Brahman—he purifies him by means of the Brahman. With the words, "May the Lord of Speech purify thee,"—for he is the purifier. With the words, "May the god Savitṛ purify thee,"—verily, impelled by Savitṛ, he purifies him.

With the words, "The deities purify him with an unbroken strainer," he purifies him so that there is no failure. With the words, "By the rays of the sun," he purifies him by means of the very body of Āditya. With the words, "O Lord of the strainer, by thy strainer," the Lord of the Strainer is indeed the sacrifice; thus he purifies it for the sake of the sacrifice. With the words, "For whomsoever I purify this, may I be able [for him]," he says, "May I be able for the sacrifice. He purifies him limb by limb, for breath follows along the limbs of a person; for when the breath becomes transverse, then one dies. If...

If he were to purify it crosswise, he would make its vital breath crosswise; it might perish, for he would thus make its vital breath [perish]. He purifies it from outside; having purified him in the world of men, he leads him, once purified, into the world of the gods.

The consecrated one is the embryo; the consecrated shed is the womb; the consecrated garment is the caul; the black antelope skin is the placenta. From this very womb, indeed, Indra was born. Having made it a nest-like dwelling, he attends upon it; therefore, the sun should not set nor rise while the consecrated one is elsewhere than in his consecrated shed. Thus he is born from his own womb. "To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, Svāhā!"—for the sacrifice is conceived and then set in motion; at the very point where one conceives the sacrifice, there one takes hold of it. "To Medhā, to Manas... [Svāhā].

With the thought "To Agni, svāhā! he approaches with wisdom and mind; with "May he be for the sacrificers," he indeed seizes the sacrifice. With "To Dīkṣā, to Tapas, to Agni, svāhā!"—for by means of consecration (dīkṣā) and austerity (tapas) one attains the sacrifice—he secures the sacrifice itself. With "To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agni, svāhā!"—Sarasvatī is speech and Pūṣan is cattle—the sacrifice is seized from speech and cattle; verily, by means of speech, he seizes the sacrifice from cattle. "The divine waters, vast, all-beneficent"—the sacrifice is indeed the waters in heaven.

The sacrifice is in the intermediate space and on the earth; Bṛhaspati is the Brahman. Truly, the sacrifice is wherever the Brahman is; wherever the sacrifice is, from there he seizes it with the Brahman. He offers these five oblations; the sacrifice is fivefold, and thus he wins the sacrifice itself. These sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) are indeed the materials for the sacrifice; if he were not to offer them, his sacrifice would be incomplete. Since he offers them, he gathers the entire sacrifice as it is. Previously, one who was not yet consecrated used to eat by means of a single oblation; indeed, they used to eat his food before this time.

For whomsoever these [oblations] are not offered, for him these are offered for the sake of consecration and for the sake of having a second [partner]. He offers with "To Agni, svāhā! To Agni, svāhā!"—Agni is all the deities; thus he wins all the deities. He offers five of these; the Audgrabhaṇa is the sixth. There are six seasons; verily, he finds firm support in the seasons.

When the sacrifice was created, the *yajus* flowed forth first; the *ṛc* drew it after, and the *sāman* followed. There are nine *sāmans*, twelve *yajus*s; therefore, they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* with nine [verses], and they offer the *udgrabhaṇa* with an *ṛc*. In that he offers the *udgrabhaṇa* with an *ṛc*, he restrains the sacrifice as it is being created by means of the *ṛc*. Indeed, Kārudveṣin used to offer the *udgrabhaṇa* with twelve [verses]; he should make it consist of twelve [drawings] and offer it—by that very means he attains that. He offers with a full ladle; for it is full.

Prajāpati attains Prajāpati himself. If he were to offer with a deficient [offering], he would make room for his rival; but the full [offering] is indeed the fulfillment of desire. Whatever desire one desires, that one effects through the full [offering]; whatever desire one desires, that one secures.

The sacrifice is to be established in its own metre; for the Anuṣṭubh is indeed Prajāpati’s own metre, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. In that he offers the Audgrabhaṇa oblation with the Anuṣṭubh, he establishes the sacrifice in its own metre. The sacrifice is indeed supported by the metres; it is to be established in the metres according to their respective nature. This [Anuṣṭubh] is as follows: of this Anuṣṭubh, one foot has seven syllables and three have eight syllables. Of those seven syllables, the three which are [part of the eight-syllable feet] go toward them [to make up the eight]; thus they become eleven. That...

The four [syllables] that belong to the Triṣṭubh become eight; these [eight] together with those [four] make twelve, which is the Jagatī. Those eight [syllables] are the Gāyatrī. The undivided Anuṣṭubh is [contained] in the Svāhā-call, and the Paṅkti is [contained] in the Svāhā-call. There are indeed only so many meters; thus he establishes the sacrifice itself, according to its meters, within the meters.

"The sacrifice, created by the gods, is to be seized with the words, 'The whole [sacrifice] of the god, the leader' (*viśvo devasya netuḥ*). Because it contains the word "leader" (*netṛ*), it belongs to Savitṛ; because of the word "mortal" (*marta*), it belongs to the Pitṛs; because of the word "whole" (*viśva*), it belongs to the Viśvedevas; because of the word "splendor" (*dyumna*), it belongs to Bṛhaspati; because of the word "may he prosper" (*puṣyatv*), it belongs to Pūṣan; and the exclamation *svāhā* belongs to Sarasvatī. There are indeed as many deities as these. Thus, one seizes the sacrifice, once created, with the deities. When the sacrifice was created, it entered into three parts: a third part into the Ṛc, a third part into the Sāman, and a third part into the Yajus. That which was its beloved body, with that it became the Yajus.

Therefore, when entering, one should not recite the *yajus* loudly; for he rends asunder the beloved body of the sacrifice, becomes devoid of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and is destined to be naked.

The sacrifice indeed departed from the gods, having become a black antelope. As it was returning, the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman* departed from it; they entered the black antelope, perceiving it to be the sacrifice—the *Sāman* being white and the *Ṛc* being black. When one undergoes consecration (*dīkṣā*) with a black antelope skin, one thereby seizes the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*. Day and Night indeed became a couple; their vigor and strength departed, and that entered the black antelope. When one undergoes consecration with a black antelope skin, one thereby seizes the vigor and strength of Day and Night. Heaven and Earth indeed became a couple...

The sacrificial luster of those two departed; it entered the black antelope skin. In that one consecrates oneself with the black antelope skin, one seizes the sacrificial luster of Heaven and Earth. With the words, "You two are the crafts of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*," he seizes the *ṛc* and the *sāman* themselves. Just as two boats intended for crossing would carry him across to the end, so [does this]. With the words, "You are a refuge; grant me a refuge," he indeed mounts both the deities and the sacrifice when he mounts the black antelope skin. For when a superior man desires, then he [desires] the inferior.

He pushes [the metres] away from the deities and pays homage to them for the sake of the sacrifice, so that they are not pushed away. Indeed, some of the metres were swift and others were not swift; those that were swift ran a race, thinking, "We shall burn up those that are not swift. Out of fear, they entered the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). Those which are swift carry the sacrifice; out of fear, thinking, "We shall follow after those that are not swift," they entered the black antelope skin. Those metres which do not carry the sacrifice attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).
He who knows this attains self-sovereignty; when he is consecrated with a black antelope skin, he secures both the swift and the non-swift meters.

The *hotrā* indeed departed from the gods; it followed after the *vaṣaṭ*-call, having become a black antelope. Therefore, the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is not spilled from the *vaṣaṭ*-call; for this reason, they grind the oblation upon a black antelope skin. The consecrated one (*dīkṣita*) is indeed the oblation; therefore, he sits upon the black antelope skin. For this reason, he does not spit, so that the oblation may not be spilled. The sacrifice and the deities are on the outside of the animals, while the fat is within. If he were to make the black antelope skin with the hair on the inside, the sacrificer would be separated from both the sacrifice and the deities.

If there should be one with hair on the inside, the sacrifice would be hidden from the deities; he should join two together, with hair on the inside and hair on the outside. If there should be only one, he should sew it along the edge; thus the sacrificer is not hidden from the sacrifice and from the deities, and the sacrifice is not hidden from the deities. With the words, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s protection, the protection of the sacrificer,"—for the sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu and the sacrificer is Vaiṣṇava—he makes himself joined on both sides by means of the sacrifice itself, which is Viṣṇu. When the sacrifice was created, its navel enveloped it.

That became the garment of the consecrated; for the embryo is consecrated when he puts on the garment of the consecrated. He thus envelops himself with his own womb. Therefore, one should not speak clearly during this great rite, for the embryo is as if covered and hidden by the caul; [he should do so] so that his speech may not become exhausted.

When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, they threw down their girdles; from them the Śara grass arose. In that the girdle is made of Śara grass, he takes hold of that very girdle. When the gods divided the vital strength (ūrj), from it the Śara grass arose. In that the girdle is made of Śara grass, he takes hold of that very vital strength. The girdle is indeed vital strength; he winds it around at the middle. Thus he places vital strength in the middle, both in the sacrificer and in his offspring; therefore, from the middle, the offspring gain vital strength and are invigorated.

He winds it around at the navel; for that part of a person which is above the navel is pure (*medhya*), while that which is below is impure (*amedhya*); [this is done] to distinguish between the pure and the impure. It is threefold (*trivṛt*); for with the threefold *stoma*, Prajāpati created offspring. The thunderbolt (*vajra*) is threefold; verily he hurls the thunderbolt at his enemy. Indra indeed hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra; that part of it which shattered became the reed (*śara*). That is the reason for the name "reed" (*śara*). The reed is indeed a thunderbolt; in that the girdle (*mekhalā*) is made of reeds, [it serves as a thunderbolt].

He hurls the very thunderbolt at his rival; he should lay him low. Whomever he hates, while girding himself, he should meditate upon him; verily, by means of the thunderbolt, he delivers him over. The girdle belongs to the man, the thong to the woman; for the girdle is female and the thong is male. Thus, as a couple, they encompass the mouth of the sacrifice for the sake of procreation. The girdle is indeed a thunderbolt, and hunger is a wide-open door, a wicked rival. In that he girds himself with the girdle, he strikes away the wicked rival by means of the thunderbolt.

The sacrifice was among the gods, and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) was among the ancestors. That sacrifice desired the sacrificial fee; the ancestors said to it, "Seek a share for us among the gods. They replied, "We shall have a share at the third pressing. Therefore, the third pressing is performed for the ancestors. He called out to her; being called, she ran toward him. Therefore, when a man is called by a woman, he runs toward her. Therefore, one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) is most desirous of women, for he is closest to the sacrifice. He united with her; Indra perceived this, and he thought: "Who..."

"Or whoever shall be born from this [womb], he alone shall become this [world]. He entered that womb, and from it he was born. He looked back again and thought, "Whoever else shall be born from this, he will be my rival. Having pursued him, he cut him off by twisting [the cord]; that became the *viṣāṇā* (horn). In that the *viṣāṇā* exists, one touches the seed of the sacrifice, the womb of Indra, the womb of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). It consists of five turns; for with five [turns] he cut him off by twisting, [the womb] of Indra.

"This is the womb of Indra; this is indeed the womb of the ploughing, for thee with a well-disposed mind"—therefore what is ploughed bears fruit. "Uptear!"—therefore plants spring up erect. He scratches with a *yajus* formula; for men scratch without a formula, [he does so] for the sake of distinction. If he were to scratch without a formula, he would scratch like Varuṇa, and even embryos would be born with skin diseases.

Speech indeed entered the gods and humans; that which remained over from it entered the trees. This very speech speaks in the trees—that which is in the drum, that which is in the flute, and that which is in the lute. As for the staff that there is, he thereby secures the excess of speech. He hands it to the Maitrāvaruṇa; he thus hands speech to him. He distributes it perpetually among the officiating priests; therefore his speech does not fail. It should be made as high as the mouth, for this much is the extent of speech that speaks; and furthermore—
For such is the power exerted by speech: one might say of a fruit-bearing tree, "May I become the essence of that which bears fruit. ||4||

"Oblation! To the sacrifice with the mind!"—for by means of the mind the sacrifice is indeed grasped. "The sacrifice has its source in Vāta; the sacrifice is in heaven, the sacrifice is in the intermediate space, the sacrifice is on earth"—for here and there indeed is the sacrifice. Wherever the sacrifice is, from there he grasps it with the mind. When he sits [in attendance] after having grasped it, he sits after having grasped the sacrifice itself. If he were to release it, he would release the sacrifice. If he were to release it, he should undergo initiation again. If he were to undergo initiation again, he would overfill the oblations. He should recite the *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Viṣṇu. The *gāyatrī* is speech, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus, by means of speech, he [re-attains] the sacrifice.

He continues [the recitation]. He should recite the verse addressed to Bṛhaspati as the subsequent one. Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; by means of the Brahman, the injury of the sacrifice is removed. By means of the Brahman alone, he removes the injury of the sacrifice. "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows"—this he should recite for Agni Vratapati. The vow of one who, having been consecrated (*dīkṣita*), does not observe his vow, goes to Vratapati. Agni is the lord of vows among the gods; from Vratapati himself, he undertakes the vow. "This one, the son of so-and-so, has been consecrated"—thus he says three times in a low voice.

Three times he announces the sacrifice aloud to the gods and to men; having seen the constellation, he releases his speech. By day indeed men perform the sacrifice, and by night the gods; thus, by means of the day, he extends it to the night and presents the sacrifice to the gods for their protection. "Perform the vow," he says—this means "perform the sacrifice. This utterance consists of five parts, and the sacrifice is fivefold; thus the speech is properly raised up. The consecrated one should not lie on his back; if he were to lie on his back...

He would turn toward the world of the gods; he should not lie on his side, for if he were to lie on his side, he would turn toward the world of the fathers. Indeed, the fathers are far from this world; if he were to come from among the people, he would be liable to die prematurely. He should lie only on his back. For the consecrated one has the intermediate space as his deity; having turned toward his own world, his own abode, he lies down. He should not lie with his back to the fire; Agni is all the deities, and [if he did so] he would cut himself off from the deities. He should lie turning toward the fire; Agni is all the deities, and thus he lies having turned toward the deities themselves—the divine thought.

With the verse, "We choose," he purifies himself with the *brahman* for the sake of brilliance; furthermore, [he does so] thinking, "May the waters not steal away my consecration (*dīkṣā*). Food indeed loathed men; the gods desired it, and the waters said, "Return to us, and we shall make these [foods] palatable for you. He returned to them. When one who is consecrated purifies himself, it is for the attainment of food.

Therefore, when food has been brought for the Brahmin, he should wash his hands; this is for the attainment of food. One who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) must neither consume what has been offered as an oblation nor what has not been offered. He consumes his fast-food (*vrata*) with the words, "O gods born of Manu. The gods born of Manu are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); thus, he consumes his fast-food as an oblation offered to his own very deity. By this, it is neither an unoffered oblation for him, nor is it not an oblation at all. While sleeping, he should address Agni with the mantra, "O Agni, you be well awake. For much of that which is to be consumed during the fast (*vrátya*) falls away while one sleeps. Agni is the first among the gods.

Having handed over the vow to the Lord of Vows, he should address Agni at dawn with the words, "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows," for he thus hands over the vow to the Lord of Vows; Agni is the Lord of Vows among the gods, and from the Lord of Vows alone he undertakes the vow. ||5||

One who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) must not offer an oblation (*havis*). For the consecrated one is indeed Rudra, and Agni is the oblation; if he were to offer it, he would deliver his own self, having become the oblation, unto Rudra. If he were not to offer it, he would cut off the sacrifice. Therefore, this is the rule: having placed [the oblation] upon a later fire, he moves toward the earlier fire; by that very means he continues the sacrifice. Just as a cow with a full udder releases her milk, even so does he who is consecrated gather the sacrifice for the gods. If he were to offer [it immediately], he would milk the sacrifice dry and cause it to flow away, just as when a cow has been milked she is exhausted.

In that he offers later on, when the time has arrived, he milks the sacrifice for the gods all at once. Indeed, everything belonging to one who is consecrated becomes the sacrificial oblation; for he undergoes consecration having assigned [all his possessions] as the offering. Whoever eats his food swallows the sacrifice; for him, the expiation is by means of the sacrifice itself.

He who is consecrated is indeed bound by a noose; for the noose belongs to Varuṇa, and he who eats his food, Varuṇa becomes his seizer. Therefore, one should not eat the food of one who is bound or imprisoned. Indeed, he who is consecrated is set apart for the gods; for what is set apart belongs to humans as a fragrant offering. Therefore, one should not eat the food of one who is consecrated. They divide the evil of him who is consecrated threefold: he who eats his food takes a third part, he who speaks indecorously takes a third part, and he who [speaks] his name...

He takes the third [portion] from that; therefore, one should not eat the food of one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*), nor should one utter what is indecorous, nor should one mention his name. For he undergoes consecration for the sake of giving; yet he commits an untruth when he accepts a gift. The consecrated one is an embryo, and an embryo destroys an embryo that has been accepted. "Pūṣan of gains, Soma of riches"—for Pūṣan is the lord of gains and Soma of riches. "Bestow this, O Soma!"—Soma indeed bestows upon him that which he desires. "Bring more, O God Savitṛ!"—for he brings him more at the time of arrival.

With the words, "Of wealth, O giver of wealth," he accepts [the gift] indeed impelled by Savitṛ, for his own non-injury. Of old, the sacrifice was not sufficient for the gods; they made it complete through sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). When one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) seeks wages (*bhṛti*), he thereby makes the sacrifice complete. Therefore, for twelve nights, the consecrated one should seek wages; as great as the sacrifice is, so much does he make complete.

One set of sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) is led away for the gods, and another for men; he assigns these [cows] as follows: "To Vāyu, thee! for the one that perishes; "To Nirṛti, thee! for the one that sinks down; "To Rudra, thee! for the one that Rudra kills; "To Varuṇa, thee! for the one that dies in water or by a tumor (bleṣka); "To Yama, thee! for the one that dies by any other form of death. These indeed are led away for the gods, while the others are for men. Through these, a virtuous Brāhmaṇa prospers even more; he who knows this prospers. "O divine waters, of the waters..."

He does not plunge into the water head-first; he avoids that which of these waters is sacrificial and fit for oblation, so as not to cause distress. The consecrated one is indeed Agni, and the waters are Agni; he plunges into them with a *yajus* formula for the sake of pacification, for the waters are a pacifier. Furthermore, he thereby places more luster within himself. If he were to plunge in without a *yajus*, the waters would be distressing; therefore, he plunges in with a *yajus*.

Therefore, the waters flow in a continuous, unbroken stream; if one should cross a boat, having placed the two kindling-sticks (*araṇi*) and the chariot upon it, he crosses over together with Agni—for Agni is all the deities—and the sacrifice—for the chariot is the sacrifice—with both the deities and the sacrifice. Having gone to the further shore, he should sit down crushing a clod of earth; by this, these [waters] do not become his companions. With the formula, "This is your seasonal womb," according to the sacrificial text, and with, "We have come to this place of divine worship on the earth," he settles upon the place of divine worship (*devayajana*).

With the words, "Crossing over by means of the *ṛc*s and *sāmans*, by means of the *yajus*," he indeed crosses over to the place of divine worship by means of the *ṛc*s and *sāmans*, and by means of the deities. ||6||

The gods and the Asuras performed the sacrifice equally. Whatever the gods did, the Asuras did that too—the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and the Cāturmāsya offerings; indeed, this was the extent of the sacrifice at that time. Those gods saw this Soma-sacrifice (saumyādhvara); they brought it forth, they consecrated themselves, and they made the Agnihotra their vow. The Agnihotra is indeed the vow; therefore, whatever is the expiation for a spilt Agnihotra, that is the expiation for a broken vow. Therefore, one has two vows.

They were consecrated; for twice they offered the Agnihotra. Of those [sacrifices], that which was the Full Moon sacrifice they made into the animal offering to Agni and Soma, which is slaughtered on the previous day. That which was the New Moon sacrifice they made into the offering to Agni, which is slaughtered at each pressing. They made the Vaiśvadeva into the morning pressing, the Varuṇapraghāsas into the midday pressing, and the Sākamedhas into the third pressing. At the third pressing, they arranged the Pitṛyajña; at the third pressing, the Tryambakas. As those Asuras were retreating, they said: "Not indeed..."

"May these [beings] become *adhvara*," he thought; that is the reason for the name *adhvara*. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who, knowing this, undergoes initiation, and he who, knowing this, initiates another, prospers in himself and his rival is defeated.

By means of this [Prāyaṇīya offering], they indeed go to the heavenly world; that is the "starting-point-ness" (*prāyaṇīyatva*) of the Prāyaṇīya. He who goes to yonder world is indeed cut off from this world. In that the Āditya [offering] becomes the Udayanīya, he finds firm support in this very world. The gods, having slain the Asuras and being afraid of retaliation for their enmity, confounded the quarters, thinking, "Lest another here recognize this [path]. Regarding this they say: "There were gods named Sādhyas who existed before the gods; they, having confounded the quarters, [reached] the heavenly world."

"Lest another should understand this world of ours," they thought; thus these later gods sought to understand it, but they did not understand it. Aditi said, "I shall choose a boon: I will proclaim these quarters for you, so that the sacrifice shall have its beginning in me and its conclusion in me. Therefore, the introductory offering belongs to Āditya and the concluding offering belongs to Āditya, for she chose that boon. She said, "Sacrifice to Pathyā Svasti; by her you shall discern the eastern quarter. Sacrifice to Agni," she said.

With that [oblation], he said, "Sacrifice to Soma for the southern quarter"; with that, he said, "Sacrifice to Savitṛ for the western quarter"; with that, he said, "I myself [sacrifice] for the northern quarter; I know both these worlds," said Aditi; for her, this upward direction is the upward one; with that, they went to the heavenly world. These very deities are thus sacrificed to for the arrangement of the quarters and for the discernment of the heavenly world. By means of Pathyā Svasti, the gods discerned the eastern quarter; Agni and Soma beheld it after her, as did Savitṛ.

"Aditi gave birth to this; upon her they stretched out the sacrifice forward. Indeed, that which is the Prāyaṇīya [offering] is gathered as the mouth of the sacrifice. When he offers to Pathyā Svasti, since the Prāyaṇīya is the mouth of the sacrifice, he thereby gathers speech itself. With Agni and Soma, he gathers the out-breath and the in-breath for the sake of impulsion. Through Savitṛ, there is impulsion; through Aditi, he gathers the mouth of the sacrifice upon her for the sake of preparation. That which is the Prāyaṇīya is set apart for the sake of arrangement. Of the Maruts, the divine host—for indeed, it is the divine host...

As it is being prepared, it conforms to the human community, since the verse for the sacrifice to the Maruts contains the words, "O Maruts, bestow well-being and wealth. Thus he prepares the divine community itself, and as that is being prepared, it conforms to the human community. He sacrifices to Pathyā Svasti; therefore, this Āditya rises in the east and sets in the west, for he moves along following Pathyā Svasti. He sacrifices to Agni; therefore, the plants first ripen from the south, for the plants belong to Agni. [Then] Soma...

He sacrifices to Agni; therefore the waters flow most abundantly toward the west, for the waters belong to Soma. He sacrifices to Savitṛ; therefore this wind blows most abundantly from the north, for it blows impelled by Savitṛ. He sacrifices to Aditi; therefore this [earth] rains upon the creatures from above. He sacrifices to these five deities; the sacrifice is fivefold; verily he wins the sacrifice itself. He cuts off a sixth portion for Agni; there are six seasons; verily he finds support in the seasons. There are ten invitatory and offering verses; the Virāj consists of ten syllables; food is the Virāj. Verily he wins food.

He finds firm support in the Virāj, in sovereignty, and in the eating of food. There are two [verses] for the Sviṣṭakṛt; the year consists of twelve months, [this is] for the attainment of the year. There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; the year indeed consists of seventeen parts: five seasons and twelve months. This, verily, is that year; from the year itself he extends the mouth of the sacrifice. 8.

He sacrifices to Pathyā Svasti; Pathyā Svasti is indeed speech, and thus he preserves his own speech. He sacrifices to Agni; whatever dry part of his body is fit to be consumed by fire, that he preserves by means of this. He sacrifices to Soma; whatever moist part of his body is not fit to be consumed by fire, that he preserves by means of this. Savitṛ is for instigation; Aditi is for completion and for firm standing. They set out by way of Pathyā Svasti and they conclude by way of Pathyā Svasti. Pathyā Svasti is indeed speech; it is by speech that they set out, and by speech that they conclude. [They sacrifice] to the Āditya.

There is a Prāyaṇīya offering and an Udayanīya offering to Āditya; by means of the opening of the sacrifice, he finds firm support in this world and in that world. The heavenly world is indeed the quarters; the quarters have these deities. In that he sacrifices with the Prāyaṇīya, he ascends to the heavenly world through the very quarters. Just as a web is woven on a loom, so is the sacrifice woven. In that the Prāyaṇīya is for Āditya and the Udayanīya is for Āditya, he ties these cords at the end like cross-bars for the sake of strength and security. Those which...

The invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) of the *prāyaṇīya* [offering] are the offering verses (*yājyā*) of the *udayanīya*; those which are the offering verses are the invitatory verses. By the very same way they set out, by that same way they rise up, for the sake of a firm footing and for the sake of full awareness. One should interlink the offering verses and the invitatory verses; for whomsoever one hates, he causes him to fall from this world and does not reach the other. Just as one rises up from a path, so it is with that; he cuts him off from both sides. The *prāyaṇīya* should be without after-offerings (*anuyāja*), and the *udayanīya* should be without fore-offerings (*prayāja*). This sacrificial food (*havis*) is indeed the same, for the sake of continuity. The self, indeed...

The fore-offerings (*prayāja*) are offspring and the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are offspring; if he were to act in this way, he would exclude both himself and his offspring, and he would die childless. Let [the two offerings] be possessed of fore-offerings and possessed of after-offerings. This sacrificial food is the same, the deity is the same, and the stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*) is the same; by that very means he maintains the continuity of the sacrifice, and he does not exclude either himself or his offspring.

"Should it be concluded? Should it not be concluded? they deliberate. "The sacrifice that is not concluded indeed flows away; following that flowing sacrifice, the sacrificer flows away along with his offspring and cattle. It must certainly be concluded. However, one should not perform the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wife, for she is then impure and unpurified, and is not capable of going to the heavenly world. One performs the *saṃyāja* for her at the *udayanīya* (concluding) offering. Just as a traveler returns to his own home, even so does the sacrificer, through the wife, find firm footing in this world. [Regarding] the food of the initiated...

For those who have sacrificed do not eat [the remains], and they do not become better off; for at that time when one performs the *prāyaṇīya* offering, one is consecrated (*dīkṣita*); and at that time when one emerges from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), one is still consecrated. One prepares the *udayanīya* offering using the scrapings of the *prāyaṇīya*. One should not eat of the *udayanīya*, for it is the food of the consecrated; thus he avoids it and becomes better off. 9.

Kadrū and Suparṇī vied with each other regarding their own forms; Kadrū won Suparṇī’s form from her. This earth is indeed Kadrū, and the sky is Suparṇī; the meters are the forms belonging to Suparṇī. Kadrū said to Suparṇī: "Soma is in the third heaven from here; fetch him, and with him ransom yourself. Suparṇī said to the meters: "Parents indeed support their sons; do not deliver me to such as these, do not ransom me from here! Thereupon she flew up as the Jagatī, consisting of fourteen syllables.

The *sati* reached [the earth] and turned back; two of her syllables were lost. She fell away, taking with her cattle and the consecration (*dīkṣā*). Therefore, the consecration approaches one who possesses cattle. Therefore they say, "The *jagatī* is the most cattle-like of the meters. The *triṣṭubh* fell away; being thirteen-syllabled, she reached [the earth] and turned back; two of her syllables were lost. She fell away, taking with her the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and austerity (*tapas*). Therefore, in the world of the *triṣṭubh*, sacrificial fees are led forth. Indeed, this is austerity: that one gives what is one's own.

Therefore they say that among the pressings (*savana*), the midday pressing is the most ascetic. That *gāyatrī* flew up while being only four syllables; she flew up clutching a goat by the ear. A goat leaped upon her; that is why the goat is called "aja" (leaper). She flew down taking those four syllables and the *soma*; she became eight-syllabled. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) ask: "Since the *gāyatrī* is the smallest of the meters, why did it go around to the beginning of the sacrifice? Why is it the most brilliant? Because it brought the *soma* from there, therefore the *gāyatrī* is so named.

The sacrifice has its opening there; therefore, she is most full of splendor. With her two feet she brought two pressings, and with her mouth the third. What she brought with her mouth, she consumed; therefore, two pressings are bright, while the third pressing is as if consumed. Therefore, they press out the *ṛjīṣa* at the third pressing. When they pour the *āśira* (milk-mixture) into the third pressing, they consider it as restoring that very third pressing.

O Indra and Agni, you pierced Vṛtra; O Indra and Varuṇa, may I [attain] the day; O Indra and Varuṇa, now for us; both of you have conquered through our joint action; for us, O Indra and Bṛhaspati; [and] Bṛhaspati for us.
O Indra and Soma, burn up the Rakṣasas; crush them, O Bulls, and cast down those who thrive in darkness.
Strike down the senseless ones, burn them away, slay them, drive them off, and sharpen your weapons against the devourers.
O Indra and Soma, let the evil-minded one who seeks to harm us be consumed by heat like a cauldron placed upon the fire.
Bestow hatred upon the hater of sacred knowledge, the flesh-eater with the terrible eye, the *kimīdin* who causes no rest.
Now may we invoke Indra and Pūṣan for friendship, for well-being, and for the winning of booty.
When Indra, the most powerful bull, brought down the great waters from the rock, Pūṣan was there with him.
O Indra and Parvata, bring hither on your lofty chariot desirable refreshments accompanied by noble heroes.
O Gods, enjoy the oblations at the sacrifices; may you both increase through our hymns, rejoicing in the sacrificial food.
May Parijman, the slayer of Vasu, exhilarate us; may Vāta, the bull of the waters, exhilarate us.
O Indra and Parvata, sharpen our wits for us; may all the gods grant us this wide space.
May we overcome with the Ṛbhus through the Ṛbhus, and with the Vibhūs through the Vibhūs in power, our own powers.
May Vāja aid us in the winning of booty; with Indra as our ally, may we overcome Vṛtra.
By your skillful power you made your parents young again; by your skillful power you fashioned the chalice for the drinking of the gods;
by your skillful power, O Ṛbhus, possessors of the treasure of booty, you fashioned the two bay steeds, the swiftest bearers of Indra.
I slew Vṛtra; you have accomplished many deeds at all times, O Indra, through this our praise. 11.
O Agni, you, the god, bestow great vital power upon the donor; Agni is the sage, the master of the house, the youthful bearer of oblations, and the ageless one.

O Fathers, you who are pervasive, radiant, and beautiful to behold for us—shine with excellent household fires and abundant food; measure out for us, directed toward us, glorious fame, you who [know] all these created beings and all forms.
And you, O Soma, being our will, let us not die; you are the Lord of the Forest, whose hymns are beloved.
Brahmā among the gods, the pathfinder for the poets, the seer among the wise, the buffalo among wild beasts,
the hawk among vultures, the axe among the forests— Soma goes forth beyond the filter, singing aloud.
Like birds plunging into water, guarding themselves, the sounding voices of the thundercloud have roared;
like waves breaking from the mountains, the hymns have celebrated Bṛhaspati with joy.
Like swans, with his loudly speaking friends, Bṛhaspati cast off the stone-made bonds;
crying out toward the cows, he praised them and, being wise, sang them forth on high.
O Indra, you of skillful action, having grown great instantly for the drinking of the pressed juice, you were born for preeminence.

Through the sacred word (*brahman*), O Indra, you have become great; you have become worthy of sacrifice at all libations. You have become the shaker of men in every battle; you are the supreme mantra, O lord of all people.
The fame of the god Mitra, the supporter of the people, is victorious; it is true and possesses most wonderful renown.
Mitra, speaking aloud, impels the people; Mitra has supported both the earth and the sky.
Mitra gazes unblinking upon the human tribes. Let us offer an oblation rich in ghee to the Truthful One.

O Mitra, let that mortal be one who offers oblations, he who strives for you, O Āditya, with sacred observance. He whom you protect is neither slain nor conquered; no distress reaches him, neither from near nor from afar.
Whatever offense we humans commit against the divine host, O Varuṇa—
whether through thoughtlessness or by violating your laws— do not harm us for that sin, O God.
Whatever the gamblers have cheated at play, whether it be truth or what we do not know—loosen all those things like a loose bond, O God; then, O Varuṇa, may we be dear to you.
So that Aditi may grant us the Rudra-power for our cattle, for our men, for our kine, and for our offspring.
Do not harm us in our children or grandchildren, nor in our life, nor in our cattle, nor in our horses.
O Rudra, do not slay our heroic men in your anger; bearing oblations, we worship you with reverence. 12.
Thus ends the twenty-third section, named *Dīkṣita*, in the *Madhyamikā* recension of the *Caraka* school of the glorious *Kāṭhaka-Yajurveda*. 23.

Now begins the twenty-fourth section. Regarding the witness-cow: one should not purchase [the Soma] with a cow that has white eyes, black tails, and black hooves; for her this is as if struck down and ground up, she belongs to the Pitṛs, and she would bring about premature death. One should not purchase it with a cow of two colors; she belongs to Vṛtra-slayer Indra, and she either conquers or is conquered. Or rather, one may purchase it for a Rājanya with such a cow, for there is no middle state for him; he either conquers or is conquered. One should purchase the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with a cow that has ears like those of the *adhīla* plant; for this is an excess among forms, and the *ṣoḍaśin* is an excess; by means of the excessive, he obtains the excessive.

With one that is brown and one year old he should purchase [the Soma]. Speech indeed is the Soma-purchasing cow; man is speech. Because he purchases with one that is one year old, therefore a man speaks speech at the age of one year. Because he purchases with one that is older, therefore an older person speaks.

The *chandāṃsi* (metres) fetched Soma from yonder world; Gāyatrī, having become a falcon, carried it off, but the Gandharvas stole it from her midway. Viśvāvasu remained there for three nights as a guest; therefore, Soma, once purchased, remains for three nights. The gods begged him back from them, but they would not give him back to them. They said, "Let us ransom him with a cow. They reflected, "If we ransom him with a cow, we shall sell him at a sacrifice. They said, "The Gandharvas are indeed fond of women; speech is a woman."

Having performed the rite, they released the illusion and thought, "We have been deprived of our offspring; we have been deprived by speech. They then lamented, "Soma is ours! The Soma-purchase-cow is ours! The Gandharvas said, "Let us call out to one another. The Gandharvas spoke the *brahman* (sacred formula), while the gods sang; the cow returned to the gods because of their singing. Therefore, a woman loves one who sings, not one who speaks the *brahman*, for she was unfaithful to the *brahman*. Therefore they say, "The Soma-purchase-cow has not been bought with Soma," for [she belonged] to the gods.

She returned again, and they said, "The Gandharvas are indeed fond of women; many among the Gandharvas couple and procreate. Enter into the waters and emerge! She emerged having become a hunchbacked old woman, for that which had been struck and ground was her form. They said, "She belongs to the Pitṛs," and therefore they kill her for the Pitṛs. They said, "Enter again and emerge! She emerged having become a two-colored cow that destroys enemies (*vārtraghnī*). By that form, she freed herself from them; therefore—

That cow was most excellent; the boon does not harm him who, knowing thus, chooses her as the boon. They said, "Having entered again, come forth! She came forth having become a reddish-brown one-year-old cow. With her they purchased [the Soma]; therefore she is the one used for the purchase of Soma; that is her form.

The third pressing is to be acquired by means of the Soma-purchase-cow; for the third pressing is indeed cattle. In that he purchases [the Soma] with a cow, by that very act he acquires the third pressing. He measures [the Soma] on a red hide; therefore, among animals, those of red color are most numerous. One should not permit the measuring to be done haphazardly, nor should one be a spectator of it being measured. Soma is the overlord of plants; it draws out what has been swallowed by him. He becomes hungry; therefore, the Soma-seller is hungry. He purchases [it] at the edge of the waters; thus he makes it full of sap.

He buys it with gold; verily, he buys it with splendor. He buys it with a goat; verily, he buys it with fervor. He buys it with a cow; verily, he buys it with the milk-mixture (*āśira*). He buys it with an ox; verily, he secures the vehicle of the sacrifice. He buys it with a male calf and a female calf; verily, he buys its pair. He buys it with a bull; verily, he buys it together with Indra. Regarding this they say: "If one sells it for a bull, one sells it for Prajāpati himself. Whosoever [does so]...

It should be a castrated bull, one that is seedless; with it he should purchase [the Soma]. By means of that very [bull], he purchases [the Soma] together with Indra, but he does not sell it to Prajāpati. He purchases it with ten [cows]; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food; verily, he establishes himself in the Virāj, in the eating of food. 2.

"Thou art swift," he says; for the cow that purchases Soma (somakrayaṇī) is indeed speech, and speech moves hither and thither. Seeing her thus, he offers the oblation for the cow that purchases Soma. The cow that purchases Soma is indeed speech; seeing her, he thus restrains her with the words, "Held by the mind. For speech is indeed held by the mind. With "Pleasant to Viṣṇu," he makes her pleasant for the sacrifice, for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice. With "In the impulse of thee, whose impulse is true, may I obtain the control of thy body, Svāhā!"—for whoever obtains the control of this [cow's] body becomes possessed of the body of Savitṛ.

He pervades the mechanism; with the utterance of *svāhā*, he indeed restrains her. Having announced [the purchase] to that Āditya, saying, "O divine Sūrya, we shall buy the Soma," one buys the Soma after having announced it to that very Āditya.

"Thou art consciousness," he says; for the Soma-purchasing cow is indeed speech; he thus instructs her, and therefore instructed offspring are born. "Thou art mind," he says, for speech is held by the mind. "Thou art intelligence," he says, for one meditates with speech in this way and that. "Thou art the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," he says, for she is indeed the sacrificial fee. "Thou art worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiyā*)," he says, for she is indeed worthy of sacrifice. "Thou art of the warrior class (*kṣatriyā*)," he says, for she is indeed of the warrior class; moreover, whoever she favors becomes a member of the warrior class. "Thou art Aditi, double-headed," he says, for she is indeed Aditi, double-headed, since she encompasses the sacrifice on both sides.

The *paribhū* verse belongs to the *prāyaṇīya* (opening) rite and to the Āditya; the *udayanīya* (concluding) rite belongs to the Āditya. [He says,] "May she be well-advanced for me and well-returning. Thus he makes her well-advanced and well-returning. [He says,] "May Mitra bind you by the foot. If she were bound by the foot, she would belong to the Pitṛs. The Soma-purchasing cow is indeed Speech, and the noose belongs to Varuṇa; if Speech were seized by Varuṇa, she would not speak. If she were seized by the ear, she would be a slayer of Vṛtra. If she were not touched and led forward...

"May Mitra bind you by the foot"—Mitra is indeed the Brahman; verily, by means of the Brahman he binds him by the foot. "May Pūṣan protect your paths"—Pūṣan is indeed this earth; verily, he entrusts her to her. "For Indra, the overseer"—Indra is indeed the most powerful among the gods; verily, he makes him her overseer. "May your mother permit you, may your father permit you"—for both her father and her mother are indeed her permitters. "Go, O goddess, to the god, to Soma for Indra"—for she is indeed a goddess, and she goes to the god, to Soma for Indra.

"May Rudra turn you back," he says; for Rudra is indeed the swiftest of the gods; he thus places him beyond her for the sake of non-participation. "For well-being, O friend of Soma, come back again," he says; he thus effects well-being for her as she turns back. ||3||

With his right foot he steps following after the right footprints; therefore the right side of the self is more powerful. He steps six times; there are six seasons, and thus he finds firm support in the seasons. There are six *pṛṣṭha* chants; those very ones he wins. He grasps the seventh footprint; there are seven domestic animals, and those very ones he wins. Sevenfold indeed this speech speaks; that very [speech] he attains. "Thou art Vastrī, thou art Rudrā"—these are indeed the names of the gods; he enters into them. "Thou art this one, thou art this one"—this is what he thereby says.

Whatever comes forth, that is truly raised up from speech: "May Bṛhaspati cause you to rest in bliss; may Rudra with the Vasus bring you hither. Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and Rudra is the most powerful among the gods; by means of those two who are the most powerful of the gods, he finally restrains her.

"I sprinkle you on the head of the earth, at the place of sacrifice to the gods"—for this place of sacrifice is indeed the head of the earth. "In the station of *iḍā*, rich in ghee, with a self-sacrifice"—this is indeed *iḍā*, and this is her footprint rich in ghee; he thus restrains her with the utterance of *svāhā*. "Here do I cut off the neck of the Rakṣas"—the Rakṣas is indeed the enemy; he thus cuts off the neck of his enemy. He traces around the footprint with the wooden sword (*sphya*); the wooden sword is a thunderbolt and the footprint is cattle; by means of the thunderbolt, he thus encloses the cattle for him.

One should trace around [the footprint] as far as the ghee flows; for ghee is cattle, and thus he wins cattle. He pours the footprint into a vessel; for cattle are Aditi and the earth is Aditi, and the vessel is made from the earth. Thus he places them in their own womb. With the words, "Rejoice in us! In us be your wealth!"—if he were to say, "In you be your wealth," he would hand over the cattle to another, and the Adhvaryu would be without cattle. By saying, "In me be your wealth," he secures the cattle for himself.

This oblation which one offers in that which is not fire is indeed unsuccessful; when he offers after placing gold down, he offers in that which possesses fire, for the sake of success. This oblation, indeed, he offers in that which is not fire; it is liable to be followed by the *rakṣases* in order to destroy it. When he pours out water, it is for the sake of pacification and for the driving away of the *rakṣases*. In that he brings back their footprint from the trench, he subjects these animals to impurity; in that he pours out water, he releases the animals themselves from impurity. He causes the wife to look at the Soma-purchase cow; this belongs to the wife herself.

It is the taking hold of the sacrifice; moreover, he places a pair at the very beginning of the sacrifice for the sake of procreation. "May we serve thee together with Tvaṣṭṛ"—for from this indeed these creatures are born, for the sake of procreation.

Having placed gold in his hand, he measures it; gold is indeed truth, so with truth he measures him. Gold is indeed immortality, so with immortality he measures him. With the words, "Thou art ours," he makes him his own. With the words, "Thy bright draught," he takes his bright portion. With the verse, "Toward that god Savitṛ... he measures him with the deities, being impelled by Savitṛ. He measures with the Atichandas metre; for the Atichandas is the highest of metres; verily, he causes both the sacrifice and the sacrificer to reach the highest state.

He measures with each one separately; thus he obtains the specific powers of these [fingers]. Therefore, we can bend them at will and extend them at will. If he were to measure with all of them together, their power would converge into the hand. He measures with the thumb; therefore, this [thumb] projects the powers of these [fingers] individually. He should not bend it down; if he were to bend it down, he would create a noose. These [fingers] belong to Varuṇa, and the noose belongs to Varuṇa; Varuṇa would seize him. Since he releases [the thumb], he frees himself from Varuṇa’s noose.

He measures twice, for there are two *śukriya* pressings; he measures ten times, for the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the *virāj* is food; verily, he establishes himself in the *virāj*, in the eating of food. If he were to measure what is limited, his life would be limited; he measures what is unlimited, therefore this life is unlimited. If he were to measure what is limited, it would be only for the sacrificer; he measures what is unlimited, and thereby it is also performed for the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*). With the words, "For the offspring thee! May the offspring breathe after thee!"—the stalks (*aṃśus*) are indeed offspring; verily, [he establishes] them in the offspring.

He bestows vital breath; there is clarified butter taken four times, for cattle are four-footed; verily he secures cattle for him. Clarified butter is indeed the form of cattle; verily he wins cattle that are of like form.

"This is thy bright body, this is thy luster," he says, as he places gold into the clarified butter. Clarified butter is indeed Agni’s beloved body, and gold is his luster; thus he endows his beloved body with luster. Gold is seed and clarified butter is cattle; when he places gold into the clarified butter, he places seed in cattle. Therefore, from seed that is boneless, offspring are born possessing bones. He ties it up for the support of the embryos so they do not fall out; he ties it with a *niṣṭarkya* cord.

Therefore, embryos are released from the womb; for were he to tie them with an unpropitious *ṛk*, embryos would not be released from the womb. He places [the fire] down with a *yajus*, he lifts it up with a *yajus*, he yokes it with a *yajus*, and he unyokes it with a *yajus*. Therefore, offspring deposit their seed facing away, yet they are born facing toward [the mother]. ||5||

One should not throw down a footprint in the east; for Agni is the Rudra of the gods who has consumed the oblations, and the footprint belongs to Rudra. He would entrust the cattle to Rudra, and he would become without cattle. He throws it down on the Gārhapatya fire; the cattle attend upon the Gārhapatya, for this is the womb of cattle; thus he places them in their own womb. Where there is a charcoal that is as if extinguished, there he should throw it down, for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. With the words, "I buy Soma from you," he proclaims the powers and the greatness of King Soma. He does not [speak of himself].

If one should bargain for it by the parts, he diminishes the power of King Soma; he declares the ruin of the sacrificer. He becomes hungry. One should say, "This is its self, this is its form, this is its offspring, this is its milk. Thus he does not diminish the power of King Soma, nor does he declare the ruin of the sacrificer; he does not become hungry.

"I buy your bright with the bright, your shining with the shining, your nectar with nectar"—thus he buys his bright with the bright, his shining with the shining, and his nectar with nectar. "That power which is yours, O cow, those [drops] of yours are shining"—thus he bestows vigor upon himself; with that which has become devoid of vigor, he sells. "Thou art the body of austerity"—for she is indeed the body of austerity. "The color of Prajāpati"—Agni is indeed Prajāpati, and goats are born from Agni. "Thriving with a thousandfold prosperity"—for she indeed thrives with the thousandfold prosperity of cattle.

For by this [purchase], he nourishes three and likewise produces two; "with the supreme animal you are bought," for this is indeed the supreme among animals. With the words, "This is your bond for us," he places its vigor within himself; with it, having become devoid of vigor, he completes the sale.

The *chandases* indeed brought Soma from yonder world; it was enveloped in darkness. That *gāyatrī*, with the *ajā*, flew up by means of light; she made it shine for him. Indeed, this [Soma] is brought for him at the very moment it is purchased; that which he purchases with the *ajā* is this very darkness between [the worlds]. He thus makes it shine for him. "Come to us as Mitra, bestowing good friendship"—for having become Varuṇa, he approaches the sacrificer; he thus makes him Mitra. He uncovers [his head], just as one of lower status uncovers [his head] for one of higher status who is approaching.

"In this very way, enter Indra’s right thigh"—for Indra indeed first placed him upon his thigh; Indra is the sacrificer, and thus he places him in his own womb. "O self-radiant one," with these words he points toward the Soma-purchasing cows. These Gandharvas were guarding them here; they brought him away from that world by means of the Gāyatrī for the protection of the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ. Therefore, these two offices are unsuccessful, and the drinking of Soma is unsuccessful for them; therefore, one should not perform the duties of the Neṣṭṛ or the Potṛ, and therefore these two seem to be in attendance together.

As he sacrifices, these [Gandharvas] follow after him; these Gandharvas indeed carry away his prosperity, and therefore the seller of Soma does not thrive. If he should suffer distress, he should fetch it back from them, for this [Soma] is purchased from those Gandharvas. With the words, "Up with life!"—according to the sacrificial formula—"Go through the wide atmosphere!"—for at this time he has the atmosphere as his deity. With the words, "We have even gone upon the path," he goes while warding off the Rakṣases, for at this time the Rakṣases attend upon him when he has departed from here but has not yet reached there; they drive away the Rakṣases as they go, and they convey him by means of the cart.

They restrain his greatness and carry him with a wagon; therefore, plants ripen as things carried by a wagon. If they were to carry him on the head, plants would ripen as things carried on the head. "Thou art the skin of Aditi; sit on the seat of Aditi"—for Soma is indeed Aditya and Aditi is the earth; [Soma] is prepared on the wagon from the earth; verily he places him in his own womb. Soma belongs to Varuṇa; he deprives him of his deity if he makes a friend of him. In that he settles him with a verse addressed to Varuṇa, he endows him with his own deity.

"He has stretched the intermediate space over the forests"—with these words he wraps it around with a cloth; for the cloth belongs to all the deities; verily, he causes him to prosper through all the deities. "I have mounted the eye of the Sun"—with these words they fasten a black antelope skin over it from the front. For at this time the Rakṣases seek to slay him as he is ascending to the heavenly world. The sun is the highest path; verily, he causes him to ascend that very path for the attainment of the heavenly world. 6.

"Descend, O Lord of the World!"—for he is indeed the lord of beings. "Over all abodes"—the abodes are the deities; verily, he causes him to descend toward the deities. "Becoming a hawk, fly away"—the hawk is the swiftest among birds; having made him a hawk, he lets him loose past the Rakṣases. "In the house of our sacrificer, well-prepared"—verily, he makes him the very dwelling-place of the sacrificer; moreover, he prepares it in the sacrificer's own house by means of the deities. "Homage to Mitra..."

"Of Varuṇa’s eye"—for having become Varuṇa himself, he approaches the sacrificer; thus he makes him Mitra. They lift up the throne-seat; just as they lift up a throne-seat for a human king who is seated, so too does he find firm support through Agni. Agni is all the deities; verily, by means of the deities, he finds firm support. Agni and Soma indeed encompass the sacrificer at this time; when he finds support with the animal victim, he delivers him over to those two. Verily, by means of Agni and Soma, he [delivers] his own self.

He who is consecrated (dīkṣate) offers up his intelligence; when he offers an animal, he thereby ransoms himself. That which is hornless and bearded has the form of a dual-deity [victim]; it is hairy and fat, having the form of a man—one should offer that. Whoever eats of it eats a man; therefore, one should not eat of it. The consecrated one indeed suffers from hunger; this [animal] is offered as a ransom for hunger. Whoever eats of it becomes hungry; therefore, one should not eat of it. By means of the power belonging to Agni and Soma, Indra slew Vṛtra. It...

This animal, the slayer of Vṛtra, is sacrificed for the sake of victory; therefore, one should eat of it. Indeed, when it was being sacrificed on the previous day, the deities did not turn toward it, thinking, "We shall be excluded from the subsequent sacrificial rite. Agni and Soma alone turned toward it, while the other deities cast it away from the sacrifice. Therefore, this animal is sacrificed to Agni and Soma; for that reason, no libation (graha) is drawn for Agni and Soma.

As those two were returning to the gods, they deposited that which was their beloved abode; the gods strove to search for it. Seeking it by crawling along, they said, "This has been crawled over (sṛpta)," and because they said "it is new (navam)," that is the essence of butter (*navanīta*). Because they said "it has been crawled over," that is the essence of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). Because the goat found it, that is the essence of sacrificial butter (*ājya*). It made a *ghṛṅ* sound, and that is the essence of ghee (*ghṛta*). Therefore, the goat wanders about making the sound *ghṛṅ*. That...

Following after the cattle, they (Agni and Soma) gathered them together; from that, by means of this [offering], they are born from the cattle. They two said, "Let us choose a boon; let this very one be our portion, he who found our dear abode. Therefore, this [animal] is sacrificed to Agni and Soma; therefore, one should eat of it, for it is a chosen boon.

One ox is unyoked and the other remains unyoked; then the guest-offering (*ātithya*) is prepared for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice. If both were unyoked, the oblation would belong to the ancestors (*pitṛdevatya*); the sacrifice would be interrupted, not continuous, and not secured. If both were unyoked, the oblation would be one that slays Vṛtra (*vārtraghna*); the sacrifice would be continuous, uninterrupted, and secured. Since one is unyoked and the other remains unyoked, the oblation becomes one that slays Vṛtra and does not belong to the ancestors; the sacrifice is thus continuous.

The sacrifice is uninterrupted and secured when he causes the wife to take hold [of him] as he pours out [the oblation].
