For the wife is the mistress of the household goods; thus he pours out the offering to the gods with her consent and her authorization. This is the wife's taking hold of the sacrifice; moreover, he places a productive pair at the mouth of the sacrifice for the sake of procreation.

As many as are the merits that follow [the guest], hospitality is offered to all of them. The *chandases* follow King Soma once he has been purchased. With "Thou art the body of Agni; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—with the Gāyatrī, he pours this out. With "Thou art the body of Soma; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—with the Triṣṭubh, he pours this out. With "Thou art the hospitality of the guest; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—with the Jagatī, he pours this out. With "For Agni, the giver of increase of wealth; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—with the Anuṣṭubh, he pours this out. With "For the Śyena, the bearer of Soma; for Viṣṇu... [he pours it out].

With the words "To thee," he offers with the Gāyatrī; for the Gāyatrī indeed brought this [sacrifice] from yonder world, therefore she is one who returns, and therefore it is performed again. In that he offers with the meters, he makes the meters themselves possess their respective shares. He offers five times; the sacrifice is fivefold, so he wins the sacrifice itself. With the words "To Viṣṇu thee! To Viṣṇu thee!"—for at this time the sacrifice belongs to Viṣṇu, since it is as yet undefined; therefore the sacrificial cake belongs to Viṣṇu. It should be prepared on three potsherds, for that indeed belongs to Viṣṇu.

That which is a cake on nine potsherds is also one on three potsherds, for those three sets of three potsherds constitute the nine potsherds; there are nine vital breaths, and by means of the vital breaths he goes forth at the beginning of the sacrifice. Moreover, he spreads out the threefold luster at the beginning of the sacrifice. In that it is on three potsherds, it belongs to Viṣṇu; in that it is on six, it belongs to the meters; thus he does not depart from either.

"The animal is to be sacrificed for King Soma," they say; "but when an animal is sacrificed for a human king, they churn the fire, for animals belong to Agni; thus he sacrifices an animal to him [Agni]. Agni is all the deities; verily he generates all the deities for Soma and for the meters that have arrived. The *prastara* (grass-bunch) is made of *aśvavāla* grass, and the *udyāma* (supporting sticks) are of sugarcane. Prajāpati was like a horse; these were his hairs, namely the *aśvavālas*, and those two were his arms, namely the *udyāmas*. Having taken hold of him, the gods [proceeded]."

When they were going to the heavenly world, the *prastara* was made of *aśvavāla* grass and the two *udvāpau* were made of *ikṣu* cane; thus he takes hold of Prajāpati for the attainment of the heavenly world. The *aśvavāla* grasses are indeed the eyelashes of Prajāpati; in that the *prastara* is made of *aśvavāla*, he extends the face of the sacrifice from Prajāpati himself.

The *rakṣases* indeed sought to destroy the sacrifice of the gods; they struck them away with the *kārṣmarya* wood. That the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are made of *kārṣmarya* is for the smiting away of the *rakṣases*. Whatever the gods accomplished by means of this [wood], by that they prospered; that is its fitness for ritual action. It is indeed called "fit for action" (*karmaṇya*); by means of it, he prospers at the very beginning of the sacrifice. There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; the year is indeed seventeenfold: five seasons and twelve months. This, verily, is that.

Year after year, he extends the mouth of the sacrifice from above. The guest-offering (*ātithya*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *upasad*s are the neck. If he were to conclude [the sacrifice] at that point, he would conclude it at the mouth; he would cut off the head from the neck of the sacrifice. It ends with the *iḍā* offering; thus he restores the head to the neck of the sacrifice. It consists of nine potsherds; therefore, the head of a man is divided into nine parts. The *anuyāja*s are, as it were, the *tanūnaptra* and the *āśis* of this [sacrifice]; therefore, there are no *anuyāja*s. 8.

The gods did not agree among themselves as to who should be the most excellent. They went forth in four groups: Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, Indra with the Maruts, and Varuṇa with the Ādityas. Those gods became weaker, while the Asuras became more prosperous. They realized, "Those [gods] are indeed becoming weaker, while the Asuras are becoming more prosperous. They then made a compact regarding their dear bodies, saying, "May this protect us from him who would act treacherously toward another among us. Therefore, one should not act treacherously toward one who has entered into the *tanūnaptra* covenant. For...

He betrays his dear body; he betrays it when they swear an oath upon the body. That is why the *tānūnaptra* (the oath) has its name. From that, the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who, knowing this, enters into the *tānūnaptra*, prospers in himself and his rivals are defeated. Yonder sun is indeed Indra; his [the sun’s] rays stood firm for the sake of preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya*). His kinsmen stand firm for the sake of preeminence—he who knows thus. In him, indeed, they deposited those bodies; therefore, he [is so called].

It burns most intensely; therefore, the Soma-libations dedicated to the deity Sūrya are offered in the greatest quantity. With the *vajra* of clarified butter (*ājya*), the gods slew Vṛtra; with the two ladles as their arms, Soma was Vṛtra. They indeed slay this Soma when they offer it in close proximity with clarified butter. With the words, "O divine Soma, may each stalk of thine swell," they cause that which they have slain and exhausted to swell again. Those who cause the Soma to swell depart from this world. With the words, "May riches come to the one who impels, to Bhaga," [they remain] in this very world.

They take their stand. He who kills an embryo harms both his father and his mother; for the embryo belongs to these two. With the two [verses], "Soma is King" and "Homage to Heaven, homage to Earth," he makes amends. "What does one gain by the consecration (dīkṣā)? they ask. "What by the intermediate consecration (avāntaradīkṣā)? One gains oneself through the consecration, and offspring through the intermediate consecration. He tightens the girdle more closely.

He undertakes a lesser vow; therefore his offspring is inferior to himself. Because he releases [the milk] for another who is true (satyā), he expands through superior and more excellent offspring—through son and grandson. The consecrated one is indeed Agni; they appease Agni with water. He purifies himself with the *madantī* waters; he consumes the *madantī* waters as his vow-food (*vratya*) for the sake of non-appeasement, for the waters are worthy of appeasement. Moreover, he thereby places greater luster within himself. Indeed, neither what has been offered nor what has not been offered should be consumed as a vow by him who is consecrated. Agni is indeed Rudra; by means of Agni, he [the consecrated] [assumes] a body.

With the words, "That Rudra-form of yours, O Agni," he undertakes the vow; he thus undertakes the vow in his own deity. Therefore, for him, it is neither an offering that has been made, nor one that has not been made. 9.

The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Of those Asuras, these were their fortresses: this earth was made of iron, the intermediate region was silver, and the sky was golden. Those gods were repeatedly defeated in battle after battle. They realized, "It is because we are without a stronghold that we are being defeated. They therefore constructed these fortresses: the *havirdhāna* from the sky, the *āgnīdhra* from the intermediate region, and the *sadas* from the earth. They said, "Let us perform the *upasad*; by means of the *upasad*, one indeed conquers a great fortress. Thus they did.

Having approached them with the Upasads, they struck them down from these worlds by means of the Upasads themselves. Therefore, they say, "By the Upasads one indeed conquers a great fortress. Having been driven out from these worlds, they entered the seasons. They approached them with the Upasads and struck them down from the seasons by means of the Upasads themselves: with two [Upasads] from yonder world, with two from the intermediate space, and with two from the earth. Having been driven out from the seasons, they entered the year. They approached them with the twelve [Upasads], and by means of the Upasads themselves—

They drove them out for a year with four [verses] from yonder world, with four from the intermediate space, and with four from the earth. Thus driven out for a year, they entered day and night. Because they approached them in the evening, they drove them out by means of the night; because [they approached them] in the morning, they drove them out by means of the day. Therefore, the cow swells in the evening what was taken in the morning, and in the morning what was taken in the evening. Driving them away from these worlds by means of the *upasad* rites, they advanced; then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. From all these worlds—

He who, knowing this, performs the *upasad* rites, advances while driving away his rival; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. One should not perform twelve *upasad* days for the *agniṣṭoma*, lest they be unappeased and wipe him out. Nor should one perform three for the *ahīna* sacrifice, lest the sacrificial rite, being too heavy, break his neck and bring him to ruin. One should perform twelve for the *ahīna* for the sake of appeasement and to prevent wiping out. One should perform three for the *agniṣṭoma* for the sake of support and stability. Thus, O Gods...

These worlds were not able to overcome the Asuras; they entered them with Agni as their mouth. In that the introductory portions of the Upasads contain Agni, it is just as when a master of a field drives away [the weeds] from his field: even so, they go forth conquering these worlds with Agni as their mouth. Verily, he who knows the Sādhyas among the gods succeeds. These worlds are indeed the Sādhyas among the gods. For what is accomplished for these [worlds], that is accomplished for him; what is accomplished for this [earth], that is accomplished for him; what is accomplished for yonder [heaven], that is accomplished for him who knows thus. He succeeds. 10.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section, named "The Witness" (Sākṣī), in the Madhyamikā branch of the Caraka school of the Śukla-Yajurveda-Kāṭhaka. 24.

Now follows the twenty-fifth section: The Arrow. The gods fashioned these Upasad rites into an arrow: Agni was the barb-tip (*śṛṅga*), Soma the shaft (*śalya*), and Viṣṇu the point (*tejana*). They said, "He among us who is the strongest, let him discharge this. They said to Rudra, "You indeed are the strongest among us; you discharge this. He replied, "I choose a boon: let me alone be the lord of cattle. They thought, "If he becomes the lord of cattle, he will consume them all. They said, "Be the lord for seven days, but not beyond that. Therefore, Rudra is the lord for seven days.

He was the lord of cattle; the Rakṣases struck him from behind. He released her (the Upasad); with her he shattered them in front. Because he shattered (*sam-aruja-t*) them, that is Rudra’s rudra-nature. He who, knowing this, performs the Upasads, releases destruction upon his rival. He should not turn back again. Of two who are engaged in combat, whichever one turns back again, he is the one defeated.

He who now approaches the Upasad rites exerts himself in the same manner; having stepped back once for all, he causes the announcement (*āśrāvayati*) for the sake of winning the sacrifice and for the striking away of the Rākṣasas. There are no *prayāja* offerings, nor are there *anuyāja* offerings. For the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s are the forepart of the sacrifice; if one were to perform the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s, one would place them at the forepart of the sacrifice, and it would be difficult to overcome. One should make the arrow blunt. He observes the fourfold vow, for the arrow has four feathers. He observes the threefold vow, for the arrow has three joints and a horn-tip.

The shaft has a point; it consists of two vows and has two joints—the arrow-shaft and the point. The point consists of one vow, for the arrow is indeed one. Having thus prepared this arrow, he releases it against his rival on the following day; moreover, he thereby attains the vow itself.

The Upasad rites are indeed the neck of the sacrifice; there are neither fore-offerings (prayāja) nor after-offerings (anuyāja). Therefore, the neck is the thinnest part of every person, yet it is employed with full vigor; thus the neck, though thin, is most powerful. There are three Upasads, for these worlds are three; therefore there are three vertebrae in a person. He sacrifices with [verses] closely joined; therefore the neck is closely joined. Moreover, he sacrifices with verses that are not exhausted in their power, and with those that are truly unexhausted. The invitatory and offering verses (yājyā-anuvākyā) are in identical meters.
One should perform this so that they may be according to one's desire; otherwise, if the Hotṛ is unacquainted with it, they would slay him. The *bhidvatī* verses are for the breaking of fortresses.

The gods and the asuras were engaged in conflict over the sacrifice. That sacrifice was afraid, thinking, "If they conquer, they will tear me apart. It hid itself away. The gods, having conquered, sought after it; searching for it in every direction, they went along. Indra passed directly over it. He said, "Who is this that has passed directly over me? "It is I," he replied, "I am here to rescue you from distress. "And who are you? [Indra asked. "It is I," he replied, "I am here to bring you out from distress. "This is a boar named Emūṣa," [Indra] said. [This was told] by means of twenty-one [verses].

"Whatever desirable wealth of the Asuras lies beyond the stone fortresses, with that he stands; slay him! He who said, 'I am the slayer in distress'—Indra, having discharged his bolt at him, shattered him. He said, 'He is slain; bring him who said, "I am the one who will bring him back from distress. Viṣṇu brought him back from the shoulder-strap; for Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice. By means of the sacrifice, they thus appropriated their sacrifice, by means of cattle their cattle, and by means of sensory power their sensory power. Thereupon the gods prospered, and the Asuras were defeated."

Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice, he thus appropriates the sacrifice of his rival; by means of cattle, he appropriates his cattle; by means of power, he appropriates his power; by himself, his rival is cast down. They desire a place for the divine sacrifice; they truly desire the sacrifice itself. Whatever they find, they find the sacrifice itself. If the ground should slope toward the north or the east, on that one should sacrifice who desires a sacrifice; for in this very way that sacrifice lay down, for the sake of obtaining the sacrifice. If it be level and well-established, on that one should sacrifice who has attained prosperity.

A firm foundation must indeed be sought by one whose prosperity has departed; for that which is level is established upon the earth, and thus he finds a foundation for himself and attains stability. One who has rivals should sacrifice on ground elevated in three places. By means of what is elevated in three places, Viṣṇu conquered these worlds and drove the Asuras away from these worlds. Thus, he conquers these very worlds and drives his rival away from these worlds.

One who desires heaven should sacrifice on a place where the center is elevated in one spot; for from there indeed the gods went to the heavenly world, for the attainment of the heavenly world. One who desires cattle should sacrifice on a place where the plants appear as many and distinct from one another; for cattle are indeed plants; verily he attains abundance of cattle. One who desires cattle should sacrifice on a place where the plants grow in difficulty, spreading out in succession; for from there indeed the gods released the cattle; verily he releases cattle.

If it is a thicket without hair, he should cause one whom he hates to sacrifice upon it; for that which is a thicket without hair is indeed devoid of plants, and since cattle are plants, he thereby deprives him of cattle.

If a path should run right through the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*), one should cause him whom he desires to sacrifice there to perform the rite, thinking, "May I cut him off from offspring and cattle. For that is indeed the place of sacrifice called "The Severed" (*vicchinna*); it cuts him off from offspring and cattle. If a path should run between the waters and the place of sacrifice, one should cause him whom he desires to sacrifice there to perform the rite, thinking, "May no other sacrifice come near him. For that is indeed the place of sacrifice called "The Encircling Path" (*parivartma*); another sacrifice avoids him.

Where waters flow together from all sides, there one desiring food should sacrifice; for it is from the quarters that food is brought to him to whom they bring it. He secures food from all the quarters. This is the sacrificial ground called *sanāman*, which becomes most prosperous among those who dwell around it.

Where the waters flow eastward from the Āhavanīya fire and westward from the Gārhapatya fire, in that place one should cause him to sacrifice whom they might deliberate upon regarding water, a vessel, or a marriage; for he whom they deliberate upon regarding water, a vessel, or a marriage is indeed pursued by evil. By means of this [place], he turns him away from evil. Where the waters, having flowed around to the south, delight toward the west and then toward the east, in that place one who desires prosperity should sacrifice; for the waters are all the deities, and thus it is a sacrificial ground favored by the deities when it is so.

He sacrifices on a place for the sacrifice to the gods that is favored by the deities themselves; he indeed prospers. On a place where the waters flow from the south toward the north, he should sacrifice if he desires kinsmen. The waters are indeed all the deities; the deities are his kinsmen; verily, he places him in the forefront of his kinsmen. He who desires prosperity should sacrifice on an artificial site; the place for the sacrifice to the gods is the self; verily, he makes it for himself. On a place where one can see both fire and water while reciting the morning litany (prātaranuvāka), he should sacrifice if he should desire, "May the sacrifice come to me from behind. Agni is indeed all...

The waters are the deities of the sacrifice; another sacrifice inclines toward him, for he sacrifices while beholding both the deities and the sacrifice. Where one may recite the *prātaranuvāka* while beholding fire, water, and the sun, there one who desires spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice. This is indeed the sacrificial ground named *triśukriya*; he becomes possessed of spiritual splendor. One who has rivals should sacrifice on a sacrificial ground that is open in front; for this world is left over for his rival.

He leaves over this much of the sacrificial ground from the front; he thus leaves over for him just as much of this world and makes it a non-world for him who, knowing this, performs the sacrifice on the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). Indeed, Agni is the sacrificial ground, for in Agni all the deities are sacrificed to. Wherever one might establish the fire and sacrifice, by that very act one prospers. The Brahmins indeed are the sacrificial ground; where many Brahmins may be in agreement, there one should sacrifice. By that very act one prospers.

He measures out the altar: he measures it thirty steps toward the west, thirty-six toward the east, and twenty-four toward the front. By means of the Virāj meter he measures it around from the west, by the Bṛhatī toward the east, and by the Gāyatrī toward the front; thus he measures it all around by means of the meters. He finds firm support in the Virāj when he brings it to completion as the Virāj. With the wooden sword (sphya) he carries away the Stambayajus; for Indra indeed hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, and it became threefold: the wooden sword was one third, the sacrificial post was one third.

The chariot is the third; the wooden sword is indeed the thunderbolt. As great as this earth is, so great is the altar; by means of the thunderbolt, he thus excludes his rival from the earth. He carries it away three times; these worlds are three; from these very worlds he thus excludes him.

He takes up the fourth [clod] silently; verily, he banishes him from the immeasurable. Having slain Vṛtra, Indra indeed laid him down with this [earth]; in that he takes up the fourth clod silently, he lays down his rival with this very [earth]. He cuts the root; verily, he cuts the root of his rival. He digs up [the clod]; therefore the plants perish in the cold season. He spreads the sacrificial grass (barhis); therefore they come forth again in the spring. "O Araru, depart from the earth, the place of sacrifice for the gods!"—for the rival is indeed Araru. Verily, he drives him away from the place of sacrifice for the gods.

With "The Araru, the adversary, I strike away from the earth," he indeed strikes away the adversary from the earth. With "May thy drop not leap up to heaven"—for that which is the essence of this [earth] is its drop, and upon it these creatures subsist—he thereby secures that very essence within her, so that it may not leap away. With "May the Araru not fall to heaven"—the Araru is indeed the adversary—he thus repels the adversary from the heavenly world.

There was indeed an Asura named Viṣa; he smeared the earth with poison. No one ate of it; whoever did eat of it became ill. When they dig [the earth], they thereby remove whatever in it is impure and unfit for sacrifice. One should even dig down to the roots for the sake of expiating what has been pierced. One should dig deep below, for its strength lies below; this is for the attainment of strength. Therefore, rice and barley ripen on well-ploughed ground. Regarding this, they say: "Its strength lies in the upper part, upon which these creatures subsist; therefore, one should not dig too deeply."

One should dig for the sake of the sacrificer’s firm foundation; one should make a hollow on the south side as the characteristic form of the sacrificial ground (devayajana) for the smiting away of the Rakṣases; it should be full of loose soil—for loose soil is indeed cattle—and thus he wins cattle for himself.

He encloses the altar with the wooden sword (*sphyá*). The wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajrá*); as great as the altar is, so great is this earth. Having thus excluded his rival from the earth by means of the thunderbolt, he encloses it for himself by means of the meters (*chándas*), saying: "May the Vasus enclose thee with the Gāyatrī meter! On the south side, the Gāyatrī is indeed splendor and sacred power (*brahman*); verily, he encloses him on the south side with splendor. [He says: "May the Rudras enclose thee with the Triṣṭubh meter! On the west side, the Triṣṭubh is indeed vigor and strength; verily, he [encloses] it with vigor.

Thereafter he encloses it from the west with the formula, "May the Ādityas enclose thee with the Jagatī metre. Cattle are indeed connected with the Jagatī; cattle have their abode in the north. Thus he provides an abode for the cattle and secures them for the sake of stability and brilliance; on both sides he thus encloses the cattle. With the words, "Before the flowing of the cruel one, O Virapśin," he obtains that brilliance of this earth which is fit for sacrifice, for that [brilliance] has gone into the moon.

He sprinkles the sacrificial fuel and the sacrificial grass. These, having been brought from the forest, are dry and impure; water is pure and fit for sacrifice. In that he sprinkles them with water, he makes these two pure and fit for sacrifice. He sprinkles the altar; he thus makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. Furthermore, as for what they dig up from it—

They perform a cruel act; he pacifies it by spreading the *barhis* grass. The *barhis* is indeed offspring, and the altar (*vedi*) is the earth; thus he establishes offspring upon the earth. He spreads the grass along the entire altar; therefore, herbs spread across the whole earth. He should spread the grass thickly, so that the sacrificer does not become hungry and the *adhvaryu* priest does not become naked. He places the *prastara* (handful of grass) upon the *barhis*; the *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer, and the *barhis* is offspring; he thus places the sacrificer himself upon the offspring. [He places it] on top.

He sets it down, for the sacrificer is higher; he sets it down separated from the sacrificer, for the sacrificer is indeed separated from the sacrificer. Having anointed the *prastara* with butter, he throws it into the fire; the *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer, and thus he causes him, having become an oblation, to go to the heavenly world. He should not throw it beyond the tip; if he were to throw it beyond the tip, the women would be born with broken hair, disheveled, and naked. He kindles the tip upon the tip; verily by the tip he unites the tip. He should throw it straight for one who desires heaven; verily he leads him straight to heaven.

He causes him whom he hates to fall from the world; indeed, he causes him to fall from the heavenly world. One desiring rain should strike downward; for whatever oblation rises from here, it causes rain to fall from there. By that very oblation, he pours down rain from heaven. He should strike upward if he should desire, "May a male son be born to him," for a male stands upright. Having spread [the hand] out, he should strike if he should desire, "May a female be born," for a female is, as it were, spread out. The sacrificer, indeed...

When he throws the prastara-bunch [into the fire], it indeed departs from this world; when he takes up a blade of grass, he restrains it in this very world. He throws it after [the other offerings] to pacify whatever cruelty they have committed by touching it or whatever injury they have caused by severing it. "Has it gone? O Agnīdh!"—"It has gone!"—by saying "it has gone," he means "it has gone to the heavenly world. "Make it heard! Let it be heard!"—he thus makes the one who has gone to the heavenly world be heard.

The gods and the Asuras were arrayed for battle. Whatever splendor and sacrificial power there was in her, that, having become like the form of a lioness and like the form of a buffalo, stood between them. They knew: "Whichever side she will join, they shall be the victors here. The gods invited her, and she said: "I shall choose a boon: let the first oblation to Agni reach me; then, through me, you shall attain all your desires. She joined the gods, and thereafter the gods prospered while the Asuras were defeated.

For one who knows this, the high altar (uttaravedi) is thus prepared; and for one who, knowing this, pours [the earth], he prospers in himself and his rival is defeated. There are ten footprints across behind, and ten on both sides.

The *vedi* is commensurate with the eastern limit; it is commensurate with the *virāj*. Whatever wealth belonged to the Asuras, that the gods found on the *vedi*; therefore, the *vedi* has its nature as "that which is found" (*vedya*). That which is to be found is [found] on the *uttaravedi*; therefore, the *uttaravedi* has its nature as "the higher found" (*uttara-vedya*). For one who knows thus, when both the *vedi* and the *uttaravedi* are prepared and the latter is strewn, he finds both the wealth and that which is to be found belonging to his rival. Indeed, the nose of Prajāpati was shattered; it became the *uttaravedi*. Prajāpati is the sacrifice; therefore, when he prepares the *uttaravedi*, he restores the sacrifice.

He restores Prajāpati’s very nose from the mouth; for it has four names: *nāsikā*, *kaśārī*, *siṃhī*, and *uttaravedi*. [He says: "Thou art the heated one" (*taptāyanī*), for he has indeed brought her to heat; "thou art the found one" (*vittāyanī*), for he has indeed found her. "Protect us from what is desired" (*avatān mā nāthitam*), for he protects them from what is desired; "protect us from what is distressed" (*avatād vyathitam*), for he protects them from what is distressed. "O Agni Aṅgiras, who art on this earth, who art on the second, who art on the third"—[he says this] because whatever of hers is attached or joined in these worlds.

He digs there with [the formula], "O Videdagni, [dig] the sky, by name. Or rather, that which was Agni’s desirable wealth, *nabha* by name—that entered this earth, down to the depth of a knee; therefore, it should be dug to the depth of a knee for the sake of obtaining that very desirable wealth. [With the words] "Thou art a lioness, thou art a buffalo," for she stood within having assumed, as it were, the form of a lioness and the form of a buffalo. [With the words] "Spread yourself out for the gods," he indeed causes them to spread out; [with the words] "Be prepared for the gods," he indeed prepares them; [with the words] "Purify yourself for the gods," he purifies them.

With "They purify them for the gods; be beautiful," he indeed makes them beautiful. With "May the radiant one drink the Soma-mead in abundance," he prepares the ends. The high altar is indeed the vessel of the gods; by means of that very vessel of the gods, he satisfies the deities. Moreover, he presents the vessel of the gods to the deities themselves. The Yatis were indeed devoured by hyenas—Pārda was [eaten]...

While they were being rubbed down as he lay there, they stepped out onto the *uttaravedi*; we could not overcome them. One among them smiled; then we were able to overcome them. We tore each one of them away from them; therefore, one should not be a person who laughs in vain. When he drives it out, he drives out whatever of this [earth] was touched by the gods and was impure. He sprinkles [it]; for this earth was only as large as the *uttaravedi*. All around it, the *rakṣases* trembled; those [beings], the gods—

Having driven away the Rakṣases with these deities, they enclose [the altar] on all sides; for these quarters belong to those deities, so by driving away the Rakṣases with these deities, he encloses himself on all sides.

For protection, indeed, this first oblation of Agni reaches it when he sprinkles [the butter] across; then he said, "Let the first oblation of Agni reach me alone, and then through me you shall attain all desires. Now, at that time, the Asuras were their rivals; they desired, "May we overcome our rivals," and with the words, "Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals, svāhā! they overcame their rivals. They desired, "May we obtain cattle," and with the words, "Thou art a lioness, possessing good offspring, svāhā!"...

They sought cattle; they desired, "May we obtain offspring. [With the words] "Thou art a lioness, well-born, a supporter—Svāhā! they thereby obtained offspring. They desired, "May we become Ādityas. [With the words] "Thou art a lioness, belonging to the Ādityas—Svāhā! they thereby became Ādityas; therefore these creatures are called Ādityas. They desired, "May we be worthy of sacrifice. [With the words] "Thou art a lioness; bring the gods for the god-loving sacrificer—Svāhā! they thereby became worthy of sacrifice. They desired, "May we go to the heavenly world. [With the words] "For the beings, thee!"...

The gods, having become beings, went to the heavenly world by means of that [rite]. For one who knows thus, and for whom the high altar (uttaravedi) is sprinkled with ghee, and for one who, knowing thus, performs the sprinkling—by this [rite] he attains all desires. These worlds were indeed held together; they trembled, and the gods steadied them with these sacrificial formulas (yajus). In that he lays the enclosing-sticks (paridhi) around with these [formulas], it is for the support of these worlds. Agni indeed departed from the gods; that first place where he fled to—[that he now takes].

It dwelt among cattle within the horns of the bull; therefore, there is the woolly tuft. That which was the second [portion] it placed among the trees, in the *pītudāru* tree; therefore, the *pītudāru* tree exists. That which was the third [portion] it placed among the plants, in the *sugandhitejana* plant; therefore, the *sugandhitejana* plant exists. Since these materials are used as preparations, he thereby gathers together whatever of his was stuck or smeared [upon him]. Returning again, he shook his body; that which was his flesh became bdellium (*gulgulu*), and that which was his bone...

The fibers of the *pītudāru* tree are fragrant resin; when these materials are used, he thereby gathers together whatever of this [fire] was stuck or smeared, for the sake of the completeness of Agni. "Thou art the nest of Agni, thou art the soil of Agni"—for this is indeed like a nest and like soil. "The sacrifice has been firmly established"—this is for the firm establishment of the sacrifice.

There were indeed four Hotṛ-priests of the gods: Bhūpati, Bhuvanapati, Bhūtānāṃ pati, and Bhūta. Three of them perished through their office as Hotṛ. Now, that which remained as Bhūta was afraid of death; he hid himself and entered the ocean. The ash he left behind in the ocean is this very mud. A fish pointed it out to him. He cursed it, saying, "May the one who comes after you slay you! Therefore, whoever pursues a fish slays it, for it is cursed. Then, having escaped from there, it entered a reed.

Therefore, the Naḍa grass was burnt; a cruel, fierce, and most dark horse, white in color, searching about, found him and scorched him. Therefore, its mouth is scorched. It cried out; that which was its voice became the bird Suśloka. Therefore, when one cries out toward someone who has lost something, one certainly finds it. The gods, having found him, led him away, saying, "You shall be our Hotṛ here. He feared death. His deceased brothers said to him, "We shall be your armor from here on among the gods."

"Let us choose a portion," they said. "Whatever oblation, having become [spilled], falls outside the enclosing-sticks (paridhi), that shall be their portion. These indeed are those enclosing-sticks. If an oblation, having become [spilled], should fall outside the enclosing-sticks, one should consecrate it with the formula: "To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā! These gods indeed have a share in what is spilled; he thus causes those gods who have a share in the spilled portion to attain it. Of these, the sacrifice is the middle one; the sacrificer is the southern half; the enemy is the northern half.

He should make the middle [post] the thickest of those belonging to the northern half, and the one on the southern half the tallest; the one on the northern half the most massive. He first girds the thickest one on the northern half, for the sacrifice is first; he girds the tallest one on the southern half, just as the sacrificer sits down to the south of the sacrifice—so it is there. And lastly he girds the one on the northern half, for the rival is indeed behind; thus by means of the sacrifice he makes the sacrificer advance further and drives away the rival by means of the sacrifice. Having anointed [the posts], he [girds] the one on the southern half.

He strikes at the sacrificer from the very mouth [of the offering], yet he gratifies him; moreover, having made him into an oblation, he causes him to go to the heavenly world. He scatters [the grain] on the northern half; thus he scatters it away from his rival. Now Āryala Kāhoḍi used to say: "Why should he sacrifice who would not become better off because of what has spilled from the sacrifice? Wherever it should spill, having poured water there, he should measure out [the ground] with his span toward the east, saying, "Svāhā to Bhūpati! toward the south, saying, "Svāhā to Bhuvanapati! and toward the west, saying, "Svāhā to Bhūtānām pati! (Lord of Beings).

That which spills away from the sacrifice goes to the common folk; for this earth is indeed the people, and he who goes to this [earth] does not return. Whatever blessing he desires for that sacrifice, that very blessing he secures for the people.

He measures out the quarters; for when the sacrifice is spilled, its blessing (*āśis*) goes to the quarters. From the quarters alone he wins back the blessing of the sacrifice. He measures with a span (*prādeśa*); for as much vigor as there is in a man—as far as his vital breaths extend—by that very vigor he gathers it together. He pours down water; for that part of the sacrifice which is spilled dies away. They sprinkle one who is exhausted with water; water is all the deities; thus he causes it to enter the deities. If it should spill at the morning pressing, [he says] "The gods have gone to the Janas."

If [the sacrifice] has gone to the waters at midday, he should follow it with the mantra: "The sacrifice has gone to the waters; may the wealth of that sacrifice, which is offered and enjoyed, come here. If it has gone to the plants, he should follow it with the mantra: "The sacrifice has gone to the plants; may the wealth of that sacrifice, which is offered and enjoyed, come here. If it has gone to the ancestors at the third pressing, he should follow it with the mantra: "The sacrifice has gone to the ancestors; may the wealth of that sacrifice, which is offered and enjoyed, come here. If it has gone to heaven and earth at night, he should follow it with the mantra: "The sacrifice has gone to heaven and earth; may the wealth of that sacrifice, which is offered and enjoyed, come here."

He should recite over it: "If [the oblation] has been hidden among the Gandharvas, the sacrifice has gone to the people; may the wealth of that sacrifice which has been offered and enjoyed come here to me. He should recite this. These deities indeed go toward the blessing of the spilled sacrifice. Having approached these very deities according to their respective domains, he secures for himself whatever blessing of the sacrifice he desires. He becomes more prosperous—he for whom they recite over the spilled sacrifice while knowing thus, and he who, knowing thus, recites over it. 7.

He sprinkles [the two] at the *havirdhāna* sheds; he thus makes them pure and fit for sacrifice. They untie the knots; intending to tie divine knots, they untie human knots. The oblation is indeed in the *havirdhāna*; they set down the oblation upon the strewn sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Therefore, they move the *havirdhāna* carts when the *barhis* is strewn. The wife anoints [the axle]; this is the wife’s participation in the sacrifice, and furthermore, she establishes a pair at the beginning of the sacrifice for the sake of procreation. Three times...

He anoints [the axle] from front to back; for humans anoint it crosswise—this is for the sake of distinction. He anoints with a *yajus* formula; for humans anoint without a formula—this is indeed for the sake of distinction. He anoints from the south, for these two [axles] turn northward from the south toward the world of men; thus he makes the human element their superior part.

If [the axle] were to break from the rear, they would not return to either of the two worlds. These two Havirdhāna carts proceed toward the heavenly world; therefore, with the verse addressed to Savitṛ, "They yoke the mind," he offers an oblation, so that, impelled by Savitṛ, he causes them to go to the heavenly world. The Havirdhānas are indeed the sacrificial offering; no offering attains its essence unless it is sprinkled with ghee. By anointing them, he maintains them as fit for sacrifice. That axle which is bound on both sides by the two naves and the two linchpins is dry and seized by Nirṛti.

When he anoints [the axle] while biting his lip, he makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. There was once an Asura named Ghoṣa; he entered the trees. The gods, having seized him, bound him on both sides. If he were to make a sound, the voice of the Asuras would speak against the sacrifice, and the Rakṣases, having followed after the sacrifice, would destroy it. They proceed holding [the axle], to prevent the Rakṣases from following after it. The Rakṣases, having followed after the sacrifice along its path, seek to slay it. He offers an oblation on the path with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; for the sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu—by means of Viṣṇu himself [he protects it].

Through sacrifice, one drives away the *rakṣas* demons. That offering which one makes in that which is not fire is indeed unsuccessful; when he makes the offering after placing gold [on top], he offers in that which possesses fire, for the sake of success. These two, having gone forth to the world of heaven, when he makes the offering on the path of the southern *havirdhāna* cart with a *gāyatrī* verse, he causes them to step upon this very earth. With a *triṣṭubh* verse, he makes the offering on the northern [cart]; he causes them to step upon the intermediate space itself. He causes them to go to the *āhavanīya* fire; he causes them to go to the world of heaven, for the *āhavanīya* is indeed the world of heaven. Three times in front...

He leaves a remnant of the strides; these are three worlds, and thus he leaves a remnant of these very worlds. With the words, "O Viṣṇu, from heaven or from earth," he drives in the pin of the southern *havirdhāna* cart. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; verily, from the very beginning of the sacrifice, he secures the blessing. Seeking that blessing at every joint, he proceeds. With the words, "Now I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu," he [drives in the pin] of the northern cart. The *havirdhāna* belongs to Viṣṇu; verily, by its own deity, he makes it prosper. With the words, "Thou art the back of Viṣṇu."

He places the roof-covering on top; by that he forms this very thing which is the upper half of the head. With the words, "O Viṣṇu, you are the forehead," he forms the forehead in front. With the words, "You are the temples of Viṣṇu," he forms the two temples on both sides.

They stitch the front beam crosswise; therefore, a man’s eyebrows are directed crosswise. With the words, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s seam; thou art Viṣṇu’s knot," he stitches the oblation-holder which belongs to Viṣṇu with its own deity, and he ties the knot with its own deity. Whatever first knot he may tie, that he should untie first for his own protection; if he were to untie another first, the Adhvaryu would die from dysentery. They bind [the poles] above the śamyā-peg.

For humans measure from behind and join from the front; they measure from below and join from the front for the sake of distinction. The *havirdhāna* (sacrificial cart) is indeed the head of the sacrifice; it is broader in the front and narrower in the back. Therefore, the head of a man is broader in the front and narrower in the back. "Thou art Vaiṣṇava; for Viṣṇu thee!"—with these words he consecrates the joined [cart]. The *havirdhāna* belongs to Viṣṇu; verily, by its own deity, he makes it successful. "That Viṣṇu is praised... [he recites].
With the words "by vigor," he causes the sacrificer to take three steps forward; having thus become Viṣṇu, he causes him to go to these worlds. ||8||

The *havirdhāna* cart is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *uparava* holes are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). He traces around [the holes] beneath the southern *havirdhāna*; this is the joint of these two, and thus he restores the vital breaths to the very mouth of the sacrifice. Therefore, the vital breaths are at the mouth. He traces around four [holes], for there are four vital breaths. He traces them out one span (*prādeśa*) each; for this much [space] do they dig without piercing these vital breaths. It is for the non-piercing of the vital breaths; were he to pierce them, he would pierce the vital breaths.

He would split them; they would die; the enemy unites them into one. Therefore, the vital breaths (prāṇas) are united by the enemy into one. With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes up the spade; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes them up with the deities. With the words, "Here I cut off the neck of the Rakṣas,"—the Rakṣas is indeed the enemy—he cuts off the neck of his enemy. With the words, "Here I cut off the neck of him who, whether equal or unequal to us, acts as an enemy," [he cuts off the neck of the adversary].

The sounding-holes (*uparava*) are indeed the vital breaths; verily, from the vital breaths he separates his rival, and [the rival] quickly perishes. "Thou art great, O great stone; utter a great voice for Indra," he says, for he indeed utters a great voice for Indra. "Slaying the Rakṣases, slaying the secret spells, belonging to Viṣṇu," he says, for the sake of striking down the Rakṣases. As to why he says "belonging to Viṣṇu": Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; verily, he endows it with its own deity. The gods and the Asuras were contending; those Asuras [attacked] the vital breaths of the gods.

They dug out the *valaga* spells; they found them at the depth of the length of an arm. Therefore, the pits should be dug to the depth of an arm, for the purpose of finding the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). With the words, "Here I root up those *valaga* spells which our equal or our unequal has buried," he roots them up, having discovered whatever here was cursed or practiced as sorcery against him. Therefore these [pits] are healing; therefore they cause one who is ill to be rubbed along [the pits].

"Thou art a sovereign ruler (samrāj), thou art a self-ruler (svarāj)"—with these [formulas] he attains sovereignty. "By the Gāyatrī metre thou art pressed down; him whom we hate, by the Triṣṭubh and the Jagatī"—there are indeed only so many metres; verily, by means of the metres he presses down his rival. "What is auspicious therein, let that be ours both"—thus he invokes a blessing. "The charm (valaga) is cast out, the malevolent one is pressed down"—this is according to the sacrificial formula. "I sprinkle the Rakṣas-slayers, the charm-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu"—this is for the striking away of the Rakṣases. As for "belonging to Viṣṇu," the sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu.

Viṣṇu himself endows it with its own deity by saying, "I sprinkle the Vaiṣṇava [stones], slayers of Rakṣases, slayers of Valagas," for the purpose of striking away the Rakṣases; furthermore, he pacifies whatever cruel thing they do while digging. By saying "the Vaiṣṇava," Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice, and he thus endows it with its own deity. He says, "I strew the Vaiṣṇava [grass], slayers of Rakṣases, slayers of Valagas," for the purpose of striking away the Rakṣases; by saying "the Vaiṣṇava," Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice, and he thus endows it with its own deity.

He completes it, sprinkles it, and strews it; therefore the vital breaths within are hairy and moist. "I sprinkle you two, the Rakṣas-slayers, the charm-destroyers, belonging to Viṣṇu," he says for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. By saying "belonging to Viṣṇu"—for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice—he completes it with its own deity. These two [pressing-skins] are indeed carved out and impure; water is pure and fit for sacrifice. In that he sprinkles them with water, he makes them pure and fit for sacrifice in their very midst. These two pressing-skins are indeed the jaws of the sacrifice; they are not pierced through.

Therefore, your jaws are not pierced; they are narrower in front and broader behind. For in this very way, there is a space of two finger-breadths between the two jaws. Therefore, this space between the jaws is like a girdle. "I place you, the Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," he says for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. By saying "belonging to Viṣṇu"—for Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice—he causes them to prosper through their own deity. "I pile around you, the Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," he says for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. By saying "belonging to Viṣṇu" [he further ensures their prosperity].

"Thus, Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he thus endows it with its own deity. He piles [the earth] around; therefore, even when not burning, the bowels are not consumed. The two lips are the two pressing-boards (*upara*), the corners of the mouth are the *sṛkka*s, and the beard is the head of the sacrifice. That which is the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*) is the vital breaths; the sounding-holes (*uparava*) are the jaws; the pressing-stones (*grāvan*) are the teeth; the skin used for pressing is the tongue; the wooden trough (*droṇakalaśa*) is the head. Prajāpati is the sacrifice. From the very mouth of Prajāpati they drink the Soma; therefore, the dregs (*ṛjīṣa*) are as if already chewed.

It is as if it were eaten, for that which is eaten with the teeth becomes so. He who knows the Virāj, which is to be milked at the beginning of the sacrifice, milks her. This earth, indeed, is the Virāj; its udder is the two pressing-boards, its teats are the *uparava* holes, its calves are the pressing-stones, and its skin is the pressing-skin. The priests milk her. He who thus knows the Virāj, which is to be milked at the beginning of the sacrifice, milks her. 9.

The *havirdhāna* shed is indeed the head of the sacrifice; the *āgnīdhra* shed is the neck; the *sadas* is the belly; and the *udumbara* wood is strength (*ūrj*). In that he erects the *audumbarī* post in the *sadas*, he places strength in the very middle—for both the sacrificer and his offspring. Therefore, offspring find strength in the middle; they thrive with vigor from that center. For this world, the *audumbarī* is erected; for yonder world, the sacrificial stake (*yūpa*). Therefore, he sprinkles the stake from here toward the distance, and the *audumbarī* from yonder toward this side, for the separation of these two worlds. The *udumbara* is indeed strength; in that he [places] the *audumbarī* from yonder toward this side...

He sprinkles [the earth] from there toward this side; he causes nourishment to flow hitherward and anoints nourishment in this very world. Indeed, the Udgātṛ priest rests upon the Udumbara post as Prajāpati; thus he anoints nourishment among the creatures. With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes up the spade; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it up with the deities. With the words, "Here I cut off the neck of the Rakṣas,"—for the Rakṣas is indeed the enemy—he cuts off the neck of his enemy.

"May the worlds, the seats of the fathers, be purified," he says; thus he purifies it. Moreover, whatever cruel thing they do while digging it, that he pacifies. He pours water mixed with barley over it; barley is food, and the udumbara is strength; thus he bestows food and strength upon it. "I strew thee for the world, the seat of the fathers," he says. For if they were to erect this [post] without a sacrificial grass-strew (*barhis*), it would surely become a pit; since the plants are on the northern half of this [earth], he erects it on the northern half of this very [earth], thereby making it not a pit. "Support the sky, fill the mid-region."
"Be firm upon the earth"—thus he indeed makes it firm. "May Nitāna Māruta strike you down"—Nitāna is the mind and the Mārutās are the vital breaths; thus he carries it away by its own deity.

The Mārutas indeed used to erect the Audumbarī post for the gods; with that very [power] he erects it. With the words, "By the firm law of Mitra and Varuṇa,"—for by Mitra these creatures are pacified and by Varuṇa they are sustained—it is for the sake of arrangement and for the sake of support. With the words, "Thee, winner of the Brahman, winner of the Kṣatra," he invokes a blessing. With the words, "Make firm the Brahman, make firm the Kṣatra," he makes firm for him the most excellent blessing. With the words, "O Heaven and Earth, fill yourselves with clarified butter," he moistens Heaven and Earth with clarified butter.

Therefore, the plants sing out unanointed. He makes an offering upon the Udumbara post with ghee; ghee is indeed brilliance and the Udumbara is food; verily, he bestows brilliance upon food. He places sap right to the very end within the trees and the plants.

"Thou art the shade of all people," he says, for this is indeed the shade of all people; for from clan after clan they creep forward toward the Audumbarī pillar. He should make the coverings face each other; for these plants are the divine clans, and the coverings are the plants, while the Audumbarī is the sacrificer. Thus he makes the offspring face the sacrificer. There is a covering, and then an inner partition; therefore there is flesh upon a man. Now, that which is the *sadas* of the sacrifice is the belly; they set it up crosswise.

Therefore, what is eaten by a man is sustained [in him]; if they were to measure it less than a man, what is eaten by a man would not be sustained. For the sacrifice is measured by the man, and the man by the sacrifice; because the Sadas is hollow on both sides, therefore the man is hollow on both sides. They sew it together; therefore the man is sewn up within. "Thou art Indra’s needle; thou art Indra’s fixed point"—the Sadas belongs to Indra; thus he sews it with its own deity and knots the knot with its own deity: "Thou belongest to Indra; for Indra, thee!"

He consecrates it as commensurate [with the sacrifice]: "The assembly hall belongs to Indra; verily, he causes it to prosper through its own deity. He should make nine roofs if it be an *agniṣṭoma*; it is commensurate with the threefold [stoma], which is brilliance. Fifteen if it be an *ukthya*; it is commensurate with the fifteenfold [stoma]; the thunderbolt is fifteenfold; it is commensurate with the thunderbolt. Seventeen if it be an *atirātra*; it is commensurate with the seventeenfold [stoma]; Prajāpati is seventeenfold; it is commensurate with Prajāpati. Twenty-one for one who desires a firm foundation.

One should make the twenty-first [post] the foundation of the *stomas*, for the sake of stability; furthermore, it is for the sake of distinguishing the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*). If he should desire, "May it rain," he should make those which are at the end the tallest, for the sky, when about to rain, becomes as if lowered. If he should desire, "May it not rain," he should make those the tallest, for the sky, when not about to rain, becomes as if raised. Those which are the southern coverings, he should make them the northern; these belong to the world of the sacrificer. Those which are...

The southern ones belong to the world of the rival; the northern ones make the sacrificer superior to his rival who does not sacrifice, for the sacrificer is indeed superior to him who does not sacrifice.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section, named "The Arrow" (Iṣu), in the Madhyamikā recension of the Caraka branch of the glorious Yajurveda-Kāṭhaka. 25.

Now follows the twenty-sixth section: The Dhiṣṇya altars. The Dhiṣṇyas are piled for the support of these two worlds; some are piled, others are not piled. By those that are piled, he supports this world; by those that are not piled, he supports yonder world, for yonder world is turned away and undefined. Agni indeed departed from the gods and entered the earth; they found him knee-deep; therefore, it should be dug knee-deep. Having found him, he piles them. He piles them from the Cātvāla pit; this is indeed the womb of Agni; verily, he piles them from their own womb. He who knows the ford of the Vedi does not [fail].

The Sadasya incurs misfortune if he passes between the Āgnīdhra fire and the Cātvāla pit toward the west; he should pass along that path, for this is the *tīrtha* (the proper passage) of the altar. He who knows thus does not incur misfortune from the Sadasya. The Adhvaryu should not pass westward across the Sadas; the Sadas is indeed the belly of the sacrifice. If he were to drag it across the belly of the sacrifice, he would perish. This [passage] is the people of the Adhvaryu; he goes to the people, and having gone from one assembly to another, he overcomes them. If he must pass across, he should do so with a verse addressed to Indra; for the Sadas belongs to Indra, and thus he passes by means of its own deity.

He does not pass beyond the *havirdhāna* shed; for the *havirdhāna* is the head of the sacrifice, and he would drag down the head of the sacrifice and perish if he were to pass beyond it. He should pass by with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; for the *havirdhāna* belongs to Viṣṇu, and thus he passes by with its own deity. Regarding this, they say: "One should pass by with a verse addressed to Kṣetrapati. This earth is the lord of the field (*kṣetra-pati*); therefore, he does not go astray from her. Indeed, Soma was in yonder world; the *dhiṣṇya* hearths guarded him. The *gāyatrī* brought him away as a protection for the *iṣṭāpūrta*.

Therefore, these two have failed as *hotṛ*s, and their Soma-drinking has failed; therefore, one must not act as the *neṣṭṛ* nor as the *potr*. Therefore, these two perform the sacrifice as if they were in close association. They followed after him, having assumed second names; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who has two names is successful. They settled around him, desiring a share; for them he assigned this share when he sprinkles the *dhiṣṇya* hearths with ghee: he thus endows them with their own respective shares. Those among them who settled closest to him—

When one attains the place of Soma-drinking—the Āhavanīya, the Āgnīdhra, and the Hotrīya—therefore these [fires] do not harm one who offers the *vaṣaṭ* call over and over again, for they are pleased with him. The Adhvaryu should not pass behind the *dhiṣṇya* hearths facing west; the *dhiṣṇyas* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and he would draw them together [into himself]. Nor should the Hotṛ pass behind [the fires] facing west; this [place] of the Hotṛ is the navel of the sacrifice. Above the navel is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and below it is the in-breath (*apāna*). He would place the out-breath into the in-breath, and he would perish.

To the south, the Rakṣases indeed overcame the sacrifice of the gods; they drove them back from the Āgnīdhra hearth. When they distribute the Dhiṣṇya hearths from the Āgnīdhra, it is for the conquest of the sacrifice and for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. There was an Asura named Jambha; he swallowed the sacrifice of the gods, yet he could not swallow even the Āgnīdhra. Because they distribute the Dhiṣṇyas from the Āgnīdhra, the sacrifice thereby remains alive and becomes fit for sacrifice. They distribute the embers at the two earlier pressings, for those two [pressings] possess brilliance, and those two splinters are brilliant.

By means of those [oblations] blazing at the third pressing, his pressings become possessed of *śukra* (pure/white) for him who knows thus. By means of eastward-directed oblations, the gods drove away some Asuras; by means of westward-directed ones, others. The *dhiṣṇya* hearths are sprinkled facing westward, while other oblations are offered facing eastward, for the sake of repelling the rival. These *dhiṣṇya* hearths are indeed the dear bodies of Agni Vaiśvānara; when he sprinkles the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, it is these very [bodies] that he [thus honors].

This Agni Vaiśvānara who is released is indeed highly exhilarating; if he were not appeased, he would be liable to burn up the sacrificer and the members of the assembly. To prevent the sacrificer from being consumed, he should cover himself at each pressing, for the blessings of the sacrifice rise up during the pressings; if he were to cover himself, he would place himself between those blessings. The ancestors recognize the navel; he should make his navel visible, yet he should cover his ears as if over them; thus he does not place himself between the blessings, and the ancestors recognize him.

They indeed kill this Soma when they press it. As many as have entered [the sacrificial ground], all of them should sing the *upagāna* at the *agniṣṭoma*. The *agniṣṭoma* is the end; having reached the very end, they thus impel him for the sake of power. A Brāhmaṇa drinks Soma for the sake of power; if he were to sing the *upagāna*, his power would flow away. Therefore, one should not sing the *upagāna*. The *agniṣṭoma* is the year. There are twelve chants (*stotra*) of the *agniṣṭoma*, and twelve months are the year; offspring are born after the pattern of the year. That which belongs to the *agniṣṭoma*...

During the *stotra*, he causes water to flow forward for the sake of procreation. Whatever the wife does at the sacrifice constitutes a pair; when the wife causes the water to flow forward, he pours seed into that very pair. He has the wife look toward the *udgātṛ*; the *udgātṛ* is indeed a bull, and from the wife offspring are produced; thus he introduces the bull into her for the sake of procreation. He causes it to flow from both thighs, for from the thighs offspring are born, for the sake of procreation. As it were, inwardly toward the deity, for she performs this heroic power inwardly.

One should draw it out far upwards; for one who is devoid of shame, no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) arises. He should not let the fee flow forward; if he were to let the fee flow forward, he would sweep away his offspring from the ancestors. He lets it flow northward and eastward; this is indeed the direction of men, and thus he causes them to be born into the world of men.

By means of the *upasads*, the gods conquered these worlds; by means of the *vaisarjana* offerings, they released them, just as a village is released from a battle—that is the reason for the *vaisarjana* nature of the *vaisarjana* offerings. They lead the *soma* eastward and lead the wife eastward; thus they proceed toward these very worlds. By means of Agni as their mouth, the gods conquered these worlds: by the *gārhapatya* fire this world, by the *āgnīdhra* fire the intermediate space, and by the *āhavanīya* fire yonder world. When there is the *gārhapatya*, he conquers this world thereby.

When he offers in the Āgnīdhra fire, he does so with the intermediate region; when he offers in the Āhavanīya fire, he does so with that [heavenly world]. Indeed, this [offering] is cast forth for the sake of the heavenly world. He makes two offerings in the Gārhapatya fire; the sacrificer has two feet, and thus he causes him to step upon this very earth. When he offers in the Āgnīdhra fire with a verse addressed to Agni, he causes him to step upon the intermediate region. When he offers in the Āhavanīya fire with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he causes him to go to the heavenly world, for the Āhavanīya is indeed the heavenly world. Verily, at this time the Rakṣases seek to destroy him who has departed from here but has not yet reached there.

With "O Soma," he offers on the *gārhapatya* fire; these creatures belong to Soma; verily, he announces him to the creatures. With "May the Waters enjoy," having made him an offering to the waters, he leads him across this earth. When he offers on the *āgnīdhra* fire with a verse addressed to Agni, having made him Agni, he leads him into the intermediate space. When he offers on the *āhavanīya* fire with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he causes him to go to the heavenly world, for the *āhavanīya* is indeed the heavenly world. Verily, he is brought from all—men, fathers, and gods—with "Thou, O Soma," [addressing] the one worthy of Soma.

He offers in the *gārhapatya* fire; these creatures belong to Soma—verily, he announces him to the creatures. With the words "The swift one, rejoicing," he announces him to the ancestors. When he offers in the *āgnīdhra* fire with a verse addressed to Agni, since Agni is all the deities, he announces him to the deities.

Soma indeed belongs to Viṣṇu; he deprives him of his deity if he offers it to various other deities. When he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu in the Āhavanīya fire, he endows him with his own deity. Varuṇa seizes all these when, for one consecrated, he seizes men, the ancestors, and the gods. With the words "O Soma," he offers a verse addressed to Soma in the Gārhapatya fire; since these creatures belong to Soma, he thereby releases the creatures from Varuṇa’s noose. With the words "The swift one, enjoying," he releases the ancestors from Varuṇa’s noose. When [he offers] with a verse addressed to Agni in the Anvāhāryapacana (or Anvāhārya) fire...

Agni offers the oblation; Agni is all the deities. It is the deities themselves that release him from the nooses of Varuṇa. Thus freed from debt, he goes forth, releasing these worlds. That is why these offerings are called "the releasings" (vaisarjana).

Therefore they say, "Even now they release [the Soma] for the wild animals. He places the pressing-stones and the Vāyavya cups in the Āgnīdhra shed and leads the Soma forward to the east. With these very things they strike him; by means of the strikers themselves, he turns him away from them and does not come face to face with the strikers—he who knows thus. If one were to approach from the front, Agni is indeed Rudra and the animals are the *aṃśu*s; he would deliver the animals over to Rudra and would become animal-less. They enter from behind toward the east. Soma is indeed prosperity (*śrī*); like one from behind, he approaches from the front.

One attains glory from behind; therefore, offspring go eastward, conquering the fields. One who has already attained glory should enter from the front; thus, facing westward from the front, he attains glory and finds firm support in this very world. They cause Soma to descend from behind, while the sacrificer enters from the front; thus, from both sides, he encompasses glory for himself. "Go through the wide atmosphere," he says, for at this moment he has the atmosphere as his deity. "Thou art the skin of Aditi; sit on the seat of Aditi," he says, for Soma is indeed Aditya.

"Aditi is the earth; from the earth, that which was not gathered is [gathered]. He places him in his own womb. "O God Savitṛ, this Soma is yours"—Savitṛ is indeed the overlord of the gods, and men guard this [Soma] from here onwards; he thus hands it over to him for protection. "Come hither, O divine Soma, to the gods"—for he is a god and approaches the gods. "Here I [return] to men, together with offspring, together with abundance of wealth"—thus, together with offspring and cattle, he returns to this world.

"Adoration to the gods! Svadhā to the fathers!"—for adoration belongs to the gods and *svadhā* to the fathers. "Free me from malice, free me from Varuṇa’s noose!"—verily, he thus frees him from malice and from Varuṇa’s noose. "I have looked upon the light"—the light is indeed these worlds; verily, he beholds these very worlds. "O Agni, guardian of vows"—verily, by means of Agni he exchanges his body [with that of the deity]; for at the *tānūnaptra* rite, he is liable to be harmed. By means of Agni, he thus restores his body to its proper state. At this time, indeed, he [unites] his body with the gods.

That is the reason for the "releasing" nature of the *vaisarjana* offerings. He should utter the first [verse] for himself; if he were to utter the first for the other, he would be liable to perish. He should utter the latter for one whom he hates; Agni is indeed Rudra, and thus he hands him over to Rudra; he perishes instantly.

One who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) must not offer an oblation. For the consecrated one is indeed *Havis* (the sacrificial offering), and Agni is Rudra. If he were to offer it, he would deliver himself, having become the *Havis*, unto Rudra; if he were not to offer it, he would exclude himself from the end of the sacrifice. If the *Soma* has been purchased, he may offer in the fire of the consecrated one, for by then the sacrifice has been released and the oblations have become as if offered. If it has not been purchased, he should take the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) and the clarified butter (*ājya*), go away, churn out the fire, and offer at the base of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; for the post belongs to Viṣṇu, and thus he [satisfies] it with its own deity.

"I have approached the gods; I have not approached others"—for he indeed approaches the gods and does not approach others. "Those whom I did not delight, I have avoided them"—for those whom he does not delight, he avoids them. "I have found you on this side of the further ones, and on the further side of the nearer ones"—for he finds him on this side of the further ones and on the further side of the nearer ones. "We delight in you, O Lord of the Forest, for the sacrifice to the gods"—for he delights in him for the sacrifice to the gods. "Delightful to Viṣṇu"—Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he makes him delightful for the sacrifice.

"May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey," he says; honey is indeed the clarified butter of the gods; thus he makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. "O plant, protect him! he says; this is like providing a coat of armor. "O axe, do not harm him! he says; the axe is indeed a thunderbolt; [this is] for the sake of non-injury. He should take the first splinter that falls away; for his brilliance follows that [splinter] as it falls away; thus he erects it with its own brilliance.

One who turns toward the south, one should not cut that [tree], for it belongs to the pit; one who turns toward the north, one should not cut that, for it belongs to the pillar. One whose branches and shoots point upward—that one he should cut, for this indeed is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); he cuts that which is truly fit to be a sacrificial post. He should cut one whose tip is not withered, which has many branches and many leaves; for plants and trees are cattle, and plants are cattle—verily, by means of cattle he makes him prosper. He should cut one whose tip is withered, which is branchless and leafless, if he should hate someone; [then] plants, trees, and cattle [belong] to him.

He deprives him of the plants by means of the cattle who leans toward the north-east; he should cut that [post] which leans toward the sacrificial essence (*medha*), for he who leans toward the sacrificial essence is indeed the sacrificial essence itself; thus he cuts that which leans toward the sacrificial essence. With the words, "Do not scratch the sky! Do not harm the mid-air! Be united with the earth!"—the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is indeed a thunderbolt; [he says this] for the non-injury of these worlds. He fixes it leaning toward the north and the east; this is indeed the world of the gods; verily, he causes it to lean toward the world of the gods.

"O Lord of the Forest, grow with a hundred branches," he says as he offers an oblation upon the stump; verily, he bestows abundance upon the lords of the forest, and therefore they grow more abundantly from that stump. "May we grow with a thousand branches," he says; verily, he invokes this very blessing. "Thee, whom this sharpened axe has brought forward for great good fortune"—for he who is brought forward for the sacrifice is indeed brought forward for great good fortune. He should cut off the branch of one whom he hates; for he who is without a womb is indeed without a foundation.

If he were to cut it at its base, he would make it rootless and without a foundation; therefore, he should cut it where its own sound arises, for that which has its own sound is possessed of a root and a foundation. He thus makes the sacrificer possessed of a root and a foundation. He should cut it at the height of the ankle, for the ankle is a joint, and it is commensurate with a joint of the sacrifice. He should cut it at the height of the knee, for the knee is a joint, and it is commensurate with a joint of the sacrifice. He should cut it at a point where the axle does not touch [the ground], for that is commensurate with a joint of the sacrifice, so that there may be no obstruction to the cattle.

It should be felled to the measure of an animal; it should be ten cubits long, for there are ten vital breaths in an animal and the self is the eleventh. It has eight joints and two sections, and the self is the eleventh; thus he fells it to the measure of an animal. It should be felled to the measure of a *stoma*; it should be nine cubits long, for it is commensurate with the *trivṛt* by its brilliance. It should be felled to the measure of fifteen cubits, for the thunderbolt is commensurate with the fifteenfold [stoma]; it is commensurate with the thunderbolt. It should be felled to the measure of seventeen cubits, for it is commensurate with the seventeenfold [stoma]; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, and it is commensurate with Prajāpati.

It should be measured at twenty-one cubits; it is commensurate with that sun, for the sun is the twenty-first, and it is commensurate with that sun. It should be measured at twenty-seven cubits; it is commensurate with the twenty-seven [nakṣatras]. These worlds are twenty-nine; it is commensurate with these worlds. It should be measured at thirty-three cubits; it is commensurate with the thirty-three [deities]. It should be measured according to the deities; it should be measured according to the meters: five cubits, commensurate with the *paṅkti* meter; six cubits, commensurate with the *aticchandas* meter.

It is equal to seven cubits for the Śakvarī; it is equal to eight cubits for the Gāyatrī; it is equal to nine cubits for the Bṛhatī; it is equal to ten cubits for the Virāj; it is equal to eleven cubits for the Triṣṭubh; it is equal to twelve cubits for the Jagatī; it is equal to thirteen cubits for the Sādhyas; it is large and unmeasured, being to be sought after. By means of the sacrificial post, the gods went to the heavenly world for the attainment of the heavenly world. Whosoever may be taller than a man, one should cut that [wood]; this indeed is—

The measure of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is exactly as much as the post itself; he cuts it accordingly. It has a top-ring (*caṣāla*); for by means of the top-ring, the deities went to the heavenly world. It is for the attainment of the heavenly world. Indra indeed hurled his bolt at Vṛtra; that part of it which was grasped shattered, and they fashioned the top-ring from it. That there is a top-ring is for the sake of firmness, so that it may be firmly grasped and not loose. It should be of such a size as that part which was grasped; one should not make it exceed the post. If one were to exceed it, he would make it overgrown.

One should extend it as far as the topmost finger-joint; this is measured by the sacrificial person (yajñapuruṣa) so that there may be no obstruction for the animals. Whatever is left over from the sacrifice is left over for the Sādhyas among the gods; thus it is left over from the sacrifice. If it is left over from the sacrificial post (yūpa), one thereby gratifies the Sādhyas among the gods. One should make the top-ring (caṣāla) from another tree than that of which the post is made, if he should desire of someone: "May I produce a rival for him. For other trees are indeed his rivals.
He causes his rival to ascend to this world; he deprives him of the world. ||4||

With the words, "For the earth thee! For the atmosphere thee! For the sky thee! he sprinkles the sacrificial post; thus he sprinkles it for these very worlds. Indeed, the Udumbara post is erected for this world, while the sacrificial post is for that [world]; therefore, he sprinkles the sacrificial post from here toward the beyond, and the Udumbara post from there toward this side, for the separation of these two worlds. With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes up the spade; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it up with the deities. With the words, "Here I cut off the neck of the Rakṣas,"—the Rakṣas is indeed the enemy.

He cuts off the very necks of his rival. With the words, "May the worlds, the seats of the fathers, be purified," he purifies it; thus he pacifies whatever cruelty they commit while digging it. He pours water mixed with barley over it. Barley is food, and the sacrificial post is brilliance; verily, he places brilliance in food. Barley is food, and the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt; verily, he places the thunderbolt in food.

With the words, "I strew thee for the world, the seat of the fathers," he lays down the grass; for if they were to erect this [post] without a base (barhis), it would become like a pit. On the northern half of this [altar], the plants are located; thus he erects it on the very northern half of this [altar]. With the words, "Thou art a non-pit, easy of access, the foremost leader of leaders," he throws down a chip of the sacrificial post; for this [chip] is smooth when planed and is not favorable to cattle; thus he erects it together with its skin. With the words, "O Heaven and Earth, be filled with ghee," he moistens both heaven and earth with ghee; therefore the plants, though unanointed, exude sap.

"May Savitṛ anoint you with honey," he says; honey is indeed the clarified butter of the gods; thus he makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. "Make the plants bear good fruit," he says as he fastens on the top-ring; he causes the plants to take fruit, and therefore these plants ripen even without being ploughed. He anoints the post at the bottom with clarified butter; clarified butter is indeed splendor; he thus endows the sacrificer, who stands at the base of the post, with splendor. He anoints it continuously to the very end, for the continuity of splendor and its non-interruption. [He should anoint] that of him whom he hates...

He should cut it; he thus deprives it of its splendor by means of that very splendor. He anoints it on all sides; he thus endows it with splendor from every side. "With the top you have touched the sky, with the middle you have filled the atmosphere, with the base you have made firm the earth"—the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*), for the support of these worlds. With the verse, "These are your dwellings," he carries it away; the post belongs to Viṣṇu, so he carries it away by means of its own deity. With the verse, "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu," he prepares it; the post belongs to Viṣṇu, so he prepares it by means of its own deity.

He prepares the fire with a deity; he should place the post facing the fire. Agni is brilliance, and the sacrificer is the post facing the fire; thus, by means of brilliance itself, he makes the sacrificer prosper. If he should hate someone, he should incline it toward that person in this way or that; by means of brilliance itself, he deprives him of his power. With the words, "Thee, winner of the priesthood, winner of the nobility," he invokes a blessing; with the words, "Make firm the priesthood, make firm the nobility," he makes the most excellent blessing firm for him. With the verse, "That highest step of Viṣṇu," he consecrates [the post] with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; for the sacrificial post belongs to Viṣṇu, and thus he consecrates it with its own deity. 5.

One should make half of the sacrificial post-hole within the altar and half outside the altar, for the sake of securing both the measured and the unmeasured.
