One should not make it visible above ground; if one were to make it visible above ground, it would become a mere pit. One should not release it without having girt it with a cord; if one were to release it without having girt it, the sacrificer would be subject to hunger and the Adhvaryu would be liable to nakedness. The cord is indeed strength (*ūrj*); he winds it around at the middle, and thus bestows strength in the very center—both upon the sacrificer and upon his offspring. Therefore, offspring are centered in the middle.

"Strength"—it strengthens the girdle. If he should hate someone, he should measure it for him; strength indeed is the girdle, and by means of strength he deprives him of his strength. He should draw it upward for one whom he hates; downward for one whom he hates; strength indeed is that [downward] girdle, and by means of strength he deprives him of his strength. If he should desire, "May it rain," he should wrap it high up and far away; for when it rains, it rains from the waters and from the plants, and the girdle is the plants; thus he brings the plants closer to the rain, and it rains quickly. If he should desire, "May it not... [he should wrap it low down and far away].

"He shall rain"—for it is indeed from the waters and the plants that he rains when it rains; by [using] plants for the girth-rope, he places the plants further away from the rain, so that it rains for a long time. "Thou art the encompasser; may the divine subjects encompass thee!"—the plants are indeed these divine subjects, and the plants are the girth-ropes; the sacrificial post is the sacrificer. Thus he makes the offspring face toward the sacrificer. "This man around with riches"—riches are indeed cattle; verily, he causes him to prosper with cattle. Of the atmosphere...

He pushes the *svaru* down with the formula, "Along with the marshy lands," for it now has the intermediate space as its deity; thus he pushes it away by its own deity, being above this world and below that one. It is below the ancestors and above humans; the girdle is at the level of the plants; above the girdle belongs to all the gods; Indra’s cupola is above the girdle; and what exceeds it belongs to the Sādhyas. Indeed, in these worlds—among the ancestors, humans, and gods—the sacrificial post belongs to all the deities; thus he [establishes] it with all [the deities].

He causes the deities to prosper. He should make the sacrificial post inclined toward the fire from its midpoint and sloping outward from the top. By making it inclined toward the fire from its midpoint, he creates a world for the sacrificer; by making it sloping outward from the top, he drives his rival away from the sacrifice.

By means of sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world. They desired, "May no one else recognize this world of ours. They hid themselves in the quarters; because they hid themselves in the quarters, that is the *yūpatva* (post-nature) of the sacrificial post. Having gone to that world, they became thirsty. They realized, "It is from giving back from there that we have come here. They gave this [sacrifice] back again, and by it they prospered. This indeed is the thread of the sacrifice, this is its highest step. Just as the warp is stretched from a peg, so from this [post] the sacrifice is stretched. Him, indeed, he used to...

They offer this very thing, having first extracted it from the ancient [sacrifice], when they offer the *svaru*—for the sake of its redemption. Thus redeemed, gratified, and made well-disposed, it stands by these worlds. With the words, "May your smoke go to heaven, your flame to the intermediate space, your ash to the earth, Svāhā! he causes it to go to these very worlds. ||6||

There were gods named Sādhyas who existed before [the present] gods; they had nothing of their own. Having churned the fire, they sat offering oblations into the fire. From that bond, cattle were born; therefore, all cattle are said to belong to Agni. In that one churning the fire and then immolates an animal, he immolates it as something already born; furthermore, he acts according to the ancient precedent. Regarding this, they say: "The fire should be churned after having immolated the animal. For Agni is all the deities; thus, by immolating the animal, he brings forth all the deities themselves.

All the pressings (savana) must be made to possess cattle and vigor by means of an animal victim. In that they proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing, thereby that [pressing] possesses cattle and vigor; in that they proceed with the sacrificial gifts at the midday pressing, thereby that [pressing] possesses cattle and vigor; and in that they proceed with the other part of the animal victim at the third pressing, thereby that [pressing] possesses cattle and vigor. All his pressings become possessed of cattle and vigor for one who knows thus.

This animal victim is indeed offered through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) from all directions. When they perform the *āprī* verses while it faces east, he thereby conquers the world of the gods. When they lead it northward after the *āprī* verses have been recited, he thereby conquers the world of men. When they carry it around to the south and cut portions from it, he thereby conquers the world of the fathers. When they carry away the collected remains toward the west, he thereby conquers that direction. When he offers while standing upright, he thereby conquers the heavenly world. By means of the animal victim, the gods [conquered] heaven.

While they move about the world, he shakes his body; the omentum is heaven, for when they proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing, it is for the attainment of the heavenly world. When they proceed with the other animal at the third pressing, it is for the redemption of the body. With one that is moist and many-leaved he should perform the upākaraṇa; plants indeed are the trees, and animals are plants; thus he causes him to prosper by means of animals. With one that is dry and leafless he should perform the upākaraṇa against whomsoever he may hate; plants indeed are the trees, and animals are plants.

Verily, he deprives him of cattle. One thunderbolt is terrible, the other is auspicious; that which is dry is terrible, that which is moist is auspicious. With that which is auspicious he performs the dedication (*upākaraṇa*). He dedicates with *barhis* grass; *barhis* is indeed cattle. Verily, by means of cattle he dedicates cattle for him. "Thou art a protector," [he says], for he indeed protects. "The divine subjects have approached the gods," [he says]; for these subjects are indeed the cattle. Verily, he dedicates cattle for him. "The carriers, the eager ones," [he says]; the priests are indeed the carriers and the eager ones. [He dedicates] to the priests.

In this way he dedicates them: "O Bṛhaspati, hold fast the treasures. Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; by means of the Brahman, creatures are produced; thus, by means of the Brahman, he causes these [creatures] to be born. "O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, delight in the treasure. Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of forms; he fashions forms for him. "O wealthy ones, rejoice! Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and cattle are the wealthy ones; by means of the Brahman, he bestows cattle upon him. "Thou art the birthplace of Agni," for this is indeed the birthplace of Agni. "Ye two are the testicles," for those that are without testicles do not [procreate].

"Creatures are born from procreation; you are Urvaśī, you are Āyu; you are Purūravas. Urvaśī is indeed the mother, Āyu is the embryo, and Purūravas is the father. Ghee is seed. When he anoints the two kindling woods with ghee, he places seed in the very union. "Be born after the Gāyatrī metre, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī"—for there are only so many metres, and by means of the metres seed placed is brought forth. By means of the metres, he causes the seed placed for him to be brought forth.

This [earth] turns toward the south; she is indeed the generative body of the Sun; verily, he is born after her. Now at this time, the two Agnis aim at the sacrificer; with the words, "Be of one mind for us," he makes them of one mind. With the words, "Do not harm the lord of the sacrifice, nor the sacrifice, O Jātavedas," he does so for his own safety. With the words, "Be auspicious to us today," he makes them auspicious. Indeed, the enclosing-sticks (paridhis) are placed around for the sake of not falling prey to the Rakṣases; that which is above and above...

One should strike the Rakṣases at the *tīrtha*, or one strikes with the edge [of the blade] joined together; or rather, one offers with the *sruva* ladle using the *tīrtha* itself; thus, by means of these two joined together, one presents the sacrificial portion.

He recites the Sāvitrī; verily, impelled by Savitṛ, he brings him forth. He recites one addressed to a single deity; verily, he brings him forth in a single way. If he were to recite one addressed to two deities, he would produce for him a second rival. He recites one addressed to Heaven and Earth for the sake of encompassing all creatures that have been born. He should not recite one accompanied by smoke; for when Indra slew Vṛtra, from wherever there was failure in his act, from that smoke arose. Verily, he is born from failure; he becomes subject to failure for him if [he recites such].

If [the fire] should not be produced while being churned, he should recite the *rakṣoghnī* verses for the purpose of driving away the Rākṣasas. He should recite them without pausing; for the Rākṣasas seek to destroy the sacrifice at every pause. Thus, he creates a non-fordable obstacle for the Rākṣasas. He should recite a *gāyatrī* verse for a Brāhmaṇa, for the Brāhmaṇa is connected with the *gāyatrī*; a *triṣṭubh* verse for a Rājanya, for the Rājanya is connected with the *triṣṭubh*; a *jagatī* verse for a Vaiśya, for the Vaiśya is connected with the *jagatī*. In this way, it is according to their respective meters.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he takes up the rope; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it up with the deities. "I bind you, the divine oblation, with the noose of Ṛta"—for that which is fit for sacrifice and pure is indeed the noose of Ṛta; with that very thing he seizes it. "Pleasant to such-and-such [deity]," he says; thus he makes it pleasant to whichever deity he is sacrificing to. "Be bold toward the human," he says; for the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt and humans are cattle; with the thunderbolt he thus bestows cattle upon him. Indeed, this [post] is a bear.

When he, being skilled, binds the animal which is impure, he makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. Indeed, animals approach the sacrificial food from the front; the vital breaths are the deities in this [animal]. In that they appease it from the front toward the back, they appease its half for the sake of the deities. With the words, "For the waters, for the plants," it is indeed for the waters and the plants that the animal is seized; thus he sprinkles it for the waters and the plants. With the words, "May your mother permit you, may your father permit you," for both his father and mother [are present].

And [the waters] are the consenter; the waters indeed are all the deities, and the animal sacrifice belongs to all the deities. Verily, he causes it to prosper through all the deities. Much indeed of this [animal] becomes impure and unfit for sacrifice when it is the animal; the waters are pure and fit for sacrifice. In that he sprinkles it with water, he makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. With the words, "Thou art the drinker of the waters," he takes up water; he thereby makes those portions which are cut from the interior pure. With the words, "The oblation is well-cooked, rich in ghee for the gods," he sprinkles back upon the breast.

Those portions which are cut from below, he makes them pure for him; he sprinkles [them] all around; verily, he endows him entirely with sacrificial essence. The Āghāra-libation is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the animal is its body; when, having performed the Āghāra-libation, he anoints the animal, he restores the head of the sacrifice to the body. With the words, "May Vāyu unite with thy breath," he causes Vāyu to enter its breath. With the words, "May the limbs unite with the worshipful ones,"—the worshipful ones are indeed the deities—he causes the deities to enter its limbs.
With the words, "May the lord of the sacrifice unite with his blessing," he endows the sacrificer with his very blessing.

He chooses the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); for the priests are indeed the meters (*chandas*), so it is the meters that he chooses. By means of those chosen and joined together, his *vaṣaṭ*-calls are joined in front. He chooses the Hotṛ; thereby he chooses the Jagatī among the meters. He chooses the Agnīdh; thereby he chooses the Paṅkti among the meters. He chooses the two Adhvaryus; thereby he chooses the Atichandas among the meters. Between the Hotṛ and the two Adhvaryus, he chooses the Agnīdh; therefore Agni has entered into the midst of the plants. When he performs the final sacrifice, [he does so]...

Therefore, being churned from above, [the fire] is born. He chooses the Maitrāvaruṇa; he thereby chooses the Gāyatrī among the meters. He chooses the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; he thereby chooses the Triṣṭubh among the meters. He chooses the Potṛ; he thereby chooses the Uṣṇih among the meters. He chooses the Neṣṭṛ; he thereby chooses the Kakubh among the meters.

The *anuṣṭubh* metre is, as it were, like a goat from behind; and this *acchāvāka* priest's office is, as it were, like a goat from behind. Therefore, they merely summon the *acchāvāka*, but do not formally choose him. Now, these are the *āprī* verses. Having created living beings, Prajāpati felt as if he were emptied out. He saw these *āprīs* and with them he gratified himself. Prajāpati is the sacrifice, and the sacrificer is the self of the sacrifice. Since these [verses] are performed in the front part of the sacrifice, he gratifies the sacrificer right at the beginning. He performs the *prayāja* offerings; for the vital breaths are indeed...

The *prayāja* offerings are indeed the vital breaths; it is them that he offers as the *prayājas*. That is why they are called *prayājas*. One should perform them without interruption for him whom one desires, "May he attain a full lifespan. The *prayājas* are the vital breaths; thus, he restores the vital breaths to him without interruption, and he attains a full lifespan. The omentum (*vapā*) of the victim is its self, and the *āprī* verses are the self of the sacrificer. When the final *āprī* verse lies around the omentum, it is as if the self itself lies around the self. This is for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice. There are eleven *prayājas*, eleven *anuyājas*, and eleven *upayajas*; so many indeed [are the parts].

The deities belong to all the gods; the animal sacrifice belongs to all the deities; he thus satisfies him with all the deities. There are indeed thirty-three deities: thirty-three are Soma-drinkers and thirty-three are non-Soma-drinkers—the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, and Vaṣaṭkāra and Prajāpati; these are the Soma-drinkers. The fore-offerings (prayāja), the after-offerings (anuyāja), and the supplementary offerings (upayāja) are the non-Soma-drinkers; therefore they are performed outside the sacrifice. With the Soma he gratifies those gods who are Soma-drinkers, and with the animal sacrifice those who are non-Soma-drinkers; both of them, being gratified, are present at his sacrifice.

Śyāparṇa Sāyakāyana once said this regarding Aṣāḍha Kaiśina: "When they lead him away from the Soma, [he said], 'If indeed you will lead me away from the Soma, you will lead me along with both kinds of gods—those who drink Soma and those who do not drink Soma; your sacrifice will be abandoned by the gods, and furthermore, when they lead me away, they will come against you and overcome you. Having deliberated on this, [the others] said, 'We have no fear from them,' and they led him back toward the south. Consequently, the Kuntis came against the Pañcālas and conquered them."

Thus he leads him [the sacrificer] to Soma; he leads him together with both kinds of gods, those who drink Soma and those who do not drink Soma. His sacrifice becomes possessed of many gods and is not left behind. Moreover, when they lead him forward, they overcome him by approaching him from that direction.

The gods and the Asuras performed the sacrifice equally; whatever the gods did, the Asuras did that too. Then the gods perceived this *upāṃśu* [cup]; they perceived the sacrifice to be completed in it, and in it they completed the sacrifice. They pressed it eight times; thereby they attained the *gāyatrī* metre. Eleven times; thereby the *triṣṭubh*. Twelve times; thereby the *jagatī*. Three times they drew it out; thereby they attained the *savana*s (pressings). Those gods, as much as...

The sacrifice, having taken hold of him, rose up to offer it; the Asuras saw them and thought, "The gods are indeed offering. Raising their thunderbolt, they rushed at them. The gods shielded themselves from them with the *antaryāma* [offering] from these worlds. Then the gods prevailed, and the Asuras were defeated. For whomsoever, knowing thus, they offer the *upāṃśu* [libation], and whoever, knowing thus, offers it—he shields his rival from these very worlds; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. Now, Aruṇa Aupaveśi used to say:

"How could he who does not know how the sacrifice is to be completed in the *upāṃśu* [cup] perform the sacrifice? Thus, he presses eight times; thereby he obtains the *gāyatrī* metre. Eleven times; thereby the *triṣṭubh*. Twelve times; thereby the *jagatī*. Three times he suspends the pressing; thereby he obtains the *savana*s (pressings). In this way, the sacrifice is completed in the *upāṃśu* cup itself; having been thus completed, it proceeds unimpaired, uninjured, and unharmable. One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should press eight times at each stage; the *gāyatrī* has eight syllables; [thus he obtains] the *gāyatrī* itself.

He extends the opening of the sacrifice over the Gāyatrī, its own brilliance, its own womb, in the heavenly world; thus the opening of the sacrifice is extended, and he who knows this becomes preeminent. He should not say, "Thou art taken with a support," for the earth is indeed the support; by it he would obstruct the vital breaths. They do not spread out the filter, for the atmosphere is the filter; by means of the atmosphere he would enclose the vital breaths and would perish. Verily, that which blows here is the vital breath; this [formula] is a withdrawal from it when he says, "Thou art taken with a support. Therefore, he does not say, "Thou art taken with a support."

They do not spread out a purifier; therefore, this [wind] is unappropriated, and it blows thus and so at will. Therefore, we breathe at will. The *upāṃśu* cup has breath as its purifier; verily, by means of the vital breaths, he purifies it. Six shoots around—

Therefore he takes six breaths; he purifies them in pairs, therefore the breaths are in pairs. From the *upāṃśusavana* stone he draws the *upāṃśu* cup; the *upāṃśusavana* is indeed breath, and the *upāṃśu* is breath; from breath itself he thus draws breath. The *upāṃśusavana* stone is above, and the *aṃśu* cups are below; the *upāṃśusavana* is breath and the *aṃśu* cups are offspring; verily he places breath within offspring, and therefore breath is the highest. ||10||
May he be the best through his wisdom; may he increase you today with excellent grace. The mortal has offered a well-fashioned hymn of praise.
O Brahman, these prayers are being offered; you who are borne by the *brahman*, sit upon the sacred grass (*barhis*). O Hero, partake of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Come hither, O sons; may those who are the hearers of the word of immortality listen to our songs; may they be very gracious unto us.
Therefore, it is possible for us to obtain great earthly and celestial wealth; great indeed is your dominion among the gods.
O Bṛhaspati, be pleased with us; O Agni, come for the feast; O Indra, [bestow] winning wealth.
May auspicious intentions come to us from every side—intentions that are undeceived, unimpeded, and victorious.
May the gods be ever-present for our prosperity, guarding us day by day with tireless care.
Come to us, O Mitra and Varuna!
Having pushed aside the waters and the darknesses, you mount the radiant chariot of Cosmic Order,
O Bṛhaspati— terrible, the subduer of enemies, the slayer of Rākṣasas, the breaker of enclosures, and the finder of heaven.
The five dawns.
O friend, turn toward your friend; like a swift horse, descend from the chariot-wheel for us, O wondrous one, with speed!
O Agni, find favor with Varuṇa, with the Maruts, and with all the radiant ones. O blazing one, grant welfare to our offspring and progeny; O wondrous one, grant us welfare!

I honor Agni as the Hotṛ-priest, the bountiful, the Vasu, the Son of Strength, Jātavedas— the wise one like a sage, Jātavedas— who, a god of perfect sacrifice, with his upward-reaching form turned toward the gods,
desires the brilliance of the clarified butter, following the flame of the offered fat. 11.

Homage to the seer, homage to the overseer, homage to the observer; homage to the knower, homage to the informant, homage to the announcer; homage to the hearer, homage to the listener, homage to the sitter; homage to the non-sitter, homage to the born, homage to the one yet to be born; homage to the being, homage to the future; homage to the eye, homage to the ear, homage to the mind, homage to speech; homage to Brahman, homage to the weary, homage to austerity, homage! 12.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section, named Dhiṣṇya, in the Madhyamikā recension of the Caraka branch of the Śrī Yajurveda Kāṭhaka. 26.
Now follows the twenty-seventh section: *Vācaspati*.

"Flow for Vācaspati"—by saying this, he means "flow for the lordship over speech. Therefore, by means of this [verse], we speak according to our desire and we utter it forth. Prajāpati was this [universe] alone; speech was his second. He united with her as a couple; she conceived a fetus and then departed from him. She created these creatures, and she entered back into Prajāpati himself. "Flow for Vācaspati"—by this very couple, one is propagated with offspring and cattle. "Flow for Vācaspati."

"Brahman indeed is the Lord of Speech; by means of the Brahman he purifies him. "By the two arms of the bull, purified by the hands"—Indra is indeed the bull; his hands are the two arms; by means of those very two he purifies him.

With the words, "Thou art the god of gods, the purifier," he assigns it to the deities. With the words, "May our foods be honey-sweet; they purify Soma with Soma; thou art the portion of those [gods]," he assigns it to the deities. With the words, "Make our foods honey-sweet," the foods indeed belong to the gods; thus he makes it sweet for the gods. With the words, "Thou art well-prepared," he makes the breath itself well-prepared. With the words, "Go through the wide atmosphere," for at this time it has the atmosphere as its deity. With the words, "For all the powers (*indriya*)," he [places it] among the gods.

He places vital breath among men with the words, "May the mind hold you fast," for by the mind indeed is the vital breath held. With "Svāhā! To thee, O Subhū, Sūrya!"—Subhū is indeed Soma—he satisfies those dear bodies of the gods in yonder sun; furthermore, by means of the *svāhā*-utterance, he mixes the oblations within him.

He offers the *sarvahuta* (the all-oblation); therefore the breath (*prāṇa*) moves straight forward. Standing upright, he offers; the sacrifice is measured by the person, for the person is continuous with the out-breathing and in-breathing (*prāṇāpāna*). To prevent the confusion of the out-breathing and in-breathing, the Adhvaryu does not fall prostrate—he who knows thus. He should offer the *upām̐śu* from the north and the *antaryāma* from the south. This sacrifice is indeed the chariot of the gods; these two, the *upām̐śu* and the *antaryāma*, are its reins. He spreads the reins of the divine chariot in front for the ordering of the year and for the sake of heaven.

For the sake of the world’s discernment, those two reins of the human chariot are drawn out; they should be offered straight so that the vital breaths do not become intermingled. One should wipe upwards if he should desire, "May it not rain," for he thereby confines the rain there above. One should wipe downwards if he should desire, "May it rain," for whatever other oblation rises upward causes the rain to fall from there; by means of the Soma-oblation alone, he pours down the rain from heaven.

With the words, "Thee for the gods who drink the rays of light," he wipes it on the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*). The gods who drink the rays of light are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇas*); verily, he gratifies them. Moreover, this is the Soma-draught of the enclosing-sticks; he wipes it on the inside, therefore the vital breaths are on the inside. Indeed, he cuts the sacrifice asunder if he brings it to completion before the pressing. When he pours out the unpressed stalks (*aṃśus*), it is for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice. He pours out the animals (the stalks), therefore there are six vital breaths in pairs; therefore the vital breaths [are six].

The vital breaths (prāṇas), though moist, remain unjoined; therefore, the vital breaths, being moist, remain unjoined. He who knows the Soma-drinking of Soma is never severed from the Soma-drinking, nor is his progeny [severed]. With the formula, "O Soma, that which is yours, the invincible, the watchful by name—to that Soma, for Soma, svāhā!"—this indeed is the Soma-drinking of Soma. Verily, he thus satisfies Soma with Soma; he who knows this is never severed from the Soma-drinking, nor is his progeny [severed], even if he should practice sorcery.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee"—with these words he should take [the Soma]. "In the exhilaration of the intoxicating, joy-bestowing [Soma], let there be falsehood; then I shall offer thee"—thus he makes it false. Soma indeed belongs to all the gods; at this time, all the deities hope for him, thinking, "He will offer to me! He will offer to me! The deities themselves, desiring the oblation, carry him up until the end of the night. If he recites the Yajus formula, he reaches the very end of his vital breath.

Verily, he cuts him off from the gods; he performs the rite with the *upāṃśu* [whispered] cup; the *upāṃśu* is indeed breath; verily, by means of breath he strikes at his breath; swiftly does he perish.

The gods, indeed, could not find a vessel for the pressed Soma with which they might draw it out, saying, "By what means shall we draw this? They saw this very earth as the vessel of the gods; by means of it, they drew it out. This earth, truly, is the vessel of the gods; they make the vessels from her clay, and the cups for Vāyu from her. He who knows thus attains a more excellent vessel. One should examine the Brāhmaṇa with the vessel; that is the vow: "Thou art taken with a support. The earth, indeed, is the support. Whatever of it spills here, it is restrained by this [earth]. His Soma does not spill, he who knows thus.

"Thou art taken with a support," [he says], for from that point the Soma juices become "taken with a support. They spread out the filter, for from that point the Soma juices become purified by the filter. Svarbhānu, the Asura, pierced the sun with darkness; he did not shine. Therefore, the gods dispelled the darkness. That which they first dispelled became the black [cow]; that which they secondly dispelled became the pale-red [cow]; that which they thirdly dispelled became the white-spotted [cow].

Therefore, they purify it; he purifies it by means of the very body of the sun. With the words, "Restrain him, O Maghavan; protect the Soma," he places his rival between these very worlds. With the words, "Make our nourishments honey-sweet," he makes it honey-sweet for the gods, for nourishment is indeed the gods. With the words, "Thou art well-prepared," he makes the out-breathing itself well-prepared. With the words, "Pervade the wide atmosphere," he does so because it now has the atmosphere as its deity. With the words, "For all powers," he [places it] among both gods and men.

He offers the downward breath (apāna) with the formula, "May Tvaṣṭṛ hold thee with the mind," for the downward breath is indeed held by the mind; "Svāhā! To thee, O auspicious one, to Sūrya!"—the auspicious one is indeed Soma; he thus gratifies those dear bodies of the gods which are in yonder sun; moreover, by means of the *svāhā*-utterance, he mixes the oblations within him.

He should set down the Antaryāma vessel. Soma is indeed vigor, and the Antaryāma is the intermediate space; thus he places vigor in the intermediate space and bestows it upon the cattle. Cattle are born after the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups, while other creatures are born after the other vessels. He offers them while they are still unseated; therefore, cattle are unseated [not tied up], yet they are born day by day. Therefore, cattle that are born on the same day stand firm within a year. "For out-breathing," he says, and sets down the Upāṃśu vessel; "for through-breathing," [he says of the Antaryāma].

With "For thee," [he takes] the Upāṃśusavana stone; with "For out-breathing (apāna) thee," the Antaryāma vessel. By means of the diffused breath (vyāna), these two, the out-breathing and the in-breathing, are held apart—one moving forward and the other backward—so that this one does not ascend upward, nor does the other descend downward. He places the diffused breath in the middle for the sake of supporting the out-breathing and the in-breathing.

The horn is the dust, the *antaryāma* cup is the semen, and the *soma*-draught is the offspring. Indeed, Rajana Kauṇeya used to think that when one sucks the horn, he is sucking these two cups. Since these two are performed at the eastern part of the sacrifice, he thereby places a pair at the mouth of the sacrifice for the sake of procreation. Therefore they say, "Offspring are born after the pattern of out-breathing and in-breathing (*prāṇa* and *apāna*). For the sacrifice is commensurate with man, and man is pervaded by out-breathing and in-breathing; thus, when these two are set down in the morning...

When [the sacrifice] has ceased after the third pressing, he continues the sacrifice by means of the out-breath and the in-breath; therefore, from a man who has fallen asleep, the out-breath and in-breath do not depart, for they are joined again at the third pressing. Therefore, having slept, one awakens; and for this reason, the two breaths move downward.

The *upāṃśu* cup is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the *antaryāma* cup is the in-breath (*apāna*), and the *aindravāyava* cup is speech. Since the *aindravāyava* is drawn after the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma*, one places speech above the out-breath and the in-breath; therefore, a person speaks after having breathed out and breathed in. The gods were indeed unable to lift up the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). At that time, Vāyu was at the third pressing. The gods carried him forward. Vāyu is the breath, and the sacrifice belongs to Indra. Since the *aindravāyava* is drawn at the morning pressing, one [performs] the sacrifice by means of the breath itself.

Having taken hold of it, they lift it up from the front. This [cup] was formerly Vāyu’s; that speech, once created, did not turn away [from him]. It simply made a sound. Indra said, "Let this be taken for me as well; I shall cause this speech to turn away [from him]. Then they drew this cup for Indra and Vāyu. Thus, this speech speaks, having been turned away by means of the organ of speech. This Soma is drawn for the turning away of speech. He who knows thus speaks in a way that is turned away from the wicked. Of the creatures that were created, those two [Vāyu and Indra] became divided; they did not [unite].

Being unable to breathe out after having breathed in, or to breathe in after having breathed out, Indra said: "Let me also be included here; I shall maintain these two, the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (apāna). Thereupon they drew this cup for Indra and Vāyu. [The Adhvaryu says: "Recite for Vāyu, for Indra and Vāyu! He places Indra in the middle and Vāyu on both sides, for the sake of separating the out-breath and the in-breath. The diffused breath (vyāna) is indeed power; by the diffused breath these two, the out-breath and the in-breath, are held apart. Thus, moving forward and backward, they do not perish; neither does this one go upward, nor does the other go downward.

It passes on; he places the *vyāna* breath in the middle for the support of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. He holds [the breath] three times; therefore speech speaks three times: softly, loudly, and then very loudly. The gods indeed said to Vāyu, "With you as our mouth, let us slay Vṛtra. He replied, "Let me choose a boon: let the cups be drawn with me at their head. Therefore the cups are drawn with Vāyu at their head, for that was the boon he chose. Indra then said, "Let them also be drawn for me here; then we shall overcome him. Thus...

They drew this cup for Indra and Vāyu; from that they slew Vṛtra. This very Soma, the slayer of Vṛtra, is drawn for the sake of victory. Soma indeed was Vṛtra; when he was slain, he became putrid. Those gods said to Vāyu, "Carry this away for us. He said, "Let me choose a boon: let the vessels be called after my own deity. He carried it away; therefore it drove away the stench. For this reason, when an animal has died, one should not smell [the Soma] from it, for it is the stench of King Soma. He who knows thus is not afflicted by consumption (*rājayakṣma*).
Therefore they pour out the *śukra*; therefore also a third cup belongs to Vāyu. Now those [vessels] are called *vāyavya*, for they are indeed chosen by him.

Formerly, they used to draw these two Soma-libations separately for Mitra and for Varuṇa. Consequently, those creatures, being unappeased and undivided, wandered about killing one another. Those gods said, "Let us draw this one together; let us appease Varuṇa with Mitra, and Mitra with Varuṇa. Thereupon, they drew it together, and by means of Mitra alone they appeased Varuṇa, and by means of Varuṇa they appeased Mitra. These creatures are thus appeased by Mitra and held apart by Varuṇa. Since the Maitrāvaruṇa cup is drawn, it is for the sake of proper arrangement and for the sake of separation. The gods, indeed...

They said to Mitra, "Let us slay Vṛtra. He replied, "No; I am Mitra; I do not strike. They said, "We shall surely slay him. He said, "I shall choose a boon: let me mix my Soma with milk. Therefore, they mix the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk, for that was the boon he chose. From that time on, they slay the Vaiśya with the Rājanya as the overseer. Because he, being Mitra, committed an untruth, Varuṇa seized him. The cattle departed from him. That Mitra then took refuge with Varuṇa himself, and he said:

"Let this Soma be drawn together with him; then I shall release you from that," he said. Therefore, they drew this [cup] together with him, and by that he released him from Varuṇa. Because the Maitrāvaruṇa cup is drawn, it is for the sake of freedom from Varuṇa. Milk is indeed cattle, for milk belongs to cattle. In that he mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk, he endows it with cattle. "This is not Soma," they say, "these are plants; milk alone is Soma. In that he mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk, he makes it Soma; and furthermore—

Whatever they strike at him while pressing [the Soma], whatever they do that is cruel, he pacifies that. He mixes it with boiled milk; for what is boiled belongs to Mitra, and the fresh milk (*pratidhuk*) belongs to Varuṇa; thus he endows these two with their own respective portions. The Brāhmaṇa belongs to Mitra and the Rājanya to Varuṇa; because this cup for Mitra and Varuṇa is drawn, therefore the Kṣatriya has a Brāhmaṇa as his domestic priest. Indeed, the head of the sacrifice was cut off; at that time, the Aśvins, who were not drinkers of Soma, were the physicians of the gods. The gods said to them, "You two are indeed physicians."

"Stay here; you two shall put on this head of the sacrifice," they said. They replied, "Let us choose a boon: let there be a draught of Soma for us among the gods, and let a cup be drawn for us. The gods, having purified them with the *bahis-pavamāna*, drew a cup for those two who had become pure and fit for sacrifice. Therefore, when the *bahis-pavamāna* has been chanted, the cup for the Aśvins is drawn. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should sit at the *bahis-pavamāna*, for it is a means of purification. Therefore, one whom he hates should be excluded from the *bahis-pavamāna*.

He wards him off from the *pavitra*. Those two, returning toward the gods, deposited that body of theirs which was healing in three parts: one third in Agni, one third in the Brāhmaṇa, and one third in the waters. If he should desire of someone who is ill, "May he live," he should announce it to a Brāhmaṇa at the end of the Agni-rite and then address the waters [with the formula]. For this much indeed is the remedy—whatever the remedy may be—that he provides for him; he lives and attains his full span of life; he does not die before his time. 4.

The cups for the dual deities (dvidevatya) are drawn with single vessels; therefore, the vital breaths (prāṇa) have a single name. They are offered with two vessels; therefore, the vital breaths exist in pairs. With the same sacrificial formula (*yajus*) by which he hands [the cup] over, with that he receives it back, for the continuity and the non-interruption of the vital breaths. He does not perform the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call (*anuvapaṭ*). If he were to perform the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call, he would bring the vital breaths to a final end and would die. Because he does not offer a subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāja*), the vital breaths do not come to a final end; they move both hither and thither. The cups for the dual deities are to be consumed first; the *iḍā* is to be invoked.

Thus they deliberate: "The *iḍā* alone should be invoked first, for the sake of the sacrifice’s priority. The dual-deity offerings are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), while the *iḍā* is cattle. If one were to act thus, he would exclude the vital breaths from the cattle and would perish. Therefore, the dual-deity offerings themselves must be consumed first; the vital breaths are internal, while the cattle are external. Having thus placed the vital breaths within himself, he invokes the cattle."

Those breaths that are in man are the cups for two deities (*dvidevatya*): speech and the breaths are the cup for Indra and Vāyu; sight and mind are the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa; hearing and the self are the cup for the Aśvins. Agni was the Hotṛ-priest; having uttered the *vaṣaṭ*, he fainted. When the *iḍā*-portion was placed in his mouth, the gods sought him with the cups for two deities. The cups for two deities are indeed the breaths; they thus gladdened him with the breaths. He responded, "The *iḍā* has been invoked. The cups for two deities are indeed the breaths; when one consumes the cups for two deities, [he gladdens] the breaths.

Verily, by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), he bestows [the breaths] upon himself; therefore, the cups for the two deities (*dvidevatya*) should indeed be consumed first, for they are the ones consumed first. The cup for the Aśvins is drawn as the tenth; for there are ten vital breaths. He offers that third [cup]; verily, he thus gathers the vital breaths into the head. Having carried it around on all sides, he consumes it; for the cup for the Aśvins is the ear, and therefore a person hears from every direction. Indeed, the *rakṣas* spirits cling to this vessel if it remains empty and unemptied at the sacrifice; [therefore, one should consume] the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) of the cup for Indra and Vāyu.

He places the *payasyā* (curd-mixture) in the vessel for Mitra-Varuṇa and the parched grains for the Aśvins, for the smiting away of the Rakṣases; therefore, the vital breaths are uninjured and not deficient. He sets them down beneath the southern *havirdhāna* cart; for that which is possessed of Agni is indeed powerful. He sets them down in that which is possessed of Agni and is powerful. The sacrifice is commensurate with man, and man is pervaded by the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and in-breath (*apāna*). Since these [vessels], once set down in the morning, remain until the third pressing, he thus maintains the continuity of the sacrifice through the out-breath and in-breath, and with one [verse]...

He releases it with these ten [verses]. If he were to release it earlier, he would cut off the vital breaths; if later, he would cause the vital breaths to be redundant, and [the sacrificer] would die. Vāyu is indeed the vital breath, and the two-deity cups are the vital breaths; thus, by means of the vital breath itself, he releases the vital breaths. Much that pertains to Vāyu is recited at the morning pressing, but only one [verse] at the third pressing; therefore, there are many upward-moving vital breaths and only one downward-moving one. If he should desire, "May they obstruct him who has attained his goal, or may he who is obstructed attain his goal," [he should recite]: "Here I [obstruct] so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, the grandson of such-a-one..."

With the words, "Enter! I lift up," he should lift up the Adhvaryu’s cup; with the words, "Here I place so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage, upon such-and-such people," he should place the Pratiprasthātṛ’s cup over it. For the Adhvaryu is superior, while the one who is excluded is inferior; indeed, one who is already excluded excludes another, and thus he causes the excluded one to be further excluded. They both become excluded immediately. He should transpose the cups if he should desire, "May there be a reversal of fortune. He should set down the Pratiprasthātṛ’s cups in the place of the Adhvaryu’s cups.

He should set down the Adhvaryu’s vessels in the place of the Pratiprasthātṛ’s vessels; for the Adhvaryu is superior and the Pratiprasthātṛ is inferior. Thus he sets down the superior in the place of the inferior, and makes the inferior worse than the inferior. Indeed, this Viṣūjana Saurāki discovered that which makes one worse than the inferior. ||5||

If he should desire, "May I place the sacrificer's rival, the non-sacrificer, before him," the Pratiprasthātṛ should take [the offering] first and he should pour it out first. For the sacrificer is indeed superior, and the non-sacrificing rival is inferior; thus he places the rival before him. Standing in the place of the Adhvaryu, he offers; for the Adhvaryu is superior and the Pratiprasthātṛ is inferior. He thus causes the rival to ascend to the sacrificer's place and deprives him of his place.

The Adhvaryu should not cause the announcement (*āśrāvayet*) while leading [the victim]; he would be without a firm foundation. He should not cause the announcement without having touched the vessel; for that which is first offered is indeed the Adhvaryu’s own self. He should offer the subsequent oblations at the same place where he offers the first oblation. For wherever one offers the first oblation, there the deities gather around. If he were to offer elsewhere, he would cause discord among the deities; thus, he directly bestows their allotted portion upon the gods.

Formerly, these two fires—the Āhavanīya and the animal-sacrifice fire—were separate. Therefore, in former times, Rudra was not a slayer of animals; for "animals" (paśavaḥ) indeed mean animals, and "aṃśavaḥ" means animals, while Agni is Rudra. When he mixes the two oblations, he hands over the animals to Rudra, and he becomes devoid of animals. Therefore, nowadays Rudra is a slayer of animals. One should offer the butter-oblations in the middle of the fire, and the animal-oblations on both sides of the Soma-oblations. Thus, one wards off Rudra with the animals; there, Rudra does not become a slayer of animals, provided that the Adhvaryu is one who knows thus.

"May we connect life; may we connect breath"—thus they connect the vital breaths themselves. Therefore, the vital breaths come together in pairs. "Heaven and earth"—thus they cause these very worlds to prosper. "Cast out are Śaṇḍa and Marka along with him whom we hate. For as great as the sacrifice is, so great are the Śukra and Manthin cups; as great as this earth is, so great is the high altar (uttaravedi). Śaṇḍa and Marka are untruth; the enemy is untruth. Thus, by means of this [formula], he casts out the enemy from both the sacrifice and the earth.

"You are the support of the divided semen; you are the support of the churned [mixture]," they say as they offer oblations into the kindled fire. Indeed, Agni was afraid of the overflowing of the oblation; therefore, the two *chalakau* sticks are thrown in to prevent the overflowing of the oblation.

The *śukra* and *manthin* cups are indeed the two eyes of the sacrifice; when the two stalks are thrown in, they place a barrier between the two eyes to prevent them from being scorched. Therefore, one says, "Offer the pressed [juice] to that Indra! Offer the pressed [juice] to that Sūrya! This is for the sake of distinguishing between the two eyes. Thus, although the eye is one and the same, it is divided into two; by offering both as entirely consumed (*sarvahuti*), they bestow the complete faculty of sight upon all creatures. He who knows the pairing of the vessels, the cups, and the *soma* juices, is procreated from that very union. The other cups [are drawn] with jars.

They draw other cups with verses addressed to Vāyu; thus they form pairs among those vessels. They mix some cups with milk, but not others; thus they form pairs among those cups. Some Soma draughts are accompanied by blessings, while others are not; thus they form pairs among the Somas. From that very union, one is procreated.

The gods and the Asuras were arrayed for battle. Bṛhaspati was the domestic priest of the gods, and Śaṇḍa and Marka were those of the Asuras. They could not prevail. Indra perceived: "Both sides are indeed possessed of the *brahman*; that is why we do not conquer. He invited them; they said, "Let us choose a boon: let there be a draught of Soma for us among the gods, and let two cups be drawn for us. To them Indra gave these two, the Śukra and the Manthin, which were his own; they approached that as their portion.

Therefore, a kingdom without a domestic priest (purohita) is liable to ruin; for that reason, one should speak untruth to an enemy. He reflected: "If I offer these [oblations] into these two Asura-Brahmans, then the Asuras will prevail along with them; but if I do not offer them, they will still prevail along with them. Taking them up, he drove them away, saying: "Śaṇḍa and Marka, together with him whom we hate, are driven away! Thereupon the gods prevailed and the Asuras were defeated. For whomsoever, knowing this, they offer the Śukra and Manthin [libations], and for whomsoever two [priests] knowing this offer them, [he prevails].

It serves for the removal of the rival; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. Prajāpati’s eye swelled; its pupil fell away and entered the *vikaṅkata* tree; it took hold there. It then entered barley; it took hold there. The cup for the *manthin* draught is made of *vikaṅkata*; he mixes it with groats. Thus he gathers the very eye of Prajāpati. The *śukra* draught has the sacrificer as its deity, while the *manthin* draught has the rival as its deity; he mixes the *śukra* with gold.

Gold is indeed brilliance; by means of brilliance he thus endows the sacrificer. Therefore, one of the two eyes is more brilliant than the other, and therefore the day is of a single form. He mixes the *manthin* cup with groats; verily, he thus removes the brilliance of his rival. Therefore, the night is of many forms. He should mix the other cups without crushing them; if he were to crush them, his offspring would suffer from eye disease, and the sacrificer would become blind. These two, the *śukra* and the *manthin*, are indeed the two eyes of Prajāpati, and the sacrifice is [his body].

When Prajāpati, having rushed forward facing eastward, offered oblations at the two openings of the Soma-pressings, he thereby placed the two eyes in the openings of the pressings; therefore, two of the pressings contain the *śukra* cup. The *śukra* is indeed this sun, and the *manthin* is the moon. Because they go forward facing eastward while covering [the cups], therefore people do not see these two as they move eastward. But because they offer while standing in front facing westward without covering [the cups], therefore people see them as they move westward.

By means of the eastern oblations, the gods drove away some Asuras; by means of the western ones, others. Standing facing westward, they offer the Śukra and Manthin cups, while the other oblations are offered facing eastward, for the repelling of the enemy. Indeed, these two do not deserve to depart from among men. "Thou art Tutha, the supporter of people; may the gods who drink the Śukra lead thee forward. "Thou art Tutha, the supporter of people; may the gods who drink the Manthin lead thee forward. Thus he leads them forward with their own deity. [May there be] offspring rich in heroes.

"Procreating, go around; procreating good offspring, go around"—thus they place a hero among the non-eating offspring and abundance among those that are eaten; therefore a hero is born from these, and therefore the others, though being eaten, do not perish.

From *śukra* (the bright cup) indeed the *atrī* progeny are born, and from *manthin* (the stirred cup) the *adya* (eaters) are born; Agni is the progenitor. When they run around Agni on opposite sides and offer [the oblations], they thus cause both kinds of progeny, the *atrīs* and the *adyas*, to be born. They should walk around the high altar (*uttaravedi*) as if panting; then his offspring are born with joints and well-formed. This high altar is indeed the nose of Prajāpati, and the *śukra* and *manthin* are his two eyes; Prajāpati is the sacrifice. When they run forward and offer [the oblations], the two eyes are placed right in front of the nose.

"Support this," for they stand on both sides of it and offer oblations; therefore the two eyes are on both sides of the nose. "Thou art unassailable," with these words they seize it; therefore the eye-socket is most deeply set.

The gods and the Asuras performed the sacrifice equally; whatever the gods did, the Asuras did that too. Those Asuras were more numerous, more excellent, while the gods were fewer, more wretched, and more like those who lag behind. Those gods saw this Āgrayaṇa cup; they drew it, and by means of it, they attained preeminence. Because they attained preeminence (*agram paryāyan*), that is the reason for the name of the Āgrayaṇa. [It should be offered] by one who is lagging behind.
Saramā found the breach in the mountain; she made the great, ancient path converge. The swift-footed one led the way for those who were to flow; knowing it well, she went first toward the roar.

With this *puroruc* verse, the *āgrayaṇa* cup is drawn; having cut down his rival, he proceeds to the summit. Speech indeed departed from the gods, seeking her share in the sacrifice. Those gods performed the sacrifice mentally for so long until they thought, "She is passing us by. Then she returned toward the *āgrayaṇa*. When one draws the *āgrayaṇa* and releases speech, he yokes speech itself once it has returned to the sacrifice. For the pursuit of the sacrifice is like that of a wild beast; the *āgrayaṇa* is the very self of the sacrifice. In that he restrains his speech, [he preserves the essence].

He indeed hastens toward the sacrifice when he releases his speech; having reached the sacrifice, he releases his speech. The Āgrayaṇa cup belongs to Prajāpati, and these officiating priests chosen for the rite are dedicated to Prajāpati. Three are engaged in the sacrifice: the Prastotṛ, the Udgātṛ, and the Pratihartṛ. When he utters the *hiṅ* sound, he chooses the Udgātṛs themselves; they, being chosen, become engaged in his sacrifice.

He draws two *dhārās* at the morning pressing, three at the midday pressing, and four at the third pressing; there are nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, and the *Āgrayaṇa* is the self of the sacrifice; he thus provides him with the very vital breaths. They indeed cut the sacrifice asunder when they conclude the pressings separately; the *Āgrayaṇa* is the self of the sacrifice; in that he draws the *Āgrayaṇa* at each pressing, he continues the sacrifice by means of its own self. [With the verse: "O gods, you eleven who are in heaven..."

By means of the thirty-three deities alone he continues the sacrifice. Prajāpati indeed is the Āgrayaṇa; when [the Soma] spills out, he thereby deposits seed; when he catches it, he procreates. He draws it with a vessel (sthālī); thus it remains unrecognizable as that with which one will offer. Therefore, one who kills an embryo is called a "slayer of the unformed" (bhrūṇahan), for the embryo is unformed. He draws it with a vessel and offers it with a cup for Vāyu. Therefore, a woman is without strength, and a man is without strength. They throw away the vessel, but not the cup for Vāyu; therefore, they cast out a woman once she has given birth.

If a cup should fail before the Āgrayaṇa, one should draw from the Āgrayaṇa; if the Āgrayaṇa should fail, one should draw from the houses. The Āgrayaṇa is indeed the father and the cups are the sons; when the son fails, he resorts to the father. This Soma is drawn for the sake of atonement. The exponents of the Veda say: "Why does the Gāyatrī, though its strength is not exhausted, carry all the pressings as it turns back? The Āgrayaṇa is indeed the calf of the Gāyatrī; when the Āgrayaṇa [is drawn] at the pressing...

He draws [the cup] at each pressing; therefore, the *gāyatrī*, being unwearied (*ayātayāmnī*), turns back toward all the pressings. Therefore, a cow, when being led away from her calf, turns back again. Having created the creatures, Prajāpati made them low (*abhihiṅkṛ*) unto himself. Prajāpati is the Āgrayaṇa; because he makes the lowing sound after drawing the Āgrayaṇa, therefore a cow lows unto her calf once it is born. ||9||

Indra indeed raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra. He said, "This strength is in me; I will give it to you, but do not strike me. He gave it to him. Indra perceived, "Truly, there is strength in him. He raised a second [thunderbolt] at him, and a third. He said, "This strength is in me; I will give it to you, but do not strike me. He gave it to him. Truly, he gave him the sacrifice; for the Ukthya is as much as the entire sacrifice.

As much as the Ukthya is for internal cohesion, so are the other cups drawn; he offered it three times, therefore they draw this one three times separately. Because, though being one, they draw it in many ways, therefore one man becomes the leader of many. The Ukthya is indeed the head of the sacrifice, the Ukthas are its limbs, and the Śukra and Manthin are its two eyes. Because these are the most frequently offered Soma-libations, therefore the eye prevails over all the limbs. Because the most numerous Soma-libations follow the Ukthya vessel, therefore one who is meritorious goes [alone].

Many follow [this path]. They indeed cut asunder the sacrifice when they conclude the pressings separately. The *ukthya* is the self of the sacrifice; in that he draws [the cup] separately at each pressing for the *ukthya*, by that very means he continues the sacrifice. With the words, "For Indra thee, accompanied by the *bṛhat*,"—for the sacrifice belongs to Indra—with the words, "For thee, for Viṣṇu,"—for the sacrifice is Viṣṇu—he thus continues the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice itself, Viṣṇu. Just as something yoked on both sides, or just as a burden-carrier [yoked] on both sides, so too are the *puroruks* and...

Now, this cup is without a *puroruk* formula; who is it that is drawn? The sacrifice is liable to be torn asunder when he draws the *ukthya*. By drawing it with the [preceding] cup still joined, he makes it firmly bound. The *ukthya* is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *ukthas* are its limbs. From behind, the sacrifice is directed forward, joined to the head by means of the *ukthyas*. When he pours down the *ukthya*, he thus joins the sacrifice, directed forward from behind, to the head by means of the *ukthas*. Therefore, from behind, a man is joined to his head from behind by means of sinews and covered with skin. Soma is indeed prosperity (*śrī*). If...

If the Adhvaryu should desire, "May I endow myself with glory," he should pour [the water] between the Āhavanīya fire and the Havirdhāna cart; for this is the world of the Adhvaryu, and thus the Adhvaryu endows himself with glory in his own world. If he should desire, "May I endow the sacrificer with glory," he should pour it between the Sadas and the Havirdhāna; for this is the world of the sacrificer, and thus he endows the sacrificer with glory in his own world. If he should desire, "May I endow the members of the assembly (sadasyāḥ) with glory," he should pour it while touching the Sadas; for this is...

He causes the members of the assembly to attain glory in their own world; for the *āgrayaṇa* is indeed the self of the sacrifice, and the *ukthya* is its limbs. When the *ukthya* is drawn following the *āgrayaṇa*, he restores the limbs to the very self of the sacrifice; therefore, the limbs are fixed within the self.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section, named Vācaspati, in the Madhyamikā recension of the Caraka branch of the glorious Yajurveda-Kāṭhaka. 27.

Now begins the twenty-eighth section: On the *dhruva* cup. The *dhruva* is indeed life (*āyus*). Life is taken as the highest; therefore, life is the highest among the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). It is taken ninth, for there are nine vital breaths. He places it alone in the northern *havirdhāna* cart; therefore, the vital breath is alone and possesses half of the vital breaths. Indeed, human beings are born after the *dhruva*; other creatures are born after the other cups. He places the *dhruva* on ground that has been strewn with sand, while he places the other cups on ground that has not been strewn; therefore, man stands firm by means of flesh, whereas animals stand firm by means of bone. The prince guards the *dhruva*.

The Rājanya is indeed the lord of the subjects; he is the firm life-force (*āyus*). He protects the life-force of the subjects, and furthermore, he protects the ruling power (*kṣatra*). If he should desire, "May those who have been driven out return, and may those who are driven out regain their place," he should lift up the *dhruva* [fire] with the formula: "Thee, the firm one, whose dwelling is firm, the most unstable among the unstable, the most unshakable among the unshakable, I lift up from such-and-such a people. For he who has been driven out is indeed the firm one, while he who is driven out [and remains there] is the unstable one. Thus, he drives out the one who has already been driven out and causes the one who is driven out to return. They both return immediately.

If one were to act in this manner, he would disturb the life-span of living beings; however, if he should pass a blade of grass over [the vessel] again and again with this mantra, by that very act he causes the obstructed [life-force] to depart, yet he does not disturb the life-span of living beings. The altar is indeed the field of the gods; as great as the altar is, so great is this earth. By means of the field of the gods, he excludes him from the field of men. He should take it full if he should desire, "May he attain a full lifespan"; verily, he takes a full lifespan for him, and he attains a full lifespan. He should take a small amount if he...

If he should desire, "May he attain a short life," he makes his life short indeed; he quickly perishes. He should take [the milk] from the upper half if he should desire of someone, "May he attain a long life"; verily, he causes him to attain a longer life.

In whatever manner he takes hold of his life-span, he takes up Vaiśvānara on both sides; therefore the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are on both sides of Vaiśvānara. With the words, "The head of heaven, the messenger of earth," he bestows life-span upon both gods and men. The sacrifice is commensurate with man and extended by man’s life-span; since this [cup] is drawn in the morning and remains until the third pressing, he thereby extends the sacrifice by means of the life-span. These two are indeed drawn in the morning, in the world of the Gāyatrī: the Āgrayaṇa and the Dhruva. They...

When he has lain down from the third pressing, he departs from the world of the Jagatī; therefore, the Gāyatrī, being unwearied, returns at the later pressing. This indeed is its allotted portion. The Gāyatrī is breath, and the Trayastriṃśa-stoma is life; because he lies down in the morning until the third pressing, therefore, as long as life is, so long is breath. Dhruva is life, and Agni is Rudra; he must not be offered alone, for he would bestow life upon the creatures, and they would become liable to die prematurely. He pours [the offering] into the Hotṛ’s cup; the Hotṛ belongs to the Viśvedevas, and these creatures belong to the Viśvedevas.

He bestows life-span upon the offspring themselves. For he makes this [sacrifice] unstable when he pours it out; indeed, following the instability of that [sacrifice], it does not prosper for the offspring. With the words, "May the divine hosts be firm; may men prosper; in heaven let there be heavenly things, in the atmosphere birds, on earth earthly things," he pours it out while making it stable (*dhruva*). Thus he makes the offspring firm in their proper place. He should pour it out when the hymn (*uktha*) has been invoked; by means of the praise itself, he continues the sequence into the recitation (*śastra*). If he were to pour it out when the hymn has been invoked, he would make the hymn redundant; if he were to do so when the recitation has been performed...

He should set aside the draught that is the middle *paridhānīyā*. He pours it down during that [verse]. These *ukthāmadāni* are indeed the limbs of the sacrifice, while the *ruvānaḥ* are the life-force (*āyus*). Half of a person’s self consists of the limbs, and half consists of the life-force. Having joined the two ends together, he places the life-force in the middle. "By what truth do the learned say that the waters, though rushing, are neither exhausted nor do they perish? [The answer is: "Because they await this very drinking of Soma (*somapītha*); for this [Dhruva] pushes them back."

Sitting facing westward, he pours [the water] out; thus he directs them toward the riverbank. He should not let it flow away prematurely. He should sit for the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. The Dhruva cup is indeed life-span; he would be letting his life-span flow away. The sacrifice is as large as the Agniṣṭoma; when he sits for the Agniṣṭoma, he enters into the very breath of this [sacrifice] and attains a full span of life. The Sadas is indeed the belly of the sacrifice; they run [to it] as if crawling out. Prajāpati is the sacrifice. When he sits for the Agniṣṭoma, he does not empty the belly of Prajāpati; he becomes free from hunger.

The gods, having slain the Asuras, were distressed by the obligation of vengeance; they became bewildered regarding the seasons and the year. The gods sought the proper arrangement of that [year] and established it by means of the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*). In that the seasonal cups are drawn, it is for the arrangement of the year and for the discernment of the heavenly world. They draw both together at the beginning, for these two approach together to arrange the year. Having arranged the year together, they are both released together, facing in both directions.

The two Ṛtu cups have openings on both sides, for the seasons indeed have two faces; for one who knows this, there is no single face of the seasons. They should not enter into one another; if they were to enter into one another, one season would be joined to another. Because they pass by one another, therefore they say, "The seasons have sniffed at each other like horses. These twelve are drawn; there are twelve months in a year, for the sake of the ordering of the year. The year is indeed the heavenly world; these Ṛtu cups are its steps and transitions. By means of them, he ascends to the height.

For the attainment of the heavenly world, there are six others and six others; for yonder sun is the season. Therefore, he moves northward for six months and southward for six. By means of the season, [he attains] six; for there are six seasons, and thus he finds firm support in the seasons themselves. By means of four seasons, [he attains] cattle, for cattle have four feet and cattle are born after the year; from the year itself, he causes cattle to be born for him. Twice by means of the season; for the sacrificer has two feet, and thus he finds support above among the cattle.

These seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*) are indeed Soma-drinkers, kinsmen of Indra’s Soma-drinkers; for he says, "Let him drink the Soma by means of the season (*ṛtu*)," and they do not offer to the season itself. These two vessels are their own, with which they offer them; therefore, a kinsman brings tribute with his own vessel, and they bring tribute to one who knows thus. They consume [the remains] separately to prevent exhaustion; therefore, it rains season after season. By that, the gods, having fashioned the year and discerned the heavenly world, departed.

This is the light of the sacrifice; they placed it at the end when the cup for Indra and Agni is drawn. Thus he places light at the very beginning of the sacrifice, for the ordering of the year and for the discernment of the heavenly world.

Therefore, for a year the light moves higher and higher; with the vessel of the seasons he draws the draught for Indra and Agni. Indra and Agni are the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the seasons are the common people (*viś*); verily, he establishes the nobility upon the common people. All the gods indeed have their share in the third pressing, yet they desired the morning pressing. Prajāpati saw that they were to be satisfied by this very draught; because the draught for the Viśve Devas is drawn at the morning pressing, he satisfies all the gods at the morning pressing. When they are satisfied and pleased, they [assist] him in the subsequent [pressings].

At the third pressing, they are poured out; he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup with the Śukra vessel. Yonder sun is indeed the Śukra, and these creatures belong to the All-gods (Vaiśvadeva). Therefore, all these creatures turn toward him, thinking, "Toward me! Toward me! || 2 ||

With the midday pressing, indeed, Indra slew Vṛtra through the Maruts and his heroic power. There is a *marutvatīya* chant, a *marutvatīya* hymn, and *marutvatīya* cups; thus he endows the sacrificer on all sides with heroic power and slays Vṛtra on all sides. The first *marutvatīya* is the preparation; the second is the departure; with the third, he releases the discharge. With the first *marutvatīya*, he raises the thunderbolt; with the second, he hurls it forward; with the third, he lays [Vṛtra] low.

If he should hate someone, he should take [the cup] for that person; the Maruts are indeed vigor—verily, by means of vigor he deprives him of his strength. When Indra was about to slay Vṛtra, he gave a gift to the gods as dakṣiṇā; it was by means of the Marutvatīya cups that he slew Vṛtra. Therefore, when the Marutvatīya has been recited, nothing should be given, for at that time Vṛtra has been slain and victory is won. He should not accept [a gift], for he causes settled cattle to depart, and he becomes without cattle. Having slain Vṛtra, Indra indeed became Mahendra.

He held other gods in contempt; he drew this cup as a special portion for Mahendra. Therefore, a king, having won a battle, performs the *nirāja* ceremony. Those gods said to him, "You have indeed spoken everything; let there be a share for us here too. He asked, "How might there be a share for you? [They replied,] "Let the *virāj* sacrifice this cup! The *virāj* is indeed the vessel of the gods; in that he sacrifices with the *virāj*, he satisfies the deities with the very vessel of the gods.

Therefore, when a king wins a battle, it is there that the Sūtas and Grāmaṇīs [sing]: by means of the Gāyatrī, the Trivṛt finds its abode; by the Triṣṭubh, the Pañcadaśa; by the Jagatī, the Ekaviṃśa. Now, this Virāj is indeed the abode of the Saptadaśa. When he sacrifices with the Virāj, he makes the Saptadaśa possess an abode. If he should hate someone, he should sacrifice for him with the Triṣṭubh. The Triṣṭubh is indeed vigor and strength; verily, by vigor and strength, he cuts him off from his abode. Being without an abode, he perishes. The gods, having slain the Asuras...

Being excluded from the *vairadeya* and other offerings, they entered into the middle of the sacrifice; they entered this very *ṛc*, namely the *virāj*. In that he sacrifices with the *virāj*, it is for the propitiation of the deities. When the Ādityas were going to the heavenly world, the Aṅgirases remained in this world together with the sacrifice. Those Aṅgirases said to the Ādityas, "To how many of you shall we carry the oblation? "To thirty-three," they replied. "Ten Vasus, with Indra as the eleventh; ten Rudras, with Indra as the eleventh; ten Ādityas, with Indra [as the eleventh]."

These deities are thirty-one; the *vaṣaṭ*-call consists of two syllables, and speech consists of one syllable. By this [speech] they are made fit for Indra. His deities attend to his oblation according to their respective shares, and his oblation goes to each deity as is appropriate. He who knows thus is chosen for the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*); for as many deities as there are, he causes them all to reach the oblation.

From the midday pressing, indeed, the gods went to the heavenly world; these are their stepping-stones and crossings, namely the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). In that one gives a sacrificial gift, having made a bridge, one goes to the heavenly world. As many breaths as one gives here, so many breaths are there in yonder world; therefore, much should be given. Therefore, they praise what has been given much here. He builds a bridge that is ever more extensive. At this time, indeed, the deities draw near most closely; therefore, at this time, this [sun] burns most fiercely.

As soon as he ascends to the heavenly world from that which is nearest, he offers with two verses addressed to Sūrya for the attainment of the heavenly world; by means of two [verses], he causes the sacrificer—who is himself two-footed—to step upon this very earth. When he offers at the Āgnīdhra altar with a verse addressed to Agni, he causes him to step into the intermediate space.

What he gives, that indeed causes him to go to the heavenly world; [with the words] "Go to the sky, go to heaven," it is for the attainment of the heavenly world. "Your form with my form, your vigor with my vigor"—clarified butter is indeed the form of cattle, and gold is their form; thus he approaches them with their own form and with vigor. "May Tutha, the all-knowing, distribute you"—Tutha the all-knowing is indeed Truth; thus he distributes them by means of the Brahman, which is Truth. "This gift of yours, O Agni, goes forth, distilling Soma"—these are addressed to Agni.

Indeed, those animals are given at the Soma sacrifice; "lead them by the path of Mitra," he says, and thus he leads them by the very path of Mitra. He leads them between the Āgnīdhra and the Sadas; for by this very path the gods went to the heavenly world, and he causes them to attain that same path.

The Rakṣases indeed conquered the sacrifice of the gods from the south; they drove them back again from the Āgnīdhra. When they lead the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā) from the Āgnīdhra toward the south, it is for the victory of the sacrifice and for the driving away of the Rakṣases. He offers at the Āgnīdhra with a verse addressed to Agni, for cattle belong to Agni; it is for the redemption of cattle. He should offer a second oblation with a verse addressed to Varuṇa if he intends to give a horse, a draft-ox, or a chariot, for horses belong to Varuṇa and trees belong to Varuṇa. Agni is all the deities; [this is] for the propitiation of the deities.

He gives a cushion; this is indeed the form of the meters; by its very form he wins the meters. He gives gold; verily, with golden light, he causes them to go to the heavenly world. With the words, "Given by us, full of sweetness, may it go to the gods," he causes them to go to the heavenly world itself.

"May he enter the giver"—therefore, one becomes destined for that world. "Go forth by the path of *ṛta*, O you whose sacrificial fee is a cow"—for he who is worthy of sacrifice and fit for the altar is indeed the path of *ṛta*; by that very path he leads them. "Today may I honor a Brāhmaṇa, one who has a father and a grandfather"—for he who is a learned scholar (*śrotriya*) and of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) is one who has a father and a grandfather; "may I find such a one," this is what he says. For he is a true giver of the sacrificial fee; that which he gives to a non-Brāhmaṇa spreads among the trees, while that which he gives to the Kaṇvas and Kaśyapas [spreads] among the sages.

With that [gift] which he gives to a Brāhmaṇa who is not learned in the Vedas, the mists spread; with that which he gives to one who is learned in the Vedas and descended from a lineage of seers (ārṣeya), the rays of light spread. By that [gift], he prospers in yonder world and it serves for his enjoyment again in this world. Therefore, he alone is to be sought after. "Behold the sky! Behold the atmosphere!"—with these words, he looks toward the Sadas.

These Brahmins are indeed Soma-drinkers; their eyes are full of splendor. These [gifts] are given as if they were hostile; they are capable of repelling him. He pays homage to them so that they do not repel him. Here he gives gold. Svarbhānu, the Asura, pierced the sun with darkness; Atri first found it again. In that he gives Atri-gold, it is for the attainment of the heavenly world. If he cannot find a descendant of Atri, he should give it to one who is of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) and well-versed in the *Saṃhitā*; by that very means he prospers. The Asuras, indeed...

They brought a sacrificial gift for the gods; they repelled it, saying, "This one has become unaffectionate. They brought another for them; they repelled that, saying, "Strength has come to this one. They brought yet another for them; they repelled that, saying, "She has run away. Regarding these, the Seer indeed recited: "They brought a sacrificial gift for the gods; they repelled it, saying, 'This one has become unaffectionate. They brought another for them; they repelled that, saying, 'Strength has come to this one. They brought yet another for them; they repelled that, saying, 'She has run away. This is what the Seer then proclaimed.
The dark drop descended into the Am̐śumatī river, fleeing with ten thousand [companions].
Indra, by his power, protected him as he blew; he, whose mind is manly, destroyed the female serpents.

Thus that female jackal, having come into being, entered the Asuras and consumed them from within. Therefore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) that has been turned back must not be accepted, nor should one drive it among the cattle; for it enters him as a female jackal and consumes him. ||4||

In that he gives a cow, by that he rescues his life-span; in that he gives a garment, by that he makes his life-span long; in that he gives a horse, he makes him shine like the sun; in that he gives a cart or a chariot, by that he rescues his limbs; in that he gives a sheep or a goat, by that he rescues his flesh; in that he gives boiled rice or a stirred drink, by that he rescues whatever is his innermost self; in that he gives a boon, by that he rescues his very self, for the self is the boon; and in that he gives to the Brahmin, he belongs to Bṛhaspati.

By what he gives to the Udgātṛ, he gratifies Bṛhaspati; for the Udgātṛ belongs to Prajāpati, and by that he gratifies Prajāpati himself. By what he gives to the Hotṛ, he gratifies the All-gods (Viśve Devāḥ); for the Hotṛ belongs to the Viśve Devāḥ, and by that all his deities become worshipped and gratified. By what he gives to the two Adhvaryus, he gratifies the Aśvins; for the two Adhvaryus are the Aśvins, and by that he gratifies the Aśvins themselves. By what he gives to the officiating priests (Ṛtviks), he gratifies the Hotrās; for the Ṛtviks are the Hotrās, and by that his Hotrās become worshipped and gratified.

That which he gives to the *sadasyas*, by that he ransoms the very Soma they drink. That which he gives to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), but not a priest (*anṛtvij*) and has come as a guest (*prasṛpta*), by that his knowledge which he possesses becomes desired and gratified for him. That which he gives to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, not learned in the Vedas, not a priest, and has come as a guest, by that his knowledge which he possesses becomes desired and gratified for him. That which he gives without desire, from that the nobility (*kṣatra*) eats the priesthood (*brahman*). That which he gives when asked, by that he [eats] his rival (*bhrātṛvya*).

That gift which he gives outside the sacrificial altar does not reach him; that gift which he gives to a kinsman who is not a priest nor has entered the ritual service, he deposits as evil upon himself. But that gift which he gives to the eldest or to one learned in the Vedas—that very faculty (indriya) by which the recipient becomes [prosperous], that becomes desired and gratified for him. ||5||

The Ādityas, having slain the Asuras, entered the gods while seeking refuge from their enmity; they entered the two-deity cups (*dvidevatya*), for these are the most numerous of the gods' companions. Therefore, the Āditya cup is drawn after the two-deity cups. Or rather, the Ādityas were born from the remnants; therefore, this Soma is drawn as a remnant. The Ādityas have the remnants as their portion; therefore, this Soma is drawn as a remnant. He draws it within an enclosure; Agni is Rudra, and the Āditya is cattle—this is for the protection of the cattle from Rudra.

The gods excluded themselves from the sacrifice; they agreed among themselves, saying, "This is your share in the mother," thus referring to the Ādityas. Having brought it as far as this point, they placed a barrier between themselves and the sacrifice. In that he draws the Āditya cup from the *pariśrita* vessel, he indeed places Rudra as a barrier between himself and the sacrifice.

The sun is indeed cattle; because this Soma is drawn in its greatest abundance, therefore cattle, though being eaten, do not perish.
