When there are many [cattle] within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), then he should draw it; thus he secures food for those very cattle. If his rival should be within the altar, then he should draw it; for the altar is the sacrificer’s own world, and the cattle are the sun; thus he appropriates the cattle of his rival in his own world. The Puroruc verses are in the Bṛhatī metre; the Bṛhatīs are cattle, and the sun is cattle; [thus he wins] in cattle itself.

He places the cattle [within]. He draws Soma first, then curds, then Soma; for curds are strength (*ūrj*) and the Ādityas are cattle; verily he places strength in the midst of the cattle. It is cooked with hot milk; therefore the raw cow yields cooked milk. If he should desire, "May it rain," he should mix it with curds from above, saying, "With that which is divine rain, I mix thee"; for curds are cattle and the Āditya is cattle; verily it rains for the sake of the cattle. When it rains, he pours down the rain for the sake of the cattle by means of the *upāṃśusavana* stone.

He mixes [the Soma]. The Upāṃśusavana stone is indeed breath, and the Āditya cup is cattle; thus he places breath within the cattle. With the formula, "O Vivasvat Āditya, this is your Soma-draught,"—for that Upāṃśusavana is indeed he—he directly endows it with the Soma-draught. If a drop of the drawn [Soma] falls, it rains immediately. Having taken it, he covers it for the support of the embryos so that they do not fall out. He causes it to move at the tenth hymn; therefore, embryos are placed in the womb during the tenth month.

They are born elsewhere; looking on, he offers the oblation. Agni is indeed Rudra, and the Āditya is cattle; [he does this] for the protection of the cattle. If he were to look on, a Brāhmaṇa as a supervisor would seize the cattle; thus, he becomes a supervisor over the cattle themselves as they are being given away. 6.

He draws the Sāvitra cup with the Antaryāma vessel. The Antaryāma is indeed cattle; cattle are produced by the impulse of Savitṛ. Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he causes them to be born. He offers it while it is not yet placed [on the fire]; therefore, cattle are not yet settled when they are born. The gods were unable to lift up the third pressing. At that time, Savitṛ was at the morning pressing. The gods said to him, "With you, let us lift this up. He said, "No; I am the chief; I shall not move backward."

They said, "The *mukhya* cup is indeed the primary one here; therefore, let us draw from it. So they drew from the *sāvitra* cup. Because the *sāvitra* is drawn, it serves as the means of drawing for the third pressing. With the verse, "O God Savitṛ, toward thee," he draws the *mukhya* at the morning pressing. Savitṛ indeed encompassed the sacrifice on all sides; he who knows thus encompasses his rival on all sides. He draws the *sāvitra* from the *āgrayaṇa* into the *antaryāma* vessel at the third pressing.

This Āgrayaṇa cup is drawn in the morning in the world of the Gāyatrī; at the third pressing, he divides it in the world of the Jagatī. Therefore, the Sāvitra cup is drawn from that Āgrayaṇa, for Savitṛ is the Gāyatra among the gods. From the overflow of the Sāvitra, he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup. This cup is indeed common [to all], for the sake of continuity. These creatures belong to the Viśvedevas; impelled by Savitṛ, creatures are born. Thus, he causes these very creatures to be born, impelled by Savitṛ. "Thou art a good refuge, a good support," [he says] over the Soma, for...

He draws the Soma; thus he makes the well-protecting upper [cup] subordinate to this one, and the well-established lower [cup] superior to that one. "To the great bull, homage! For the homage of the gods is indeed great, and that of the fathers is [great]. The fathers have a share in the *uktha* hymns, not a share in the *stoma* chants; therefore, at the very place where he recites the *uktha* for them, he draws the cup for them.

The Pātnīvata cup is indeed procreation. Whatever is performed at the sacrifice as a Pātnīvata rite is truly procreation. He draws it with the Upāṃśu vessel; the Upāṃśu is breath, and from breath offspring are born. For the sake of procreation they proceed with the Upāṃśu, and they rise with the Upāṃśu vessel. The Upāṃśu is breath; verily by breath they proceed, and by breath they rise. With the words, "Of thee, pressed by Bṛhaspati,"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and from the Brahman offspring are born; verily by the Brahman he [produces] them.

"Generating Indra"—thus he places seed. "Possessing power"—power indeed is progeny; "the Soma-draught in Agni, accompanied by the wives"—he thus creates a pair. "In unison with Tvaṣṭṛ, drink the Soma"—Tvaṣṭṛ is the fashioner of forms; he fashions forms for him. This cup indeed did not stand apart from the wives; the gods, having made the clarified butter a thunderbolt, struck it. In that he mixes the Pātnīvata cup, it is for the sake of striking down. He mixes it with the residue for the sake of continuity. He mixes it on top; therefore—

The female is prone to baldness; for he offers this Soma as cooked, while the others he offers uncooked. Therefore a woman is without vigor, and a man is without vigor. The Hotṛ does not sacrifice for him, for he [the Hotṛ] is like one who has gone behind; he should pass around the vital breaths from behind. Agni sacrifices for him, for he is like one who stands in front; he does not sacrifice after the vital breaths. If he were to sacrifice after them, he would exclude the vital breaths by means of Agni, and he would die. He consumes this Soma as cooked; therefore Agni is prone to impotence, for procreation is indeed [the essence].

Therefore, the Pātnīvata [cup] becomes one that possesses many cattle. Together with the vessel, it creeps toward the Neṣṭṛ; he thus causes the wives to partake of the Soma-drink. He should not sit upon the lap; if he were to sit upon the lap, he would become a eunuch. He creeps between the Neṣṭṛ and the Dhiṣṇya hearth; for the Neṣṭṛ is female and the Dhiṣṇya is male; verily, he deposits seed in the union of a couple.

Indra, indeed, slew Vṛtra; he split open his head, and it became the *droṇakalaśa* (the wooden trough). From that, the Soma which flowed out became the *hāriyojana*. Indra, having slain Vṛtra, poured Soma from his lungs and heart, and that became the *hāriyojana*. He thought: "If I offer this while it is uncooked and without a companion, the Asuras will follow after it; but if I do not offer it, they will likewise follow after it. Thus, the Soma remained prepared, and the [oblations] were offered.

Then he stepped forward to offer the enclosing-sticks; Agni said to him, "You shall not offer this uncooked [oblation] to me without a companion. He poured parched grains (*dhānā*) into it; he offered it once it was cooked and had a companion. When he pours the parched grains, it is for the sake of cooking and for the sake of having a companion. Whatever cattle were in Vṛtra, those very cattle he thus secures as wish-fulfilling cows; for they fulfill every desire. The two bay steeds (*harī*) of Indra are indeed the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*; this is their share.

In that there are the *hāriyojana* vessels as supports and the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), and in that he offers the *hāriyojana* when the enclosing-sticks have been cast out, he thereby provides fodder for these two while they are without support. Prajāpati indeed is the *āgrayaṇa*; from the *āgrayaṇa*, this Soma is left over. Whatever is left over in the sacrifice is left over for Prajāpati. In that he offers this leftover Soma, therefore this Prajāpati is "leftover" (excessive) and bestows offspring. The Unnetṛ offers the *hāriyojana* with the *droṇakalaśa* vessel; it is the leftover.

The *droṇakalaśa* is indeed the surplus of the vessels; the *unnetṛ* is the surplus of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); and the *hāriyojana* cup is the surplus of the Soma-pressings. By means of the surplus, he obtains the surplus. They seek the invitation (*upahava*) from the *unnetṛ* in order to secure whatever Soma-drinking (*somapītha*) exists therein. Those animals which were in Vṛtra, these very ones they are when [the vessel] is broken. If he were to break it, the small cattle would attend him as those who have been torn apart (*saṃśārukā*). For he destroys them; but if he does not break it, many [cattle] attend him as those who are unscathed (*asaṃśārukā*).

The animals, while eating, should stand near; for he does not harm them, as it were, when he takes the portions together; he thus accomplishes both purposes, and many animals, while eating, attend upon him. He should not scatter [the grain] away, so that he may obtain whatever portion of Soma exists there. He pours it out on the high altar (uttaravedi); the high altar is indeed cattle, and the *hāriyojanī* grains are cattle; thus he places cattle within cattle. ||9||

The cups are employed for the support of these two worlds: some are joined and others are not. Those which are employed sustain this world; those which are not employed sustain that [other] world, for that world is turned away and is undefined. The *upāṃśu* cup is employed; thereby goats are produced among cattle. He draws it three times; therefore she gives birth to three, or else two. Because the *upāṃśu* cup is employed, he thereby supports goats among cattle. Then the *antaryāma* cup.

When the Antaryāma vessel is employed, sheep are born after the cattle; by that means he supports sheep among the cattle. When the two Ṛtu vessels are employed, horses are born after the cattle; therefore, the hoof of a horse is found beneath those two. When the two Ṛtu vessels are employed, it is horses among the cattle that he supports. When the Ukthya vessel is employed, wild animals are born after the cattle; therefore, when they have been penned and come to the village, people kill them.

When the Ukthya cup is employed, he thereby supports the wild animals; the Śukra cup is employed, and through it the Atri people are born after [the gods]; the Manthin cup is employed, and through it the Ādya people are born after [the gods]. When these two are employed, he thereby supports both the Atri and the Ādya people. The two Ṛtu cups are employed before the Śukra cup; for the Śukra is yonder sun and the Ṛtus are the rays; therefore these two are employed first, for these are indeed first.

From this [Aditya cup] as the lowest, the Aditya vessel is employed; verily, cattle are born after it when the Aditya vessel is employed; he thereby supports cattle among animals. The Agrayana vessel is employed; verily, all creatures are born after it when the Agrayana vessel is employed; he thereby supports all creatures. The Dronakalasa is employed; the Dronakalasa is indeed Prajapati. When the Dronakalasa...

Therefore this is employed; therefore Prajāpati knows offspring. Therefore this is a place of destruction. So many indeed are the cups drawn in the morning; they must be made possessed of stotras, possessed of śastras, possessed of foundations, and possessed of abodes. Having drawn these nine, they chant the Bahiṣpavamāna with nine verses; thereby they are possessed of stotras. In that he returns and draws the Āśvina cup, it is by means of Soma that it becomes possessed of a stotra. In that the Hotṛ recites the consecratory formula over the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma when they have been offered, thereby those two become possessed of śastras.

In that there is the draught for Indra and Vāyu, by that the draught for Indra and Vāyu possesses the *uktha*; in that there is the draught for Mitra and Varuṇa, by that the draught for Mitra and Varuṇa possesses the *uktha*; in that there is the draught for the Aśvins, by that the draught for the Aśvins possesses the *uktha*; in that there is the exclusive (*niṣkevalya*) draught, by that the Śukra and Manthin possess the *uktha*; in that there is the draught for the Viśve Devas, by that the Āgrayaṇa possesses the *uktha*; and in that the chanters of the *ukthas* recite the *ukthas*, by that the *ukthya* sacrifice possesses the *uktha*. So many indeed are the draughts drawn in the morning; he thus makes them possessed of the *stotra*, possessed of the *uktha*, possessed of their foundation (*nidāna*), and possessed of their abode (*āyatana*). He who knows thus becomes possessed of his foundation and possessed of his abode. 10.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth section, named Āyuṣya, in the Madhyamikā recension of the Caraka branch of the Śrī Yajurveda Kāṭhaka. 28.

Now the twenty-ninth section: Dīrghajihvī. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Those gods were repeatedly defeated in battle after battle. They realized, "It is because we are without a stronghold that we are being defeated. They made these [cakes] their strongholds; those [strongholds] did not hold them, being themselves without a foundation. They saw these sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and offered them at each pressing (anusavana). With them they fortified the front; indeed, they made the pressings their strongholds. Because they fortified the front (puro 'dṛmhan), that is the reason for the name of the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa). Because [they were offered] at each pressing...

He offers the *puroḍāśa* cakes for the support of the pressings and for victory; therefore, one should eat of the *puroḍāśa* at each pressing for the support of the Soma-drinking. One should eat from where it has been smeared with ghee, for by means of the thunderbolt of clarified butter the gods slew Vṛtra, and Vṛtra is Soma; thus it is for the non-injury of the Soma-drinking. Regarding this they say: "Nothing other than clarified butter is fit to be combined in an *ahīna* sacrifice. Whatever they purify, all that becomes the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). One should not eat of whatever might remain unpurified. Dīrghajihvī indeed...

The gods desired the sacrifice; they longed for the morning pressing (*prātassavana*), and it became exhilarated. It turned into *payasyā* (curd-mixture). Therefore, the *āmikṣā* is as if exhilarated. In that there is *payasyā* at the morning pressing, it is for the prosperity of the morning pressing. It belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa at the morning pressing, but it does not partake in the later pressings. Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing; thus he preserves out-breathing and in-breathing at the very beginning. Therefore, out-breathing and in-breathing are at the beginning. Indeed, no cooked offering is prepared in the sacrifice without a *stotra* or a *śastra*.

These five oblations he thus prepares as a fivefold sequence in the sacrifice. The sacrifice is indeed a fivefold sequence of oblations, and it is a fivefold sequence of *nārāśamsa* cups; for there are these five oblations, and thus it is a fivefold sequence of oblations. There are two *nārāśamsas* at the morning pressing and two at the midday pressing, while there is one *nārāśamsa* at the third pressing; thus it is a fivefold sequence of *nārāśamsas*. The animal victim for Agni and Soma is one, the three pressings are another, and the barren cow to be immolated (*vaśā*) and the *anūbandhyā* cow are yet another; thus it is a fivefold sequence. He who understands these forms of the sacrifice in this way prospers.

The gods and the Asuras were arrayed for battle. The *mahimānaḥ* (powers) departed from the gods and went over to the Asuras. Those many hundreds of the Asuras slew the gods; these were the *chandas* (metres) which do not carry the sacrifice. The gods were afraid, thinking, "In this very way, the Asuras will surely overcome us all. They entreated those [metres], and they said, "Let us choose a boon. They chose the *parivāpa-puroḍāśa* (the enclosing-oblation cake). That [cake] approached as their share. Indeed, the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* had departed from them.

The cattle, the organ of speech, and the out-breath and in-breath—Indra thought, "These indeed have become this. He attained union with them. [With the words] "May Indra, accompanied by the two bay horses (*hari*), eat the parched grains," for the two bay horses of Indra are indeed the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*; thus he attained union with the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*. [With the words] "May Pūṣan, accompanied by [the offering], eat the groats," for Pūṣan is indeed the cattle; thus he attained union with the cattle. [With the words] "May Sarasvatī, accompanied by Bhāratī, eat the parched grain," for Sarasvatī is indeed speech; thus he attained union with speech. [This was] the cake for Indra.

Thus, "indra" means the sense-faculty (*indriya*); he attained union with that very sense-faculty. With the words, "The curd of Mitra and Varuṇa," [he offers]; Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed out-breath and in-breath; he thus attains union with out-breath and in-breath. He attains union with the greatness of these very [deities], he reaches a full lifespan, he becomes possessed of cattle, and he does not meet with sacrificial misfortune—he who knows thus. 1.

This nest of the sacrifice is indeed being constructed when it is performed with the *yajus*; for it is performed loudly with the *ṛc* and the *sāman*. In that there are *ṛc*s as *puroruks*, it is for the sake of firmness and for support so that it may not be loose. He utters aloud with the *ṛc* and restrains with the *yajus*; he causes [the cup] to go forth with the *graha*. Indeed, with the *ṛc* one takes the cup for the *stotra*, and with the *yajus* for the *śastra*. Therefore these two are joined together, for the *stotra* and the *śastra* are joined together. At this point, the sacrifice has turned away and the deities have turned away at the third pressing.

From the sacrificer, he performs the circum-oblation with a verse addressed to Agni in the east, one addressed to Soma in the middle, and one addressed to Viṣṇu in the west. Agni is indeed all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus he obtains both the deities and the sacrifice. For they indeed slay this Soma when they press it; this offering to Soma is its "anustaraṇī" (funeral cow). He offers it in the southern half of the fire-altar, for the south belongs to the ancestors. He makes a single cutting, for what is cut once belongs to the ancestors. When he makes a second cutting with the stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*), by that very act it becomes as if cut once. They carry it away to the Udgātṛs.

The *sāman* indeed has Soma as its deity; [he eats it] for the sake of the *sāman*'s possession of vigor and for the sake of having a body. "Should he eat it? Should he not eat it?"—thus they deliberate. If he were to eat it, he would become a mere eater of what is cooked (*prākāruka*); if he were not to eat it, he would be without food (*ahavis*). He should smell it; thus he accomplishes both. He who, being capable of eating food, does not eat food, should eat it. This food is indeed supreme, namely that which belongs to the Fathers; by means of that supreme food, he secures inferior food for himself. The gods prepared this as a remedy for the sacrifice, namely the *saumya* [oblation]; this is that very thing.

Therefore, it is to be consumed by the sick man as a remedy. May the Fathers rejoice; may they rejoice, those whose faces are like Soma. May we attain the god-appointed lifespan. Drunk by Indra, far-sighted, may we attain the god-appointed lifespan. Touching the heart, touching the will, you are the bestower of splendor; bestow splendor upon me.
Whatever mind of mine has gone to Yama, or whatever has not yet returned from him—that we maintain within ourselves by means of King Soma.

Thus he should look upon the Soma-vessel. Whatever he does here that is measured out for himself goes to the ancestors; when he looks upon the Soma, he preserves that very thing for himself. He should look around as it were; in that he looks around, he looks around at himself. With his entire body, he dwells together with him in yonder world, who, knowing thus, looks upon the Soma. The Upasad rites are indeed vigor, while the third pressing is devoid of vigor; they are performed outside the sacrifice. In that they proceed with the Soma-vessel at the third pressing, [it serves] the third pressing.

Thus he bestows vigor; for these deities are sacrificed to during the Upasad rites. With a verse addressed to Agni he sacrifices first in front, and with one addressed to Soma he sacrifices around it, thinking, "Lest they should attack the sacrifice. With a verse addressed to Viṣṇu he sacrifices afterwards, thinking, "Lest they should attack the Soma-offering in the Agniṣṭoma. He strews grass on both sides so that they do not attack. With a verse addressed to Agni he sacrifices of the clarified butter, with one addressed to Soma of the Soma-portion, and with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu of the clarified butter afterwards; thus he arranges the deities in their proper order. 2.

The *saṃsthitayajūṃṣi* (concluding formulas) are indeed the vital breaths; these are nine formulas. With nine [verses] they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna*; there are nine vital breaths. By means of the vital breaths they go forth, and by means of the vital breaths they rise up. He offers continuously for the sake of the continuity and non-interruption of the vital breaths. If he should desire of someone, "May he die," having drawn [the soma] nine times, he should offer each one with a formulaless [utterance]. The *saṃsthitayajūṃṣi* are indeed the vital breaths; verily, he separates him from the vital breaths, and he quickly perishes. Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, was indeed [the embodiment] of the sacrifice.

He beholds both the unsuccessful and the successful; there are these six verses (ṛc). Whatever of his is unsuccessful, that he makes successful by means of them. There are three sacrificial formulas (yajus); that is indeed successful. There are six verses; for there are six seasons; verily, he finds firm support in the seasons. There are three sacrificial formulas; these worlds are three; verily, he prospers in these very worlds.

Whatever indeed is redundant in the sacrifice, Varuṇa seizes that. This which is redundant in the sacrifice is the *ṛjīṣa*, the *audumbarī* post, and the two *adhiṣavaṇa* pressing-skins; with these they go down to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). Water is indeed Varuṇa; [they go] for the sake of release from Varuṇa. They should not descend into flowing water, for the *ṛjīṣa* is cattle; they would wipe away his cattle, and he would become without cattle. They should not descend facing north; if they were to descend facing north, Varuṇa would seize the offspring from the front. Not toward the south, for if it were toward the south, the offspring would be swept away to the fathers. [Therefore, they descend] facing north.

They descend toward the east, for the sacrifice, being released from Varuna’s noose, goes forward from behind. They cause the water to flow from stationary vessels; for Varuna is visibly present in what is stationary, and thus they offer a sacrifice to Varuna by means of Varuna himself. With the words, "For King Varuna has made wide room; a hundred are your physicians, O King, a thousand," [he acts]. With the verse, "The face of Agni has entered the waters," he pours the *āghāra* libation; this is for the sake of kindling and for brilliance. Wherever he sees grass or wood, there he should pour back the libation; thus he offers into that which possesses fire.

He performs the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) with the *barhis* excluded for the sake of prosperity; the *barhis* is indeed offspring, and thus he releases offspring from death. He performs the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga); the two butter-portions are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing, and thus he releases offspring from the noose of Varuṇa by means of out-breathing and in-breathing. Now, this cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla) belongs to Varuṇa for the sake of freedom from Varuṇa’s power; for a man cannot be reached by means of potsherds, but he reaches him all at once. He makes the offering together to Agni and Varuṇa; thus he releases him from the noose of Varuṇa from both sides—from Agni and from Varuṇa—entirely.

This sacrifice is indeed manifold; much is done for it and much is not done. If he were to conclude the sacrifice, he would cause Varuṇa to seize it; if he does not conclude it, he releases the sacrifice from the noose of Varuṇa. With the words, "In the ocean is thy heart, within the waters,"—for the sacrifice has the ocean as its womb—he causes it to go to its own womb. With the words, "O Lord of the Sacrifice, thee for the sacrifice," he makes it an oblation. With the words, "O purifying bath, Nicuṅkuṇa," he thereby releases it from both kinds of sin: that committed against the gods and that committed against men.

"O divine waters, this is your embryo"—for he is indeed the embryo of the waters; thus he causes him to go to his own womb. "The noose of Varuṇa is stepped over; the noose of Varuṇa is cast down"—thus they cast down the very noose of Varuṇa. "Of thee, O divine Soma, washed in the waters," with these words he sips a drop; this is for the attainment of that which is the drinking of Soma therein.

When he sips water, Varuṇa might otherwise seize him; by saying, "Thou art taken with a grip," he seizes him as it were, and thus effects both [the avoidance of Varuṇa's grasp and the taking of the water]. By saying, "Cast off is the noose of Varuṇa; homage to the noose of Varuṇa," he indeed casts off the noose of Varuṇa. By saying, "Rise up, bestowing offspring, life, and luster," he invokes a blessing.

"Fuel art thou; may we prosper"—thus, having offered a portion to Varuṇa, they approach the fuel as it blazes. "Kindling art thou; may we kindle thee"—thus he invokes a blessing. "Radiance art thou; bestow radiance upon me"—thus he places radiance within himself. "I have moved along the waters today; we have united with their essence"—this is according to the sacrificial formula (yajuḥ). 3.

The head of the sacrifice was indeed cut off; the essence that flowed from it became the barren cow (*vaśā*). In that the barren cow is the *anūbandhyā* (the cow bound after the sacrifice), it is for the sake of providing the sacrifice with its essence. Mitra indeed takes hold of the well-sacrificed part of the sacrifice, while Varuṇa takes hold of the ill-sacrificed part. In that the barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa is the *anūbandhyā*, he releases the sacrifice from both [Mitra and Varuṇa] and hands it over to the sacrificer. Just as one cleaves the soil with a plough, so is the sacrifice split apart by the *Ṛg* and *Sāman* verses. Just as...

He thus causes the mind to follow after it; for that which is the *anūbandhyā* cow is bound after [the sacrifice] for the sake of the sacrifice’s pacification. What flowed out first, Bṛhaspati received; what flowed out second, Mitra and Varuṇa; what flowed out third, the Viśve Devas. If there should be three *anūbandhyā* cows, one should perform the first as dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa, then the one to the Viśve Devas, and then the one to Bṛhaspati—for the sake of the completeness and sapidity of the sacrifice, since here and there indeed lies the undiminished essence (*rasa*) of the sacrifice, as well as its deities and the sacred formulation (*brahman*).

And for him who sacrifices with the Soma, these two offerings to the Viśvedevas and to Bṛhaspati are made; this is for the sake of the unfailing vigor of both the deities and the Brahman. The offering to the Viśvedevas is in the middle; the Viśvedevas are these creatures, and thus he places seed within his own creatures. He sacrifices in a low voice, for seed is unexpressed. That to Bṛhaspati is last; Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; having reached the very end, he becomes established in spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

Just as a bull or a horse, when unyoked, runs away, even so do the deities and the sacrifice run away from one who has sacrificed with Soma. He offers a cake on five potsherds to Agni as the concluding oblation (*udavasānīya*). Agni is indeed all the deities, and the sacrifice is fivefold; thus he wins back both the deities and the sacrifice. Agni is of the *gāyatrī* nature and the *gāyatrī* is his metre; he deprives him of his metre if he makes it a cake on five potsherds. It should be made on eight potsherds; the *gāyatrī* has eight syllables, and Agni is of the *gāyatrī* nature and the *gāyatrī* is his metre; thus he [restores] him by means of his own [nature].
He causes it to prosper through the meters; the invitatory and offering verses consist of five parts, and the sacrifice consists of five parts; thus he does not depart from the sacrifice.

Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, the luminous, I take thee, the luminous; for Dakṣa, the increaser of skill; for those whose tongue is Agni, who live by Truth, who drink the Wind, whose self is Parjanya, whose eldest is Indra, whose king is Varuṇa; for Earth thee, for Atmosphere thee, for Heaven thee; for what is, thee, for what is not, thee, for the past thee, for the future thee; from whom offspring were born unbroken, to that Prajāpati, the all-pervading giver, I offer thee—Svāhā! Soma has overcome the waters.

The waters long for the Soma as cows long for their calves; through their coming together, they strike one another. In the same way, these two, coming together and being in accord, strike out each other’s power and vigor. Both of these—the Soma and the waters—belong to Prajāpati. Curds are the essence of the waters. Just as when two sons fight, the father provides for them, so the father pacifies them in their own world with their own portion. He who has this [oblation] taken for him with curds sacrifices indeed with a sacrifice that is fully successful.

All the pressings (savana) should be made to possess cattle and vigor. In that they proceed with the *payasyā* at the morning pressing, thereby it possesses cattle and vigor; in that they proceed with the *dadhigharma* at the midday pressing, thereby it possesses cattle and vigor; in that there is the *āśira* at the third pressing, thereby it possesses cattle and vigor. All his pressings become possessed of cattle and vigor for one who knows thus. 5.

The gods, having conquered the sacrifice from the Asuras, went along taking the cups (grahas) one after another. Prajāpati reflected: "Whoever shall take the first cup, he alone shall possess this world. He beheld this *aṃśu* cup; he took it while breathing outwards. He reached the end of prosperity while breathing outwards. One who desires prosperity should take this cup; he should breathe outwards and not breathe inwards. If he breathes inwards, he reaches the end of prosperity while breathing outwards; he meets with misfortune, or he perishes, or he is deprived of all his possessions, if [he does so].
If he should desire, "May I be equal," let him neither breathe out nor breathe in; he indeed becomes equal. The vessel is four-cornered; there are four quarters; he prospers in all the quarters.

He touches it with gold; gold is indeed immortality; verily, he unites him with immortality. He draws [the draught] from that which has been pressed once; for Prajāpati cannot be reached by the pressings (savana); verily, he reaches him all at once. He does not recite a Ṛc verse, nor does he utter a Yajus formula; for Prajāpati cannot be reached by speech; verily, he reaches him by means of the mind. He who knows the abode of the Aṃśu becomes possessed of an abode; while drawing the Aṃśu, he should meditate upon the Vāmadevya with his mind—this indeed...

He who knows thus becomes possessed of a dwelling, for the sun is the dwelling. He recites over the gold; gold is indeed life, and thus he endows himself with life. He sprinkles it with water; water is indeed immortality, and thus he causes him to rejoice with immortality.

Now, these are the *atigrāhya* cups. Whatever supreme vigor and strength has not been secured, for the securing of that [they are offered]. That which is dedicated to Agni—Agni is indeed brilliance; by that, he places brilliance in front. That which is dedicated to Indra—Indra is indeed power; by that, he places power in the middle. That which is dedicated to Sūrya—this Āditya is indeed spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); by that, he places spiritual luster at the top. Agni is indeed brilliance, Indra is power, and this Āditya is spiritual luster; thus, by means of brilliance and spiritual luster, [he secures them].

He grasps both the axle-pins for himself from both sides; for these Atigrāhyas are the support of the sacrifice, as are the two wheels and the Pṛṣṭha-stotras. If these were not taken, the Pṛṣṭhas, being heavier, would crush the sacrifice from above as it moves forward. Since these are taken, he places the two wheels in front after having supported the sacrifice, so that it may be steady. He should take them at the morning pressing; for this is the most vigorous of the pressings, and thus he takes them by means of vigor itself.

The gods were indeed all alike; they did not attain distinction. Then they saw these cups: Agni [saw] the cup for Agni, Indra the cup for Indra, and Sūrya the cup for Sūrya. Thereupon they attained distinction and the preeminence among the gods. He among his peers for whom these are drawn attains distinction and preeminence. Prajāpati assigned the portions to the gods; he considered the sacrifice itself to have entered within himself. Those three who were his beloved ones remained there.

He set these cups aside; indeed, it was those cups he then set aside. With whatever sacrifice one desires to proceed, in that very sacrifice one should draw these cups. He thus gathers them all together for the sake of prosperity—himself whole, with his strength, his source, and his body.

Formerly, these [cups] were in Vṛtra. When Indra had slain Vṛtra, he found this [cup] belonging to Agni; he gave it to Agni, saying, "Hold this for me. He found that one belonging to Sūrya; he gave it to Sūrya, saying, "Hold this for me. Having found the one belonging to Indra, he asked for those two back again. They did not give them back to him. They entered these worlds separately: Agni this [world], Indra the intermediate space, and Sūrya yonder [world]. By means of these cups, they indeed prospered in these worlds; by means of these, they [prospered] for themselves.

By means of these, one attains sovereignty over the worlds; he who has these drawn for him prospers and attains sovereignty over all these worlds. That which is the splendor of the Virāj belongs to Agni; that which is of the Śakvarī belongs to Indra; that which is of the Revatī belongs to Sūrya. Wherever these Sāmans are present, there one should draw these [cups], for the sake of the splendor of the Sāmans. Now, these are both the oblations and the portions for consumption; by means of these, Bambha and Viśvavayas came to know these worlds, both those directed hitherward and those directed awayward, for whomsoever these are [drawn].

These worlds, both those facing this way and those facing away, are grasped together; indeed, by their power, Agni shines upward from here, the sun burns downward, and the wind blows crosswise. Well-known indeed is that world from here, but from there it is difficult to perceive. He, however, perceives this world from there as being near, for whom these [fires] are taken up.

The animal dedicated to Agni, the one to Soma, and the one to Bṛhaspati are sacrificed with the same sacrificial portion. In that there is one for Agni—Agni is indeed brilliance; verily, by that he places brilliance at the front. In that there is one for Soma—Soma is indeed power; verily, by that he places power in the middle. In that there is one for Bṛhaspati—Bṛhaspati is indeed the sacred formulation (*brahman*); verily, by that he places spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) at the rear. Agni is brilliance, Soma is power, and Bṛhaspati is the sacred formulation; thus, by means of both brilliance and spiritual luster, he places power on both sides of his self.

He takes hold [of them] from the right. Indeed, the Rakṣases sought to strike at the sacrifice of the gods from the right; therefore, those deities who are most powerful are sacrificed on the right for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases. "What is performed in the set of eleven [animals]? ask the exponents of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinaḥ); [they say it is] because the common people (viś) seek support from the ruling power (kṣatra). Those deities who are most powerful are sacrificed on the right.

Those that are weaker, he makes them higher than those; therefore the commoner (viṭ) seeks support from the power of the ruling class (kṣatra). He should make a depression on the south side, which is the form of the sacrificial ground (devayajana), for the purpose of striking away the Rākṣasas; therefore, on the south side of fords there is a shallow place. Those three [posts] which are nearest the fire (agniṣṭha), he should make them equal, for cattle attend upon Agni; this is for the attainment of cattle. The post nearest the fire is the self, while the other two are his rivals; he should make those two more prosperous, for he thus makes his rival lower. Those two which are further away...

Those two [posts] should be equal to the one at the fire-altar (agniṣṭha), for they are its own; he should measure them thus up to the furthest limit (parārdha) for the sake of excluding misfortune. Moreover, he thereby makes his rival inferior. If he should desire, "May the people (viś) be more powerful than the nobility (kṣatra)," he should make those [posts] to the north of the agniṣṭha taller; thus he makes the people more powerful than the nobility.

Those [stakes] which are south of the *agniṣṭha* he should make taller if he should desire, "May the nobility (*kṣatra*) be more powerful than the common people (*viś*). Verily, he makes the nobility more powerful than the common people. He should make them all equal if he should desire, "May there be a state of mutual degradation. Verily, he brings about a state of mutual degradation. They are measured crosswise for the separation of the quarters; they are measured upright for the separation of these worlds. He should not set up a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) outside the altar, nor should he let it extend beyond the altar. The sacrificer is indeed the sacrificial post; as great as this earth is, so great is [the extent].

If he were to erect the sacrificial post outside the altar, he would exclude the sacrificer from the earth; if he were to exceed the altar, he would leave a space for his rival. He should erect it level with the edge of the altar; thus he neither excludes the sacrificer from the earth nor leaves a space for his rival. He should erect it level with the top [of the altar] if he should desire, "May I prosper in the world of the fathers"; verily he prospers in the world of the fathers. He should erect it level with the girdle if he should desire, "May I prosper in the world of men"; [verily he prospers] in the world of men.

He prospers. If he should desire, "May I prosper in the world of the gods," he should measure [the post] to the height of a *caṣāla*; thus he prospers in the world of the gods. He prospers in all these worlds. He measures it with the axle of a chariot; for the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt (*vajra*) and the chariot is a thunderbolt; verily, he places a thunderbolt upon a thunderbolt. All [posts] should be made so that they face the fire; those which do not rest against the central post, he should pile around the fire; by that very means, all are made to face the fire.

In that they distribute the ropes from the one standing near the fire (the *agniṣṭha*), by that very means all [posts] are made to stand near the fire. Two ropes reach each post; therefore women are in excess over men, and for this reason one man finds many wives, but not one woman many husbands. The spare post (*upaśaya*) is the twelfth; the year has twelve months, so it is for the attainment of the year. Having carried it around to the south, they set it down; for on the south side the Rakṣases sought to destroy the sacrifice of the gods. The sacrificial post is a thunderbolt, for the striking away of the Rakṣases.

If he should practice sorcery, he should make a human victim, saying, "I bind so-and-so, the son of such-and-such a man and such-and-such a woman," and he should fasten the cord upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). For the post is indeed a thunderbolt; thus he binds him with a thunderbolt, and he quickly perishes. If he does not practice sorcery, he should designate a wild animal; he must not eat of it. Or rather, the wild animals attend upon the *upaśaya* (the post lying near). The domestic animals attend upon the set of eleven posts (*ekādaśinī*). Since the altar is measured by means of the *ekādaśinī*, therefore the domestic animals appear as if subdued and tranquil.
Because he lies in a place of rest as if in a cave, therefore wild animals roam as if in a cave, as if toward a dwelling-place, as if toward a place of concealment. 8.

Prajāpati, having created living beings, felt as if he were emptied out. He saw this set of eleven [sacrificial animals] and took it; with it, he gratified himself. Whoever feels as if he is emptied out should take this set of eleven at whatever sacrifice [he performs]. For there are ten vital breaths in a person, and the self is the eleventh; thus he gratifies his entire self. Agni is all the deities; these deities are obtained through Agni. The self belongs to Agni, and Sarasvatī is speech; in that there is an animal for Sarasvatī, he thereby obtains speech.

He yokes a pair to himself; now, Soma belongs to the *saumya* [deity], and Soma is the placer of seed—he thus places seed in the very union. Then there is the offering to Pūṣan; Pūṣan is indeed cattle—he thus causes them to be born. Then there is the offering to Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati is the *brahman*—he thus extends the *brahman* over the cattle. Then there is the offering to the Viśvedevas; these creatures belong to the Viśvedevas—he thus unites the creatures with the *brahman*. Then there is the offering to Indra; Indra is indeed the *kṣatra*—he thus extends the *kṣatra* over the creatures. Then there is the offering to the Maruts; the Maruts are indeed the *viś* (the common people).

He unites the people with the ruling power itself; then [he offers] to Indra and Agni—for Indra and Agni are might and vigor—with might and vigor he drives the people toward the ruling power for the sake of impulsion. [The offering] to Savitṛ is for the sake of instigation; that to Varuṇa is for the sake of release from Varuṇa’s noose. Prajāpati created the creatures; they departed from him, they went upward. He desired, "May they turn back to me. He practiced fervor; he offered himself as a victim at the sacrifice. They turned back to him. They were afraid of him; they were cast down. Therefore, animals are bent downward. They...

Moving from afar, these offered him tribute: the earth with the sacrificial ground, the plants with the sacrificial grass, the waters with the sprinkling water, the trees with the fuel and the sacrificial post, goats and sheep with the sacrificial animals, and the cows with the milk-mixture and the clarified butter. These indeed are the deities who receive offerings; they are the sacrifice, Prajāpati. To him who knows this, all these bring tribute, and they bring tribute unto him.

He was afraid of their departure; he brought their paired powers into himself. The self is indeed Agni, Vāc is Sarasvatī, and the sense-organ is Soma; thus he brings both speech and the sense-organ into himself. Then [the offering] for Pūṣan, then that for Bṛhaspati; Pūṣan is indeed cattle and Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; thus he brings both cattle and the Brahman into himself. Then [the offering] for the Viśvedevas, then that for Indra; the Viśvedevas are indeed vigor and Indra is power; thus he brings both vigor and power into himself. Then...

The Marut cup is for strength, for the Maruts are indeed strength; the Indra-Agni cup is for vigor, for Indra and Agni are vigor; he thus bestows both strength and vigor upon himself for the sake of impulsion. The Sāvitra cup is for instigation, and the Vāruṇa cup is for release from Varuṇa’s noose.

One desiring spiritual luster, one desiring offspring, one desiring cattle, or one desiring the office of a domestic priest, should sacrifice these together: an animal for Agni, one for Sarasvatī, one for Soma, and one for Bṛhaspati. As for the one for Agni, the Brāhmaṇa is indeed of the nature of Agni; as for the one for Sarasvatī, Sarasvatī is indeed speech, for he speaks speech; as for the one for Soma, he indeed drinks Soma; as for the one for Bṛhaspati, Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; thus, having brought about the four-footed Brahman, he establishes it, and he becomes possessed of spiritual luster. Then there is the one for Pūṣan; Pūṣan is indeed cattle.

O Brahmin, he indeed binds the cattle to the Brahman; then [the animal] for Indra-Agni, and then for Indra. Indra and Agni are the Kṣatra, and Indra is the Kṣatra; having thus brought about the Kṣatra, he establishes it. Moreover, by means of the Kṣatra itself, he brings the cattle near to the Brahman. That for Agni is in the middle, and those for Indra are on both sides. The Brāhmaṇa is indeed related to Agni, and the Rājanya is related to Indra; by means of the Brahman, he causes the Kṣatra to descend into the middle. He who knows this attains the office of the domestic priest (purodhā). Indra and Agni are the sharers of the cattle in the greatest measure.

The Āgneya cup belongs to Agni; the Aindra belongs to Indra; the Aindrāgna belongs to both Indra and Agni together. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya are the greatest sharers among subjects. Then follows the Vaiśvadeva cup, then the Māruta. The All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ) are indeed the people (viś); the Maruts are the people. Having thus brought about the people, he subjects them to the nobility (kṣatra). Having made the nobility have the priesthood (brahman) as its head, he subjects the people to it for the sake of impulsion: the Sāvitra cup is for impulsion; the Vāruṇa cup is for release from Varuṇa’s noose. He thus properly marshals the priesthood and properly marshals the nobility. He makes them harmonious.

Wherever the *ekādaśinī* (set of eleven victims) is prepared and sacrificed, there it is made fit for the subjects: the Brāhmaṇa becomes a Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya a Rājanya, and the Vaiśya a Vaiśya. Indeed, this world is not fit for the subjects unless it is prepared by means of the *ekādaśinī*. This indeed is that *ekādaśinī*; the Kāpeyas know it as such. One should sacrifice this very one at the final day of the *atirātra* sacrifice. By means of this, these creatures move about in this [world] on the other day; this is the rule for the days, for these days have those deities as their essence. 10.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth section, named Dīrghajihvī, in the Madhyamikā recension of the Caraka-śākhā within the auspicious Kāṭhaka Yajurveda. 29.

Now the thirtieth section: The Pātnīvata offering. The Pātnīvata is indeed procreation; whatever Pātnīvata rite is performed at the sacrifice, that is indeed procreation. At this point, the sacrifice has turned away and the deities have turned away; Tvaṣṭṛ belongs to the turned-away ones. Into these very turned-away deities he introduces Tvaṣṭṛ as a bull; he thereby creates a pairing for him. This set of eleven [animals] is a thunderbolt that is gathered in front; it is capable of turning the sacrifice back toward itself. When the Pātnīvata is offered, it serves to support and stabilize it. Of Manu...

As many Asuras as they (the gods) struck down with those skull-bones, so many were utterly defeated. At that time, there were two Tristavarutris who were Asura-Brahmins. The Asuras said to them, "Beg for these Manu-skull-bones. They approached Prātaritvan and said, "O Vāyu! O Agni! O Vāyu! O Indra! He asked, "What do you two desire? They replied, "Give us these skull-bones. He gave them to them. Having carried them away into the forest, they ground them together. Thereupon, Manu’s cattle stood around them.

The bull bellowed; as many Asuras as heard him bellowing perished. Then the two Prātaritvanas approached them, saying, "To Vāyu! To Agni! To Vāyu! To Indra! He asked, "What do you two desire? They replied, "Let us cause ourselves to be sacrificed with this bull. Thereupon the wife arrived, reciting a Yajus formula. *Dyaus* (Heaven) took possession of her speech. As she spoke, as many Asuras as heard her perished. Therefore, at night, a woman speaks more clearly. Those two—

The two who come early in the morning approached [him], saying, "Vāyu! Agni! Vāyu! Indra! He asked, "What do you two desire? They said, "Let us cause you to sacrifice with this wife. She had already been circumambulated by fire. Then Indra perceived: "Manu, whose god is Faith, has deprived his wife of her husbandly power through the Triṣṭubh and the Avarutrī, the Asura and the Brahman. He went to him and said, "Let me cause you to sacrifice with these two. He said, "No; I have no mastery over these two. He said, "The master of the guest is indeed the master of the guest. He gave them to him. He...
A neighbor, while preparing the sacrificial altar, sat down; they asked him, "Who are you? He replied, "A Brahmin. They asked, "Which one is a Brahmin?"
Why do you ask about the Brahmin’s father, or why do you ask about his mother? If the Veda has been heard by him, he is that father and he is that grandfather.

"Thus they did not find her; was it Indra? he asked. They both flew toward her. With the sprinkling waters that were there, he released [the victim] and cut off its head. Those two became the *vṛṣa* and the *yavāṣa* plants; therefore, those two wither in the rains, for they were struck by water. He drove away that [victim] after it had been carried around the fire. By means of it, Manu prospered. These are the offspring of Manu (*manāvyāḥ*). In that he drives away the Pātnīvata after it has been carried around the fire, he attains that very prosperity which Manu attained. "Should it be completed? Should it not be completed? they ask.

They deliberate: "The sacrifice indeed flows away while it is not yet concluded; as it flows away, the sacrificer flows away after it, along with his offspring and his cattle. Therefore, one should conclude the sacrifice for the sake of its stability. If he were to conclude it, he should cut portions from the clarified butter (ājya) equal in number to the portions of the animal victim, for that which is clarified butter belongs to Prajāpati and is never exhausted; and since Prajāpati is never exhausted among the gods, he thus concludes it by means of that very [butter]. Yet, he does not truly conclude it; he performs both [the conclusion and the non-conclusion] at once.

At the beginning, the cups are drawn with the Aindravāyava first, then those with the Śukra first, and then those with the Āgrayaṇa first. The Aindravāyava belongs to the Gāyatrī, the Śukra to the Triṣṭubh, and the Āgrayaṇa to the Jagatī. These indeed are the meters; by means of the meters the gods went to the heavenly world, and by means of the meters he goes to the heavenly world. On the fourth day, the Āgrayaṇa comes first; for the Āgrayaṇa is of the Jagatī, and this three-night rite has the Jagatī at its opening. Whatever meter he attains on that day, by that he extends the subsequent three-night rite. On the fifth day, the cups have the Aindravāyava first.

The cup for Indra and Vāyu is indeed Gāyatra; the Gāyatrī is breath. He thus places breath in the middle; therefore breath is in the middle. The cups beginning with the Śukra are on the sixth day; the Śukra is Traiṣṭubha, and this three-night period ends in the Triṣṭubh. He thus raises it up toward the end. The cups beginning with the Śukra are on the seventh day; the Śukra is Traiṣṭubha, and the Triṣṭubh is the mouth of this Chandoma. This is for support and stability, and also because by whatever metre he attains, by that he extends the subsequent three-night period. The cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa...

On the eighth day, there is the *āgrayaṇa* cup for the *jagatī*; this *chandoma* sacrifice has the *jagatī* in the middle, and thus it arranges itself according to the arrangement of the metres. At the introductory rite (*prāyaṇīya*), the cups begin with those for Indra and Vāyu; at the concluding rite (*udayanīya*), they likewise begin with those for Indra and Vāyu. The cup for Indra and Vāyu is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); by means of the vital breath they set out, and by means of the vital breath they return. The cups are indeed the vital breaths; he confuses them when he draws them in an alternating manner. If he were to draw them beginning with the foremost ones [in both cases], he would hold them fast until the time of setting them down. The cups are indeed the vital breaths; he thus places the vital breaths themselves into their proper abodes.

Then, having extended further, they are indeed taken. Thus, at the felling of the tree-trunk for Keśin Dālbhya, they took the draughts; Luśākapi Khārgali said to him, "How did you take the draughts? They replied to him, "In such and such a manner. He said, "His offspring will be threefold. Thereupon the Pañcālas divided into three groups. For whomsoever the draughts are taken in this way, his offspring becomes threefold. ||2||

One who desires, "May it be well-ordered for my offspring according to their seniority," should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu. Indeed, following the order of the sacrifice, things become well-ordered for the offspring; following the disorder of the sacrifice, they do not become well-ordered. Thus he makes it well-ordered for the offspring according to their seniority; the younger does not overstep the elder. He should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu for one who is ill. For he whose illness afflicts him is deprived of his vital breath (*prāṇa*); the cup for Indra and Vāyu is the vital breath. Verily, he endows him with the vital breath. [Then] those beginning with the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa...

They should draw [the cups] for those initiated ones among whom one dies; for those initiated ones among whom one dies, they are deprived of out-breath and in-breath (*prāṇa* and *apāna*). Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed out-breath and in-breath; thus they preserve out-breath and in-breath at the very beginning. Therefore, they should draw the cups beginning with those for the Aśvins. One who is inferior in rank should draw them first; for the Aśvins were the two most inferior among the gods, yet they attained the foremost place. The Aśvins are the deity of him who is inferior in rank; he takes hold of them, and they lead him to the foremost place. He should draw the cups beginning with the *śukra*.

"Take [the cups]; this sun has lost its splendor, for this *śukra* cup is the end; having reached the end of his prosperity, a man returns. From the very end he seizes the end; he does not become worse off than he was when he sacrificed. One practicing sorcery should take the *manthin* cups first; the *manthin* cup is indeed a vessel of affliction; verily, he causes death itself to seize him. One against whom sorcery is practiced should take the *ukthya* cups first; the *ukthya* cup contains the sensory power and vigor of all the vessels; verily, he overpowers him with his entire sensory power."
May we not come to your desolate fields; do not shrink away; do not fail us with your milk.
May we not suffer for the sin committed by another; O Sarasvatī, lead us toward greater wealth.

Thus, these are indeed the fields of Death, the *araṇas*; by means of them, one does not go to the fields of Death. One should draw the *āgrayaṇa* cups first for one whose father and grandfather were virtuous, but who has not yet attained that [status]. He who has a virtuous father and grandfather is deprived of speech and vital power (*indriya*). Since he has not attained it, this [cup] is like the chest of the sacrifice, and the *āgrayaṇa* is like speech; verily, he endows him with speech and vital power. One should draw full cups for one who is ill; [for] his vital breaths...

Suffering afflicts him who is ill; the *grahas* release that very suffering from his vital breaths (*prāṇa*). One should draw the full cups when Parjanya does not rain. For at the time when Parjanya does not rain, suffering afflicts the vital breaths of creatures; the *grahas* are the vital breaths, and they thus release the vital breaths of creatures from suffering. Immediately it rains.
O Lord of the Field, milk for us a honeyed wave, as a cow yields her milk—sweet-dropping, well-purified like clarified butter. May the Lords of Eternal Order show us mercy.
You are taken with a support; for Aditi, the four-uddered, you!
Raise yourselves up, O Maruts, from the ocean; you who possess abundance, cause the rain to fall.
Your milch-cows, O wonder-workers, never fail; your chariots have rolled forth after your glorious journey.
You are taken with a support; for Aditi, the four-uddered, you!

We invoke for protection the Earth, the mother of those who observe holy vows, the consort of Eternal Order— Aditi, the mighty ruler, the undecaying, the far-reaching, the provider of good shelter and excellent guidance.

"You are taken with a support; for Aditi, the four-breasted, you! This is your womb; for Aditi, the four-breasted, you! Rain indeed departed from the gods; it took refuge in these worlds. The gods strove to seek it out; they saw this cup and drew it. By means of it, they caused rain to fall down from these worlds. One who desires rain should draw this cup, [with the verse]: "O Lord of the Field, the honeyed wave... For he who is yonder is indeed the Lord of the Field; from there he rains, so cause him to send it forth.

"From the ocean, O Maruts..."—thus they lead the rain sent forth by the Maruts to the earth. "The great mother of the well-vowed ones..."—this is Aditi; it rains upon her. These deities indeed rule over the rain; he has recourse to them and causes the rain to fall from these very worlds. The vessel has four nipples; there are four quarters; thus he causes the rain to fall from the quarters. Whichever nipple the rain first reaches, from that quarter it rains toward this [spot], even while the vessel is being prepared.
When it rains, one catches [the water] with an earthen vessel; one offers oblations with a wooden ladle, for an earthen vessel cannot contain the oblation. ||4||

You are taken with a support; for Prajāpati, for the creatures, you! This is your womb; for Prajāpati, for the creatures, you! You are taken with a support; for the creatures, for Prajāpati, you! This is your womb; for the creatures, for Prajāpati, you! You are taken with a support; for the intermediate space, for the trees, you! This is your womb; for the intermediate space, for the trees, you! You are taken with a support; for the trees, for the intermediate space, you! This is your womb...

The womb is from the trees; for the atmosphere, you are taken with a support; for the waters, for the plants—this is your womb; for the waters, for the plants, you are taken with a support; for the plants, for the waters—this is your womb; for the plants, for the waters.
Those rays bear aloft that god Jātavedas, Sūrya, so that everyone may behold him.
You are taken with a support; for Sūrya you are; this is your womb; for Sūrya you are.
We invoke today for our protection Vācaspati, the all-maker (Viśvakarman), who is yoked by thought, in this contest;
may he, the source of all well-being and performer of good deeds, come most near to our invocations for our aid.
You are taken with a support: for Indra Viśvakarman you! This is your resting place: for Indra Viśvakarman you!

We invoke for our protection the Earth, the mother of those who observe holy vows, the consort of Eternal Order— Aditi, the possessor of great dominion, the ageless, the far-reaching, the provider of excellent shelter, and the excellent guide.

"You are taken with a support; for Aditi you! This is your womb; for Aditi you! These cups are indeed a continuous succession. Just as a house, so is the year; just as the two sides of a house, so are the two sides of the year; just as the central ridge-pole, so is the *divākīrtya* chant. If these were not drawn, the two sides of the year would fall apart in opposite directions and they would meet with ruin. Since these are drawn, [it is] just as the two sides of a house [support] the center.

They fasten it to the central beam; in the same way, they extend the two wings of the year toward the *divākīrtya* chant. All of them are taken up together at the *divākīrtya*. Just as the central beam is the support, so is the *divākīrtya*; for if there were no *saubala*, it would fall apart.

Because these [cups] are not drawn [on other days], they are drawn on this day with a view toward firmness and to prevent looseness; they are drawn with the *śukra* as their foremost [cup]. For the *śukra* is of the *triṣṭubh* metre, and this day is of the *triṣṭubh* metre; it is for the sake of support and stability. On this day, an animal dedicated to Sūrya is sacrificed, and the cup for Sūrya is drawn. Yonder sun is indeed this day; thus they directly prosper that very thing. Six *atigrāhya* cups are drawn on this day, and the animal is the seventh; there are seven vital breaths. Yonder sun is the head of creatures; [it is] right in the head.

He bestows the vital breaths; therefore there are seven vital breaths in the head. Indra, having slain Vṛtra, conquered these worlds; that world up there remained unconquered for him. Becoming Viśvakarman, he conquered it. In that the cup for Viśvakarman is drawn, it is for the conquest of that world. Those who draw the cup for Viśvakarman depart from this world, for they do not ascend as it were; they are liable to perish. They should draw the Āditya cup on the following day, so that by means of that [cup] they remain in this very world.

From the half-yearly period of a year, they should take one [cup] after another as they settle; by means of one they perform all rites, and by means of the other they find firm support in this world. Both are drawn together at the Mahāvrata; having reached the very end, they prosper in both worlds. With the Vaiśvakarman [offering], there is the Arkya hymn for that Āditya cup in yonder world and for this one here; the Arkya is indeed food, and through it they find firm support as eaters of food. ||5||
I pluck you out for Agni with the Gāyatrī metre; I pluck you out for Indra with the Triṣṭubh metre; I pluck you out for the Viśvedevas with the Jagatī metre.
May Agni Vaiśvānara, the maker of all, the source of all well-being, protect us at the morning libation.
May he, the purifier, bestow wealth upon us; may we be long-lived and share in the sacrificial food together.
May all the gods, the Maruts, and Indra not abandon us at this second libation;
may we, being wise and speaking what is pleasing to them, become masters of riches.
This is the third libation for the sages who, with the eternal truth, set the chalice in motion;
may the sons of Sudhanvan, having attained immortality, lead us toward well-offered sacrifice and greater prosperity.

I take your bright [essence] with the bright, in the form of the day, in the rays of the sun. I shake you in the flight-path of the *reśīs*; I shake you in the flight-path of the *māndās*; I shake you in the flight-path of the *kṛtās*; I shake you in the flight-path of the *bhandanas*; I shake you in the flight-path of those that go to the gods.
The fierce ones have brought down from heaven an unceasing stream; the lofty form of the bull shines brightly.

Soma is the precursor of Soma; Śukra is the precursor of Śukra. O Soma, that which is your invincible, watchful name—for that Soma of yours, Svāhā! Three times you have flowed for the Vasus; three times you have flowed for the Rudras; three times you have flowed for the Ādityas. With that form by which you flowed for Prajāpati, with that flow pure for me, O divine Soma. By means of the Gāyatrī metre, go to the path of Agni; as a controller, O divine Soma, by means of the Triṣṭubh metre, go to the path of Indra from us.
O divine Soma, friend, with the Jagatī metre, go unto the path of all the gods. ||6||

The gods and the Asuras performed the sacrifice equally; whatever the gods did, the Asuras did that as well. Those gods saw this Adābhya cup and drew it, saying, "For Agni I draw thee, with the Gāyatrī metre. By this they obtained both the deities and the metres. Saying, "May Agni protect us at the morning pressing," they obtained the pressings. Saying, "Thy bright [juice] I draw with the bright," they obtained the forms of day and night. [With the words,] "Thee of the Reśīs..."

With the words, "I shake [the Soma] upon the seat," he attains the very forms of the waters. Having encompassed the entire sacrifice, those gods offered it; when the Asuras perceived that it had been offered, they said, "They have not deceived us. That is its *ādābhya* nature (un-deceivable). Furthermore, because they were unable to deceive them, that is its *ādābhya* nature. This [cup] is drawn for the very purpose of deceiving one's rival.

He draws the *nigrābhya* waters; Soma indeed draws from the curd, for curd is Soma. The vessel is four-cornered; there are four quarters, and thus he finds firm support in the quarters. Verily, they strike this Soma when they press him; this [cup] is his body that delivers him from harm (*ādābhya*). By following it, he is delivered from the world of heaven when it is struck. Following that, the sacrificer is delivered from the sacrifice. For that belongs to the sacrificer; indeed, he whose [cup] is drawn possesses his entire body in yonder world. Verily, he thus divides the sacrifice.

He cuts [the sacrifice] when he causes the rite to conclude before the pressing has begun; he cuts it when he pours in stalks that have not been pressed. This is for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice. "They say there is no cup without a *sāman* or a *uktha*, for it would be without a foundation," they say. "Three times you have descended for the Vasus"—this is the *uktha*; the *Gaurīvīta* is the *sāman*. When the gods divided the *brahman*, that which remained over became the *Gaurīvīta*. The *Gaurīvīta* is indeed what is excessive, and the *atigrāhya* cups are likewise excessive.

Verily, by means of the redundant one he obtains what is redundant; wherever there may be the Gaurīvita Sāman, there he should also take many *atigrāhya* cups. By that very means he makes them possessed of the Sāman, possessed of the *uktha*, possessed of a foundation, and possessed of an abode. He who knows thus becomes possessed of a foundation and possessed of an abode. 7.
The offspring of Prajāpati, those being born and those already born—announce them to him; may he, the wise one, grant his approval.
The creatures of Paśupati are both diverse and similar; may he who is self-ruling approve that one whom the gods have chosen among them.
The ancients, fully aware, received the vital breath as it issued forth from the limbs. Offered, go by the paths traveled by the gods; take your stand among the plants with your bodily remains.
Those who, being bound, followed after what was being bound, observing it with mind and eye—
may the god Agni release them first, Prajāpati, in harmony with his offspring.

May the divine Vāyu, together with Viśvakarman, first release those wild animals which are multiform, though being diverse in appearance, they are of one form in many ways; may he do so, rejoicing in his progeny.
Of those animals over whom Paśupati is lord—whether they be four-footed or two-footed—may they, being redeemed, go to their sacrificial portion; may the abundance of wealth enter the sacrificer.
Releasing the seed of the world, O gods, grant a path for the sacrificer. Whatever has been offered and prepared that stood firm, let it go to the dear domain of the gods.
May the various breaths of the sacrificer, together with the animal, go as a sacrifice to the gods by the path of the gods;
may the sacrifice properly bestow long life upon the lord of the sacrifice.
O Śamitṛs, you who are endowed [with skill], the oblation has been prepared for the gods; release the noose from the animal, the noose from the lord of the sacrifice.
May Aditi release these bonds; homage be to the cattle and to the Lord of Cattle!
May he who hates us fall low; upon him we fasten these bonds.
Thee, O Agni, those [gods] have established as the first one to be beheld, as the maker of the cooked oblation and as the one worthy of sacrifice.
Having become of one body with the skillful [gods], O Jātavedas, then carry the offering to the gods.
O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum, for you have become the first Hotṛ-priest.
O Agni, unite with a body of clarified butter; may the desires of the sacrificer come true. (8)

The cattle were born from Prajāpati, both those already born and those yet to be born; they belong to Rudra. He who slaughters an animal belonging to these two without having asked them for permission acts with cattle that are deprived of their rightful owner. Having asked for permission from those to whom the animal belongs, and being permitted and impelled by them, he prospers. "A living animal must be made to go to the heavenly world," they say, "for a dead one is not fit to go to the heavenly world. Knowing this, they accept [the animal] first while it is still alive, [so that] it may go to the heavenly world while living.

He causes [the sacrificer] to go to the world; and those domestic animals and those wild animals—when this [victim] is being immolated, they meditate upon it. That sacrificer is liable to perish, becoming devoid of cattle, [if he does not do so]. "Those wild animals which are being bound after [the victim] is being bound, the multiformed ones"—this is the complete liberation of the cattle. He offers these five oblations; cattle are fivefold; as great as the cattle are, so great he causes them to go to the heavenly world.

When he causes [the animal] to smell [the offering], he thereby sacrifices that very one which has been designated. "The sacrifice is indeed an animal; from the sacrifice, the sacrificer sacrifices this animal," they say. "Where, then, is the sacrificer at this moment? [He replies: "The breath of the sacrificer is separate from that of the animal. Thus he separates the breaths of the two. "Verily, by saying 'The breath is separate,' he deprives him of the sacrifice. [He says: "May the sacrifice bestow full life upon the lord of the sacrifice. Thus he makes him prosper through the sacrifice. These two, the rope and the animal, are indeed above in yonder world.

And by means of this [formula], the sacrificer does not release the bond from those two [the two posts]. [The formula is: "O preparers, approach! The oblation of the gods has been prepared; release the bond of the animal, release the bond of the lord of the sacrifice. Thus he indeed releases the bond from these two. He who acts thus [is freed] from the noose of Varuṇa and remains unaging in that world. If he should practice sorcery, he should strike a post or a piece of wood with the words: "May he who hates us fall low; upon him we fasten these bonds. Thus he fastens the bond upon him.

In that he prepares the animal-cooking fire, he diminishes the Āhavanīya fire which is Varuṇa’s noose; [he counters this] with the verse, "Thee, O Agni, they have established as the first beholder," whereby he makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. With the words, "O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum," he causes him to go to the heavenly world. Whatever in the sacrifice of the seers and the gods was unpurified, that they purified by means of these [verses]; whatever in his sacrifice is unpurified, that he purifies by means of these. By means of these, they drove away the *āvya* (the impurity);
that is the reason for the name *apāvya* (driving away). By means of these, he drives away the *āvya*. 9.

In the third heaven, indeed, was the Soma; Gāyatrī fetched it, and a leaf of it was torn off; that became the *parṇa* tree. That is the reason for the name of the *parṇa*. Therefore all trees possess leaves, and this very thing is called *parṇa* when it is a branch of the *parṇa* tree. By means of that very [branch], one secures the Soma. The gods, indeed, deliberated upon the Brahman; the *parṇa* heard that. He is truly named Suśravas (the Well-hearing); he who knows thus does not become deaf. When he causes [the victim] to move forward with a *parṇa* branch, [it is for this reason].

Verily, by means of the *brahman*, he impels them. Prajāpati created cattle; this god (Agni) became intent upon them; he quieted him with the *śamī* tree; that is the reason for the *śamī*'s name as "the pacifier" (*śamī*). When he impels [the animals] with a branch of the *śamī*, it is for the sake of peace. Darbha grass is indeed the brilliance of the waters and of the plants; when he impels them with blades of darbha grass, he impels them by means of the brilliance of the waters and of the plants. With the words, "For food thee! For strength thee! he bestows food and strength upon the sacrifice. With the words, "Ye are for Vāyu,"—Vāyu is indeed the overseer of the atmosphere, and these [animals] have the atmosphere as their deity.

The animals are indeed Vāyu; he entrusts them to the intermediate space. When he says, "O you who belong to Vāyu," he truly releases them. For Vāyu belongs to the wild, and by saying, "O you who have fodder," he secures the animals for the sacrificer. With the words, "May the god Savitṛ impel you," it is for the sake of impulsion. With the words, "For the most excellent rite,"—the sacrifice is indeed the most excellent rite—he says, "Swell up, O inviolable ones, for the portion of the gods. Formerly, these cows swelled for the sake of both calves and men; now, however, he makes them swell for the gods alone.

"May they swell, rich in offspring, free from disease, and free from consumption"—thus he makes them indeed prosperous, free from disease, and free from consumption. "May neither thief nor ill-wisher master you"—he thus invokes a blessing. "May the missile of Rudra avoid you"—he thus spares the cattle from Rudra; Rudra becomes harmless toward the cattle of him who, knowing this, and who, knowing this, drives out the cows for the oblation. "May they be steadfast with this lord of cattle"—thus he makes them firm; "may they be many"—thus he increases them.

He causes them to reach abundance. With the words, "Protect the cattle of the sacrificer," he hides the branch facing inward for the protection of the sacrificer's cattle; therefore, domestic animals return from the forest to the village in the evening. If he were to hide it facing away, they would be lost in the forest.
Thus ends the thirtieth section, named the Pātnīvata, in the Madhyamikā Caraka-śākhā of the Kāṭhaka Śrī-Yajurveda, which is divided into one hundred and one branches of the Adhvaryu tradition. 30.
And this Madhyamaka is complete.
Now follows the Orimikā.
Now begins the thirty-first section:
the Puroḍāśa Brāhmaṇa.

Prajāpati indeed knows the plants joint by joint; the horse is related to Prajāpati; when he strews the sacrificial grass with the horse’s rib, it is for the non-injury of the plants. With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes it up, impelled by Savitṛ and with the deities. With the words, "Thou art the seat of cattle," he bestows wealth upon the sacrificer. With the words, "The Rakṣas is burnt away," he drives away the Rakṣases from the very mouth of the sacrifice. With the words, "This Dhiṣaṇā has gone forth toward the sacrificial grass,"—for Dhiṣaṇā is knowledge—he approaches it with knowledge. It was fashioned by Manu and by the Svadhā-call.

"Vitaṣṭā"—for she was indeed fashioned by Manu with the *svadhā* offering; "vitaṣṭorvantarikṣaṃ vīhi" (fashioned, enter the wide mid-air); [he says this] for the sake of completeness. "Indrasya pariṣūtamasī" (Thou art the portion set aside for Indra)—whatever exists here, all that is the portion set aside for Indra. Just as one performs a rite after announcing it to a superior, even so he cuts the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) after announcing it to Indra. As much as he indicates by pointing out, if he does not cut all of that, it is an excess of the sacrifice. Whatever is an excess of the sacrifice, by that he increases his rival. He should indicate only a single tuft; that [he should cut].

Everything [is for] the non-excess of the sacrifice; whatever portion one does not leave over for the cattle as their livelihood—whether one leaves over one *śnuṣṭi*, or two—one does not cause an excess in the sacrifice, yet one leaves over a livelihood for the cattle. [One should cut with the formula: "May I prosper neither below nor above, but on the surface; may I succeed. He should cut [thinking], "May this not harm you. For as much as the ignorant Adhvaryu cuts from the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), so much is diminished from his own self; he whose self is not diminished is he who knows thus: "O divine *barhis*, hundred-branched..."

"O plant, grow forth"—he thus bestows abundance upon the plants. "May we grow forth with a thousand branches"—thus he invokes a blessing. "Thou art Aditi’s girdle"—Aditi is this earth; he thus makes her his girdle. "The binding of Indrāṇī"—Indrāṇī was the first among the deities to bind herself; she attained success, for the sake of prosperity. He binds the sacrificial grass (barhis); the sacrificial grass is indeed offspring; it is for the non-separation of offspring, therefore offspring are connected by sinews.

"May Pūṣan tie your knot"—Pūṣan is indeed nourishment; verily he bestows nourishment upon the sacrificer. "May it not slip from you"—this is for the sake of non-injury. "I lift you up with the arms of Indra"—verily he lifts it up with the arms of Indra. "I carry you on the head of Bṛhaspati"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; verily he carries it by means of the Brahman. "You are one that goes to the gods"—much of this [Soma] spills when it is being carried on the previous day; verily he presents it to the gods without spilling.

Regarding this, the seers recite: "The seers indeed bring it forward from the front. The seers are the Brahmins, for it is the Brahmins who bring this forward. With the words, "Sit here upon the sacred grass (barhis), which is pleasing to the gods," he makes it pleasing to the gods.

"You are the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams; you are the purifier of the Vasus, with a thousand streams. This purifier is indeed the portion of the Vasus; he thus makes it for them. Prajāpati created offspring; his two fire-pan lids (ukhā) became exhausted. He saw these two [pans], and with them he took hold. In that these two fire-pan lids exist, he restores the two fire-pan lids of Prajāpati himself. "Free from disease, I unite you with offspring"—thus he makes them free from disease. "May they become abundant through the increase of wealth"—thus he says.

He causes them indeed to go to abundance with the words, "Swell, rich in honey and rich in ghee"; thus he makes an offering for the gods that is rich in honey and rich in ghee. With the words, "Living, living, may we come unto you," he invokes a blessing.
