With the words, "Thou art the heat of Mātariśvan," he [refers to] the atmosphere, for the heat of Mātariśvan is indeed the atmosphere. With "Thou art the sky; thou art the earth," he makes her (the milking vessel) like the sky and the earth. With "By the supreme support of Viśvadhāyas, thou art unshaken; do not shake," he makes her firm. He covers her with a filter and thus mixes together the milk of plants and of cattle. With the words, "She is all-life, she is all-extensive, she is all-sustaining"—the sky is indeed all-life, the atmosphere is all-extensive, and this earth is all-sustaining—he [establishes] these very worlds in their proper order.

These worlds cause [the milk] to be given to him, just as they were previously bestowed; he milks the three with the *yajus* formula and consecrates them with the *yajus*. These are the three worlds; verily, he places essence in these very worlds. Therefore, creatures subsist upon these worlds; he who knows thus becomes one upon whom others subsist.

He consecrates [the drop] with the formula: "The offered drop, the offered spark—svāhā to Agni, the great vault! Indeed, this earth is Agni, the great vault. Much of what is being milked here spills; he thus establishes it upon this very earth so that it does not spill. One should not milk into a wooden vessel, for a wooden vessel belongs to Agni; one would be sacrificing with sacrificial food that has lost its potency. Regarding this, the Dārteyas used to say: "Sacrificial food has the cake as its mouth; indeed, there is no loss of the sacrificial food from this [vessel] to that. It must simply be milked. One should not do so.

A Śūdra should not milk [the cow], for he is born from what is unreal (asat) and would thus become unreal; moreover, that which passes beyond the filter is indeed the oblation of the Agnihotra, and a Śūdra should not milk that, for they do not purify it. He pours it back with the words, "Be united, O you who flow with nectar," for the sake of cooking it, since the gods desire cooked food.

With the words, "I anoint thee, Indra’s portion, with Soma," he makes it indeed Soma. Soma is, as it were, the *sānnāyya* offering of the gods in secret. For him who, knowing this, sacrifices with the *sānnāyya*, the drinking of Soma becomes continuous. With the words, "Thou art a receptacle for Viṣṇu,"—Viṣṇu being the sacrifice—he makes it a receptacle for the sacrifice. He should not cover it with an earthen vessel; for if he were to cover it with an earthen vessel, the oblation would belong to the Pitṛs. He covers it with a wooden vessel; for a wooden vessel contains fire, and thus the oblation is indeed placed within fire.

"Guard it, O water-rich one! he says; the waters are slayers of the Rākṣasas, for the purpose of striking down the Rākṣasas. "O Viṣṇu, guard the oblation! he says; thus Viṣṇu himself guards the oblation. "O waters, be watchful! he says; the waters are indeed the guardians of the sacrifice; to them he entrusts this.

He leads forward the waters; the sacrifice is indeed the waters, so it is the sacrifice itself that he proceeds with after leading them forward. The waters are the dear abode of the gods; having led forward the dear abode of the gods, he proceeds. The waters are slayers of the Rakṣases, for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases. The waters are a thunderbolt; he hurls the thunderbolt at his rival. The waters are faith; the gods and men have faith in him for whom one who knows this leads forward the waters. With the words, "For the sake of the rite, you two," he washes his hands, for this rite is now being performed.

"You are of the forest trees; the Rakṣas is burnt away"—thus he drives away the Rakṣas from the very mouth of the sacrifice. "Go through the wide atmosphere"—this is for the sake of reaching together. "Thou art the yoke-pole; injure him who injures us"—for this fire is indeed the yoke-pole; if one were to pass over it without touching it, he would afflict the sacrificer with pain. There are two kinds of enemies for a man: him whom he hates and him who hates him; these two he afflicts with pain.

"You are the best bearer for the gods"—thus he makes it a bearer for the gods. "Thou art Viṣṇu’s stride; thou art unshakable; O Soma-holder, be firm, do not waver"—thus he makes it firm. "I gaze upon thee with the eye of Mitra"—thus he makes it Mitra. "Wide for thee, O wind"—whatever the wind does not blow over, that belongs to Varuṇa; thus he frees it from Varuṇa’s power. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ"—impelled by Savitṛ, he offers it to the deities. "To such-and-such, agreeable"—[he says].

He makes it pleasing to whichever deity he offers it; with the words "May the five hold you," he indeed gratifies the five seasons. Those seasons, being gratified, become favorable to him; the seasons become favorable to him who knows thus.

"For protection from thee, not from misfortune"—this is for the striking away of the *rakṣases*. "This is of the gods, this is ours together"—this is for separation. "I have looked upon the light"—verily, he enters as it were into darkness when he goes around the enclosure; [by saying this] he looks out clearly as if toward the light. These worlds, indeed, trembled when the oblation had been taken; the gods steadied them with this *yajus*: "May the dwellings be firm"—thus he makes these very worlds firm. He should say, "Pervade the wide atmosphere"; otherwise the *adhvaryu* would be liable to perish in the wide atmosphere.
The Adhvaryu becomes free from fatigue if he knows thus. He sets it down with the words, "O Agni, protect the oblation! and so Agni himself protects the oblation.

With the words, "By Viṣṇu’s mind you are purified," he purifies them; with "May the god Savitṛ purify you," he purifies them by means of the deities, impelled by Savitṛ. With "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he sprinkles it for the deities, impelled by Savitṛ. With "Pleasant to such-and-such [deity]," he makes it pleasant for whichever deity he is sprinkling for. With "May the vessels be cleansed for the sacrifice to the gods," he cleanses these for the gods. With "The Rakṣas is shaken off, the enemy is shaken off," [he shakes the grass-broom].

With the words, "For the driving away of the Rākṣasas; thou art the skin of Aditi," he makes this very skin of hers. With the words, "Thou art the pressing-sieve, made of wood," he makes it indeed a pressing-sieve. With the words, "Thou art the body of Agni, the release of speech," for this is indeed the body of Agni and the release of speech; for when cattle eat plants, they then release their speech. With the words, "Thou art the great stone, made of wood," having thus made it a stone, he prepares the oblation. With the words, "O preparer of the oblation, come! he calls him who is the most excellent preparer of the oblation among the gods.

He calls out three times, for the gods are true to their word. "Thou art the stone, the maker of the hymn; the Rakṣas is smitten away, the enemy is smitten away"—this is for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. "May we conquer every host, every host"—verily, he conquers every hostile host.

The speech of the sacrificer, the god Manu Śraddhādeva, had entered the sacrificial implements as a slayer of the Asuras. Of those [implements], as many Asuras as heard them were defeated. If one who knows this should sacrifice after settling in the midst of his rivals, he takes away the sensory power and vigor of as many of his rivals as hear the sacrificial implements; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. With the words, "Thou art grown by rain; may that which is grown by rain recognize thee," it is indeed a pairing.

By means of the husks, the gods drove away the *rakṣases* from the cattle; by means of the chaff, they drove them away from the plants. With the words, "The *rakṣas* is winnowed away! The enemy is winnowed away! he drives the *rakṣases* away from the sacrifice by this much alone. With the words, "The evil-plotters are cast out,"—for the evil-plotters are indeed one's rivals—he casts out his rival. "May Vāyu separate [the grain] for sap and vigor"—Vāyu is indeed the purifier of the gods; he thus purifies them. He makes them well-husked; he makes them pure and fit for sacrifice. He husks them three times, for the gods are true to the number three.

"The Rakṣas is shaken off; the enemy is shaken off"—thus, by means of the removal of the Rakṣases, [he says]. "Thou art the skin of Aditi"—thus he makes this very earth his skin. "Thou art Dhiṣaṇā, the daughter of the mountain; may the skin of Aditi recognize thee; do thou make firm the earth"—thus he indeed makes the earth firm. "Thou art Dhiṣaṇā, the daughter of the mountain; may the daughter of the mountain recognize thee; do thou make firm the sky"—thus he indeed makes the sky firm. "Thou art the pillar of the sky"—with these words he lays down the *śamyā* (peg). These two [worlds] were indeed together; they moved apart by the measure of a *śamyā*, by the measure of a *śamyā*.

The *vajra* is the *śamyā*; in that he places the *śamyā*, it is for the sake of separating these two. "Thou art grain; prosper the gods"—by the power of this *yajus*, as much as one deity might desire, so much does the offering of this [oblation] expand. "For out-breathing thee, for diffused-breathing thee, for in-breathing thee"—he thus bestows out-breathing, diffused-breathing, and in-breathing upon the sacrificer. "Along the long extension, for life thee"—verily, he bestows life upon him. "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you"—[thus he says], as if toward the front.

These [drops] indeed spill; [he offers with the formula] "for stability, with unimpaired vision I behold," for the protection of the eye, for the increase of wealth, and for good offspring—he thus invokes a blessing.

"The Rakṣas is burnt away, the enemy is burnt away"—this is for the driving away of the Rakṣases. "O Agni, drive away the Agnimāda"—having thus driven away that raw-flesh-eating Agnimāda, he places [the fire] upon the sacrificial ground fit for sacrifice. In that he turns the ember downward, he thereby bestows light upon this world; in that he turns it upward, he thereby bestows light upon the intermediate space. That very sun becomes his light in yonder world; all these worlds become luminous for him. Three...

He lays down the *samīcī* bricks; there are three vital breaths—prāṇa, vyāna, and apāna—and he places these very breaths within the sacrificer. These are the three worlds; verily, he prospers in these worlds. "Thou art firm; make the earth firm!"—verily, he makes the earth firm. "Give life, give breath!"—verily, he invokes this blessing. "Thou art the supporter; make the atmosphere firm!"—verily, he makes the atmosphere firm. "Give sight!"—verily, he invokes this blessing. "Thou art the sustainer; make the sky firm!"—verily, he makes the sky firm. "Give vigor, give strength!"—verily, he invokes this blessing.

"Give," he says; verily he invokes a blessing. "Thou art Dharma; make firm the quarters," he says; verily he makes the quarters firm. "Give wealth, give prosperity," he says; verily he invokes a blessing. "The bond of hope is thine; make firm hope," he says; verily he makes hope firm. "Give form, give color," he says; verily he invokes a blessing.

Prajāpati, indeed, when he first came into being, came into being as exactly this much; for in the beginning, one skull of the head comes into being, then a second, then a third, then a fourth, then a fifth, then a sixth, then a seventh, then an eighth. When he lays down eight bricks joined together, the sacrificer thereby prepares his own self; having been prepared, he follows after that [self] in yonder world. In that he lays down eight, he obtains the Gāyatrī metre.

In that there are eleven [bricks], he makes them measured by the *triṣṭubh* meter; in that there are twelve, he makes them measured by the *jagatī* meter. Thus he lays them down as precisely measured by their meters. By saying, "Ye are piled, ye are piled around," he makes them all possessed of the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). By saying, "Be heated by the heat of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases," he heats them with the heat of these very deities. By saying, "The potsherds which the wise pile upon the *gharma*,"—for the *gharma* is indeed yonder sun, and the quarters are its potsherds—he thereby releases them according to their proper place. These belong to Pūṣan as well. As for the vow...
"O Indra and Vāyu, let [the chariot] be unyoked"—by this, he makes Indra and Vāyu their unyokers.

With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he, impelled by Savitṛ, pours it out for the deities. With the words, "Pleasant to such-and-such [a deity]," he makes it an oblation for whichever deity he is pouring it out for; he indeed makes it acceptable to that deity. He pours it out over the strainers; thus he makes it an oblation. He pours water upon it; water is immortality, so he makes the oblation immortal. With the words, "The waters together with the plants, the plants together with their sap," he unites them; for one set of these [plants] quickens the other. With the words, "O wealthy ones, [bestow] wealth upon us... [he completes the rite].

"That which is yours, the sacrificial, from the sacrificial; that which is yours, the moving, from the moving"—the *revatī* verses are indeed the waters, and the *madhumatī* verses are the plants; the *jagatī* verses are cattle. Having thus combined the waters, the plants, and the cattle into a single whole for him, he makes them full of sweetness.

With "For Janayati thee," he mixes [the flour]; thus he creates a pair. With "Thou art the head of Makha"—Makha is indeed the sacrifice—he thereby makes the head of the sacrifice. With "The Gharma, the life of all, spread wide; may the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for thee," he causes it to expand. With "The Rakṣas is burnt up," he drives away the Rakṣas from the very mouth of the sacrifice. That cake which is offered every half-month is indeed the Gharma; if it were not appeased, it would be liable to burn up the cattle of the sacrificer. In that he performs the carrying of fire around it (paryagni-karoti), [he pacifies it].

He makes it like an animal for the sake of peace and so that it may not burn; he carries it around three times, for these worlds are three; verily, from these worlds he pacifies it. When the sacrificial cake was placed upon the fire, the Rakṣases sought to destroy it; that fire in heaven named Nāka is the slayer of Rakṣases, and it drove the Rakṣases away from it. With the words, "May the god Savitṛ bake you upon the highest firmament," he effects the driving away of the Rakṣases. With the words, "May Agni not injure your body," he causes the skin to take hold [of the cake] for the sake of non-injury.

Therefore, the brain is enclosed; and those which are these skull-bones of the head are the *kapālas*. The brain is the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). If he were not to cover it, the brain would be exposed; because he covers it, therefore the brain is hidden. He covers it with ashes; therefore bone is covered with flesh. He strews it over with the *veda* (grass-bundle); therefore the head is covered with hair. Those gods did not find that place upon which they might sprinkle the cruel part of the sacrifice. Agni said: "I shall clothe it."

"I shall produce one in whom you may rub the cruel part of the sacrifice," he said; he then struck the waters with a coal, and from that Ekata was born. From that [second strike], Dvita was born; from that [third], Trita. That which he fashioned from himself is the self-nature of those belonging to the self; that which he fashioned from the waters is the water-nature of those belonging to the waters. He pours it out within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi); thereby he secures it. He sprinkles it with a firebrand for the sake of cooking, for the gods desired cooked [meat]. They went away having cleaned themselves excessively; they cleaned themselves when the sun had risen.

One who has risen before the sun; one who has set after the sun; one who has set after the sun; one with deformed nails; one with deformed nails; one with black teeth; one with black teeth; one whose younger brother marries before him; one whose younger brother marries before him; one who causes his younger brother to marry before him; one who causes his younger brother to marry before him; one who marries before his elder brother; one who marries before his elder brother; one who marries the widow of his deceased younger brother; one who marries the widow of his deceased younger brother; one who kills a hero; one who kills a hero; one who kills a Brahmin; one who kills a Brahmin; one who kills an embryo; [the sin] of one who kills an embryo does not pass away. 7.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he takes up the wooden sword (*sphya*); thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it up with the deities. "Thou art the right arm of Indra, thousand-spiked, hundred-edged"—the wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt; thus he sharpens the thunderbolt, intending to strike his rival. "O Earth, place of sacrifice to the gods! May I not harm thy root, O herb!"—this is for the non-injury of plants. "Go to the pen, the cow-stall"—the pen and the cow-stall are indeed the *chandas* (metres); thus he provides the *chandas* as a pen for him.

He makes a stall for the cattle with the words, "May the sky rain for you"; verily, he brings down the rain. With the words, "Bind him, O God Savitṛ, upon the furthest earth with a hundred fetters," he binds both of a man's rivals—him whom he hates and him who hates him—upon the furthest earth with a hundred fetters. With the words, "May your drop not leap to the sky," he restrains within this earth that very essence which is its drop, upon which these creatures subsist.

"Lest it fall upon the *araru* on the earth"—for the *araru* is indeed the rival; he thus drives the rival away from the heavenly world. There was once an Asura named Araru who feared, "The gods will overcome us by means of the sacrifice. He smeared the earth with poison, making it impure. When Indra slew Vṛtra, this [earth] flowed after him with blood, and it became impure. In that they dig out [the earth], they remove whatever is impure and unfit for sacrifice in her. There was once an Asura named Araru...

He was afraid, thinking, "The gods will exclude me from the earth. He crept up to the earth and lay down. Indra perceived him and said, "Drive him away from the earth, the place of sacrifice for the gods; drive him away from the place of sacrifice on earth! They drove him away from the earth. He flew toward the sky, thinking, "Let him not fall upon me from the sky! Indra pushed him back from the sky. Then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. For whomsoever, knowing thus, the *stambayajus* is carried out, and by whomsoever, knowing thus, it is carried out—for him he excludes his rival from these very worlds.

He prospers by his own self, and his rival is defeated. This earth belonged to the Asuras. Those gods said, "Give us a portion of this. They replied, "You yourselves must ask for it. Then Agni conquered the eastern quarter; the Vasus, the southern; the Rudras, the western; and the Ādityas, the northern. Those gods thus took possession of this earth from the Asuras. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who, knowing this, encloses the altar with these deities, takes possession of this very earth from his rival.

He finds prosperity for himself; his rival becomes defeated. Indeed, from the earth, the pure and the impure separated: the pure went out toward the east and north, while the impure went out toward the west and south. One should make the altar (vedi) sloping toward the east and north; thus one makes it sacrificially pure in its center. Furthermore, this is for the sake of distinguishing between the pure and the impure. He raises the two arms toward the east; thereby he encompasses the Āhavanīya fire. The two hips face westward; thereby he encompasses the Gārhapatya fire.

The Rakṣases indeed drink after the roots; one should not cut them with the fingernail—for if one were to cut them with the fingernail, he would become one with deformed nails. He cuts them with the wooden sword (sphya); for the wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt (vajra), and by means of the thunderbolt he strikes down the Rakṣases. ||8||

Ghee and honey were indeed Prajāpati; from that which was honey, he created offspring. Therefore, there is a generative quality in honey; for this reason, they do not perform the ritual with honey, for it is exhausted. They perform it with ghee, for this is unexhausted. That which is clarified butter (*ājya*) belongs to Prajāpati; it is unexhausted. Prajāpati, who belongs to the gods, places it over the *gārhapatya* fire. The wife looks upon it; this is the wife’s taking hold of the sacrifice. Moreover, she thereby establishes a couple at the beginning of the sacrifice for the sake of procreation.

Whatever the wife does at the sacrifice constitutes a pair; when the wife looks [at the oblation], she creates a pair. That which the wife looks upon is indeed impure and unfit for sacrifice; he places it over the Āhavanīya fire, and thus he makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. The gods and the Asuras performed the sacrifice equally; whatever the gods did, the Asuras did that too. Indra perceived this opening (avakāśa) and looked with it; by that he overcame the Asuras. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.

He who, knowing thus, gazes at the clarified butter with this [formula], truly overcomes his rival; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. With the words, "The Rakṣas is burnt up," he drives away the Rakṣases from the very mouth of the sacrifice. With the words, "You are sharpened, destroyers of rivals," he indeed makes them sharp. He wipes the spoons; he purifies them. First he wipes the *sruva* ladle; he thereby sharpens the male among them first. Then the *juhū*, then the *upabhṛt*, then the *dhruvā*. That [heaven] indeed...

The *juhū* is the intermediate space, the *upabhṛt* is this [earth], and the *dhruvā* is yonder [heaven]; thus he cleanses these very worlds in their proper order. The *juhū* has the sacrificer as its deity, while the *upabhṛt* has the rival as its deity. When taking four portions in the *juhū*, he takes more clarified butter; when taking eight in the *upabhṛt*, he takes less. Thus, he makes the rival a subordinate for him.

With the words, "O divine waters, you who go before," he leads forward the sacrifice itself; with "Lead this sacrifice forward, further the lord of the sacrifice," he invokes a blessing. The sacrificial essence (medhas) of Agni departed, having become a black antelope; it entered the trees. [He says: "You are sprinkled; you are the black one dwelling in the pen; I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni"—thus he wins that very sacrificial essence. Moreover, for whichever deity he sprinkles him, he makes him acceptable to that deity. [He says: "You are the altar; I sprinkle you, acceptable to the sacrificial grass (barhis)."

"Thou art the sacrificial grass; I sprinkle thee, acceptable to the ladles. The sacrificial grass is indeed offspring, and the altar is the earth; thus he establishes offspring upon the earth. "Go to the earth with strength"—he thereby bestows strength upon the earth. Therefore, offspring subsist upon the earth. He who knows this becomes one who is to be subsisted upon.

One should set down many; for as many *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-waters as he sets down, so many waters are there for him in yonder world. Therefore, many should be set down. He takes the *prastara* bundle from the front; thus he makes the sacrificer preeminent. He should take as much as he can grasp with his hand; the sacrificer becomes free from hunger and the *adhvaryu* priest remains unexposed. He should not shake it; if he were to shake it, he would shake off both his offspring and his cattle. He should not wipe it; whatever is his own, whatever is his wealth, and whatever is to be known—that is [preserved].

He wipes it, yet he should not wipe it; for whatever is coming toward him, that he repels. He spreads the girding-bunch to the south; therefore the knot (*nīvi*) is on the right. Holding the *prastara* as a support, he lays down the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). The *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer; thus the sacrificer himself encloses his own self for the warding off of the *rakṣases*. He lays down the enclosing-sticks joined together so that the *rakṣases* may have no passage through them. He does not lay one down in front, for that very Sun rises from this [place].

He repels the Rakṣases from the front; he places two kindling-sticks upright; thus he smites the Rakṣases from above. He places two [sticks]; verily he creates a pair. "Ye are the arms of Savitṛ, the support of the divine folk," for these are indeed the arms of Savitṛ, the support of the divine folk. "Thou art the seat of the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas"—verily, for those very deities whom he has conquered, he prepares this seat. "Come, O ladle, dripping with ghee"—this, indeed, is their beloved abode, that which possesses ghee.

He causes them to prosper with their own dear abode. "They have settled, firm in the womb of Truth; protect them, O Viṣṇu!"—by saying this, he says to Viṣṇu: "This is your portion; guard it. It is just as if one were to say: "This is your clarified butter; guard it."

"Thou art the world; spread out!"—thus he causes [the fire] to spread. "Agni is the sacrificer; here is homage"—for by paying homage, they approach one who is superior. "Come, O Agni, thou art summoned for the sacrifice to the gods"—Agni is all the deities; thus he wins all the deities. "Come, O Upabhṛt, the god Savitṛ summons thee for the sacrifice to the gods"—impelled by Savitṛ, he proceeds and does not meet with misfortune. "With my foot, O Viṣṇu, may I not step upon you two"—this is according to the sacrificial formula. "Protect me, O Agni, from evil conduct; do not lead me..."

"Partake of good conduct"—this he says to strike away evil. "Depart from one another; do not burn me"—this is for his own non-injury. "O makers of the world, create a world for me"—thus he invokes a blessing. "The station of Viṣṇu"—this is for stability. "Upright is the sacrifice, touching the sky"—the sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; this is for the upward elevation of the sacrifice. "Unassailed is the sacrifice of the Lord of Sacrifice"—this is for prosperity. "Accompanied by Indra, great-luminous, Svāhā!"—the sacrifice belongs to Indra; thus he presents the sacrifice to Indra at its very beginning, so that it remains possessed by Indra.

The sacrifice becomes [united] with light by the words, "Light with light. For the sacrifice is indeed light; he thus continues the sacrifice within the sacrifice itself. With the words, "By the impulse of strength, through the divinity Agni-Soma, I conquer," he drives away that rival who has previously surpassed him. With the words, "By the impulse of strength, through the divinity Agni-Soma, I repel so-and-so," he drives away that rival who stands behind him. Thus he drives away a superior rival and repels an inferior one.

"Thou art for the earth, thou art for the atmosphere, thou art for the sky"—with these words he causes him to go to these very worlds. "Licking the offered [oblation], let them go forth with vigor"—thus he makes it palatable. "The spotted cow of the Maruts, having become dappled, go to the sky"—the *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer; thus he causes him, having become the oblation, to go to the heavenly world. "From there, send down rain for us"—verily, he secures rain. "Infallible is the breath"—thereby the Adhvaryu arranges the vital breaths from the beginning. "Thou art the protector of sight; protect my sight."

"For the protection of the eye, that fence which you have placed around yourself, O divine Agni, when being kindled by the Paṇis"—by this, Agni, who is all the deities, secures for himself all the deities. "Spread out the sacrificer," he says; thus he causes him to expand and leads him to abundance. "Those who share in the remnants of the oblation," with these words he makes offerings over the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*); he thus gratifies them with their own respective portions.

"O Agni, of unassailable life, of uninjured body"—whatever they omit and whatever cruel thing they do, he pacifies that [with these words]. "Make our food free from poison"—he thus makes the food palatable for him. "The earth, a good seat for those of good seats"—he thus establishes him on a good seat. The sacrificial altar (vedi) indeed departed from the gods; they found it with the *veda* (sweeping-broom), and that is why the *veda* has its name. That there is a *veda* is for the purpose of finding the altar. The altar is female and the *veda* is male; when he sweeps the altar with the *veda*, it is indeed a productive union.

The Veda is indeed the beard of Prajāpati. If he should desire of a wife, "May she obtain a son," he creates a union for her by placing [the Veda] upon her lap with his mouth. He indeed cuts the sacrifice asunder when he brings it to a conclusion at the half-month; in that he spreads the Veda continuously from the Āhavanīya fire, he thereby makes the sacrifice continuous. He offers it continuously during the subsequent half-month.

The upaveṣa is indeed the encircler of the trees; for one who knows thus, his dwellings (veśāḥ) become unassailable. He strikes it toward the west from the front; therefore the dwellings are situated facing westward. He strikes it from the thickest part so that the dwellings do not speak over him. Indeed, the sacrifice is performed for the serpents; the upaveṣa is a serpent, the ant-hill is the rubbish-heap (utkara). In that he throws the upaveṣa onto the rubbish-heap, therefore the ant-hill is the home of the serpents.

Indeed, an Adhvaryu who, not knowing the union of the offering-spoons (*sruk*), responds when called "Adhvaryu! Adhvaryu!", is cut off from the deities; he becomes childless and without cattle. But an Adhvaryu who, knowing the union of the offering-spoons, responds when called "Adhvaryu! Adhvaryu!", is not cut off from the deities; he becomes possessed of offspring and cattle. With the call "Āśrāvaya" (Make it heard!), he unites the *juhū* spoon; with "Astu śrauṣaṭ" (Let there be hearing!), he unites the *upabhṛt* spoon; with "Yaja" (Sacrifice!), he unites the *dhruvā* spoon; and with "Ye yajāmahe" (We who sacrifice), he unites the butter-vessel; [all] by means of the *vaṣaṭ*-call.

Yonder [sun] is indeed the *sruva* ladle; the atmosphere is the *juhū*; this [earth] is the *upabhṛt*; the quarters are the *dhruvā*; the sun is the vessel for the clarified butter (*ājyadhānī*); and speed is yonder [sun]. Yonder [sun] bestows this [earth], and this [earth] bestows upon yonder [sun]. Therefore, whatever [clarified butter] he pours from the *juhū*, with that he replenishes the *dhruvā*; and whatever [he pours] from the *dhruvā*, with that he replenishes the *juhū*. For yonder [sun] bestows upon this [earth], and this [earth] bestows upon yonder [sun]. To him who knows thus, it is bestowed continuously and without interruption.
Be seated comfortably for me on this pleasant seat upon the earth—broad, wide, and expanding in the heavenly realm.

You are the sacrificial ladle, sharpened with ghee, the destroyer of rivals; sit in heaven, in the intermediate space, and upon the earth, so that I may become supreme and my rivals be cast beneath me.

Ascend the path that leads to the gods, where the ancient seers of old first went. O swift one with golden wings and well-formed limbs, carry me to that highest world of the doers of good deeds, where I may be supreme and my rivals be beneath me.
With the *upabhṛt* ladle I drive away my enemy—the born rivals and those yet to be born. I milk the sacrifice like a cow that yields well; may I be supreme, and may my rivals be beneath me.

O Agni, whoever, malicious in heart, has assailed us with word or thought, acting as an enemy from afar—may his intention fall lower than this firm earth; may I be the highest, and my rivals be the lowest.

O Agni, whatever of this sacrifice of mine may be harmed, or whatever of the clarified butter may be spilled, O Viṣṇu—with that I strike down the malevolent rival; I place him in the lap of Destruction. Whoever here desires our youngest [offspring], let him [be struck] for me, the sacrificer, at this sacrifice.
May Indra and Agni drive those beings away; may I obtain offspring rich in food and endowed with brave sons.
This Veda has found the earth, which was hidden in secret places within the depths;
may it find a world for me, the sacrificer, and may he, rich in seed, make the sacrifice flawless.
Strew the sacrificial grass; enclose the altar; do not harm the sacrificial ladle lying there.
Strew it with golden-colored darbha grass; let these be the gold neck-ornaments for the sacrificer.
In this sacrifice of mine, let there be further abundance; I set up the enclosing-sticks for the sake of non-disturbance.
May the Sustainer, the Ordainer, the Supporter, and the Most Firm One drive away all hostilities.
The four-crested young woman, the good wife, being led forth for great good fortune;
milking out ghee for the people, may she, Aditi, milk for me all things desired for prosperity.

By means of sacred knowledge they discovered the altar upon the earth; that earth spread itself out for the sake of all that is earthly. She bears the germ within the worlds, and from thence the sacrifice is performed at all times.
Driving away the stinginess of the people, [these two goddesses] push aside every born enemy and the malevolent one;
settling as goddesses in the world of the well-performed deed, may they both drive away all hostilities.
May Dhruvā, worthy of sacrifice, swell with clarified butter for the sake of the gods who seek the sacrifice;
may she, like the udder of Sūryā in the lap of Aditi, yield her milk in abundance at this sacrifice.
Place milk in the earth, milk in the plants, milk in the heavens, and milk in the intermediate space;
may the quarters of space be full of milk for me. 14.

The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed a complete sacrifice. To whom do the deities come for the sacrifice, and to whom do they not? Among many sacrificers who perform the sacrifice on the same day, those deities come to the sacrifice on the following day for him who takes hold of them on the previous day. With the words, "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations," he first takes hold of Agni. Since Agni is all the deities, he thus takes hold of the deities themselves on the previous day and worships them on the following day. On the full moon day, they enter upon the vow with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

In ancient times, on the new moon night, before the calves were driven away, the husband and wife would eat after washing their hands; standing to the south of the fire, he should say: "O Agni, lord of vows, undertake the vow. For Agni is indeed the lord of vows and the Brāhmaṇa is the bearer of the vow; having addressed the lord of vows, he undertakes the vow, and his vow succeeds for him. If he should undertake the vow when the sun has set, he should worship the fire and recite this Yajus: "Agni has entered there as the Hotṛ; I invoke him. For at that time, Agni has indeed entered [the sun].

He touches the vessel with which he is about to pour out the oblation. The deities are indeed difficult to grasp, and the sacrifice is difficult to grasp; thus he grasps both the deities and the sacrifice. With the words, "May the gods come, being well-disposed,"—these are indeed the divine invocations (devahūti) of the gods; the gods come to his invocation, and he is not cut off from the sacrifice who knows thus. With the words, "May the gods partake of this my oblation," he invokes a blessing.

With the words, "I yoke thee with divine prayer," he speaks as the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are being laid around; this is indeed the sacrifice of Agni, and by means of the sacred word (*brahman*), he yokes Agni. Yoked, he carries the oblation for the gods to him. With the words, "May the Aṅgirases protect the first recitations of this sacrifice," this is the yoking of the *sāmidhenī* verses; through those verses being yoked, whatever blessing he desires, that he obtains. With the words, "Agni is kindled, he is offered to," this is the kindling itself. [With the words,] "Thou art the mind, belonging to Prajāpati; enter me with the mind that is existence," [he addresses] the mind.

Verily, Prajāpati is like this; the sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati; he thus makes the sacrifice continuous. This speech is Indra’s, the destroyer of rivals; with speech and with power she enters him; for speech is indeed power; verily, he wins power itself.

Truly, they do not know this: whether Brāhmaṇas sacrifice in spring, or whether it rains for the Brāhmaṇas, or for whomever they declare [the victim], or for whichever rain-god he sacrifices while declaring his name—it is to that [deity] the sacrifice goes; it does not approach another. When choosing the *pravara* (ancestral invocation), he should say: "O gods, O fathers, O gods, being who I am, sacrifice. Whosoever he may be, to him the sacrifice goes; it does not approach another. Thus he entrusts the sacrifice to the gods and the fathers; they [protect] it for him.

They protect him by means of his combined sacrificial offerings and works of public utility; he goes to the heavenly world, and that for him becomes inexhaustible and immeasurable. "I gratify the spring among the seasons"—there are five seasons; he thus gratifies the seasons themselves. The seasons, being gratified, become favorable to him who knows this. ||15||
Thus ends the thirty-first section, named the *Puroḍāśabrāhmaṇa*, in the *Orimikā* of the *Caraka-śākhā* within the illustrious *Kāṭhaka-Yajus*. 31.
Now the thirty-second section: The Brāhmaṇa on the Sacrificer.

"By means of Agni and Soma, the sacrifice becomes sighted"—for Agni and Soma are indeed the two eyes of the sacrifice; by means of the eye of the sacrifice itself, he bestows sight upon himself. He who knows thus becomes sighted. "Agni is the lord of food"—Agni is indeed the eater of food among the gods; he causes him to obtain the eating of food among men. He who knows thus becomes an eater of food. "You are a piercer; may I become unpierced; may I pierce so-and-so"—by this very piercing-power (dabdhi), the gods indeed pierced the Asuras. By that same power, [he pierces] his rival.

He who knows thus—the one wishing to harm him does not harm him; he harms no one. "Agni and Soma, slayers of Vṛtra"—for by means of the power of Agni and Soma, Indra slew Vṛtra; by those two alone he lays low his rival. "By the sacrifice to the gods, Agni and Indra, may I become possessed of vigor and heroic power"—for Agni and Indra are indeed vigor and heroic power; verily, he places vigor and heroic power within himself. "By the sacrifice to the god Indra, may I become possessed of sensory power"—for Indra is indeed sensory power; verily, he places sensory power within himself.

"By the sacrifice to Mahendra, may I attain victory and abundance"—verily he attains victory and abundance. "By the sacrifice to Indra Vimṛdha, may I be without a rival"—verily he becomes without a rival. "By the sacrifice to Indra Indriyāvan, may I be rich in cattle"—cattle are indeed power; verily he bestows cattle upon himself. "By the sacrifice to Sarasvatī, may I nourish speech and the eating of food"—Sarasvatī is indeed speech; verily by speech he secures the eating of food. "Of Pūṣan, I..."

"Through the sacrifice to the gods, may I become possessed of nourishment and cattle"—Pūṣan is indeed nourishment; verily, he secures nourishment for himself. "Through the sacrifice to the goddess Aditi, may I attain a firm foundation"—Aditi is this very earth; verily, he finds a firm foundation upon her.

"Through the sacrifice to all the gods, may I attain union with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Thus he attains union with the vital breaths. "Through the sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, may I be procreated with offspring and cattle. Thus he approaches Prajāpati. "Through the sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, may I attain stability in life. Thus he bestows life upon himself and stands firm through the sacrifice. He who knows the deities, the sacrifice, and those who are to be satisfied in the sacrifice, is satisfied with offspring.

The Soma-drink inclines toward him with cattle; for at this time all the deities are present, since it is at the time of the *sviṣṭakṛt* that he unites and sacrifices to them all. This *sviṣṭakṛt* is indeed the sacrifice manifest before one's eyes. By saying, "He has satisfied the sacrifice in the sacrifice," he satisfies both the deities and the sacrifice within the sacrifice; thus he himself is satisfied with offspring and cattle, and the Soma-drink inclines toward him. With the words, "Agni has sacrificed for Agni’s dear abodes," he thereby secures spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). With the words, "He has sacrificed for Soma’s dear abodes..."

"By that [offering], he has sacrificed for the nobility (kṣatra) of Agni and Soma; 'the beloved abodes'—this he utters in a low voice, unexpressed, and thereby he wins the unexpressed. 'He has sacrificed for the beloved abodes of Agni and Soma'—this he utters aloud, expressed; thereby he wins both the unexpressed and the expressed, for this world consists of both the unexpressed and the expressed. Thus, for the winning of both, he wins both the dry and the green; for what is dry belongs to Agni, and what is green belongs to Soma. This world indeed consists of both the dry and the green, and it is for the winning of both. 'He has sacrificed for the beloved [abodes] of the gods who drink the clarified butter (ājyapāḥ)..."

Regarding the word "abodes" (*dhāmāni*): the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s are indeed the gods who drink the clarified butter (*ājyapa*). He thus gratifies both of them; they, being gratified, participate in his sacrifice. ||1||

"Make me great with strength; make me strong with the strength of Vāmadevya"—for Vāmadeva indeed saw this [verse] regarding the names of cattle, and *iḍā* is cattle; thus he bestows cattle upon cattle. "In what is pleasing may I find thy pleasure; invited, may I obtain thy invitation"—the sacrifice has two blessings (*āśis*); it is for the sake of the sacrifice that he invokes this blessing. "Come to me with a good invocation"—he thereby makes her one who possesses a good invocation. "Together with increase of wealth"—thus he approaches together with prosperity. "May Indra bestow power upon us"—this is the milking of *iḍā*.

"May he milk this very *iḍā* for us; may the liberal lords (*maghavan*) attend us with riches"—riches indeed are cattle, and the liberal lords are cattle; thus he places cattle within himself. "May our blessings be fulfilled"—he thereby invokes a blessing. "Conquering the lands by force, O Indra, making my other rivals lowly"—he thereby makes his rival lowly.

"May the Brahman-splendor swell for me; may the Kṣatra-power swell for me"—this is indeed the *iḍā* (sacrificial food) that milks everything for him who knows this; all this comes to pass for him who knows thus. "In me be that great power (*indriya*)," [he says]; for the waters are indeed power; verily, he places power within himself. "O radiant one (*bradhna*), swell! May the quarters be established!"—the radiant one is indeed yonder sun; when he rises, then the quarters become established for him who knows this. That which a non-Brahmin eats is a spilt oblation; of that, Vasiṣṭha alone is the consumer.

He knew the expiation: with the words, "O radiant one, swell," he touches the sacrificial cake; thus he establishes the sacrifice upon the very *dakṣiṇīyas*. It becomes unspilled and undisturbed. Indeed, even that portion of his which a non-Brahmin eats becomes as if offered. Now, Kapiṇava Bhauvāyana used to say: "How could he perform a sacrifice who does not milk the sacrifice like a cow? This [sacrifice] is indeed easier to milk than a cow. With the words, "May the lord of the sacrifice attain his blessings," the sacrificer eats the sacrificer's portion. The sacrificer, indeed...
The sacrifice is the lord of the sacrifice; it is the sacrificer's portion. If the sacrificer eats the sacrificer's portion, he establishes the sacrifice in the very lord of the sacrifice. ||2||

"Through the sacrifice to the god Barhis, may I become possessed of offspring"—for by means of the Barhis, Prajāpati created offspring; verily, he creates offspring. "Through the sacrifice to the god Narāśamsa, may I become possessed of cattle"—for by means of the Narāśamsa, Prajāpati created cattle; verily, he creates cattle. "Through the sacrifice to the god Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, may I attain long life and a firm foundation"—verily, he bestows long life upon himself and stands firm through the sacrifice. "May the blessings yield for me"—the blessings.

Those who desire milk wait upon the sacrificer; just as milch-cows, when not milked, turn away, so indeed do they turn away from that sacrificer. But he who knows thus milks the very blessings: "May this my true blessing go to the gods"—having caused his true blessing to go to the gods, he chooses a boon.

"From the beloved, may she go to the more beloved"—thus he makes her even more beloved than the beloved. "From the praiseworthy, may she go to the more praiseworthy"—thus he makes her even more praiseworthy than the praiseworthy. "With a mind free from malice, go to the gods"—this is what he says; "by that path which leads to the gods, go to the gods"—he thus causes him to attain that very path which leads to the gods. "May Agni cause you to go to the deity by means of the ruddy one; may Indra cause you to go to the deity by means of the two bay horses"—the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is indeed the sacrificer; he thus makes him, having become an oblation, ascend to heaven.

"He leads him to the world; with the words, 'O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice, go to the lord of the sacrifice,' he causes him to go to his very own womb. He who knows the life-span of the sacrifice reaches the full span of life. With the words, 'Thou art the life-span of the sacrifice; may the sacrifice bestow life upon me,' this indeed is the life-span of the sacrifice; he who knows thus reaches the full span of life. When a yoked horse, having been unyoked, either makes the chariot shake or damages it, [he says], 'I loosen thy traces, I loosen thy reins'—this is its unyoking. Having caused the deity to go to the heavenly world, [he performs] this."
Having established [the post], he releases it with the formula, "At the end of Viṣṇu’s sacrifice. Since the sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu, he thus establishes the sacrifice at its very end. ||3||

"The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus, the giver of wealth by the Yatis"—this is indeed the milking of the sacrifice; he thus milks the sacrifice itself. "May the wealth of that sacrifice, well-offered and properly performed, come to me"—thus he invokes a blessing. "The Aṅgirases have offered for me with the morning litany (prātaranuvāka) of this sacrifice"—this is the milking of blessings. "The sacrifice is wealthy, the sacrifice is rich in goods"—thus he makes the sacrifice wealthy. "May the wealth of that wealthy sacrifice come to me"—thus he invokes a blessing. "Soma is the depositor of seed."

Soma is indeed the placer of seed among the gods; Soma himself places seed for him. Tvaṣṭṛ is the fashioner of forms; Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of forms, and he fashions forms for him. "The wives of the gods, Agni the lord of the house—this is the couple for the sacrificer": this is indeed the couple of the New and Full Moon sacrifices; by means of the couple of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, he places a couple within himself. "By the sacrifice to these two gods, may I procreate through a couple"—thus he says, and he is propagated with offspring and cattle.

Or rather, his wife should sit down right behind him; for if he were not to say this, Agni might burn up her offspring. By saying, "O wife, this is your place," he makes a place for her, and so Agni does not burn up her offspring. With the words, "May the wife go with the husband to the good deeds," this is indeed the wife’s taking hold of the sacrifice from behind; "may you both dwell together in the heavenly world, Svāhā! Svāhā to the well-sacrificed, Vaṣaṭ to the ill-sacrificed!"—for both the well-sacrificed and the ill-sacrificed are joined together in the sacrifice of one who [performs it].

He whose sacrifice is well-offered attracts the sacrifice; he becomes more prosperous. He whose sacrifice is ill-offered attracts the sacrifice; he becomes worse off. By means of the well-offering alone, he makes his sacrifice successful and becomes more prosperous. "O Agni, [be] free from sin and free from reproach. For "free from sin" (ayās) is indeed the name of a body of Agni. Regarding this, they say: "O men, by steadfastness. This [formula] belongs to both that atonement of the sacrifice which we know and that which we do not know, and to both that part of the sacrifice which is performed and that which is not performed.

"An expiation for Sarasvatī, the sister of Veśa, svāhā!"—this is indeed the subduing of the dwelling. Even those who live by his means wait upon him, saying, "We wait upon the speech of this Brāhmaṇa or Rājanya," he who knows thus. "With the measure, the counter-measure, the over-measure, and the exact-measure of the sacrifice, I encompass thee"—the Gāyatrī is indeed the measure of the sacrifice, the Triṣṭubh the counter-measure, the Jagatī the over-measure, and the Anuṣṭubh the exact-measure. So many indeed are the meters that carry the sacrifice;
with them he encompasses it, and in them he establishes it. 4.

"Full art thou; may I become full for myself"—with these words, he fulfills those very desires for which he was deficient. Agni indeed consumes the sacrificer who is greater [than himself]; he causes [the water] to flow in an unbroken stream. As the waters are released, the sacrificer is released along with them; moreover, by means of the waters, he thus interposes his own self between himself and Agni to prevent being consumed. Indeed, all of this sacrifice of his—that is, the house and the cattle—is cleansed of its impurity and sinks down in grief. "May the gods, the officiating priests, cleanse [us] from the eastern quarter"—these, indeed, are the purifications of the sacrifice.

These are the pacifications; his sacrifice becomes purified, and Paśupati, the peaceful and non-injurious, [protects] the cattle. With the words, "Viṣṇu strode across the earth with the Gāyatrī metre," [it is said]: the gods, having Viṣṇu as their head, drove away the Asuras from these worlds by means of the metres. In the same way, the sacrificer, having Viṣṇu as his head, drives away his rival from these worlds by means of the metres. With the words, "We have gone to heaven," he indeed goes to heaven. With the words, "We have united with light,"—for the sacrifice is light—he continues the sacrifice within the sacrifice itself.

"Following the turning of the sun, I turn"—thus he turns according to the turning of that very Āditya; moreover, the sacrifice thus turns back. "I entwine the breath of him who hates us and whom we hate"—verily, he entwines the breath of him whom he hates. "Thou art brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me"—verily, he bestows brilliance upon himself. "May I be united with offspring, and may offspring be united with me"—verily, he bestows offspring upon himself. "May I be united with the increase of wealth, and may the increase of wealth be united with me"—cattle, indeed, are the increase of wealth.

"May I obtain abundance of wealth; may I place cattle within myself"—with this he places cattle within himself. "By the splendor of Agni, may I become splendid"—with this he places splendor within himself. "By the life-span of Vāyu, may I become long-lived"—with this he places life-span within himself. "By the luster of Sūrya, may I become lustrous"—with this he places luster within himself. "By the power of Indra, may I become powerful"—Indra is indeed power; with this he places power within himself.

"May Dhātṛ bestow upon me well-being with his support"—thus Dhātṛ indeed bestows well-being upon him with his support. "May I become possessed of offspring through the offspring of Prajāpati"—thus he places offspring within himself. He who strides forth with the *prakrama* steps indeed falls away from this world, for by means of the meters he ascends away [from it]. He is liable to perish; therefore, with the words, "O Agni Gṛhapati," he worships the Gārhapatya fire. Thus he finds firm support in this very world. ||5||

"The gods have gone to the people at the sacrifice"—for that which spills from the sacrifice goes indeed to the people; thus he secures the blessing of the sacrifice from the very people. "I take thee for the support of the five winds"—he who blows here is indeed the sacrifice, and the sacrifice is fivefold; verily, he secures the sacrifice for him. "I take thee for the support of the five waters"—the waters are indeed cattle; verily, he secures cattle for him. "I take thee for the support of the five ridges"—the ridges are indeed the sacrifice.

Verily, he takes up the sacrifice for him; for by this [formula], the New and Full Moon sacrifices become possessed of the *pṛṣṭha* chants. "I take thee for the support of the five quarters," he says; there are indeed five quarters; verily, he takes up the quarters for him, and he conquers all the quarters, and all the quarters become conquered for him. "I take thee for the support of the five peoples," he says.

The *chandāṃsi* (Vedic meters) are indeed the five *pañcajanāḥ* (five classes of beings); the sacrifice is the *chandāṃsi*, and thus the sacrifice bows down toward him. With the words, "May there be prosperity for us; may the oblation reach the gods; may blessings reach the sacrificer," he secures prosperity for himself, while the oblation goes to the gods and the blessings to the sacrificer. With the words, "I take you for the support of the five-holed *caru*,"—the *caru* is these worlds and the five holes are these very worlds—he thereby secures these worlds for him. With the words, "You are the abode, the dear, unassailable place of sacrifice for the gods," he takes the clarified butter (*ājya*) from a well-known spot, as if traveling by a familiar path.

The sacrifice does not fail for him, nor does the sacrifice fail for one who knows thus. Indeed, the sacrifice departed from the gods; they found it by means of the *veda* (sacrificial grass bundle); that is the "Veda-ness" of the *veda*. That there is a *veda* is for the recovery of the sacrifice. The altar (*vedi*) is female and the *veda* is male; when he sweeps the altar with the *veda*, he creates a productive pair. These are indeed the beard of Prajāpati which is the *veda*. If he should desire of a wife, "May she obtain a son," he places [the *veda*] upon her lap with his mouth; thus he creates a productive pair.

The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *veda* grass-bundle is its hair. When he wipes the sacrificial cake with the *veda*, it is for the completeness of the sacrifice. The *veda* is indeed plants, and plants are cattle; that which is between the two fires is the stall of cattle. In that he spreads the *veda* between the two fires, he appropriates the cattle of his rival in their own stall. Difficult to follow is the sacrifice over there; in that there is a *veda*, it is for the attainment of the sacrifice. The sacrifice is indeed split asunder when it reaches completion every half-month.

As he goes continuously from the Āhavanīya fire, he spreads [the grass] and thus maintains the continuity of the sacrifice; he offers that continuous sacrifice in the subsequent half-month. Indeed, there are gods who destroy the sacrifice and those who steal the sacrifice; they dwell in these worlds, seizing and plundering him who gives and him who sacrifices. With the words, "Those gods who destroy the sacrifice and steal the sacrifice, who dwell upon the earth," he passes beyond those very gods who destroy and steal the sacrifice on earth and goes to the intermediate space (antarikṣa). "May we go to the world of the doers of good deeds."

With "We," he indeed invokes a blessing. "Those gods who, being destroyers of the sacrifice and stealers of the sacrifice, dwell in the intermediate space"—having passed beyond those very gods who are destroyers and stealers of the sacrifice dwelling in the intermediate space, he goes to heaven. With "May we, the doers of good deeds, go," he indeed invokes a blessing. "Those gods who, being destroyers of the sacrifice and stealers of the sacrifice, dwell in heaven"—having passed beyond those very gods who are destroyers and stealers of the sacrifice dwelling in heaven, he goes to the world of heaven. With "May we, the doers of good deeds, go," he indeed invokes a blessing.

"Rich in cattle, O Agni, rich in sheep, rich in horses is this sacrifice"—thus he makes the sacrifice indeed rich in cattle, rich in sheep, and rich in horses. "A friend of men, forever unassailable"—for he is indeed a friend of men, forever unassailable. "Full of refreshment, O Asura, full of progeny"—verily he invokes a blessing. "Long-lasting wealth, broad-based, with a gathering place"—verily he causes it to expand. "O Agni, I have performed thy vow"—Agni is indeed the Lord of Vows among the gods; verily he hands over the vow to the Lord of Vows.

The Āhavanīya fire is indeed the abode of the gods; that which is between the two fires belongs to the cattle; the Gārhapatya fire is for men, and the Anvāhāryapacana fire is for the ancestors. Having strewn sacrificial grass around both the eastern and the western fires, he says: "For men, indeed, is the new dwelling, the beloved new dwelling"—thus they have made it for the sake of its being fit for sacrifice (*medhya*). All the deities indeed come to the sacrifice of him who knows this and is about to sacrifice. With the words, "Thou art the body of Agni, the release of speech," he pours out the grains for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); for this is the drawing of the cup (*graha*) for the deities—he has thus drawn them for the deities. Now Aruṇa used to say:

"Aupaveśi said: 'Even when the oblations have not yet been offered, I cause the deities to reach the sacrificial food; by means of the completed sacrifice, may I attain completion. He who knows thus—indeed, even when his oblations have not been offered, the deities reach the sacrificial food, and by means of the completed sacrifice, he attains completion. When about to lead forward the water, one should restrain speech. By means of the mortar and the upper grinding stone, the gods struck away the Rakṣases from the mouth of the sacrifice. With the mind, Prajāpati extended the sacrifice; the Adhvaryu [should act] after the mortar has been raised."

The sacrificer and his wife should restrain their speech; having become Prajāpati himself, he performs the sacrifice mentally. All the sacrificial implements are to be thrown into the fire together; if they were done one by one, that would be human. Two at a time are thrown in, for that is the form of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. He fasts; thus he obtains both kinds of cattle, those of the village and those of the forest. In that he does not eat what belongs to the village, he thereby obtains the cattle of the village; in that he eats what belongs to the forest, he thereby obtains the cattle of the forest, as well as vital power (*indriya*).

Whatever is forest-grown, that indeed secures the sense-faculties. He should not eat beans; beans are indeed impure. He should not eat in the evening that which he intends to offer in the morning. By means of an offering that has not been tasted, the gods attained a state of greater prosperity; by means of one that had been tasted, the Asuras were defeated. By means of an offering that has not been tasted, the sacrificer attains a state of greater prosperity. Indeed, he who sacrifices without having first undertaken faith becomes worse off. Faith is water; he does not grasp it with speech, nor...

By means of the *yajus*, these waters indeed overflow their speech, but they do not overflow their mind. Therefore, when he is about to take up the waters, he should then meditate upon this [earth] with his mind. This earth is indeed the vessel for these waters; by means of her alone he takes them up. Taking hold of faith itself, he performs the sacrifice and becomes more prosperous.
Thus ends the thirty-second section, titled the *Yajamāna-brāhmaṇa*, in the *Orimikā* of the *Caraka-śākhā* within the illustrious *Kāṭhaka* of the *Yajurveda*. 32.
Now follows the thirty-third section: The Sattras.

Cows indeed performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), desiring to obtain horns. In the tenth month, horns grew upon them. They said, "Let us rise from here; we have attained that desire for which we sat down. But some among them said, "Or rather, let us stay for as long as it takes to complete a year—twelve months—and then let us rise. As they were rising, others said to them, "Faith has not yet come to us. Of those cows that sat for twelve months, horns [grew].

They proceeded, either with faith or without faith; those which were barren (tūparāḥ) are these [cows] here, therefore twelve months are barren. They move about as ten horned ones, or rather both kinds [of cows]; those that had horns prospered, while the others obtained nourishment (ūrj). They prosper in ten months, they prosper in twelve who know thus. This is the prosperous journey (ṛddham ayana); therefore they proceed by this. Indeed, one finds what is lost by means of a footprint; therefore this [journey] wins cattle.

"The Atirātra is the highest of the sacrificial rites (yajñakratu)," say the exponents of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinaḥ). "Why then do they perform it first? Because when they perform the Atirātra, they actually perform the Agniṣṭoma first, then the Ukthya, then the Ṣoḍaśin, and then the Atirātra; thus they approach the sacrificial rites in their proper order. Having approached these, having seized and encompassed them, they sit drinking Soma. They perform the Jyotiṣṭoma first; for the Jyotiṣṭoma is the mouth of the Stomas. Thus they employ the Stomas from the very beginning. [They employ] the Virāj...

The Jyotiṣṭoma, when fully accomplished, exceeds by one [verse] the Gaurīvatī and is deficient by one the Āyuṣmatī; these, when chanted together, result in the Virāj. Two verses remain over. The Virāj is indeed the heavenly world, and the sacrificers are two-footed; thus the two-footed sacrificers find firm support in that heavenly world, in the Virāj.

The *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant. This earth, indeed, is the *rathantara*; they sit having taken hold of this very earth. "The *rathantara* is by day, the *rathantara* is by night," so say the exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*). "By what means is there non-repetition (*ajāmi*)? [They reply: the *saubhara* is the *brahmasāman* at the third pressing; it becomes the *bṛhat*. He places it in the middle for the sake of supporting the *rathantara*; thereby there is non-repetition. From the *atirātra*, they proceed to the twenty-fourfold day (*caturviṃśamahaḥ*). There are twenty-four half-months in a year; thus the year is composed of half-months.

It is obtained by half-months; thus they obtain it year by year. It has three hundred and sixty *stotrīya* verses, for there are indeed three hundred and sixty days in a year. Day by day they obtain the year; day by day they obtain the year. There is an *ukthya* [rite]; the *ukthas* are cattle; verily they win cattle. The *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha*; the *bṛhat* is the world of heaven; verily by it they obtain the heavenly world. The *sāman* is named *trayastrim̐śa*.

It occurs during the midday *pavamāna* chant. There are thirty-three gods; they do not reach those [other] gods. Indeed, they enter upon this year; they have reached the gods, they have reached the heavenly world, they have reached cattle, they have reached the year by way of the half-months, and they have reached the day by means of the recitation. On the twenty-fourth day, having encompassed all the deities, they sit drinking Soma. Those who enter upon the year from here forward do not attain well-being for themselves; however, those who enter upon it from there backward, they [do].
By this they cross over safely; for it is thus that they approach from yonder toward this world. 2.

They undertake the Jyotiṣṭoma first; by it they find firm footing in this world. They undertake the Goṣṭoma second; by it they find firm footing in the intermediate space. They undertake the Āyuṣṭoma last; by it they find firm footing in this world. This world is indeed light, the intermediate space is the cow, and that which is here is life. In that they undertake these Stomas, the performers of the sacrificial session proceed finding firm footing in these very worlds. The Jyotiṣṭoma is perfected as the Virāj; the Goṣṭoma exceeds it by one [verse], and the Āyuṣṭoma falls short of it by one.

When they have been fully praised, they attain the Virāj; for the Virāj is indeed nourishment (*ūrj*). By means of these Stomas, the performers of the sacrificial session (*sattrin*) go while securing nourishment for themselves; thus they do not suffer from the pain of hunger and become free from hunger. For the performers of the sacrificial session are, as it were, oppressed by hunger. The Agniṣṭomas are on both sides like the outer rims, and the Ukthyas are in the middle like the nave. This, indeed, is the revolving wheel of the gods. When they proceed with this six-day period, they mount the very wheel of the gods for their safety; they thereby attain well-being.

They proceed with the *Ubhayatojyotis* (light on both sides). The heavenly world is indeed light; thus the performers of the *sattra* sacrifice proceed while firmly establishing themselves on both sides in the heavenly world. They proceed by means of a six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*). There are six seasons; thus they proceed while firmly establishing themselves in the seasons. There are two six-day periods; these amount to twelve days. There are ten vital breaths in a person and two breasts—making twelve; thus they revolve around the person. There are three six-day periods; these amount to eighteen days: nine others and nine.

The vital breaths revolve around those vital breaths. There are four six-day periods; these amount to twenty-four days. There are twenty-four half-months in a year; thus the year is obtained month by half-month. They revolve around that year. There are five six-day periods; these amount to thirty days. There are ten fingers, ten toes, and ten vital breaths—that makes thirty. The Virāj consists of thirty syllables, and the Puruṣa is of the nature of the Virāj. That...

"They revolve around the person; for they say that the year is indeed not established, being superior to its own foundation. Such, O Brāhmaṇa, is the explanation of the year: as much as there is in a month, so do those who know this proceed, finding support month by month.

These days are nine; for there are indeed nine heavenly worlds: the four quarters, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith as the ninth. When they undertake these days, the performers of the *sattra* sacrifice proceed while firmly establishing themselves in the nine heavenly worlds. "The *agniṣṭoma*s should be performed with the *parasāman*s," they say, for the heavenly world is commensurate with the *agniṣṭoma*. There are twelve *agniṣṭoma* chants; twelve months are a year, and the year is the heavenly world. Therefore they say that; but one should not heed that—the [days] should be *ukthya*s.

"The *parasāman* chants are to be performed," they say; for the *ukthas* are indeed cattle, [and this is] for the attainment of cattle. The *viśvajit* and *abhijit* are *agniṣṭomas*; the *ukthya* rounds have the *saptadaśa* stoma and the *parasāman* chants; the *divākīrtya* has the *ekaviṃśa* stoma. When these are chanted together, they result in the *virāj*. Two verses remain over; the *virāj* is indeed the heavenly world, and the sacrificers are two-footed. Thus, in that heavenly world, in the *virāj*, the two-footed sacrificers find firm support.

That which is the *rathantara* should be performed on the first day, the *bṛhat* on the second, the *vairūpa* on the third, the *vairāja* on the fourth, the *śākvara* on the fifth, and the *raivata* on the sixth; thus they do not depart from the *pṛṣṭha* chants. These *atigrāhya* cups are drawn as a continuous sequence among the *parasāman* days; when these are drawn, the sacrificers, having made these very worlds continuous, ascend to the heavenly world. These *atigrāhya* cups are drawn as a pair among the *parasāman* days; when these are drawn—

By these [libations], they indeed obtain a pair. This Sūrya cup is drawn as an *atigrāhya* on the twenty-first day; its name must not be uttered directly, for it is exceedingly brilliant, more piercing than a firebrand, and dangerous either through burning or through the absence of a vessel. "In various places, engendering deeds"—this is the unexpressed *prājāpatya* cup, drawn as an *atigrāhya* on the twenty-first day; it is all-encompassing, conducive to long life, and beneficial to cattle. He who is Prajāpati is indeed Indra; thus, they do not depart from the gods.

In the first month they perform the *pṛṣṭha* days; in the middle [month] they perform them; in the last [month] they perform them. In that they perform the *pṛṣṭha* days in the first month, they find firm support in this world; in that they perform them in the middle [month], they find firm support in the intermediate space; in that they perform them in the last [month], they find firm support in yonder world. "The *pṛṣṭha* days should be performed month by month," they say, for the *pṛṣṭha* days are indeed the milking of the sacrifice. Regarding this they say: "This one day of the gods is indeed the year. And which [day] it is...

They sit near for three days; she yields but little with the two subsequent milkings. "How will she yield when they sit near her twelve times? they ask. They should perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants only once, in the final month. Indeed, those who undertake the year-long rite plunge into an ocean that is shoreless and boundless. One should proceed by means of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*; for the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* are the boat of the gods. By means of that boat of the gods, they cross the ocean, the flood, as if in the middle of the sea.

They should avoid floating [in this manner]. Thus, if they were to omit the Bṛhat and Rathantara [stotras] before the year is complete, it would be a failure to perform the omission. Having proceeded with the Bṛhat and Rathantara, having attained a firm foundation, they should perform the Pṛṣṭha-stotras only once in the final month. Indeed, the junction (sandhi) milks all desires; thus, through the sacrifice and the Pṛṣṭhas, they milk all desires from the year.

This is the twenty-onefold [stoma]. By means of this twenty-onefold, the gods caused Āditya to ascend from here to the heavenly world. This very one is the twenty-onefold from here; of it, there are ten days below and ten above. He is established on both sides of the Virāj, for he is indeed established on both sides of the Virāj; therefore, he goes between these two worlds while establishing himself in all the heavenly worlds. The gods were afraid that Āditya might fall down from the heavenly world; him they [established] in three heavenly worlds.

They placed him in the worlds; fearing that he might step beyond them, they supported him from behind with three heavenly worlds. Thus, he is established on both sides in six heavenly worlds—for stability, for support, so that there may be no stepping down and no stepping beyond.

The gods, indeed, were afraid of the collapse of the seventeenfold [stoma]; they enclosed them from below with all the *stomas* and from above with all the *stomas*. Therefore, the *Abhijit*, consisting of all *stomas*, is below the seventeenfold [stomas], and the *Viśvajit*, consisting of all *stomas*, is above.

Beyond the seventeen-fold [stoma], for the sake of support and non-collapse: the gods were afraid that the sun might fall from the heavenly world; they placed it upon those which are the summit and the overlords of the heavenly worlds. For the thirty-four-fold stomas are indeed the summit and the overlords of the heavenly worlds. Now, of the twenty-one-fold day, there are three seventeen-fold stomas below and three above; these are three sets of thirty-four-fold stomas, two by two. Upon them, indeed, this [sun] is placed for support and for stability.

"Neither for falling down nor for overstepping. For he is indeed placed at the summit of the heavenly worlds; therefore, one who knows thus rises above all beings, attaining the summit of his own kin and supreme lordship. The gods, indeed, were afraid that [the sun] might fall from the heavenly world of Āditya; they raised him up with five rays, and the *divākīrtyas* are those rays. Therefore, on the twenty-first day, five *divākīrtyas* are performed: those which are in the *gāyatrī* metre are performed in *gāyatrī* verses on the two subsequent days.

The *mahādivākīrtya* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant for the two *pavamāna* lauds; the *vikarṇa* is the *brahmasāman*, and the *bhāsa* is the *agniṣṭoma*. Now, as to why five *divākīrtya* chants are performed on the twenty-first day: it is by means of these five that they cause Āditya to rise with his five rays—for the sake of support, for stability, so that there may be no falling away and no over-stepping.

Now, these are the *sparas*. By means of the *sparas*, the gods indeed caused the Āditya to reach the heavenly world; because they caused him to reach it (*aspṛṇvan*), that is the *spara*-nature of the *sparas*. The *sparas* cause him who knows this and praises with them to reach the heavenly world. Now, these are the *paras*. By means of the *paras*, the gods indeed caused the Āditya to cross over to the heavenly world; because they caused him to cross over (*apārayan*), that is the *para*-nature of the *paras*. The *paras* cause him who knows this and praises with them to cross over to the heavenly world. They are indeed *anuṣṭubhs*.

In that they have the form of *ayātayāma* (unworn-out), those [verses] are the *parāḥ*; therefore, the *parāḥ* are performed in the *anuṣṭubh*s. In that the *parāḥ* are performed in the *anuṣṭubh*s, they thereby make the *anuṣṭubh* full of vigor for the attainment of the heavenly world.

"Should one discontinue [the sacrifice], or should one not discontinue? they deliberate. Regarding this, they say: "One must indeed discontinue. These full-moon sacrifices are indeed the out-breath and in-breath of the year; if they were not to discontinue, they would bind themselves for the entire year, and the performers of the sacrificial session (*sattra*) would die from urinary obstruction. "They say it should be discontinued on the full moon and the new moon, for these two carry the sacrifice. Regarding this, they say: "But one must not discontinue those two which share in the sacrifice in between. They say it should be discontinued on the first *vyaṣṭakā* day, for that month is the month of dissolution (*viśara*).

Thus, they should not omit what has been prescribed, nor should they omit what has been prescribed; rather, when the *paryāplava* occurs during the middle of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), they should complete the month with six-day periods and then omit that which is the seventh day. They extend the six-day period and breathe out for a year. On whichever day they omit, they should offer in the morning a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Vasumat, curd for Indra, and at midday a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Marutvat, and [an offering] for the Viśvedevas.

For those who observe the seasonal rites, there should be a cake on twelve potsherds in the afternoon, and an animal sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati. The morning pressing belongs to Agni Vasumat; when they offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vasumat in the morning, they thereby make the deity a sharer in the rite so that she is not excluded. This curd for Indra is indeed Soma entered into the plants; by providing it, they do not deprive Indra of his share. They approach the pressing with eight [verses]; indeed, those animals which are brought forward in the morning are these very ones.

The midday pressing belongs to the Vasus and to Indra accompanied by the Maruts; when they offer a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra accompanied by the Maruts at midday, they thereby make the deity a sharer in the sacrifice so that she may not be excluded.

They proceed with the third pressing by means of eleven [verses]. The third pressing belongs to the Viśve Devas who possess the seasons (*ṛtumat*). When they offer a cake on twelve potsherds to the Viśve Devas who possess the seasons in the afternoon, they thereby make the deities partakers so that the pressing is not abandoned. They proceed with the pressing by means of twelve [verses]. There is an animal sacrifice for Prajāpati; Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice, [offered] so that the sacrifice is not abandoned. For six months from here, the *abhīvarta* is the *brahmasāman*; the *abhīvarta* is indeed the *brahman*.

It is by means of the *brahman* alone that they go, causing the world of heaven to turn toward them. For this world of heaven is, as it were, adverse. The *pragāthas* are similar, while the *sāmans* are various and different; for the *sāmans* are worlds and the *ṛcs* are worlds. Thus, ascending to the heavenly worlds by means of the worlds themselves, they go. There is one and the same *sāman* while the *ṛcs* are various and different; for the *sāmans* are heavenly worlds and the *ṛcs* are worlds. Thus, ascending to the heavenly worlds by means of the worlds themselves, they return.
O Indra, bring us wisdom, just as a father provides for his sons. Teach us, O much-invoked one, on this path; living, may we attain the light.

Thus, for those coming from yonder, the Brahmasāman is performed for six months; this world is light, and progeny is light. Beholding this very world and addressing one another, they come; for this world is the foundation of all worlds.

Now, these are the *parasāman* chants. Of those *parasāman* chants, that which is first is the last, and that which is last is the first; that which is in the middle remains in the middle. By the very same path by which they go [to the world of heaven], they return from there again, for the continuity and the preservation of these worlds. Above the *viśvajit*, they perform the descending *stoma*s. Regarding this, they say: "These indeed conquer and then suffer defeat; they perform the descending *stoma*s after having turned back, and thus they turn away from the heavenly world toward the downward direction."
