"Stretching out the sacrifice"—thus they proceed for five months, and of the sixth month, they perform three *Abhipravas*, two days, and the *Go* and *Āyus* [Sāmans]. They undertake the *Pṛṣṭha* [Stotras]. The *Pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the milking of the sacrifice; [they think], "Let us milk the sacrifice, and let us obtain cattle and immortality; let us stretch out the sacrifice forward. The *Pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the seasons; thus they proceed, finding firm support in the very seasons. The *Pṛṣṭhas* are the heavenly world; thus they proceed, finding firm support in the heavenly world itself.

The *stomas* of the *devakṣatra* are indeed the domain of the gods; thus they proceed ascending toward that very domain of the gods. They enter upon the *chandomas*; the *chandomas* are cattle; verily, they obtain cattle. They enter upon the tenth day, which is procreative, belonging to Prajāpati, and a firm foundation; verily, they obtain procreation, offspring, and a firm foundation. They enter upon the day of the *Mahāvrata*. Regarding this, they say: "This day is indeed the *viṣuvant*; one should enter upon the *Mahāvrata* at the *viṣuvant*. Then they say: "Or rather, it belongs to Prajāpati..."
"This day, the Mahāvratīya, is to be undertaken in the latter half of the year. Indeed, he who is born in the sixth month or the seventh month perishes; one does not enjoy prosperity through him.

Indeed, seed that has been deposited is brought forth within a year. When they perform the Mahāvrata day at the latter half of the year, they cause that seed deposited in the year to be born. They arrange the seasons according to their proper times; as before, they bring forth progeny. They employ the twenty-five-fold Stoma, the Puruṣastoma: ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, two arms, two thighs, and the self is the twenty-fifth. In that they employ this Stoma, it is from its own source.

Through the *stoma*, the performers of the sacrificial session produce themselves for prosperity. Regarding this, they say: "This day belongs to Prajāpati; it is the Mahāvrata day. On it, all the cups (*graha*) should be drawn, for Prajāpati encompassed everything. [Others say: "Only one cup should be drawn, for Prajāpati is one. [Still others say: "Three cups should be drawn, for these worlds are three; thus they prosper in these very worlds."

Five cups are to be drawn; the sacrifice consists of five parts, so they win the sacrifice itself. Seven cups are to be drawn; there are seven domestic animals, so they win those very animals. Nine cups are to be drawn; there are nine vital breaths, so they become firmly established in the vital breaths. Fifteen cups are to be drawn; there are fifteen nights in a half-month, and through the half-month the year is obtained; thus, by means of the half-month, they obtain the year. Seventeen cups are to be drawn; Prajāpati is seventeenfold.

They attain Prajāpati himself. Twenty-one cups are to be drawn; yonder sun is the twenty-first; they attain yonder sun. Twenty-seven cups are to be drawn; these worlds are twenty-seven-fold; they prosper in these very worlds. Thirty-three cups are to be drawn; there are thirty-three deities; they find firm support in the deities themselves. ||8||
Thus ends the thirty-third section, named "The Sattras," in the *Orimikā* of the *Caraka* recension of the *Kāṭhaka* of the glorious *Yajurveda*. 33.

Now begins the thirty-fourth section: The Ekādaśinī. They proceed with the sets of eleven [animals]. The Ekādaśinī is indeed the vital breaths; thus, they proceed while establishing themselves in the vital breaths. Regarding this, they say: "If they proceed with the sets of eleven, either the days will be in excess, or the highest animal will not be attained on the final day. Therefore, if they should desire the Ekādaśinī, they should undertake the Ekādaśinī in the first month and also in the last. The Ekādaśinī is indeed the vital breaths; thus, they commence with the vital breaths at the beginning and establish themselves in the vital breaths at the end. Indeed, the animal for Indra and Agni should be unchanging.

Indra and Agni are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing; thus, they go while establishing themselves in out-breathing and in-breathing. Indra and Agni are brilliance; thus, they go while establishing themselves in brilliance. Indra and Agni are vigor and heroism; thus, they go while establishing themselves in brilliance, vigor, and heroism. Indra and Agni are all the deities; therefore, when the animal victim belongs to Indra and Agni, they go while gratifying all the deities.

On whichever day the *Rathaṃtara* Sāman is used, on that day they should immolate an animal for Agni; on whichever day the *Bṛhat* [Sāman] is used, on that day it belongs to Indra, and thus it belongs to Indra-Agni. On whichever day the *Rathaṃtara* Sāman is used, on that day they should immolate an animal for Agni-Indra; on whichever day the *Bṛhat* is used, on that day it belongs to Indra-Agni. In this way, they arrange the deities in their proper sequence and immolate the animals in the correct order; they proceed by means of Indra and Agni alone. On the sixth day, they should immolate a white-backed animal for Bṛhaspati; the Brahman is indeed...

Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; thus they find support at the end of the sacrifice for Bṛhaspati. Indeed, the white-backed one belongs to Bṛhaspati by deity. On the seventh day, they should immolate a cow for Heaven and Earth in the first Chandoma; for Heaven and Earth are the foundation of the sacrifice. Thus they find support at the end of the sacrifice in Heaven and Earth. Indeed, the cow belongs to Heaven and Earth by deity. On the eighth day, they should immolate a calf for Vāyu in the middle Chandoma; [for] breath...

Vāyu is indeed the vital breath; thus they find firm support at the end of the sacrifice. The calf is indeed dedicated to Vāyu by its deity. On the ninth day, they should immolate a speckled cow (*pṛśni*) for Vāc on the last *Chandoma* day; for the speckled cow is speech, and speech is the foundation. Thus they find firm support at the end of the sacrifice in speech itself. The speckled cow is indeed dedicated to Vāc by its deity. On the tenth day, they should immolate a barren cow (*vaśā*) for Aditi; for this earth is indeed Aditi, and this earth is the foundation. Thus they find firm support at the end of the sacrifice in this very earth. [The barren cow] is dedicated to the Ādityas.

Indeed, they should sacrifice a barren cow to the deity Vaiśvakarman and a bull on the Mahāvrata day. Having slain Vṛtra, Indra became Viśvakarman; having created offspring, Prajāpati became Viśvakarman; "The year is Viśvakarman," they say, "after whom these creatures are born. It should be three-colored: that which is its first form is Indra's; that which is its second is Prajāpati's; and that which is its third is the form of the year—Indra, the bull.
"Prajāpati is the bull; they say that the year is his bull, for these creatures are born after him. Therefore, there should be a bull. 1.

Indeed, having made the non-divine color depart from him, brilliance, sensory power, vigor, offspring, and cattle go away from him whose sacrificial post sprouts; that sacrificer is liable to become worse off. He should offer a multi-colored animal to Tvaṣṭṛ. Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of forms; he approaches him with his own share, and he causes brilliance, sensory power, vigor, offspring, and cattle to return to him again. Those among the consecrated who die are liable to meet with misfortune. If they were to cast him out...

As if for those who have committed cruel deeds, the world would say to them, "Seize him! Burn him! Having placed him on the southern half of the altar, they should praise him with the verses of Sarparājñī; for this earth is indeed Sarparājñī, and it is through her that they impel him forward. Regarding this, they say: "That which is praised but not recited is indeed unsuccessful. Therefore, the Hotṛ—being the first among those initiated—should put on the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), go around the Mārjālīya fire, and, without speaking, proclaim the verses of Sarparājñī; for this earth is the queen of all that creeps, and it is through her that they impel him forward.

They indeed purify him by this; moreover, they take away his darkness. For those initiated ones for whom one dies, they go as if into darkness. They should perform "O Agni, you purify the lives" (*agna āyūm̐ṣi pavase*) as the introductory verse (*pratipad*) of the Soma sacrifice. Thus they purify themselves and place life within themselves; moreover, they proceed possessed of light. Those for whom an initiated person dies are indeed unsettled. Their Soma sacrifice should have the *rathaṃtara* as its *sāman*. The *rathaṃtara* is this earth; thus they find firm support upon this very earth. 2.

If they should take away what has not been purchased, another must be bought; if it has been purchased, he who is nearest shall fetch it and press it for the king’s food. However, if something is given to him, he does not thereby become fully purchased. If they should not find *soma*, they should press *pūtīka* plants; if no *pūtīkas* are found, [they should press] *ārjunī* plants. Indeed, Gāyatrī, having become a hawk, carried off the *soma*. The guardian of the *soma* let go his claw, and from it a nail was severed; the stalk that fell loose became the *pūtīka*. These are indeed called *pūtīkas*.

When they press the *pūtīka* plants, they provide the impulse for the sacrifice. When Indra slew Vṛtra, that which was his blood became those white *ārjuna* plants with red cotton-wool; and the sap that flowed from his severed neck became those white *ārjuna* plants with brown cotton-wool. This [plant] is indeed Soma, yet it is as if non-divine (*asurya*); therefore, it should not be pressed. There is fresh milk at the morning pressing and *pūtīkas*; curd at the midday pressing and *pūtīkas*; boiled milk at the third pressing and *pūtīkas*. For this [Soma] is indeed vital power (*indriya*).

One is deprived of the drinking of Soma whose Soma they carry away; he enters into the plants and the cattle. When they press both of these together, he recovers the drinking of Soma from both the plants and the cattle. ||3||

If two Soma sacrifices should be performed on the same day, one should commence the Prātaranuvāka during the latter part of the night; thus he wins the sacrifice first, the deities first, and the meters first. He should use a *pratipad* containing the word "vṛṣan" (bull), for Indra is indeed the bull; from the very morning pressing, he thereby wins Indra for them. Regarding this, they say: "It should be performed at every opening of the pressings"; from each opening of the pressings, he thereby wins Indra for them. [He offers: "To the lying down, to the sitting down, to the Gāyatrī meter, the overcomer, svāhā!"

"To the Triṣṭubh, to the Jagatī, to the Anuṣṭubh, to the metre that overcomes, for lying down, for sitting down, Svāhā!"—so many indeed are the metres; by means of the metres the gods wrested the metres of the Asuras; by means of the metres he wrests their metres.

The *sajanya* is to be recited; the *vihavya* is to be recited; the *kayāśubhīya* of Agastya is to be recited. As much as exists—namely, as much as exists from the intermediate space, from heaven, from earth, and from day and night—from all these he excludes them. If the pitcher should break at the morning pressing, they should chant at the midday *pavamāna* on verses addressed to Viṣṇu containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*. Whatever exceeds in the sacrifice, that exceeds toward Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa; for this is excessive, it is excessive.

One attains the redundant through that which is indeed redundant: if they should perform a Sāman with a *vaṣaṭ*-call as its *nidhana* before the Ārbhava-pavamāna at the midday pressing, or if they do so at the third pressing; for the *vaṣaṭ*-call is the foundation of the sacrifice—they thus cause him to reach the very foundation.

Having ascended the throne-seat (*āsandi*), the Udgātṛ chants the Mahāvrata; having ascended the swing (*preṅkha*), the Hotṛ recites the Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*); standing upon their respective pedestals (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the two Adhvaryus respond with the *pratigara*; the others sit upon grass-mats (*kūrca*). Food is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); from yonder it is bestowed, and upon this earth it is produced. That which they perform with the Mahāvrata while seated in the intermediate space is for the sake of producing that [food] for the intermediate space. It is for the attainment of food-eating; moreover, they cause the sacrifice to be performed as witnesses for the gods in the assembly, as they are ascending to the heavenly world.

They go forth as both accusers and defenders. One among them praises the sacrificial sessions, while another censures; he who praises praises that which among them is well-sung and well-recited, whereas he who censures strikes down that which among them is well-sung and well-recited. A Śūdra and an Ārya struggle over a hide.

The gods and the Asuras contended for the Āditya; the gods conquered it. He causes the noble class (Ārya) to be uplifted; he causes himself to be uplifted. One who is noble should be within the sacrificial altar (Antarvedi), one who is a Śūdra outside the altar (Bahirvedi). There should be a white, circular hide, the form of the Āditya. On all its corners, drums resound; by that, they win whatever speech is in the quarters. There is a ground-drum; by that, they win whatever speech is in this earth. Lutes resound; by that, they win whatever speech is in domestic animals.

The *kāṇḍavīṇā* lutes speak that speech which is in the plants; by means of them, they obtain that speech. The *nāḍītūṇava* drums speak that speech which is in the trees; by means of them, they obtain that speech. The lute has a hundred strings; man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundredfold vigor; thus he obtains both life and vigor.

A celibate student and a harlot go about together; for all beings indeed speak words, and they move about as a couple. For a year these, being procreative, perform a sacrificial session (*sattra*); their procreation is obstructed by the year itself. When they move about as a couple, it is for the attainment of the procreativity of the year. They attend upon women with water-jars for the sake of prosperity. Singing "This is sweet," they go around clad in armor, thereby magnifying the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*), and also for the sake of having Indra present.

The splendor of the Brahman is one thing, and the splendor of the Kṣatra is another. When he is consecrated, wearing a black antelope skin over his garment, that is the splendor of the Brahman; when he is armored and has strung his bow, that is the splendor of the Kṣatra. Thus he becomes both, for the attainment of both splendors.

Prajāpati fashioned the twelve-day rite from out of himself. Prajāpati is the year; he took three nights from each of four months, and that became the *dīkṣā* (initiation). He took three nights from each of the next four months, and those became the *upasads*. He took three nights from each of the final four months, and that became the *sutyā* (pressing day). Therefore they say, "As great as the year is, so great is the twelve-day rite," for it was fashioned from out of the entire year.

On the first day he created the *ihīḍa* chant and this world, Agni as the light; on the second day he created the *ūrdhveḍa* chant and the intermediate space, Vāyu as the light; on the third day he created the *iḍābhiraiḍa* chant and yonder world, Sūrya as the light; on the fourth day he created the *paristubdheḍa* chant and that light which is splendor in the world; on the fifth day he created the *adhyardheḍa* chant and that light which is truth in the world; and on the sixth day he created [the same].

And in that world he created the *hoiḍa* Sāman, the *brahman* light, and the seventh day; and in that world he created the *punarnitunnā* *iḍā*, the *tapas* light, and the eighth day; and in that world he created the *viṣvagaiḍa* Sāman, the *ṛta* light, and the ninth day; and in that world he created the *hoiḍa* Sāman, the *brahman* light, and the tenth day; and in that world he created the *dvīḍa* Sāman, the *amṛta* light, which is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the introductory [day], and the in-breath (*apāna*).

Therefore, whatever is performed at the opening ceremony (*prāyaṇīya*) is likewise performed at the concluding ceremony (*udayanīya*). For as great as the out-breath (*prāṇa*) is, so great is the in-breath (*apāna*). He who, knowing this, performs the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), wins these worlds, these *sāmans*, these lights, and these splendors.

Prajāpati desired, "May I create offspring. He beheld this twelve-day rite within himself; he fashioned it from himself and with it he created offspring. The Gāyatrī metre was created after it. It [the Gāyatrī] desired, "May I encompass this [twelve-day rite] on all sides. She encompassed it with brilliance at the beginning, with power in the middle, and with the metre at the end. Thus she indeed surpassed it on all sides. Whoever knows this surpasses his rival on all sides. There are two forms of the year: months and days.

The six seasons are one thing, and the twelve months are another; by the former he obtains the year, and by the latter he obtains it. Through both these forms, he obtains the year. The Gāyatrī is indeed the Brahman, and the twelve-day rite is the Kṣatra; the Kṣatra awakens him, and he who knows this attains the office of a domestic priest.

The other *chandas* were created for the sake of the sacrifice, but the *bṛhatī* was created for sovereignty itself; therefore, they do not utter the *vaṣaṭ* call with the *bṛhatī*. If they were to utter the *vaṣaṭ*, they would consign the cattle to the fire. Having attained them through speech, they win the cattle; for these four cattle—the wild ox, the horse, the goat, and the sheep—reside in speech. Therefore, when summoned by speech, the cattle rise up, and having been accomplished through speech, they return. Those who sit through these nights attain the *bṛhatī*; for these nights are thirty-six, and the *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables.

The *bṛhatī* is great; it knows the heavenly world. Those who sit through these nights reach the heavenly world. Indeed, those who sit through these nights reach the worlds of the gods. These nights are thirty-six; there are thirty-six worlds of the gods: eight *vasus*, eleven *rudras*, twelve *ādityas*, the *vaṣaṭ*-call, and Prajāpati, as well as these three worlds. Those who sit through these nights reach all those worlds of the gods. Both the gods and humans were once undifferentiated; those [who performed the rite] were the gods.

By means of this twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), they purified themselves through initiation (*dīkṣā*), they gathered the sacrifice through the *upasads*, and having cast off the body, they went to the heavenly world by means of the pressing day (*sutyā*). He who, knowing thus, undertakes the twelve-day rite, purifies himself through initiation, gathers the sacrifice through the *upasads*, and having cast off the body, goes to the heavenly world by means of the pressing day. Prajāpati, desiring heaven, indeed performed this [twelve-day rite], but he did not succeed; for this is an eleven-day rite (*ekādaśāha*). He placed an *atirātra* at both ends, above and below.
He carries it around; indeed, this [fire] is carried around on both sides for the attainment of the heavenly world. ||7||

Prajāpati desired, "May I procreate. He sacrificed with the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and by it he procreated. He who knows thus procreates indeed. Now, when the waters that are fit for sacrifice and pure were created, even one of them was not created; rather, blood (*asṛk*) was created there. That is why blood has its name *asṛk*. Therefore, whenever blood is shed, then one becomes fit for sacrifice and pure. This [gift] which one accepts from a *sattrin* is commensurate with a man; he truly eats the man. And indeed, for the man whom he eats, there is no [share] in this world.

It does not happen in that case either; for the first *atirātra* is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and the latter is the in-breath (*apāna*). The first *atirātra* is this [earth], and the latter is that [sky]. The first is the fire *agniṣṭoma*, and the latter is the sun. These two are indeed internal to these two; therefore they are employed as internal. Regarding this they say: "Since the sacrifice begins with an *agniṣṭoma*, why are the two *atirātras* employed first? To this they reply: "The two *atirātras* are the eyes of the sacrifice, and the *agniṣṭomas* are the pupils. If they were to employ the two *agniṣṭomas* first...

If they were to place the outer eyelashes outside, the offspring would be born blind; since the two *atirātra*s are employed as the two preceding [sacrifices], one places the two eyes of the sacrifice first and then places the two pupils in the middle. The former *atirātra* is indeed what has been, and the latter is what is to be; thus he who knows this becomes established in these ten days in the middle. Verily, he who knows the *gāyatrī* with wings of light reaches the heavenly world with a luminous splendor: the two *atirātra*s are its two wings, and the two *agniṣṭoma*s are its two lights.
The eight Ukthya-stotras in the middle are his body; this Gāyatrī indeed has light for its wings. He who knows the Gāyatrī with light for its wings goes to the heavenly world with a radiant luster.

These [days] are indeed birds; having become birds, they settle wherever they desire by flying away. This twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) is Prajāpati distributed in twelve parts: the two *atirātras* are the two wings, the two *agniṣṭomas* are the two eyes, and the eight intermediate *ukthya*s are the body. This very Prajāpati is what the performers of the sacrificial session (*sattrin*) satisfy; that is the "session-nature" (*sattratva*) of the *sattra*. The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the "real" (*sat*); it is the vital breaths they thus satisfy. Of all these creatures...

Those who live by their vital breaths perform a sacrificial session; therefore, people ask, "Are these men performers of a sacrificial session? He who knows this becomes beloved by all creatures when he rises.

Prajāpati desired, "May I come into being. He sacrificed with the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and by it he came into being. Therefore they say, "The sacrifice is for one who desires to become. The months caused him, while he was consecrated, to perform the sacrifice while remaining unconsecrated themselves; therefore, they cause one who is consecrated to perform the sacrifice while they themselves remain unconsecrated. To them he gave food and strength; that [strength] prospered within the months. Prajāpati prospered through what was given; the months prospered by receiving it. He who, knowing this, gives, prospers; he who receives, prospers. One should be fat when consecrated; whatever of his limbs wastes away, he offers that as an oblation. It is just as if...

Just as spring rises up shining with new grass, even so does he rise up shining with new grass. Penance (*tapas*) is indeed the glue of the sacrifice; just as there is glue for a chariot, so there is penance for the sacrifice. He who is without penance has a sacrifice that is not held together. Therefore, one should be a performer of penance; thus he holds the sacrifice together. These half-months desired, "May we become months. They undertook the twelve-day rite, making the thirteenth day their Brahman priest; having seen [the goal] in him, they rose up. Therefore—

He who has no fixed abode depends upon others; therefore, one should not perform the *brahman* office with a thirteenth day in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). Twelve should undergo initiation for the sake of the year, for the year has twelve months as its abode; having the year as their abode, they thus prosper. Thirteen should undergo initiation for the sake of the year, for the year has thirteen months as its abode; having the year as their abode, they thus prosper. Fifteen should undergo initiation for the sake of the half-month, for there are fifteen nights in an half-month; having the half-month as their abode, they [prosper].

Seventeen should consecrate themselves; they prosper, having Prajāpati as their abode, for Prajāpati is seventeenfold; having Prajāpati as their abode, they indeed prosper. Twenty-one should consecrate themselves if they desire luster; yonder sun is the twenty-first, he is the bestower of luster; he bestows luster upon them. Twenty-four should consecrate themselves if they desire spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*); the Gāyatrī has twenty-four syllables, the Gāyatrī is brilliance, and spiritual splendor is brilliance; verily, they win brilliance and spiritual splendor.

They should undergo initiation for twenty-seven days; the Triṇava has twenty-seven as its abode, and these worlds have twenty-seven as their abode; thus they prosper in their own abode. They should undergo initiation for thirty days; the month has thirty as its abode, and the nights have thirty as their abode; thus they prosper in their own abode. They should undergo initiation for thirty-three days; the deities have thirty-three as their abode, and there are thirty-three deities; thus they prosper in their own abode. Those desiring vigor and those desiring strength should undergo initiation for forty-four days; the Triṣṭubh has forty-four syllables, and the Triṣṭubh is vigor and strength; thus they prosper in vigor itself.

They obtain vigor. Forty-eight should be consecrated by those desiring cattle; the Jagatī meter has forty-eight syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the Jagatī; verily, they obtain cattle. An unlimited number should be consecrated for the attainment of the unlimited; Prajāpati is unlimited; verily, they prosper through Prajāpati. The seasons were indeed the younger brothers of the months; those months desired, "May we attain the seasons. They undertook a twelve-day rite, making the thirteenth day their Brahman priest, and having suppressed the seasons with the cold season (śiśira), they attained them.

Spring arose against their summer. He who, knowing this, undergoes initiation in the cool season (śiśira), having overcome his rival by means of austerity alone, rises up against his food and vigor. For him who, knowing this, undergoes initiation in the cool season, the cool season is the departure and spring is the conclusion; thus he prospers. 9.

The exponents of Brahman say: "What does one obtain by the first day of the twelve-day rite? "Radiance and spiritual luster. "What by the second? "Speech and food. "What by the third? "These three worlds. "What by the fourth? "Four-footed cattle. "What by the fifth? "The four directions and the fifth, the upward direction. "What by the sixth? "The six seasons. "What by the seventh? "The seven-syllabled Śakvarī meter. "What by the eighth? "The eight-syllabled Gāyatrī meter. "What by the ninth? "The nine vital breaths."

"What by the tenth?"—by means of the Virāj of ten syllables; "what by the eleventh?"—by means of the Triṣṭubh of eleven syllables; "what by the twelfth?"—by means of the Jagatī of twelve syllables. Truly, there is only as much as exists; having attained all that exists, he secures it, he prospers, and he becomes more prosperous—he who, knowing this, sacrifices with the twelve-day rite.

There are four sets of three [pots] each; with those that are the first, he purifies his self; with those that are the second, he becomes fit for sacrifice; with those that are the third, he cleanses his limbs; and with those that are the fourth, he shakes off whatever impurity is within him and whatever is on the outside. Indeed, those who cause one to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite devour the man himself: he who eats the animal eats him as flesh; he who eats the *vājina* (whey) eats him as blood; he who eats the parched grains eats him as bone; and he who eats the clarified butter eats him as marrow.

The marrow is that which is the *parivāpa* (fried grains); the hair is that which is the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake); the brain is that which is the *rājā* (king Soma); the sweat is that which is the *karambha* (barley meal mixed with curds); and the dandruff is that which is the *niṣpad* (the residue). Truly, he who speaks untruth eats the sacrificial food (*sattriya*). For one who knows thus, his sacrificial food becomes well-tasted; his sacrificial food does not remain uneaten. ||11||

He undergoes initiation for twelve days; he is indeed born then, for that which is born from austerity is truly born, not that which is born from a woman. He undergoes initiation for twelve days; there are indeed twelve impure things in a person: hair, skin, blood, flesh, bone, marrow, spleen, liver, tears, rheum of the eyes, sweat, and that which one urinates. These are the twelve impure things in a person. In that he undergoes initiation for twelve days, he removes those very things. He undergoes initiation for twelve days.

There are twelve *upasads* and twelve *prasūts*; these amount to thirty-six. The *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables; cattle are connected with the *bṛhatī*. Thus, he obtains cattle in the *bṛhatī*, and having obtained cattle in the *bṛhatī*, he secures them. Then, those four syllables which remain over are the four-footed *anuṣṭubh*; the *anuṣṭubh* is speech. Thus, he obtains cattle in speech, and having obtained cattle in speech, he secures them. Therefore, cattle recognize their names by means of speech, and they exist as established through speech.

Prajāpati desired, "May I become more, may I become better, may I prosper. He consecrated himself with the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) and sacrificed with it; he prospered. Therefore, one person alone should sacrifice with the twelve-day rite, for he alone prospered—namely Prajāpati. Verily, following the prosperity of Prajāpati, he who, knowing this, sacrifices with the twelve-day rite as a single individual, prospers. With it, three deities consecrated themselves for the luminous realms; they sacrificed with it and they prospered. Therefore, three persons should sacrifice with the twelve-day rite, for those three prospered. This [is the case] here.

These worlds indeed prosper following the prosperity of these very worlds for those who, knowing this, perform the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) in groups of three. By means of it, six deities consecrated themselves; by means of it they sacrificed; they prospered. Therefore, six should perform the twelve-day sacrifice, for those six prospered. The seasons indeed prosper following the prosperity of the seasons for those who, knowing this, perform the twelve-day sacrifice in groups of six. By means of it, twelve deities consecrated themselves; by means of it they sacrificed; they prospered. They...

They prospered during the former fortnights and invited the latter fortnights; therefore, twelve should sacrifice with the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), for they prospered by twelves. Indeed, it is the months that cause the months to prosper. Those who, knowing this, sacrifice with the twelve-day rite for twelve [days], should undergo initiation on the thirteenth day during the *upasads*; for some know him and others do not know him, and indeed, some know the thirteenth month and others do not know it.

Prajāpati [is present] in the mind; Sārasvata when speech is released; Dhātṛ during the consecration; Brahma during the vow; Savitṛ during the maintenance; Aṃśa, Accheta, Divya, Suparṇa, and Pratikhyāta during the Upasads; Aditi at the introductory sacrifice (*prāyaṇīya*); Paśusthā when the grains are scattered; Rudra while being winnowed; the *Chandāṃsi* while being measured; Varuṇa when tied up; Pūṣan at the Soma-purchase cow; Bhaga while bargaining for the price; Asura when purchased; Śipiviṣṭa when being placed on the lap; Bṛhaspati when lifted up; Vāyu while being carried; and Adhipati [is present] when it is placed upon [the cart].

The Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice being led forward is the guest; Varuṇa, the sovereign, seated on the *dūroṇasat* seat, is the guest-offering (*ātithya*); the Aindrāgna [offering] being placed on the *āsandyā* seat; the Aindrāgna [offering] when the fire is churned; the Sāman during the *tānūnaptra* rite; austerity during the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*); the earth during the *upasada*; the intermediate space during the *upasada*; the sky during the *upasada*; the measuring out, the over-measuring, and the counter-measuring of the sacrifice while the altar (*vedi*) is being prepared; the animals on the *uttaravedi*; the sky on the *havirdhāna* shed; the intermediate space on the *āgnīdhra* shed; and the earth on the *sadas*. ||14||

The *prāṇa* [is the deity] in the *uparava* holes; the *bhrātṛvya* (rival) in the *dhiṣṇya* hearths; cattle in the *barhis*; Prajāpati when the altar (*vedi*) is being strewn; the waters at the *vaisarjana* libation; Prajāpati when being led forward; Agni at the *āgnīdhra* hearth; Viṣṇu during the preparatory rites; the hand when released; Viṣṇu in the sacrificial post; the plants in the girdle; the sacrifice itself in the *āprī* verses; the oblation when the fire has been carried around it; the Pitṛs when it is being immolated; the pair of the sacrifice in the *pannejana* water; the portion of the Rākṣasas in the *vapā* as it is being extracted; the sacrifice itself...

The lineage [of the Soma] is transferred into the Vasatīvarī waters; the cow is the sacrificial fee for Indra and Agni when it is placed on the western corner of the northern high altar; the cow is placed for Mitra and Varuṇa on the northern corner of the northern high altar; the meters are at the Āgnīdhra shed; the oblation is brought down on the Upavasatha day; the offering to Sarasvatī is at the morning litany (prātaranuvāka), or rather, it has been poured out; Prajāpati is being distributed; the deities are distributed; Indra is the slayer of Vṛtra;
Indra is the overcomer of enemies; Indra is the conqueror of Vṛtra; Āyu is being led forward; Yama is the one pressed in the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups. 15.

The *nibhūya* is in the *pūrādhavanīya*; the well-purified *pūḥ* is in the *pūtabhṛt*; the *śukraśrī*, the *kṣīraśrī*, and the *kakuhassaktuśrī* are in the vessels; Vāyu is in the *bahiṣpavamāna*; the *hotrās* are in the *pravara*; the Vasus are in the *prayājas*; the animal sacrifice has the same deity as the Soma offering; the *unnīyamāna* belongs to the Viśvedevas; the *unnīta* belongs to Indra and Agni; Rudra is the one being offered; Vāk is the one offered; the troop of Maruts is the one turned toward; Mitra is the one looked upon; Indra is the one seated; the *bhakṣa* is being consumed; the friend is the one consumed; the *nārāśamsa* belongs to the Pitṛs; [the cake] belongs to Agni.

The morning pressing belongs to Indra; the midday pressing is the sacrifice; at the time of the sacrificial fee, the *pṛṣṭha* chants belong to Indra; the third pressing belongs to the Viśvedevas; the *agniṣṭoma* chant belongs to Vaiśvānara; the hymn of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest belongs to Indra and Varuṇa; that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin belongs to Indra and Bṛhaspati; that of the Acchāvāka belongs to Indra and Viṣṇu; the *ṣoḍaśī* chant belongs to Indra; the night belongs to the wives; the *rathaṃtara* *saṃdhi* chant belongs to Agni; the day belongs to Sūrya and the Aśvins; the sacrifice belongs to the Ādityas in the *anuyāja* offerings; and that which is performed between these is the ocean.

Varuṇa is at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath); the ocean is at the *ṛjīṣa*. That which is the ford on this side is the *prāyaṇīya* (opening sacrifice), and that which is the ford on the other side is the *udayanīya* (concluding sacrifice). Viṣṇu is in the barren cow; Brahmā is in the *samiṣṭi* (final oblation).

Just as a chariot moves by resting upon each individual spoke, so does the sacrifice proceed by resting upon each individual body [of the ritual]. Before the performance begins, the oblations must be offered in the Āgnīdhra fire. Regarding this, Vāsiṣṭha Sātyahavya said: "When it is announced, 'The Soma has spilled,' do not be heedless; proceed with the rite! For it was at dawn that I completed the Soma. The Soma of one who knows thus does not spill. Indeed, he used to sit upon a throne-seat, stirring the Soma with barley meal and drink it. I—

"Verily, he who knows these [oblations] knows the sacrifice in its entirety; [thinking] 'He shall not harm me,' the Soma, whether drunk or not yet drunk, does not harm him who drinks Soma knowing this. When they said to him, 'Why do you sit here drinking Soma after churning it with barley meal?', he replied, 'I am establishing the sacrifice among the deities. For one who knows this, for whomsoever a learned priest offers the expiation for the failure of the sacrifice when such a failure occurs, he establishes the sacrifice among the deities."

One should offer the *yajñārti* oblation for the sake of having a common origin. There are indeed thirty-three bodies of the sacrifice: twenty-nine *stomabhāgas*, three *savana*s, and the sacrifice itself as the fourth. By means of the *stomabhāgas*, he thus joins the *stomabhāgas*; by means of the *savana*s, the *savana*s; and by means of the sacrifice, the sacrifice. Verily, all the bodies of his sacrifice become joined, all attained, and all secured. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, for Bṛhaspati, let there be praise"—for whatever indeed Savitṛ [bestowed] upon the gods...

Therefore, they prosper; impelled by Savitṛ, they praise, they succeed, and they are successful. Indeed, his hymns of praise (stomas) are successful, the sacrifice is successful, it is successful for the sacrificer, it is successful for his offspring, it is successful for his cattle, and it is successful for his sacred word (brahman)—for him who knows thus, and for him who has a Brahman priest who knows thus.

He who indeed knows the extensions and the responses of the *stomabhāgas* should be the *brahman* priest at a completed *soma* sacrifice. When the *prastāva* has been chanted during the *bahispavamāna*, he should say: "Chanted for food, chanted for strength, chanted; at the impulse of the god Savitṛ, impelled by Bṛhaspati. These indeed are the extensions and responses of the *stomabhāgas*. He who knows thus should be the *brahman* priest at a completed *soma* sacrifice. In whichever direction the two *somas* have been praised, toward that direction he should look about, saying: "This one, the son of such-and-such a man and such-and-such a woman..."

"May I pierce them with grief," he should say to one of the officiating priests; thus he indeed pierces them with grief. Whosoever, being ignorant of the *stomabhāgas*—both their sequence and their responses—becomes the *brahmán*, he is deprived of his strength on all sides. When the *bahiṣpavamāna* has been introduced and the chant begun, [the *brahmán*] should look down upon the *brahmán* from above, saying: "Praise for food! Praise for strength! Praise! At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, impelled by Bṛhaspati! By doing so, he makes his enemy truly low. When [the *brahmán*] says, "O *brahmán*, the Soma has spilled," he means, "The sacrifice has spilled. Wherever it should spill, having poured water there—
Savitar the God has become worthy of our praise;
indeed, he is now to be invoked by men at the beginning of the day—he who distributes treasures to human beings, so that he may grant us the most excellent wealth here.

Thus he should consecrate the waters: "The waters are indeed all the deities; verily, he establishes the sacrifice among the deities. Wherever the Brahman priest sees another being given more [of the sacrificial fee], that Soma becomes inclined downward. If the Brahman priest should see another being given more, he should say to the sacrificer, "I take away the sensory power and vigor of such-and-one, the son of such-and-one"; thus he takes away his very sensory power and vigor.
With their insights, men have generated from the two fire-drills by the movement of their hands the praiseworthy Agni—the far-seeing lord of the house, the active one.
By fire is fire kindled—the sage, the master of the house, the youth, the bearer of oblations, whose mouth is the sacrificial ladle.
Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven the seers, and seven your beloved abodes;
knowing them, fill the seven sacrificial vessels and the seven wombs with clarified butter.
May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it extend this sacrifice of ours unharmed.
May the gods come to this seven-threaded sacrifice spread out for us, being well-disposed toward us.

The thirty-three threads with which they wove this sacrifice, those who bestow it with the *svadhā* call—may we mend whatever breach there is therein; may this sacrifice go to the gods with the cry of *svāhā*.
Whatever flaw there is in my mind, or in my speech, or in my heart—
may this god Bṛhaspati fill that up with wealth.
May Viśvakarman, enjoying this oblation, extend this sacrifice through continuous lineages;
may he unite with us those dawns that have shone forth and those that are setting, by means of the oblation of clarified butter.
O Agni, you are without guile and without reproach; you are indeed truth, for you are without guile.
Being without guile, you have been fashioned by the mind; being without guile, you carry the oblation. As one without guile, bestow healing upon us.

O Agni, you who are wise, may you ward off from us the wrath of the god Varuṇa; as the best of sacrificers, the most excellent bearer of oblations, and the brightly shining one, release from us all those who hate us.
As such, O Agni, be our protector, most near to us at the dawning of this morning.
Being gracious, release us from Varuṇa; seek our mercy, and be easy for us to invoke.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth section, named the Ekādaśinī, in the Orimikā of the Caraka-śākhā within the Śrī Yajus Kāṭhaka. 34.
Now begins the thirty-fifth section:
Expiation.

O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious. With steady limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya of unharmed wheels grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
May the Maruts, whose steeds are spotted, whose mother is Pṛśni, who move in splendor and frequent the assemblies,
who have Agni for their tongue, who are wise and possess the sun as their eye— may all those gods come here to me with their protection.
A hundred autumns are before us, O gods, within which you have ordained the aging of our bodies;
wherein sons become fathers—do not harm us in the midst of our journeying life.
O Agni, youngest one, shine forth before us, blazing with your unceasing beam; unto you come all our constant offerings.

With my words, I approach the vault of heaven, praising with speech the one of keen hearing, the seer, the one to be known; from whatever fear there may be, let there be safety for us—O Agni, protect us from the wrath of the gods! O Ikṣvāku, be gracious!
With the Agnis in harmony, make Agni your god— the most excellent sacrificer, the messenger at the rite—
who is steadfast among mortals, the upholder of *ṛta*, whose head is flame, who feeds on ghee, and who is the purifier.
Agni has ghee for his face, ghee for his back; he has ghee for his oblation and ghee is his abode.
May the green, ghee-sprinkling steeds carry you hither; drinking the clarified butter, O God, worship the gods. 1.
O Agni, carry these most desirable oblations, you who are unwearied, toward the assembly of the gods; may they accept these fragrant offerings from us.

Seven are yours, O Agni; thirty-three are yours. Whatever [is] of my mind, Viśvakarman, I yoke the fire for you. Being kindled, may Agni, being praised, protect me with the gods worthy of praise who belong to the earth. May Vāyu, being praised, protect me with the gods worthy of praise who belong to the intermediate space. May Sūrya, being praised, protect me with the gods worthy of praise who belong to heaven. May Viṣṇu, being praised, protect me with the gods worthy of praise who belong to the quarters. May Agni with the *yajus*-verses and Pūṣan with the *svagā*-utterances protect this sacrifice; may they protect me. I take hold of you; do you take hold of me. 2.

O Earth, most abundant one! O Sinīvālī, O Urandhra! May your mind be directed toward us; may your heart be ours. That wave of yours which is worthy of oblation and endowed with power—may I prosper through it. You are the clarified butter of Soma; you are the oblation of the oblation, the light of the light. You are the portions of the Viśve Devas; I take you for the enjoyment of the gods.
May the Maruts pour forth together; may Pūṣan, Dhātṛ, and Bṛhaspati pour forth together.
May this Agni pour forth for you with offspring and with wealth; make me long-lived.
The slow-moving ones are the barren cows.
The divine waters were indeed ghee; these waters bear Agni and Soma.
Intense is the essence of those honey-blended ones, reaching the immortal realm; may it come to me with breath and with splendor.

From the very beginning I see you, or else I hear you; the sound of you comes to me, and your speech has entered my mouth. Having partaken of immortality, I then perceived you—when I was satisfied by you, O golden-hued ones.
Some flow together, others approach; the rivers fill the same expanse.
The pure waters have surrounded him—the pure, shining Son of the Waters.
O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss; grant us strength so that we may behold great joy.
Whatever most auspicious essence there is, may you grant us a share of it here, as longing mothers do for their children.
Therefore, let us come quickly to you, for whose abode you quicken us; O Waters, give us life.

As a bull, he generates the embryo within them; as a child, he sucks them, and they lick him. He, the Son of Waters, strengthening himself within the waters, shines forth for the one who bestows wealth.
May cattle be born here, may horses be born here, may men be born here;
may the increase of wealth, accompanied by a thousand sacrificial fees, be produced here.
May this sacrifice increase with cattle and horses; may this altar be rich in offspring and heroic sons. May this sacred grass surpass all other grass; may all the gods protect this sacrifice.
He in whose house dwells the well-milking cow, he swells with the self-sustaining power (*svadhā*); being strong, he eats the food.
He, the Son of the Waters, of unblemished color, has entered here as it were with the body of another. 3.
The sky has spilled, the earth has spilled, this entire oblation has spilled;
all beings have eaten what was spilled—may the spilled oblation be born anew.
Here are the cows; here is the sacrifice.
The waters are full of milk, the plants are full of milk, and my speech is full of milk;
may that milk which belongs to the waters increase together with us.

Whatever [impurity] the bird has smeared upon you with its beak, O Nirṛti—may the consumer of oblations, the purifier of ghee, cleanse all that which is undesirable. Whatever [impurity] the bird has smeared upon you with its beak, O Nirṛti—may the carrier of oblations, the purifier of ghee, cleanse all that which is undesirable. May prosperity increase through curds and ghee; may it release the sacrifice for the sake of the sacrifice, Svāhā! May prosperity increase through ghee; may it release this sacrifice, and may it release the lord of the sacrifice from sin, Svāhā!

O Agni, those logs of yours that are within the waters, upon the height of the earth, and before the sun—let those oblations of clarified butter go to you, O divine one, for the protection of the sacrificer. 4.

For you two, O Indra and Agni, are the officiating priests of the sacrifice; by your arrangement, may you both satisfy yourselves with what has been offered and what has not been offered, with the oblation and that which is not an oblation.
Of that which has been offered and that which has not been offered, of that which was not offered and that which was offered.
O Indra and Agni, come and partake of this golden-hued Soma offering; drink! Come hither!
May darkness not find this sacrifice, nor the mortal priests, nor these creatures;
may he who drinks this Soma not find it, for both [the pure and the impure] have been mixed together.
May our fathers not be angry, nor the gods; may neither one of our own kin nor one of a different kin harm us.
May the ill-wisher and the malevolent one have no power over us; may this unassailable sacrifice reach the gods.
Seven are the officiating priests, seven the portions in this assembly; ten are their fingers, O Aśvins, and fivefold is the strength.
Out-breath, diffused-breath, in-breath, mind, and intention—Agni, Svāhā! May the gods enjoy this oblation. ||5||
The soul of the sacrifice, pressed for speed, flows as the effused juice; the seer protects the ancient hymns.
O Indu, you are the winner of cattle, the winner of men, the winner of horses, and the winner of booty; you are the primordial soul of the sacrifice.
The self-possessing sky yields clarified butter and milk; from the womb of Cosmic Order, immortality is born.
The bounteous ones, acting in concert, find pleasure therein; the men, the pourers, pour forth that which is beneficial.

May the gods take their place among the gods; may the first ones take their place among the second; may the second ones take their place among the third. You who are three times eleven, and thirty-three, and three hundred and three, and three thousand and three—may they protect this sacrifice; may they protect me. I take hold of you; do you take hold of me. 6.
May the Vasus raise you up; may the Rudras cause you to swell; may the Ādityas lift you aloft; may the Viśvedevas make you firm.
Firm is the sky, firm is the earth, firm is this entire world;
by the power of Dharma the gods are firm, and the sacrificer is firm through his cattle.

Make firm those things in heaven that belong to heaven; make firm those things in the intermediate space that belong to the intermediate space; make firm those things on earth that belong to the earth.
I have brought you hither; be within, O Earth, and stand firm, unshakable.
Let all the people desire you; let not the sacrifice fall away from you.
With the firm oblation we lead the firm oblation, Soma, down;
so that Indra may make the clans bring us tribute exclusively.

Svāhā! From heaven, swell; svāhā! From the intermediate space, swell; svāhā! From earth, swell. You are the bestower of life, O steadfast one; bestow life upon me. You are the bestower of vigor, O steadfast one; bestow vigor upon me. You are the protector of the body, O steadfast one; protect my body. You are the protector of the eye, O steadfast one; protect my eye. You are the bestower of luster, O steadfast one; bestow luster upon me.
O Adhvaryu, let this sacrifice be for the gods, for the plants, for the cattle, and for my wealth.
May he be firm for every living being; O divine sacrifice, swell with clarity like clarified butter, O God.
Be right here; do not waver, like a mountain that does not shake.
Stand firm here like Indra; maintain the sacrifice here.
Indra has established this as firm with a firm oblation;
for him Soma has spoken in favor, and for him Brahmaṇaspati.
Firm is the sky, firm is the earth, and firm are these mountains;
firm is this entire world, and firm art thou, O King, of the people. (7)
Hail to Asu, hail to Vasu, hail to the Bestower of Wealth, hail to the Lord of the Earth, hail to the Lord of the World, hail to the Lord of Beings, hail to Being!
The drop has fallen upon the earth and across the sky; following this womb and that which was before, I offer the drop as it moves along its common source, according to the seven priestly offices.
That drop of yours which spills, that stalk of yours which has fallen from the arm onto the lap of the *dhiṣaṇā* bowl,
or that which [falls] from the *adhvaryu* or from the filter— that I offer for you with my mind, consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* call.
That drop, that stalk which has fallen upon the earth— from the parched grain, from the sacrificial cake, from the groats,
from the fried grains, from the Soma, from the stirred drink, from the bright [Soma]— that which is consecrated with Svāhā, I offer it to Indra for Indra.
That drop of yours which is honeyed, endowed with power, consecrated by Svāhā, and returns again to the gods—
whether from the Adhvaryu or from the filter— I offer that to you with my mind, accompanied by the Vaṣaṭ-call.
Whatever drop of yours spills, whatever stalk of yours falls, and whatever [part] is beyond the sky—may this god Bṛhaspati pour that back together with wealth. 8.

May the seasons—spring, summer, the honeyed rains, autumn, and winter—liberating the speech, dripping with ghee, full of moisture, and bringing bliss, dwell together in the two worlds of space. May they, overflowing with water, inhabit the heavens.
Bring us offspring; O Agni, you are the guardian of the vows of the gods.
O gods, whatever vows of yours we, being more ignorant than the wise,
have violated— Agni, the knowing one, shall fulfill all that through the seasons by which he ordains the gods.

Madhu and Mādhava are the two spring seasons; Śukra and Śuci are the two summer seasons; Nabhas and Nabhasya are the two rainy seasons; Iṣa and Ūrja are the two autumn seasons; Sahas and Sahasya are the two winter seasons; Tapas and Tapasya are the two cool-seasons. May these protect this sacrifice; may they protect me. I take hold of you; do you take hold of me. 9.

Hail to Asu! Hail to Vasu! Hail to Vibhu! Hail to Vivasvat! Hail to Śūṣa! Hail to Saṃsarpa! Hail to Malimluca! Hail to Gaṇaśrī! Hail to Candra! Hail to Jyotis! Hail to Abhibhū! Hail to Adhipati! Hail to Divāpati! You are Indra’s cup; you have been taken, you are to be taken by the gods. You are their fullness; I enter you, I resort to you, together with my house, together with my progeny, together with my cattle, together with the officiating priests, and together with the members of the assembly.

Together with the Soma, together with those worthy of sacrificial gifts, together with the sacrifice, and together with the lord of the sacrifice—O Indra and Agni, O divine Vāta, I enter into my previously established boundaries, along with the gathering of cattle, horses, and men, and whatever belongs to me; for safety and freedom from distress, for resting and sitting, for the Gāyatrī metre, the all-conquering, Svāhā! For safety and freedom from distress, for resting and sitting, for the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and the Anuṣṭubh metres, the all-conquering, Svāhā! ||10||

May Heaven and Earth mix you; may Day and Night mix you; may Speech and Mind mix you; may Waters and Herbs mix you; may the Ṛg-veda and the Sāman-veda mix you; may the Stoma and the Yajus mix you; may the Bṛhat and the Rathantara mix you; may the Sacrifice and the Dakṣiṇā mix you; may the Sun and the Moon mix you; may the New Moon and the Full Moon mix you; may the Brahman and the Kṣatra [mix you].

May the sun and the horse-sacrifice blend with you; may you be blended, may I be blended. O drop, I have come to the drop; of that [drop] of yours, which possesses power and has been drunk by Indra, of which all the hosts partake and which is shared by all the hosts, being invited, I partake of the invited portion. 11.
O Agni, through you may we cross over all enemies, as one crosses over streams of water.
O Goddess, you who are the most excellent among the waters of the Aṣṭakas, you are skillful in your work;
as such, we shall worship you with this oblation. You are Varuṇa’s own mediator in the sacrifice.
To Śrutkarṇa.
O Anumati, grant your approval for this which we prepare as a remedy for our bodies—
[that which is] for you in our children, our persons, our progeny, in our cattle, in the plants, and in the waters.
Hiraṇyagarbha.
The wise man does not doubt that state from which the deceased returns again as a living being;
the threefold world is like a chariot, wherein the living one is the embryo, not the dead—svāhā!
Swell up; may your milks be gathered together.
Swell, O most exhilarating Soma, with all your rays; become for us a most glorious friend for our prosperity. 13.
O Agni, in the waters.
Burn, O Agni, the enemies within; burn away the curse of the hostile stranger. O Vasu, you who are observant, burn those who are thoughtless; let your ageless, tireless flames spread abroad.
O Agni, whoever, being ungrateful, would seek to harm us, or whoever, O you who are great as Mitra, would plot against us from within—
burn him with your own ageless bulls, O most burning burner, you who are full of heat through your fervor.
May he provide a signal for him, even at night, though he be far away,
when the ageless purifier consumes the lords of the forest.
O Agni, no mortal has ever consumed the cruel part of your body; the monkey consumes its own whetted point, like a cow its afterbirth.
Like a ram, he chews up and chews down;
when he devours the plant of the highest one, he moves head with head and chest with chest, and he consumes the stalk with his golden jaws.
The fair-winged ones have fashioned their song; the black, impetuous ones have danced upon the back of heaven.
They descend headlong to the appointed place of the lower world; bright as the sun, they have deposited abundant seed.

By means of fire, he obtained ascetic heat; by the sun, brilliance; by the wind, the vital breaths; by Indra, the gods; by Yama, the ancestors; by Sarasvatī, human beings; by the seventeenfold hymn, the stomas; by the Vāmadevya, the Sāmans; by the Gāyatrī, the meters; by the amulet, forms; by gold, splendors; by the crosswise antelope skin, serpents; by the python, water-dwellers; by the hawk, winged birds; by the tiger, wild animals; by the eagle, fowls; by the aśvattha tree, forest trees; by the cooked rice, foods; by barley, medicinal herbs; by the stallion, one-hoofed animals.

Cattle [are sustained] by the bull; cows by the breeding bull; birds by the ram; goats by the ewe; the stars by the moon; speech by the Brahmin; the deities by speech; the Virāj by the woman; the mountains by the pressing-stone; the waters by the ocean; truth by the waters; the Ṛta by truth; austerity by the Ṛta; the Parameṣṭhin by austerity; Death by the Parameṣṭhin; creatures by Death; Sagara by his progeny; Prajāpati by those gods. May I be followed by prosperity, may I be followed by abundance, may I become the most excellent among Brahmins. 15.

If one's *droṇakalaśa* vessel runs dry, his vital breath (*prāṇa*) follows after it as it runs dry, for Soma is indeed the vital breath. Regarding this, they say: "One should pour milk into it. But on the other hand, they also say: "This milk is, as it were, concealed; one should rather pour water into it and draw out gold. Water is immortality and gold is life; thus he bestows immortality and life upon himself from the immortal. Four boons should be given: to the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, the Hotṛ, and the Adhvaryu. These are indeed the Indras of the sacrifice; he thus gratifies them. That is the rule.

In that regard, the expiation for one whose *camasa* (cup) spills is as follows: as the cup itself spills, his vital breath (*prāṇa*) spills after it; for Soma is indeed the vital breath. Whatever final draught the Adhvaryu might take, he should pour out its residue as an expiation. For Soma is taken for the sake of expiation; thus, by means of expiation, he effects an expiation for him, and he attains a full lifespan. That is the expiation in that case. As for one whose pressing-stone (*grāvan*) shatters, he is deprived of cattle; for the pressing-stones are indeed cattle, belonging to Dyutāna Māruta.

They should praise with the *brahmasāman*. The Maruts are indeed the radiant ones; verily, by means of its own *sāman*, he unites him [the sacrifice], and he becomes possessed of cattle. That itself is the expiation in that case. He should pour out those [Soma shoots] unfit for consumption into the *uparava* holes with the formula, "To Prajāpati, svāhā! Soma belongs to Prajāpati; verily, he causes him to attain his very foundation. That itself is the expiation in that case. If someone should burn the Soma, the Adhvaryu should secure the cups, the Udgātṛ the chants (*stotra*), and the Hotṛ the recitations (*śastra*); then they should proceed with the sacrifice as before.

Five choice gifts should be given; the sacrifice consists of five parts, and thus he secures the sacrifice itself. Having gone to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) and returned, he should undergo consecration again before the twelfth day. If he were to let the twelfth day pass, he would be excluded from the rite; in that case, he should give those very sacrificial fees which he intended to give at the previous consecration—this is the expiation for that occasion. ||16||

He who, having added fuel to the fire, undertakes the vow, causes all his desires to enter into that fire. If he were to depart without having sacrificed, his desires—being ungratified—would not follow him; he would be lacking luster and devoid of vigor. Therefore, when about to depart, he should offer an oblation.
To you, O best of the Aṅgirases, all those secure dwellings have separately submitted for your desire, O Agni.

Thus he places desires themselves within him; desires, being gratified, follow after him. He becomes radiant and full of vigor. Continuity indeed belongs to that sacrifice when one who has established the sacred fires enters upon the vow (*vrata*); if his fire should go out before the sacrifice is completed, that would be a rupture for him. Having drawn it out toward the east, he should stand worshipping it with his mind. For Prajāpati is like the mind, and the sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati; thus he maintains the continuity of the sacrifice itself. He should utter the *vyāhṛti*, "Bhūḥ! For Prajāpati is "Being" (*bhūta*); he thus approaches prosperity (*bhūti*). By means of life-span and vigor...
If the fire of an Āhitāgni goes out, he is deprived of his prosperity; as far as one could strike with a *śamyā*, if it should go out within that distance, he should re-establish it.
This is one for you, and that beyond is another; enter into union with the third light.
Being gracious to your body through this union, be dear to the gods in the highest birthplace.

Thus he gathers it with the *brahman* itself; that indeed is the expiation in that case. If it should blow away further away, he should go after it and dwell there; that indeed is the expiation in that case. The milk of one for whose oblation the calves suckle while they have been driven away enters the plants and the cattle. He should offer a barley gruel to Vāyu; Vāyu is the giver of milk. He approaches him with his own portion, and he bestows milk upon him. Then he should drive the calves away for the subsequent oblation; that indeed is the expiation in that case. ||17||

Half of this sacrifice is indeed lost for him whose evening-milk offering meets with disaster. Having set aside rice-grains for Indra, he should fast; for plants are milk, and by thus beginning with milk, he fasts having grasped milk itself. They should prepare a hundred [grains] for that which was intended for the morning, and the other cake should be for Indra. For plants are milk; verily, by means of milk he causes milk to be bestowed upon him. Then he should drive away the calves for the subsequent offering; that indeed is the expiation in that case. Verily, he provides both classes of gods with their respective portions.

Those who come to the house of the sacrificer both morning and evening cause him to diminish. If the sacrificial milk of one whose offering is spoiled by damage occurs both morning and evening, he should offer a five-platter oblation of cooked rice. He should worship Agni first among the deities; thus he gratifies the deities with Agni as their mouth. Those deities who follow Agni and those who follow Indra—he gratifies both groups of them. Then, for the subsequent offering, he should drive away the calves; that indeed is the expiation in that case. If he should offer with [milk] into which insects have fallen, he will be childless.

The sacrificer would be without cattle if he were to pour it out in a place that is not its proper abode; he would be without an abode. He should pour it out within the enclosing stones with the middle leaf of the palāśa branch and with a verse addressed to Heaven and Earth. Heaven and Earth are indeed the foundation of the sacrifice; verily, he causes him to reach that very foundation. That itself is the expiation in that case. If, while the *prayāja* offerings have not yet been performed, a coal should fall toward the east, it would bring misfortune to both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer; if toward the south, it would bring misfortune to both the Brahman and the sacrificer; if toward the west, it would bring misfortune to both the Hotṛ and the wife.
If there should be harm to the fire-priest, or to the sacrificer, or to the sacrificial animals, one should hurl that [missile] toward the north.

The thousand-horned bull, Jātavedas, whose back is the Stoma, who is rich in clarity and beautiful of countenance—may he not desert me, nor may I, being in need, abandon him. Grant me the nourishment of a thousand and the nourishment of cattle.

Thus he strikes it with the very *brahman*; that itself is the expiation in that case. Half of this sacrifice is indeed lost for him whose wife becomes one who does not touch [him] on the day of the vow; having excluded her, he should perform the sacrifice. Thus he sacrifices with the entire sacrifice; having sacrificed, he should call her back.
You are she, I am he; I am he, you are she. Come, let us two unite for the sake of producing a male son, for the increase of wealth, for good offspring, and for heroic vigor.
He thus causes her to share in half of this [world]; that indeed is the expiation in that case. ||18||

If he were to offer while it has not rained upon him, a deformed offspring would be born to him; if he were to return [without offering], he would become worse off; if he were not to offer at all, he would meet with calamity.
Mitra, knowing all, impels men; Mitra has supported both the earth and the sky.
Mitra gazes unblinking upon the peoples; let us offer to Mitra an oblation rich in ghee.

Having thus offered a fuel-stick with the verse addressed to Mitra, he should sacrifice; for Mitra is indeed the pacification of the sacrifice, and by means of Mitra he pacifies it. Having sacrificed that, he should then milk another cow and sacrifice again; that itself is the expiation in that case. If he should sacrifice with [milk] into which an insect has fallen, the sacrificer will be without offspring and without cattle; if he should not sacrifice at all, he would meet with calamity. He should pour it out into an anthill with the verse addressed to Prajāpati; for the anthill belongs to Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice; thus he establishes the sacrifice within the sacrifice itself.

Having offered that, one should offer another after milking again; that itself is the expiation in this case. If, when the first oblation has been offered, the subsequent oblation spills, the sacrificer would be deprived of two-footed animals; if he were to pour it back onto the fire, the sacrificer would be deprived of four-footed animals.
O Lord of the Forest, wherever you know the secret names of the gods, there bring our oblations.

Having thus placed a fuel-stick with a verse addressed to the Lord of the Forest (*vanaspati*), one should offer the oblation; for by means of the Lord of the Forest alone, he maintains both the afflicted and the unafflicted offerings. Having offered that, and having then milked another [cow], one should offer again; that indeed is the expiation in that case.

The gods and the Asuras were both in this world. Prajāpati desired, "May I drive away the Asuras and create offspring. He saw these Cāturmāsya sacrifices; by means of the Cāturmāsyas he drove away the Asuras, and by means of the Cāturmāsyas he created offspring. He who, knowing thus, performs the Cāturmāsyas drives away his rival and is propagated with offspring and cattle. Having fashioned the Vaiśvadeva sacrificial rite from the Agniṣṭoma, Prajāpati [created] offspring.

Having fashioned the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice from the Ukthya, he caused the creatures to be seized by Varuṇa; having fashioned the Sākamedha sacrifice from the Atirātra, Indra slew Vṛtra. By means of the Vaiśvadeva, he indeed drove away the Asuras; by means of the Vaiśvadeva, he created the creatures.

Some creatures were already created, while others were not yet created. Then Prajāpati desired, "May I create offspring. The sacrifice is indeed the year, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. From his own self, he fashioned forth these two milks: that which is for the cow-pen (*audhanya*) and that which is for the cart (*vahnya*). Then, from these deities, he assigned these oblations as their shares; with them, he created offspring. Those offspring were indeed born from the seasons; these five oblations are the seasons, for there are five seasons. Thus one is born from them—Agni himself.

Soma caused the seed to be cast forth; Agni and Soma constitute a pair. Savitṛ impelled it; Savitṛ is indeed the year, and the year consists of twelve months; therefore, the cake is offered on twelve potsherds. Moreover, it is offered on twelve potsherds for the sake of its being dedicated to the All-gods (vaiśvadeva). He sacrifices silently, for the year is undefined. Sarasvatī placed speech within her as she was created; they released Pūṣan as their foundation.

Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and Pūṣan is cattle; speech and cattle are a productive pair. From the middle, offspring are released; from the end, they are born spreading in all directions from the productive pair. Thus, it is from Prajāpati himself that offspring are released from the middle, and then from the end, they are born spreading in all directions from the productive pair on both sides. These oblations are indeed slayers of Vṛtra. With Agni as his vanguard, Indra slew Vṛtra, impelled by Soma the king, by Savitṛ, and by Sarasvatī the mother;
Pūṣan stood by him with his heroic powers. These oblations are truly victory. 20.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth section, named "Expiation," in the *Orimikā* of the *Caraka* recension within the glorious *Kāṭhaka* of the *Yajurveda*. 35.

Now the thirty-sixth section: The Cāturmāsya sacrifices. When Indra had slain Vṛtra, his *indriya* and *vīrya* departed; it entered into all this—the waters, the plants, and the trees. Because of that, the gods exerted themselves. They brought together this [substance], which is the *sānnāyya* offering. Both curd and milk are indeed a pair; when they are mixed together, it appears like cream, like whey, as if it were something solidified. That is indeed the embryo. From heat (*tapas*) offspring are born; it attains the state of heat when it reaches the state of being boiled; from that very state it is born.

In that he created offspring with the curdled milk (āmikṣā) dedicated to the Viśvedevas, therefore these offspring belong to the Viśvedevas; for the Viśvedevas are indeed the drops (stoka), and it is them he thus worships, for offspring subsist upon what is given from beyond.

This is indeed the womb of creatures; the Maruts desired it, and from them, being unseized, they were emitted. Because [the offering] is for those who possess their own property (*svatavat*), it is for the sake of self-possession and for the sake of expiation. The Maruts are indeed cattle; this cake on seven potsherds is for the sake of procreation among cattle. There are seven Maruts; it is for the sake of complete release. Moreover, by this he wins the food of the village. Those [creatures], created by the Vaiśvadeva [offering], went apart in all directions; he encompassed them with the Dyāvāpṛthivī [offering]. This is for the sake of the creatures that have been created.

Because it consists of a single potsherd, it belongs to Prajāpati; thus the deities find firm support in Prajāpati. The cake on one potsherd is indeed the sacrificer, and the Āhavanīya fire is the heavenly world; he offers it as a complete oblation (*sarvahuta*), and having become an offering, he causes him to go to the heavenly world. The cake on one potsherd is his very self.

Animals are ghee; when he fills [the vessel] with ghee, he causes him to prosper through animals themselves. If he were to fill it [completely], the animals would attend upon him while consuming him, for he makes him inferior to the animals. It should be made with the back exposed; thus he makes him superior to the animals, and the animals attend upon him while consuming him. Therefore, one need not worry about that; he should simply fill it up, for animals do not fail to consume. He places it on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for stability. The sacrificer indeed...

When the sacrificer falters, the subjects falter after him; when the sacrificer is firmly established, the subjects become firmly established after him. He should be offered straight and well-established for the sacrificer’s firm establishment. ||1||

Then he is bound in three ways; the fuel is bound in three ways, for the Cāturmāsya sacrifices are ordained in three ways by the year. One should sacrifice in spring for the sake of procreation; one should sacrifice on sloping ground for the sake of procreation; there are plants growing there, [thinking] "May they bring me forth. They do not throw up the high altar for the sake of procreation; one churns the fire for the sake of procreation, for cattle are born after the fire; and furthermore, he thus generates this bull for the sacrificer. The speckled butter is indeed cattle, which are of various forms.

Therefore, animals are of various forms: the ghee belongs to Agni, the curd belongs to Indra, and the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) belongs to Indra and Agni by deity. Indra and Agni are out-breathing and in-breathing; offspring have their origin in the couple, for out-breathing and in-breathing are the couple. Thus, from that very couple, one is born as progeny.

If he should sacrifice in spring, he should spread [the underlayer] twice and pour [the clarified butter] once; thus he establishes the plants. If he should sacrifice in the rainy season, he should spread [the underlayer] once and pour [the clarified butter] twice; thus with rain itself he sprinkles the cattle. From the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), indeed, creatures are born; these nine oblations are the vital breaths, and the deity is the self (*ātman*); from that very source he is born. There are nine *prayāja*s and nine *anuyāja*s, two *ājyabhāga*s, eight oblations—he cuts off for Agni and sacrifices to the *vājina*s; that is so.

The Virāj consists of thirty syllables; the Virāj is food. Verily, he finds firm support in the Virāj, in the eating of food. The Virāj indeed consists of thirty syllables; from the womb of the Virāj, creatures are born. From the very womb of the Virāj, he causes them to be born.

There are thirty nights in a month; that which is a month is indeed a year, and the year is Prajāpati. Thus, from this very union of Prajāpati and Virāj, [the sacrifice] is born. Indeed, with each single oblation, they won twelve nights each. As many as are the nights of the year, so great is their number; by this calculation, they win the year itself from their rival. With the Vaiśvadeva, they won four months; with the Varuṇapraghāsas...

Four [months] beyond those they drove away by means of the Sākamedha offerings, and four [months] beyond those they likewise drove away their rivals; because they drove them away for four months at a time, that is the reason for the Cāturmāsya (four-monthly) nature of these rites. ||2||

One who desires offspring or cattle performs the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, but not the Varuṇapraghāsas nor the Sākamedhas. Every man is born with a thousand-fold [potential], yet he reaches only as much vigor as his generative power allows. The Vaiśvadeva is a sacrificial oblation that is generative; he sacrifices it thinking, "May I reach my own full measure. When he should reach a thousand cattle, then he should perform the Varuṇapraghāsas; by that very thousand he has reached, he expiates that sin. One is a performer of the seasonal sacrifices (Ṛtuyājī), while the other is a performer of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.

He who sacrifices thinking, "Spring has been," "The rainy season has been," "Autumn has been," is a performer of the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtuyājī*). He who brings about a thirteenth month performs sacrifice unto that thirteenth month; he is a performer of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices. Having performed three straight [series of] sacrifices, he should omit the fourth; having performed two subsequent straight series, he should omit the third. Those which are indeed the three years, their full-moon sacrifices number thirty-six; those which are the two [years], their [full-moon sacrifices] number twenty-four. Of the thirty-six, they reach the twenty-four that are in excess; this indeed is that.

The thirteenth month—this he thereby perfects; it is that he sacrifices to. When he sacrifices to *barhis* in the fore-offerings (*prayāja*), he sacrifices to the plants; when he sacrifices to *barhis* in the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), he sacrifices to the fruit; when he sacrifices to the *barhis* of the *vāritī* grass, he sacrifices to that which is produced from the fruit. When he sacrifices to the *duraḥ*, he sacrifices to the womb; when he sacrifices to Dawn and Night, he sacrifices to both the rising and the setting; when he sacrifices to the two *joṣṭrī*, he sacrifices to what has been born and what is yet to be born; when he sacrifices to the two *ūrjāhuti*, he sacrifices to that which one eats.

He drinks and he offers that [oblation] which belongs to the divine *hotṛ*s; these indeed are the divine *hotṛ*s, and it is to them that he offers when he offers to the three goddesses. The three goddesses are indeed speech; it is speech itself that he offers when he offers to them. Speech is indeed the meters; it is the meters themselves that he offers. He offers to Narāśaṃsa. The sacrifice, when it has set forth, is Tanūnapāt, but Narāśaṃsa is [the sacrifice] when it has not yet set forth. Now, at this point, the sacrifice has indeed set forth; therefore, he offers to Narāśaṃsa in the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s). He offers to Tvaṣṭṛ, for he is the one who transforms forms.
He sacrifices to Vanaspati; Soma is indeed Vanaspati, and these creatures belong to Soma; verily, he bestows vigor upon the creatures. ||3||

He sacrifices to the *vājins*; the *vājins* are indeed cattle; it is them he thus sacrifices. This is not like a well-performed sacrifice, for when the sacrifice has been completed and the enclosing-sticks have been cast away, he offers.
