In that the Hotṛ recites the offering-verse without drawing breath, by that the sacrifice is performed. He performs the after-sacrifices (*anuyāja*s); Agni is the *samiṣṭi*, Agni is the foundation. It is for the sake of the foundation through the *samiṣṭi*. The *vājins* are indeed cattle; if he were to bring the sacrifice to a conclusion, he would conclude those [cattle], for these [cattle] are born perpetually without being concluded. While pouring [the butter] over the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he follows.

He takes [the portion] from the bulls themselves; he places seed in offspring, for offspring are indeed the *barhis* and seed is strength (*vājina*). Sitting with his knees raised, he performs the sacrifice; for the animal has its knees raised, and thus he places seed in the animal. Having invited one another, they consume [it], for this is like a drinking of Soma. All the officiating priests eat it, saying, "May the *vājins* carry my sacrifice," so that he may eat it for himself; verily, he places strength in himself.

They were indeed created by Prajāpati through the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice; Varuṇa seized them while they were still young. Then he brought them back, and as they were passing beyond him, he caused them to be seized by Varuṇa. Therefore, one must not pass beyond [the father]. Indeed, Prajāpati created offspring through the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice; the Maruts scrambled his oblation, and from that, they were born seized by evil (*aṃhas*). He sought a remedy for them; he sought it within himself. From himself, he fashioned forth milk. With that, he ransomed them from evil, from *aṃhas*.

This Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice is indeed an "encircling" (aveṣṭi); for Varuṇa seizes one who has consumed what is forbidden; therefore it is called Varuṇapraghāsa. As much sin as exists in a child before it is born, so much sin belongs to him who performs the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices. Now, these five oblations are for the sake of continuity.

The cake for Savitṛ is on eight potsherds, for Savitṛ is the Gāyatra among the gods. The cake for Indra and Agni is on twelve potsherds for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva nature. When those creatures seized by Varuṇa were as if writhing, then Indra and Agni bestowed strength upon them. Varuṇa did not seize them while they were breathless; indeed, they were not breathing. Indra and Agni are out-breathing and in-breathing; thus out-breathing and in-breathing are placed in the middle. Varuṇa seized those creatures when they were weak; Indra and Agni are vigor and heroism; thus vigor and heroism are placed in the middle.

The offering to the Maruts is for the sake of release from Varuṇa; the offering to Varuṇa is for the sake of freedom from Varuṇa. The offering to Ka is for Kanva; or rather, because Ka was born from those women seized by Varuṇa, it is called Kāya. Prajāpati indeed caused those creatures to be seized by Varuṇa; Ka is Prajāpati, and thus he releases them from Varuṇa by means of himself. Sacrifice is truth and reality, while woman is untruth. She commits an act of untruth who, having been purchased by her husband, then behaves toward others. By performing this rite, she casts off that untruth and attains truth and reality. When he makes her recite [the formula], he renders her fit for sacrifice.
He makes [the fire] fit for sacrifice; he should not speak falsely, for if he should speak falsely, he would be driven away by that which is most dear. ||5||

They are made of raw grain for the removal of all sin; if they were roasted, the removal of sin would be skinless. Varuṇa seized those creatures by means of the vessels; by using the vessels, he releases them from Varuṇa’s grasp. There is one for each person, so that he removes the sin for each person individually. There is one extra, by which he removes the sin from the embryos. Varuṇa seized those creatures by means of food; they carry food with a winnowing-basket, therefore it is offered with a winnowing-basket. A man and a woman [are required].

They offer as a pair; thus they release offspring from Varuṇa. Standing facing each other, they offer from the front; verily, they drive away evil from the front at the beginning. By means of the vessels, they drive away evil from the front for those two-footed animals that exist in pairs. By means of the ram and the ewe, they drive away evil from above for those four-footed animals that exist in pairs. Thus they drive away evil from both sides—from the front and from above.

Having offered the vessels, he cleanses the fire with the mantra: "In that which they have driven away evil and purified, therein let him sacrifice to the deities. For when Varuṇa seizes creatures, he does not seize *śamī* and barley; for Varuṇa belongs to the two winter months (*hemanta*), therefore these two do not wither in winter. By means of those two which are not seized by Varuṇa, he releases these [creatures] from Varuṇa. Barley indeed belongs to Varuṇa and has Varuṇa as its deity; thus he propitiates Varuṇa with his own share. Now, these are the cattle of falsehood, for those creatures [were seized] because of falsehood.

Varuṇa seized these because they were animals of falsehood; verily from Varuṇa he releases them from falsehood. They become a male and a female, for it is through a pair that offspring is released from Varuṇa. They have hair, for the sake of purity; for as many hairs as the animals possessed, so much did they attain to the sacrificial essence (*medha*). There are *śamī* leaves, for the sake of peace. This tree is indeed named *bhūrja*; its ladles should be made. Prajāpati did not obtain food; he obtained it by means of fuel-sticks of *śami* wood—more than a hundred.

The rites for the attainment of food are to be performed by the thousands; indeed, the thousand-fold fuel-pile has encompassed the entanglement of sin. The rites for the entanglement of sin are to be performed by the thousands.

The *sālāvṛkī* wolves indeed devoured the ascetics (*yatīn*); these date-palms (*kharjūra*) are their heads. This rising [sun] is the drinking of Soma; that there are *karīra* fruits is because he thereby secures for himself the drinking of Soma. These mountains are the eldest offspring of Prajāpati; they were winged and flew away wherever they desired. At that time, this earth was loose; Indra cut off their wings, and with them he made firm this earth. Those which were the wings became the clouds (*jīmūta*).

Therefore they overflow the mountain, for this is their source; therefore it rains most abundantly on the mountain. That which flowed forth became the *karīra* fruits; thus, in the rainy season, the clouds overflow. They sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings; verily, he extends the rain. Therefore it rains most abundantly then, for he extends the rain. At the Vaiśvadeva, they do not throw up the high altar (*uttaravedi*); they throw it up here [at the Varuṇapraghāsas]. Verily, he encompasses the offspring already born. That which is the northern altar, that which is the *atrīḥ*...

Those are the offspring; that [altar] is their source, and they are born after it. That which is the southern altar is the source of those who are the first-born offspring, and they are born after it. Thus he procreates both kinds of offspring here: those who are descendants and those who are first-born. This [northern altar] was indeed the hand; this second altar is not [the hand], for by means of it they found this second hand. Therefore, this one is its server, for it is subsequent; therefore, the younger serves the elder. They should be made equal, for these two hands are equal, and they should be unconfused.

If they were to break [the altar] without having performed the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice, their sin would remain unexpiated; therefore, they break it along the single wooden splint (*ekasphyā*) for the sake of continuity. They throw up the northern part [of the altar], not the southern, so as not to ascend back toward what has already been reached.

Varuṇa is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the Maruts are the common people (*viś*); they sacrifice separately for the sake of distinguishing between the worse and the better. Whatever the Adhvaryu does, the Pratiprasthātṛ does that; therefore, what the King (the sacrificer) does, the common people do. There are not thirty oblations in the Vaiśvadeva, nor in the Sākamedhas; it is in the Varuṇapraghāsas alone that there are thirty oblations. Man is of the nature of the *virāj*; he has ten fingers on his hands, ten on his feet, and ten vital breaths—that makes thirty. The *virāj* consists of thirty syllables; man is of the nature of the *virāj*.

When he now performs the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), he expiates his own sin. Whatever part of the sacrifice does not reach the *svagā* formula, Varuṇa seizes that. When he performs the purificatory bath with the scrapings (*niṣkāṣa*), he thereby makes amends to Varuṇa for what has been seized by Varuṇa; furthermore, it is for the expiation of whatever was deposited there belonging to Varuṇa. They return without looking back, so as not to fall into the power of Varuṇa. With the words, "O fuel, may we prosper through thee," they approach the fuel after having made amends to Varuṇa. "Thou art kindling."
"May we prosper"—thus he utters a blessing; "Thou art brilliance, bestow brilliance upon me"—thus he places brilliance within himself. ||7||

Having created offspring and overcome distress, he desired, "May I slay Vṛtra. He, having joined together with these deities—the Maruts as his host, Agni as his vanguard—rushed forward. Having approached Vṛtra and seen him, he stood there seized by a great paralysis, unable to attack. The Maruts, on wind-driven chariots made of reeds, pursued him; they reached his vital parts, and he became motionless. They indeed scorched him thoroughly; therefore, the Sākamedha offerings are called *sāṃtapana* (scorching) and *vārtraghna* (slaying Vṛtra).

Indra slew Vṛtra with Agni as his vanguard; it is for the sake of having a vanguard that this Agni is the commander-in-chief of the gods. This is indeed the rite for the raising of the army. Indra, indeed, was unable to lift the thunderbolt against Vṛtra; he offered this portion to the Maruts. The Maruts heated it for the sake of heroic power; with that heroic power he lifted up the thunderbolt. They heated it thoroughly, therefore they are called the Sāṃtapanas (the Heaters). It should be offered at midday, for then it burns both ends. It is a *caru* (oblation of boiled rice), for that—

The gods indeed scorched Vṛtra from all sides, yet they did not find his vital spot; the Maruts pierced him with a razor-edged thunderbolt, and they thoroughly scorched him; therefore, they are called the Sāṃtapanas. ||8||

Desiring to slay Vṛtra on the morrow, they stayed overnight and said, "To whom will this belong tomorrow? For whom shall we cook it? They cooked this rice; they sought after cattle, thinking, "Whichever of us these will desire tomorrow, they shall be the victors. They set out toward them with this [rice] and caught them with this; this is indeed the acquisition of cattle. Desiring to conquer on the morrow, they stayed overnight and said, "To whom will this belong tomorrow? For whom shall we cook it? They cooked this rice, and they said:

"Let us eat the Māhuta!"—with these words they offered it to the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhas. The Maruts, the Gṛhamedhas, are indeed cattle; it was to them that they thus made the offering. When they were engaged in battle, those Asuras sent hunger against the gods. The gods, having perceived it, cooked this rice-mess (odana). Hunger, finding no place among the gods, returned again to the Asuras and consumed them. Therefore, even if one cooks rice for a neighbor, he sends hunger to his rival, and she consumes him.

That which belongs to the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed that of the Pākayajña; it is among these that there is abundance of cattle. The Gṛhamedha is indeed a Pākayajña; no Prayājas are offered, no Anuyājas are offered, he does not recite the Sāmidhenī verses, yet he offers the two Ājyabhāgas—thereby the sacrifice is performed. He makes the portions for Agni; Agni is the *samiṣṭi* (the completed offering), Agni is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhiti*). It is for the sake of this foundation through the *samiṣṭi*. The Gṛhamedhas are indeed cattle, and the *iḍā* is cattle; therefore they invoke the *iḍā*. The scrapings (*niṣkāṣa*) are deposited for the sake of continuity. Of both these [sets of offerings], Indra is...

The gods departed, leaving this portion for Indra, thinking, "May he choose us tomorrow when his portion has been set aside. The Vaṣaṭ-call then roared, "They have called away the bull of the Asuras themselves; may he procreate us! In calling the bull, he calls upon Indra himself; furthermore, he thus snatches away the prosperity of his rival.

Cows dwell with their calves for the sake of the *Sākamedha* sacrifice. If the wife were not to eat, they would be without the *Sākamedha*; since the wife eats, it is for the sake of the *Sākamedha*. Verily, Nirṛti seizes that part of the sacrifice which the woman eats; for a woman is indeed Nirṛti, and this ladle (*darvī*) is the hand of a woman. In that he offers with the ladle, he expiates Nirṛti by means of Nirṛti herself. Whatever part of the sacrifice does not reach the utterance of *svagā*, Nirṛti seizes that. The ladle is indeed seized by Nirṛti, for it moves about while heated when used with the ladle.

He offers [the oblation]; even as one seized by Nirṛti, he thus expiates Nirṛti. He set out the next day to slay Vṛtra; the Maruts came along, playing around him. Having reached him, they drove him away; they overcame him. Therefore, they are called "the players" (krīḍayaḥ). They were engaged in battle; those gods did not see the furthest limit of the Asuras. Then the Maruts saw them playing, and they thought, "These ones are surely of conquered mind. For them, he set apart this portion; then they conquered. Having conquered—

This very sun is indeed Indra; the rays are the *krīḍayas*. Together with the rays they move forth for the sake of victory. The gods, indeed, did not recognize Vṛtra when he had been slain; the Maruts played (*akrīḍan*) over him, and therefore they are called *krīḍayas*. Now, these five oblations are for the sake of continuity. Then there is the offering to Indra and Agni; Indra and Agni struck him with the thunderbolt. Moreover, they say: "May Indra and Agni bear the thunderbolt for him. Then there is the offering to Indra; by this indeed Indra slew Vṛtra, and he took this as his portion (*uddhāra*), a portion indeed.

This is his portion; and then [he offers] for Viśvakarman with the words, "May all my deeds be accomplished," for he indeed became Viśvakarman after slaying Vṛtra. With the words, "O Agni, perform the office of the Hotṛ, perform the office of the messenger," he pours the libation (āghāra), for the fulfillment of the oblations and for the attainment of the thirty [deities]. ||10||

Having created offspring and having overcome the darkness, and having slain Vṛtra, they desired immortality. The heavenly world is indeed immortality; the year consists of twelve months, and the heavenly world is the year. In that there are twelve oblations, he thereby secures immortality. He has indeed traversed the year; he has reached the year in that he brings together six by six. There are six seasons; it is thus the seasons he establishes again. Following those seasons as they are established, he himself becomes established; from that he is born. This, indeed, transcends...

In that he has entered the year by means of twelve oblations, he turns around the year itself; for he has indeed reached this year—the Pitṛs and the Seasons—and he procreates it. Following him as he is being procreated, they too are procreated. Indeed, the year has become sacrificed to by him, and the Seasons have been sacrificed to; but his Pitṛs were not yet sacrificed to. When this Pitṛyajña is performed, his Pitṛs become sacrificed to and gratified.

It should be set out on the south, for the south belongs to the ancestors; it may also be set out on both sides, for both [gods and ancestors] are worshipped there. But that need not be considered; let it be set out only on the south, for the south belongs to the ancestors. There is a cake on six potsherds; the seasons are indeed six, and by this the seasons become propitiated and pleased for him. Neither with parched grains nor with the stirred drink is the sacrifice truly performed; it is by means of this cake that the sacrifice is accomplished. Now, these parched grains are indeed nectar; they are unlimited in yonder world throughout the year.

These very nights of his become desired and gratified by these [offerings]. Indeed, the sacrifice to the ancestors is neither with parched grains nor with the sacrificial cake; rather, it is because of this stirred drink (*mantha*) that it is a sacrifice to the ancestors. It is made from the milk of a cow whose calf has been taken away, for she is closest to the ancestors. He stirs it with a single [finger], for the ancestors occupy a single world. He stirs it on the south side, for the south belongs to the ancestors. He stirs it without grasping [the vessel], for thus it goes to the ancestors. 11.

He does not dig up the ground toward the east, for the sacrifice to the ancestors is not a southern sacrifice; he digs between the two directions, for both [classes] are worshipped, and thus he reaches both—the gods and the ancestors. The altar has four corners, for the ancestors are in all directions. They cause the sacrifice to be performed within an enclosure, for the ancestors are hidden from yonder sun, and likewise the ancestors are hidden from both the gods and men. He cuts the sacrificial grass (barhis) near its root; by that which is with the root it belongs to the ancestors, and by that which is without the root it belongs to the gods—thus to both.

He goes around spreading the sacrificial grass (barhis) on all sides; for the seasons go around him, encompassed on all sides. He who goes around the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) indeed departs from this world. In that he goes around again after having spread the grass, he returns to this very world. Indeed, in that former [world], the deities sacrifice. If he were to sacrifice there, he would mingle the oblations and cause a conflict. They prepare the cooked offering on the Gārhapatya fire; by that the sacrifice is performed. They bring the fire from the cooking of the rice-porridge (odana); that which is brought from elsewhere is already cooked.

With the verse, "Desiring you, we invoke you," he recites; for the fathers desire [him]. He recites an Anuṣṭubh; the Anuṣṭubh is the end, and the fathers are at the end. Moreover, the Anuṣṭubh contains all the meters. He recites a single verse; for the fathers are in a single world. He recites it thrice; for the fathers are in the third world. In that he recites a single verse, by that he honors the fathers; in that he recites it thrice, by that he honors the gods. Thus both are honored. He does not choose an ancestral seer (ṛṣi) nor a Hotṛ priest; verily, he releases them from death. He performs the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) without the sacrificial grass (barhis); for the sacrificial grass is offspring.

In this way, one releases the offspring from death; indeed, one wraps [the garment] around for the sake of men when about to perform [the rite]. To the south, one wraps it over the left shoulder for the sake of the gods. Now, in this case, it should be worn with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta) for the sake of distinction. Having cut off the portion to the south and having stepped across toward the north, he turns to the south and offers the oblation, for the south belongs to the ancestors.

He sacrifices to Soma first; Soma, indeed, is the deity of the ancestors, for Soma belongs to the ancestral deities. In that he sacrifices to Soma Pitṛmat, he sacrifices to those ancestors who drink Soma. In that [he sacrifices] to the Barhiṣads, he sacrifices to the sacrificers; in that [he sacrifices] to the Agniṣvāttas, he sacrifices to the householders. In that [he sacrifices] to Agni Kavyavāhana—Agni has two bodies: by his *havyavāhanī* (oblation-bearing) form, he carries the oblation to the gods; by his *kavyavāhanī* (ancestral-oblation-bearing) form, he carries it to the ancestors. Agni is the *samiṣṭi* (completion), Agni is the foundation; it is for the sake of completion and for the sake of a firm foundation. Five, five.

He cuts [the portions] five times, for there are five seasons; he utters "svadhā namaḥ" as the *vaṣaṭ*-call, for *svadhā* belongs to the ancestors and the salutation (*namaskāra*) belongs to the gods. Two indeed are the invitatory and offering verses (*anuvākyā* and *yājyā*) of the gods: by the one he offers, and by the other he causes [the deity] to go. Now, in this case, three should be performed for the sake of distinction: two invitatory verses and one offering verse. The ancestors are indeed beyond the gods; by this third [verse], he hands it over to them.

Indeed, human fathers drink after the gods and the ancestors; thus he has now caused the gods and the ancestors to drink. He places them at the corners (of the altar); thereby he sacrifices to the human ancestors. He places them three times, for there are three ancestors here: the father, the son, and the grandson; he thus proclaims them in succession for the sake of continuity. He places them at all the corners; he causes them to go to all the quarters, for the ancestors are in all the quarters. He should not place them on this [earth]; if he were to place them on this earth, he would deliver them to death.

One should take hold of that [ladle]; they follow it. By the very act of wiping it upon that [ladle], he gratifies them. With the words, "O Fathers, rejoice here," they go out; they approach the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "Thee, who art fair to behold, we [approach]. They remain standing until the light fades away. Those who enter upon the Pitṛyajña reach the end of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); by making Agni their witness, they reach the end of the vital breath. With the words, "Depart, O Soma-loving Fathers," they return. For the Fathers have followed after them; [they return] for the sake of separation.

With the words, "The fathers have rejoiced," they enter; they lay down either wool or a fringe. Whatever they step upon there, he offers an oblation for that as an atonement. He sprinkles water around and purifies them. Not sprinkling again, he goes around; for those who enter upon the Pitṛyajña enter that world. Prajāpati alone is able to lead them out from here. When he recites this undefined verse addressed to Prajāpati, "Creating various forms and deeds," it is Prajāpati himself who leads them out from there.

The sacrifice has indeed gone to the ancestors; they return by means of the fivefold [rite], for the sacrifice is fivefold; thus they return together with the sacrifice. His mind goes to the ancestors; with the words, "We call the mind hither," he thereby calls it back again. ||13||

Verily, this year has been sacrificed to by him, and the Pitṛs have been sacrificed to; now his Rudras remain unsacrificed—the Rudras are the Tryambakas. Since these are Tryambakas, thereby his Rudras become sacrificed to and propitiated. They are offered one for each person; verily, he thus pays off Rudra one for each person. There is one additional cake; thereby he pays off Rudra for the embryos. They are prepared on a single potsherd (ekakapāla); for a man cannot be reached by means of [many] potsherds; he reaches him all at once. It should be sprinkled with clarified butter.

"Should it be sprinkled with clarified butter? they deliberate. "It must indeed be sprinkled, for there is no oblation that is not sprinkled. [But] if he were to sprinkle it, he would cause Rudra to descend upon the cattle; therefore, it should not be sprinkled. They carry a single firebrand, for the Rudras belong to a single firebrand. They carry it smoking, for the Rudras belong to what is smoking. They carry it away from here, for they carry Rudra away from here. They carry it toward this quarter, for in this quarter are the dwellings of the Rudras; thus he propitiates Rudra right in his own dwelling.

"I make the rat your victim," saying this, he scatters one grain of *akhukiri* for the sake of the animals; thus he propitiates Rudra with the very animals. Therefore, Paśupati is a slayer of them. They cause him to sacrifice at a crossroads, for the dwellings of the Rudras are at the crossroads; it is in their dwellings that he propitiates Rudra. "This is your portion, O Rudra, together with your sister Ambikā; enjoy it, Svāhā! Autumn is indeed Rudra’s sister Ambikā; he follows after her, and therefore he kills most in the autumn. It is with her that he [propitiates] him.

He makes amends with the middle leaf and offers with it, for that [leaf] is untouched by demons. If he were to offer with a domestic leaf, Rudra would strike down his cattle; therefore, it is offered with a wild leaf. With the words, "O Mother, we have appeased Rudra," they have indeed become free from debt. With the words, "A remedy for the cow, the horse, and the man," having become free from debt, they have provided the remedy.

With the verse, "We worship Tryambaka," they walk around [the fire]. Any woman who desires a husband should also walk around; thus they effect the winning of a husband for her. They throw those [beans] away and recover them; having become free from debt, they recover their fortune (*bhaga*). They pour them together for the sacrificer; thus they pour his fortune together for him. For a woman who desires a husband, they should pour them together for her; thus they pour her fortune together for her. Having placed them in a cloth, they hang them on a tree with the words: "This, O Rudra, is thy portion; with it as thy provision, go beyond the Mūjavat mountains."

The mountain is indeed the womb of Rudra; from there he descends. By means of his own portion, he causes him to go to his own womb. They come back without looking back, so that they do not fall under the sway of Rudra. With the words, "Thou art fuel; may we prosper," they approach the fuel after having offered a portion to Rudra. With the words, "Thou art a kindler; may we be kindled," he invokes a blessing. With the words, "Thou art brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me," he places brilliance within himself. A woman is indeed *ambī* (mother), and she is called *bhagā* (fortune). Therefore, the *tryambaka* offerings are [for her]. He for whom [the sacrifice] is unestablished is indeed unstable.

The oblation is not established; the Tryambaka offerings are not performed, nor the Prayājas, nor the Anuyājas, nor does he recite the Sāmidhenī verses. He offers a pap to Aditi; for Aditi is this [earth], she is the foundation; verily, upon her he finds firm support. ||14||

That essence of the waters which is in their flow, that I take for this man, for so-and-so, for the descendant of such-and-such, for the sake of splendor and luster. That essence of the waters which is in their wave, that I take for this man, for so-and-so, for the descendant of such-and-such, for the sake of vigor and sovereign power. That essence of the waters which is in their midst, that I take for this man, for so-and-so, for the descendant of such-and-such, for the sake of progeny and nourishment. That body of the waters which is worthy of sacrifice, that I take for this man, for so-and-so, for the descendant of such-and-such, for the sake of life and long-livedness.
In the chariot, in the axles, in the vigor of the bull, in the wind, in Parjanya, and in the breath of Varuṇa—
that blessed goddess who gave birth to Indra has come here, in harmony with splendor.
She who is within the elephant, the leopard, the gold, the cattle, the horses, and within men—
the blessed goddess who gave birth to Indra— she has come here, in harmony with splendor.
The splendor that is in the lion, the tiger, and the adder; that which is in fire, in the Brahmin, and in the sun;
the auspicious goddess who gave birth to Indra—that very one has come here, in harmony with radiant luster.
That goddess who is in the drum of the nobleman, in the neighing of the horse,
and in the magic power of man— she, the fortunate one who gave birth to Indra, has come here, in harmony with splendor.

You are the Rāj, you are the Virāj, you are the Samrāj, you are the Svarāj. For Indra, the honeyed one, I mix you, the honeyed; for Indra, the powerful one, I mix you, the powerful; for Indra, the milky one, I mix you, the milky; for Indra, the long-lived one, I mix you, the long-lived. You are luster; bestow that upon me; I bestow that upon you. You are power; bestow that upon me; I bestow that upon you. You are milk; bestow that upon me; I bestow that upon you. You are life; bestow that upon me; I bestow that upon you.
May my face be radiant; may my head be radiant.
May I be radiant on every side; endow me with radiance from all quarters.
May my face be full of vigor; may my head be full of vigor.
Being vigorous in every direction, endow me with vigor from all sides.
May my mouth be full of milk; may my head be full of milk.
May I be full of milk on every side; nourish me with milk.
May my mouth be endowed with long life; may my head be endowed with long life.
O Long-lived One, facing me from every side, do thou endow me with long life.

With this Gāyatrī metre, with the Trivṛt Stoma, with the Rathantara Sāman, with Agni as the deity, I take from you, O *asau*, brilliance and luster. With this Triṣṭubh metre, with the Pañcadaśa Stoma, with the Bṛhat Sāman, with Indra as the deity, I take from you, O *asau*, vigor and sovereign power. With this Jagatī metre, with the Saptadaśa Stoma, with the Vairūpa Sāman, with the Viśve Devas as the deity, I take from you, O *asau*, progeny and prosperity. With this Anuṣṭubh...
By means of the twenty-one-fold Stoma, the Vairāja Sāman, and Prajāpati as the deity, I take from you [Name] long life and longevity.
O Agni, immerse him in long life and splendor; O Varuṇa, sharpen his keen vigor.
Like a mother, O Aditi, grant him protection, so that all the gods may see him reach old age.
Viśvakarman, Viśvadeva, Viśvajit, Viśvadarśata—these have generated you with a stream of clarified butter for preeminence.
From whence the wind is as swift as thought, and from whence the rivers flow—
by the splendor of all those [waters], I consecrate you with luster.
I have sprinkled you with splendor, together with sacrifice and milk;
may Savitar make you such that you are an increaser of friends.
All songs have magnified Indra, who is as expansive as the ocean,
the best of charioteers among charioteers, the true lord of spoils, the master.

With that essence which is in the flowing of the waters, I consecrate this man, the son of such-and-such a lineage and of such-and-such a mother, for splendor and for the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). With that essence which is in the wave of the waters, I consecrate this man, the son of such-and-such a lineage and of such-and-such a mother, for vigor and for sovereign power (*kṣatra*). With that essence which is in the midst of the waters, I consecrate this man, the son of such-and-such a lineage and of such-and-such a mother, for progeny and for nourishment. With that body of the waters which is worthy of sacrifice, I consecrate this man, the son of such-and-such a lineage and of such-and-such a mother, for life and for long-livedness. 15. [2321]
Thus ends the thirty-sixth section, named the Cāturmāsyas, in the Orimikā of the Caraka recension of the Śrī Yajurveda Kāṭhaka. 36.

Now follows the thirty-seventh section. Regarding the *savas*: Prajāpati created offspring; they departed from him. He desired, "May they turn back toward me. He cooked this rice-offering (*odana*); it stood there as food itself, unified. Not finding food elsewhere, those offspring turned back toward Prajāpati alone for the sake of eating food, all together. Indeed, however many creatures speak speech here, they all turn back toward him who is consecrated by this rite for the sake of eating food, all together. This is the *odanasava*. [He recites: "Thou art a sovereign (*rāj*), thou art a universal ruler (*virāj*"); all these [names] indeed [are used].

All foods exist; all men exist. He secures all foods and all men. He gives gold to the Brahmin; thereby he purchases splendor (tejas). He gives a bow with three arrows to the Rājanya; thereby he purchases vigor (ojas). He gives a goad to the Vaiśya; thereby he purchases nourishment (puṣṭi). He gives a bowl of beans to the Śūdra; thereby he purchases life-span (āyus). He fastens on the gold; thus he establishes it in him.

When he eats the boiled rice, he thereby secures all this and places it within him in a single mass. It is performed under the Rohiṇī asterism; for the Brahmins are Rohiṇī, therefore it is performed when the sun has risen. For this is the form of Prajāpati when he rises: all these creatures indeed rejoice at him. He becomes one who is desirable to behold and beautiful to look upon. They deliberate: "Has he reached the avabhṛtha (concluding bath), or has he not? In that he purifies [the sacrificer] with bunches of darbha grass, he thereby reaches it; yet he does not reach it. Thus he accomplishes both.

He purifies with two; truth and untruth—by means of truth alone he purifies away his untruth. With two [he purifies]: out-breath and in-breath. He purifies with three; for the gods are threefold in truth, and moreover, there are three vital breaths: out-breath, diffused breath, and in-breath. He purifies with five; for these Darbha blades are the brilliance of the waters and the plants. In that he purifies with Darbha stalks, he consecrates him with the very brilliance of the waters and the plants.

There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Bṛhaspati, a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma, a pap for Sarasvatī, a cake of barley on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth. As for the cake for Agni: the Brāhmaṇa is indeed related to Agni; as for the pap for Soma: the Brāhmaṇa is indeed related to Soma; as for the [cake] for Savitṛ: it is for impulsion, for Savitṛ is the impeller; as for the [pap] for Bṛhaspati: Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; this is the lordship of speech belonging to the Brāhmaṇa; as for the [cake] for Agni-Soma: he is indeed related to Agni and related to Soma.

When these two [Soma cups] meet, then one becomes possessed of vigor. That which belongs to Sarasvatī is indeed speech, for Sarasvatī is speech; this is the manifest lordship of speech belonging to the Brāhmaṇa. That which belongs to Varuṇa is for the sake of release from Varuṇa’s noose. For whoever is consecrated, regardless of who he may be, he is subject to Varuṇa; thus there is that which belongs to Varuṇa. As for that which belongs to Heaven and Earth: Indra, when he raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra, Heaven and Earth did not approve of it. They approved of it through this share. This is indeed an imitation of the thunderbolt; one should be consecrated with the thunderbolt approved by both.

Thus, when there are eight oblations—the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, the Gāyatrī is the Brahman—[the sacrificer] is consecrated upon the black antelope skin with the thought, "May he be consecrated by means of the Brahman. For the black antelope skin is the form of the Ṛc and the Sāman; verily, he is consecrated upon the Ṛc and the Sāman. With gold he purifies the clarified butter for the sake of brilliance and luster; since he is consecrated with clarified butter, thereby he attains preeminence. ||2||

There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Pūṣan, a cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for the Viśve Devas, a cake on eight potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ, a cake made of barley on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts, and a dappled barren cow for the Maruts. As for the offering to Agni: it is for prosperity, for prosperity indeed has Agni as its mouth. As for the offering to Pūṣan: Pūṣan is nourishment; the Vaiśya is indeed nourishment. As for the offering to Savitṛ: it is for instigation, for Savitṛ is the impeller. As for the offering to the Viśve Devas: the Vaiśya belongs to the Viśve Devas. As for the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ: Tvaṣṭṛ indeed fashions forms. As for the offering to Varuṇa...

It is for the sake of freedom from Varuṇa that there is an offering to Varuṇa; for whoever is consecrated while being [still] a common man, he belongs to Varuṇa. As for the offering to the Maruts, it is because a Vaiśya belongs to the Maruts. There are seven oblations, for the Maruts are seven. Now, this spotted cow is for the Maruts; its portions belong to Agni. Then he is consecrated. The Maruts are indeed the people (viś); thus he is consecrated from the midst of the people. Therefore, he is dear to the people, for he is consecrated from the midst of the people. He is consecrated upon the skin of a bull, for he is a progenitor, [this serving] for procreation. He is consecrated with sour milk; the sour milk is soft, and so he makes him soft.
Let us magnify with sacrifices the greatness of these, the worshipful Narāśaṃsa,
who are wise, pure, and supporters of prayer— the gods who enjoy both kinds of oblations.

He who sacrifices with Soma performs the *devasava*; he who sacrifices with an animal performs the *devasava*; he who sacrifices with an *iṣṭi* performs the *manuṣyasava*. The gods indeed gave their approval to this [rite] for the sake of the earth; with it they consecrated him. He also brought forth the wild animals. Truly, whatever creatures here speak speech, of all of them he is consecrated when he is consecrated by this [rite]. He is consecrated by means of concealment; he is consecrated with a verse addressed to Nārāśaṃsa, for man is Nārāśaṃsa—whatever [is human].

In the Rājasūya, that which is not performed on the Uttaravedi is performed here in its entirety. Now, there is this Marut offering on twenty-one potsherds; for it, there is a portion set aside for Agni. Then he is consecrated. There are indeed thrice seven Maruts; the Maruts are the people (*viś*). Thus he is consecrated from the very midst of the people; therefore, he is dear to the people, for he is consecrated from the very midst of the people. ||4||
May thy milks come together, and let thy strengths and thy bull-like powers, which overcome the assailants, unite.
Swelling for the sake of immortality, O Soma, bestow upon us the highest glories in heaven.

Indeed, there is no pressing of Soma with Soma, for Soma is already pressed; they kill Soma, and what is killed is not pressed. He is consecrated with a *triṣṭubh* verse addressed to Soma, for that is the pressing of Soma; he is also consecrated with one addressed to Soma during the birth of a cow, for she is the depositor of seed and Soma is seed. Whatever else is in the Rājasūya except for the *stomas*, all that is performed here. Now, this cake on twenty-one potsherds is for the Maruts; it has its portioning-off for Agni, and then he is consecrated. For the Maruts are thrice seven.
The Viṇmaruts are the people (viś); he is consecrated from the midst of them; therefore he is dear to the people, for he is consecrated from the midst of the people. ||5||

That which is the Rājasūya is the consecration of Varuṇa; that which is the Vājapeya is the consecration of a sovereign (samrāj). Prajāpati is the sovereignty (sāmrājya); Parameṣṭhin is self-sovereignty (svārājya). This very [sacrifice] is the Gosava; for as is a cow, so indeed does he become who is consecrated by this [rite]. He is consecrated with the Pratiduh vessel, for that is self-sovereignty. The Bṛhat Sāman is used, for that is self-sovereignty. Ten thousand is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), for that is self-sovereignty. They chant the Kaṇvarathantara during the Pavamāna laud. He is consecrated to the south of the Āhavanīya fire, while it has not yet been dug out.

This is indeed the cow; he is consecrated without any interval from her. There is the thirty-sixfold hymn-form (*ṣaṭtriṃśastoma*); this is the "Hymn-form of Cattle" (*paśustoma*), and by means of it, it is the *gosava*.

The Trivṛt-stoma is indeed spiritual luster; by means of spiritual luster he is consecrated. The Rathantara-sāman is indeed spiritual luster; by means of spiritual luster he is consecrated. The Agniṣṭoma-stoma is indeed spiritual luster; by means of spiritual luster he is consecrated. The Pravargya is performed; the Pravargya is indeed spiritual luster; by means of spiritual luster he is consecrated. The Hotṛ wears a wreath, he is tawny-eyed and blind, and he possesses the three Śukriyas; this indeed—

The form of *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster) is by means of its very form that he wins *brahmavarcasa*. This pressing is indeed one, for there is a single *stoma*, a single *chandas*, and he should give eleven [cows] at each pressing; this is for the distinction of the pressings. They amount to thirty-three; the deities are thirty-three, and thus he wins the deities themselves. He gives a horse as the thirty-fourth; Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth, and thus he attains Prajāpati. Indeed, the gods did not trust Bṛhaspati; him they [consecrated] with this...

Prajāpati caused [the sacrifice] to be performed; then they placed their faith in him. This is the Bṛhaspatisava; one who desires spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should sacrifice with this, and he becomes possessed of spiritual luster. Its rule is this very one: all his subjects become Brāhmaṇas possessed of spiritual luster. ||7||

The fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśastoma*) is indeed vigor and strength; by means of vigor and strength he is consecrated. The *Bṛhat* chant is indeed vigor and strength; by means of vigor and strength he is consecrated. The fifteenfold hymn-form is indeed vigor and strength; by means of vigor and strength he is consecrated. The fifteenfold hymn-form is indeed vigor and strength; by means of vigor and strength he is consecrated. The *Ukthya* hymn-form is indeed vigor and strength; by means of vigor and strength he is consecrated. The *Indra*-related *stotra* and *śastra*, the *Pavamāna* chants in the *Triṣṭubh* meter—these are indeed vigor and strength; for the *Triṣṭubh* is vigor and strength, and by means of vigor and strength he is consecrated. Indeed, all adversaries, all destroyers, and all [obstacles] [assail] Indra.

Desiring to destroy him, the Rakṣases sought to harm him; Prajāpati caused him to sacrifice with this [rite], and he overcame all adversaries, all destroyers, and all Rakṣases. When the sacrificer, being Indra, performs this sacrifice, he likewise overcomes all adversaries, all destroyers, and all Rakṣases. This is the Indrasava.
Bestow, O God Savitṛ, upon our first father his height and his vastness;
then, O Savitṛ, pour forth for us day by day many desirable things and cattle.
Being himself a being, he moves among beings; having entered them, he has become their sovereign.
While death performs the Rājasūya sacrifice for him, may that King grant his approval for this kingdom.
With those crafts by which Prajāpati spread out the earth, with which he made firm the sky,
and with which he fashioned speech in its manifold forms— that imperishable power— with that, anoint this man here first with splendor.
With those rays by which the Āditya shines forth, with which the Sun of brilliant luster is seen,
and with those imperishable, lotus-like [rays] by which he [produces] speech— with those, anoint this man here first with splendor.
May he come with power over the five peoples; may he be like Indra, the eldest among all creatures.
May there be abundance in him, O Citrabhānu; may he fill the measured expanse with his radiance.
O Kaśyapa, that art of yours which is radiant, powerful, abundant, and of wondrous luster—
in which the seven suns are placed together— upon that let us establish this king.
O tiger, stride with valor upon the tiger-skin;
may the great quarters, all the people, and the celestial waters rich in milk desire you.
The waters that are celestial, which have come together with the milk, those that are in the intermediate space and those that are terrestrial—
with the luster of all of them, I consecrate you with splendor.
I have sprinkled you with splendor, together with sacrifice and milk;
may Savitṛ make you such that you are an increaser of friends.
All songs have magnified Indra, who is as expansive as the ocean—
the best of charioteers among charioteers, the true lord and master of spoils.
Advance, display your heroism; be fierce, a mindful slayer of rivals. Ascend, you who increase your friends; the gods have spoken in favor of you.
Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra; your two bay steeds have been yoked by our sacred prayer.
May the pressing-stone, with its resonant sound, turn your mind toward us.
As he stood firm, all [the gods] adorned him; clothed in splendors, he moves, self-luminous.
That name of this Asura is great; as the omniform one, he has taken his stand upon the immortal realms.
May Indra rejoice after you, may Bṛhaspati, may Soma, and may Agni favor you.
May all the gods favor you, and the seven kings who have been consecrated with water.
May Mitra and Varuṇa favor you here; may Heaven and Earth with the plants favor you;
may Sūrya with the days favor you; may the Moon with the constellations have favored you.
May Heaven and Earth, the wise ones, and the sacrifice and the great sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), protect you.
May *Svadhā* take heed; may Soma and Agni, and Savitṛ with his impulse (*sava*), protect you.
With these [praises], they urge on the tiger, the lion who embraces [the world], for the sake of great wealth.
They groom the tiger within the waters, like those of noble form who have stood up against the ruddy one.

May *bodha* and *pratibodha* protect me from the east; may *asvapna* and *anavadrāṇa* protect me from the south; may *gopāyamāna* and *rakṣamāṇa* protect me from the west; and may *jāgṛvi* and *aruṃdhatī* protect me from the north.
Make us without enemies from below; O Indra, make us without enemies from above. Make us without enemies from behind; make us without enemies from the front.

May we be united with days free from enemies; O All-Gods, may our dawns and our sunsets be free from enemies. May the six wide expanses and the five directions protect us; may they establish us in friendship, and may there be fearlessness for us.
Those who attend to you by night, and those who remain watchful among living beings, and those who protect all cattle—may they remain watchful for our own selves.

“O Awakening, O Counter-Awakening, O Sleepless, O Unslumbering, O Protecting, O Guarding, O Watchful, O Restraining—those gods who are the protectors of the body, do you protect my body here! “Awakening” is indeed the sun; “Counter-Awakening” is Agni. “Sleepless” is the moon; “Unslumbering” is he who blows (the wind). “Protecting” is the day; “Guarding” is the night. “Watchful” is the sacrifice; “Restraining” is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). These indeed are the gods who sustain the kingdom (*rāṣṭrabhṛt*); it is them that he worships for his own protection.

Those who are the sustainers of the kingdom and those who are the followers of the kingdom—to them he entrusts him; for these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed they, and it is to them that he entrusts him. These are their wives; he follows after them with these [oblations]. Here too, an act must be performed for them; it is for their sake that this is done, for one who desires the office of domestic priest (*purodhā*) follows after them.

One should perform [this rite]; it unites both the Brahman and the Kṣatra. If one should practice sorcery against the Kṣatra, he should say: "May this Brahman protect him here, not the Kṣatra. For the Kṣatra is established in the Brahman; by means of the Brahman alone the Kṣatra perishes. It quickly falls away when one seeks to seize it. One should perform it in battle; one should perform it for those who are the sustainers of the kingdom and the supporters of the kingdom—toward them he should resort, and they support the kingdom for him. This is the pairing of these worlds.

The Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings know him; his kingdom does not falter. Agni and his mind, Vāyu and the intermediate space, the sacrifice and the sun, the sky and the moon—these seven are his protectors, for they carry him away from danger. There are thrice-seven armored ones, thrice-seven quiver-bearers, thrice-seven weapon-bearers; to them the ruler of the realm should entrust him. These indeed are the vital breaths; it is to them that he entrusts him. On both sides of the Agniṣṭoma, the gods and the Asuras were arrayed; at the Agniṣṭoma the gods prevailed, while at the Ukthas the Asuras prevailed.

When the gods came to the *ukthas* and when they had conquered the *ukthas*, Indra said, "Who and I shall we two bring this? Varuṇa replied, "I [and you]. Varuṇa supported him; Indra brought it. He said, "Who and I shall we two bring this? Bṛhaspati replied, "I [and you]. Bṛhaspati supported him; Indra brought it. He said, "Who and I shall we two bring this? Viṣṇu replied, "I [and you]. Viṣṇu supported him; Indra [brought it].

"Let him take it with these deities; for by union with these deities, the gods took the kingdom of the Asuras. Having taken the kingdom from his rival by union with these very deities, and having made that kingdom secure, he offers it to those who are the sustainers of the kingdom and those who maintain the kingdom, thinking, 'May they sustain this; may this not perish. Indeed, yonder sun is the kingdom, and the seasons are the sustainers of the kingdom; to them he offers it, thinking, 'May they sustain this; may this not perish'—this being the seventh."

This [oblation] is Prajāpati himself. If one were to offer it in the middle, he would shake him off. It should be offered beyond the reach of the cattle-pen (parogavyūti); thus he does not shake him off. He offers while standing upright, for standing upright one is more vigorous. He offers with a full ladle; Prajāpati is full; verily he attains Prajāpati. ||11||

Commentary: Both the gods and the asuras performed the sacrifice equally; whatever the gods did, the asuras did that too. Those gods saw these *rāṣṭrabhṛt* (kingdom-sustaining) offerings. With the first [offering], they excluded from themselves Agni and the plants; with the second, Sūrya and the mental faculties (*manāṃsi*); with the third, Candramas and the constellations (*nakṣatrāṇi*); and with the fourth, the sacrifice and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Deprived of the sacrifice, deprived of the fee, and deprived of the constellations, whatever those asuras did, they did it as mere sorcery (*kṛtyā*). Therefore, one should not perform [a rite] without a sacrificial fee.

One should prepare the oblation in the house; for when one performs [the sacrifice], he performs a *kṛtyā* (magical spell). With the fifth [offering], he appropriates Prajāpati and the *ṛks* and *sāmans*; with the sixth, Vāyu, the waters, the plants, and vigor. Truly, there is only so much as exists, and by means of these [offerings], they appropriated all that existed for themselves. That which is the seventh is Prajāpati himself; by means of him, they drove them away. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. One who has rivals should sacrifice with these; for truly, there is only so much as exists, and by means of these, he appropriates everything belonging to his rival. That which is the seventh is [Prajāpati].

This is Prajāpati himself; with him he repels [the enemy], and he prospers in his own person while his rival is defeated. With these [sacrifices] one should cause a king engaged in battle to sacrifice. For as much as there is, so much is this [world]; by means of these [offerings], he appropriates all that belongs to them. This seventh [offering] is Prajāpati himself; with him he repels [the enemy] for the sake of victory, and he indeed conquers. With these [offerings] one should cause him to sacrifice if his kingdom should be as if loose or carried away. Having yoked as many chariots as they possess, of whichever one among them is the best—

Having lifted up the right wheel of the chariot, he should offer an oblation upon a reed. The chariot is indeed vigor; by means of vigor, he causes their kingdom to fall apart. They split the chariot wheel; the chariot is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt, they split their evil. If the prepared offering passes over, it is prepared for them. He upon whose reed he offers the oblation is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); this is for the sake of prosperity.

Who are you? Which one are you? What is your name? For whom are you? To which one are you? For what purpose do I place you upon me? As such, O God, protect us with the *gāyatrī* metre during the day; you are the merciful one, you show mercy to the two-footed and the four-footed. You are Āditya; you are the seed of the stallion; you are the missile of the gods; you are my missile—slay him! As such, O God, protect us with the *triṣṭubh* metre during the night; you are the destroyer, destroy that two-footed and four-footed one! You are the pillar.
This is the noose of King Varuṇa; bind that one for the day! You are the leech; this is the noose of Nirṛti; bind that one for the night! To Agni, whose anger has been appeased, Svāhā!
By that same means through which Indra struck down Vṛtra by means of the Anuṣṭubh meters, by that auspicious speech do I today strike him down from his dwelling. 13.

The gods and the Asuras were arrayed for battle. At that time, the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*) was among the Asuras; it was within the mouth of Śuṣṇa the Dānava, whom he carried inside his own mouth, thinking, "Lest it destroy the gods. Those who belonged to the gods, Śuṣṇa had suffused with the nectar; they became exhausted. Indra knew this: "The nectar of immortality is indeed among the Asuras, with Śuṣṇa the Dānava. Having become a honey-lump (*madhvaṣṭhīlā*), he lay down on the path. Śuṣṇa opened his mouth toward it. Indra, having become a falcon (*śyena*), seized it from his mouth and snatched away the nectar. Therefore, this—

Among birds, he is the most powerful; for this is one of Indra’s bodies, and he who knows this bears immortality. If one should desire of someone, "May he live free from disease," one should open his mouth and breathe over him; verily, one breathes over him with immortality. He lives, he reaches a full lifespan, and he does not die before his time.

The gods and the asuras were arrayed for battle. Those gods slew the asuras; of them, those who remained fled after the gods. Pursuing them and casting them back, they came upon them. The gods held a council; they perceived these two, the *brahmayātu* and the *devayātu*. They discharged them against [the asuras], and they burned them up. Pursuing them and casting them back, those two returned. Of them, those who escaped entered into human beings; they are the *yātudhānas* born from that [origin].
The others are meat-eaters; indeed, neither sorcerers, nor flesh-eaters, nor *piśācas*, nor *rakṣases* have power over him, and neither a curse nor malevolent magic reaches him who knows this.

If they should say of him, "He is a Yātudhāna," he must not deny it; for these two indeed are his Yātus. [The priest asks: "Who are you? Which one are you? This one is indeed the Brahman-Yātu; he entrusts him to that very one. [The priest says: "O God, do thou protect us with the Gāyatrī metre during the day. Thus he entrusts himself to the day. [He says: "Thou art gracious; thou art gracious to bipeds and quadrupeds. Thus he entrusts both his bipeds and his quadruped cattle to him. [He says: "Thou art Āditya; thou art the seed of the stallion; thou art the Yātu of the gods; thou art my Yātu; prosper me!"

"Kill him!"—this is indeed the one who goes to the gods; he thus entrusts him to that very one. "Do thou, O God, protect us from the night with the Triṣṭubh metre"—he thus entrusts himself to the night. "Crush! Crush the two-footed and the four-footed of such-a-one!"—he thus entrusts both his two-footed and four-footed cattle to him.

"You are the pillar; you are the fetter"—these two are indeed Yama’s horses, Day and Night. These two, seeking to exclude human beings, are being hurled from here; with these two he thus covers him over. When these two, seeking to exclude him, are being hurled from here, if he should feel as if he were sinking down, he should offer an oblation with the words, "To Agni, whose anger has been appeased, svāhā! For the malevolent sorcerer is liable to become unappeased and turn back against him; this [offering] is for the sake of pacification. ||14||

Hail to the earth! Hail to the intermediate space! Hail to the sky! Hail to desire! Hail to sleep! Hail to the day! Hail to the night! You are satisfied; I am satisfied; my out-breath is satisfied; my diffused breath is satisfied; my in-breath is satisfied; my eye is satisfied; my ear is satisfied; my speech is satisfied; my self is satisfied. Heaven is my father; the earth is my mother; the sun is my eye; the wind is my breath. I am named Unsatisfied. He (the Unsatisfied) has entrusted his self to heaven and earth; may I find refuge in them.

In the prowess of these two, protect me for my preservation; do not harm me, do not harm me! Protect me from the enemy, protect me from injury, protect me from the godless curse! You are a stone, a protector of the body; as such, protect my body here!

In you is my vital core; in Bṛhaspati is my life-breath. O Death, protect me from uttering an improper word, from losing my mental composure, from failing in my senses, from losing my offspring, or from losing my cattle. May he who seeks to harm me from this quarter meet with destruction. O Indra and Agni, protect me from this quarter! O Fathers, protect me from this quarter! O Savitṛ, protect me from this quarter! O Mitra and Varuṇa, protect me from this quarter! O Bṛhaspati, protect me from this quarter! O Giver of Life, O Consort of Life, O You who possess the *svadhā* offering, you are our guardians and protectors; let no one strike us down, and may we not perish. 15.

Those [deposits] which the Asuras deposited for the gods, those the gods perceived; those which the gods deposited for the Asuras, those the Asuras did not perceive. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. Where another does not perceive, there one should deposit these [deposits], for the sake of the non-perception of the rival; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. "To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā! To the sky, svāhā!"—thus three times.

These are the worlds; he thus entrusts him to these very worlds. "To desire, svāhā!"—life is indeed the supreme desire; by this, he preserves life for him. "To sleep, svāhā!"—those destructive powers (*nāṣṭrā*) which seek to harm him while he sleeps, from them he protects him by means of sleep. "To day, svāhā! To night, svāhā!"—day and night are indeed two seasons; by means of these two, he entrusts him. He offers these seven oblations; there are seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*); he thus places those very breaths in him and distributes them within him.

He makes them inseparable from him. He anoints the stone with ghee; for at this time, ghee is his own self and ghee is brilliance. As great as his self is, he anoints that very self with brilliance. He anoints it on all sides; verily, he endows him with brilliance on every side. "Satisfied art thou, satisfied am I"—thus he proclaims his two greatnesses, which are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), for the vital breaths are the greatnesses. "The sky is my father, the earth is my mother, the sun is my eye, the wind is my breath"—by means of these very deities, he entrusts himself, being unharmed.

"By name am I; he [is] this; I entrust myself to Heaven and Earth"—thus he entrusts himself to Heaven and Earth. "In their support, in their prowess"—for he who exerts prowess in these two does not suffer. "Exerting prowess in these two, for my protection, preserve me; do not harm me"—this is for his own safety. "Protect me from enemies, protect me from injury, protect me from the godless curse"—thus he invokes a blessing.

He carries the stone all around; for it protects him from every side. He digs up a clod of earth from the edge, for this much is the extent of the self. He digs a pit as deep as an arm, for man is of that same measure. Having placed [the body] therein, he then places the stone and then the gold upon its northern half. It remains unburied; he buries it up to the navel, for the navel supports the vital breaths—both those that go upward and those that go downward—for the maintenance of the vital breaths. He makes it touch the gold; for gold is indeed immortality.

With gold he joins him together with immortality. He should dig out these [bricks] of his—namely *udvāc*, *unmanīṣā*, and *amati*—and thus he raises them up. The altar is of the measure of the body, for armor is of the measure of the body; if it were not of the measure of the body, it would not be made for the self. As great as this earth is, so great is the altar; he has thus placed forts at its ends. These are indeed the fortresses of the gods, which he has made as protectors for these quarters for the sake of guarding.

The ṛṣis did not see Indra face to face; Vasiṣṭha alone saw him face to face. He was afraid that he would reveal [the secret] to the other ṛṣis. He said, "I will tell you a *brāhmaṇa*, so that offspring shall be born with you as their domestic priest (*purohita*); but do not tell this to the other ṛṣis. To him he spoke these *stomabhāga* formulas. Thereupon, with Vasiṣṭha as their domestic priest, offspring were born. Indeed, the *stoma* is the share of these; therefore they are called *stomabhāgas*.

The state of being a *stomabhāga* is expressed by the formulas: "Thou art a ray; for dwelling thee, quicken the dwelling!"—the dwelling indeed is the gods; thus he announces the sacrifice to the gods. "Thou art an impulse; by Law thee, quicken Law!"—Law indeed is human beings; thus he announces the sacrifice to human beings. "Thou art a following; for the sky thee, quicken the sky! Thou art a junction; for the atmosphere thee, quicken the atmosphere! Thou art a support; for the earth thee, quicken the earth!"—these are the three worlds; thus he announces the sacrifice to these very worlds.

"You are the support; for rain, you; quicken the rain"—thus he secures rain itself. "The one who goes forth, the one who returns"—thus he creates a pair. "The eager one are you; for the Vasus, you; quicken the Vasus. The conscious one are you; for the Rudras, you; quicken the Rudras. The well-disposed one are you; for the Ādityas, you; quicken the Ādityas. There are eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, Vāc as the thirty-second, and Svar as the thirty-third. [He says this] for the sake of the deities, having announced the sacrifice to the deities. "Strength are you; for the Pitṛs, you."

"Enliven the fathers"—he thus extends the line of the gods to the fathers. "Thou art the thread; for offspring, enliven offspring"—he thus extends the line of offspring to cattle. "Thou art the subduer of armies; for cattle, enliven cattle"—he thus extends the line of offspring to cattle. "Thou art wealthy; for plants, enliven plants"—he thus establishes cattle in the plants. "Thou art victorious; for Indra, the yoke-seizer, enliven Indra"—the *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed the thunderbolt.

"Thou art distinguished from others; therefore, thou art a Vajra distinguished from others. Thou art the overlord. For out-breathing, thee! Quicken the out-breathing!"—thus he secures the out-breathing. "Thou art the supporter. For down-breathing, thee! Quickenthe down-breathing!"—thus he secures the down-breathing. "Thou art the glider. For sight, thee! Quickenthe sight!"—thus he secures the sight. "Thou art the bestower of vigor. For hearing, thee! Quickenthe hearing!"—thus he secures the hearing.

This indeed makes him a man; from this he attains the vital breaths. "Thou art threefold (*trivṛt*), for thee who art threefold; thou art well-threefold (*savṛt*), for thee who art well-threefold; thou art forth-threefold (*pravṛt*), for thee who art forth-threefold; thou art after-threefold (*anuvṛt*), for thee who art after-threefold"—thus he creates a pair. "Thou art the upward-growing (*saṃroha*), thou art the diverging (*viroha*), thou art the forward-growing (*praroha*), thou art the after-growing (*anūroha*)"—this is Prajāpati himself. "Thou art Vasuku, thou art Vasvaṣṭi, thou art Veṣaśrī"—this is the firm foundation itself. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, for Bṛhaspati, the praise!"—whatever indeed Savitṛ impelled for the gods, that [he now impels].

Thus they prosper; impelled by Savitṛ, they praise and they prosper—provided that for one who knows this, there is a Brahman priest who, knowing thus, performs with the Stomabhāgas. He becomes more prosperous. ||17||

I mix you, the sweet with the sweet, the sharp with the sharp, the immortal with the immortal, the honeyed with the honeyed; you are Soma, be prepared for the Aśvins, be prepared for Sarasvatī, be prepared for Indra the Good Protector.
Pour out the pressed juice on all sides; this Soma is the supreme oblation.
He who, flowing as a hero within the waters, has pressed the Soma with the stones.
May the purified wind purify you.

The Brahman, the Kṣatra, brilliance, and sensory power flow forth; the pressed Soma, well-blended with the *surā*, is for exhilaration. O God, satisfy the deities with your bright [light]; bestow nourishment upon the sacrificer with your essence.
Come now, O you who possess barley, just as those who have barley reap it in due order, separating it out;
prepare food here for those who have not come to the trimming of the sacred grass with their homage.
You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to the Aśvins, to Sarasvatī, and to Indra the Good Protector. This is your seat: for splendor you, for heroism you, for strength you.
For manifold indeed is the seat prepared for you two by the gods; do not mingle in the highest heaven! You are Surā, the spirited;

this is Soma—do not harm me as you enter your own womb. You are taken with a support: the splendor of the Aśvins, the vigor of Sarasvatī, the strength of Indra. This is your womb; for delight you, for bliss you, for greatness you!

May she who protects against the tiger, the cholera-demon, and the wolf; who protects against the falcon, the bird of prey, and the lion—may that Soma protect us from evil. You are united; unite me with what is auspicious. You are separated; separate me from evil. 18.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh section, named Savā, in the Orimikā of the Caraka recension of the Śrī Yajurveda Kāṭhaka. 37.
Now begins the thirty-eighth section:
the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. King Soma, the pressed nectar, through the *ṛjīṣa* [residue], has abandoned death.

By means of the Cosmic Order (Ṛta), the Truth, the potent power, the digestion of the bright food—the vital force of Indra, this milk, the nectar, the honey. With the sacred verse, the Swan dwelling in the pure realm drank the Soma from the waters.
By means of the Cosmic Order, the Truth, the potent power, the digestion of the bright food—the vital force of Indra, this milk, the nectar, the honey.
The first-born Kruñ, the Aṅgiras, drank the milk by means of inspired thought.
By the Eternal Law, he drank the true, potent, and bright draught of the soma-juice—this milk, the immortal honey, which is the very power of Indra.
From food he extracted the essence; by means of the sacred word (brahman), the ruling power (kṣatra) drank it.
By cosmic order (ṛta), the truth, the sensory power, the drink, the bright essence of the soma-plant—this is the milk, the nectar, the honey, the very sense-power of Indra.
The seed and urine are cast off as the organ enters the womb;
the embryo, enveloped by the placenta, casts off the amnion at birth.
By the Eternal Law, this truth, the power of the senses, the drinking of the bright essence of the soma-plant—this is the vital power of Indra, the milk, the nectar, the honey.
By means of the Veda, Prajāpati drank the forms [of the world], both the pressed and the unpressed;

by means of the Cosmic Order (Ṛta), he drank the Truth, the sensory power, the drinking-vessel, the bright essence of the plant-juice—this milk, the nectar, the honey, which is the sensory power of Indra.

Having seen the forms, Prajāpati distinguished truth from falsehood; Prajāpati placed lack of faith in falsehood and faith in truth. Through Truth, the power of Indra—the drinking-vessel, the bright, the invigorating—this milk, the nectar, the honey, has become the sensory strength of Indra.
Having seen the flowing juice, Prajāpati drank the bright with the bright, the milk, the Soma.
By the Eternal Law, the truth, the potent drink, the bright essence of the plant—this is the milk, the nectar, the honey, the power of Indra. 1.
With reverence, the mighty ones impel the sacrifice, rich in Soma, seated upon the sacred grass, and abounding in heroes;
offering Soma among the gods in heaven, they, the sacrificers of noble praise, exhilarate Indra with their intoxication.
Whatever essence is gathered in the plants, whatever vigor of Soma pressed with skillful art—
thereby, with that exhilarating joy, quicken the sacrificer, Sarasvatī, the Aśvins, Indra, and Agni.
Yama, the two Aśvins, and Sarasvatī extracted this from the Asura Namuci for the sake of vital power.
Here I consume this very King Soma, the bright, honeyed, and exhilarating drop.
Whatever of this flavorful pressed juice has been left over here, which Indra drank by his powers—
I, with a gracious mind, partake here of that Soma, the King.

Svadhā and obeisance to the fathers who partake of the svadhā; svadhā and obeisance to the grandfathers who partake of the svadhā; svadhā and obeisance to the great-grandfathers who partake of the svadhā. The fathers have eaten; the fathers have rejoiced; the fathers have been satisfied. O fathers, be purified!
May the Soma-loving fathers purify me; may the grandfathers purify me;
may the great-grandfathers purify me with the hundred-year-old purifier.
May the grandfathers purify me; may the great-grandfathers purify me. Through this purifier that grants a hundred-year life, may I attain a full lifespan. O Agni, you purify our lives.
May the divine folk purify me; may they purify me with their minds and their thoughts. May all beings purify me; O Jātavedas, do thou purify me.
Purify me with the purifier, O shining god, with your bright luster; O Agni, [purify] my mental powers according to your wisdom.
That purifier of yours which is spread within your flame, O Agni—may the sacred word (*brahman*) purify me with it.
May Pavamāna, the light-winner, the all-seeing one who purifies with the filter, he who is the cleanser—may he purify me.
O God Savitṛ, purify me on all sides with both the filter and the impulse.
The purifying goddess, belonging to all the gods, has come—she whose forms here have smooth backs. Rejoicing with her in our common feasts, may we be masters of riches.
Those ancestors who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama—for them let there be a world, svadhā, and obeisance; may the sacrifice be prepared among the gods.
May those living beings who are equal to me and of one mind among all living beings— may their prosperity be ordained for me in this world for a hundred years.
I have heard of two paths of the fathers, and of the gods and mortals;
along these two, all this moving world comes together—that which is between the father and the mother.
May this oblation be productive for me, with ten heroes and a full assembly, for my well-being.
May it win me the self, win progeny, win cattle, win safety, and win the world.
May Agni make my progeny abundant; bestow upon us food, milk, and seed. 2.
With lead as the warp, the wise weave the ritual with their minds; with woolen thread, the seers weave it.
The Aśvins, Savitṛ, and Sarasvatī [weave] the sacrifice; Varuṇa [provides] the healing for Indra’s form.

The three deities, acting in harmony through their powers, bestowed upon him this immortal form: his body hairs became grass-blades in many ways, his young shoots became the hair on his head, his skin became flesh, and the parched grains became his fat.
Then the two Aśvins, the physicians whose path is like that of Rudra, and Sarasvatī weave a beautiful form within;
they fashion bone and marrow with the *māsara* mixture, placing them upon the skin of cows.
Sarasvatī weaves with her mind a skillful treasure for the two Nāsatyas—a beautiful form;
she yields a red juice like flowing liquor, as the hero spins out the warp of the loom.
Through milk they produce semen, the immortal generative power; from wine and urine they produce seed.
Driving away ignorance and ill-will, they cast far away the entrails, the wind, and all that [evil].

Indra, the protector, generated truth with his heart; Savitṛ generated it with the sacrificial cake. Varuṇa, acting as a physician, fashioned the liver and the lungs; he does not diminish the bile through the Vāyu-offerings.
The entrails are the cooking pot overflowing with honey; the intestines are the vessels like a cow that yields milk well.
The spleen is like the wing of a hawk through its powers; the navel is the throne-seat, and the belly is like a mother.
The cauldron is the rectum, the progenitor by its powers, in which, at the beginning, the embryo dwells within the womb;
the bladder is manifest as the hundred-streamed well; like a cauldron, it yields the *svadhā* offering to the ancestors.
The mouth is the seat of the assembly; with his head he strives, the tongue is the filter, and Sarasvatī is the Aśvins.
His loins are the caul, the physician is his covering; his penis is the bladder, impetuous with heat.
From the two Aśvins, [he received] immortal vision; from the two cups, brilliance through the goat and the cooked oblation;
the eyelashes were fashioned with wheat and water-lilies; like a skilled artisan, he clothes himself in white and black.
The unaging ram for strength, the immortal path of breath through the two cups,
Sarasvatī with the *upavāka* hymns, and the *barhis* grass with jujube fruits— these have generated the diffused breath (*vyāna*) within the nostrils.
The bull is the form of Indra for the sake of strength; from his two ears comes immortal hearing through the two cups.
The sacrificial grass is like barley, the curls are on his brows; the jujube fruit was born as honey from the bee from his mouth.
On his body there is no hair like that of a wolf; on his face there is no beard like the fur of a tiger;
on his head there are no hairs for the sake of glory and splendor; the crest is the fur of a lion, and his brilliance is the power of the senses.
Then the Aśvins, the physicians, restored his limbs to himself; Sarasvatī joined the self with the limbs, as Indra’s form, a hundredfold life, and immortal light through the moon.
Sarasvatī, the consort, bears within her womb the well-fashioned embryo for the Aśvins;
the King, generating Indra for the sake of glory, does so in the waters with the essence of the waters, with Varuṇa, and with the Sāman.

The luster of cattle, the oblation endowed with sensory power, the foaming liquor, the honey of the bees, and the milk—these have been milked by the two physicians, the Aśvins, and by Sarasvatī, for the sake of the pressed and the unpressed, as the immortal Soma-drop. 3.
You are the navel of the kṣatra; you are the womb of the kṣatra; you are pleasant; you are a good seat; sit upon the pleasant one, sit upon the good seat; may it not harm you, may you not harm me.
Varuṇa, firm in his vows and of excellent wisdom, sat down within the dwellings for the sake of universal sovereignty.

At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you with the healing power of the Aśvins for the sake of splendor and spiritual luster. At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you with the healing power of Sarasvatī for the sake of virility and the enjoyment of food. At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you with the power of Indra for the sake of strength, prosperity, and glory. Who are you? What is your name?
For whom you? For Ka you? O you of fair renown, O you of auspiciousness, O you whose kingship is truth!
Prosperity is my head, glory is my face, splendor is my hair and beard;
the King is my breath, the Immortal is my sovereign power, and the Virāj is my hearing.
My tongue is prosperity, my speech is greatness, my mind is fury, and my wrath is self-ruling splendor; my joys and delights are my fingers, my limbs are my strength, and my friend is my power.
My arms are strength and power; my hands are action and vigor; my chest is the self and the ruling power.
My backbones are the kingdom, my belly and shoulders are the neck and hips; my thighs, forearms, and knees are the subjects—my limbs on every side.
My navel is consciousness; my mind is the anus, which is the ash. My two testicles are joy and delight; my phallus is fortune and good luck.
Through my shanks and feet, I am Dharma, established as the king of the people;
I am established in the ruling power, established in the kingdom, established among the horses, and established among the cattle.
I establish myself in the secondary limbs, I establish myself in the vital breaths and in nourishment;
I establish myself in heaven and earth, and in the sacrifice.
The three gods, the eleven, and the thirty-three, the bounteous ones, impelled by Bṛhaspati at the instigation of the god Savitṛ.

May the gods protect me with the gods: the first with the second, the second with the third, the third with truth; may truth with sacrifice, sacrifice with the *yajus* formulas, the *yajus* formulas with the *sāmans*, the *sāmans* with the *ṛc* verses, the *ṛc* verses with the *yājyās*, the *yājyās* with the *vaṣaṭ* calls, and the *vaṣaṭ* calls with the oblations fulfill my desires. *Bhūḥ svāhā!*
My body hair is my effort; my skin is my bowing, my arrival; my flesh is my approach; my wealth is my bone, my marrow is my bowing. 4.
O gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed, O gods, may Agni release me from that sin and from all distress.
Whether by day or by night we have committed sins, may Vāyu release me from that evil and from all distress.
Whether we have committed sins while awake or while dreaming, may Sūrya release me from that sin and from all distress.
Whatever sin we have committed in the village, whatever in the forest, whatever in the assembly hall, whatever in the senses, whatever toward a Śūdra or toward an Ārya,
whatever against the law of another— that is your means of expiation.

When we swear by the waters, O Varuṇa, saying "O inviolable ones," then, O Varuṇa, release us! O *avabhṛtha*, you who plunge deep; you are the one who glides down, you who plunges deep.
