Thou art the path of the world through the work of the gods; thou art the path of the world through the work of the waters. With the Vasus as deities, with the Gāyatrī metre, I yoke thee; with the oblation of the spring among the seasons, I consecrate thee. Thou art the path of the world through the work of the gods; thou art the path of the world through the work of the waters. With the Rudras as deities, with the Triṣṭubh metre, I yoke thee; with the oblation of the summer among the seasons, I consecrate thee. Thou art the path of the world through the work of the gods; thou art the path of the world through the work of the waters. With the Ādityas as deities, with the Jagatī metre...

I yoke you with the *chandas* [meter], with the rain of the seasons, I consecrate you with the oblation; you are the path of the work of the gods. With all the gods as your deity, I yoke you with the *anuṣṭubh* meter; with the autumn of the seasons, I consecrate you with the oblation; you are the path of the work of the gods. With the Aṅgirases as your deities, I yoke you with the *paṅkti* meter; with the winter and the cool season of the seasons, I consecrate you with the oblation; you are the path of the work of the gods.

By means of the rite, I have ascended the path of the departing immortal; I have mounted the consecration, the consort of the immortal. By the Gāyatrī metre and by the sacred word (*brahman*), I have established the cosmic order (*ṛta*) in truth, and truth in the cosmic order. [I have taken refuge] in the great, well-protecting [goddess Aditi]. 9.

Hail to the one who utters "iṃ," hail to the one who has uttered "iṃ"! Hail to the one who cries out, hail to the one who calls aloud! Svāhā! To him who will step out, svāhā! To him who is stepping out, svāhā! To him who has stepped out, svāhā! To him who will walk about, svāhā! To him who is walking about, svāhā! Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Vāyu! Svāhā to Sūrya! You are the essence of the Ṛta; you are the Ṛta; you are the Truth; you are the truth of truth; you are the path of the Ṛta; you are the shadow of the gods; you are the name of the Ṛta. That is the Truth: that you are Prajāpati.

When the clans vie for him as for a prize-winning steed, like the splendors of the sun in heaven, he flows on, choosing the waters, acting like a seer; like a watchful herdsman, he moves all around like a vigilant protector.

Now the third speech, the response:
"May the sacrifice come hither toward me from yonder; may he who is the domestic priest of the seers [come] to me."
Having rendered it godless and powerless, let Viṣkandha perish upon him who hates us;
let the body, the impurity of sacrifice and the debt, settle upon him who hates us.
O Sacrifice, with that splendor which belongs to the Sacrifice, come over to me;
through the austerity of the Sacrifice, I invoke these Brahmins, the officiating priests, and the gods.
With what is desirable, I call upon you who are cooked; here am I. I gather for you your well-performed merit, your offspring, and your cattle.

I have gathered for you the commands, the kindling verses, the two libations of clarified butter, the portions of clarified butter, the call "Āśrāvaya," the response "Pratyāśrāvaya," the invocation "Āśr̥ṇomi te," the fore-offerings, the after-offerings, the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, the Iḍā, and the blessings; I have won the light of heaven.
With Agni, Indra, Soma, Sarasvatī, Viṣṇu, and the deities;
with the invitatory and offering verses, I call upon you. Here I take up this sacrifice for you; may it be consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* cry.
I have appropriated for myself the Stotra, the Śastra, the Pratigara, the Graha, the Iḍā, the Āśis, and the Svar.
I call upon you for the Patnīsaṃyājas; here I take for myself the Samiṣṭayajus, which is yours.

I invoke for you the cattle, the pressed soma, the sacrificial cakes, the libations, and indeed the sacrifice; I call upon all the gods together with Indra, those who have Agni as their mouth and Soma as their companion. 1.

Homage to the past, the present, and the future; vaṣaṭ, svāhā, homage to the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus; vaṣaṭ, svāhā, homage to the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī meters; vaṣaṭ, svāhā, homage to the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky; vaṣaṭ, svāhā, homage to food, agriculture, and rain; vaṣaṭ, svāhā, homage to the father, the son, and the grandson; vaṣaṭ, svāhā, homage to the prāṇa, vyāna, and apāna breaths; vaṣaṭ, svāhā, homage to bhūr, bhuvas, and svar; vaṣaṭ, svāhā, homage! 2.
May houses be mine, may progeny be mine; may the heroic sacrifice enter into me.
May the divine, sacrificial waters enter me; may the abundance of a thousandfold wealth not forsake me.
May the cups come to me; may the Puroruc and the Stotra-Śastra enter me together.
May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus be my fellow-sitters in the assembly. May the abundance of the thousandfold not fail me.
May the Agniṣṭoma enter me, may the Ukthya and the Atirātra enter me, and may the Āpiśarvara enter me.
May the well-offered oblations enter me through the intermediate day; may the abundance of the thousandfold not abandon me. 3.

By means of fire he obtained fervor; by speech, the sacred formulation (*brahman*); by the jewel, forms; by gold, luster; by water, the earth; by wind, the intermediate space; by the sun, the sky; by the moon, the stars; by Yama, the ancestors; by the king, human beings; by fruit, edible plants; by the python, serpents; by the tiger, wild animals; by the falcon, birds; by rice, grains of food; by barley, medicinal herbs; by the *udumbara* tree, vigor; by the *nyagrodha* tree, the lords of the forest; by the stallion, horses; by the bull, cattle; by the ram, sheep; by the goat, the *gāyatrī* meter.
By means of the *chandāṃsi* he [wins] the *stomas* consisting of nine parts; by means of the *rathantara*, the *sāmans*; and by means of the *brāhmaṇa*, speech. ||4||

Svāhā to the one who has meditated upon the meditation; svāhā! Svāhā to the meditation for the mind; svāhā! Svāhā to the mind for Prajāpati; svāhā! Svāhā to Ka; svāhā! Svāhā to Katama; svāhā! Svāhā to Aditi; svāhā! Svāhā to Aditi Mahī; svāhā! Svāhā to Aditi Sumṛḍīkā; svāhā! Svāhā to Sarasvatī; svāhā! Svāhā to Sarasvatī Pāvakā; svāhā! Svāhā to Sarasvatī Bṛhatī; svāhā! Svāhā to Pūṣan; svāhā! Svāhā to Pūṣan Prapathya; svāhā! Svāhā to Pūṣan Naraṃdhiṣa; svāhā! Svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ; svāhā! Svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ Turīpa.
To Tvaṣṭṛ of many forms, Svāhā! To Viṣṇu, Svāhā! To Viṣṇu who protects the hidden, Svāhā! To Viṣṇu who protects what is near, Svāhā! May the All protect the leader of the god. ||5||

Thus ends the third recitation, named *Anuvacana*, in the fifth book called the *Aśvamedha* within the *Caraka-śākhā* of the illustrious *Kāṭhaka-Yajus*. 3.
Now follows the fourth speech; the recitation for the ram:

May the ram protect thee with cooked offerings, the red-necked one with goats, the *śalmali* tree with prosperity, the *parṇa* tree with sacred knowledge (*brahman*), the *plakṣa* tree with wisdom (*medha*), the *nyagrodha* tree with cups (*camasa*), the *udumbara* tree with strength (*ūrj*), and the *gāyatrī* with the meters. May the *trivṛt* hymns and the *avanti* verses protect thee; may the *avantis* protect thee. We invoke thee, the beloved of the beloved, the most excellent of those worthy of attainment, the lord of hosts among hosts, O Vasu, mine! We invoke thee, the beloved lord of the beloved, O Vasu, mine! We invoke thee, the lord of treasures among treasures, O Vasu, mine! 1.

Hail to the wells! Hail to the rivulets! Hail to the cooking-pots! Hail to the pits! Hail to the threshing-floors! Hail to the lakes! Hail to the ponds! Hail to the pools! Hail to the marshes! Hail to the tanks! Hail to the waters of rain! Hail to the waters of drought! Hail to the sprinkled waters! Hail to the hailstones! Hail to the stagnant waters! Hail to the flowing waters! Hail to the river-waters! Hail to the waters of the Indus! Hail to the oceanic waters! Hail to all the waters! 2.

Svāhā to the waters! Svāhā to those that flow! Svāhā to those that carry [them] to the ocean! Svāhā to those that carry [them] everywhere! Svāhā to those that carry [them] fiercely! Svāhā to those that carry [them] dreadfully! Svāhā to those that carry [them] swiftly! Svāhā to those that carry [them] rapidly! Svāhā to the waters! Svāhā to the clouds! Svāhā to the great ones! 3.
Varuṇa strikes down that mortal who seeks to kill the courser; even further off is the dog.
May you and I, O slayer of Vṛtra, agree upon the most excellent boons;
even the enemy, O wielder of the stone, shall acknowledge us, O Hero—for auspicious are the gifts of Indra.
O Indra, by your wisdom you have become preeminent; on earth your greatness has pervaded the realms.
For with your own power you have struck down Vṛtra; no enemy has found the end of your weapon.

Homage to the King! Homage to Varuṇa! Homage to the Horse! Homage to Prajāpati! Homage to the Overlord! You are the overlord; make me an overlord! May I become the overlord of creatures! Bestow [your power] upon me; place [it] in me! Svāhā to the one brought near! Svāhā to the one seized! Svāhā to the one offered! 5.
May the wind blow auspiciously; may the sunbeams enter the plants full of vigor.
May they drink from the fatness that brings life to all creatures; O Rudra, be gracious to our bipeds and quadrupeds.
Those who are alike, those who are diverse, those who are of one form, whose names Agni knows as *niṣṭyās*—
those whom the Aṅgirases have brought here through austerity— to them, O Parjanya, grant great protection.
Those who extended their bodies among the gods, whose every form Soma knows— those,
swelling with milk and rich in offspring, O Indra, bestow upon us in our cow-pen.
Prajāpati, bestowing these upon me, in harmony with all the gods worthy of sacrifice—may they, becoming numerous, quickly come to our cow-pen; may we be united with them through progeny.
Here is support, svāhā! Here is separation, svāhā! Here is delight, svāhā! Here is rejoicing, svāhā! [We invoke] the great one, the excellent protector... ||6||
Who indeed wanders alone? Who, verily, is born again?
What is the remedy for cold? And what is the great sowing ground?
The sun moves alone; the moon is born again; fire is the remedy for cold; the earth is the great vessel for sowing.
Who was Pūrvacitti? What was Bṛhadvaya? Who was Pilippilā? And who was Piśaṅgilā?
The sky was the first thought; the horse was the great bird;
the ram was the slippery one; the night was the speckled one.
I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask you about the navel of the world.
I ask you about the seed of the stallion; I ask you about the highest heaven of speech.
They call the altar the furthest limit of the earth; they call the sacrifice the navel of the world.
They call Soma the seed of the virile horse; the Brahman is indeed the supreme sky of speech. 7.
"O Amba, O Ambālī, O Ambikā! No one is leading me away, O fortunate dweller of Kāmpīla, you whose horses are well-fed!"

In the heavenly world, may you two envelop me; I give birth to you as the placer of the embryo, and you give birth to me as the placer of the embryo. Together, let us both extend our four feet. May the bull, the depositor of seed, deposit his seed in you. Place the testicle within the thighs; anoint the anointing-place, following the anointing-place.
He who is the life and sustenance of women, who cleanses their dwellings,
who is dear even to beloved women, and who is marked with dark spots— he has struck down the one who was devouring the earth.
O Amba, Ambālī, and Ambikā, let no one lead me away; my little horse has fallen asleep.
Raise her up on high with your voice, like a load of bamboo;
then let her waist swell, as if purifying herself in a cool breeze.
"Mother," he said.

When the doe eats barley, she does not consider the animal to be well-nourished; when a Śūdra woman has a noble lover, she does not desire wealth for the sake of sustenance. Thus it was said: "O Mother!"
This little bird, saying "Alas!", deceives me; when it is struck, the female bird cries out, "My foot is caught in its own throat."
"Mother," he said.
Both your mother and your father grow upon this tree;
"I shall bring forth," so saying, your father struck his fist against the womb.
I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan; [and] the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed... (āpo hi ṣṭhā). 8.
May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre; may the Rudras anoint you with the Triṣṭubh metre; may the Ādityas anoint you with the Jagatī metre.
Since the wind has gone to the waters, to the beloved body of Indra—
by this path, O praiser, bring back this horse of ours to us again.
O Prajāpati, eat this food, eat this food—this food of the one who wins grain, the one who wins horses, the one who wins fame, and of me, for the sake of barley and cattle, O Gods!
They harness the ruddy, flaming one as he moves; those who stand around him behold him. The luminous realms shine in heaven.
They yoke his two beloved bay horses to the chariot on either side—red, bold, and bearers of the hero.
Making a banner for that which was without a banner, O men, providing a form for that which was formless, you were born together with the dawns. 9.

Hail to the out-breath, hail to the diffused breath, hail to the in-breath! Hail to the sinews, hail to the continuities, hail to the connections! Hail to the joints, hail to the unions, hail to the bodies! Hail to the sacrifice, hail to the sacrificial fee, hail to heaven, hail to the world! Hail to all! 10.
Thus ends the fourth section, named the Recitation of the Sheep, in the fifth book called the Aśvamedha, within the Caraka recension of the glorious Kāṭhaka Yajurveda. 4.

Hail to the one who has closed his eyes! Hail to the about-to-breathe-out! Hail to the breathing-out! Hail to the one who has breathed out! Hail to the about-to-breathe-in! Hail to the breathing-in! Hail to the one who has breathed in! Hail to the about-to-speak! Hail to the speaking! Hail to the one who has spoken! Hail to the about-to-silence! Hail to the silencing! Hail to the one who has become silent! Hail to the about-to-think! Hail to the thinking! Hail to the one who has thought! Hail to the about-to-meditate! Hail to the meditating! Hail to the recalling! Hail to the one who has recalled! Hail to the about-to-understand! Hail to the understanding! Hail to the one who has understood! Hail to the about-to-realize! Hail to the realizing! Hail to the one who has realized! Hail to the about-to-attain! Hail to the attaining! Hail to the one who has attained! Hail to the about-to-accomplish! Hail to the accomplishing! Hail to the one who has accomplished! Hail to the about-to-complete! Hail to the completing! Hail to the one who has completed! Hail to the about-to-finish! Hail to the finishing! Hail to the one who has finished! Hail to the about-to-conclude! Hail to the concluding! Hail to the one who has concluded! Hail to the about-to-release! Hail to the releasing! Hail to the one who has released! Hail to the about-to-liberate! Hail to the liberating! Hail to the one who has liberated! Hail to the about-to-freedom! Hail to the freedom! Hail to the one who

Svāhā to the days, svāhā to the *ṛc*s, svāhā to the *yajus*es, svāhā to the *sāman*s, svāhā to the Aṅgirases, svāhā to the Vedas, svāhā to the *gāthā*s, svāhā to the *nārāśaṃsī*s, svāhā to the *raibhī*s, svāhā to everything! 2.

To the one with teeth, svāhā! To the toothless, svāhā! To the breathing one, svāhā! To the breathless, svāhā! To the one with a nose, svāhā! To the noseless, svāhā! To the one with a mouth, svāhā! To the mouthless, svāhā! To the one with eyes, svāhā! To the eyeless, svāhā! To the one with ears, svāhā! To the earless, svāhā! To the one with a head, svāhā! To the headless, svāhā! To the one with feet, svāhā! To the footless, svāhā! To the one who breathes, svāhā! To the one who does not breathe, svāhā! To the one who speaks, svāhā! To the one who does not speak, svāhā! To the one who sees, svāhā! To the one who does not see, svāhā! To the one who hears, svāhā! To the one who does not hear, svāhā!

Hail to the one possessing mind, hail to the mindless! Hail to the one possessing semen, hail to the seedless! Hail to offspring, hail to procreation! Hail to the one possessing hair, hail to the hairless! Hail to the skin, hail to the skinless! Hail to the one possessing hide, hail to the hideless! Hail to the one possessing blood, hail to the bloodless! Hail to the one possessing flesh, hail to the fleshless! Hail to the sinews, hail to the sinewless! Hail to the one possessing bone, hail to the boneless! Hail to the one possessing marrow, hail to the marrowless! Hail to the one possessing limbs!
Svāhā to the bodiless one; svāhā to the one possessing a self; svāhā to the selfless one; svāhā to everything! 3.

Agni was the sacrificial animal; with him he sacrificed, and he won this world in which Agni dwells—this is your world, you shall win it; now, smell [the smoke]. Vāyu was the sacrificial animal; with him he sacrificed, and he won this world in which Vāyu dwells—this is your world, you shall win it; now, smell [the smoke]. Āditya was the sacrificial animal; with him he sacrificed, and he won this world in which Āditya dwells—this is your world, you shall win it; now, smell [the smoke]. ||4||

The sky is your back, the earth your seat, the atmosphere your self, and the ocean your womb; the sun is your eye, the wind your breath, the moon your hearing, the quarters your feet, and the intermediate quarters your cattle; the stars are your form, the months and half-months your joints, the seasons your limbs, and the year your majesty. 5.

Hail to exertion! Hail to distress! Hail to weariness! Hail to effort! Hail to exhaustion! Hail to rising! Hail to grief! Hail to heat! Hail to the burning one! Hail to fervor! Hail to the glowing one! Hail to hunger! Hail to the slaying of the embryo! Hail to everything! 6.
To Jumbaka, svāhā! To the final bath, svāhā! To everything, svāhā! ||7||
To Death, Svāhā! To the final purificatory bath, Svāhā! To everything, Svāhā! ||8||

Who yokes you? Let him yoke you. May Viṣṇu yoke you for the success of this sacrifice—for my devotion, for such-and-such a desire, for life, for you, for out-breath, for you, for diffused breath, for you, for in-breath, for you, for the dawning, for you, for wealth, for you, for prosperity, for you, for nourishment, for you, for sound, for you, for sound from afar, for you, for departure, for you. Who unyokes you? Let him unyoke you. May Viṣṇu unyoke you, having prospered for the success of this sacrifice—for my devotion, for such-and-such a desire, for life, for you.

For out-breath thee, for diffused breath thee, for in-breath thee; for dawning thee, for wealth thee, for prosperity thee, for nourishment thee, for sound thee, for sound from afar thee, for stability thee. 9.

To Agni, who is associated with the *gāyatrī* metre, the *trivṛt* stoma, the *rathaṃtara* sāman, and the spring season, [there is] an offering on eight potsherds; to Indra, who is associated with the *triṣṭubh* metre, the *pañcadaśa* stoma, the *bṛhat* sāman, and the summer season, [there is] an offering on eleven potsherds; to the Viśvedevas, who are associated with the *jagatī* metre, the *saptadaśa* stoma, the *vairūpa* sāman, and the rainy season, [there is] an offering on twelve potsherds; to Mitra and Varuṇa, who are associated with the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *ekaviṃśa* stoma, the *vairāja* sāman, and the autumn season, [there is] an offering of curdled milk (*payasyā*); and to Bṛhaspati, who is associated with the *paṅkti* metre, the *triṇava* stoma, the *śākvara* sāman, and the winter season.

A cake on twelve potsherds for Caruṣvitra Āticchandasa Trayastrim̐śa Raivata Śaiśira; a pap for Aditi Viṣṇupatnī; a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara; a pap for Anumati; and a cake on one potsherd for Kāya. ||10||
In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha came into being; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists.
He supported this earth and yonder sky. To which god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. Of you, the sky is the greatness, the stars are the form, and the sun is the brilliance. To that greatness, to Prajāpati, svāhā! ||11||
By this manifestation, generating heroic deeds— for he is the glowing one, the wide path for the sake of space—
he has risen up toward the ruddy summit of the honeyed [light], when his own body impelled his body.

You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. The intermediate space is your greatness, the waters and birds are your form, and Vāyu is your brilliance. To that greatness, to Prajāpati, svāhā! ||12||
He who by his greatness alone became the sole king of the breathing and blinking world;
he who rules over its bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. Earth is your greatness, herbs and trees are your form, and Agni is your brilliance. To that greatness, to Prajāpati, svāhā! 13.

O Brahman, may a Brahmin endowed with Vedic luster be born in this kingdom; may a Kshatriya be born who is skilled in archery, heroic, and a great chariot-warrior; may there be a milch-cow that yields milk, a draft-ox that carries the load, a swift steed, a victorious warrior standing in the chariot, a woman who is a bringer of prosperity, and a youthful son of this sacrificer who is fit for the assembly. May Parjanya rain for us according to our every desire; may our plants ripen with fruit; may our security and prosperity be established. 14.

The prize-winning steed has stepped upon the earth; the prize-winning steed has made Agni his yoke-fellow. The prize-winning steed has stepped into the mid-air; the prize-winning steed has made Vāyu his yoke-fellow. The prize-winning steed has stepped upon the sky; the prize-winning steed has made Sūrya his yoke-fellow. O prize-winning steed, you are the yoke-fellow of Vāyu; I take hold of you—convey me safely across. O prize-winning steed, you are the yoke-fellow of Vāyu; I take hold of you—convey me safely across. O prize-winning steed, you are the yoke-fellow of Āditya; I take hold of you—convey me safely across. You are the upholder of the out-breath; make my out-breath firm. You are the upholder of the through-breath; [make] my through-breath firm.
O firm one, make my drinking firm; you are sight, bestow sight upon me; you are hearing, bestow hearing upon me; you are life, bestow life upon me; may I attain a full span of life. 15.

The steed has stepped forward with strides, in harmony with all the gods worthy of sacrifice; lead us to the world of the well-performed deed, and may we rejoice in the offering of that which belongs to you. 16.

The seed has been born; Parjanya has rained. The path is ready; the crops have good fruit; these plants are for easy treading upon; Agni is easy to approach; the atmosphere is well-supervised; Pavamāna is easy to traverse; the sky is a gracious place of refuge; that sun shines auspiciously. Day and night follow as before; the half-months consist of fifteen days; the months consist of thirty days; the seasons are duly arranged; the year is peaceful. 17.

There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, a pap for Pūṣan, a pap of Gavidhuka seeds for Rudra, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara at the deer-trap; if he does not arrive, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Amhomuc, milk for Sūrya, and a portion of clarified butter for Vāyu. 18.

To Agni Amhomuc, a cake on eight potsherds; to Indra Amhomuc, a cake on eleven potsherds; a pap for Vāyu and Savitṛ, the two who drive away the cow; a milk-curd offering (payasyā) for Mitra and Varuṇa, the two who drive away the cow; parched grains (dhānā) for the Aśvins, the two who drive away the cow; a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts, the ones who drive away sin; a cake on twelve potsherds for the All-gods, the ones who drive away sin; a pap for Anumati; a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara; and a cake on two potsherds for Heaven and Earth, the two who drive away the fire. 19.

They have bowed down to Agni; they have bowed down to the Earth. As Agni has bowed down to the Earth, so may auspicious bows bow down to me. They have bowed down to Vāyu; they have bowed down to the Atmosphere. As Vāyu has bowed down to the Atmosphere, so may auspicious bows bow down to me. They have bowed down to Sūrya; they have bowed down to Heaven. As Sūrya has bowed down to Heaven, so may auspicious bows bow down to me. They have bowed down to Varuṇa; they have bowed down to the Waters.

As Varuṇa was in harmony with the waters, so may the auspicious ones who bow down be in harmony for me; as the Sāman was in harmony with the Ṛc, so may the auspicious ones who bow down be in harmony for me. As the Sāman was in harmony with the Ṛc, so may the auspicious ones who bow down be in harmony for me. As the Brahman was in harmony with the Kṣatra, so may the auspicious ones who bow down be in harmony for me; as the Brahman was in harmony with the Kṣatra, so may the auspicious ones who bow down be in harmony for me. As the King was in harmony with the people, so may the auspicious ones who bow down be in harmony for me; as the King was in harmony with the people, so may the auspicious ones who bow down be in harmony for me. As the King was in harmony with the people, so may the auspicious ones who bow down be in harmony for me.

May the auspicious convergences converge for my chariot; they have converged for the horses, and as the chariot has converged with the horses, even so may the auspicious convergences converge for me. 20.
With kindled fires, with which [hymn] shall we [serve you]?

Who today yokes to the pole of the Cosmic Order the impetuous, fierce, and ill-disposed bulls—those who carry arrows in their mouths, pierce the heart, yet grant bliss? Only he who provides for their maintenance shall live.
Thus ends the fifth recitation, named *Mitānuvacana*, in the fifth book called the *Aśvamedha* within the *Caraka-śākhā* of the venerable *Kāṭhaka-Yajurveda*. 5.
Now begins the sixth recitation:
the *Jīmūtānuvacana*.
Like the appearance of a cloud, so is his countenance when the armored warrior goes into the lap of battle;
with an uninjured body, may you be victorious—may the greatness of this armor protect you.
With the bow may we win cattle, with the bow may we conquer in battle; with the bow may we overcome fierce adversaries.
The bow turns the enemy's will away; with the bow may we conquer all the quarters.
As if about to speak, she goes toward the ear, embracing her dear friend;
like a woman, this bowstring twangs upon the stretched bow, carrying us across in the encounter.
Moving together like a woman to her husband, may they bear [the arrow] in their lap like a mother her son;
may these two bow-ends, acting in concert and vibrating, pierce the enemies and strike down the foes.
He is the father of many, his sons are many; having entered the fray, he makes a whizzing sound.
With his quiver fastened upon his back, he conquers all armies when he is urged forward.
Standing in the chariot, the skillful charioteer guides the horses forward wherever he desires. Marvel at the greatness of the reins: the traces follow behind, obeying the mind.
Making loud noises, the horses with strong hooves, striving for the prize along with the chariots,
trampling the enemies with their forefeet, destroy the foes without turning back.
The chariot-bearer is his name, wherein his weapons and his armor are laid;
there let us sit upon the auspicious chariot, being well-disposed toward him, every single day.
The Fathers, who sit at the sweet draught, bestowers of vitality, who have taken refuge in hardship, powerful and profound;
they who possess wondrous armies, whose strength lies in their arrows, never-failing, heroes of truth, vast and conquerors of hosts.

May the Brāhmaṇas, our Soma-loving ancestors, and the auspicious, blameless Heaven and Earth be gracious to us. May Pūṣan protect us from misfortune, O increasers of Truth; guard us, and let no malevolent speaker have power over us.
She wears the feathers of an eagle; her tooth is of deer-horn; bound with cow-hide, she flies forth when discharged.
Where men run together and apart, there may the arrows grant us protection.
O Vṛjinī, avoid us; let our bodies be as stone. May Soma speak in our favor, and may Aditi grant us protection.
Like a serpent with its coils, it encircles the arm, warding off the strike of the bowstring;
the hand-guard, knowing all the ways, may it protect the man from every side.
They strike their flanks; they strike upon their haunches. O horse-whip, you who are wise, urge the horses forward in battles.
O Lord of the Forest, may you be firm-limbed, our friend, a furtherer, and rich in heroes;
you are bound with cow-hides, so be firm, and may your rider win all that is to be won.
The vigor brought forth from heaven and earth, the conquering strength gathered from the trees,
the power of the waters encompassed by the rays of light— worship with an oblation the chariot that is Indra’s thunderbolt.
The thunderbolt of Indra, the vanguard of the Maruts, the offspring of Mitra, and the navel of Varuṇa— O divine chariot, enjoying this our offering of oblations, accept these gifts.
Cause the earth and the sky to resound; let the world, established in many places, take heed of you. O drum, in harmony with Indra and the gods, drive our enemies far, even to the furthest distance.
Roar aloud, bestow strength and vigor upon us; thunder forth, driving away all misfortunes.
O drum, drive away misfortune from here; you are the fist of Indra—be firm!
O King, turn these [enemies] back; the drum resounds with its banner.
Our heroes, winged by horses, advance together; O Indra, may our chariot-warriors be victorious! 1.

Kindled by our hymns, O Agni, you consume the sacrificial food; swelling with honeyed clarified butter, you, the prize-winning steed who carries the prize, bring us to the beloved dwelling-place of the gods, O Jātavedas.
Anointing the paths leading to the gods with ghee, may the steed, knowing them well, go to the gods.
O courser, let the quarters follow you; bestow your own power upon this sacrificer.
O Steed, you are worthy of praise and worship; you are swift and fit for sacrifice.
May Agni Jātavedas, in harmony with the gods and the Vasus, carry you—the beloved bearer—forward.
The sacrificial grass is strewn, well-spread; may Aditi, in harmony with the gods, rejoicing in it as it extends wide and broad upon the earth, making it a pleasant seat, establish us in prosperity.
These doors, truly blessed with rain, possessing all boons, swelling wide with their lofty frames,
being adorned by the seers— may the divine doors be easy of passage.
Moving between Mitra and Varuṇa, they are the mouth of the sacrifices, acting in perfect harmony.
I seat you two, O Uṣas, rich in gold and well-fashioned, here in the womb of Cosmic Order (Ṛta).

The first two of you, golden-hued gods who share one chariot, beholding all worlds— having extended your impulsion and measured it out, O Hotṛ-priests, you point out the light by means of the quarters of space.
May Bhāratī with the Ādityas desire our sacrifice; may Sarasvatī together with the Rudras protect us.
May Iḷā, invoked along with the Vasus, the goddess, bestow our sacrifice upon the immortals.
Tvaṣṭṛ begot the hero who desires the gods; from Tvaṣṭṛ was born the swift, impetuous horse.
Tvaṣṭṛ brought forth this entire world; O Hotṛ, worship here the maker of much.
Anointed by itself with ghee, let the horse go to the gods according to the seasons;
may Vanaspati, knowing the world of the gods, carry the offerings made savory by Agni.
O Agni, increasing through the ascetic fervor of Prajāpati, as soon as you were born, you desired the sacrifice.
As the leader, come with the oblation consecrated by *svāhā*; may the gods eat the offering in your company. 2.
When you cried out.
I recognized you as my own self with my mind, like a bird flying through the sky;
I beheld your head, the winged one, hastening along easy paths that are free from dust.
Here I beheld your supreme form as you strove to win the nourishment at the station of the cow;
when the mortal attained your enjoyment, then, O most voracious one, you swallowed and awakened the plants.
After you, O steed, follows the chariot; after you, the young man; after you, the cattle; after you, the fortune of maidens.
After you, the hosts have followed for your friendship; the gods have measured out their heroic power according to yours.
His horns are of gold, his feet are of iron; swift as thought was Indra, who followed behind him. The gods came to eat his sacrificial oblation—he who was the first to mount the courser.
With swelling haunches, with tails like porcupine quills, these divine stallions are heroes;
like swans they draw up in rows when the horses have reached their divine course.
Your body flies like a bird; your mind is swift as the wind.
Your horns are fixed in many places; they move flickeringly in the forests.
The Unborn One is led in front; his kinship follows behind him, as the sages and the singers proceed.
He has approached the highest dwelling place, toward his father and mother who are near. Today he shall go to the gods as one most beloved; then he prays for desirable boons for the donor. 3.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Indra, Ṛbhukṣan, and the Maruts not overlook us,
when we proclaim in the assembly the precious gifts of the prize-winning steed, born of the gods.
When they lead before him the captured gift of wealth covered by the cleansing cloth, may the goat,
bleating and assuming every form, go straight forward to the beloved path of Indra and Pūṣan.
This goat, the portion of Pūṣan, is led before the vigorous horse as one belonging to all the gods;
when they lead the beloved sacrificial cake around with the steed, Tvaṣṭṛ impels it for the sake of glory.
When men lead the horse three times around the path that goes to the gods, according to the seasons, as an offering.
Therein, the goat, the first portion for Pūṣan, goes forth, announcing the sacrifice to the gods.
The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Āvayā, the Agnimindha, the Grāvagrābha, and the wise Śaṃstṛ—
with this well-prepared, well-offered sacrifice, fill the channels of the belly.
May the approval of those who hew the sacrificial post, those who carry the post, those who carve the top-ring for the horse’s post, and those who prepare the cooking-vessel for the steed,
further us.
He has come near; a well-intentioned prayer has been offered. With his smooth-backed form, he has approached the quarters of the gods.
May the wise seers rejoice after him; desiring the prosperity of the gods, we seek Subandhu.
Whatever halter binds the swift steed, whatever head-stall or cord belongs to him,
or whatever grass has been placed in his mouth as fodder— may all these of yours be among the gods.
Whatever of the horse’s raw flesh the flies have eaten, or whatever remains smeared on the sacrificial post or the axe;
whatever is on the hands of the immolator or on his nails—all that of yours let there be among the gods.
Whatever foul odor emanates from the belly, whatever stench there is from the raw flesh—
let the immolators make that well-prepared, and let them cook the sacrificial victim until it is thoroughly cooked.
The inspection of the cauldron for cooking the flesh, the vessels for pouring the broth,
the warming-covers for the pots, and the hooks— these adorn the horse.

Whatever from your body, as it is being cooked by fire, drips down after you have been impaled on the spit—let that not cling to the earth, let it not cling to the grass; let it be offered to the gods who desire it.
Those who look upon the horse when it is cooked, and those who say, "It smells good, take it away!"—[to them be this offering].
And those who wait upon the horse for a portion of its flesh—may their approval also further us.

Let not the smoke-scented fire belch at you; let not the radiant cauldron, when overturned, strike you. The gods accept that horse which has been sacrificed, offered, approved, and consecrated with the cry of *vaṣaṭ*.
The stepping forth, the sitting down, the rolling over, and the foot-fetter of the steed;
whatever he drank and whatever fodder he ate—may all those of yours be among the gods.
Whatever of yours was pained by the heel or by the whip when you were urged on with great force in the gallop—
at the sacrifices, like a ladle of oblation, I soothe all those [pains] of yours with a sacred prayer (*brahman*).
When they spread out a garment for the horse, an upper covering, and the golden ornaments; when they bring the halter, the foot-rope, and the dear trappings for the steed among the gods.
The axe meets the thirty-four ribs of the horse, the steed of the friend of the gods; make the limbs free from injury with skill; having proclaimed joint by joint, dissect [the body].
One is the dismemberer of the horse of Tvaṣṭṛ; two are the bearers [of the sacrifice], and likewise the season.
Those of your limbs which I prepare according to the seasons, those I offer as balls of meat into the fire.
Let not your dear self burn you as you enter it; let not the axe linger upon your body.
Let not the greedy disemboweler, overstepping the bounds, pierce through your vital parts with the sword, nor cut them haphazardly.
Verily, you do not die here, nor do you suffer harm; you go to the gods by easy paths.
Your two bay steeds and the two spotted mares have been yoked; the vigorous steed has taken his place at the pole behind the donkey.
May the prize-winning steed grant us abundance of cattle, abundance of horses, male children, and all-nourishing wealth;
may Aditi grant us freedom from sin, and may the sacrificial horse win for us sovereign power. 5.
Thus ends the sixth recitation, named *Jīmūtānuvacana*, in the fifth book called the *Aśvamedha* of the *Kāṭhaka* of the illustrious *Yajurveda*, belonging to the *Caraka* branch. 6.

Now follows the seventh speech: the response to Indra. For King Indra, a boar; for King Varuṇa, a black antelope; for King Yama, a porcupine; for King Ṛṣabha, a gayal; for King Śārdūla, a gaur-bull; for the King of Men, a monkey; for the swift hawk, a quail; for the blue-horned ox, a worm; for King Soma, a kuluṅga antelope; for the Sindhu, a porpoise; for the Himavat, an elephant. 1.

The mayu belongs to Prajāpati; the ulūka, the halikṣṇa, and the vṛṣadaṃśa belong to Dhātṛ; the śāri bird, white and speaking like a man, belongs to Sarasvatī; the parrot, white and speaking like a man, belongs to Sarasvat; the wild goat, the mongoose, and the śaka belong to Pūṣan; the krauñca belongs to Vāc. 2.

The Jhaṣa is for Apāṃ Napāt; the Ākra, the Makara, and the Pulīra are for the Waters; the Paiṅgarāja is for the cry of the oar; the Kuṣītaka is for Bhaga; the Ātī and the Vāhasa are for the Darvī; the Cakravāka is for the quarters and for Vāyu. 3.

For strength, the python; for the mouse, the *sṛjaya*; for the egg-born, the *śayāṇḍaka*; these are yours as friends. For death, the black snake; for fury, the self-biting; for the *kaumbhīnasa*, the *puṣkarasād*; for the red-streaked, the *lohitāhi*; these belong to Tvaṣṭṛ. For the echo, the *vāhasa*. ||4||

The male deer belongs to the Moon; the iguana, the *kālakā*, and the woodpecker belong to the Trees; the female antelope belongs to the Day; the black bird, the *piṅgā*, and the blue-headed one belong to the Night; the heron belongs to Aryaman; and the crab belongs to Dhātṛ. ||5||

The crane is for Sūrya; the peacock and the hawk are for the Gandharvas; the francolin partridge is for the Vasus; the partridge is for the Rudras; the red deer, the kuṇḍṛṇācī, and the golattikā are for the Apsarases; the sṛmara is for the Forest.

The spotted antelope belongs to the Viśvedevas; the *bidva* and the *nyaṅku* belong to Kaśa; the *anyavāpa* belongs to Anumati; the *kaśyapa*, the *kuvayi*, and the *kuṭaru* belong to the half-months and the months; the *dātyauha* belongs to Sinīvālī; and the *śimyuṭa* belongs to Bṛhaspati. ||7||

The Śaka is for the Earth; the Pāṅkta, the Kaśa, and the Manthīlava are for the Pitṛs; the Jahakā is for the Seasons; the Lopā, the Kapota, and the Ulūka are for the Saṃvatsara; and the Śaśa is for Nirṛti; the Kukavāku is for Savitṛ. ||8||

The Ruru antelope for Rudra; the Kṛkalāsa lizard and the Śakuni bird, the Pippakā, these for the Arrow-shaft; the Harina deer for the Maruts; the Śārga for Brahman; the Tarakṣu hyena, the black dog, the four-eyed dog, and the donkey, these for the Itarajanas; the Dhūṅkṣā vulture for Agni.

The *alaja* is for the atmosphere; the *udra*, the *madgu*, and the *plava*—these are for the Waters; the *haṃsa* and the *sāci* are for Aditi; the *kīrṣā*, the *gṛdhra*, the *śitikakṣī*, and the *vārdhrīṇasa*—these are for Aditi; the porcupine is for Heaven and Earth. 10.

The Suparṇa belongs to Pārjanya; the Haṃsa, the Vṛka, and the Vṛṣadaṃśa belong to Indra; the Udra belongs to the Waters; the Lopāśa belongs to Aryaman; the Siṃha, the Nakula, and the Vyāghra belong to Mahendra; the Parasvān belongs to Kāma. ||11||
Thus ends the seventh section, named *Indrānuvacana*, in the fifth book titled *Aśvamedha* within the *Caraka-śākhā* of the *Śrī Yajurveda Kāṭhaka*. 7.

Now follows the eighth section: the recitation concerning the ram. A black-necked goat is for Agni; a ewe is for Sarasvatī; a brown one is for Soma; a dark-grey one is for Pūṣan; a white-backed one is for Bṛhaspati; a speckled one is for the Viśvedevas; a ruddy one is for Indra; a dappled one is for the Maruts; a compact one is for Indra and Agni; a dark-bellied one is for Savitṛ; and a ram is for Varuṇa. 1.

The horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal are for Prajāpati; two black-necked ones are for Agni; two with hairy thighs are for Tvaṣṭṛ; two white-backed ones are for Bṛhaspati; the speckled one is for Dhātṛ; and the white ram is for Sūrya. 2.

For Agni Anīkavat, a red-marked ox; two for Savitṛ, both reddish-brown; two for Pūṣan, with silvery navels; two for the Viśvedevas, tawny and hornless; one for the Maruts, speckled; one for Agni, a black goat; one for Sarasvatī, a ewe; and one for Varuṇa, a black ram with a single white foot. 3.
Thus ends the eighth section, named the Recitation of the Petva, in the fifth book called the Aśvamedha, within the Caraka-śākhā of the glorious Yajurveda-Kāṭhaka. ||8||
Now follows the ninth statement: the recitation concerning the Rohitas.

The Dhūmralohita, the Karkandhurohita, and the Prājāpatya Babhru; the Aruṇababhru and the Śukababhru, those belong to Rudra; the Śyeta, the Śyetākṣa, and the Śyetagrīva, those belong to the Pitṛs; three black barren cows belong to Varuṇa; three white barren cows belong to Sūrya; and hornless bulls with smoke-colored marks on their foreheads belong to Mitra and Bṛhaspati. ||1||

The speckled, the cross-speckled, and the upward-speckled—these belong to the Maruts; the pale, the red-wooled, and the white-eyed—these belong to Sarasvatī; the spotted, the small-spotted, and the large-spotted—these belong to the Viśvedevas; three dark-brown barren cows belong to Pūṣan; three ruddy barren cows belong to Mitrā; and reddish-brown hornless bulls with white marks on their foreheads belong to Indra and Bṛhaspati. 2.

Those with white forelegs on one side, those with white forelegs on both sides, and those that are white all over are for Indra and Vāyu; those with white hooves on one side, those with white hooves on both sides, and those that are white all over are for Mitra and Varuṇa; those with clean tails, those with entirely clean tails, and those with jewel-like tails are for the Aśvins; three brindled cows are for the Viśvedevas; three tawny ones are for Parameṣṭhin; and hornless, dark-spotted goats are for Soma and Pūṣan. ||3||

The *unnata*, the *ṛṣabha*, and the *vāmana* are for Indra and Varuṇa; those with white backs, white rumps, and white buttocks are for Indra and Bṛhaspati; those with white feet, white lips, and white eyebrows are for Indra and Viṣṇu; three speckled barren cows are for Viśvakarman; three spotted cows are for Dhātṛ; and hornless white ones with black spots on their foreheads are for Pūṣan. ||4||

Three black-eared ones are for Yama; three gentle ones with white marks on their heads are for Agni; three for the youngest Agni (Agni Yaviṣṭha) are mongooses; three red cows are for the Triyavi; three reddish-brown ones are for the Vasus; three ruddy ones with white spots on their foreheads are for the Rudras; and those hornless ones with brown marks on their foreheads are for Soma and Indra.

There are three Śuṇṭha-Vaiṣṇavas with dark ears; three Viṣṇus, Urukramas, with spotted bellies; three Viṣṇus, Urugāyas, with five udders; three Ādityas with three-year-old calves; three Aṅgirases; and hornless bulls, black-spotted on the forehead, for Agni and Indra.

For Indra the King, three with white backs; for Indra the Overlord, three with white humps; for Indra the Self-Ruler, three with white rumps; three four-year-old cows for the Sādhyas; three six-year-old cows for the Viśvedevas; and hornless oxen marked with white spots on their foreheads for Indra and Viṣṇu. ||7||

Three red-spotted ones for Aditi; three black-spotted ones for Indrāṇī; three ruddy-spotted ones for Kuhū; three milch-cows for Rākā; three oxen for Sinīvālī; and hornless bulls with red marks on their foreheads for Agni-Viṣṇu. ||8||

Three gentle, tawny ones for Soma the King; three dappled ones for Parjanya; three goats with pendulous dewlaps, having the color of the sky, for Indrāṇī; three ewes for Aditi; and hornless, long-haired ones for Heaven and Earth. 9.

Three with black spots on the forehead are for Varuṇa; three with red spots on the forehead are for Varuṇa, the destroyer of enemies; three with tawny spots on the forehead are for Śilpa; three speckled ones are for the Viśvedevas; three dappled ones are for all the deities; and hornless ones with dark spots on the forehead are for Indra and Sūrya. ||10||
Thus ends the ninth section, named the Recitation on the Rohita, in the fifth book called the Aśvamedha, within the Caraka-śākhā of the Śukla-Yajurveda-Kāṭhaka. 9.

Now follows the tenth statement: the recitation for Soma. For Soma, the self-ruling king, two oxen that draw the cart; for Indra and Agni, the givers of vigor, two camels; for Indra and Agni, the givers of strength, two plow-oxen; two ewes; two cows belonging to the earth; for the quarters, two mares; two cows belonging to the earth; for the Vairāja meters, two female humans; two cows belonging to the earth; for Vāyu, two oxen that draw the mounting-ladder; two oxen belonging to Varuṇa; two black barren cows; two wild oxen belonging to the sky; two bulls that wander about. 1.

In the morning, eleven bovine animals are sacrificed: a spotted goat, a *kikidivi* bird, and a *vidīgaya*—these two belong to Tvaṣṭṛ; nine white barren cows dedicated to Sūrya are the *anūbandhya* victims; and those dedicated to Agni, Indra-Agni, and the Aśvins are sacrificed at the *viśāla* sacrificial post.

Three tawny ones for the spring; three dappled ones for the summer; three spotted ones for the rainy season; three speckled ones for the autumn; three with speckled thighs for the winter; three smeared ones for the cool season; and three with hair on their chests for the year. ||3||

For Spring he sacrifices *kapiñjala* partridges; for Summer, *kalaviṅka* sparrows; for the Rains, *tittiri* partridges; for Autumn, *vartika* quails; for Winter, *kakara* pheasants; and for the Cool Season, *vikara* pheasants. ||4||
May Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Anuṣṭubh, along with Paṅkti, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇih, and Kakubh, pierce you with their needles.
Those with two feet, those with four feet, those with three feet, and those with six feet—
those with regular meters and those with irregular meters— may they sew you together with needles.
The Mahānāmnīs, the Revatīs, and all the quarters that bring forth progeny.
May the pure, lightning-like words pierce you with their needles.
Silver, gold, and lead—these are joined together by their functions;
let them fasten you with needles upon the skin of the vigorous horse.
Let the women, your wives, comb your hair with their wits;
let the wives of the gods stitch you together with needles.
kuvidaṅga ||5||
Who carves you? Who dissects you? Who smooths your limbs?
And who is your wise preparer?
May the seasons, the dissectors, cut you into portions according to the seasons;
may they prepare you with the nourishment of the year and with their skillful arts.
May the divine Adhvaryus cut you apart and direct you; may the preparers prepare your limbs joint by joint as they perform their work.
May the half-months and the months, healing you, knit together your joints;
may the Maruts, day and night, heal what is injured in you.
May the Earth, together with the intermediate space, heal the wound for you, O Vāyu;
may the Sky, along with the constellations, restore your form, O Sādhya.
May there be peace for your upper limbs, may there be peace for your lower limbs;
may there be peace for the marrow within you, and may there be peace for your entire body.
Thus ends the tenth section, named *Somānuvacana*, in the fifth book called *Aśvamedha* within the *Caraka-śākhā* of the illustrious *Kāṭhaka-Yajus*. 10.
Now follows the eleventh statement, the statement of salutation:
"Homage to Agni; homage to Gāyatrī; homage to Trivṛt; homage to Rathantara; homage to Spring; homage to the eastern direction; homage to the out-breath; homage to the Vasus. (1)

Homage to Indra; homage to the Triṣṭubh meter; homage to the Pañcadaśa stoma; homage to the Bṛhat sāman; homage to the summer season; homage to the southern quarter; homage to the Vyāna breath; homage to the Rudras. 2.

Homage to the Maruts; homage to the Jagatī meter; homage to the Saptadaśa stoma; homage to the Vairūpa sāman; homage to the rainy season; homage to the western quarter; homage to the apāna breath; homage to the Ādityas. 3.

Homage to all the gods; homage to the Anuṣṭubh meter; homage to the twenty-first [stoma]; homage to the Vairāja sāman; homage to the autumn season; homage to the northern quarter; homage to the Saman; homage to the moon. 4.

Homage to Mitra and Varuṇa; homage to the Paṅkti [meter]; homage to the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa [stomas]; homage to the Śākvara and Raivata [sāmans]; homage to the winter and the dewy season; homage to the upward direction; homage to the udāna breath; homage to Viṣṇu. 5.

Homage to the Earth, homage to Agni, homage to the Past, homage to the Eye; homage to the Atmosphere, homage to Vāyu, homage to the Future, homage to the Ear; homage to the Sky, homage to Sūrya, homage to that which is to be, homage to the Mind. 6.
Thus ends the eleventh section, titled "The Words of Salutation," in the fifth book named Aśvamedha, within the Caraka recension of the glorious Yajurveda-Kāṭhaka. 11.
Now the twelfth utterance:
the recitation for the *alivandā*.
To the *alivandā*, svāhā! To the *balivandā*, svāhā! To everything, svāhā! ||1||
Thus ends the twelfth section, named the Recitation for the Ant-hill, in the fifth book called the Aśvamedha, within the Caraka-śākhā of the glorious Yajurveda-Kāṭhaka. 12.

Now follows the thirteenth recitation, the *śādānuvacana*. With his teeth he should eat the *śāda* grass; with the roots of his teeth, the *avakā* plants; with his tusks, the *tegā* fish; with his jaws, the frogs; with his palate, the *ādaka* birds; with his lips, he should consume vigor; with his tongue, the wild *jāmbīla* fruit; with his gums, the clay; with his phlegm, the gravel; with his saliva, the *avakā* plants; with his spittle, the gravel; with his tongue-tip, the tongue itself; and with the tip of his tongue, Sarasvatī. ||1||

He placed strength in the jaws, the waters in the mouth, the Ādityas in the beard, the *upayāma* vessel in the lower lip, and the *sadas* in the upper lip; he placed the inner light within the nasal cavity and the outer light with the light itself; he placed thunder in the palate, the sun and fire in the two eyes, lightning in the pupils, the thunderbolt in the brain, and power in the marrow. ||2||

From the tortoise, he took speed from its hooves, the *kapiñjala* bird from its ribs, the *sāman* chant from its humps, swiftness from its shanks, healing medicine from its knees, valor from its two secret parts, fear from its moving limbs, the Aśvins from its shoulders, Aditi from its head, and Nirṛti from its bald head.

With the yoktra [he purifies] the vultures; with the yoke, bent down, the mind; with the neck-ropes, the Saṃghoṣas; with the vital breaths, the skin; with the outer space, the interior; with the mosquitoes, the hair; with the Indra-hymn, the *svapa* [song]; with the *vaha*, Bṛhaspati; with the *śakunisāda*, the chariot; with the *uṣṇihā* meters, [the chariot]. ||4||

Mitra and Varuṇa with the two buttocks; Indra and Agni with the two tufts of hair; Indra and Bṛhaspati with the two thighs; Indra and Viṣṇu with the two knee-caps; Savitṛ with the tail; the Gandharvas with the penis; the Apsarases with the testicles; Pavamāna with the anus; the Purifier with the two lips of the prepuce; the stepping forward with the two humps; the stepping back with the two hollows. ||5||

The breast belongs to Indra; the belly to Aditi; the collar-bones to the quarters; the heart and its appendages to the clouds; the atmosphere to the pericardium; the sky to the stomach; Indrāṇī to the spleen; the anthills to the lungs; the mountains to the entrails; the ocean to the abdomen; and Vaiśvānara to the ashes.

The rectum belongs to Pūṣan; the thick entrails belong to Āndhāhi; the intestines to the serpents; the ribs to the seasons; the back-bone to the sky; the first rib belongs to the Vasus, the second to the Rudras, the third to the Ādityas, the fourth to the Aṅgirases, the fifth to the Sādhyas, and the sixth to the Viśvedevas.

Ojas with the necks, Nirṛti with the ribs, Indra with the well-fashioned vehicle, the shoulder of Rudra as the mover; the second of day and night, the third of the half-months, the month the fourth, the fifth of the seasons, the sixth of the year. 8.

To Ānanda and Nandathu, [I assign] desire; to the two nearby ones, fear; to the two cool ones, instruction; to the two rulers, command; to the kidneys, the sun and moon; to the two testicles, the dark and the speckled; to form, the dawning; to formlessness, the setting. 9.

By means of the flesh [he formed] the day, by the fat the night; by the broth the water, by the essence the clarified butter; by the marrow the *śyāmā* plant, by the fatty secretions the *hraduni* plant; by the beard the clouds, by the form the sky, by the reflection the stars, by the skin the earth, by the hide the poets. To that which is offered, svāhā! To that which is seized, svāhā! To that which is sacrificed, svāhā! 10.

The wing of Agni; the counter-wing of Sarasvatī; the third of Soma; the fourth of the Waters; the fifth of the Plants; the sixth of Rudra; the seventh of the Maruts; the eighth of Bṛhaspati; the ninth of Mitra; the tenth of Varuṇa; the eleventh of Indra; the twelfth of the Viśvedevas; the side of Heaven and Earth; the breast of Yama Pāṭara. 11.

The wing of Vāyu, the under-wing of Sarasvatī, the third of the Moon, the fourth of the Nakṣatras, the fifth of Savitṛ, the sixth of the Year, the seventh of the Serpents, the eighth of Aryaman, the ninth of Dhātṛ, the tenth of Tvaṣṭṛ, the eleventh of Indrāṇī, the twelfth of Aditi, the side of Heaven and Earth, and the breast of Yami. 12.

He [drives away] the paths with the two *anuvṛk* [vessels], the continuity with the two *snāvanī* [vessels], the *śuka* [diseases] with the bile, the jaundice (*hariman*) with the liver, the *halīkṣṇa* [worms] with the bad wind, the *kūṣma* [diseases] with the *śaka* [vessels], the *śavarta* [diseases] with the *ūvadhya* [contents of the stomach], the dogs with the *viśasana* [entrails], the serpents with the smell of blood, the birds with the smell of cooked meat, and the ants with the *praśāda* [remnants]. 13.
Thus ends the thirteenth section, named the Recitation for the Śāda, in the fifth book called the Aśvamedha, within the Caraka-śākhā of the glorious Yajurveda-Kāṭhaka. 13.
Thus ends the fifth book, named the Aśvamedha, in the Caraka-śākhā of the Kāṭhaka Śrī-Yajurveda, which is divided into one hundred and one distinct branches of the Adhvaryu school. 5.
And the Caraka branch is complete.
